## Bench

```bench
id: contrastive-lineup
title: Picking the true match out of a lineup
fallback: An anchor, a positive and several negative embeddings in 2D. Move any point and watch the similarity scores, softmax probabilities and the resulting contrastive loss update.
```

**Try this**

1. Move the positive closer to the anchor and watch the loss fall.
2. Move one negative very close to the anchor instead and watch the loss rise, even with the positive unchanged.
3. Lower the temperature and see how much more sharply the probabilities concentrate on whichever candidate is closest.

**What you should notice:** the loss cares about *relative* closeness, not absolute distance — a positive that is close to the anchor but has a negative almost as close still produces a meaningfully higher loss than a positive that clearly stands out.

## Where it appears in AI

* **SimCLR and similar vision methods** generate positive pairs by applying two different random augmentations (crop, colour jitter, flip) to the same image, treating every other image in the batch as a negative.
* **CLIP-style models** apply the same contrastive principle across *different modalities* — pulling an image and its matching caption's embeddings together, pushing mismatched image-caption pairs apart.
* **The choice of negatives matters a great deal in practice**: "hard" negatives (similar but genuinely different) teach the model more than negatives that were already obviously dissimilar.

## Common pitfalls

* **Forgetting the loss is relative, not absolute.** A positive's raw similarity score alone doesn't determine the loss; how it compares to the negatives in the same batch does.
* **Using too small a batch (too few negatives).** Contrastive learning's negatives come from the batch itself in most implementations, so a small batch gives a much easier (and less informative) task.
* **Picking an augmentation strategy that destroys the thing you actually want the model to learn.** If augmentations are too aggressive, "same source" pairs may no longer share the structure you intended to teach.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. What makes a pair "positive" in contrastive learning, typically?</summary>
Both members come from the same original source (such as two different augmented views of the same image), generated automatically with no human labelling.
</details>

<details><summary>2. What does lowering the temperature τ do to the softmax probabilities?</summary>
It sharpens them, concentrating probability more heavily on whichever candidate has the highest similarity score.
</details>

<details><summary>3. In the worked example, why is the loss low even though negative₂'s score isn't very negative?</summary>
The positive's score (1.988) is still comfortably the highest, so it captures the large majority of the softmax probability regardless of how the negatives compare to each other.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Anchor, positive, negative:** the reference example, its true match, and unrelated distractor examples in a contrastive training batch.
* **Temperature (τ):** a scaling constant controlling how sharply the softmax concentrates on the closest candidate.
* **InfoNCE loss:** the standard contrastive loss, a softmax cross-entropy over similarity scores against one true positive.

[[Self-Supervised Learning]] · [[Embeddings and Similarity Search]] · [[What Deep Networks Learn]] · [[Data Augmentation]]

## Generative Deep Learning

[[Generative vs Discriminative Models]] on the Machine Learning planet draws the line; this district walks the deep architectures that learn to generate rather than only recognise, from a bottleneck that reconstructs to one that denoises.

Topics on this stretch of the road:

* [[Variational Autoencoders]]: an autoencoder whose bottleneck is a distribution you can sample from.
* [[Generative Adversarial Networks]]: two networks trained against each other, one generating and one judging.
* [[Training Instabilities in GANs]]: why that contest is hard to referee, and what helps.
* [[Normalizing Flows]]: building a generator out of operations you can exactly invert and measure.
* [[Diffusion Models]]: learning to generate by learning to reverse a gradual noising process.

## Variational Autoencoders

A plain [[Autoencoders|autoencoder]]'s bottleneck is one fixed vector per input — useful for compression, but there's no obvious way to "make up" a new, realistic vector to decode into something new. A **variational autoencoder (VAE)** fixes that by making the bottleneck a whole probability distribution instead of a single point, trained so that sampling *any* reasonable point from a known, simple distribution produces a plausible decoded output.

**You need:** [[Autoencoders]] and [[Generative vs Discriminative Models]].

## The question it answers

"A trained decoder can reconstruct known inputs — but how do I generate *new* ones that were never in the training set?" Train the encoder to describe each input as a small Gaussian distribution (a mean and a variance) rather than a single point, and push all those distributions to resemble a standard normal distribution — then sampling from that standard normal and decoding gives you new, never-seen data.

## Intuition: a neighbourhood, not a pin

A plain autoencoder places each input at one exact point in latent space — a pin on a map. A VAE instead places each input as a small cloud (a Gaussian) around a point — a neighbourhood, not a pin — and requires nearby points in that neighbourhood to decode into something similar. Because every input's cloud is also pushed to resemble a single shared standard normal shape, the *whole* latent space ends up densely, smoothly covered by overlapping neighbourhoods: any point you pick, even one never specifically seen during training, lands inside *some* input's learned neighbourhood and decodes into something plausible.

## Definitions

```text
encoder outputs:  μ (mean), log(σ²) (log-variance), per latent dimension

reparameterization trick:  z = μ + σ · ε,     ε ~ N(0, 1)   (sampling, but still differentiable in μ, σ)

loss = reconstruction error  +  KL( N(μ, σ²) ‖ N(0, 1) )
KL(N(μ, σ²) ‖ N(0, 1)) = ½(σ² + μ² − 1 − log σ²)
```

The KL term is what pulls every input's latent distribution toward the shared standard normal shape; without it, the model could ignore the "distribution" framing and collapse back toward a plain autoencoder's sharp points.

## A worked example

An encoder outputs `μ = 0.5`, `log(σ²) = −0.2` for one latent dimension. Sampling with a drawn standard-normal value `ε = 1.2`:

```text
σ = exp(−0.2 / 2) = exp(−0.1) ≈ 0.9048

z = μ + σ·ε = 0.5 + 0.9048 × 1.2 ≈ 1.5858

KL(N(0.5, 0.8187) ‖ N(0, 1)) = ½(0.8187 + 0.5² − 1 − (−0.2)) = ½(0.8187 + 0.25 − 1 + 0.2) ≈ 0.1344
```

A small KL value (0.1344) here means this particular input's distribution is already fairly close to the shared standard normal shape — not yet exactly there, but the training pressure is pulling it further in that direction with every step.

## Bench

```bench
id: vae-sample
title: Sampling from a learned distribution
fallback: An adjustable mean and log-variance for one latent dimension, plus a draggable random sample ε. See the resulting latent value z, and how far this distribution's KL divergence sits from the standard normal target.
```

**Try this**

1. Set μ and σ to match the standard normal (μ=0, log-variance=0) and watch KL drop to exactly 0.
2. Push μ or σ far from the standard normal and watch KL grow.
3. Change ε and watch z move, while μ and σ (and so KL) stay exactly the same.

**What you should notice:** ε is pure randomness drawn fresh every time; μ and σ are what the encoder actually learned for this input, and are the only part of z's computation that training can push toward (or away from) the standard normal.

## Where it appears in AI

* **Generating new samples** at inference time simply means sampling `z ~ N(0, 1)` directly (no encoder needed) and running it through the decoder.
* **The reparameterization trick** is what makes training possible at all — sampling on its own isn't differentiable, but expressing the sample as a differentiable function of μ, σ and an independent random ε is.
* **[[Generative Adversarial Networks|GANs]] and [[Diffusion Models]]** are alternative generative approaches that solve the "generate something new" problem by entirely different means, each with their own trade-offs against a VAE's approach.

## Common pitfalls

* **Forgetting the KL term's role.** Without it, nothing pushes different inputs' latent distributions to overlap or resemble a common shape, and sampling randomly from the prior would likely land in "empty" regions the decoder never learned to handle.
* **Treating z as fully determined by the input.** It genuinely depends on a random draw (ε) as well as the encoder's output — the same input produces a different z (though from the same distribution) on repeated encodings.
* **Expecting VAE samples to be as sharp as GAN samples.** VAEs are well known for often producing somewhat blurrier outputs than adversarial approaches, a direct consequence of how their loss is structured.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. What does a VAE's encoder output, instead of a single vector?</summary>
A mean and variance (describing a Gaussian distribution) for each latent dimension.
</details>

<details><summary>2. Why is the reparameterization trick necessary?</summary>
Directly sampling from a distribution isn't differentiable; rewriting the sample as μ + σ·ε (with ε drawn independently) keeps μ and σ differentiable, so gradients can still flow through the sampling step during training.
</details>

<details><summary>3. What does the KL divergence term in the loss encourage?</summary>
It pushes each input's learned latent distribution to resemble the standard normal distribution, so that the whole latent space is smoothly, densely covered and sampling from the standard normal at generation time produces plausible outputs.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Variational autoencoder (VAE):** an autoencoder whose bottleneck is a learned probability distribution rather than a fixed vector.
* **Reparameterization trick:** expressing a random sample as a differentiable function of learned parameters and independent noise.
* **KL divergence:** a measure of how different two probability distributions are, used here to pull latent distributions toward the standard normal.

## Related

[[Autoencoders]] · [[Generative vs Discriminative Models]] · [[Generative Adversarial Networks]] · [[Diffusion Models]]

## Generative Adversarial Networks

A **generative adversarial network (GAN)** trains two networks against each other: a **generator** that turns random noise into fake samples, trying to fool the second network, and a **discriminator** that tries to tell real samples from the generator's fakes. Training is a contest — as one gets better, it forces the other to improve too.

**You need:** [[Variational Autoencoders]] and [[Generative vs Discriminative Models]].

## The question it answers

"Is there another way to train a generative model, besides a VAE's distribution-and-reconstruction approach?" Yes: instead of an explicit loss measuring reconstruction quality, let a second network — one explicitly trying to catch the first one's fakes — supply the training signal.

## Intuition: a forger and a detective, improving together

A forger (the generator) tries to paint fakes good enough to pass as originals; a detective (the discriminator) examines paintings and tries to spot the fakes. Neither starts out skilled. But as the detective gets better at spotting specific tells, the forger is forced to eliminate exactly those tells; as the forger's fakes get subtler, the detective is forced to look harder. Run this contest long enough, and (ideally) the forger's fakes become good enough that even a skilled detective can't reliably tell them from the real thing.

## Definitions

```text
generator G:        fake = G(noise)                 (turns random noise into a fake sample)
discriminator D:     D(x) = P(x is real), a probability in (0, 1)

discriminator loss:  −[ log D(real) + log(1 − D(fake)) ]      (wants D(real) high, D(fake) low)
generator loss:       −log D(fake)                              (wants D(fake) high — fool the discriminator)
```

The two losses pull in opposite directions on the same `D(fake)` value — exactly the adversarial contest.

## A worked example

A discriminator currently scores a real example `D(real) = 0.9` and a generated fake `D(fake) = 0.3`:

```text
discriminator loss = −[log(0.9) + log(1 − 0.3)] = −[log(0.9) + log(0.7)] ≈ 0.4620
generator loss (non-saturating form) = −log(0.3) ≈ 1.2040
```

The discriminator's loss is fairly low (0.4620) — it's doing a reasonable job, correctly leaning toward "real" for the real example and "fake" for the fake one. The generator's loss is considerably higher (1.2040) — it's currently being caught fairly easily, and that higher loss is exactly the training signal pushing it to produce more convincing fakes next.

## Bench

```bench
id: gan-losses
title: The forger and the detective's two losses
fallback: Adjustable discriminator scores for a real and a fake example. See the discriminator's loss and the generator's loss move in opposite directions as those scores change.
```

**Try this**

1. Push `D(fake)` toward 0 (confidently caught) and watch the generator's loss climb.
2. Push `D(fake)` toward 1 (the generator fooled the discriminator) and watch the generator's loss drop while the discriminator's loss rises.
3. Find settings where both losses are simultaneously low or high, and think about whether that's a stable state for the contest.

**What you should notice:** `D(fake)` pulls the two losses in opposite directions — good news for the generator (`D(fake)` near 1) is exactly bad news for the discriminator, and vice versa, which is the whole adversarial structure in miniature.

## Where it appears in AI

* **Image generation** was GANs' first major success, producing photorealistic faces, objects and scenes years before diffusion models became the dominant approach.
* **Style transfer and image-to-image translation** (turning sketches into photos, day scenes into night scenes) have used GAN-based architectures extensively.
* **The adversarial training signal itself** — one network's loss derived directly from another network's current performance — has influenced training setups well beyond pure generation.

## Common pitfalls

* **Expecting GAN training to be as stable as ordinary supervised training.** The adversarial setup is well known for instability (see [[Training Instabilities in GANs]]), unlike a VAE's single, well-behaved loss.
* **Confusing the discriminator's job with the final goal.** The discriminator is a training tool; at the end, only the generator is kept and used.
* **Forgetting that a "perfect" discriminator early in training can stall the generator.** If the discriminator becomes too good too fast, the generator may receive almost no useful gradient to improve from.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. What does the discriminator's loss want D(real) and D(fake) to be?</summary>
D(real) close to 1 (correctly spotting real examples) and D(fake) close to 0 (correctly spotting fakes).
</details>

<details><summary>2. What does the generator's loss want D(fake) to be?</summary>
Close to 1 — meaning the discriminator was fooled into thinking the fake is real.
</details>

<details><summary>3. In the worked example, why is the generator's loss higher than the discriminator's?</summary>
The discriminator is currently doing fairly well at telling real from fake (D(real)=0.9, D(fake)=0.3), which is exactly the situation that produces a high loss for the generator, since its fakes are being caught.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Generator:** the network that turns random noise into fake samples.
* **Discriminator:** the network trained to distinguish real samples from the generator's fakes.
* **Adversarial training:** training two networks against each other's objectives simultaneously.

## Related

[[Variational Autoencoders]] · [[Generative vs Discriminative Models]] · [[Training Instabilities in GANs]] · [[Diffusion Models]]

## Training Instabilities in GANs

A [[Generative Adversarial Networks|GAN]]'s two networks are not cooperating toward one shared loss the way an ordinary supervised model's layers do — they are actively working against each other. That adversarial setup is exactly why GAN training is notoriously harder to keep stable than most other deep learning.

**You need:** [[Generative Adversarial Networks]] and [[Vanishing and Exploding Gradients]].

## The question it answers

"If the generator and discriminator are both just being trained by gradient descent, why is this specific setup so much harder to get right?" Because each network's loss landscape keeps shifting underneath it as the *other* network changes — and a couple of specific failure patterns show up again and again as a result.

## Intuition: two failure patterns worth knowing by name

**Mode collapse**: the generator discovers a small handful of outputs that reliably fool the current discriminator, and — having no incentive to explore further once those work — keeps producing just those, with little variety. **Vanishing gradients for the generator**: if the discriminator becomes too confident too early (correctly spotting fakes with near-certainty), the generator's naive loss formula can give it almost no useful gradient to learn from, right when it most needs guidance.

## Definitions

```text
original minimax generator loss:   log(1 − D(fake))     — saturates (near-zero gradient) when D(fake) is small
non-saturating generator loss:     −log(D(fake))          — stays large (strong gradient) when D(fake) is small
```

The non-saturating version is almost universally used in practice for exactly this reason: it gives the generator its *strongest* signal exactly when it is doing worst (being caught easily), rather than its weakest.

## A worked example

Comparing the gradient (with respect to `D(fake)`) of both loss formulations when the discriminator is confidently catching the generator's fakes, `D(fake) = 0.01`:

```text
original minimax loss gradient:    d/dD[log(1−D)] = −1/(1−D) = −1/0.99 ≈ −1.0101
non-saturating loss gradient:      d/dD[−log(D)]   = −1/D     = −1/0.01 = −100.0000
```

At exactly the moment the generator is being caught almost every time — precisely when it most needs a strong push to improve — the original loss's gradient magnitude is a modest 1.01, while the non-saturating loss's gradient magnitude is a massive 100. The non-saturating form gives roughly 100 times stronger training signal in this situation.

## Bench

```bench
id: saturating-grad
title: Saturating vs non-saturating generator gradients
fallback: A slider for D(fake). Compare the gradient magnitude of the original minimax generator loss against the non-saturating version, especially as D(fake) gets small.
```

**Try this**

1. Move D(fake) toward 0 (the generator being caught easily) and watch the two gradient magnitudes diverge sharply.
2. Move D(fake) toward 1 (the generator fooling the discriminator) and see the two formulas behave more similarly.
3. Find roughly where the two gradients cross over in magnitude.

**What you should notice:** the gap between the two formulas is largest exactly where training needs the most help — when the generator is currently losing badly.

## Where it appears in AI

* **The non-saturating loss is the practical default** in almost every real GAN implementation, specifically to avoid the vanishing-gradient trap shown here.
* **Mode collapse detection and mitigation** (tracking output diversity, specialised loss terms, architectural tweaks) is an entire sub-area of GAN research in its own right.
* **Alternative training objectives** (Wasserstein GANs and others, not covered in depth here) were developed specifically to make GAN training more stable, reformulating the adversarial game to behave better numerically.

## Common pitfalls

* **Assuming a GAN that trains without crashing is training well.** Stable-looking losses can still hide mode collapse — checking actual output diversity matters, not just the loss curves.
* **Using the original (saturating) minimax loss by default.** It is the textbook formula, but the non-saturating version is almost always the practical choice.
* **Treating instability as purely a hyperparameter problem.** Some of it is structural to the adversarial setup itself, not something any single learning rate or architecture choice fully eliminates.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. What is mode collapse?</summary>
The generator settling on producing a small handful of outputs that reliably fool the discriminator, rather than a diverse range of outputs.
</details>

<details><summary>2. Why does the original minimax generator loss give a weak gradient exactly when the generator is doing poorly?</summary>
Its gradient, −1/(1−D(fake)), stays small in magnitude when D(fake) is small (the generator being easily caught) — the opposite of where strong training signal is most needed.
</details>

<details><summary>3. Why is the non-saturating loss preferred in practice?</summary>
Its gradient, −1/D(fake), grows large exactly when D(fake) is small, giving the generator a much stronger training signal precisely when it is losing badly.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Mode collapse:** a generator producing a narrow range of outputs rather than diverse ones.
* **Saturating gradient:** a gradient that shrinks toward zero in exactly the situation where a strong training signal is most needed.
* **Non-saturating loss:** a generator loss formulation chosen specifically to avoid that vanishing-gradient trap.

## Related

[[Generative Adversarial Networks]] · [[Vanishing and Exploding Gradients]] · [[Normalizing Flows]] · [[Diffusion Models]]

## Normalizing Flows

Neither a [[Variational Autoencoders|VAE]] nor a [[Generative Adversarial Networks|GAN]] can tell you the exact probability their model assigns to a specific data point — a VAE only has an approximation, and a GAN has no likelihood at all. A **normalizing flow** builds its generator entirely out of transformations that are **invertible** and have a computable [[Jacobian]], which buys back an exact likelihood for every single point, in exchange for a real architectural constraint.

**You need:** [[Variational Autoencoders]] and [[Jacobian]].

## The question it answers

"Is there a generative model where I can compute the exact probability it assigns to any given data point, not just sample from it?" Yes — if every transformation from the simple base distribution to the data is invertible, the classic change-of-variables formula from probability gives you that exact probability for free.

## Intuition: stretching a dough, and tracking exactly how much it thinned

Imagine rolling out a ball of dough into a specific shape: every point in the original ball maps to exactly one point in the final shape, and the mapping can be reversed. Wherever the dough was stretched more, it got correspondingly thinner — that local stretching factor is exactly what the Jacobian measures. A normalizing flow builds a generator as a chain of such invertible "stretches," and the change-of-variables formula uses the *total* stretching factor to convert the simple base distribution's density into the correct density for the transformed data.

## Definitions

```text
x = f(z),    z ~ (simple base distribution, e.g. standard normal)
f must be invertible: z = f⁻¹(x)

change of variables:   p_x(x) = p_z(f⁻¹(x)) · |det(∂f⁻¹/∂x)|
                      = p_z(z) / |det(∂f/∂z)|            (for one invertible step)
```

Stacking several invertible transformations, each with its own computable Jacobian determinant, multiplies the correction factors together — still exactly computable, as long as every step was chosen to be invertible with a tractable Jacobian.

## A worked example

A single affine flow step, `x = f(z) = 2z + 3`, with `z ~ N(0, 1)`. The Jacobian here is just the scale factor, `2`. Evaluating the exact density at `x = 5`:

```text
z = f⁻¹(x) = (5 − 3) / 2 = 1

p_z(z=1) = standard normal density at 1 ≈ 0.2420

p_x(x=5) = p_z(z) / |2| = 0.2420 / 2 ≈ 0.1210
```

The transformation stretched the distribution by a factor of 2 (every unit of `z` becomes 2 units of `x`), so the density correspondingly thins out by that same factor — exactly what the `/ |det|` term in the formula accounts for.

## Bench

```bench
id: flow-density
title: Stretching a distribution and tracking its density
fallback: A simple affine flow with adjustable scale and shift. See the base distribution, the transformed distribution, and the exact density computed at a chosen point via the change-of-variables formula.
```

**Try this**

1. Increase the scale factor and watch the transformed distribution spread out while its peak density drops.
2. Decrease the scale factor below 1 and watch the opposite: a narrower, taller transformed distribution.
3. Move the evaluation point and check the computed density against reading the transformed curve directly.

**What you should notice:** the transformed density's peak height is inversely proportional to the scale factor — stretching a fixed amount of probability "mass" over a wider range necessarily thins out how densely packed it is at any one point.

## Where it appears in AI

* **Exact likelihood matters for some applications directly** — density estimation, certain scientific modelling tasks — where knowing precisely how probable a point is (not just being able to sample) is the whole point.
* **Real normalizing flows use far more expressive invertible transformations** than a simple affine map, specifically designed to have a Jacobian determinant that is still cheap to compute despite the transformation being complex.
* **Flows, VAEs, GANs and [[Diffusion Models|diffusion models]] are different trade-offs on the same underlying problem** — generate realistic samples — each giving up or keeping different things (exact likelihood, training stability, sample sharpness, generation speed).

## Common pitfalls

* **Assuming any invertible network qualifies as a usable flow.** The architecture also needs a Jacobian determinant that's cheap to compute — an arbitrary invertible network's Jacobian can be computationally intractable.
* **Forgetting the correction factor's job.** It is not optional bookkeeping; without dividing by the Jacobian determinant, the "density" computed would not actually integrate to 1 and wouldn't be a valid probability distribution.
* **Expecting flows to always outperform GANs or diffusion models on sample quality.** Exact likelihood is flows' specific advantage, not necessarily the sharpest or most realistic samples in every setting.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. What capability do normalizing flows provide that VAEs and GANs don't?</summary>
An exact, computable likelihood (probability density) for any given data point, rather than an approximation or none at all.
</details>

<details><summary>2. In the worked example, why does the density at x=5 come out smaller than the density at z=1?</summary>
The transformation stretched the distribution by a factor of 2, thinning out the density by that same factor at the corresponding point.
</details>

<details><summary>3. What property must every transformation in a normalizing flow have?</summary>
It must be invertible, with a Jacobian determinant that is tractable (cheap) to compute.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Normalizing flow:** a generative model built from invertible transformations with computable Jacobians.
* **Change of variables:** the probability formula relating a base distribution's density to a transformed distribution's density via the Jacobian determinant.
* **Jacobian determinant:** the local stretching (or shrinking) factor a transformation applies to volume (or, in 1D, length).

## Related

[[Variational Autoencoders]] · [[Jacobian]] · [[Generative Adversarial Networks]] · [[Diffusion Models]]

## Diffusion Models

A **diffusion model** learns to generate by learning the opposite of something easy: gradually turning clean data into pure noise is a simple, fixed process with no learning involved at all; a diffusion model trains a network to run that process **backward**, turning noise back into data, one small denoising step at a time.

**You need:** [[Normalizing Flows]] and [[Variational Autoencoders]].

## The question it answers

"Generation from scratch is hard — is there an easier problem to train on that still gets you a generative model?" Yes: train a network to undo one small, fixed amount of noise at a time, repeated enough times, and starting from pure noise and running that trained denoiser repeatedly produces a sample.

## Intuition: un-developing a photograph, one grain at a time

Imagine a photograph progressively ruined by adding a little grainy noise, over and over, many times, until nothing recognisable remains — pure static. That forward process needs no learning; it's just adding noise on a fixed schedule. The hard, trained part is the *reverse*: a network that looks at a noisy image and predicts roughly what noise was just added, so it can be subtracted back out. Chain enough of these small denoising steps together, starting from pure static, and a recognisable image gradually emerges.

## Definitions

```text
forward process:  x_t = √(ᾱ_t) · x₀ + √(1 − ᾱ_t) · ε,     ε ~ N(0, 1)

ᾱ_t = ∏ (1 − β_s) for s = 1 to t      (cumulative product of per-step "keep" factors)
β_t = the (small, scheduled) amount of noise added at step t
```

This "jump directly to step t" formula is one of diffusion's most useful properties: you never need to simulate every intermediate noising step one by one — you can sample `x_t` straight from `x₀` and a single noise draw, using only `ᾱ_t`.

## A worked example

A toy 4-step noise schedule, `β = (0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.4)`:

```text
step (t)    ᾱ_t      signal weight √ᾱ_t    noise weight √(1−ᾱ_t)
1          0.9000    0.9487                 0.3162
2          0.7200    0.8485                 0.5292
3          0.5040    0.7099                 0.7043
4          0.3024    0.5499                 0.8352
```

By step 3, the signal and noise weights are almost equal (0.7099 versus 0.7043) — the data and the noise contribute almost equally to `x₃`. For `x₀ = 1` and a drawn noise value `ε = 0.5` at step 3: `x₃ = 0.7099 × 1 + 0.7043 × 0.5 ≈ 1.0621`. By step 4, the noise weight (0.8352) has clearly overtaken the signal weight (0.5499) — the original data is nearly swamped.

## Bench

```bench
id: diffusion-noise
title: Noising a value, step by step
fallback: A clean value and a noise schedule. Step forward through the noising process and watch the signal and noise weights trade off, then see how a trained reverse step would need to subtract the noise back out.
```

**Try this**

1. Step forward through the schedule and watch the signal weight shrink while the noise weight grows.
2. Find roughly which step the signal and noise weights cross over.
3. Try a gentler schedule (smaller β values) and see how many more steps it takes to reach the same amount of noise.

**What you should notice:** the signal weight and noise weight always satisfy `(signal weight)² + (noise weight)² = 1` — they trade off along a fixed budget, never both staying large or both shrinking together.

## Where it appears in AI

* **Modern state-of-the-art image generation** is largely built on diffusion models, having displaced GANs as the dominant approach for photorealistic image synthesis in recent years.
* **The reverse (denoising) network** is usually a large convolutional or attention-based architecture, trained to predict the noise that was added at a given step, given the noisy input and the step number.
* **Sampling requires running the reverse process many times** (often dozens to hundreds of steps), which is a genuine speed trade-off against GANs' single forward pass — a major area of ongoing research is reducing the number of steps needed.

## Common pitfalls

* **Assuming the forward (noising) process involves any learning.** It is entirely fixed and known in advance; only the reverse (denoising) process is trained.
* **Confusing the per-step noise schedule (β_t) with the cumulative signal/noise weights (ᾱ_t and its square root).** The schedule sets how much noise is added at each individual step; the cumulative weights describe the total effect by step t.
* **Expecting diffusion sampling to be as fast as a GAN's single forward pass.** Generating one sample typically requires many sequential denoising steps, a real computational cost diffusion pays for its other advantages.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. What does the forward diffusion process do, and does it require training?</summary>
It gradually adds noise to data according to a fixed schedule, turning it into pure noise; no training is involved in this direction.
</details>

<details><summary>2. What does a diffusion model's network actually learn to predict?</summary>
Roughly how much noise was added at a given step, so that noise can be subtracted back out during the reverse (generation) process.
</details>

<details><summary>3. In the worked example, what happens to the balance between signal weight and noise weight as t increases?</summary>
The signal weight shrinks and the noise weight grows, with the two becoming roughly equal partway through the schedule and noise dominating by the final step.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Forward (noising) process:** the fixed, un-learned process of gradually adding noise to data.
* **Reverse (denoising) process:** the trained process of removing noise step by step, used to generate new samples.
* **Noise schedule:** the sequence of per-step noise amounts (β_t) controlling how quickly data is noised.

## Related

[[Normalizing Flows]] · [[Variational Autoencoders]] · [[Generative Adversarial Networks]] · [[Training Instabilities in GANs]]

## Graphs, Structure and Beyond Grids

Not every input is a grid of pixels or a left-to-right sequence. This short district covers architectures built for data with a different shape: networks of relationships, continuous-time processes, and models that grow a team of specialists instead of one block.

Topics on this stretch of the road:

* [[Graph Neural Networks]]: learning from data that is a network of related items.
* [[Neural ODEs]]: treating a network's depth as continuous time instead of discrete layers.
* [[Mixture of Experts]]: routing each input to a handful of specialist sub-networks instead of running the whole model.

## Graph Neural Networks

A [[Convolutional Neural Networks|convolution]] aggregates each pixel's fixed, grid-shaped neighbourhood. A **graph neural network (GNN)** generalises that same idea to data that isn't a grid at all — a social network, a molecule, a road network — where each node aggregates information from whichever other nodes it happens to be connected to, however many that is.

**You need:** [[Why Depth Helps]] and [[Graphs and Networks]].

## The question it answers

"Convolution relies on every pixel having the same fixed-shape neighbourhood — what do you do when your data's connections are irregular, with every node having a different number of neighbours?" Replace "the fixed 3×3 window" with "whatever nodes this one happens to be connected to," and aggregate over that instead.

## Intuition: updating your opinion from your actual friends, not your neighbours on a grid

On a grid, "who's nearby" means fixed, identical positions relative to you. In a social network, "who's nearby" means your actual friends — a different number for everyone, with no fixed layout at all. A GNN layer updates each node's representation by combining its own current value with some aggregate (commonly a sum or average) of its neighbours' current values — exactly the way you might update an opinion partly from your own view and partly from averaging what people you're actually connected to think.

## Definitions

```text
one GNN layer, for node v:

h_v' = combine( h_v,  aggregate({ h_u : u is a neighbour of v }) )

aggregate is often mean or sum;  combine is often a small dense layer (weights + activation)
```

Stacking `k` GNN layers lets information reach up to `k` hops away — a direct graph analogue of how stacking convolutional layers grows a [[Receptive Fields and Depth|receptive field]].

## A worked example

A 4-node graph — `A—B`, `B—C`, `B—D` (B is the hub) — with initial scalar features `A=1, B=2, C=3, D=4`, updated by averaging each node with the mean of its neighbours:

```text
A's only neighbour is B:          mean = 2;      A' = (1 + 2) / 2   = 1.500
B's neighbours are A, C, D:       mean = 2.667;  B' = (2 + 2.667)/2 = 2.333
C's only neighbour is B:          mean = 2;      C' = (3 + 2) / 2   = 2.500
D's only neighbour is B:          mean = 2;      D' = (4 + 2) / 2   = 3.000
```

Notice `B`, with three neighbours, pulls in information from all of `A`, `C` and `D` in a single layer; `A`, `C` and `D`, each with only `B` as a neighbour, only see `B`'s value directly — they'd need a second layer to be influenced by each other, since right now they only connect through `B`.

## Bench

```bench
id: gnn-aggregate
title: Updating a node from its graph neighbours
fallback: A small graph with editable node features. See one mean-aggregation GNN layer update every node's value from its own neighbours, and step through a second layer to watch information reach further.
```

**Try this**

1. Change one node's feature and see which other nodes' updated values shift after one layer.
2. Add a second layer and see values that were two hops away start to influence each other.
3. Compare a node with many neighbours to one with only a single neighbour, and see how differently their updates behave.

**What you should notice:** a node with many neighbours blends in information from all of them at once; a node with few neighbours changes more slowly, and needs more layers before distant parts of the graph can influence it at all.

## Where it appears in AI

* **Molecules, social networks, recommendation systems and road networks** are all naturally graphs, and GNNs are a standard tool for prediction tasks over this kind of data.
* **Message passing** is the general name for the "aggregate from neighbours, then update" pattern this topic describes; many GNN variants differ mainly in how they aggregate and combine.
* **Graph structure can also appear inside otherwise grid- or sequence-shaped data** — for instance, treating distant words connected by a dependency parse as graph neighbours, rather than only immediate sequence neighbours.

## Common pitfalls

* **Forgetting a node only directly sees its immediate neighbours in one layer.** Information from further away needs more layers to arrive, exactly as in the worked example.
* **Using sum aggregation on graphs where node degree varies wildly.** A node with a hundred neighbours and a node with two can end up with very differently-scaled aggregated values unless this is accounted for (mean aggregation, as used here, is one common fix).
* **Treating a GNN as interchangeable with a plain dense network over a flattened adjacency matrix.** The whole point of message passing is that it respects the graph's actual, irregular structure rather than imposing an arbitrary fixed ordering.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. What does a GNN layer do differently from a plain convolution's fixed window?</summary>
It aggregates over whatever nodes happen to be graph-neighbours of a given node, however many there are, instead of a fixed-size, fixed-shape neighbourhood.
</details>

<details><summary>2. In the worked example, why does node A's updated value only reflect node B, not nodes C or D?</summary>
A's only direct neighbour is B; C and D are two hops away through B, which a single GNN layer cannot reach.
</details>

<details><summary>3. How many GNN layers would it take for node C's value to start influencing node D?</summary>
Two layers — the first layer lets B's value absorb information from C, and the second layer lets D (B's neighbour) pick up that updated value from B.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Graph neural network (GNN):** a network whose layers aggregate information from each node's actual graph neighbours.
* **Message passing:** the aggregate-then-update pattern a GNN layer performs.
* **Hop:** one edge's worth of distance in a graph; a GNN with k layers can reach information up to k hops away.

## Related

[[Why Depth Helps]] · [[Graphs and Networks]] · [[Receptive Fields and Depth]] · [[Mixture of Experts]]

## Neural ODEs

A [[Residual and Skip Connections|residual block]]'s update, `h_(t+1) = h_t + F(h_t)`, looks suspiciously like a single step of a very basic way to solve a differential equation. A **Neural ODE** takes that resemblance seriously: instead of a fixed number of discrete residual blocks, it treats "depth" as continuous time and solves `dh/dt = F(h, t)` directly with an ODE solver.

**You need:** [[Residual and Skip Connections]] and [[Rate of Change]].

## The question it answers

"A ResNet's depth is a fixed number you choose ahead of time — what if the transformation it's approximating is more naturally continuous?" Treat it as one: define how `h` changes *per unit of continuous depth* (a rate of change, `dh/dt`), and let a numerical ODE solver decide how finely to step through it, rather than fixing the number of steps in advance.

## Intuition: counting discrete floors versus riding a continuously moving elevator

A plain deep (or residual) network is like a building with a fixed number of floors — however coarse or fine, that number is baked in when it's built. A Neural ODE is more like a continuously moving elevator: you specify the *rate* at which it moves at any given position, and a solver figures out how many stops (steps) to actually take to get you there accurately, potentially using more small steps where the rate is changing quickly and fewer where it isn't.

## Definitions

```text
residual block:    h_(t+1) = h_t + F(h_t)              — looks like one step of Euler's method
Neural ODE:         dh/dt = F(h, t, θ)                  — the continuous version
                     h(T) = h(0) + ∫₀ᵀ F(h, t, θ) dt     — solved by any ODE solver, with any step size

Euler's method (the simplest solver):   x_(n+1) = x_n + h · f(x_n)     (h = step size)
```

A plain ResNet is, in effect, always using Euler's method with a step size fixed at exactly 1, for exactly as many steps as it has residual blocks.

## A worked example

Solving the simple differential equation `dx/dt = x` (true solution `x(t) = x₀eᵗ`) from `x₀ = 1` to `t = 2`, using Euler's method with different step sizes:

```text
step size h=1    (2 steps):   x(2) ≈ 4.0000
step size h=0.5  (4 steps):   x(2) ≈ 5.0625
step size h=0.25 (8 steps):   x(2) ≈ 5.9605

true value:  e² ≈ 7.3891
```

Smaller steps get steadily closer to the true value — exactly the trade-off a Neural ODE's solver can make automatically: more (smaller) steps where accuracy matters, fewer (larger) steps where it doesn't, rather than committing to one fixed number of "layers" for the whole network regardless of how complex the underlying transformation actually is.

## Bench

```bench
id: euler-steps
title: Solving a differential equation with more or fewer steps
fallback: A step-size slider for Euler's method solving dx/dt = x from x₀ = 1 to t = 2. See the approximation converge toward the true value as the step size shrinks (more steps).
```

**Try this**

1. Start with a large step size and compare the result to the true value.
2. Shrink the step size and watch the approximation steadily improve.
3. Think about what a plain ResNet is implicitly committing to by using one fixed step size, forever.

**What you should notice:** this is exactly the resemblance Neural ODEs exploit — a ResNet's depth is, numerically, a step-size (and step-count) choice baked into the architecture, which a continuous-time formulation can instead leave to an adaptive solver.

## Where it appears in AI

* **Memory efficiency** is a practical advantage: a Neural ODE's "depth" at inference is a solver choice, not a fixed number of stored layer weights, which can save memory during training via the adjoint method (not covered in depth here).
* **Irregularly-sampled time series** (medical records, sensor data with gaps) are a natural fit, since a Neural ODE can evaluate the hidden state at *any* continuous time, not just at fixed, evenly-spaced layer indices.
* **Normalizing flows** (see [[Normalizing Flows]]) have a continuous-time variant built on exactly this same differential-equation framing.

## Common pitfalls

* **Assuming Neural ODEs are always more efficient than a plain deep network.** Solving an ODE accurately can require many solver evaluations, sometimes costing more compute than a fixed-depth network for the same task.
* **Expecting Euler's method specifically to be used in practice.** It's the simplest solver (and the one that looks most like a plain residual block), but real Neural ODE implementations typically use far more accurate adaptive solvers.
* **Confusing "continuous depth" with "continuous input."** The continuity here is about how the *hidden state* evolves with depth, not necessarily about the kind of input data the network accepts.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. What does a plain ResNet's residual update resemble, numerically?</summary>
One step of Euler's method, solving a differential equation with a fixed step size of 1.
</details>

<details><summary>2. In the worked example, why does a smaller Euler step size give a more accurate result?</summary>
Smaller steps better approximate the true, continuously changing rate, accumulating less error over the same total interval.
</details>

<details><summary>3. What does a Neural ODE replace a fixed number of residual blocks with?</summary>
A differential equation describing the hidden state's rate of change, solved by a numerical ODE solver that can choose its own step size (and count).
</details>

## Key terms

* **Neural ODE:** a network whose depth is treated as continuous time, with the hidden state's evolution defined by a differential equation.
* **Euler's method:** the simplest way to numerically solve a differential equation, taking fixed-size steps along the rate of change.
* **Adaptive step size:** letting a solver choose smaller steps where accuracy requires it and larger steps where it doesn't.

## Related

[[Residual and Skip Connections]] · [[Rate of Change]] · [[Normalizing Flows]] · [[Why Depth Helps]]

## Mixture of Experts

A plain dense layer runs every input through the exact same weights. A **mixture of experts (MoE)** layer instead keeps several separate sub-networks ("experts") and a small **router** that decides, per input, which handful of experts to actually run — getting the capacity of many experts' worth of parameters while only paying the compute cost of the few that are actually used.

**You need:** [[The Multilayer Feedforward Network]] and [[Softmax and Cross-Entropy in Practice]].

## The question it answers

"More parameters usually means more compute per input — is there a way to have a much bigger model without a proportionally bigger cost for every single input?" Yes, if most of that extra size is split into many specialist experts and a lightweight router sends each input to only a handful of them, rather than running the whole thing every time.

## Intuition: routing a question to a specialist, not asking everyone

A large hospital doesn't make every patient see every single specialist — a triage step routes each patient to the one or two specialists most relevant to their case. An MoE layer works the same way: a small router network looks at the input and decides which experts (out of possibly dozens) are most relevant, and only those few actually process it. The rest of the experts — and their parameters — sit idle for that particular input, contributing nothing to its compute cost.

## Definitions

```text
router:  logits = router(x);   probs = softmax(logits)     (one score per expert)
top-k selection:  keep only the k highest-scoring experts; renormalise their probabilities to sum to 1

output = Σ (renormalised weight_i) · expert_i(x),   summed only over the selected top-k experts
```

Every expert is a full sub-network in its own right (often the same size as what a plain dense layer would have been); the total parameter count across all experts can be enormous, while the compute for any single input only involves the `k` selected ones.

## A worked example

A router scores 4 experts for one input: logits `(1.2, 0.3, 2.5, −0.5)`. Keeping only the top 2 (experts at index 2 and 0):

```text
full softmax over all 4:   (0.1902, 0.0773, 0.6978, 0.0347)

top-2 experts: index 2 (score 0.6978) and index 0 (score 0.1902)
renormalised among just these two:  (0.7858, 0.2142)

expert 2's output = 5,  expert 0's output = 3

combined output = 0.7858 × 5 + 0.2142 × 3 ≈ 4.5717
```

Experts 1 and 3 (indices 1 and 3) contribute nothing at all to this particular input's output or compute — their parameters exist, and may matter a great deal for a *different* input the router routes to them, but are entirely irrelevant here.

## Bench

```bench
id: moe-routing
title: Routing an input to its top experts
fallback: Four experts with adjustable router scores and outputs. See the full softmax, which experts the top-k selection keeps, their renormalised weights, and the resulting combined output.
```

**Try this**

1. Adjust one expert's router score higher and watch it dominate the combined output more.
2. Change `k` (how many experts are kept) and see how the combined output shifts as more or fewer experts contribute.
3. Set two experts' router scores very close together and watch the combined output become a near-even blend of both.

**What you should notice:** an expert that isn't selected contributes exactly zero to this input's output, however large or carefully trained its own parameters are — the routing decision is all-or-nothing per input, not a soft blend across every expert.

## Where it appears in AI

* **Very large language models** increasingly use mixture-of-experts layers to scale total parameter count far beyond what would be affordable if every parameter had to be used on every input.
* **Load balancing across experts** is an active practical concern: if the router consistently favours a small subset of experts, the rest go undertrained, which specialised auxiliary losses are often added to discourage.
* **The router itself is trained end to end** along with the experts, typically learning to specialise experts for different kinds of input without being told explicitly what that specialisation should be.

## Common pitfalls

* **Assuming MoE layers always reduce total compute.** They reduce compute *per input* relative to the total parameter count, but running many experts across a large batch of varied inputs still requires real computation — the saving is in not running *every* expert for *every* input.
* **Forgetting the renormalisation step.** Without it, the selected experts' weights wouldn't sum to 1, and the combined output's overall scale would drift depending on how many experts happened to be selected.
* **Expecting experts to specialise in humanly interpretable ways.** Any specialisation that emerges is a trained, emergent property of the router and experts jointly, not something designed in by hand.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. What does the router in a mixture-of-experts layer decide?</summary>
Which (typically a small number, k, of) experts should process a given input.
</details>

<details><summary>2. Why are the selected experts' weights renormalised after top-k selection?</summary>
So they sum to exactly 1 among just the selected experts, keeping the combined output's scale consistent regardless of which experts were chosen.
</details>

<details><summary>3. In the worked example, do experts 1 and 3 affect this input's output at all?</summary>
No — they were not among the top-2 selected experts, so they contribute nothing to this particular input's combined output or compute.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Expert:** one of several separate sub-networks in a mixture-of-experts layer.
* **Router (gating network):** the small network that scores and selects which experts handle a given input.
* **Top-k selection:** keeping only the k highest-scoring experts and renormalising their weights.

## Related

[[The Multilayer Feedforward Network]] · [[Softmax and Cross-Entropy in Practice]] · [[Graph Neural Networks]] · [[Scaling Laws and Model Capacity]]

## Efficiency and Deployment

A network that trains well is not automatically one you can afford to run. This district covers shrinking a trained network and finding its architecture automatically, so it fits a budget of memory, latency or power.

Topics on this stretch of the road:

* [[Model Pruning]]: removing weights or units a trained network turns out not to need.
* [[Quantization]]: storing and computing with numbers that use fewer bits.
* [[Knowledge Distillation]]: training a small network to mimic a large one.
* [[Neural Architecture Search]]: searching for a good architecture instead of hand-designing it.
* [[Edge and On-Device Deep Learning]]: what changes when a network must run on a phone, not a server.

## Model Pruning

A trained network rarely needs every single weight it ended up with. **Pruning** removes the ones that matter least — often simply the weights closest to zero — shrinking the model with, ideally, only a small cost to accuracy.

**You need:** [[The Multilayer Feedforward Network]] and [[Overfitting and Double Descent]].

## The question it answers

"A trained network has millions of weights — are they all actually necessary?" Usually not: many end up tiny, contributing almost nothing to the output, and can be removed (set to exactly zero) with little effect on what the network computes.

## Intuition: trimming the dead branches, not the trunk

A weight with a value very close to zero barely changes the output no matter what multiplies it — it's a dead branch on an otherwise healthy tree. **Magnitude pruning** cuts the smallest-magnitude weights first, on the reasoning that they were contributing the least anyway. **Structured pruning** goes further, removing whole units, channels or filters at once (not just individual weights), which — unlike scattered individual-weight pruning — actually speeds up computation on ordinary hardware, since it shrinks the matrices themselves rather than leaving sparse holes in them.

## Definitions

```text
magnitude pruning:   remove the weights with the smallest |w|, setting them to exactly 0
structured pruning:  remove whole units/channels/filters, not just scattered individual weights

sparsity = (number of zeroed weights) / (total weights)
```

## A worked example

A 6-weight layer, `w = (0.9, −0.05, 0.6, 0.02, −0.8, 0.1)`, computing a dot product against an input of all 1s:

```text
full output = 0.9 − 0.05 + 0.6 + 0.02 − 0.8 + 0.1 = 0.77

prune the 3 smallest-magnitude weights (0.02, 0.05, 0.10) → set to 0:
pruned w = (0.9, 0, 0.6, 0, −0.8, 0)

pruned output = 0.9 + 0.6 − 0.8 = 0.70

relative error = |0.77 − 0.70| / |0.77| ≈ 9.1%
```

Removing half the weights (50% sparsity) only shifted the output by about 9% — exactly the trade-off pruning aims for: a large reduction in parameters for a comparatively small change in behaviour.

## Bench

```bench
id: prune-weights
title: Pruning the smallest weights
fallback: A short weight vector and an input. Adjust how much to prune (by magnitude) and watch the sparsity, the output, and the relative error against the unpruned output.
```

**Try this**

1. Increase the pruning amount gradually and watch when the relative error starts climbing sharply.
2. Set one weight to be very large and watch how much sparsity you can apply before it (the largest weight) has to be touched.
3. Compare pruning amounts that remove "obviously small" weights versus amounts that start cutting into meaningfully-sized ones.

**What you should notice:** error tends to stay small while pruning only removes genuinely tiny weights, then rises more sharply once pruning starts removing weights that were actually contributing something.

## Where it appears in AI

* **Deploying models on resource-constrained devices** (see [[Edge and On-Device Deep Learning]]) often combines pruning with [[Quantization]] and [[Knowledge Distillation]] to meet strict size and speed budgets.
* **Iterative pruning and fine-tuning**, not covered in full detail here, alternates pruning a little, retraining to recover accuracy, and pruning further — usually reaching much higher sparsity than a single one-shot cut.
* **The "lottery ticket hypothesis"**, an influential line of research, found that some pruned sub-networks, if retrained from their *original* initial weights, can match the full network's accuracy — suggesting much of a large network's benefit comes from giving training many chances to find a good sparse sub-network, not from needing every weight at inference time.

## Common pitfalls

* **Assuming unstructured pruning (scattered individual weights) speeds up a model on ordinary hardware.** It reduces parameter count and storage, but a sparse matrix with scattered zeros usually needs specialised hardware or software support to actually run faster.
* **Pruning too aggressively in one shot.** Accuracy often degrades sharply past some point; gradual pruning with retraining in between usually reaches much higher sparsity safely.
* **Forgetting pruning changes the model permanently.** Unlike dropout (training-time only), pruned weights are typically gone for good at inference.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. What does magnitude pruning remove?</summary>
The weights with the smallest absolute value, on the reasoning that they contribute the least to the output.
</details>

<details><summary>2. Why does structured pruning speed up computation on ordinary hardware, while unstructured pruning often doesn't?</summary>
Structured pruning removes whole units or channels, actually shrinking the matrices involved; unstructured pruning leaves scattered zeros inside matrices of the same shape, which ordinary hardware doesn't automatically skip over.
</details>

<details><summary>3. In the worked example, what was the cost (in relative error) of removing half the weights?</summary>
About 9.1% — a comparatively small change in output for a 50% reduction in the number of non-zero weights.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Pruning:** removing weights (or whole units) from a trained network to shrink it.
* **Magnitude pruning:** removing the smallest-magnitude weights specifically.
* **Sparsity:** the fraction of a network's weights that have been pruned (set to zero).

## Related

[[The Multilayer Feedforward Network]] · [[Overfitting and Double Descent]] · [[Quantization]] · [[Knowledge Distillation]]

## Quantization

A weight stored as a 32-bit float can represent an enormous range of values with high precision — far more precision than most trained weights actually need. **Quantization** stores (and often computes) the same weights using far fewer bits — commonly 8 — accepting a small, bounded rounding error in exchange for a model that is smaller and faster.

**You need:** [[Floating Point]] and [[Model Pruning]].

## The question it answers

"Do weights really need 32 bits of precision each?" Usually not — rounding each weight to one of a much smaller number of evenly-spaced levels loses only a small, predictable amount of accuracy, while shrinking the model's size by a large, fixed factor.

## Intuition: a ruler with fewer markings

A ruler with millimetre markings is far more precise than one with only centimetre markings, but for most everyday measurements, the coarser ruler is still good enough — you just round to the nearest mark. Quantization rounds every weight to the nearest of a fixed, small set of evenly-spaced levels (say, 256 of them for 8-bit quantization), instead of keeping each weight's full floating-point precision.

## Definitions

```text
range [min, max],  b bits  →  2^b evenly-spaced levels

scale = (max − min) / (2^b − 1)

quantize:    q = round((x − min) / scale)        (an integer, 0 to 2^b − 1)
dequantize:  x̂ = min + q · scale                   (the approximate value actually used)

maximum possible rounding error = scale / 2
```

## A worked example

Five weights, quantized to 8 bits (256 levels) over the range `[−1, 1]`:

```text
scale = (1 − (−1)) / 255 ≈ 0.007843

weight     −0.800   0.300   0.950   −0.200   0.600
quantized   q=25    q=166   q=249    q=102    q=204
dequantized −0.8039  0.3020  0.9529  −0.2000  0.6000
error       0.00392  0.00196 0.00294  0.00000  0.00000
```

Every weight's error is well under the theoretical maximum of `scale / 2 ≈ 0.00392`, and most are far smaller — a tiny rounding cost in exchange for storing each weight in 8 bits instead of 32, a 4× reduction in storage for the weights alone.

## Bench

```bench
id: quantize-weights
title: Rounding weights to a fixed set of levels
fallback: Adjustable weights, a bit-width slider, and the chosen value range. See each weight's quantized integer code, its dequantized approximation, and the resulting rounding error.
```

**Try this**

1. Lower the bit-width from 8 toward 2 or 3 and watch the rounding error grow sharply.
2. Widen the value range without changing the bit-width and watch the error grow too, even though the bit-width didn't change.
3. Narrow the range to just barely cover the actual weights and watch the error shrink.

**What you should notice:** error depends on both the bit-width *and* how tightly the chosen range actually fits the weights being quantized — a wider range than necessary wastes precision on values that never occur.

## Where it appears in AI

* **8-bit (and even 4-bit) quantization** is now routine for deploying large models efficiently, especially combined with [[Model Pruning]] and [[Knowledge Distillation]].
* **Quantization-aware training**, not covered in full detail here, trains a model while simulating quantization's rounding effects, so the model learns weights that are more robust to that rounding than a model quantized only after training.
* **Different parts of a model are often quantized to different precisions** — some layers more sensitive to rounding than others — rather than applying one fixed bit-width everywhere.

## Common pitfalls

* **Choosing too wide a value range.** It wastes available precision on values that never actually occur, increasing error for no benefit.
* **Assuming quantization is free.** There is a real, bounded accuracy cost; very aggressive quantization (very few bits) can noticeably hurt a model's outputs if not done carefully.
* **Forgetting that quantizing after training ("post-training quantization") and training with quantization in mind are different strategies** with different accuracy trade-offs.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. What is the maximum possible rounding error introduced by quantizing to a given scale?</summary>
Half the scale (half the spacing between adjacent quantized levels).
</details>

<details><summary>2. Why does widening the chosen value range increase quantization error, even with the same bit-width?</summary>
The same number of levels must now be spread over a wider range, so the scale (spacing between levels) grows, and so does the maximum possible rounding error.
</details>

<details><summary>3. In the worked example, why did two of the five weights have exactly zero error?</summary>
Those particular weight values happened to land exactly on one of the 256 quantization levels, so rounding introduced no change at all.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Quantization:** representing values with a smaller, fixed set of discrete levels instead of full floating-point precision.
* **Scale:** the spacing between adjacent quantization levels, determined by the value range and bit-width.
* **Dequantization:** converting a quantized integer code back into its approximate real value.

## Related

[[Floating Point]] · [[Model Pruning]] · [[Knowledge Distillation]] · [[Edge and On-Device Deep Learning]]

## Knowledge Distillation

A large, accurate **teacher** network's final prediction is one number per class — but its *full* output, before being squashed into near-certainty, carries far more information: how confident it was, and how it ranked the classes it got wrong. **Knowledge distillation** trains a small **student** network to mimic that fuller picture, not just the teacher's single correct answer.

**You need:** [[Model Pruning]] and [[Softmax and Cross-Entropy in Practice]].

## The question it answers

"A big, accurate model is too slow or large to deploy — can a much smaller model learn almost as much, directly from the big one, rather than from raw labels alone?" Yes — train the small student to match the teacher's *softened* output distribution, which reveals relative confidence across all classes, not just which one "won."

## Intuition: learning from a tutor's full reasoning, not just their final answer

A teacher's ordinary softmax output is usually extremely confident — one class near 100%, everything else near 0% — which hides almost all of the teacher's more nuanced judgement about which *wrong* answers were still plausible. **Temperature** softens that peak: dividing the logits by a temperature `T > 1` before the softmax flattens the distribution, revealing the teacher's relative ranking of all the classes — information a hard 0-or-1 label could never have conveyed on its own.

## Definitions

```text
softened softmax:   P_i = softmax(z / T)_i        (T = 1 is ordinary softmax; T > 1 softens it)

distillation loss:  cross-entropy between the student's softened output and the teacher's softened output
                     (often averaged with an ordinary loss against the true hard labels)
```

## A worked example

Teacher logits `(3.0, 1.0, 0.5)` for 3 classes, compared at ordinary temperature and a softened one:

```text
T = 1 (ordinary):  P = (0.8214, 0.1112, 0.0674)     — very peaked, almost all weight on class 1
T = 4 (softened):  P = (0.4669, 0.2832, 0.2499)     — reveals class 2 is a noticeably closer runner-up than class 3
```

A student with its own logits `(2.0, 1.2, 0.8)`, softened the same way, gives `(0.3907, 0.3199, 0.2894)` at `T = 4`. Comparing the two softened distributions with cross-entropy gives a distillation loss of about `1.0714` — a loss that specifically rewards the student for matching the teacher's *relative* ranking of all three classes, not merely picking the same top class.

## Bench

```bench
id: distill-temp
title: Softening a teacher's output with temperature
fallback: Adjustable teacher logits and a temperature slider. See the teacher's softmax distribution flatten as temperature rises, and compare a student's distillation loss against the softened teacher target.
```

**Try this**

1. Set temperature to 1 and note how sharply the teacher's distribution favours one class.
2. Raise the temperature and watch the distribution flatten, revealing the relative order of the other classes more clearly.
3. Adjust the student's logits to better match the teacher's ranking and watch the distillation loss fall.

**What you should notice:** at a high temperature, a student is rewarded for matching the teacher's *entire* ranking of classes, not just its top pick — which is exactly the extra signal ordinary hard labels don't provide.

## Where it appears in AI

* **Deploying a smaller, faster model** that approximates a larger one's behaviour, when the larger model is too slow or large for the deployment target (see [[Edge and On-Device Deep Learning]]).
* **Distillation is often combined with [[Model Pruning]] and [[Quantization]]** as part of a broader model-compression pipeline.
* **Self-distillation**, a variant not covered in detail here, uses a model to distill into a smaller or even same-sized version of itself, sometimes improving results beyond ordinary training.

## Common pitfalls

* **Forgetting to also use the true hard labels, where available.** Distillation loss alone, with no grounding in the actual correct answers, can let a student learn the teacher's mistakes just as readily as its correct judgements.
* **Using too low a temperature.** Near `T = 1`, the teacher's output is almost as peaked as a hard label, losing much of the extra signal distillation is meant to provide.
* **Assuming the student can match the teacher at any size.** A sufficiently small student may lack the capacity to capture everything the teacher's full output is conveying, however good the distillation signal.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. What extra information does a softened teacher output provide beyond a hard label?</summary>
Its relative confidence across every class, not just which one it predicted — including how it ranked the classes it got wrong.
</details>

<details><summary>2. What happens to a softmax distribution as temperature increases?</summary>
It flattens, spreading probability more evenly across classes and revealing finer distinctions in relative confidence.
</details>

<details><summary>3. Why is distillation loss often combined with an ordinary loss against the true hard labels?</summary>
Relying only on the teacher's output risks the student learning the teacher's mistakes as faithfully as its correct judgements; grounding in true labels helps avoid that.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Teacher / student:** the large, already-trained model and the smaller model being trained to mimic it.
* **Temperature:** a scaling factor that softens (or sharpens) a softmax distribution.
* **Distillation loss:** cross-entropy between a student's and teacher's softened output distributions.

## Related

[[Model Pruning]] · [[Softmax and Cross-Entropy in Practice]] · [[Quantization]] · [[Edge and On-Device Deep Learning]]

## Neural Architecture Search

Depth, width, kernel sizes, how layers connect — every architecture in [[CNN Architectures: From LeNet to ResNet|the CNN lineage]] was designed by hand, by researchers trying ideas and comparing results. **Neural architecture search (NAS)** automates that process: search over a space of possible architectures, score each candidate, and let the search itself find a good trade-off between accuracy and cost.

**You need:** [[CNN Architectures: From LeNet to ResNet]] and [[Hyperparameter Tuning]].

## The question it answers

"Must a good architecture always come from human intuition and trial and error?" Not entirely — if you can define a space of possible architectures and a way to score any candidate from that space, search methods (grid search, random search, evolutionary search, reinforcement learning, gradient-based relaxations) can explore it automatically.

## Intuition: treating the architecture itself as something to tune

[[Hyperparameter Tuning]] already searches over settings like learning rate or batch size; NAS just widens what counts as a "setting" to include the architecture itself — number of layers, layer widths, which operations to use where. The score for any candidate typically balances accuracy against cost (compute, memory, latency), since the "best" architecture is rarely just the biggest one.

## Definitions

```text
search space:   the set of architecture choices considered (depth, width, kernel sizes, …)
search strategy: how candidates are proposed (grid, random, evolutionary, RL-based, gradient-based)
score(candidate):  typically accuracy on a validation set, minus some penalty for cost
```

## A worked example

A tiny, deliberately simple grid search over depth `d ∈ {2, 3, 4}` and width `w ∈ {8, 16, 32}`, scoring each with a toy accuracy-proxy (saturating with more capacity) minus a cost penalty (growing quadratically with capacity):

```text
accuracy proxy(d, w) = 1 − 1/(1 + 0.1·d·w)
cost penalty(d, w)   = 0.0005·(d·w)²
score = accuracy proxy − cost penalty

d=2, w=8:   accuracy 0.6154,  cost 0.1280,  score  0.4874   ← best
d=2, w=16:  accuracy 0.7619,  cost 0.5120,  score  0.2499
d=2, w=32:  accuracy 0.8649,  cost 2.0480,  score −1.1831
d=4, w=32:  accuracy 0.9275,  cost 8.1920,  score −7.2645
```

The architecture with the *highest raw accuracy proxy* (`d=4, w=32`) has by far the *worst* overall score, because its cost penalty overwhelms the accuracy gain — the grid search correctly picks the small `d=2, w=8` architecture instead, exactly the kind of trade-off NAS is meant to automate.

## Bench

```bench
id: nas-grid
title: Searching a small architecture grid
fallback: A grid of depth and width choices, each with an accuracy proxy and a cost penalty. See every candidate's score and which one the search picks as best, and adjust the cost penalty's weight to see the choice shift.
```

**Try this**

1. Look at the full grid of scores and find which candidate wins.
2. Increase the cost penalty's weight and watch the winning candidate shrink toward smaller architectures.
3. Decrease the cost penalty's weight toward zero and watch the largest architecture start to win instead.

**What you should notice:** the "best" architecture is entirely a function of how accuracy and cost are weighed against each other — there's no universal winner, only a winner relative to a chosen trade-off.

## Where it appears in AI

* **Mobile and embedded models** (see [[Edge and On-Device Deep Learning]]) are a common target for NAS, since cost (latency, memory, power) matters as much as raw accuracy for these deployments.
* **Real NAS search spaces and strategies are vastly larger and more sophisticated** than this toy grid — reinforcement learning and gradient-based methods (like DARTS) can search spaces far too large to enumerate exhaustively.
* **NAS itself can be extremely expensive to run**, since naive versions require training (or at least evaluating) many candidate architectures — a real engineering trade-off search methods are specifically designed to reduce.

## Common pitfalls

* **Treating NAS as free.** Searching over architectures, especially by training each candidate from scratch, can cost more compute than training one well-chosen architecture by hand.
* **Forgetting the score function's design drives everything.** Changing how accuracy and cost are weighed (or what "cost" even measures — latency? memory? energy?) can completely change which architecture the search prefers.
* **Assuming a found architecture generalises to a very different deployment target.** An architecture optimised for one hardware/cost trade-off may be a poor choice for a very different one.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. What does neural architecture search widen "hyperparameter tuning" to include?</summary>
The architecture itself — depth, width, kernel sizes and connection patterns — not just training settings like learning rate.
</details>

<details><summary>2. In the worked example, why does the architecture with the highest accuracy proxy score worst overall?</summary>
Its cost penalty grows quadratically with capacity and ends up far outweighing its accuracy advantage.
</details>

<details><summary>3. Is there a single "best" architecture independent of how the score function is defined?</summary>
No — the winning candidate depends entirely on how accuracy and cost are weighed against each other in the score.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Search space:** the set of architecture choices a NAS method considers.
* **Search strategy:** the method used to propose and evaluate candidate architectures.
* **Accuracy-cost trade-off:** balancing a candidate's performance against its compute, memory or latency cost.

## Related

[[CNN Architectures: From LeNet to ResNet]] · [[Hyperparameter Tuning]] · [[Edge and On-Device Deep Learning]] · [[Choosing an Architecture for a Problem]]

## Edge and On-Device Deep Learning

Running a model on a phone, a smartwatch, or a tiny embedded chip is a different problem from running it on a server: memory, compute, power and network connectivity are all far more constrained, and often there's no network connection to a server at all. **Edge deployment** combines everything from this district — pruning, quantization, distillation — to fit a model within those limits.

**You need:** [[Quantization]], [[Model Pruning]] and [[Knowledge Distillation]].

## The question it answers

"A model trained on a data centre's GPUs needs to run on a phone with a tiny fraction of that power — how do you get it to actually fit?" By stacking compression techniques together: a smaller architecture (via distillation or direct design), fewer non-zero weights (pruning), and lower-precision numbers (quantization) — each buying back some of the budget a server-sized model would otherwise need.

## Intuition: packing for a trip with a much smaller bag

A server can carry a huge, roomy suitcase. A phone's "bag" for a model is tiny by comparison — limited memory, a battery that drains with every computation, and often no cloud connection to lean on. Shrinking a model for the edge is exactly like packing for that much smaller bag: everything that isn't earning its keep (pruning), stored more compactly (quantization), and ideally designed smaller to begin with (distillation into a purpose-built small architecture) rather than crammed in as an afterthought.

## Definitions

```text
on-device inference:  running the model entirely on the local device, no network round-trip needed

benefits:  lower latency (no network delay), works offline, keeps data private (never leaves the device)
costs:     limited memory, compute and power compared to a server
```

## A worked example

A 100 MB model, compressed in stages:

```text
original (32-bit, dense):                        100 MB

structured pruning (removes 50% of channels):     50 MB     (2× smaller)
8-bit quantization (32-bit → 8-bit, 4× smaller):   50 MB / 4 = 12.5 MB

combined reduction:  2× (pruning) × 4× (quantization) = 8× smaller overall
final size:           100 MB / 8 = 12.5 MB
```

Pruning and quantization attack different kinds of redundancy (how many weights, versus how precisely each one is stored), so their size reductions multiply rather than merely add — an 8× total reduction from two techniques that individually only gave 2× and 4×.

## Bench

```bench
id: compression-stack
title: Stacking compression techniques
fallback: A starting model size, with pruning and quantization reduction factors as sliders. See each stage's resulting size and the combined reduction factor.
```

**Try this**

1. Apply pruning alone and note the resulting size.
2. Apply quantization alone (reset pruning) and compare.
3. Apply both together and confirm the combined reduction is the product of the two individual factors.

**What you should notice:** the two techniques compound multiplicatively because they reduce different things (weight count versus bits per weight) — stacking them is far more effective than relying on either alone.

## Where it appears in AI

* **On-device voice assistants, cameras and keyboards** run models locally specifically for latency and privacy — no round trip to a server, and raw data (what you said, what you typed) never has to leave the device.
