Attention mixes information across every position in the sequence; the feed-forward sublayer processes each position entirely independently, with no access to any other position's content.
</details>

<details><summary>2. In the worked example, what fraction of hidden units survived the ReLU activation?</summary>
2 of 8 — the other 6 were negative before the activation and got zeroed out by ReLU.
</details>

<details><summary>3. What is the conventional relationship between the feed-forward hidden dimension and d_model?</summary>
The hidden dimension (d_ff) is conventionally 4 times d_model — for example, 3072 for a 768-wide model.
</details>

## Key terms

* **d_ff:** the width of the feed-forward sublayer's hidden layer, conventionally 4 times d_model.
* **Position-wise:** applied identically and independently to each position in a sequence, with no mixing between positions.
* **Expansion-then-projection:** widening a vector to a larger hidden dimension before compressing it back to the original width.

## Related

[[Residual Connections in Transformers]] · [[The Artificial Neuron and Activation Functions]] · [[Modern Feed-Forward Variants: SwiGLU and GeGLU]] · [[Mixture-of-Experts Transformer Blocks]]

## Modern Feed-Forward Variants: SwiGLU and GeGLU

[[The Feed-Forward Sublayer|The plain feed-forward sublayer]] expands, activates, and projects back down with one activation function applied directly. Most modern large transformers use a small but consistent twist instead: two parallel projections, where one *gates* the other through an activation, before the result is projected back down.

**You need:** [[The Feed-Forward Sublayer]].

## The question it answers

"Is applying an activation function directly to one projection the only way to introduce nonlinearity into the feed-forward sublayer?" No — a **gated** feed-forward sublayer computes two separate projections of the input instead of one, passes one of them through an activation function, and multiplies the two together element by element before projecting back down. SwiGLU (using the SiLU activation) and GeGLU (using GELU) are the two most common instances of this pattern.

## Intuition

The plain feed-forward sublayer decides how much each hidden unit fires using only its own linear combination of the input, run through an activation. A gated version splits that job in two: one projection (the **gate**) decides, through an activation, "how open is this channel?" while a second, purely linear projection (the **up** projection) carries "what value would flow through if it were fully open?" Multiplying the two together lets the network learn a much more flexible, input-dependent filter than a single activation function can express on its own.

## Definition and notation

```text
plain FFN:   out = W_down · activation(W · x)
gated FFN:   gate = activation(W_gate · x)
             up   = W_up · x
             out  = W_down · (gate ⊙ up)        (⊙ is elementwise multiplication)
```

SwiGLU uses `activation = SiLU` (`x · sigmoid(x)`); GeGLU uses `activation = GELU`. Both drop the bias terms common in a plain feed-forward sublayer, matching standard practice. Because there are now *three* weight matrices (`W_gate`, `W_up`, `W_down`) instead of two, `d_ff` is usually shrunk somewhat to keep the total parameter count close to a plain feed-forward sublayer's.

## A worked example

The same input as [[The Feed-Forward Sublayer|the previous topic's example]], `x = [0.5, -0.3, 0.8, 0.1]`, through a SwiGLU sublayer with `d_ff = 6`:

```text
gate (after SiLU):     [0.048, -0.077, 0.046, 0.010, -0.086, 0.133]
up (linear, no activation): [0.127, -0.371, -0.221, 0.218, 0.592, -0.220]
gated (elementwise product): [0.006, 0.029, -0.010, 0.002, -0.051, -0.029]

output: [0.0032, -0.0338, -0.0029, 0.0310]
```

Notice the gated values are much smaller in magnitude than either the gate or the up projection alone — the elementwise product squeezes down wherever either side is small, giving the sublayer a genuinely different shape of nonlinearity than a single activation applied directly.

Parameter count: a SwiGLU sublayer at this size needs `3 × (6 × 4) = 72` weights (three same-shaped matrices, no biases); a plain feed-forward sublayer at `d_ff = 6` needs `2 × (6 × 4) + 6 + 4 = 58` (two matrices plus biases) — the gated version costs more per hidden unit, which is exactly why `d_ff` is usually reduced to compensate when switching to a gated design.

## Bench

```bench
id: gated-ffn
title: Two projections, one gating the other
fallback: Push a vector through a SwiGLU-style gated feed-forward sublayer and compare the gate, the up projection and their product against a plain feed-forward sublayer's output.
```

**Try this**

1. Compare the gate and up projections side by side, then look at their elementwise product.
2. Switch the gating activation between SiLU and GELU and see how the gated values shift.
3. Compare the parameter count of a gated sublayer against a plain one at the same `d_ff`.

**What you should notice:** the gated output is shaped by *two* learned projections working together, not one activation applied to a single projection — giving the sublayer more expressive power per hidden unit, at the cost of an extra weight matrix.

## Where it appears in AI

* **SwiGLU and its relatives are the standard feed-forward design in most modern large transformers** — a direct, practical successor to the plain ReLU feed-forward sublayer from the original transformer paper.
* **The gating idea itself predates transformers**, echoing the gating mechanisms inside [[Long Short-Term Memory|LSTMs]] on [[Deep Learning]], where a learned gate also controls how much of a signal passes through.
* **[[Assembling One Transformer Block|the next topic]] can use either a plain or a gated feed-forward sublayer** — the rest of the block's structure (attention, residuals, normalization) doesn't change either way.

## Common pitfalls

* **Assuming gating doubles the parameter count for free performance.** It genuinely costs more parameters per hidden unit — real models compensate by shrinking `d_ff`, not by ignoring the cost.
* **Confusing the gate and the up projection's roles.** Only the gate passes through an activation function; the up projection stays purely linear, and swapping which one is which changes the computation.
* **Treating SwiGLU and GeGLU as fundamentally different mechanisms.** They are the identical gated structure, differing only in which activation function (SiLU vs. GELU) is used for the gate.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. What are the two projections in a gated feed-forward sublayer, and which one passes through an activation function?</summary>
The gate projection and the up projection; only the gate passes through an activation function (SiLU for SwiGLU, GELU for GeGLU) — the up projection stays linear.
</details>

<details><summary>2. How do SwiGLU and GeGLU differ from each other?</summary>
Only in which activation function gates the output — SiLU for SwiGLU, GELU for GeGLU; the overall gated structure is identical.
</details>

<details><summary>3. Why is d_ff typically reduced when switching from a plain feed-forward sublayer to a gated one?</summary>
A gated sublayer needs three weight matrices instead of two, costing more parameters per hidden unit — shrinking d_ff keeps the total parameter count comparable to a plain feed-forward sublayer.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Gate:** a projection passed through an activation function, controlling how much of a parallel projection's value passes through.
* **SwiGLU / GeGLU:** gated feed-forward designs using SiLU or GELU, respectively, as the gating activation.
* **Elementwise multiplication (⊙):** multiplying two vectors position by position, combining the gate and up projections.

## Related

[[The Feed-Forward Sublayer]] · [[Long Short-Term Memory]] · [[Assembling One Transformer Block]]

## Assembling One Transformer Block

Every piece needed is now on the table: [[Multi-Head Attention|attention]] itself, [[Residual Connections in Transformers|residual connections]], [[Layer Normalization Placement: Pre-Norm vs Post-Norm|normalization placement]], and [[The Feed-Forward Sublayer|the feed-forward sublayer]]. This topic puts them together into the one block that gets stacked, unchanged, a dozen or a hundred times to build an entire transformer.

**You need:** [[Multi-Head Attention]], [[Residual Connections in Transformers]], [[Layer Normalization Placement: Pre-Norm vs Post-Norm]], [[The Feed-Forward Sublayer]].

## The question it answers

"What is the exact sequence of operations inside one transformer block, from input to output?" A pre-norm block (the modern default) runs two residual sublayers in order: normalize, then attend, then add back to the input; normalize again, then feed forward, then add back to that result. Every piece covered earlier on this planet has exactly one job inside this sequence.

## Intuition

Think of the block as two "detours," each one leaving from and returning to the same running total (the residual stream). The first detour: take a cleaned-up look at the whole sequence (normalize), gather information from every other position (attend), then merge whatever was gathered back into the running total. The second detour: take another cleaned-up look at just this position's own current content (normalize again), process it in isolation (feed forward), then merge that back in too. Nothing about the running total itself is ever replaced — only added to.

## Definition and notation

```text
pre-norm transformer block, for a sequence of position vectors X:

1. X₁ = X + SelfAttention(LayerNorm(X))
2. X₂ = X₁ + FeedForward(LayerNorm(X₁))     — applied to each position independently

output: X₂
```

Every sublayer follows the identical shape: normalize an input, transform it, add the result back to the (untouched) residual stream. The exact same block, with its own trained weights, is stacked many times — the output `X₂` of one block becomes the input `X` of the next.

## A worked example

A 3-position, 4-dimensional toy sequence, pushed through one complete pre-norm block (random small weights, for traceability):

```text
input X, three positions' vector norms:        1.28, 1.61, 0.96

step 1 — LayerNorm(X), then self-attention, then add back (X₁):
  X₁'s vector norms:                           1.08, 1.79, 1.34

step 2 — LayerNorm(X₁), then feed-forward, then add back (X₂, final output):
  X₂'s vector norms:                           1.40, 1.91, 1.42
```

Every position's output norm ended up larger than its input norm — each residual addition contributed something new on top of the original signal, exactly as [[Residual Connections in Transformers|residual connections]] are designed to do, without ever discarding what came before.

## Bench

```bench
id: transformer-block
title: One block, start to finish
fallback: Trace a small sequence of vectors through one complete pre-norm transformer block — attention sublayer, then feed-forward sublayer, each wrapped in normalization and a residual connection.
```

**Try this**

1. Step through the block one sublayer at a time and watch each position's vector change.
2. Compare the input and final output vector norms for each position.
3. Stack the same block's output back through itself as a second block, and see the norms grow further.

**What you should notice:** nothing about this process depends on how many times the block is repeated — the same four-step recipe (normalize, attend, add; normalize, feed forward, add) is exactly what every layer of a real transformer runs, with its own independently trained weights at each depth.

## Where it appears in AI

* **It is literally the building block of every transformer**, from a small research model to a frontier-scale one — the only things that change between models are the number of blocks, their width, and small variant choices (RMSNorm vs LayerNorm, gated vs plain feed-forward) covered earlier in this district.
* **[[Encoder-Only Architectures|Encoder-only]], [[Decoder-Only Architectures|decoder-only]] and [[Encoder-Decoder Architectures as a Pattern|encoder-decoder]] architectures**, covered next, differ only in what masking is applied to the attention sublayer and whether a second, cross-attention sublayer is added — the block's core shape stays the same.
* **[[Capstone: Assembling a Tiny Transformer from the Ground Up|the planet's own capstone]]** extends exactly this worked example into a full, multi-block transformer.

## Common pitfalls

* **Forgetting the feed-forward sublayer is applied position by position.** Only the attention sublayer mixes information across positions; the feed-forward sublayer, inside the same block, processes each position independently.
* **Mixing up pre-norm and post-norm while assembling a block.** The order of normalize-then-sublayer versus sublayer-then-normalize changes which quantity is being added to the residual stream.
* **Assuming every block in a stack is identical in its weights.** The structure is identical at every depth, but each block has its own independently trained parameters.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. How many sublayers does one transformer block contain, and what does each one do?</summary>
Two: a self-attention sublayer that mixes information across positions, and a feed-forward sublayer that processes each position independently — both wrapped in normalization and a residual connection.
</details>

<details><summary>2. In a pre-norm block, what exactly gets added back to the residual stream after the attention sublayer?</summary>
The output of self-attention applied to the normalized input — the residual stream itself (the unnormalized `X`) is never altered directly, only added to.
</details>

<details><summary>3. What changes between a transformer's blocks when they're stacked, and what stays the same?</summary>
Each block's own weights are independently trained and different; the overall structure — normalize, attend, add; normalize, feed forward, add — is identical at every depth.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Transformer block:** the repeated unit of a transformer, containing one attention sublayer and one feed-forward sublayer, each wrapped in normalization and a residual connection.
* **Sublayer:** one of the two main computations (attention or feed-forward) inside a transformer block.
* **Stacking:** repeating the same block structure many times, with independently trained weights at each depth, to build a full transformer.

## Related

[[Multi-Head Attention]] · [[Residual Connections in Transformers]] · [[The Feed-Forward Sublayer]] · [[Encoder-Only Architectures]] · [[Capstone: Assembling a Tiny Transformer from the Ground Up]]

## Positional Information Beyond Sinusoids

The fixed sinusoidal encoding from [[Deep Learning]] was the original transformer's answer to "where is this token in the sequence?" — but it was never the only answer, and modern models mostly use something else. This district covers the alternatives and why they displaced it.

Topics on this stretch of the road:

* [[Learned Positional Embeddings]]: treating position like any other token, with a vector learned from data.
* [[Relative Position and RoPE]]: encoding how far apart two tokens are instead of their absolute positions.
* [[ALiBi and Length Extrapolation]]: biasing attention directly by distance, to generalize past the training sequence length.

## Learned Positional Embeddings

The sinusoidal encoding from [[Deep Learning]] computes a position's vector from a fixed formula — nothing about it is trained. The simplest alternative skips the formula entirely: treat position exactly like a token, and learn a vector for each one.

**You need:** [[Token Embeddings and Embedding Scaling]].

## The question it answers

"Must positional information come from a fixed mathematical formula, or can the model simply learn what each position's vector should be?" It can simply learn it: build a second embedding table, indexed by position instead of by token id, and add the result to the token embedding at that position — the exact same lookup-and-add mechanism as token embeddings, just keyed by a different index.

## Intuition

A token embedding table answers "what vector represents *this word*?" A learned positional embedding table answers the parallel question "what vector represents *this position*?" Both are ordinary trainable lookup tables; adding the two together gives the model a vector that encodes both what the token is and where it sits in the sequence. Because the table is trained like any other parameter, the model is free to learn whatever positional pattern turns out to be useful — not constrained to the particular sinusoidal shape derived in [[Deep Learning]].

## Definition and notation

```text
positional table P: shape max_length × d_model, trained like any other parameter

input to the transformer at position i:
  token_embedding(token_id) + P[i]
```

Unlike the sinusoidal formula, which can in principle be evaluated at any position, a learned table has a fixed `max_length` — it has no entry at all for a position beyond however many rows it was built with.

## A worked example

A 5-row, 4-dimensional positional table, applied to the *same* token embedding `[0.5, -0.2, 0.1, 0.4]` at two different positions:

```text
P[0] = [ 0.106, -0.184,  0.019, -0.201]
P[3] = [-0.158, -0.181,  0.078,  0.143]

token at position 0:  [0.5,-0.2,0.1,0.4] + P[0] = [0.606, -0.384, 0.119, 0.199]
token at position 3:  [0.5,-0.2,0.1,0.4] + P[3] = [0.342, -0.381, 0.178, 0.543]
```

The exact same word produces two visibly different vectors purely because of where it sits in the sequence — exactly the disambiguation positional information is supposed to provide, here coming entirely from two learned rows of a table rather than a formula. This table costs `5 × 4 = 20` parameters at this toy size; a real model's table scales with its actual maximum sequence length and width.

## Bench

```bench
id: learned-pos-embed
title: A trained row instead of a formula
fallback: Add a learned positional vector to the same token embedding at different positions, and see how the resulting vector changes with position.
```

**Try this**

1. Compare the same token's final vector across several different positions.
2. Try a position beyond the table's size and see that there's simply no row to look up.
3. Compare the parameter cost of the table at a few different maximum lengths.

**What you should notice:** nothing in this mechanism explains or constrains *what* each positional row should contain — unlike the sinusoidal formula's built-in structure, a learned table's positional vectors are whatever training happens to settle on.

## Where it appears in AI

* **It was the positional scheme used by several early, influential transformer models**, valued for its simplicity — one more embedding table, trained the same way as every other.
* **Its fixed-length limitation is exactly the problem [[Relative Position and RoPE|relative position schemes]] and [[ALiBi and Length Extrapolation]] solve directly** — both of the next two topics specifically target handling sequences longer than anything seen during training.
* **It contrasts directly with the sinusoidal encoding on [[Deep Learning]]**: same role, same place in the computation, but one is fixed and formula-based while the other is trained and data-driven.

## Common pitfalls

* **Assuming a learned table generalizes past its trained maximum length.** There is no row to look up past `max_length` — the model simply cannot represent a position it never saw a table entry for.
* **Expecting the learned positions to form any particular pattern.** Unlike the sinusoidal encoding's deliberate frequency structure, a learned table's values are whatever training found useful, with no guaranteed interpretable shape.
* **Forgetting the parameter cost scales with maximum sequence length.** A model built for very long sequences pays for a correspondingly large positional table.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. How does a learned positional embedding table get its positional vectors, as opposed to the sinusoidal encoding?</summary>
By training, exactly like a token embedding table — there is no formula; the values are learned parameters, indexed by position instead of token id.
</details>

<details><summary>2. In the worked example, what caused the same token's final vector to differ at position 0 versus position 3?</summary>
The two different rows of the positional table, `P[0]` and `P[3]`, added to the identical token embedding.
</details>

<details><summary>3. What is a learned positional table's main limitation compared to a formula-based encoding?</summary>
It has a fixed maximum length — there is no table entry at all for a position beyond however many rows it was trained with.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Positional table:** a trained embedding table indexed by sequence position instead of token id.
* **max_length:** the largest sequence position a learned positional table has an entry for.
* **Absolute position:** a token's fixed index within the sequence (0, 1, 2, …), as opposed to its position relative to another token.

## Related

[[Token Embeddings and Embedding Scaling]] · [[Relative Position and RoPE]] · [[ALiBi and Length Extrapolation]]

## Relative Position and RoPE

Both the sinusoidal encoding and [[Learned Positional Embeddings|learned positional embeddings]] tell a token its *absolute* position — "you are token number 7." Rotary position embedding (RoPE) asks a different question: instead of encoding where a token is, what if positional information only ever showed up as *how far apart* two tokens are, built directly into the attention computation itself?

**You need:** [[Learned Positional Embeddings]], [[Multi-Head Attention]].

## The question it answers

"Can positional information be built into attention so that only the *relative* distance between two tokens matters, with no notion of absolute position anywhere?" RoPE's answer: rotate each query and key vector by an angle proportional to its position, before computing attention scores. Because rotating two vectors by different amounts and then taking their dot product depends only on the *difference* between the two rotation angles, the resulting attention score ends up depending only on how far apart the two tokens are — never on their absolute positions.

## Intuition

Picture a query vector and a key vector as two hands on two separate clocks. Instead of writing a token's absolute position somewhere in the vector, RoPE spins each vector's clock hand by an angle proportional to its position. When two spun vectors are compared (via a dot product), the comparison naturally only "sees" how far apart the two clocks were spun relative to each other — spinning both clocks forward by the same extra amount changes nothing about how they compare to each other. That's exactly the relative-position property this topic is after.

## Definition and notation

For a 2D pair of a vector's components `(x₁, x₂)` and position `pos`, RoPE applies a rotation by angle `pos × θ`:

```text
rotate(x₁, x₂, angle) = (x₁ cos(angle) − x₂ sin(angle),  x₁ sin(angle) + x₂ cos(angle))
```

A full query or key vector is split into pairs of dimensions, each pair rotated by a position-dependent angle (different pairs typically use different frequencies, the same idea as the sinusoidal encoding's varying frequencies). The key mathematical fact: for query position `m` and key position `n`, `dot(rotate(q, m), rotate(k, n))` depends only on `m − n`, never on `m` and `n` individually.

## A worked example

A single 2D query `q = [1, 0.5]` and key `k = [0.3, -0.8]`, rotated by position and then compared via dot product, at several different absolute positions but the same relative distance:

```text
positions (m=2, n=5),   relative distance −3:  dot = 0.233063
positions (m=10, n=13), relative distance −3:  dot = 0.233063
positions (m=0, n=3),   relative distance −3:  dot = 0.233063

positions (m=5, n=5),     relative distance 0:  dot = −0.100000
positions (m=100, n=100), relative distance 0:  dot = −0.100000
raw dot(q, k), no rotation at all:              −0.100000
```

Three completely different pairs of absolute positions, all three at a relative distance of `−3`, produce the *exact same* attention score. And a relative distance of `0` always recovers the original, unrotated dot product — whatever the shared absolute position actually is.

## Bench

```bench
id: rope-relative
title: Rotation that only sees relative distance
fallback: Rotate a query and a key vector by two chosen positions and see that their dot product depends only on the distance between the two positions, not where they are absolutely.
```

**Try this**

1. Fix the relative distance between two positions and slide both positions together — watch the dot product stay fixed.
2. Change only the relative distance and watch the dot product change.
3. Set both positions equal (distance 0) and confirm the result matches the unrotated dot product.

**What you should notice:** the dot product is a function of exactly one number — the relative distance — no matter how large or small the two absolute positions themselves are.

## Where it appears in AI

* **It is the positional scheme used by many modern large language models**, directly addressing [[Learned Positional Embeddings|the fixed-table problem]]: there's no table to run out of, since the rotation formula is defined for any position.
* **It composes naturally with [[Multi-Head Attention]]**: the rotation is applied to queries and keys before the usual scaled dot-product computation, with nothing else about attention changed.
* **[[ALiBi and Length Extrapolation|the next topic]] takes a different, even simpler route** to a related goal — generalizing well to sequences longer than anything seen during training.

## Common pitfalls

* **Assuming RoPE adds anything to the vectors.** Unlike the sinusoidal encoding or learned embeddings, nothing is added — RoPE only rotates the existing query and key vectors.
* **Forgetting RoPE applies to queries and keys, not values.** The rotation specifically targets the vectors used to compute attention scores; the values being averaged together are untouched.
* **Expecting the relative-distance property to hold for arbitrary transformations.** It specifically relies on rotation's particular mathematical structure (rotating by `m` then comparing to rotating by `n` depends only on `m − n`) — not every positional scheme has this property.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. What does RoPE do to a query or key vector, and what does it never do?</summary>
It rotates the vector by an angle proportional to its position; it never adds anything to the vector, unlike the sinusoidal encoding or learned positional embeddings.
</details>

<details><summary>2. In the worked example, why did three different position pairs all produce the exact same dot product?</summary>
Because all three pairs shared the same relative distance (−3), and RoPE's rotation makes the dot product of two rotated vectors depend only on that relative distance, not on the absolute positions themselves.
</details>

<details><summary>3. What happens to the dot product when two positions are equal (relative distance 0)?</summary>
It equals the original, unrotated dot product of the two vectors — rotating both by the same angle doesn't change their relationship to each other.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Relative position:** positional information expressed as the distance between two tokens, rather than either token's absolute index.
* **Rotation angle:** the position-proportional angle RoPE uses to rotate a vector's paired dimensions.
* **Rotary position embedding (RoPE):** a positional scheme that rotates queries and keys so attention scores depend only on relative distance.

## Related

[[Learned Positional Embeddings]] · [[Multi-Head Attention]] · [[ALiBi and Length Extrapolation]]

## ALiBi and Length Extrapolation

[[Relative Position and RoPE|RoPE]] builds relative position into attention through rotation. ALiBi (Attention with Linear Biases) takes an even more direct route to a related goal: skip rotating anything, and just subtract a penalty from each attention score, proportional to how far apart the two tokens are.

**You need:** [[Relative Position and RoPE]], [[Multi-Head Attention]].

## The question it answers

"Can a model trained only on short sequences still behave sensibly on much longer ones it never saw during training?" [[Learned Positional Embeddings|A learned positional table]] clearly cannot — there's no row for a position past its trained maximum. ALiBi's answer is to make distance penalization the *entire* mechanism: subtract a bias proportional to distance directly from each attention score, with a different penalty steepness (slope) per head. Because that formula is defined for any distance at all, it keeps producing sensible, well-behaved scores far past any sequence length seen during training — this is **length extrapolation**.

## Intuition

Instead of telling a token "you are at position 47," or rotating vectors to encode distance mathematically, ALiBi takes the plainest possible approach: just make attention scores naturally prefer nearby tokens, by subtracting more from the score the farther away a token is. Different attention heads use different penalty steepnesses — some heads have a steep penalty and effectively only look at very nearby tokens, while others have a shallow penalty and can still attend fairly broadly. Because "subtract a number proportional to distance" works identically whether the distance is 5 or 5,000, nothing about the mechanism breaks down on sequences far longer than training ever included.

## Definition and notation

```text
bias(query_pos, key_pos) = −slope × |query_pos − key_pos|
masked score = raw attention score + bias       (added before the softmax)

slopes for h heads: slope_i = 2^(−8(i+1)/h),  for i = 0, …, h−1
```

Each head gets its own fixed, never-trained slope, geometrically spaced from steep (heavily penalizing distance) to shallow (barely penalizing it).

## A worked example

Eight attention heads' slopes, following the standard geometric spacing:

```text
slopes: 0.500, 0.250, 0.125, 0.0625, 0.0313, 0.0156, 0.00781, 0.00391
```

The bias applied at a few distances, for the steepest head (slope 0.5) and the shallowest (slope 0.00391):

```text
distance   steep-head bias   shallow-head bias
   1            −0.500            −0.0039
   5            −2.500            −0.0195
  20           −10.000            −0.0781
 100           −50.000            −0.3906
```

The steep head's penalty grows harsh very quickly — by distance 20, it's already subtracting 10 points from the raw score, likely pushing that position's attention weight toward zero after the softmax. The shallow head's penalty barely registers even at distance 100. Crucially, this same formula computes a sensible bias at distance 2,000, or 20,000, exactly as easily as at distance 5 — there is no "table" to run out of, and no retraining needed to handle a longer sequence than the model ever saw.

## Bench

```bench
id: alibi-slopes
title: A distance penalty, different per head
fallback: Compare the ALiBi bias at a chosen distance across several attention heads with different slopes, and see how the penalty scales to very long distances.
```

**Try this**

1. Compare the bias at a short distance across heads with steep and shallow slopes.
2. Push the distance far beyond anything a model would realistically train on and confirm the bias still computes a sensible number.
3. Compare how quickly a steep-slope head's bias grows versus a shallow-slope head's.

**What you should notice:** the bias formula never runs out of range — unlike a learned positional table, there is no maximum distance beyond which it stops being defined.

## Where it appears in AI

* **It is specifically designed for length extrapolation** — running a trained model on sequences longer than anything in its training data, a real, practical need for long-document and long-context use cases.
* **It removes positional information from the vectors entirely**, unlike every other scheme on this planet — ALiBi adds nothing to queries, keys or embeddings; it only modifies the attention scores directly, alongside the masks from [[Attention Masks: Padding and Causal Masking]].
* **The different slopes across heads give the model a built-in range of "attention spans"** for free, without any slope ever being trained — a structural choice baked into the architecture rather than learned.

## Common pitfalls

* **Confusing ALiBi's bias with a mask.** A mask sets a score to negative infinity (fully blocking a position); ALiBi's bias is a graded, finite penalty that reduces — but doesn't necessarily eliminate — attention to a distant position.
* **Assuming the slopes are trained.** They are fixed by the geometric formula before training ever starts, the same for every model using this scheme at a given head count.
* **Expecting arbitrary extrapolation with zero cost.** Length extrapolation under ALiBi is dramatically better than under a fixed-table scheme, but extremely long distances still eventually push attention weights toward negligible, which is in fact the intended, graceful behaviour.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. What does ALiBi add to a transformer's queries, keys or embeddings?</summary>
Nothing — ALiBi only modifies attention scores directly, by subtracting a distance-proportional bias before the softmax.
</details>

<details><summary>2. In the worked example, why did the steep-slope head's bias grow so much faster than the shallow-slope head's?</summary>
Because the bias is the slope multiplied by the distance, and a larger slope value scales that penalty up much more steeply as distance increases.
</details>

<details><summary>3. Why does ALiBi handle sequences longer than anything seen in training, unlike a learned positional table?</summary>
Its bias is a simple formula (slope times distance) defined for any distance at all, with no maximum length built in — unlike a learned table, which has no entry past its trained size.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Length extrapolation:** a model's ability to behave sensibly on sequences longer than anything seen during training.
* **Slope:** a fixed, per-head constant controlling how steeply ALiBi's bias penalizes distance.
* **Linear bias:** a penalty that grows proportionally with distance, subtracted directly from an attention score.

## Related

[[Relative Position and RoPE]] · [[Learned Positional Embeddings]] · [[Attention Masks: Padding and Causal Masking]]

## Architectural Families

The same transformer block supports three very different overall shapes, depending on which direction information is allowed to flow. This district names those shapes, the famous models that popularized each one, and how to choose between them.

Topics on this stretch of the road:

* [[Encoder-Only Architectures]]: every position attends to every other position, built for understanding a fixed input.
* [[Decoder-Only Architectures]]: each position only attends to what came before it, built for generating one token at a time.
* [[Encoder-Decoder Architectures as a Pattern]]: a full encoder feeding a decoder through cross-attention.
* [[Choosing an Architecture Family for a Task]]: matching the shape of a problem to one of these three patterns.

## Encoder-Only Architectures

[[Attention Masks: Padding and Causal Masking|The masking topic]] introduced two patterns: padding masks and causal masks. An encoder-only transformer uses only the first — every real token attends freely to every other real token, in both directions. That single choice is what makes BERT-style models good at *understanding* a complete piece of text rather than generating one token at a time.

**You need:** [[Attention Masks: Padding and Causal Masking]], [[Assembling One Transformer Block]].

## The question it answers

"What does a transformer look like when it's allowed to use the entire input at once, with nothing hidden from any position?" An encoder-only architecture: no causal mask anywhere, only padding masking where needed — every position can attend to every other position, before *and* after it in the sequence. This bidirectional view is exactly what makes these models well suited to a task like filling in a masked word, where the surrounding context on both sides is genuinely useful information.

## Intuition

Reading a sentence with one word blacked out, a person naturally uses *both* the words before the gap and the words after it to guess what's missing — "The ___ sat on the mat" is far easier to fill in with "the mat" visible than without it. An encoder-only transformer is built around exactly that assumption: since the whole input is available at once (there's no left-to-right generation happening), there's no reason to hide the right-hand context from any position. Every attention computation in the stack sees the complete sequence.

## Definition and notation

```text
encoder-only attention mask: padding mask only — no causal restriction
  allowed(i, j) = (j is not padding)
```

Training typically uses **masked language modeling (MLM)**: replace some tokens with a special `[MASK]` symbol, and train the model to predict the original token at each masked position, using the bidirectional context around it.

## A worked example

The sentence `The cat sat on the mat` (6 tokens), with the third token, `sat`, masked. Compare how much context is available to predict it under two schemes:

```text
encoder-only (bidirectional), mask row for position 2:  [1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1]
  → sees all 5 other tokens: "The", "cat", "on", "the", "mat"

causal (as in a decoder-only model), mask row for position 2: [1, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0]
  → sees only 2 tokens: "The", "cat"
```

An encoder-only model predicting the masked word has access to the entire sentence except the masked position itself — including "on the mat," which strongly suggests a word like "sat." A causally-masked model at the same position could only ever see "The cat," with no access to what follows.

## Bench

```bench
id: encoder-mask
title: How much context is available to fill a gap
fallback: Mask one token in a short sentence and compare how many surrounding tokens are visible to predict it, bidirectionally versus causally.
```

**Try this**

1. Move the masked position toward the end of the sentence and watch the causal case's available context shrink to almost nothing.
2. Compare the total number of visible tokens under each scheme, for the same masked position.
3. Consider what the causal case would need to do differently to ever use the right-hand context at all.

**What you should notice:** the gap between the two schemes grows as the masked position moves later in the sequence — bidirectional access to context is most valuable exactly where a causal model is most starved for it.

## Where it appears in AI

* **BERT and its many descendants are encoder-only architectures**, trained with masked language modeling — a direct, practical application of the bidirectional masking shown here.
* **It is the natural fit for understanding tasks**: classification, extracting a span of text, or filling in a gap — anything where the complete input is available up front and the goal is to understand it, not generate new text one token at a time.
* **[[Decoder-Only Architectures|the next topic]] makes the opposite choice**, and the reason it must is directly visible in this topic's worked example: generating text one token at a time means the "future" tokens genuinely don't exist yet to attend to.

## Common pitfalls

* **Assuming encoder-only models can generate text left to right.** Nothing stops information from flowing backward through the sequence, which is exactly what makes naive autoregressive generation incoherent with this architecture.
* **Forgetting padding masking still applies.** "No causal mask" doesn't mean "no masking at all" — padding positions are still excluded, exactly as in [[Attention Masks: Padding and Causal Masking]].
* **Assuming MLM is the only possible training objective for this architecture.** It's the most common one, but the bidirectional *architecture* itself is a separate choice from any particular training objective layered on top of it.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. What single masking choice defines an encoder-only architecture?</summary>
No causal mask — only padding masking is applied, so every real token can attend to every other real token in both directions.
</details>

<details><summary>2. In the worked example, why did the causal case have so much less context available than the bidirectional case?</summary>
A causal mask only allows a position to attend to itself and earlier positions, so at position 2 it could only see positions 0 and 1 — the bidirectional case had no such restriction and could see all 5 other positions.
</details>

<details><summary>3. What training objective is commonly paired with encoder-only architectures, and why does it need bidirectional attention?</summary>
Masked language modeling — predicting a masked-out token using the full surrounding context, which requires seeing tokens on both sides of the gap, not just the ones before it.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Encoder-only:** a transformer architecture using only padding masking, with no causal restriction — every position attends to every other.
* **Bidirectional attention:** attention that allows looking both backward and forward in a sequence, as opposed to causal (backward-only) attention.
* **Masked language modeling (MLM):** a training objective that predicts a masked-out token from its surrounding bidirectional context.

## Related

[[Attention Masks: Padding and Causal Masking]] · [[Decoder-Only Architectures]] · [[Choosing an Architecture Family for a Task]]

## Decoder-Only Architectures

[[Encoder-Only Architectures|The previous topic's]] bidirectional attention works because the whole input is available at once. Generating text one token at a time breaks that assumption completely: the tokens after "now" genuinely don't exist yet. A decoder-only architecture is built around that constraint from the ground up — causal masking, everywhere, always.

**You need:** [[Encoder-Only Architectures]].

## The question it answers

"What does a transformer look like when it has to generate its output one token at a time, each one depending only on what came before?" A decoder-only architecture: every attention computation in the stack uses a causal mask, so a position can never attend to anything later than itself. This isn't an arbitrary restriction — it's the only option that makes sense once the goal is producing the next token in a sequence that doesn't fully exist yet.

## Intuition

Imagine writing a sentence one word at a time, where each new word has to be chosen based only on the words already written — you can't peek ahead at a word you haven't written yet, because it doesn't exist until you write it. A decoder-only transformer is in exactly that position at every single token it generates: predict the next token using only the tokens generated (or given) so far, then append that new token to the sequence and repeat. This is called **autoregressive** generation — each new output feeds back in as part of the input for the next step.

## Definition and notation

```text
decoder-only attention mask: causal mask only
  allowed(i, j) = (j ≤ i)

generation, one step at a time:
  step t:  predict token at position t, using only positions 0 … t−1
  append the predicted token, now position t is "known" too
  step t+1: predict position t+1, using positions 0 … t
```

Every layer of a decoder-only transformer applies this same causal restriction — there is no point in the stack where a position can see ahead of itself.

## A worked example

Generating a 5-token sequence, tracking exactly how much context is visible at each generation step:

```text
step 1: predicting position 0 — context: {}               (0 tokens visible)
step 2: predicting position 1 — context: {0}               (1 token visible)
step 3: predicting position 2 — context: {0, 1}             (2 tokens visible)
step 4: predicting position 3 — context: {0, 1, 2}           (3 tokens visible)
step 5: predicting position 4 — context: {0, 1, 2, 3}         (4 tokens visible)
```

Compare this to [[Encoder-Only Architectures|the previous topic's]] worked example, where every position saw all 5 other tokens simultaneously, regardless of position. Here, the visible context grows by exactly one token at each step — never more, and crucially, never including anything "ahead" of the position currently being predicted.

## Bench

```bench
id: decoder-generate
title: Generating one token, with only what came before
fallback: Step through generating a sequence one token at a time, watching exactly which positions are visible to the model at each step.
```

**Try this**

1. Step through generation and watch the visible context grow by exactly one position each time.
2. Compare the final step's visible context to the encoder-only bench's full-sentence visibility.
3. Consider what would happen if a later position's information somehow leaked into an earlier prediction.

**What you should notice:** the causal mask isn't an arbitrary training-time restriction — it's the architecture correctly matching the actual information available at generation time, step by step.

## Where it appears in AI

* **GPT-style models are the canonical decoder-only architecture**, trained to predict the next token given everything before it — exactly the generation process traced in the worked example.
* **This is the architecture [[LLMs|most modern large language models]] are built on**, since their core capability — generating fluent, coherent text one token at a time — is precisely what causal masking makes consistent between training and actual use.
* **[[KV-Caching for Autoregressive Inference|KV-caching]], covered later on this planet**, exists specifically because decoder-only generation repeats the same growing-context computation at every single step — a real cost this architecture's generation process creates.

## Common pitfalls

* **Assuming a decoder-only model could use bidirectional attention if trained differently.** The mismatch between bidirectional training and strictly left-to-right generation would make training and actual use inconsistent — training would see context the model will never have at generation time.
* **Confusing "decoder-only" with "has no encoder, so it can't understand anything."** Decoder-only models still build up a rich internal understanding of the input — the causal restriction limits what they attend to, not what they're capable of representing.
* **Forgetting every layer applies the same causal mask.** It isn't just the final output step that's restricted — every attention computation in every layer, at every depth, respects the same causal boundary.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. What masking choice defines a decoder-only architecture, and why is it necessary rather than arbitrary?</summary>
Causal masking everywhere — necessary because generation produces tokens one at a time, and later tokens genuinely don't exist yet when an earlier one is being predicted.
</details>

<details><summary>2. In the worked example, how does the visible context change from one generation step to the next?</summary>
It grows by exactly one token — predicting position t uses positions 0 through t−1, and once that token is generated, predicting position t+1 can use positions 0 through t.
</details>

<details><summary>3. What does "autoregressive" mean in this context?</summary>
Each newly generated token is appended to the sequence and becomes part of the input context for predicting the next one.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Autoregressive:** generating output one step at a time, where each new output becomes part of the input for the next step.
* **Causal masking:** restricting attention so a position can only see itself and earlier positions, never later ones.
* **Decoder-only:** a transformer architecture using causal masking throughout, suited to generating text one token at a time.

## Related

[[Encoder-Only Architectures]] · [[Encoder-Decoder Architectures as a Pattern]] · [[Choosing an Architecture Family for a Task]] · [[KV-Caching for Autoregressive Inference]]

## Encoder-Decoder Architectures as a Pattern

[[Encoder-Only Architectures|Encoder-only]] and [[Decoder-Only Architectures|decoder-only]] architectures each use one kind of self-attention throughout. An encoder-decoder architecture uses both — a full bidirectional encoder stack, a full causal decoder stack, and a third kind of attention connecting them: the decoder looking directly at the encoder's finished output.

**You need:** [[Encoder-Only Architectures]], [[Decoder-Only Architectures]].

## The question it answers

"What does a transformer look like when the task is genuinely two different jobs — fully understand one piece of text, then generate a different piece of text based on it?" An encoder-decoder architecture: the encoder stack reads the input bidirectionally, exactly as in [[Encoder-Only Architectures]]; the decoder stack generates output causally, exactly as in [[Decoder-Only Architectures]]; and a new attention sublayer, **cross-attention**, lets every decoder position look at the *entire* finished encoder output, with no causal restriction at all.

## Intuition

Think of translating a sentence from one language to another. Understanding the full source sentence benefits from seeing it all at once, in both directions — exactly the encoder's job. Producing the translation, word by word, has to respect that later words don't exist yet — exactly the decoder's job. But generating each word of the translation also needs to look back at the *entire* source sentence, not just the part already covered — translating the first word of the output might still depend on something near the end of the input. Cross-attention is exactly that: a decoder position's query, compared against keys and values drawn from the finished encoder output, with no restriction on which source positions it can see.

## Definition and notation

```text
encoder:  bidirectional self-attention, same as Encoder-Only Architectures
decoder (per block):
  1. causal self-attention among the decoder's own positions so far
  2. cross-attention: decoder queries, encoder keys and values — no masking
  3. feed-forward sublayer, as usual
```

Cross-attention uses the same scaled dot-product formula as self-attention — the only difference is that queries come from one sequence (the decoder) while keys and values come from a different, already-computed sequence (the encoder's output).

## A worked example

A 3-position encoder output and a 2-position decoder, so far, both 4-dimensional:

```text
decoder's own causal self-attention weights:
  position 0: [1.000, 0.000]        (can only see itself)
  position 1: [0.509, 0.491]        (sees itself and position 0)

cross-attention weights (decoder position → encoder positions), no masking:
  decoder position 0: [0.341, 0.327, 0.333]   (sums to 1.000)
  decoder position 1: [0.322, 0.344, 0.334]   (sums to 1.000)
```

Both decoder positions spread their cross-attention across *all three* encoder positions, regardless of how little of the decoder's own sequence has been generated so far — position 0, despite only having itself available in self-attention, still has full access to the entire encoder output through cross-attention.

## Bench

```bench
id: cross-attention-demo
title: Looking back at the whole source while generating
fallback: Compare a decoder position's causal self-attention (restricted to earlier decoder positions) against its cross-attention (full access to every encoder position), side by side.
```

**Try this**

1. Compare how restricted decoder self-attention is for an early position against how unrestricted its cross-attention is.
2. Add more decoder positions and watch self-attention's visible context grow while cross-attention's stays full every time.
3. Consider what cross-attention would need to be masked for a task like translation with aligned padding.

**What you should notice:** causal restriction applies only to the decoder's own, still-being-generated sequence — it says nothing about the encoder's already-complete output, which stays fully visible through cross-attention at every single decoder step.

## Where it appears in AI

* **T5 and other sequence-to-sequence transformer models follow exactly this pattern**, and it is the direct transformer-era descendant of [[Encoder-Decoder Architectures with Attention|the RNN-based encoder-decoder attention]] covered on [[Deep Learning]] — same cross-attention idea, built from transformer blocks instead of recurrent ones.
* **It is the natural fit for genuinely input-to-output tasks**: translation, summarization, and other jobs where the output is a transformation of a complete input, not a continuation of it.
* **[[Choosing an Architecture Family for a Task|the next topic]] weighs this pattern's extra cost and complexity** (two stacks instead of one, plus cross-attention) against when it's actually worth it over a simpler architecture.

## Common pitfalls

* **Assuming cross-attention is masked like decoder self-attention.** It generally isn't — the encoder's output is already complete and fixed, so there's no "future" to hide from it (padding masking on the encoder side still applies).
* **Confusing cross-attention with a second self-attention pass.** Queries and keys/values come from two different sequences here, unlike self-attention, where they all come from the same one.
* **Treating this as strictly more powerful than encoder-only or decoder-only.** It solves a genuinely different kind of task (transforming one sequence into another) at the cost of two stacks instead of one — not a universal upgrade.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. What are the three kinds of attention present in an encoder-decoder transformer block?</summary>
Bidirectional self-attention in the encoder, causal self-attention in the decoder, and cross-attention connecting the decoder's queries to the encoder's keys and values.
</details>

<details><summary>2. In the worked example, why did cross-attention weights sum to 1 across all three encoder positions, for every decoder position?</summary>
Cross-attention has no causal restriction — every decoder position's query is compared against the entire, already-complete encoder output, with the softmax normalizing the weights over all of it.
</details>

<details><summary>3. What distinguishes cross-attention from self-attention, mechanically?</summary>
Cross-attention's queries come from one sequence (the decoder) while its keys and values come from a different, already-computed sequence (the encoder) — self-attention draws all three from the same sequence.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Cross-attention:** attention where queries come from one sequence and keys/values come from a separately computed sequence.
* **Encoder-decoder architecture:** a transformer combining a bidirectional encoder stack, a causal decoder stack, and cross-attention connecting them.
* **Sequence-to-sequence:** a task that transforms one complete input sequence into a different output sequence, such as translation.

## Related

[[Encoder-Only Architectures]] · [[Decoder-Only Architectures]] · [[Encoder-Decoder Architectures with Attention]] · [[Choosing an Architecture Family for a Task]]

## Choosing an Architecture Family for a Task

Three architecture families, three different attention patterns, three different costs. This topic puts a number on that difference for a single concrete input/output shape, and turns the earlier topics' structural differences into an actual decision.

**You need:** [[Encoder-Only Architectures]], [[Decoder-Only Architectures]], [[Encoder-Decoder Architectures as a Pattern]], [[Why Attention Replaced Recurrence]].

## The question it answers

"Given a task's input and output shape, which architecture family actually fits, and what does each one cost?" The deciding factor is almost always what the task's input and output actually look like: a single input with no generated output (classification, understanding) fits encoder-only; one continuous stream the model both reads and extends (open-ended generation, chat) fits decoder-only; two genuinely separate sequences, one transformed into the other (translation, summarization into a fixed target format) fits encoder-decoder.

## Intuition

Encoder-only has nothing to generate — it reads once and produces a judgment, so bidirectional, single-pass attention is exactly what's needed and nothing is wasted on a decoder it would never use. Decoder-only treats the prompt and the generated continuation as one and the same kind of thing — appropriate when there's no meaningful boundary between "input" and "output," just one growing sequence. Encoder-decoder keeps the input and output as two separate sequences on purpose, useful exactly when that separation is real and worth preserving — the output isn't a continuation of the input, it's a transformation of it.

## Definition and notation

Using the same quadratic attention-cost accounting as [[Why Attention Replaced Recurrence]] (attention pairs ≈ sequence length squared, summed appropriately for causal attention):

```text
encoder-only:    cost ≈ N²                              (one bidirectional pass, N input tokens)
decoder-only:    cost ≈ Σ_{t=1}^{N+M} t                  (causal self-attention over the whole N+M sequence)
encoder-decoder: cost ≈ N² + Σ_{t=1}^{M} t + M·N          (encoder + decoder self-attn + cross-attention)
```

## A worked example

An input of `N = 6` tokens and an output of `M = 4` tokens, compared across all three architectures:

```text
encoder-only (classification, no generation): 6² = 36 attention pairs
decoder-only (one growing sequence, 6+4=10 tokens total): Σ_{t=1}^{10} t = 55 attention pairs
encoder-decoder (6 → 4, as a transformation): 6² + Σ_{t=1}^{4} t + 4×6 = 36 + 10 + 24 = 70 attention pairs
```

At this small scale, encoder-only is cheapest (it never generates anything), encoder-decoder is most expensive (two full stacks plus cross-attention), and decoder-only sits in between — but the real decision almost never comes down to this cost difference alone: it comes down to whether the task actually has an input-only shape, a single growing sequence, or two genuinely separate sequences.

## Bench

```bench
id: architecture-choice
title: Match the task shape to the architecture
fallback: Pick a task shape — understanding only, one growing sequence, or two separate sequences — and see which architecture family fits and its attention-pair cost at a chosen input and output length.
```

**Try this**

1. Pick each task shape in turn and read which architecture it matches.
2. Change the input and output lengths and watch each architecture's cost scale differently.
3. Find input/output lengths where decoder-only and encoder-decoder's costs are close, and consider what would still make one the better practical choice anyway.

**What you should notice:** cost alone rarely decides the choice — a classification task fed through a decoder-only architecture would work, but it would be paying for a growing causal sequence it doesn't actually need, since there's no "generation" involved at all.

## Where it appears in AI

* **Most large language models in current practice are decoder-only**, in part because a single, flexible growing-sequence architecture handles an enormous range of tasks (including ones that look like classification, by framing the answer as generated text) without needing a second stack.
* **Encoder-decoder remains the natural fit for genuinely structured sequence-to-sequence tasks** — translation, where a fixed, separate target sequence is really being produced from a fixed, separate source.
* **Encoder-only remains the standard choice for pure understanding tasks** — classification, retrieval, and other jobs with no generated output at all.

## Common pitfalls

* **Treating the cost formula as the deciding factor.** The task's actual shape — is there a generated output at all, and if so, is it a transformation of a separate input or a continuation of the same sequence — matters far more than the attention-pair count at any one scale.
* **Assuming decoder-only can't do understanding tasks.** It can, by framing them as generation (producing a label as if it were text), just not with the quadratic savings an encoder-only model gets from never generating anything.
* **Forgetting encoder-decoder's cost includes two full stacks.** The formula above counts only attention pairs, not the two separate sets of feed-forward sublayers each stack also needs.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. What is the single biggest factor in choosing between the three architecture families?</summary>
Whether the task has a generated output at all, and if so, whether that output is a transformation of a separate input sequence or a continuation of the same one.
</details>

<details><summary>2. In the worked example, why was encoder-only the cheapest of the three?</summary>
It never generates anything — its entire cost is one bidirectional pass over the input, with no causal self-attention or cross-attention to pay for at all.
</details>

<details><summary>3. Why might a task that looks like classification still be handled by a decoder-only model in practice?</summary>
A decoder-only model can frame a classification answer as generated text, trading away encoder-only's cost advantage for the flexibility of a single, general-purpose architecture.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Task shape:** whether a task has no generated output, one continuous growing sequence, or two separate input/output sequences.
* **Attention-pair cost:** the number of query-key comparisons an attention computation makes, used here as a simple proxy for compute cost.
* **Sequence-to-sequence task:** a task whose output is a genuine transformation of a separate input, the natural fit for encoder-decoder.

## Related

[[Encoder-Only Architectures]] · [[Decoder-Only Architectures]] · [[Encoder-Decoder Architectures as a Pattern]] · [[Why Attention Replaced Recurrence]]

## Efficient and Scaled Attention

Plain multi-head attention gets expensive fast: its cost grows with the square of sequence length, and its memory traffic during inference grows with every token generated. This district covers the engineering responses to both problems.

Topics on this stretch of the road:

* [[Multi-Query and Grouped-Query Attention]]: sharing key and value projections across heads to shrink memory traffic.
* [[KV-Caching for Autoregressive Inference]]: avoiding recomputation by storing keys and values as generation proceeds.
* [[Sparse and Local (Windowed) Attention]]: letting each token attend to only a limited neighbourhood.
* [[Linear Attention Approximations]]: reformulating attention to scale linearly instead of quadratically.
* [[IO-Aware Attention Computation]]: computing exact attention faster by minimizing slow memory traffic, not by approximating it.

## Multi-Query and Grouped-Query Attention

[[Multi-Head Attention|Standard multi-head attention]] gives every head its own query, key and value projections. That costs something specific at inference time: every head's keys and values have to be stored and reused as generation proceeds. Multi-query and grouped-query attention keep the per-head queries but share the keys and values across heads — shrinking exactly that storage cost.

**You need:** [[Multi-Head Attention]].

## The question it answers

"Does every attention head really need its own separate keys and values, or only its own queries?" Multi-query attention (MQA) answers no: give every head its own query projection, but share a single key and value projection across *all* heads. Grouped-query attention (GQA) is the middle ground: split the heads into a handful of groups, and share one key/value projection per group. Both leave the query side fully multi-head — only the keys and values, the part that has to be stored and reused during generation, get shared.

## Intuition

In standard multi-head attention, every one of the 8 (or more) heads keeps its own separate copy of "what does every past token mean, as a key and a value" — redundant storage, since much of that information overlaps across heads. MQA asks every head to share one single copy of that key/value information, while still letting each head query it differently. GQA compromises: a handful of shared key/value copies, a middle point between MQA's single shared copy and standard attention's one copy per head.

## Definition and notation

```text
standard (MHA):  num_kv_heads = num_heads        — one K/V projection per head
GQA:             num_kv_heads = num_groups        — one K/V projection per group of heads
MQA:             num_kv_heads = 1                 — a single, shared K/V projection for every head

KV cache size per token ∝ num_kv_heads × head_dim × num_layers
```

Only `num_kv_heads` changes between the three schemes — the number of query heads, and everything else about the attention computation, stays the same.

## A worked example

A model with `d_model = 512`, 8 heads, `head_dim = 64`, and 12 layers, comparing the per-token KV cache cost:

```text
MHA (num_kv_heads = 8):  12,288 floats per token
GQA (num_kv_heads = 2):   3,072 floats per token   (4× smaller than MHA)
MQA (num_kv_heads = 1):   1,536 floats per token   (8× smaller than MHA)
```

For a sequence of 2,048 tokens (4 bytes per float), the full KV cache comes out to:

```text
MHA: 100.66 MB
GQA:  25.17 MB
MQA:  12.58 MB
```

Switching from standard multi-head attention to MQA shrinks the KV cache that needs to be stored and read back at every generation step by a full 8×, at this configuration — with only the key/value side of attention changed.

## Bench

```bench
id: kv-heads-cache
title: Shrinking what has to be cached
fallback: Set the number of KV heads and see the per-token and per-sequence KV cache size change, from standard multi-head attention down to a single shared KV head.
```

**Try this**

1. Move from 8 KV heads down to 1 and watch the cache size shrink proportionally.
2. Try an intermediate value (2 or 4) to see GQA's middle-ground cost.
3. Increase the sequence length and watch the absolute cache size at each KV-head setting.

**What you should notice:** the cache size scales linearly with `num_kv_heads` — going from 8 to 1 KV head doesn't just help a little, it's a direct, proportional 8× reduction in exactly the thing that has to be stored during generation.

## Where it appears in AI

* **It directly sets up [[KV-Caching for Autoregressive Inference|the next topic]]**: the whole reason the number of KV heads matters this much is the cache that gets built and reused during generation.
* **GQA in particular is a widely-used practical compromise** in many modern large language models — most of MQA's memory savings, with less of the capacity loss that comes from sharing key/value information across every single head.
* **It is a pure inference-time efficiency choice**: the training objective and the rest of the architecture are unaffected — only how keys and values are shared across heads changes.

## Common pitfalls

* **Assuming MQA or GQA shrinks the query side too.** Only the key/value projections are shared; every head still computes its own distinct query.
* **Treating this as free.** Sharing key/value information across heads does cost some representational capacity compared to giving every head its own — the savings come with a genuine, if often small, trade-off.
* **Confusing "num_kv_heads" with "num_heads."** The query side's head count is unchanged by this topic entirely — only how many *distinct* key/value projections exist changes.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. What is shared across heads in multi-query attention, and what stays separate per head?</summary>
A single key and value projection is shared across all heads; each head still has its own separate query projection.
</details>

<details><summary>2. In the worked example, by what factor did the KV cache shrink going from standard multi-head attention to MQA?</summary>
8×, directly matching the drop from 8 KV heads to 1.
</details>

<details><summary>3. What does grouped-query attention trade off, relative to multi-query attention?</summary>
More KV heads than MQA's single shared one (so a larger cache, less savings) in exchange for more representational capacity than fully sharing key/value information across every head.
</details>

## Key terms

* **num_kv_heads:** the number of distinct key/value projections, which can be fewer than the number of query heads.
* **Multi-query attention (MQA):** sharing a single key/value projection across every attention head.
* **Grouped-query attention (GQA):** sharing one key/value projection per group of heads, a middle ground between standard multi-head attention and MQA.

## Related

[[Multi-Head Attention]] · [[KV-Caching for Autoregressive Inference]]

## KV-Caching for Autoregressive Inference

[[Decoder-Only Architectures|Generating text one token at a time]] means recomputing attention at every single step. Without care, that recomputation redoes work that was already done at every previous step — KV-caching is the fix: compute each token's key and value exactly once, and simply reuse them forever after.

**You need:** [[Decoder-Only Architectures]], [[Multi-Query and Grouped-Query Attention]].

## The question it answers

"When generating token by token, does every generation step really need to recompute the keys and values for every token seen so far?" No — a token's key and value vectors depend only on that token itself (and its position), never on what comes after it. Once computed, they never change. KV-caching simply stores them the first time and looks them up on every later step, instead of recomputing them from scratch.

## Intuition

Imagine writing a long essay, and before adding every new sentence, re-reading and re-summarizing the entire essay so far from the beginning — wasteful, since most of that summary hasn't changed since the last sentence. KV-caching is the obvious fix: keep a running set of notes (the keys and values) for everything written so far, and when adding a new sentence, just write new notes for it and append them to the pile, without redoing any of the old ones.

## Definition and notation

```text
without caching, generating N tokens:
  at step t, recompute K and V for all t tokens seen so far
  total K/V computations = Σ_{t=1}^{N} t = N(N+1)/2

with caching:
  at step t, compute K and V only for the one new token
  total K/V computations = N
```

The query for the new token is still computed fresh every step (it has to be — it's a brand-new token), but the keys and values for every *earlier* token are pulled straight from the cache instead of being recomputed.

## A worked example

Generating sequences of various lengths, comparing total key/value computations with and without caching:

```text
N = 10:   without cache: 55     with cache: 10     →  5.5× fewer computations
N = 50:   without cache: 1,275  with cache: 50      →  25.5× fewer computations
N = 100:  without cache: 5,050  with cache: 100     →  50.5× fewer computations
N = 500:  without cache: 125,250  with cache: 500   →  250.5× fewer computations
```

The savings aren't a fixed multiple — they keep growing as the generated sequence gets longer, since recomputing from scratch gets quadratically more wasteful while caching stays perfectly linear.

## Bench

```bench
id: kv-cache-savings
title: Compute each key and value exactly once
fallback: Set a generation length and compare the total key/value computations needed with and without caching, as the sequence grows.
```

**Try this**

1. Increase the generation length and watch the speedup factor grow.
2. Compare the shape of the "without cache" and "with cache" cost curves as length increases.
3. Connect this back to [[Multi-Query and Grouped-Query Attention]] — consider how a smaller `num_kv_heads` affects what actually needs to be stored in this cache.

**What you should notice:** without caching, generation cost grows quadratically with length purely from redundant recomputation — not from any new work the model is actually doing — which is exactly the waste caching eliminates.

## Where it appears in AI

* **It is standard practice in essentially every deployed autoregressive transformer** — without it, generating long text would be prohibitively slow, scaling quadratically for no computational benefit.
* **It is also the main memory cost of serving a decoder-only model**: the cache has to be stored for the whole generation, which is exactly why [[Multi-Query and Grouped-Query Attention|shrinking num_kv_heads]] matters so much in practice.
* **[[Inference Serving Trade-offs|later in this planet]], batching multiple requests together means managing many of these caches simultaneously** — a real systems problem built directly on top of this mechanism.

## Common pitfalls

* **Assuming the cache needs to store queries too.** Only keys and values are cached — queries are always freshly computed for the current token being generated, never reused.
* **Forgetting the cache grows with every generated token.** Longer generations need more memory for the cache, not just more computation — the two costs (speed savings and memory cost) are two sides of the same mechanism.
* **Treating caching as changing what the model computes.** It changes nothing about the *result* — the same keys and values are produced either way; caching only avoids redundantly recomputing them.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. Why can a token's key and value be safely cached and reused at every later generation step?</summary>
A token's key and value depend only on that token itself and its position — nothing about later tokens changes them, so they never need to be recomputed.
</details>

<details><summary>2. In the worked example, why does the speedup factor keep growing as the generation length increases?</summary>
Recomputing from scratch costs grows quadratically (Σt ≈ N²/2) while caching costs grow only linearly (N), so the ratio between the two keeps widening as N grows.
</details>

<details><summary>3. What is still computed fresh at every generation step, even with caching?</summary>
The query for the newly generated token, and that token's own key and value (which then get added to the cache for future steps).
</details>

## Key terms

* **KV cache:** stored keys and values for every token generated so far, reused instead of recomputed at each new step.
* **Quadratic recomputation:** the wasted cost of recomputing every earlier token's key and value at every single generation step, without caching.
* **Autoregressive generation:** producing a sequence one token at a time, each depending on everything generated before it.

## Related

[[Decoder-Only Architectures]] · [[Multi-Query and Grouped-Query Attention]] · [[Inference Serving Trade-offs]]

## Sparse and Local (Windowed) Attention

[[KV-Caching for Autoregressive Inference|KV-caching]] fixes redundant recomputation, but the underlying attention computation itself still scales with the square of sequence length. Windowed attention attacks that directly, by simply refusing to compute most of those pairs in the first place — each position only attends to a fixed-size neighbourhood around itself.

**You need:** [[Attention Masks: Padding and Causal Masking]], [[Why Attention Replaced Recurrence]].

## The question it answers

"Does every position really need to attend to every other position, or would a fixed-size local neighbourhood capture most of what matters?" Windowed (local) attention restricts each position to attending only within a fixed radius — not the whole sequence — using exactly the same masking mechanism from [[Attention Masks: Padding and Causal Masking]], just with a banded pattern instead of a triangular or all-ones one. The attention computation's cost drops from scaling with the square of sequence length to scaling only linearly with it.

## Intuition

Most of what a word's meaning depends on tends to come from nearby words — the sentence it's in, maybe the one before or after. Full attention computes every pair regardless, including distant ones that, for many tokens, contribute little. Windowed attention makes that assumption explicit: give every position a fixed-size window of neighbours it's allowed to attend to, and simply never compute anything outside it. The window slides along with the position — position 50's window is centred on position 50, position 51's window shifts along with it.

## Definition and notation

```text
windowed mask: allowed(i, j) = |i − j| ≤ radius

full attention cost:      ≈ n²
windowed attention cost:  ≈ n × (2·radius + 1)       (a fixed band width per position)
```

As `radius` shrinks relative to the sequence length `n`, the windowed cost grows linearly in `n` instead of quadratically — a structural change in how the cost scales, not just a smaller constant factor.

## A worked example

An 8-position sequence with a window radius of 2 (each position sees up to 2 neighbours on either side):

```text
position 0: [1,1,1,0,0,0,0,0]
position 1: [1,1,1,1,0,0,0,0]
position 2: [1,1,1,1,1,0,0,0]
position 3: [0,1,1,1,1,1,0,0]
position 4: [0,0,1,1,1,1,1,0]
position 5: [0,0,0,1,1,1,1,1]
position 6: [0,0,0,0,1,1,1,1]
position 7: [0,0,0,0,0,1,1,1]

allowed pairs: 34 of 64 possible — 53.1%
```

At this small scale the saving is modest. At a realistic scale — `n = 1000`, `radius = 4` — the picture changes completely: full attention computes `1,000,000` pairs; windowed attention computes only `8,980` — a **111× reduction**, purely from refusing to compute pairs the window excludes.

## Bench

```bench
id: windowed-attention
title: A sliding neighbourhood instead of the whole sequence
fallback: Set a sequence length and window radius, and compare the number of attention pairs computed against full attention at the same length.
```

**Try this**

1. Shrink the window radius and watch the allowed-pairs percentage drop.
2. Increase the sequence length at a fixed radius and watch the savings grow dramatically.
3. Set the radius equal to half the sequence length and see the windowed and full costs converge.

**What you should notice:** the savings grow with sequence length even at a fixed radius — windowed attention's advantage over full attention gets *more* dramatic the longer the sequence, exactly because full attention's cost grows quadratically while windowed attention's stays linear.

## Where it appears in AI

* **It is one of several practical answers to attention's quadratic cost**, alongside the different approach taken next in [[Linear Attention Approximations]].
* **It trades some global context for efficiency** — a real cost, since information more than `radius` positions away can only reach a given position indirectly, through multiple layers, rather than in a single attention computation.
* **Stacking several windowed-attention layers lets information still travel further than one window's radius**, the same way stacking convolutions on [[Deep Learning]] expands an effective receptive field beyond a single layer's kernel size.
