## Common pitfalls

* **Assuming windowed attention can see nothing beyond its radius, ever.** A single layer can't, but information can still propagate further across multiple stacked layers, each extending the effective reach a little more.
* **Picking a radius without considering the task.** A radius too small can genuinely lose information a task depends on; the right radius is task- and data-dependent, not a universal default.
* **Confusing this with causal masking.** Windowed masking restricts by distance in both directions (unless explicitly combined with a causal mask); causal masking restricts only by direction.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. What determines whether a position can attend to another position under windowed attention?</summary>
Whether the distance between them is within the fixed window radius — nothing else about the two positions matters to the mask itself.
</details>

<details><summary>2. In the worked example, why did the savings become so much larger at n = 1000 than at n = 8?</summary>
Full attention's cost grows with the square of sequence length while windowed attention's cost grows only linearly (for a fixed radius), so the gap between the two widens dramatically as the sequence gets longer.
</details>

<details><summary>3. How can information travel further than one layer's window radius?</summary>
Across multiple stacked layers — each layer can pass information one window's width further, so depth extends the effective range beyond any single layer's radius.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Window radius:** the fixed distance within which a position may attend to its neighbours under windowed attention.
* **Local attention:** attention restricted to a neighbourhood around each position, instead of the full sequence.
* **Effective receptive field:** how far information can travel across multiple stacked layers, even when each individual layer's range is limited.

## Related

[[Attention Masks: Padding and Causal Masking]] · [[Why Attention Replaced Recurrence]] · [[Linear Attention Approximations]]

## Linear Attention Approximations

[[Sparse and Local (Windowed) Attention|Windowed attention]] cuts cost by refusing to compute most pairs at all. Linear attention takes a different route to the same destination: keep every pair's influence, but restructure the arithmetic — using a different order of matrix multiplication — so the expensive n×n score matrix never has to exist in memory in the first place.

**You need:** [[Sparse and Local (Windowed) Attention]], [[Matrix Multiplication]].

## The question it answers

"Is there a way to avoid ever computing the full n×n attention matrix, without throwing away any pairs the way windowed attention does?" Yes — if the softmax is replaced with a simpler, positive "feature map" applied to queries and keys separately, matrix multiplication's associativity lets the exact same mathematical result be computed in a completely different order: one that multiplies a `d×d` matrix instead of an `n×n` one, however long the sequence is.

## Intuition

`(A · B) · C` and `A · (B · C)` always give the same answer for matrices whose shapes allow it — that's just associativity, true regardless of what the matrices mean. Standard attention computes `(φ(Q) · φ(K)ᵀ) · V` — forming the full query-by-key score matrix first, an `n × n` object, however long the sequence is. Reorder the same three matrices to `φ(Q) · (φ(K)ᵀ · V)` instead, and the first thing computed is `φ(K)ᵀ · V` — a `d × d` matrix, whose size depends only on the model's width, never on sequence length. The `n × n` matrix is never built at all.

## Definition and notation

```text
quadratic order:  (φ(Q) · φ(K)ᵀ) · V      — forms an n × n matrix first; cost ∝ n²·d
linear order:     φ(Q) · (φ(K)ᵀ · V)      — forms a d × d matrix first; cost ∝ n·d²
```

`φ` is a positive feature map applied to queries and keys (a common choice is `elu(x) + 1`), standing in for the softmax — this substitution is the actual approximation: it changes what attention computes, trading the softmax's exact normalization for a function that makes the reordering trick valid.

## A worked example

A 5-position sequence, 3-dimensional queries, keys and values, computed both ways:

```text
quadratic order output: identical to linear order output, to the digit — e.g. first row [4.665, 4.233, 5.187]
```

Both orders produce the exact same result, confirming the reordering itself is mathematically exact — only the feature map `φ` is an approximation of softmax, not the reassociation. Comparing the actual arithmetic cost (multiply-adds) at a few scales:

```text
n = 5,     d = 3:   quadratic 150        linear 90          →   1.7× fewer
n = 1,000, d = 64:  quadratic 128,000,000  linear 8,192,000  →  15.6× fewer
n = 10,000, d = 64: quadratic 12,800,000,000  linear 81,920,000 → 156.3× fewer
```

The advantage isn't fixed — it grows with sequence length, because the quadratic order's cost scales with `n²` while the linear order's scales with just `n`.

## Bench

```bench
id: linear-attention-order
title: Same answer, two different costs
fallback: Compute the same small attention result two ways — the usual quadratic order and the linear order — confirm they match, and compare their arithmetic cost at larger scales.
```

**Try this**

1. Confirm both orders produce the same output on the same small example.
2. Increase the sequence length and watch the cost gap between the two orders widen.
3. Change the model width `d` and see how it affects the linear order's cost specifically.

**What you should notice:** the two orders are the *same computation*, not two different algorithms producing different answers — the entire benefit comes from the order of operations alone.

## Where it appears in AI

* **It is a genuinely different strategy from [[Sparse and Local (Windowed) Attention|windowed attention]]**: windowed attention throws away distant pairs entirely; linear attention keeps every pair's influence, approximated through the feature map, while changing how the computation is organized.
* **The feature map choice is itself an active area of design** — different choices trade off how closely the approximation matches true softmax attention against other practical considerations.
* **[[IO-Aware Attention Computation|the next topic]] takes yet another angle on the same underlying problem**: computing *exact* softmax attention faster, not approximating it at all.

## Common pitfalls

* **Assuming linear attention computes exactly the same thing as softmax attention.** The reassociation trick is exact; the feature map replacing softmax is not — real approximation error is introduced there, not in the reordering.
* **Expecting the linear order to help at short sequence lengths.** At small `n` relative to `d`, as the worked example's first row shows, the saving can be modest — the real advantage shows up at long sequences.
* **Forgetting causal masking complicates this trick.** The simple reordering shown here assumes no masking; making it work with causal masking (needed for decoder-only generation) requires a more careful, running-sum version of the same idea.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. What mathematical property makes the linear-order computation valid?</summary>
Associativity of matrix multiplication — (A·B)·C and A·(B·C) always give the same result when the shapes allow it, regardless of what the matrices represent.
</details>

<details><summary>2. In the worked example, what was the actual source of approximation error — the reordering, or something else?</summary>
The feature map φ replacing softmax — the reordering itself is exact, confirmed by both orders producing identical output.
</details>

<details><summary>3. Why does the cost gap between the two orders grow with sequence length?</summary>
The quadratic order's cost scales with n² while the linear order's scales with n — the ratio between the two necessarily grows as n increases.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Feature map (φ):** a function applied to queries and keys in place of softmax, chosen to make the linear-order computation valid.
* **Associativity:** the property that matrix multiplication gives the same result regardless of grouping, which the linear-order trick relies on.
* **Linear attention:** an attention computation reorganized to scale linearly, rather than quadratically, with sequence length.

## Related

[[Sparse and Local (Windowed) Attention]] · [[Matrix Multiplication]] · [[IO-Aware Attention Computation]]

## IO-Aware Attention Computation

[[Linear Attention Approximations|Linear attention]] changes what gets computed — trading exact softmax for an approximation. This topic changes nothing about what's computed at all. The exact same softmax attention, computed in a different order, without ever holding the full n×n score matrix in memory at once.

**You need:** [[Linear Attention Approximations]], [[Sparse and Local (Windowed) Attention]].

## The question it answers

"Can exact softmax attention be made faster without approximating anything?" Yes — a large part of attention's real-world cost isn't the arithmetic itself, it's moving data between slow and fast memory. FlashAttention-style computation processes attention in small tiles that fit in fast on-chip memory, using a running ("online") version of softmax that never needs the full row of scores available at once — producing the mathematically identical result to ordinary softmax attention, just computed with far less data shuffled through slow memory.

## Intuition

Ordinary softmax needs every score in a row before it can normalize any of them — compute the max, subtract it from everything, exponentiate, sum, divide. That seems to require holding the whole row at once. The **online softmax** trick shows this isn't actually true: process the row in small chunks, keeping a running maximum and a running sum, and correct the running total each time a new chunk reveals a larger maximum than seen so far. The correction factor exactly accounts for everything computed before — no information is lost, nothing is approximated, and the full row never needs to exist in memory simultaneously.

## Definition and notation

```text
process keys/values in blocks. Maintain running max m, running sum l, running weighted output acc.
for each block:
  m_new = max(m, max(block scores))
  correction = exp(m − m_new)                      — rescales everything computed so far
  l = l × correction + Σ exp(block scores − m_new)
  acc = acc × correction + Σ exp(block scores − m_new) × block values
  m = m_new
final output = acc / l
```

This is exact — not an approximation of softmax, unlike [[Linear Attention Approximations|linear attention's]] feature map. It only changes *when* each piece of the computation happens, never *what* the final answer is.

## A worked example

Eight keys and values, 3-dimensional, processed in blocks of 3 (so three blocks: sizes 3, 3, 2):

```text
naive (full-row) softmax output:   [0.564455, -0.043759, -0.412017]
online (block-by-block) output:    [0.564455, -0.043759, -0.412017]

match: exact, to the digit
```

Processing the same 8 keys and values in three separate chunks — never holding all 8 scores at once, correcting the running totals each time a new chunk arrives — produces precisely the same output as computing the full softmax in one shot.

## Bench

```bench
id: online-softmax
title: The same softmax, one block at a time
fallback: Step through computing attention in blocks using the online softmax trick, and compare the running result against the naive full-row computation at the end.
```

**Try this**

1. Step through the blocks one at a time and watch the running max and running sum update.
2. Compare the block-by-block result against the naive full-row result once all blocks are processed.
3. Change the block size and confirm the final result doesn't change, only how many update steps it took.

**What you should notice:** the running correction factor exactly undoes any bias from an outdated running maximum — the math guarantees the final answer never depends on how the row happened to be chopped into blocks.

## Where it appears in AI

* **It is the core idea behind FlashAttention and similar exact, memory-efficient attention implementations**, widely used in practice because they compute identical results to standard attention while running meaningfully faster on real hardware.
* **It complements rather than replaces the other efficiency topics on this planet**: nothing stops combining IO-aware computation with [[Sparse and Local (Windowed) Attention|windowed]] or [[Multi-Query and Grouped-Query Attention|grouped-query]] attention — they address different costs (compute pattern, memory bandwidth, and cache size respectively).
* **The online-softmax trick itself is useful anywhere a softmax needs to be computed over data too large to hold at once** — not specific to attention at all.

## Common pitfalls

* **Confusing this with an approximation technique.** Unlike linear attention, nothing about the final numerical result changes — this is purely about the order and locality of computation.
* **Assuming block size affects correctness.** It doesn't — the worked example's match confirms the result is identical regardless of how the row is chunked; block size affects only performance, not the answer.
* **Assuming this removes the need for other efficiency techniques.** It specifically targets memory-movement cost, not the fact that attention still compares every allowed pair — windowed or linear attention address that different cost.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. What, if anything, does IO-aware attention computation approximate?</summary>
Nothing — it computes the exact same softmax attention result as the naive approach, just reorganized to avoid holding the full score row in memory at once.
</details>

<details><summary>2. What role does the "correction factor" play in the online softmax algorithm?</summary>
It rescales everything accumulated from earlier blocks whenever a new block reveals a larger maximum score, keeping the running total mathematically consistent with what a single, full-row computation would have produced.
</details>

<details><summary>3. How does IO-aware computation relate to windowed and linear attention?</summary>
It addresses a different cost (memory movement, not compute pattern) and can be combined with either of the other two rather than replacing them.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Online (running) softmax:** computing softmax incrementally over blocks, using a running maximum and sum, instead of requiring the full row at once.
* **IO-aware:** designed around minimizing data movement between slow and fast memory, not just minimizing arithmetic operations.
* **Correction factor:** the rescaling term that keeps a running softmax computation consistent as new blocks of data arrive.

## Related

[[Linear Attention Approximations]] · [[Sparse and Local (Windowed) Attention]] · [[Multi-Query and Grouped-Query Attention]]

## Scaling the Block

Making a transformer bigger raises three separate questions: whether every parameter has to run on every input, how big "bigger" actually is in concrete numbers, and how a single block's computation gets spread across hardware that no longer fits it on one device. This district answers each in turn.

Topics on this stretch of the road:

* [[Mixture-of-Experts Transformer Blocks]]: routing each token to a handful of specialist feed-forward sublayers instead of running all of them.
* [[Counting a Transformer's Parameters and FLOPs]]: working out exactly how big and how expensive one block is.
* [[Splitting a Transformer Across Devices]]: dividing a single block's own weight matrices and sequence dimension across hardware.

## Mixture-of-Experts Transformer Blocks

[[The Feed-Forward Sublayer|The feed-forward sublayer]] runs the same, single network on every position. A mixture-of-experts (MoE) transformer block replaces that one network with several parallel "expert" networks and a small router that decides, per token, which handful of experts actually get to run.

**You need:** [[The Feed-Forward Sublayer]], [[Mixture of Experts]].

## The question it answers

"Can a transformer block have far more total parameters without every token paying the full compute cost of all of them?" Yes — swap the single feed-forward sublayer for several parallel copies (experts) of the same shape, add a small **router** that scores every expert for a given token and selects only the top few, and run *only* those selected experts for that token. Total capacity scales with the number of experts; the actual compute any one token pays for stays small and fixed.

## Intuition

Imagine a large team of specialists instead of one generalist handling every request. A small dispatcher (the router) looks at each incoming request and sends it to just the two or three specialists best suited to it — not the entire team. Most of the team's combined expertise exists and keeps growing as more specialists are added, but any single request still only ever gets handled by a small, fixed number of them. This is exactly how [[Mixture of Experts|the generic mixture-of-experts idea]] from [[Deep Learning]] gets applied specifically inside a transformer block: it replaces the feed-forward sublayer, nothing else in the block changes.

## Definition and notation

```text
router(x) = softmax(W_router · x)              — a probability per expert
top-k selection: run only the k experts with the highest router probability

block output = Σ (over the k selected experts) router_prob_i × expert_i(x)
```

Everywhere else — attention, residual connections, normalization — stays exactly as described earlier in [[The Transformer Block]]; only the feed-forward sublayer is replaced by this routed structure.

## A worked example

Eight experts (each a small feed-forward sublayer with 76 parameters, as in [[The Feed-Forward Sublayer|the earlier worked example]]), routing a single token `x = [0.5, -0.3, 0.8, 0.1]` with top-2 selection:

```text
router probabilities: [0.166, 0.206, 0.120, 0.091, 0.131, 0.086, 0.086, 0.114]
top-2 selected: expert 1 (p=0.206), expert 0 (p=0.166)

total parameters (all 8 experts):      8 × 76 = 608
active parameters for this token:      2 × 76 = 152   (25.0% of the total)
```

The block holds `608` feed-forward parameters in total — far more than a single plain feed-forward sublayer of the same size — but this particular token's forward pass only actually runs `152` of them, a quarter of the full capacity.

## Bench

```bench
id: moe-router
title: A router choosing which experts run
fallback: Route a chosen input through a mixture of experts, see which ones the router selects, and compare the active parameter count against the full total.
```

**Try this**

1. Change the input vector and watch which experts the router selects change.
2. Increase the number of experts selected (top-k) and watch the active-parameter percentage grow.
3. Increase the total number of experts while keeping top-k fixed, and watch the active percentage shrink.

**What you should notice:** the total parameter count and the active (per-token) parameter count move independently — adding more experts grows total capacity without growing the compute any single token actually pays for, as long as top-k stays fixed.

## Where it appears in AI

* **It is how several very large modern models scale total parameter count far beyond what running every parameter on every token would allow** — Mixtral and Switch Transformer are well-known examples of MoE applied specifically to the feed-forward sublayer.
* **[[Counting a Transformer's Parameters and FLOPs|the next topic]] has to count MoE blocks differently from plain ones** — total parameters and active (compute-relevant) parameters genuinely diverge here, unlike every other block structure covered so far.
* **The routing decision is itself trained**, alongside the experts' own weights — which experts specialize in what is learned, not hand-assigned.

## Common pitfalls

* **Confusing total parameters with compute cost.** A model built from many experts can have an enormous total parameter count while running cheaply per token — the two numbers are genuinely different things for an MoE block.
* **Assuming every expert gets equal use.** Router behaviour is learned and can become imbalanced, with some experts selected far more often than others — a real training challenge MoE models have to manage.
* **Forgetting the router itself adds a (small) extra cost.** It's a small additional computation on top of whichever experts are actually selected.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. What does the router in a mixture-of-experts block decide?</summary>
Which small number (top-k) of expert feed-forward sublayers actually process a given token, out of the full set of available experts.
</details>

<details><summary>2. In the worked example, why was only 25% of the total feed-forward parameters active for the given token?</summary>
Only 2 of the 8 experts (top-2 out of 8) were selected by the router, and 2/8 = 25% of the total parameter count.
</details>

<details><summary>3. What stays unchanged in a transformer block when its feed-forward sublayer is replaced with a mixture of experts?</summary>
Everything else — the attention sublayer, residual connections, and normalization all work exactly as in a plain transformer block; only the feed-forward sublayer's internal structure changes.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Router:** a small learned network that scores each expert for a given input and selects the top few.
* **Expert:** one of several parallel feed-forward sublayers in a mixture-of-experts block.
* **Active parameters:** the subset of a model's total parameters actually used to process a given input — can be far smaller than the total in an MoE model.

## Related

[[The Feed-Forward Sublayer]] · [[Mixture of Experts]] · [[Counting a Transformer's Parameters and FLOPs]]

## Counting a Transformer's Parameters and FLOPs

Every number quoted for a transformer's size — "110 million parameters," "175 billion parameters" — comes from literally adding up the matrices covered earlier on this planet. This topic does that addition explicitly, and checks the result against a real, published model.

**You need:** [[Assembling One Transformer Block]], [[Weight Tying]], [[The Feed-Forward Sublayer]].

## The question it answers

"Where does a transformer's parameter count actually come from, and can it be computed by hand from first principles?" Yes — almost entirely from two things repeated at every layer: the four attention projection matrices (query, key, value, output) and the two feed-forward matrices, plus one embedding table shared (if tied) between input and output. Everything else — normalization scale and shift parameters, biases — is small enough to be a rounding error at any realistic model size.

## Intuition

A transformer's size is mostly just "how many of these matrices, how big." Each layer repeats the identical structure: four `d_model × d_model` attention matrices, two feed-forward matrices sized by `d_model` and `d_ff`. Multiply by the number of layers, add one embedding table, and that single sum accounts for the overwhelming majority of a transformer's parameters — there's no hidden complexity, just arithmetic applied consistently at every layer.

## Definition and notation

```text
per-layer attention parameters: 4 × d_model²                     (Wq, Wk, Wv, Wo)
per-layer feed-forward parameters: 2 × d_model × d_ff
per-layer total: 4·d_model² + 2·d_model·d_ff

with the common convention d_ff = 4·d_model:
  per-layer total = 4·d_model² + 8·d_model² = 12·d_model²

total (non-embedding) parameters ≈ 12 × num_layers × d_model²
plus one embedding table (tied): vocabulary_size × d_model
```

## A worked example

BERT-base's published configuration: `d_model = 768`, `num_layers = 12`, `d_ff = 3072` (exactly `4 × 768`), vocabulary `30,522`:

```text
attention params per layer:  4 × 768² = 2,359,296
feed-forward params per layer: 2 × 768 × 3072 = 4,718,592
total per layer: 7,077,888  — exactly matching 12 × 768² = 7,077,888

total across 12 layers: 7,077,888 × 12 = 84,934,656
embedding table (tied, from Weight Tying): 30,522 × 768 = 23,440,896

grand total: 84,934,656 + 23,440,896 = 108,375,552 ≈ 108.4 million
```

This lands within a few percent of BERT-base's commonly cited **~110 million parameters** — the small remaining gap is normalization scale/shift parameters and biases, each tiny compared to the matrices counted here.

## Bench

```bench
id: param-counter
title: Add up the matrices, layer by layer
fallback: Set a model's width, depth, feed-forward size and vocabulary, and see its total parameter count build up from the attention and feed-forward matrices at each layer.
```

**Try this**

1. Match the worked example's configuration and confirm the total lands near 108 million.
2. Change `d_ff` away from `4 × d_model` and watch the convenient `12·d_model²` shortcut stop applying.
2. Scale up `d_model` and `num_layers` together and watch the total grow much faster than either alone.

**What you should notice:** the total is overwhelmingly dominated by the `num_layers × d_model²` term — doubling the width roughly quadruples the per-layer cost, while doubling the depth only doubles it, a genuinely different kind of scaling.

## Where it appears in AI

* **It is the basis for every "model size" number quoted about a transformer** — not a separate measurement, but this exact arithmetic applied to that model's specific configuration.
* **[[Mixture-of-Experts Transformer Blocks|MoE blocks]] break the simple relationship between total and active parameters** covered here — the formula above still applies to counting *total* capacity, but a separate, smaller count is needed for compute actually spent per token.
* **A rough FLOPs-per-token estimate follows directly from the parameter count**: roughly `2 × parameters` floating-point operations per token for a forward pass, a widely-used approximation in scaling-law analysis.

## Common pitfalls

* **Forgetting the `12·d_model²` shortcut only holds when `d_ff = 4·d_model`.** It's an extremely common convention, but not a law — a different `d_ff` ratio needs the full `4·d_model² + 2·d_model·d_ff` formula.
* **Double-counting the embedding table.** With weight tying (see [[Weight Tying]]), it's one matrix, not two — counting it twice overstates the total noticeably at smaller model sizes.
* **Assuming parameter count alone determines compute cost.** It's closely related but not identical — see [[Mixture-of-Experts Transformer Blocks]] for a case where they genuinely diverge.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. What two matrix groups, repeated at every layer, account for almost all of a transformer's parameters?</summary>
The four attention projection matrices (query, key, value, output) and the two feed-forward matrices.
</details>

<details><summary>2. In the worked example, why did 12 × d_model² exactly match the sum of the attention and feed-forward terms?</summary>
Because d_ff was exactly 4 × d_model (3072 = 4 × 768), the common convention under which 4·d_model² (attention) + 8·d_model² (feed-forward, since 2 × d_model × 4·d_model = 8·d_model²) simplifies to 12·d_model².
</details>

<details><summary>3. What accounts for the small gap between the worked example's 108.4 million and BERT-base's commonly cited ~110 million?</summary>
Normalization scale/shift parameters and biases, which this worked example's formula omits since they are small compared to the matrices it counts.
</details>

## Key terms

* **d_ff:** the feed-forward sublayer's hidden width, conventionally 4 times d_model.
* **Non-embedding parameters:** a model's parameters excluding the embedding table, often reported separately in scaling-law analysis.
* **FLOPs (floating-point operations):** a measure of computational work, roughly proportional to parameter count for one forward pass through a token.

## Related

[[Assembling One Transformer Block]] · [[Weight Tying]] · [[Mixture-of-Experts Transformer Blocks]] · [[Splitting a Transformer Across Devices]]

## Splitting a Transformer Across Devices

[[Counting a Transformer's Parameters and FLOPs|A large transformer's matrices]] can be far too big to fit on one device at all. Tensor parallelism splits a *single* weight matrix across several devices, so no one device ever needs to hold the whole thing — a genuinely different problem from the data-parallel training covered on [[Deep Learning]], which copies the *entire* model onto every device instead.

**You need:** [[Counting a Transformer's Parameters and FLOPs]], [[Distributed and Data-Parallel Training]].

## The question it answers

"When even one transformer block's weight matrices are too large for a single device's memory, how is the computation itself split up?" Tensor parallelism splits the matrices directly: part of each weight matrix lives on each device, each device computes its own partial result from the piece it holds, and the partial results are combined — summed, in the standard pattern — to reconstruct the exact same answer a single device would have produced.

## Intuition

[[Distributed and Data-Parallel Training|Data parallelism]] puts a full copy of the model on every device and splits the *data* across them. Tensor parallelism does the opposite: every device sees the same input, but only holds a *slice* of the model's own weights. For the feed-forward sublayer specifically, the standard split is: cut the first matrix's output dimension into chunks (each device computes a different slice of the hidden layer), then cut the second matrix's input dimension to match (each device computes a partial contribution to the final output), and sum the partial outputs together — a single communication step, instead of needing every device to hold the whole matrix.

## Definition and notation

```text
split d_ff across D devices, chunk size = d_ff / D

device d computes:
  hidden_d = activation(W1_d · x)            — W1_d: a chunk of W1's rows
  partial_d = W2_d · hidden_d                — W2_d: the matching chunk of W2's columns

combine (all-reduce, i.e. sum):
  output = Σ_d partial_d
```

Each device only ever stores `1/D` of `W1` and `1/D` of `W2` — the full matrices never need to exist on any single device at once.

## A worked example

A feed-forward sublayer (`d_model = 4`, `d_ff = 8`, 64 total weights) split across 2 devices, on input `x = [0.5, -0.3, 0.8, 0.1]`:

```text
single-device output:        [0.29676, 0.03862, -0.00036, -0.07130]
2-device (tensor-parallel) output:  [0.29676, 0.03862, -0.00036, -0.07130]

match: exact

device A's weight parameters: 32 (half of 64)
device B's weight parameters: 32 (half of 64)
```

Splitting the computation across two devices produces an output identical to the single-device computation — and each device only ever needs to store exactly half the weights, confirming neither device needed the full matrices to participate.

## Bench

```bench
id: tensor-parallel-ffn
title: Split the matrix, sum the results
fallback: Split a feed-forward sublayer's weights across a chosen number of devices and confirm the combined output matches the single-device result, while each device's memory footprint shrinks accordingly.
```

**Try this**

1. Confirm the split-and-summed output matches the single-device result exactly.
2. Increase the number of devices and watch each device's share of the weights shrink proportionally.
3. Consider what has to be communicated between devices (and when) for this scheme to work.

**What you should notice:** the result is identical regardless of how many devices the computation is split across — tensor parallelism changes where the computation happens, never what it computes.

## Where it appears in AI

* **It's what makes training and running models far larger than any single device's memory possible at all** — a genuinely different scaling axis from [[Distributed and Data-Parallel Training|data parallelism]], and the two are routinely combined in practice.
* **The same splitting idea applies to the attention sublayer's matrices too** (not just the feed-forward sublayer shown here), typically splitting across attention heads so each device handles a subset of heads end to end.
* **[[Mixture-of-Experts Transformer Blocks|MoE blocks]] add a natural, related option**: placing different experts on different devices, since each token only ever needs a few of them at once.

## Common pitfalls

* **Assuming tensor parallelism and data parallelism solve the same problem.** Data parallelism needs every device to hold the *whole* model; tensor parallelism exists specifically because the whole model doesn't fit on one device at all.
* **Forgetting the combination step requires communication.** The sum across devices (an all-reduce) is a real, non-free step — splitting a matrix doesn't eliminate the need for devices to exchange their partial results.
* **Splitting a matrix the wrong way.** The worked example's column-then-row pattern is specifically chosen so only one communication step (summing the final outputs) is needed — a careless split can require far more cross-device communication.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. What is split across devices in tensor parallelism, as opposed to data parallelism?</summary>
The model's own weight matrices are split, with every device seeing the same input; data parallelism instead copies the whole model and splits the input data across devices.
</details>

<details><summary>2. In the worked example, how was the single-device output exactly reproduced by two devices?</summary>
By splitting the first matrix's rows (output dimension) and the second matrix's matching columns across the two devices, then summing their two partial outputs together.
</details>

<details><summary>3. What real cost does splitting a matrix across devices introduce that a single device never pays?</summary>
Communication — the partial results computed on each device have to be combined (summed, in this pattern), which requires devices to exchange data.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Tensor parallelism:** splitting a single weight matrix's rows or columns across multiple devices.
* **All-reduce:** combining (here, summing) partial results computed on different devices into one final result.
* **Chunk:** the portion of a split weight matrix stored and computed on one device.

## Related

[[Counting a Transformer's Parameters and FLOPs]] · [[Distributed and Data-Parallel Training]] · [[Mixture-of-Experts Transformer Blocks]]

## Transformers Beyond Text

Nothing about the transformer block is specific to language — it only needs a sequence of vectors to attend over. This district covers what counts as a "sequence" once that assumption is taken seriously.

Topics on this stretch of the road:

* [[Vision Transformers]]: treating an image's patches as tokens.
* [[Graph Transformers]]: applying full attention to a graph's nodes, instead of only passing messages between neighbours.
* [[Multimodal Transformers as an Architecture Pattern]]: combining tokens from more than one modality in a single sequence.

## Vision Transformers

[[Tokenizing Beyond Text|Patches became a token sequence]] several districts ago. This topic finishes the job: linearly project each patch into the model's width, prepend a special summary token, add positional information, and run the exact same transformer block machinery already built for text.

**You need:** [[Tokenizing Beyond Text]], [[Learned Positional Embeddings]], [[Assembling One Transformer Block]].

## The question it answers

"Once an image is a sequence of flattened patches, what turns that sequence into something a transformer can actually classify?" A Vision Transformer (ViT) does exactly what a text transformer does with token ids: project each patch into a `d_model`-wide vector (the patch's "embedding"), add positional information so the model knows where each patch sat in the image, and run the whole sequence through ordinary transformer blocks — no convolutions, no image-specific machinery anywhere in the stack.

## Intuition

A patch, once flattened, is just a long list of numbers — not yet in the shape the rest of the transformer expects. A single learned linear layer fixes that, the same role [[Token Embeddings and Embedding Scaling|a token embedding table]] plays for words, just computed by a projection instead of a lookup (since there's no fixed "vocabulary" of patches). One more addition makes classification possible: prepend a special, learned **`[CLS]` token** to the sequence, with no patch of its own — after attention lets it gather information from every patch, its final vector is used as the whole image's summary representation.

## Definition and notation

```text
1. patches = patchify(image, P)                          — from Tokenizing Beyond Text
2. patch_embeddings = W_proj · patch, for each patch       — a learned linear projection
3. sequence = [CLS_token, patch_embedding₁, …, patch_embeddingₙ]
4. sequence += positional_embeddings                       — one per position, CLS included
5. run the sequence through ordinary transformer blocks
6. classification uses the final layer's CLS token output only
```

Everything from step 5 onward is identical to a text transformer — the only genuinely image-specific parts are patchifying and the linear patch projection.

## A worked example

An 8×8 image, patchified into four 4×4 patches (16 numbers each, as in [[Tokenizing Beyond Text]]), projected into a 4-dimensional model width:

```text
4 patches, each projected to 4 dimensions:
  patch 1: [-0.261, 0.047, -0.077, -0.221]
  patch 2: [-0.316, 0.083, -0.143, -0.261]
  patch 3: [-0.700, 0.330, -0.605, -0.544]
  patch 4: [-0.755, 0.365, -0.671, -0.585]

sequence with a prepended CLS token: 5 positions total

after adding positional embeddings and running one self-attention sublayer,
the CLS token's output (the eventual classification signal):
  [-0.554, 0.254, 0.040, -0.178]
```

The CLS token started with no patch information of its own — its final vector is entirely built from attending to the four patch tokens, exactly the mechanism that lets it summarize the whole image for classification.

## Bench

```bench
id: vit-pipeline
title: From patches to a classification token
fallback: Patchify a small image, project the patches, prepend a CLS token, and watch its vector change as it attends over the patch sequence.
```

**Try this**

1. Change the image and watch the patch embeddings change accordingly.
2. Compare the CLS token's vector before and after the attention step.
3. Increase the patch count (smaller patch size) and see the sequence length grow.

**What you should notice:** nothing about steps 5–6 cares whether the sequence came from patches or from word tokens — the exact same attention, residual, and feed-forward machinery applies either way.

## Where it appears in AI

* **It is the standard architecture for applying transformers to image classification**, and the clearest demonstration that nothing about the transformer block itself is specific to language.
* **It directly reuses [[Assembling One Transformer Block|the full block]] built earlier on this planet** — a genuine example of the same machinery generalizing to a new modality with minimal new parts.
* **[[Multimodal Transformers as an Architecture Pattern|the next topic]] builds on exactly this**: once image patches are vectors in a sequence, nothing stops combining them with text tokens in a single sequence.

## Common pitfalls

* **Assuming a Vision Transformer needs any convolutional layers.** It doesn't — patchifying and a linear projection are the only departures from an ordinary text transformer's input pipeline.
* **Forgetting the CLS token has to be learned too.** It's an additional trainable parameter, not a fixed or hand-computed value — a parameter like any other embedding.
* **Expecting classification to use every patch token's final output.** Only the CLS token's final vector is typically used for the classification decision, even though every patch token still participates in attention throughout the stack.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. What two steps are specific to images, and what's identical to a text transformer from there on?</summary>
Patchifying the image and linearly projecting each patch are image-specific; prepending a CLS token, adding positional embeddings, and running the transformer blocks are identical to a text transformer.
</details>

<details><summary>2. What does the CLS token's final-layer output represent, and how does it get there?</summary>
A summary of the whole image, built entirely through attention over the patch tokens — the CLS token starts with no patch information of its own.
</details>

<details><summary>3. Why doesn't the patch-projection step use a lookup table the way token embeddings do?</summary>
There's no fixed vocabulary of patches to look up — each patch is a unique vector of raw pixel values, so a learned linear projection, not a lookup, is used instead.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Patch embedding:** a learned linear projection turning a flattened image patch into a model-width vector.
* **[CLS] token:** a special, learned token prepended to a sequence, whose final output summarizes the whole input for classification.
* **Vision Transformer (ViT):** a transformer applied to image patches, using no convolutional layers.

## Related

[[Tokenizing Beyond Text]] · [[Learned Positional Embeddings]] · [[Assembling One Transformer Block]] · [[Multimodal Transformers as an Architecture Pattern]]

## Graph Transformers

[[Graph Neural Networks|A graph neural network]] restricts every node to messages from its direct neighbours, layer after layer. A graph transformer removes that restriction entirely — every node attends to every other node, exactly like a text transformer — and puts the graph's actual structure back in through a bias on the attention scores instead of through the mask.

**You need:** [[Graph Neural Networks]], [[ALiBi and Length Extrapolation]].

## The question it answers

"If a transformer can attend across an entire sequence, why not apply the same thing to a graph's nodes, instead of restricting attention to direct neighbours?" A graph transformer does exactly that: full, unrestricted attention among every node, with no adjacency mask at all. But a graph's structure still has to influence the result somehow, or the model would be blind to the topology entirely — the standard fix borrows [[ALiBi and Length Extrapolation|ALiBi's]] trick, adding a bias to each attention score based on the shortest-path distance between two nodes in the graph, instead of position distance in a sequence.

## Intuition

A message-passing GNN is structurally conservative: information only ever reaches a node from its immediate neighbours, and reaching a distant node takes as many layers as the shortest path between them. A graph transformer takes the opposite stance: let any node attend to any other node directly, in a single layer — but bias that attention so nearby nodes (by graph distance) are naturally favoured over distant ones, the same way ALiBi biases sequence attention by sequence distance. The structure isn't enforced through a hard mask anymore; it's a soft nudge built into the score itself.

## Definition and notation

```text
GNN-style (message passing): allowed(i, j) = adjacency(i, j)     — hard restriction to direct neighbours
graph transformer:            allowed(i, j) = true, for all i, j  — full attention
                               bias(i, j) = −slope × shortest_path_distance(i, j)
```

The shortest-path distance is computed once from the graph's actual edges (via breadth-first search), the same role sequence position plays for ALiBi — except here, "distance" means hops along the graph, not position in a line.

## A worked example

A 5-node cycle graph (edges `0-1, 1-2, 2-3, 3-4, 0-4`), compared two ways:

```text
GNN-style adjacency mask (self + direct neighbours only):
  node 0: [1,1,0,0,1]   — sees nodes 0, 1, 4
  node 2: [0,1,1,1,0]   — sees nodes 1, 2, 3

shortest-path distances (all pairs):
       0  1  2  3  4
  0 [  0  1  2  2  1 ]
  2 [  2  1  0  1  2 ]

graph transformer bias (slope 0.5, −0.5 × distance), full attention:
  node 0 → node 1 (distance 1): bias −0.50
  node 0 → node 2 (distance 2): bias −1.00
```

Node 0's attention is never *blocked* from node 2, the way the GNN-style mask would block it — but the bias still pushes the attention weight toward closer nodes, with the exact amount of push determined by actual graph distance.

## Bench

```bench
id: graph-transformer-bias
title: Full attention, with the graph's shape as a bias
fallback: Compare a GNN-style adjacency mask against a graph transformer's full attention with a distance-based bias, on a small graph.
```

**Try this**

1. Compare which nodes a given node can see under GNN-style masking versus graph-transformer attention.
2. Change the bias slope and watch how strongly distant nodes get penalized without ever being fully blocked.
3. Try a different graph shape and see how the shortest-path distances, and so the bias pattern, change.

**What you should notice:** a graph transformer can still, in principle, let information flow between any two nodes in a single layer — something a message-passing GNN genuinely cannot do, however many layers it stacks, without literally adding the edges.

## Where it appears in AI

* **It is a genuinely different architecture family from [[Graph Neural Networks]]**, not a variant — full attention with a structural bias, rather than restricted message passing.
* **It directly reuses the bias-based trick from [[ALiBi and Length Extrapolation]]**, just computed from graph distance instead of sequence position — a concrete example of an idea from one modality transferring cleanly to another.
* **It trades [[Graph Neural Networks|GNN's]] cheaper, locally-restricted computation for full-attention's quadratic cost** (in the number of nodes) — a genuine trade-off, not a strict improvement.

## Common pitfalls

* **Assuming a graph transformer ignores the graph's structure.** It doesn't restrict attention, but the distance-based bias still makes the structure matter — a far cry from treating the graph as an unordered set of nodes.
* **Forgetting full attention over nodes is quadratic in the number of nodes.** For very large graphs, this cost can make graph transformers less practical than a sparser message-passing GNN.
* **Confusing graph distance with any notion of sequence position.** There's no inherent ordering to a graph's nodes — distance here specifically means shortest-path hops along actual edges.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. What's the key structural difference between a GNN and a graph transformer?</summary>
A GNN restricts each node to messages from its direct neighbours (hard masking by adjacency); a graph transformer allows full attention among all nodes, injecting structure through a bias instead.
</details>

<details><summary>2. In the worked example, why was node 0's attention to node 2 not blocked, unlike under the GNN-style mask?</summary>
A graph transformer applies no adjacency mask at all — every node can attend to every other node; the graph distance only biases the attention score, it never fully blocks a pair.
</details>

<details><summary>3. What can a graph transformer do in a single layer that a message-passing GNN fundamentally cannot?</summary>
Let any two nodes directly influence each other's attention, regardless of distance — a GNN needs as many layers as the shortest path between two nodes for information to travel that far.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Shortest-path distance:** the minimum number of edges connecting two nodes in a graph, computed via breadth-first search.
* **Structural bias:** an attention-score adjustment based on graph structure, used in place of a hard adjacency mask.
* **Message passing:** a GNN's mechanism for propagating information only between directly connected nodes.

## Related

[[Graph Neural Networks]] · [[ALiBi and Length Extrapolation]] · [[Multimodal Transformers as an Architecture Pattern]]

## Multimodal Transformers as an Architecture Pattern

[[Vision Transformers|Image patches]] and text tokens both end up as the exact same thing by the time attention sees them: a vector of width `d_model`. Once that's true, nothing stops putting both kinds of vectors in the *same* sequence and letting one attention computation mix freely across both.

**You need:** [[Vision Transformers]], [[Token Embeddings and Embedding Scaling]].

## The question it answers

"How does a transformer combine information from genuinely different kinds of input — text and images — in a single model?" By making every modality produce vectors of the same width, however each one gets there: a text token through the embedding-table lookup from [[Token Embeddings and Embedding Scaling]], an image patch through the linear projection from [[Vision Transformers]]. Concatenate both sets of vectors into one sequence, and ordinary self-attention does the rest — every position, text or image, can attend to every other position, with no architectural distinction between the two once they're in the sequence.

## Intuition

Attention doesn't actually know or care where a vector in its input sequence came from — it just computes queries, keys and values from whatever vectors it's handed and compares them. That's exactly what makes multimodal transformers possible with so little new machinery: get text and images into the same vector width through their own, separate front-ends, lay them out one after another as a single longer sequence, and the self-attention mechanism built for one modality turns out to require no changes at all to mix information across two.

## Definition and notation

```text
text_embeddings  = [embedding_table[id] for id in text_token_ids]       — d_model-wide
patch_embeddings = [W_proj · patch for patch in image_patches]          — d_model-wide

combined_sequence = text_embeddings ++ patch_embeddings
run the combined sequence through ordinary transformer blocks
```

Each modality keeps its own front-end (an embedding table for text, a linear projection for patches) — only the output width has to match for the sequences to be concatenated and processed together.

## A worked example

A combined sequence of 2 text tokens and 2 image patches, all projected to `d_model = 4`, run through one self-attention sublayer:

```text
combined sequence: [text₀, text₁, patch₀, patch₁]   (4 positions total)

text position 0's attention weights over all four positions:
  [0.2027, 0.2683, 0.2706, 0.2584]    (sums to 1.0000)

attention spent on the two image patches alone: 0.2706 + 0.2584 = 0.5290
```

A text token's attention spreads across *both* the other text token and both image patches, in a single computation — more than half its attention mass (52.9%) went to the image patches here, with no special mechanism needed to let that happen; it's the same self-attention formula used throughout this entire planet.

## Bench

```bench
id: multimodal-attention
title: One sequence, two modalities
fallback: Combine a few text tokens and image patches into one sequence and see how attention spreads across both modalities at once.
```

**Try this**

1. Compare how much of a text position's attention goes to text versus image positions.
2. Change the number of text tokens or image patches and watch the attention distribution shift.
3. Consider what would need to change if text and image embeddings had different widths.

**What you should notice:** the attention computation itself has no notion of "modality" at all — it only sees a sequence of same-width vectors, and whatever structure the sequence has (which vectors came from text, which from images) is entirely a property of how the sequence was built, not of attention itself.

## Where it appears in AI

* **It is the standard pattern behind models that jointly process text and images**, extending cleanly to audio, video, or any other modality with its own front-end producing `d_model`-wide vectors.
* **It requires no new attention mechanism at all** — every efficiency and architecture topic covered earlier on this planet (masking, positional schemes, KV-caching) applies to a multimodal sequence exactly as it would to a single-modality one.
* **It closes the loop this planet opened in [[Tokenizing Beyond Text]]**: once anything can become a token sequence, combining several different anythings into one sequence is a natural, almost free extension.

## Common pitfalls

* **Assuming multimodal transformers need a fundamentally different attention mechanism.** They don't — the entire trick is getting every modality into the same vector width before attention ever runs.
* **Forgetting positional information needs care across modalities.** A position in the text portion and a position in the image portion aren't comparable the same way two text positions are — real multimodal models often use modality-aware positional schemes.
* **Expecting equal attention split across modalities by default.** Nothing enforces a particular split — how much a position attends to each modality is entirely learned, as the worked example's roughly-even-but-not-exact split shows.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. What has to be true of text and image embeddings before they can be combined into one sequence?</summary>
They have to be the same width (d_model) — each modality can use its own front-end to get there, but the output dimension has to match for concatenation to make sense.
</details>

<details><summary>2. In the worked example, what fraction of the text token's attention went to the image patches, and what does that demonstrate?</summary>
About 53% — demonstrating that a single attention computation genuinely mixes information across modalities, with no special cross-modal mechanism required beyond ordinary self-attention.
</details>

<details><summary>3. What, if anything, does the attention computation itself need to know about which positions are text and which are images?</summary>
Nothing — attention only operates on vectors and has no built-in notion of modality; any distinction between modalities exists only in how the sequence and its positional information were constructed.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Modality:** a type of input data (text, image, audio) with its own front-end producing vectors of a shared width.
* **Combined sequence:** a single sequence built by concatenating vectors from more than one modality.
* **Cross-modal attention:** attention weights spreading across positions from different modalities within one computation.

## Related

[[Vision Transformers]] · [[Token Embeddings and Embedding Scaling]] · [[Tokenizing Beyond Text]]

## Transformers in Practice

The last stretch of the road is about running a trained transformer well, and a capstone that walks the whole planet in one place.

Topics on this stretch of the road:

* [[Inference Serving Trade-offs]]: batching, latency and throughput when serving a transformer to real traffic.
* [[Capstone: Assembling a Tiny Transformer from the Ground Up]]: one small project, tracing every piece this planet covered through a single forward pass.

## Inference Serving Trade-offs

Everything so far on this planet has been about making a single forward pass efficient. Serving a transformer to real traffic adds a different question entirely: many requests arrive at once, and how they're grouped together changes both how much total work the hardware gets through and how long any individual request actually waits.

**You need:** [[KV-Caching for Autoregressive Inference]], [[Multi-Query and Grouped-Query Attention]].

## The question it answers

"Should requests be processed one at a time, or grouped together, when serving a transformer to many users at once?" Grouping them — **batching** — turns out to be dramatically more efficient, for a specific hardware reason: processing one request barely uses a modern accelerator's parallel compute capacity, so most of the cost of running a batch is fixed overhead, nearly independent of how many requests ride along in it. The trade-off is latency: a request in a larger batch may have to wait for that batch to be assembled before processing even starts.

## Intuition

Imagine a delivery van that costs the same to send out whether it carries one package or thirty — most of the cost is the trip itself, not the cargo. Sending one package at a time means paying for a trip per package; waiting to fill the van with thirty packages means thirty deliveries share one trip's cost, at the price of the first package having to wait for the van to fill up. Batching a transformer's inference requests is the same trade: processing time per *batch* barely grows with batch size (a GPU has spare parallel capacity at small batch sizes), so grouping requests multiplies throughput — but anyone whose request has to wait for the batch to fill pays in added latency.

## Definition and notation

```text
batch processing time ≈ T_fixed + T_marginal × batch_size
  T_fixed:    overhead paid once per batch, largely independent of its size
  T_marginal: small additional time per request added to the batch

throughput (requests/second) = batch_size / batch_processing_time
```

Because `T_fixed` dominates at small batch sizes, throughput grows much faster than processing time as batch size increases — the central reason batching is worth doing at all.

## A worked example

With `T_fixed = 10 ms` and `T_marginal = 0.5 ms` per request, comparing three batch sizes:

```text
batch size  1:  processing time 10.5 ms   →   95.2 requests/second
batch size  8:  processing time 14.0 ms   →  571.4 requests/second
batch size 32:  processing time 26.0 ms   → 1230.8 requests/second
```

Going from batch size 1 to 32 increased processing time by only 2.5× (10.5ms → 26ms) but increased throughput by nearly 13× (95.2 → 1230.8 requests/second) — the fixed overhead that dominates a batch of 1 becomes almost negligible once spread across 32 requests.

## Bench

```bench
id: batching-tradeoff
title: Throughput and the cost of waiting for a full batch
fallback: Set a batch size and see processing time and throughput change, alongside the latency cost of waiting for that batch to fill before processing starts.
```

**Try this**

1. Increase batch size and compare how much throughput grows versus how much processing time grows.
2. Consider a request that arrives just after a batch starts filling — how long might it wait before the next batch begins?
3. Change `T_fixed` relative to `T_marginal` and see how much that shifts the throughput benefit of larger batches.

**What you should notice:** the throughput gain from batching has a real latency cost attached — not in the processing time itself, which grows slowly, but in how long an individual request may sit waiting for its batch to be assembled in the first place.

## Where it appears in AI

* **Every production transformer-serving system has to make this trade-off explicitly**, usually by capping batch size or the maximum wait time before processing a partially-filled batch, rather than choosing one extreme.
* **[[Multi-Query and Grouped-Query Attention|KV-cache size]] directly limits how large a batch can grow**: each request in a batch needs its own growing cache, so memory — not just compute — caps batch size in practice.
* **[[Capstone: Assembling a Tiny Transformer from the Ground Up|the planet's capstone]] closes by tracing a single request through the whole pipeline this planet has built**, end to end.

## Common pitfalls

* **Assuming bigger batches are always better.** Past some point, GPU parallel capacity really does run out, and `T_marginal` starts dominating — throughput gains taper off, while latency keeps growing.
* **Forgetting batch-fill waiting time is a separate cost from processing time.** The worked example only accounts for processing time; a request's *total* latency also includes however long it waited for its batch to be ready.
* **Treating this as purely a software scheduling problem.** It's fundamentally a hardware-utilization fact — GPUs have spare parallel capacity at low batch sizes, which is what makes the whole trade-off exist in the first place.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. Why does batch processing time grow much more slowly than batch size itself?</summary>
Most of the cost is fixed overhead, largely independent of batch size, because a GPU has spare parallel capacity that a single request doesn't fully use — adding more requests to the batch is nearly free until that capacity runs out.
</details>

<details><summary>2. In the worked example, what was the throughput gain going from batch size 1 to batch size 32, and why was it so much larger than the processing-time increase?</summary>
Nearly 13× (95.2 to 1230.8 requests/second), versus only a 2.5× increase in processing time — because the fixed overhead dominating a batch of 1 request gets spread across far more requests at batch size 32.
</details>

<details><summary>3. What latency cost does batching introduce that isn't captured by processing time alone?</summary>
The time a request spends waiting for its batch to be assembled before processing even starts — a real cost on top of the processing time itself.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Batching:** grouping multiple inference requests together to process in a single pass, amortizing fixed per-batch overhead.
* **Throughput:** the rate at which requests are processed, typically requests or tokens per second.
* **Latency:** the total time a single request takes, including both time spent waiting to be batched and time spent being processed.

## Related

[[KV-Caching for Autoregressive Inference]] · [[Multi-Query and Grouped-Query Attention]] · [[Capstone: Assembling a Tiny Transformer from the Ground Up]]

## Capstone: Assembling a Tiny Transformer from the Ground Up

This capstone traces one phrase through every stage this planet built, in order: tokenizing it, embedding and scaling the pieces, adding positional information, running one full transformer block, and projecting back to a prediction over the vocabulary — checking that every piece still fits together exactly as each individual topic claimed.

**You need:** [[Byte Pair Encoding]], [[Token Embeddings and Embedding Scaling]], [[Learned Positional Embeddings]], [[Weight Tying]], [[Assembling One Transformer Block]].

## The question it answers

"Do all of this planet's individually-verified pieces actually compose into one working pipeline?" This capstone builds the pipeline directly, stage by stage, reusing the same tokenizer, embedding scaling, transformer block, and tied output projection verified separately throughout the planet — and checks that a genuinely novel input flows cleanly from raw text to a predicted next token.

## The pipeline

```text
1. Tokenization (Byte Pair Encoding)
2. Scaled embedding lookup (Token Embeddings and Embedding Scaling)
3. Add positional information (Positional Information Beyond Sinusoids)
4. One transformer block: attention + residual + norm, feed-forward + residual + norm
   (Assembling One Transformer Block)
5. Output projection via the tied embedding table, then softmax
   (Weight Tying)
```

## A worked walkthrough

The exact same BPE merges from [[Byte Pair Encoding]], applied to the exact same unseen word, `lowest`:

```text
1. tokens: ["low", "est</w>"]
```

A tiny 5-entry, 4-dimensional tied embedding table (`low`, `est</w>`, plus three distractor pieces), scaled by `√4 = 2`:

```text
2. scaled embeddings for "low" and "est</w>":
   [-0.383, 0.488, 0.065, 0.304]
   [-0.798, 0.508, -0.782, -0.631]

3. with positional vectors added:
   [-0.361, 0.593, 0.018, 0.414]
   [-0.610, 0.516, -0.877, -0.446]
```

One full pre-norm transformer block (self-attention, then feed-forward, each wrapped in normalization and a residual connection):

```text
4. block output at the final position (after "est</w>"):
   [-1.2839, 1.1197, -1.4763, -0.7382]
```

Projecting that final hidden vector back through the *same tied* embedding table used in step 2, then softmax:

```text
5. logits:  [0.3585, 1.6070, 0.6746, 0.8445, 0.4250]
   probabilities:
     low:      0.1169
     est</w>:  0.4075   ← highest
     er</w>:   0.1604
     new:      0.1901
     wid:      0.1250
```

The model's top prediction after "lowest" is `est</w>` itself — not a meaningful prediction (the weights here are untrained, small random numbers), but a complete, working pipeline: a word the BPE merges never saw during training was still tokenized sensibly, embedded, positioned, transformed through a full attention-and-feed-forward block, and turned into a genuine probability distribution over the vocabulary, using nothing but the pieces this planet built one at a time.

## Bench

```bench
id: nn-capstone-transformer
title: One phrase, the whole pipeline
fallback: Trace a word through tokenization, embedding, one transformer block and the output projection, watching each stage's output in turn.
```

**Try this**

1. Step through each stage and watch the vectors (or tokens, or probabilities) change.
2. Try a different word and see how its tokenization and final prediction differ.
3. Compare the final probabilities' spread — notice how flat they are with untrained, random weights.

**What you should notice:** every stage's output is exactly consistent with that stage's own topic earlier on this planet — nothing here is special-cased for this capstone; it's the same functions, called in sequence.

## Where it appears in AI

* **This is, structurally, exactly what a real transformer does on every input** — the only difference from a production model is scale (far more layers, far wider vectors, trained weights) and the specific architectural variants (RoPE instead of simple positions, RMSNorm, gated feed-forward) covered as options earlier on this planet.
* **It demonstrates this planet's central claim**: a transformer is not one monolithic mechanism, but a composition of independently-understandable pieces, each doing one job, stacked and connected in a fixed, learnable pattern.
* **From here, [[LLMs|training this pipeline on real data at real scale]]**, generating many tokens autoregressively, and grounding it in retrieved documents or tool use are the next planets' jobs — this planet's job was the architecture itself.

## Common pitfalls

* **Expecting a meaningful prediction from untrained weights.** The point of this worked example is that the *pipeline* works correctly end to end, not that small random weights produce useful output.
* **Assuming a real transformer differs structurally from this capstone.** It doesn't — more layers, wider vectors, and trained weights are scale and training differences, not architectural ones.
* **Forgetting the tied embedding table is used in both directions.** The same matrix that looked up "low" and "est</w>" at the start is the matrix the final hidden vector is projected back through at the end.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. What are the five stages this capstone traces a phrase through, in order?</summary>
Tokenization, scaled embedding lookup, adding positional information, one transformer block (attention and feed-forward, each with residual connections and normalization), and output projection through the tied embedding table followed by softmax.
</details>

<details><summary>2. Why was the word "lowest" specifically chosen for this worked example?</summary>
It was never part of the BPE training corpus, so successfully tokenizing and processing it demonstrates the pipeline generalizing to unseen input, not just replaying memorized training examples.
</details>

<details><summary>3. What does this capstone's result demonstrate about the planet's topics as a whole?</summary>
That the individually-verified pieces — tokenization, embedding scaling, the transformer block, and tied weights — genuinely compose into one working pipeline, with each stage's output consistent with what its own topic claimed.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Pipeline:** the ordered sequence of stages — tokenization, embedding, transformer blocks, output projection — that turns raw text into a prediction.
* **End-to-end:** covering every stage from raw input to final output, with no stage skipped or special-cased.
* **Untrained weights:** randomly initialized parameters, used here to verify the pipeline's mechanics rather than to produce a meaningful prediction.

# Generative AI

## Generative AI

Every generative model so far on this road — the GANs, VAEs, normalizing flows and diffusion models of [[Deep Learning]], the decoder-only transformers of [[Transformers]] — already learned how to represent and produce data. This planet is what happens *after* that: how a trained model is actually turned into text, an image, a sound or a video at generation time, how that generation is steered, how the result is judged, and what can go wrong when the output is trusted too far. It needs [[Deep Learning]] (GANs, VAEs, diffusion, autoencoders) and [[Transformers]] (decoder-only architectures, cross-attention, KV-caching); where a topic here builds directly on one of those, it says so under **You need**. Nothing here re-derives how a GAN, VAE or diffusion model is trained — this planet is generation-time behavior, conditioning, modality-specific pipelines, evaluation and responsible use, not the training mechanics themselves.

Each topic asks one question, explains it in plain language with a small worked example, lets you experiment in a **bench**, and ends with where the idea shows up in practice.

## The road

1. [[Decoding and Prompting]]: turning a trained model's raw probabilities into an actual sequence, and steering that process with the input you give it.
2. [[Conditioning and Guidance]]: pushing a generative model's output toward what you asked for, during generation itself.
3. [[Image Generation and Editing]]: text-to-image pipelines and the editing operations built on top of them.
4. [[Audio and Speech Generation]]: turning model output into sound — speech, voices and music.
5. [[Video, 3D and Code Generation]]: extending generation past still images and language into motion, three dimensions and source code.
6. [[Multimodal Generation]]: models that generate across more than one modality from a single shared representation.
7. [[Evaluating Generative Models]]: how to tell whether generated output is actually good, with no single ground truth to compare against.
8. [[Risks and Responsible Generation]]: what generative models get wrong, whose content they were trained on, and how misuse is detected and limited.
9. [[Generative AI in Practice]]: adapting and serving a generative model as a real product, ending with a capstone that assembles decoding and guidance into one small working generator.

From here the road leads on to [[LLMs]], [[RAG]] and [[Agents]].

## Decoding and Prompting

A trained language model outputs a probability distribution over the next token, not a finished sentence. This district covers the algorithms that turn those probabilities into actual output, and the input-side counterpart: writing the prompt that shapes what those probabilities will look like in the first place.

Topics on this stretch of the road:

* [[Greedy and Beam Search Decoding]]: always taking the single most likely continuation, or tracking several at once.
* [[Temperature and Nucleus (Top-p) Sampling]]: injecting controlled randomness instead of always taking the most likely token.
* [[Repetition and Length Control]]: stopping a model from looping on itself, and controlling how long its output runs.
* [[Constrained and Structured Generation]]: forcing output into a required shape, like valid JSON or a fixed grammar.
* [[Self-Consistency and Best-of-N Sampling]]: generating several candidate answers and picking (or combining) the best one.
* [[Prompting and In-Context Learning]]: steering a model's behavior entirely through the input, with no retraining.
* [[Few-Shot and Zero-Shot Generation]]: how many examples a prompt needs before a model performs a new task well.

## Greedy and Beam Search Decoding

A trained language model hands back a probability distribution over the next token at every step, not a finished sentence — something has to decide, step after step, which token actually gets written down. This note covers the two oldest answers to that question: always take the single most likely token, or track several promising candidates at once.

**You need:** [[Decoder-Only Architectures]], [[Softmax and Cross-Entropy in Practice]].

## The question it answers

"Given a model's next-token probabilities at every step, how do you turn them into one finished sequence?" The simplest rule — **greedy decoding** — always takes the single most probable token at each step. It's fast and deterministic, but it's a *local* choice: the token that looks best right now can lead down a path whose *total* probability is worse than a path that looked slightly less promising at step one. **Beam search** fixes this by keeping several candidate sequences alive at once (the *beam*), extending each of them every step, and keeping only the best few by total score — trading some extra computation for a better chance at the globally best sequence.

## Intuition

Imagine choosing a hiking route one step at a time by always taking the path that looks steepest-uphill right now. That greedy choice can strand you on a lower peak, while a path that looked slightly less steep at the first fork actually led to the summit. Beam search is hiking with a few scouts: at every fork, send scouts down the best few routes seen *so far*, drop the ones falling behind, and keep going — more exploration than one greedy hiker, but far less than checking every possible route.

## Definition and notation

```text
greedy:  pick argmax P(token | prefix) at every step
beam search (width k): keep the k highest cumulative log-probability
  sequences after each step; extend every kept sequence by every
  possible next token, then keep only the best k of the results
cumulative score: log P(seq) = Σ log P(tokenᵢ | token₁...tokenᵢ₋₁)
```

Beam search with width 1 is exactly greedy decoding — it's the special case where only one candidate survives each step.

## A worked example

A tiny two-step toy model over the vocabulary `{A, B, C, <eos>}`, whose first-step logits very slightly favor B over A:

```text
step 1 (from start):        logits [A: 1.0, B: 1.3, C: 0.1, eos: −5]
step 2 (after A):           logits [A: 0.2, B: 0.2, C: 3.0, eos: −5]
step 2 (after B):           logits [A: 0.2, B: 1.0, C: 1.0, eos: −5]
```

Greedy decoding takes B at step 1 (its logit is highest), then — among A, B and C tied-ish after B — picks B again:

```text
greedy:  "B B"   log-probability ≈ −1.6117
```

But brute-force checking every two-token sequence finds a better one: A, followed by C, which was *very* likely once A was chosen:

```text
A C   log-probability ≈ −1.1299   ← the actual best sequence
B B   log-probability ≈ −1.6117   ← what greedy found
```

Beam search with width 1 reproduces greedy's "B B". Beam search with width 2 or more keeps both the A and B branches alive after step 1, and finds "A C":

```text
beam width 1:  B B   (−1.6117)
beam width 2:  A C   (−1.1299)  ·  B B   (−1.6117)
beam width 3:  A C   (−1.1299)  ·  B B   (−1.6117)  ·  B C   (−1.6117)
```

Greedy's single-step shortsightedness cost it the better sequence; keeping just one extra candidate alive was enough to recover it here.

## Bench

```bench
id: decode-greedy-beam
title: Greedy vs. beam search
fallback: Compare the sequence greedy decoding finds against the sequence beam search finds on a tiny toy model, at different beam widths.
```

**Try this**

1. Set beam width to 1 and confirm it matches greedy decoding exactly.
2. Raise the width to 2 and watch the kept sequence change to the better one.
3. Raise it to 3 and check whether a third candidate changes anything here.

**What you should notice:** going from width 1 to width 2 is the only change that matters on this toy model — once beam search can see past the single best first step, it finds the sequence greedy missed, and keeping a third candidate doesn't improve on that.

## Where it appears in AI

* **Machine translation and summarization** historically relied heavily on beam search, where a locally-tempting word choice can derail the rest of a sentence.
* **Modern [[Decoder-Only Architectures|decoder-only chat models]] mostly don't use beam search** — it tends to produce short, repetitive, "safe" text for open-ended generation, which is why [[Temperature and Nucleus (Top-p) Sampling|sampling-based decoding]] is more common there; beam search still shows up for tasks with one clearly correct output.
* **Beam width is a real latency knob**: width k costs roughly k times the compute of greedy decoding, since every candidate has to be extended every step.

## Common pitfalls

* **Assuming a wider beam always finds a better sequence.** It finds a sequence with higher *total probability* under the model, which is not the same as a better sequence by human judgment — beam search famously produces duller, more generic text as width grows past a point.
* **Forgetting beam width 1 is just greedy.** They're the same algorithm; beam search is the generalization, not a different approach.
* **Confusing cumulative log-probability with per-step probability.** A sequence can contain one very likely step and still lose overall to a sequence of several merely-good steps, because log-probabilities add up over the whole sequence.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. Why does greedy decoding sometimes miss the sequence with the highest total probability?</summary>
Because it commits to the single best token at each step without looking ahead — a slightly less likely first token can lead to a much more likely second token, and greedy never considers that trade-off.
</details>

<details><summary>2. What does a beam width of 1 reduce beam search to?</summary>
Exactly greedy decoding — only one candidate sequence is ever kept alive.
</details>

<details><summary>3. In the worked example, what sequence did width-1 beam search (greedy) find, and what did width-2 find instead?</summary>
Width 1 found "B B" (log-probability ≈ −1.6117); width 2 found "A C" (log-probability ≈ −1.1299), which is the actual best two-token sequence.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Greedy decoding:** always choosing the single highest-probability next token.
* **Beam search:** keeping the k highest-scoring candidate sequences alive at every step, for beam width k.
* **Cumulative log-probability:** the sum of the log-probabilities of every token in a sequence, used to rank candidate sequences.

## Related

[[Decoder-Only Architectures]] · [[Temperature and Nucleus (Top-p) Sampling]] · [[Self-Consistency and Best-of-N Sampling]]

## Temperature and Nucleus (Top-p) Sampling

Greedy and beam search both chase the highest-probability sequence, which makes open-ended text feel flat and repetitive — real writing isn't always the most predictable continuation. This note covers the two controls used to inject (and limit) randomness into generation instead.

**You need:** [[Greedy and Beam Search Decoding]], [[Softmax and Cross-Entropy in Practice]].

## The question it answers
