"How do you make a model's output vary, without letting it wander into nonsense?" **Sampling** draws the next token randomly according to the model's probability distribution instead of always taking the most likely one. Two controls shape that distribution before sampling: **temperature** rescales how sharp or flat it is, and **nucleus (top-p) sampling** truncates it to only the most probable tokens that together make up a probability mass of `p`, so a long tail of implausible tokens never gets a chance to be picked at all.

## Intuition

Think of the model's probabilities as a bag of weighted lottery balls — one ball per possible next token. Temperature is how hard you shake the bag before drawing: shake it hard (high temperature) and the odds flatten, so unlikely balls get a real chance; barely shake it (low temperature) and the heaviest ball is drawn almost every time. Nucleus sampling, separately, is removing every ball past a certain combined weight from the bag entirely before you draw — so even with a hard shake, you can never draw one of the longshot balls that individually barely register.

## Definition and notation

```text
temperature scaling:  P'(i) = softmax(logits / T)
  T < 1: sharper distribution (more like greedy as T → 0)
  T > 1: flatter distribution (more uniform as T grows)
  T = 1: the model's own distribution, unchanged

nucleus (top-p): sort tokens by probability, descending; keep the
  smallest prefix whose cumulative probability ≥ p; renormalize
  the kept probabilities to sum to 1; sample only from those
```

## A worked example

The toy logits `[A: 1.0, B: 1.3, C: 0.1, <eos>: −5]` from [[Greedy and Beam Search Decoding]], at temperature 1.0:

```text
T = 1.0:  P(A)=0.3625  P(B)=0.4893  P(C)=0.1474  P(eos)=0.0009
```

Lowering the temperature sharpens the distribution toward B, the already-favored token; raising it flattens the gap between A, B and C:

```text
T = 0.5:  P(A)=0.3347  P(B)=0.6099  P(C)=0.0553  P(eos)≈0.0000
T = 2.0:  P(A)=0.3510  P(B)=0.4078  P(C)=0.2238  P(eos)=0.0175
```

At T = 1.0, nucleus sampling with different thresholds keeps different numbers of tokens:

```text
top-p = 0.9:  keeps {B: 0.4897, A: 0.3628, C: 0.1475}  — 3 of 4 tokens (excludes <eos>)
top-p = 0.5:  keeps {B: 0.5744, A: 0.4256}             — just 2 of 4 tokens
```

Dropping `p` from 0.9 to 0.5 removes C from consideration entirely — not because its probability changed, but because the cumulative-probability cutoff got stricter.

## Bench

```bench
id: temp-topp-sampling
title: Temperature and top-p shape a distribution
fallback: Adjust temperature and top-p and watch which tokens remain eligible to be sampled, then draw a sample.
```

**Try this**

1. Lower the temperature toward 0.2 and watch the distribution collapse toward the single most likely token.
2. Raise it toward 2.0 and watch the bars flatten out.
3. At temperature 1.0, lower top-p until only one or two tokens remain eligible.
4. Sample repeatedly at a few different settings and see how often each token comes up.

**What you should notice:** temperature reshapes every bar's height, while top-p simply removes bars past a cutoff without changing the relative heights of the ones that remain — they're independent, composable controls.

## Where it appears in AI

* **Chat and creative-writing models sample by default**, almost always with both a temperature and a top-p (or top-k) setting exposed as API parameters — "temperature 0.7, top-p 0.9" is a common default pairing.
* **Temperature near 0 approximates greedy decoding**, which is why some APIs let you set temperature to 0 directly for deterministic output instead of true sampling.
* **[[Self-Consistency and Best-of-N Sampling|sampling multiple candidates and combining them]] depends on this randomness existing in the first place** — greedy decoding would produce the same candidate every time.

## Common pitfalls

* **Setting temperature very high expecting "more creative" output.** Past a point it just produces incoherent text, because even implausible tokens start getting picked regularly.
* **Confusing top-p with top-k.** Top-p's cutoff adapts to the shape of the distribution (keeping more tokens when probability is spread out, fewer when it's concentrated); top-k always keeps a fixed number of tokens regardless of how the probability is distributed.
* **Forgetting top-p renormalizes.** The kept tokens' probabilities are rescaled to sum to 1 before sampling — they aren't sampled using their original (smaller) probabilities.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. What happens to a probability distribution as temperature approaches 0?</summary>
It sharpens toward the single highest-probability token, approaching greedy decoding in the limit.
</details>

<details><summary>2. In the worked example, why does top-p = 0.5 exclude token C while top-p = 0.9 includes it?</summary>
Because C's probability (0.1474) isn't needed to reach a cumulative probability of 0.5 once B and A are included (0.4893 + 0.3625 already exceeds 0.5), but it is needed to reach 0.9.
</details>

<details><summary>3. How do temperature and top-p differ in what they do to a distribution?</summary>
Temperature rescales every token's probability, changing how sharp or flat the whole distribution is; top-p removes the lowest-probability tail entirely, without changing the relative probabilities of the tokens it keeps.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Sampling:** drawing the next token randomly according to its probability, rather than always taking the most likely one.
* **Temperature:** a scaling factor applied to logits before softmax that sharpens (T<1) or flattens (T>1) the resulting distribution.
* **Nucleus (top-p) sampling:** restricting sampling to the smallest set of highest-probability tokens whose combined probability reaches a threshold `p`.

## Related

[[Greedy and Beam Search Decoding]] · [[Repetition and Length Control]] · [[Self-Consistency and Best-of-N Sampling]]

## Repetition and Length Control

Left alone, a decoding loop can get stuck: once a model starts favoring a short cycle of tokens, each repetition can make that same cycle even more likely next time. This note covers two practical levers for taming generation length and repetition directly at decoding time.

**You need:** [[Temperature and Nucleus (Top-p) Sampling]].

## The question it answers

"How do you stop a model from looping forever, and how do you control how long its output runs?" A **repetition penalty** reduces the logit of any token in proportion to how many times it has already appeared, making an already-used token progressively less attractive. A **length bias** directly nudges the end-of-sequence token's logit — suppressing it before a minimum length, boosting it past a target length — without touching any other token's score.

## Intuition

Repetition penalty is like a conversation where repeating yourself gets harder to justify each time — the first repeat barely registers, but by the fifth time you're saying the same thing, it's clearly time to say something else. A length bias is a separate, blunter lever: it doesn't care what's being said, only how long the model has been talking, nudging it to wrap up (or keep going) purely based on position.

## Definition and notation

```text
repetition penalty (applied per distinct token, count = times seen so far):
  logit' = logit × penaltyᶜᵒᵘⁿᵗ      if logit < 0
  logit' = logit / penaltyᶜᵒᵘⁿᵗ      if logit ≥ 0
  (penalty = 1 is a no-op; larger penalty punishes repeats harder,
   and the exponent means the second repeat is punished more than the first)

length bias (on the <eos> logit only):
  logit'(<eos>) = logit(<eos>) − bias    if step < minLen
  logit'(<eos>) = logit(<eos>) + bias    if step ≥ softCapLen
```

## A worked example

A toy model over `{the, cat, sat, again, <eos>}` whose transitions form a loop: `cat → sat → again → sat → again → ...`. With no repetition penalty, greedy decoding loops for the full 20-step budget:

```text
no penalty:   cat sat again sat again sat again sat again sat again ... (hits the length limit)
```

With a repetition penalty of 2.5, the "sat" / "again" cycle gets progressively more expensive each time either token reappears. By the third repeat of the cycle, the (still unpenalized) `<eos>` logit of 0.50 finally beats the heavily-penalized "sat" logit of 0.45:

```text
penalty 2.5:  cat sat again sat again <eos>     (6 tokens — the loop breaks on its own)
```

Separately, a length bias can force an early stop regardless of what the content-token logits say. Boosting `<eos>` by 3 once the sequence reaches 2 tokens overrides the model's preference for continuing:

```text
soft cap at step 2, bias 3:  cat sat <eos>      (3 tokens — stopped well before the natural loop)
```

## Bench

```bench
id: repetition-length-control
title: Breaking a loop, and stopping on time
fallback: Adjust a repetition penalty and a soft length cap and watch a looping toy model's generated sequence change.
```

**Try this**

1. With no repetition penalty, confirm the model loops for the full 20-token budget.
2. Raise the penalty until the loop breaks on its own, and watch how many repeats it takes.
3. Set the penalty back to 1 and lower the soft length cap instead — notice this stops generation immediately, with no regard for whether the content "wanted" to continue.

**What you should notice:** the two controls solve different problems — repetition penalty makes the model *want* to stop by making the loop itself unattractive, while a length bias can force a stop regardless of what the model wants.

## Where it appears in AI

* **Chat APIs commonly expose both as separate parameters** (often named `repetition_penalty` or `frequency_penalty`, and `max_tokens` or a length-based stop condition), because they address different failure modes.
* **Open-ended generation without any repetition control is a classic early-GPT-era failure mode** — tight loops of a few repeated phrases were common before penalties like this became standard practice.
* **[[Few-Shot and Zero-Shot Generation|task-oriented prompts]] often rely on length control to keep an answer concise** rather than letting the model keep elaborating past the point of being useful.

## Common pitfalls

* **Setting the repetition penalty too high.** Past a point it can push the model away from words that legitimately need to repeat (like "the" in ordinary prose), producing stilted text.
* **Expecting a length bias to produce exactly the target length.** It shifts the odds toward stopping; the content-token logits can still occasionally win out, especially with a small bias.
* **Applying repetition penalty to every past token equally regardless of count.** The worked example's penalty grows with each repeat specifically so that a single earlier use barely matters, while persistent looping is punished hard — a flat, count-independent penalty behaves quite differently.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. Why does a repetition penalty eventually break a loop that a flat (count-independent) penalty might not?</summary>
Because the penalty compounds with each repeat (it scales by the count of prior occurrences), so a token that keeps reappearing gets progressively more expensive, until even the end-of-sequence token becomes more attractive.
</details>

<details><summary>2. What's the difference between what a repetition penalty and a length bias each act on?</summary>
A repetition penalty adjusts the logits of tokens that have already appeared; a length bias adjusts only the end-of-sequence token's logit, based purely on how many tokens have been generated so far.
</details>

<details><summary>3. In the worked example, how many tokens did it take for a repetition penalty of 2.5 to break the loop?</summary>
Six tokens: "cat sat again sat again &lt;eos&gt;" — the loop ran through one full cycle before the penalty made &lt;eos&gt; more attractive than continuing.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Repetition penalty:** a logit adjustment that makes an already-generated token progressively less likely to be generated again.
* **Length bias:** a direct adjustment to the end-of-sequence token's logit, used to encourage stopping earlier or later.
* **Soft cap:** a length past which generation is nudged (but not forced) to stop, as opposed to a hard limit that cuts generation off outright.

## Related

[[Temperature and Nucleus (Top-p) Sampling]] · [[Constrained and Structured Generation]] · [[Self-Consistency and Best-of-N Sampling]]

## Constrained and Structured Generation

A model's raw next-token distribution has no idea your downstream code needs valid JSON, a specific grammar, or a well-formed arithmetic expression — it just assigns probabilities, and the most likely token at a given step can easily be an invalid one. This note covers forcing output into a required shape by editing the distribution itself, before a token is ever chosen.

**You need:** [[Greedy and Beam Search Decoding]].

## The question it answers

"How do you guarantee a model's output always matches a required structure?" Rather than generating freely and hoping the result parses, **constrained (or grammar-masked) decoding** tracks which tokens are valid at the current position according to some grammar or schema, and sets every other token's logit to `−∞` before choosing the next token. An invalid token can then never be selected — not because the model was discouraged from it, but because it was made literally impossible to pick.

## Intuition

It's the difference between asking someone to write only words from a given list and hoping they comply, versus physically removing every other page from the dictionary in front of them. Prompting a model to "please output valid JSON" is the first approach — it helps, but nothing stops an off-token from slipping through. Grammar masking is the second: whatever the model's draft impulse was, only the tokens that keep the output valid are ever actually available to pick.

## Definition and notation

```text
grammar mask at step t, given parser state s:
  allowed(s) = the set of tokens valid at state s
  logit'(i) = logit(i)   if i ∈ allowed(s)
  logit'(i) = −∞         otherwise
→ softmax(logit') assigns exactly 0 probability to every disallowed token
```

The parser state updates after each token is chosen, the same way a parser would track position while reading — so `allowed(s)` can change from one step to the next.

## A worked example

A toy model generating tokens from `{1, 2, 3, +, -, *, <eos>}`, meant to produce a simple arithmetic expression (a number, then alternating operators and numbers). Its *raw* logits happen to favor an operator as the very first token — which is invalid, since an expression can't start with `+`:

```text
unconstrained (raw argmax at every step):   + 1 + 1 +
```

That's not a valid expression: it starts with an operator and ends with one dangling. Applying a grammar mask — at the "need a number" state, only `{1, 2, 3}` are allowed; at the "need an operator or stop" state, only `{+, -, *, <eos>}` are allowed — changes what's even selectable at step one, and every step after:

```text
constrained (grammar-masked at every step):   1 + 1 + 1
```

Every step still picks whatever is highest-logit *among the allowed tokens* — the model's own preferences are respected as much as possible — but the result is guaranteed valid by construction, not by hoping the model cooperates.

## Bench

```bench
id: constrained-grammar
title: Masking out invalid tokens as you generate
fallback: Toggle a grammar mask on and off and watch whether the toy model's output is valid arithmetic.
```

**Try this**

1. With the mask off, check whether the raw output is valid arithmetic.
2. Turn the mask on and compare the new output.
3. Notice that the masked output still uses the model's own logit preferences — just restricted to what's currently valid.

**What you should notice:** the model's underlying preferences didn't change between the two runs — only which tokens it was *allowed* to express those preferences over.

## Where it appears in AI

* **"JSON mode" and function-calling features in production LLM APIs are grammar-constrained decoding** applied to a JSON-schema or function-signature grammar, guaranteeing parseable output.
* **[[Code Generation and Program Synthesis|code generation]] can use the same idea with a programming language's actual grammar**, so a model can never emit a syntactically invalid program.
* **It composes with sampling**: a grammar mask can be applied before temperature or top-p filtering, so the output is simultaneously varied *and* guaranteed valid.

## Common pitfalls

* **Assuming a good prompt is a substitute for a grammar mask.** A prompt can only make invalid output less likely; a mask makes it impossible — the difference matters whenever downstream code can't tolerate a parse failure.
* **Forgetting the mask can only enforce syntax, not meaning.** A grammar-masked arithmetic expression is guaranteed well-formed, but nothing stops it from being mathematically meaningless or wrong — syntax validity and correctness are different guarantees.
* **Not updating the allowed set as state changes.** A grammar mask has to track parser state and change what's allowed at every step — a single fixed allowed-token set for the whole generation wouldn't enforce much of anything.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. How does grammar-masked decoding guarantee valid output, rather than just making valid output more likely?</summary>
It sets the logits of every invalid token to −∞ before sampling or taking the argmax, giving them exactly zero probability — an invalid token can never be selected, as opposed to merely being discouraged.
</details>

<details><summary>2. In the worked example, why did the unconstrained model produce an invalid expression?</summary>
Its raw logits simply favored an operator token as the most likely first token, and nothing stopped that invalid choice from being selected.
</details>

<details><summary>3. What does grammar masking guarantee, and what does it not guarantee?</summary>
It guarantees the output is syntactically valid according to the grammar; it does not guarantee the output is correct, meaningful, or the best possible completion.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Grammar (or schema) mask:** setting the logits of every token invalid at the current position to −∞ before sampling.
* **Parser state:** the tracked position within a grammar, used to determine which tokens are currently allowed.
* **Constrained decoding:** generation that guarantees structural validity by restricting which tokens can ever be chosen.

## Related

[[Greedy and Beam Search Decoding]] · [[Code Generation and Program Synthesis]] · [[Self-Consistency and Best-of-N Sampling]]

## Self-Consistency and Best-of-N Sampling

A single sampled answer is a coin flip against the model's own uncertainty — if it's right 50% of the time per try, one sample is right about half the time, full stop. This note covers the simple fix: ask more than once, and combine the answers.

**You need:** [[Temperature and Nucleus (Top-p) Sampling]].

## The question it answers

"If one sampled answer is unreliable, can asking several times help?" **Best-of-N sampling** generates N independent candidate answers and keeps the single best one by some scoring rule. **Self-consistency** is a specific, scoring-free version of that idea for tasks with a discrete final answer: generate N candidates and take whichever answer appears most often — a majority (or plurality) vote. It works whenever the model's mistakes are more scattered across wrong answers than its correct answers are, which is a weaker requirement than "the model is always right."

## Intuition

Ask one person a trivia question and they might guess wrong. Ask the same question to a room of people who each have an *independent* shot at the right answer, and even if no individual is reliable, the most common answer in the room is usually right — their individual mistakes tend to scatter across different wrong answers, while people who know the right answer all converge on the same one. Self-consistency is running that room-of-guessers trick with one model, sampled multiple times.

## Definition and notation

```text
best-of-N: generate candidates c₁, ..., c_N independently;
           keep argmax score(cᵢ) by some scoring rule

self-consistency: generate candidates c₁, ..., c_N independently;
                   tally identical final answers;
                   keep the answer with the highest tally (majority/plurality vote)
```

## A worked example

A toy model answering a fixed question, where it samples the correct answer "4" about half the time, and splits the rest of its probability across three wrong answers:

```text
P(answer):  4 → 0.50   (correct)
            3 → 0.25
            5 → 0.15
           22 → 0.10
```

With a single sample, accuracy is exactly the probability of sampling the correct answer: about 49% over 2,000 simulated trials (matching the 0.50 probability, within simulation noise). Taking a majority vote over several independent samples does much better, because the wrong answers are split three ways while the correct answer isn't split at all:

```text
N =  1:  49.0% correct
N =  3:  72.3% correct
N =  5:  74.8% correct
N =  9:  84.1% correct
N = 15:  89.3% correct
```

Going from one sample to nine roughly cuts the error rate by two thirds (51% wrong → 16% wrong), without changing the underlying model at all — only how many times it's asked and how the answers are combined.

## Bench

```bench
id: self-consistency-vote
title: One sample vs. a vote over many
fallback: Compare the accuracy of a single sampled answer against a majority vote over several samples, at different sample counts.
```

**Try this**

1. Set N to 1 and note the accuracy is close to the model's raw per-sample correctness rate.
2. Raise N and watch accuracy climb well past that rate.
3. Compare the jump from N=1 to N=3 against the jump from N=9 to N=15 — notice the gains shrink as N grows.

**What you should notice:** accuracy keeps improving with more samples, but with diminishing returns — the biggest single jump comes from going from one sample to just a few.

## Where it appears in AI

* **Math and reasoning benchmarks routinely report "self-consistency@N" scores** alongside single-sample accuracy, since the gap can be large for exactly the reason shown here.
* **It costs N times the inference compute** of a single sample, which is the real trade-off being made — accuracy for cost, not accuracy for free.
* **[[Prompting and In-Context Learning|chain-of-thought prompting]] and self-consistency are often used together**: sample several different reasoning paths, then vote on the final answers they arrive at, rather than voting on the reasoning text itself.

## Common pitfalls

* **Expecting self-consistency to help when the model's wrong answers all agree with each other.** The method relies on correct answers being more consistent across samples than incorrect ones; if the model has one specific, confidently wrong answer it always converges on, voting won't fix it.
* **Using it on tasks without a clean final answer to tally.** Self-consistency needs a discrete answer to vote over; for open-ended generation, a scored best-of-N (not a vote) is the applicable version.
* **Forgetting the N samples must be independent.** Voting over N samples that are all small variations of the same single draw doesn't capture the same independent-error-scattering effect.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. Why can a majority vote over several samples beat the per-sample accuracy of the model generating them?</summary>
Because the model's incorrect answers tend to scatter across several different wrong options, while its correct answers all land on the same value — so the correct answer is more likely to be the most frequent one, even if it's not the most frequent on every individual sample.
</details>

<details><summary>2. In the worked example, roughly how much did going from N=1 to N=9 reduce the error rate?</summary>
From about 51% wrong to about 16% wrong — a reduction of roughly two thirds.
</details>

<details><summary>3. What's the real cost of self-consistency or best-of-N sampling?</summary>
It requires N times the inference compute of generating a single answer, since N independent samples have to be generated and then combined.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Best-of-N sampling:** generating N candidates and keeping the one with the highest score under some rule.
* **Self-consistency:** best-of-N with a majority (or plurality) vote over final answers, used for tasks with a discrete answer.
* **Majority vote:** keeping whichever sampled answer occurs most often among the generated candidates.

## Related

[[Temperature and Nucleus (Top-p) Sampling]] · [[Prompting and In-Context Learning]] · [[Human Evaluation of Generated Content]]

## Prompting and In-Context Learning

None of the decoding controls so far change what the model "knows" — they only change how its existing distribution gets turned into tokens. This note covers a different lever entirely: changing the *input*, with no retraining, to change what that distribution looks like in the first place.

**You need:** [[Decoder-Only Architectures]].

## The question it answers

"How can a model perform a task it was never specifically trained on, with no weight updates at all?" **Prompting** is simply choosing what text to put in front of a model before it starts generating. **In-context learning** is the specific, striking version of this: giving the model a few examples of a pattern *inside the prompt itself*, after which it continues the pattern on a new, unseen case — purely by reading the context, not by learning in the usual sense.

## Intuition

A plausible mechanical story behind this (confirmed by looking inside real transformer attention patterns) is a **copying** operation: somewhere in a sequence, find an earlier position where the *current* token last appeared, and look at whatever token came right after it back then — then guess that again. If a prompt reads "dog → bark, cat → meow, bird → chirp, dog → ", a model doing exactly this copying trick finds the earlier "dog", looks at what followed it, and answers "bark" — not because it looked anything up, but because the pattern was right there in the context to copy from.

## Definition and notation

```text
induction-style copy completion:
  given tokens t₁, t₂, ..., tₙ (tₙ is the token to complete after)
  find the largest i < n such that tᵢ = tₙ
  return tᵢ₊₁ as the completion (or: no completion, if no such i exists)
```

This is a simplified model of one real, measured mechanism ("induction heads") behind in-context learning — not the whole story of how it works, but enough to see why more examples in context make a difference.

## A worked example

A prompt that repeats one earlier token at the very end:

```text
dog · bark · cat · meow · bird · chirp · dog → ?
```

Scanning backward from the final "dog", the only earlier occurrence of "dog" is at the very start, immediately followed by "bark" — so the completion is "bark", recovered correctly by copying, with nothing about dogs or barking "known" ahead of time.

```text
completion:  bark
```

This copying trick isn't magic, though — it only works when the *pattern itself* is a repetition the model can find. A prompt built around a function instead of a repeated token, like "2 → 4, 3 → 6, 5 → 10, 4 → ?" (doubling), finds the earlier "4" from the very first pair and copies whatever followed *that* occurrence — "3" — which is not the doubled value at all:

```text
prompt:  2 · 4 · 3 · 6 · 5 · 10 · 4 → ?
copy completion:  3   (wrong — 4 doubled is 8)
```

Copying solves "find the pattern that already repeated here"; it does not, by itself, solve "apply a general rule to a new input."

## Bench

```bench
id: induction-copy
title: Completing by copying, not by knowing
fallback: Pick a prompt and watch a copy-based completion find (or fail to find) an earlier matching token to copy from.
```

**Try this**

1. Try the dog/cat/bird prompt and confirm the completion correctly copies "bark".
2. Try the prompt that never repeats a token at all, and see what happens when there's nothing to copy from.
3. Compare this to what [[Few-Shot and Zero-Shot Generation|more examples in the prompt]] would do to the chance of finding a match at all.

**What you should notice:** the completion only succeeds when the exact token at the end genuinely reappeared earlier in the prompt — it's pattern-matching against the prompt's own content, not recalling a fact.

## Where it appears in AI

* **"Prompt engineering" as a skill is largely about shaping context so the right pattern is available to be found or copied**, rather than about phrasing a request more politely.
* **Induction heads were identified by directly inspecting attention patterns in trained transformers** — a rare case where a mechanistic hypothesis about *why* a capability works was checked against the actual weights, not just behavior.
* **It explains why example *order and format* in a prompt matters**: the pattern has to be literally present and consistent for a copying mechanism to latch onto it.

## Common pitfalls

* **Assuming in-context learning means the model is truly learning a general rule.** The worked example's doubling-function failure shows the copying mechanism specifically solves repetition, not arbitrary function learning — real models combine this with other mechanisms, but the gap is real.
* **Treating prompting and fine-tuning as the same lever at different strengths.** Prompting changes what's visible in context for one generation; it leaves the model's weights completely untouched, unlike [[Parameter-Efficient Adaptation for Generation|fine-tuning]].
* **Forgetting the pattern has to appear *before* the point it's needed.** A copying mechanism can only look backward in the context it's already seen.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. What does the simplified copy-completion rule in this note actually do?</summary>
It looks backward from the final token for the most recent earlier occurrence of that same token, and returns whatever token immediately followed it back then.
</details>

<details><summary>2. Why did the copy rule fail on the doubling-function prompt?</summary>
Because the rule only knows how to repeat a pattern that already occurred verbatim — it found the earlier "4" and copied what followed it, which doesn't correspond to applying the doubling rule to that same "4" the second time.
</details>

<details><summary>3. Does in-context learning update a model's weights?</summary>
No — it only changes what's in the input context for that one generation; the model's parameters are completely unchanged.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Prompting:** choosing the input text given to a model to shape its output, with no change to its weights.
* **In-context learning:** a model performing a task demonstrated by examples placed directly in its input, without any training step.
* **Induction head:** a simplified name for an attention mechanism that copies whatever token followed an earlier occurrence of the current token.

## Related

[[Few-Shot and Zero-Shot Generation]] · [[Decoder-Only Architectures]] · [[Self-Consistency and Best-of-N Sampling]]

## Few-Shot and Zero-Shot Generation

The copying mechanism in [[Prompting and In-Context Learning]] only works when the pattern it needs is actually present in the prompt — which raises a direct, practical question: how many examples does a prompt need before that pattern reliably shows up?

**You need:** [[Prompting and In-Context Learning]].

## The question it answers

"Does a prompt need zero, one, or many examples to work?" **Zero-shot** means asking for a task with no examples at all, relying entirely on an instruction. **Few-shot** means including a handful of worked examples in the prompt before the real question. Whether few-shot helps — and how many examples are enough — depends on whether a model's in-context mechanisms (like the copying trick from the previous note) actually get a chance to find a matching pattern; more examples simply raise the odds that one of them matches.

## Intuition

If a copying-style mechanism needs the *current* situation to have occurred once already somewhere earlier in the prompt, then zero examples means there is nothing to match against at all — the model is guessing blind. Each additional example is another independent roll of the dice for "does one of these happen to match what I'm asked about now?" More shots don't make the model smarter; they make it more likely the exact pattern needed is already sitting somewhere in the context.

## Definition and notation

```text
zero-shot:  prompt = instruction only, no worked examples
k-shot:     prompt = instruction + k worked examples, then the real query

if each example independently has probability q of matching
the query's category:
  P(at least one of k examples matches) = 1 − (1 − q)ᵏ
```

## A worked example

A toy setup with 5 possible categories, where a prompt includes k random example pairs before a query from one of the same 5 categories. The chance that at least one of the k examples happens to share the query's category (`q = 1/5`, so `1 − q = 0.8`):

```text
k = 0:  1 − 0.8⁰ = 0.000   (0.0% — zero-shot, nothing to match)
k = 1:  1 − 0.8¹ = 0.200   (20.0% match rate)
k = 2:  1 − 0.8² = 0.360   (36.0% match rate)
k = 3:  1 − 0.8³ = 0.488   (48.8% match rate)
k = 5:  1 − 0.8⁵ = 0.672   (67.2% match rate)
k = 8:  1 − 0.8⁸ = 0.832   (83.2% match rate)
```

Simulating 5,000 random prompts at each k matches this formula closely (k=3 simulated at 49.5%, k=8 at 83.6%, both within simulation noise of the exact values above) — confirming that the benefit of more shots here is entirely about the growing odds of a usable match existing in the prompt at all, with sharply diminishing returns as k grows past a handful.

## Bench

```bench
id: fewshot-matchrate
title: Shots in the prompt vs. chance of a match to copy
fallback: Adjust the number of example shots in a toy prompt and watch the chance of a usable match rise toward its theoretical curve.
```

**Try this**

1. Set shots to 0 and confirm the match rate is exactly zero.
2. Raise shots to 3 and compare the simulated rate to the formula's prediction.
3. Keep raising shots past 5 and notice how much the rate's growth slows down.

**What you should notice:** the match rate rises quickly at first and then flattens — going from 0 to 1 shot gains 20 percentage points, but going from 5 to 8 shots gains only about 16 more, even though it's three more examples.

## Where it appears in AI

* **Zero-shot performance is a common benchmark baseline**, specifically because it isolates what a model can do from instructions alone, with no chance for in-context pattern-matching to help.
* **Few-shot prompting became a headline result for large language models** precisely because performance on many tasks jumped sharply from a handful of in-context examples, with no training at all.
* **Beyond a task-specific pattern match, more shots also cost more input tokens** — every example in the prompt is tokens the model has to process and (on most APIs) tokens you pay for, so few-shot has a real, direct cost unrelated to accuracy.

## Common pitfalls

* **Assuming more shots always helps, without limit.** This worked example's own curve shows sharply diminishing returns; very long prompts can also push useful context out of a model's effective attention span.
* **Treating zero-shot failure as proof a model "can't" do a task.** It may only mean the task needs a demonstrated pattern to follow — the same model might do fine with just one or two well-chosen examples.
* **Picking unrepresentative examples.** A few-shot prompt whose examples don't resemble the real query's pattern can actively mislead a model, since in-context mechanisms are matching against whatever pattern the examples actually show, not the one you intended.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. Why does zero-shot prompting have nothing for the copying mechanism from the previous note to use?</summary>
Because there are no worked examples in the prompt, so there is no earlier occurrence of a matching pattern for the mechanism to find and copy from.
</details>

<details><summary>2. In the worked example, roughly how much does the match rate improve from k=5 to k=8 shots, compared to k=0 to k=1?</summary>
From k=0 to k=1 the rate jumps 20 percentage points (0% to 20%); from k=5 to k=8 it only rises about 16 points (67.2% to 83.2%) despite adding three more examples instead of one — clearly diminishing returns.
</details>

<details><summary>3. What's a direct, non-accuracy cost of adding more few-shot examples?</summary>
Every example adds input tokens the model must process (and that are usually billed), independent of whether those extra examples actually improve accuracy.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Zero-shot:** prompting a model to perform a task with no worked examples, instruction only.
* **Few-shot:** including a small number of worked examples of a task directly in the prompt.
* **Diminishing returns:** each additional example improving performance by less than the one before it.

## Related

[[Prompting and In-Context Learning]] · [[Self-Consistency and Best-of-N Sampling]] · [[Parameter-Efficient Adaptation for Generation]]

## Conditioning and Guidance

Decoding controls how output is assembled token by token; this district covers a different lever — how a generative model's output is pushed toward a specific condition, image, or structure during generation itself, most concretely in diffusion models.

Topics on this stretch of the road:

* [[Classifier Guidance]]: using a separate classifier's gradients to steer a diffusion model's denoising steps.
* [[Classifier-Free Guidance]]: steering generation by contrasting a conditioned and unconditioned pass, with no separate classifier.
* [[Cross-Attention Conditioning for Generation]]: letting a text (or other) embedding directly attend into the generation process.
* [[ControlNet-Style Structural Conditioning]]: conditioning generation on a structural signal like an edge map or pose skeleton.
* [[Latent Space Interpolation and Manipulation]]: moving through a model's latent space to blend, edit or explore its outputs.

## Classifier Guidance

A [[Diffusion Models|diffusion model]] learns to denoise toward its training data in general — nothing in that process knows you specifically want a *dog*, or a *red* one. This note covers the first practical fix: using a separate classifier's own gradient to nudge each denoising step toward a chosen class.

**You need:** [[Diffusion Models]].

## The question it answers

"How do you make a diffusion model generate a specific class or concept, using a classifier trained separately from it?" **Classifier guidance** adds the gradient of a classifier's log-probability for the target class, scaled by a guidance strength, directly onto the diffusion model's own score (its learned gradient of log-density) at every denoising step. The classifier doesn't generate anything itself — it only tells the sampling process which direction would make the current (partially denoised) sample more convincingly belong to the target class, and that direction gets added to the ordinary denoising step.

## Intuition

Picture a hiker (the diffusion process) walking generally toward higher ground (higher data density) with no particular peak in mind. A park ranger (the classifier) standing somewhere specific calls out directions toward where they are, and the hiker blends that suggestion into their own sense of which way is uphill. A louder ranger (higher guidance scale) gets listened to more — and if they shout loud enough, the hiker will walk straight toward them even across terrain that isn't particularly uphill at all.

## Definition and notation

```text
unconditional score:      ∇x log p(x)                (the diffusion model's own gradient)
classifier gradient:      ∇x log p(y | x)             (a separately trained classifier)

classifier-guided score:  ∇x log p(x) + s · ∇x log p(y | x)
  s: guidance scale — s = 0 ignores the classifier entirely;
     larger s pulls samples more strongly toward class y
```

## A worked example

Two toy data clusters sit at `(−2, 0)` and `(2, 0)`. Starting exactly at the origin `(0, 0)` — equidistant from both, so the diffusion model's own score there is exactly zero — a classifier's gradient (built from a simple sigmoid separating the clusters along the first coordinate) pulls toward cluster 1:

```text
scale  0:  combined score (0.000, 0.000)  →  one step lands at (0.000, 0.000)
scale  2:  combined score (1.000, 0.000)  →  one step lands at (0.500, 0.000)
scale  5:  combined score (2.500, 0.000)  →  one step lands at (1.250, 0.000)
scale 10:  combined score (5.000, 0.000)  →  one step lands at (2.500, 0.000)
```

With no guidance, the point doesn't move at all — the diffusion model itself has no preference between the two equally likely clusters here. As guidance scale rises, the single step moves further toward cluster 1, overshooting its center `(2, 0)` once the scale gets large enough that the classifier's pull dominates completely.

## Bench

```bench
id: classifier-guidance
title: Steering a denoising step with a classifier
fallback: Adjust a guidance scale and watch a toy denoising step move toward one cluster, pulled there by a separate classifier's gradient.
```

**Try this**

1. Set guidance scale to 0 and confirm the point doesn't move — the diffusion model alone has no preference here.
2. Raise the scale and watch the point move toward cluster 1.
3. Push the scale high enough to see it overshoot the cluster center.

**What you should notice:** guidance scale directly controls how much the classifier's opinion outweighs the diffusion model's own sense of where the data lives — at scale 0 it's ignored completely, and past a point it dominates entirely.

## Where it appears in AI

* **Classifier guidance was the first widely used technique for controllable diffusion generation**, letting a single unconditional diffusion model be steered by any classifier trained on the same kind of data.
* **It requires training (or having) a separate classifier for the target labels** — a real cost that [[Classifier-Free Guidance|classifier-free guidance]] was specifically designed to remove.
* **The same mechanism generalizes past class labels**: any differentiable function of x whose gradient points toward "more of what you want" can be added the same way.

## Common pitfalls

* **Pushing guidance scale too high.** Past a point, samples start looking distorted or artifact-heavy — the classifier's gradient can point toward regions a classifier is confident about without those regions being realistic data at all.
* **Forgetting the classifier must be applicable to partially noised data.** A classifier trained only on clean images generally needs to be retrained (or adapted) to give useful gradients on the noisy intermediate samples a diffusion process actually works with.
* **Assuming guidance changes what the diffusion model learned.** It doesn't modify the model at all — it only adds an extra term to the sampling step, entirely at generation time.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. What two things get added together to form the classifier-guided score?</summary>
The diffusion model's own unconditional score, and a separately trained classifier's gradient of log-probability for the target class, scaled by a guidance strength.
</details>

<details><summary>2. In the worked example, why did the point not move at all when guidance scale was 0?</summary>
Because the starting point was exactly equidistant from both data clusters, so the diffusion model's own score there was exactly zero — with no classifier contribution, there was nothing to move toward.
</details>

<details><summary>3. What does classifier guidance require that classifier-free guidance avoids needing?</summary>
A separate classifier, trained specifically to give useful gradients on partially noised samples.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Score:** the gradient of log-density, ∇x log p(x) — the direction a diffusion model nudges a sample toward higher data density.
* **Classifier guidance:** adding a scaled classifier gradient to a diffusion model's score at sampling time, to steer generation toward a chosen class.
* **Guidance scale:** the strength with which a guidance signal is blended into the denoising step.

## Related

[[Diffusion Models]] · [[Classifier-Free Guidance]] · [[ControlNet-Style Structural Conditioning]]

## Classifier-Free Guidance

[[Classifier Guidance]] works, but it needs a second model — a classifier trained specifically to work on noisy, partially-denoised samples. This note covers the technique that replaced it almost everywhere: getting the same steering effect from one model alone.

**You need:** [[Classifier Guidance]].

## The question it answers

"Can you guide generation toward a condition without training a separate classifier at all?" **Classifier-free guidance (CFG)** trains a single model to produce both an *unconditional* score (ignoring the condition) and a *conditional* score (using it), typically by randomly dropping the condition during training some fraction of the time. At sampling time, the two scores are combined by extrapolating *past* the conditional score, away from the unconditional one — which pushes samples more strongly toward the condition than simply using the conditional score on its own would.

## Intuition

Imagine knowing both what someone would say about a photo with no hint of what it's of, and what they'd say once told "it's a cat." The *difference* between those two answers is exactly the part attributable to "cat." Classifier-free guidance doesn't just take the "told it's a cat" answer — it takes that difference and adds *more than one copy of it* on top of the unconditional answer, deliberately overshooting past what simply conditioning on "cat" would give you, to produce something even more unmistakably cat-like.

## Definition and notation

```text
uncond score:  ∇x log p(x)          (no condition used)
cond score:    ∇x log p(x | y)      (condition y used)

CFG score:  uncond + g · (cond − uncond)
  g = 0:  pure unconditional generation
  g = 1:  exactly the plain conditional score — no extrapolation
  g > 1:  overshoots past the conditional direction (typical production values: 2–8)
```

## A worked example

The same two-cluster toy setup as [[Classifier Guidance]], with the "condition" now being an entire target distribution centered at `(2, 0)` rather than a classifier's opinion. Starting from the origin (where the unconditional score is exactly zero):

```text
g = 0:  score (0.000, 0.000)  →  step lands at (0.000, 0.000)   (pure unconditional)
g = 1:  score (2.000, 0.000)  →  step lands at (1.000, 0.000)   (plain conditional)
g = 2:  score (4.000, 0.000)  →  step lands at (2.000, 0.000)   (right at the cluster center)
g = 4:  score (8.000, 0.000)  →  step lands at (4.000, 0.000)   (overshoots past it)
```

At `g = 1`, the result exactly matches what plain conditioning (ignoring the unconditional score entirely) would give. At `g = 2`, the extrapolation already lands beyond where a single conditional step would — and by `g = 4`, the step has overshot the cluster's own center by a factor of two, which is the real, documented trade-off CFG makes: stronger adherence to the condition, at the cost of sometimes pushing past what the data distribution itself would naturally produce.

## Bench

```bench
id: cfg-extrapolate
title: Classifier-free guidance overshoots on purpose
fallback: Adjust a CFG guidance scale and watch a toy denoising step move past where plain conditioning would land.
```

**Try this**

1. Set guidance scale to 1 and confirm it matches plain conditional generation.
2. Raise it toward 2 and watch the step land right at the target cluster's center.
3. Push it to 4 and notice the step overshoots well past the cluster.

**What you should notice:** guidance scale 1 is not "no guidance" — it's exactly what conditioning alone gives you; guidance only starts extrapolating *past* that once the scale exceeds 1.

## Where it appears in AI

* **Classifier-free guidance is the standard conditioning method in modern [[Text-to-Image Pipelines|text-to-image models]]**, specifically because it needs no separate classifier and trains naturally alongside the main model.
* **Typical production guidance scales (often 5–8) are well past g=1**, confirming that real systems deliberately overshoot the plain conditional direction to get sharper adherence to a text prompt.
* **Too high a scale is a known failure mode** — oversaturated colors, exaggerated or distorted features — directly caused by extrapolating too far past the conditional score.

## Common pitfalls

* **Thinking g=1 means "no guidance."** g=0 means no guidance (purely unconditional); g=1 means ordinary conditioning, with no extrapolation at all.
* **Assuming higher guidance scale is strictly better.** It trades diversity and realism for stronger condition-adherence — past a point, output quality visibly degrades.
* **Forgetting this needs the model trained to produce both scores.** CFG only works because the model was trained (typically by randomly dropping the condition during training) to represent the unconditional distribution as well as the conditional one — it's not a free property of any conditional model.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. What's the key difference between classifier-free guidance and classifier guidance?</summary>
Classifier-free guidance needs only one model, trained to produce both conditional and unconditional scores; classifier guidance needs a second, separately trained classifier that can evaluate noisy samples.
</details>

<details><summary>2. In the worked example, what guidance scale reproduces plain conditional generation exactly?</summary>
g = 1 — at that scale, the CFG formula reduces to exactly the conditional score, with no extrapolation.
</details>

<details><summary>3. Why would a practitioner deliberately choose a guidance scale greater than 1, knowing it overshoots?</summary>
Because the overshoot produces output that adheres more strongly and unambiguously to the condition (e.g. a text prompt), which is often worth the trade-off against sample diversity and realism, up to a point.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Classifier-free guidance (CFG):** steering a single model's generation by extrapolating past its conditional score, away from its unconditional score.
* **Guidance scale:** how far past the conditional score to extrapolate; g=1 is no extrapolation, g=0 is no guidance at all.
* **Condition dropping:** randomly training without the condition some fraction of the time, so one model learns both the conditional and unconditional distributions.

## Related

[[Classifier Guidance]] · [[Text-to-Image Pipelines]] · [[Cross-Attention Conditioning for Generation]]

## Cross-Attention Conditioning for Generation

Guidance (as in [[Classifier-Free Guidance]]) steers generation toward a condition through the score itself; this note covers a completely different way a condition enters a generative model — directly inside its architecture, through [[Encoder-Decoder Architectures as a Pattern|cross-attention]], letting the generated content look at the condition at every layer.

**You need:** [[Encoder-Decoder Architectures as a Pattern]].

## The question it answers

"How does a text prompt's embedding actually influence pixel generation, mechanically?" In most modern text-to-image and text-to-video models, every position being generated (an image patch, say) acts as a cross-attention *query* against the prompt's token embeddings, which serve as the *keys and values*. Each generated position attends over the whole prompt and pulls in — weighted by relevance — whichever words matter most to it, the same cross-attention mechanism used in encoder-decoder transformers, just with "generated content" and "condition" standing in for decoder and encoder.

## Intuition

Picture painting a canvas while a sentence describing the scene is pinned to the wall beside you. Before placing each brushstroke, you glance at the sentence and focus on whichever word is most relevant to that particular patch of canvas — "red" might draw your eye for one patch, "cat" for another. Every patch gets its own glance, and its own personalized mix of which words mattered — nothing forces every patch to react to the whole sentence equally.

## Definition and notation

```text
queries:        one per position being generated (e.g. an image latent patch)
keys, values:   one per conditioning token (e.g. a word embedding from the prompt)

attention(Q, K, V) = softmax(QKᵗ / √d) · V
→ each query's output is a weighted blend of the condition's value vectors,
  weighted by how similar that query is to each conditioning token's key
```

## A worked example

Two image-latent positions attend over three text-conditioning tokens — "a", "cat", "red" — using identity projections so the raw similarity is easy to trace. The first latent is built to resemble "a", the second to resemble "cat":

```text
latent 0 (≈ "a"):    attention weights  a: 0.419   cat: 0.254   red: 0.327
latent 1 (≈ "cat"):  attention weights  a: 0.274   cat: 0.408   red: 0.318
```

Each latent's highest attention weight lands on the text token it's closest to — latent 0 on "a" (0.419), latent 1 on "cat" (0.408) — and its output becomes a blend of all three conditioning values, dominated by whichever one it attended to most. Nothing forced this; it falls directly out of the same dot-product similarity that drives every other attention computation on this road.

## Bench

```bench
id: cross-attn-conditioning
title: An image latent attends over the prompt
fallback: Pick an image-latent position and see which word in a text prompt it attends to most, and by how much.
```

**Try this**

1. Pick the latent built to resemble "a" and check that it attends most to "a".
2. Pick the one built to resemble "cat" and compare.
3. Pick the blended latent and notice its attention is more evenly split.

**What you should notice:** each latent's attention weights are its own — there's no single, shared "how much does the prompt matter" number; every generated position gets its own personalized read of the condition.

## Where it appears in AI

* **Stable Diffusion-style text-to-image models insert cross-attention layers between the image's spatial positions and the text encoder's token embeddings** at multiple resolutions throughout the network, exactly this mechanism, repeated many times.
* **It's why some words in a prompt visibly "attach" to specific regions of a generated image** — attention maps for individual prompt tokens can be visualized directly, showing which pixels attended most to which word.
* **It composes with [[Classifier-Free Guidance|guidance]]** rather than replacing it: cross-attention is how the condition gets *used* inside the network; guidance is a separate, sampling-time lever for how strongly to *weight* that condition's influence overall.

## Common pitfalls

* **Confusing this with [[Classifier-Free Guidance|guidance]].** Guidance operates on the score at sampling time and needs no architectural change; cross-attention conditioning is built into the model's layers and runs during every forward pass, with or without any guidance on top.
* **Assuming every generated position attends equally to the whole prompt.** The worked example shows the opposite — attention weights differ sharply from one position to the next, based on each one's own query.
* **Forgetting this is the exact same mechanism as encoder-decoder cross-attention.** Nothing about it is specific to generation — "queries from one sequence, keys and values from another" is the whole idea, wherever it shows up.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. In cross-attention conditioning, what plays the role of queries, and what plays the role of keys and values?</summary>
The positions being generated (e.g. image patches) are the queries; the conditioning input's tokens (e.g. text embeddings) supply the keys and values.
</details>

<details><summary>2. In the worked example, why did latent 1 attend most strongly to "cat"?</summary>
Because latent 1's query vector was built to closely resemble the "cat" token's key vector, giving their dot-product similarity (and so their attention weight) the highest value among the three conditioning tokens.
</details>

<details><summary>3. How does cross-attention conditioning differ from guidance, mechanically?</summary>
Cross-attention is built into the model's architecture and runs on every forward pass regardless of any guidance setting; guidance is a separate adjustment applied to the model's output (its score) at sampling time, with no architectural change required.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Cross-attention conditioning:** using a condition's embeddings as the keys and values that generated positions attend over.
* **Attention map:** the per-position attention weights over a conditioning input, often visualized to see which words or regions influenced which output.
* **Query, key, value:** the three attention roles — here, generated positions supply queries, and the condition supplies keys and values.

## Related

[[Encoder-Decoder Architectures as a Pattern]] · [[Classifier-Free Guidance]] · [[Text-to-Image Pipelines]]

## ControlNet-Style Structural Conditioning

Guidance and cross-attention both steer generation toward a *concept* — a class, a prompt — expressed as a direction or an attended-to embedding. Neither one *forces* an exact structure. This note covers conditioning that does: locking part of the output to a given structural signal and letting the rest be generated around it.

**You need:** [[Classifier Guidance]].

## The question it answers

"How do you generate an image that must follow an exact pose, edge map, or layout — not just resemble one?" **Structural conditioning** (the idea behind ControlNet) treats some of the output as *fixed* to a given control signal (an edge map, a depth map, a pose skeleton) at every step of generation, while the rest of the output is still produced by the ordinary denoising process, informed by what the fixed part implies about the surrounding content.

## Intuition

It's like tracing part of a drawing from a stencil while freehand-sketching everything around it to match. The stencil-traced lines don't move no matter what — they're locked. But the shading, color and detail you add around them still have to make sense given what the stencil shows, the same way a free hand naturally fills in a face around a pair of stencil-traced eyes.

## Definition and notation

```text
at every denoising step, for a point x = (x_controlled, x_free):
  x_controlled is pinned to the control signal c, every step: x_controlled := c
  x_free is updated normally, using the score at the *current* (partially
    locked) point — so it still "sees" the controlled part's influence
```

The locked coordinates never move; the free coordinates evolve exactly as they would in ordinary score-based generation, except that every gradient they follow is computed at a point that already has the control signal baked in.

## A worked example

Two toy data clusters at `(−2, −1)` and `(2, 1)` — so the first coordinate and the second coordinate are correlated within each cluster. Locking the first coordinate to a control value and letting the second evolve freely for 5 steps, starting from `(0, 0)`:

```text
control x = 2:   free coordinate settles at y ≈ 0.760   → point ≈ (2.000, 0.760)
control x = -2:  free coordinate settles at y ≈ -0.760  → point ≈ (-2.000, -0.760)
with no control (free start, symmetric):  stays at (0.000, 0.000)
```

Locking x to 2 pulls the point into the neighborhood of the cluster at `(2, 1)`, and the free y-coordinate follows along, settling toward (though not exactly reaching, in just 5 steps) that cluster's own y-value of 1. The locked coordinate never wavered from exactly 2; everything else in the result is downstream of that one fixed value.

## Bench

```bench
id: controlnet-structural
title: A locked structural coordinate steers the rest
fallback: Lock one coordinate to a control value and watch where the free coordinate settles as a toy denoising process runs.
```

**Try this**

1. Set the control value to 2 and watch the free coordinate drift upward toward the matching cluster.
2. Set it to −2 and watch the free coordinate drift downward instead.
3. Set it to 0 (between both clusters) and see which way the free coordinate goes, if either.

**What you should notice:** the locked coordinate is never influenced by the free one — only the reverse. Structural conditioning is a one-way constraint, not a negotiation between the fixed and free parts.

## Where it appears in AI

* **ControlNet-style conditioning lets a single pretrained text-to-image model accept an edge map, pose skeleton, or depth map as an additional, exact structural input**, without retraining the base model from scratch.
* **It composes directly with [[Cross-Attention Conditioning for Generation|text conditioning]] and [[Classifier-Free Guidance|guidance]]**: a generated image can simultaneously follow an exact pose *and* a text prompt describing style and content.
* **[[Inpainting and Outpainting|inpainting]] is a close relative**: a mask marks which pixels are "controlled" by the original image and which are free to be generated.

## Common pitfalls

* **Expecting the free part to influence the locked part.** The constraint only runs one way — the controlled coordinates are pinned regardless of what the free coordinates' gradients would otherwise suggest.
* **Over-constraining a structure that conflicts with the content being asked for.** A control signal pulled from one kind of scene, paired with a text prompt for a totally different kind of scene, can produce an image where the two pull against each other.
* **Assuming structural conditioning alone determines the output's style or content.** It only fixes the part of the output it directly controls; the rest is still shaped by whatever other conditioning (text, guidance) is present.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. What's locked, and what's free, in structural conditioning?</summary>
A subset of the output's coordinates (the structural control signal, like an edge map or pose) is pinned exactly and never changes; the remaining coordinates are generated normally by the denoising process.
</details>

<details><summary>2. In the worked example, why did locking x to 2 cause the free y-coordinate to drift toward positive values?</summary>
Because the data cluster near x=2 is centered at y=1, so the denoising score at points near x=2 points the free y-coordinate upward, toward that cluster's own y-value.
</details>

<details><summary>3. Does the free coordinate's evolution ever affect the locked coordinate?</summary>
No — the constraint is one-directional; the locked coordinate is reset to the control value at every step regardless of what's happening to the free coordinate.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Structural conditioning:** pinning part of a generated output to an exact control signal throughout generation, while the rest is generated normally.
* **Control signal:** the structural input being enforced exactly — an edge map, depth map, or pose skeleton, for example.
* **One-way constraint:** the locked part of the output influences the free part, but never the reverse.

## Related

[[Classifier Guidance]] · [[Inpainting and Outpainting]] · [[Cross-Attention Conditioning for Generation]]

## Latent Space Interpolation and Manipulation

Every conditioning technique so far steers generation toward something. This note is about moving *between* two already-generated results, smoothly — and about why the obvious way to do that (a straight line) isn't usually the right one.

**You need:** [[Variational Autoencoders]].

## The question it answers

"How do you smoothly morph between two generated outputs, through their latent representations?" **Linear interpolation (lerp)** draws a straight line between two latent vectors. **Spherical interpolation (slerp)** instead follows the arc between them on the sphere of a given radius — and for latents whose *norm* matters to how a decoder interprets them (common when latents are drawn from something like a Gaussian, where most of the probability mass sits at a fairly consistent distance from the origin), slerp keeps that norm roughly constant along the path, while lerp doesn't.

## Intuition

Walking in a straight line between two points on the surface of a globe takes you *through* the globe, not along it — the direct path dips below the surface before rising back up to the destination. Walking the great-circle arc instead stays on the surface the whole way. Latent interpolation has the same geometry problem: a straight line between two latent vectors of similar length passes through points *closer to the origin* than either endpoint, which — for many generative decoders — corresponds to a point that doesn't look like a confident sample of anything.

## Definition and notation

```text
lerp(a, b, t)  = (1−t)·a + t·b                                    t ∈ [0, 1]

slerp(a, b, t) = sin((1−t)θ)/sin(θ) · a  +  sin(tθ)/sin(θ) · b
  θ = angle between a and b
```

## A worked example

Two unit-length latent vectors 90° apart, `a = (1, 0)` and `b = (0, 1)`:

```text
t = 0.00:  lerp (1.000, 0.000) |1.000|    slerp (1.000, 0.000) |1.000|
t = 0.25:  lerp (0.750, 0.250) |0.791|    slerp (0.924, 0.383) |1.000|
t = 0.50:  lerp (0.500, 0.500) |0.707|    slerp (0.707, 0.707) |1.000|
t = 0.75:  lerp (0.250, 0.750) |0.791|    slerp (0.383, 0.924) |1.000|
t = 1.00:  lerp (0.000, 1.000) |1.000|    slerp (0.000, 1.000) |1.000|
```

At the midpoint, linear interpolation's norm has shrunk to 0.707 — about 71% of either endpoint's length — while spherical interpolation's norm stays exactly 1.000 the entire way. Both paths start and end at exactly the same two points; only what happens *between* them differs.

## Bench

```bench
id: latent-interpolation
title: Interpolating between two latents
fallback: Slide between two latent vectors using linear and spherical interpolation and compare their paths and norms.
```

**Try this**

1. Move t from 0 to 1 and watch both paths trace out between the same two endpoints.
2. Watch the lerp path's norm dip in the middle while slerp's stays constant.
3. Compare the two curves drawn on the canvas — one is a straight line, the other follows the circle.

**What you should notice:** the two interpolations agree exactly at the endpoints (t=0 and t=1) and diverge everywhere in between, with lerp cutting the "inside" of the arc that slerp follows along its edge.

## Where it appears in AI

* **GAN and diffusion-model latent-space exploration tools almost always use slerp**, not lerp, specifically to avoid passing through lower-norm regions that tend to decode into blurrier or less coherent intermediate samples.
* **[[Variational Autoencoders|VAE]] latents are typically drawn to resemble a standard Gaussian**, where almost all the probability mass sits near one particular distance from the origin — exactly the setting where norm-preserving interpolation matters.
* **"Latent space walks"** — a common way to visualize what a generative model has learned — are built by interpolating (usually spherically) between sampled latents and decoding each intermediate point.

## Common pitfalls

* **Assuming lerp and slerp always differ meaningfully.** When two latents are nearly identical (θ close to 0) or when the decoder doesn't care about latent norm, the two methods barely differ in practice.
* **Forgetting slerp is undefined (or numerically unstable) at θ = 0.** When the two latents point in exactly the same direction, there's no unique arc between them — most implementations fall back to lerp in that case.
* **Interpolating in the wrong space.** Interpolating raw pixel values between two images produces a ghostly double-exposure, not a smooth morph — the whole point of latent interpolation is that the *latent* space, not pixel space, is where intermediate points decode into plausible content.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. What's the key geometric difference between lerp and slerp?</summary>
Lerp follows a straight line between two points; slerp follows the arc between them along a circle (or sphere) of roughly constant radius.
</details>

<details><summary>2. In the worked example, what happened to each method's norm at the midpoint?</summary>
Lerp's norm dropped to about 0.707, noticeably shorter than either endpoint's length of 1.000; slerp's norm stayed at exactly 1.000 throughout.
</details>

<details><summary>3. Why might a shrunken-norm latent point decode into a worse sample?</summary>
Because many generative decoders are built around latents drawn from a distribution (like a standard Gaussian) where most of the probability mass sits at a fairly consistent distance from the origin — a point much closer to the origin than that is an atypical input the decoder wasn't well-trained on.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Linear interpolation (lerp):** a straight-line blend between two points, parameterized by t ∈ [0, 1].
* **Spherical interpolation (slerp):** an interpolation that follows the arc between two vectors, keeping their norm roughly constant along the path.
* **Latent space walk:** a sequence of decoded outputs along an interpolated path between two (or more) latent points.

## Related

[[Variational Autoencoders]] · [[ControlNet-Style Structural Conditioning]] · [[Any-to-Any Generative Models]]

## Image Generation and Editing

With decoding and conditioning covered as general mechanisms, this district applies them to the modality generative AI is best known for: pictures — generating them from text, and then editing what's already there.

Topics on this stretch of the road:

* [[Text-to-Image Pipelines]]: assembling a text encoder, conditioning and a diffusion model into one text-to-image system.
* [[Super-Resolution and Upscaling]]: generating a higher-resolution image from a lower-resolution one.
* [[Inpainting and Outpainting]]: generating new pixels inside a masked region, or extending an image past its original border.
* [[Image-to-Image Translation and Style Transfer]]: transforming an image into a different style or domain while keeping its structure.
* [[Instruction-Based Image Editing]]: editing an image by describing the change in words, instead of painting a mask.

## Text-to-Image Pipelines

Every mechanism on the previous district's road — guidance, cross-attention conditioning — exists to answer one practical question: given a sentence of text, how do you actually get a picture out the other end? This note assembles them into one pipeline.

**You need:** [[Classifier-Free Guidance]], [[Cross-Attention Conditioning for Generation]].

## The question it answers

"How do a text prompt and a diffusion model actually combine into a finished image?" A text-to-image pipeline has three cooperating parts: a **text encoder** turns the prompt into embeddings; those embeddings condition every denoising step through **cross-attention**, letting the image-in-progress look at the prompt; and **classifier-free guidance** controls how strongly the final image is pulled toward matching that conditioning, versus simply being a plausible image in general. None of the three parts is new — this is where they're wired together.

## Intuition

A diffusion model without any conditioning is like a sculptor chipping away at marble with no brief beyond "reveal something that looks like it belongs in this studio." Text conditioning hands the sculptor a written description to consult at every stage. Guidance is how insistently they follow it — ignore it entirely, follow it as one consideration among many, or let it override everything else about what "looks right" on its own.

## Definition and notation

```text
pipeline, per denoising step:
  1. encode prompt → conditioning embeddings  (text encoder, done once)
  2. image-in-progress attends over those embeddings  (cross-attention, every step)
  3. combine conditional and unconditional scores  (classifier-free guidance, every step)
  4. take one denoising step using the combined score
→ repeat steps 2–4 until the image has fully denoised
```

## A worked example

Three toy "concepts" sit at fixed positions: cat at `(−2, 2)`, dog at `(2, 2)`, bird at `(0, −2.5)`. Starting every prompt from the same neutral point `(0, 0)` and running 6 CFG-guided denoising steps (guidance scale 3) toward whichever concept the prompt names:

```text
prompt "cat":   final position (-1.970, 2.012)   target (-2, 2)
prompt "dog":   final position ( 1.970, 2.012)   target ( 2, 2)
prompt "bird":  final position ( 0.000, -2.412)  target ( 0, -2.5)
```

Each prompt's own conditioning pulled the same starting point toward a different target, landing within a few percent of the exact concept position after only 6 steps — the entire pipeline, from "which word was in the prompt" to "where the generated point ended up," runs through nothing but conditioning and guidance applied repeatedly.

## Bench

```bench
id: text-to-image-pipeline
title: Text prompt → denoised image latent
fallback: Choose a prompt and step through a toy denoising process that pulls a point toward the matching concept.
```

**Try this**

1. Choose each of the three prompts and step through their denoising paths.
2. Compare how closely each path's final step lands on its target concept.
3. Notice all three paths start from the exact same point — only the prompt changes where they end up.

**What you should notice:** the three concepts are generated by the exact same stepping procedure; the prompt only changes which direction the conditioning pulls, not how the pulling itself works.

## Where it appears in AI

* **Every major text-to-image system (Stable Diffusion, DALL·E, Imagen) follows exactly this three-part structure**, differing mainly in which text encoder, which denoising architecture, and what guidance scale they default to.
* **The text encoder is often a model trained on a completely different task** (frequently a contrastive text-image model), reused here purely to produce conditioning embeddings.
* **[[Vision Transformers|the image side of this pipeline]] usually isn't a single pass over raw pixels** — most pipelines denoise a compressed latent representation, decoded to pixels only at the very end.

## Common pitfalls

* **Thinking the text encoder "draws" the image.** It only produces the conditioning embeddings; all the actual image content comes from the denoising process reading and reacting to those embeddings over many steps.
* **Assuming one pass through the pipeline is instant.** Realistic pipelines run tens to hundreds of denoising steps, each one a full cross-attention-and-guidance pass — this worked example's 6 steps is a deliberately small illustration.
* **Forgetting guidance and cross-attention are doing different jobs.** Cross-attention is how the condition gets read at all; guidance is how strongly the result is pulled toward matching it. Removing either changes the result in a different way.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. What are the three cooperating parts of a text-to-image pipeline?</summary>
A text encoder (turns the prompt into conditioning embeddings), cross-attention (lets the image-in-progress read those embeddings at every step), and classifier-free guidance (controls how strongly the result is pulled toward the condition).
</details>

<details><summary>2. In the worked example, what determined where each prompt's final position landed?</summary>
Only the target concept position named by the prompt — every prompt started from the exact same point and ran the same guided-denoising procedure.
</details>

<details><summary>3. Does the text encoder generate any part of the image's content directly?</summary>
No — it only produces conditioning embeddings; the image content is produced by the denoising process, which repeatedly reads those embeddings through cross-attention.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Text encoder:** the component that turns a text prompt into conditioning embeddings for the rest of the pipeline.
* **Text-to-image pipeline:** a text encoder, cross-attention conditioning, and classifier-free guidance combined to turn a prompt into an image.
* **Denoising step:** one iteration of the diffusion process, informed by the conditioning at every step.

## Related

[[Classifier-Free Guidance]] · [[Cross-Attention Conditioning for Generation]] · [[Super-Resolution and Upscaling]]

## Super-Resolution and Upscaling

A low-resolution image has fewer pixels than you want — every upscaling method has to invent the missing ones somehow. This note covers the spectrum from the cheapest possible answer to a genuinely learned one.

**You need:** [[Text-to-Image Pipelines]].

## The question it answers

"How do you produce a higher-resolution image from a lower-resolution one?" The simplest answer, **nearest-neighbor upsampling**, just repeats each existing pixel to fill the new grid — fast, but visibly blocky. **Bilinear upsampling** instead linearly blends between each pixel's neighbors, producing smoother (if slightly blurry) transitions. Learned super-resolution models go further still, using a trained network (often diffusion-based) to hallucinate plausible fine detail that was never in the low-resolution image to begin with, rather than merely smoothing between the pixels that were.

## Intuition

Blowing up a small photo in basic image-editing software without any smart scaling gives you visibly chunky squares — that's nearest-neighbor, each original pixel's color simply repeated across a block. Blur the result slightly and the blockiness softens into gradients — that's roughly what bilinear interpolation does mathematically. Neither one adds information that wasn't there; a learned super-resolution model is the first step that actually can, by having seen many pairs of low- and high-resolution images and learned what plausible fine detail tends to look like.

## Definition and notation

```text
nearest-neighbor:  output pixel = nearest input pixel's value (repeated into a block)

bilinear:  output pixel = weighted average of the 4 nearest input pixels,
           weights determined by how close the output position is to each
```

## A worked example

A tiny 2×2 low-resolution grid `[[10, 20], [30, 40]]`, upsampled 2× to a 4×4 grid two different ways:

```text
nearest-neighbor:        bilinear:
10 10 20 20               10.00 12.50 17.50 20.00
10 10 20 20               15.00 17.50 22.50 25.00
30 30 40 40               25.00 27.50 32.50 35.00
30 30 40 40               30.00 32.50 37.50 40.00
```

Nearest-neighbor produces four hard-edged blocks of exactly the original four values. Bilinear instead produces a smooth gradient between them — every value strictly between 10 and 40, changing gradually across the grid rather than jumping at block boundaries. Neither method invents detail finer than what a smooth blend between the original four values can represent.

## Bench

```bench
id: super-resolution-upsample
title: Blocky vs. smooth upsampling
```
