```bench
fallback: Compare nearest-neighbor and bilinear upsampling of the same tiny low-resolution grid at different scale factors.
```

**Try this**

1. Compare the two grids at the default scale factor.
2. Raise the scale factor and watch the nearest-neighbor side get blockier while bilinear stays smooth.
3. Consider what neither method can do: add detail finer than a smooth blend of the original four values.

**What you should notice:** bilinear always looks smoother, but it's still fundamentally limited to interpolating between the original pixels — it cannot add genuinely new information, which is exactly the gap a learned super-resolution model is trained to fill.

## Where it appears in AI

* **Diffusion-based super-resolution models condition a denoising process on the low-resolution image** (much like [[Text-to-Image Pipelines|text conditioning]], but with an image instead of text), letting the model hallucinate plausible detail rather than merely interpolate.
* **Nearest-neighbor and bilinear are still used constantly as cheap building blocks** — inside learned models (to resize feature maps between layers), and anywhere upscaling needs to be instant rather than learned.
* **Real super-resolution benchmarks measure against a known ground-truth high-resolution image**, which is exactly the setup [[Distributional Metrics (FID, Inception Score and CLIP Score)|distributional image metrics]] were built to score.

## Common pitfalls

* **Assuming any interpolation method can recover true lost detail.** Interpolation can only ever produce a smooth function of the pixels that exist — recovering plausible *new* detail requires a model that has learned what that detail tends to look like from other examples.
* **Confusing "smoother" with "more accurate."** Bilinear's smoothness is a side effect of linear blending, not evidence it's closer to what a higher-resolution camera would have actually captured.
* **Forgetting learned super-resolution models can hallucinate wrong detail.** Because they invent plausible-looking content rather than recovering real information, they can confidently add detail that looks reasonable but doesn't match what was actually there.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. What's the key difference between nearest-neighbor and bilinear upsampling?</summary>
Nearest-neighbor repeats each original pixel's value across a block, producing hard edges; bilinear linearly blends between neighboring pixels, producing a smooth gradient instead.
</details>

<details><summary>2. In the worked example, why couldn't either method add detail finer than what's visible in the 2×2 original?</summary>
Because both are purely interpolation methods — they compute new pixel values as some combination (a copy, or a weighted blend) of the existing pixels, with no mechanism for introducing information that wasn't already present.
</details>

<details><summary>3. How does a learned super-resolution model differ fundamentally from interpolation?</summary>
It has been trained on many pairs of low- and high-resolution images, letting it generate plausible fine detail that was never present in the low-resolution input, rather than only smoothing between existing values.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Nearest-neighbor upsampling:** filling a larger grid by repeating each original pixel's value across a block.
* **Bilinear upsampling:** filling a larger grid by linearly blending between each position's four nearest original pixels.
* **Super-resolution:** producing a higher-resolution version of an image, ranging from simple interpolation to learned detail hallucination.

## Related

[[Text-to-Image Pipelines]] · [[Instruction-Based Image Editing]] · [[Distributional Metrics (FID, Inception Score and CLIP Score)]]

## Inpainting and Outpainting

[[ControlNet-Style Structural Conditioning|structural conditioning]] locks part of a generated output to an exact value. This note covers the specific, very common case where that "exact value" comes from a real image: part of the output is known (because it's an existing photo), and the rest has to be generated to match.

**You need:** [[ControlNet-Style Structural Conditioning]].

## The question it answers

"How do you fill in a missing region of an image, or extend one past its original edges?" **Inpainting** fills a masked-out region that's surrounded by known pixels on multiple sides, so the generation has strong evidence from every direction about what belongs there. **Outpainting** extends an image past its original border, where the generated region has evidence from only one direction — and, intuitively, should become progressively less certain the further it gets from the known content.

## Intuition

Filling in a torn-out piece from the *middle* of an old photograph is a much better-constrained problem than guessing what's past its *edge* — in the middle, the surrounding pixels on every side all constrain the answer; past the edge, only the content immediately bordering it offers any clue, and that clue gets weaker and weaker in influence the further out you go. The mechanism in both cases is the same locking idea from [[ControlNet-Style Structural Conditioning|structural conditioning]], but where the known pixels sit around the gap determines how confident the result can be.

## Definition and notation

```text
inpainting: minimize Σ(x_{i+1} − x_i)²  given both endpoints fixed
  → the exact minimizer is linear interpolation between the two known values
    (a discrete harmonic / smoothness-prior solution)

outpainting: minimize Σ(x_{i+1} − x_i)² + λ·Σxᵢ²  given only one endpoint fixed
  → the solution decays from the known value toward the prior mean (here, 0)
    as it moves away from the anchor; larger λ decays faster
```

## A worked example

Filling 3 missing values between two known anchors, 10 and 50, by minimizing total squared adjacent differences — the exact solution is linear interpolation, confirmed by gradient descent landing on the same answer:

```text
inpaint 10 → 50 over 5 positions:  10.00  20.00  30.00  40.00  50.00
```

Extending past a single known anchor of 50, with no second anchor to pull toward, instead decays toward a prior mean of 0 — and how fast it decays depends entirely on how strongly that prior pulls (λ):

```text
λ = 0.30 (strong pull to prior):  50.00  29.25  17.28  10.49   6.86   5.27
λ = 0.05 (weak pull to prior):    50.00  41.78  35.65  31.30  28.52  27.16
```

Inpainting's result is fully determined by two known values and stays exactly linear between them. Outpainting's result starts at the known value but drifts toward an arbitrary prior the further it goes — exactly the intuition that content "far from the edge" should get less certain, not more.

## Bench

```bench
id: inpaint-outpaint
title: Filling a gap vs. extending past the edge
fallback: Compare values generated between two known anchors against values generated past a single anchor, at different prior strengths.
```

**Try this**

1. Look at inpaint mode and confirm the filled values interpolate linearly.
2. Switch to outpaint mode and watch the generated sequence decay away from the known anchor.
3. Raise the prior strength λ and watch the decay happen faster.

**What you should notice:** inpainting's result only depends on the two known values and λ plays no role; outpainting's result depends on both the one known value and how strongly λ pulls it toward a generic answer.

## Where it appears in AI

* **Production inpainting tools (removing an object from a photo, filling a torn region) rely on exactly this "constrained from multiple sides" property** to produce confident, consistent fills.
* **Outpainting tools (extending a photo's canvas) are a known weaker guarantee** — content generated far from the original image's edge is, by the nature of the problem, less constrained by real evidence.
* **[[Video Editing and Interpolation|frame interpolation]] is inpainting applied along the time axis instead of space**: filling in a frame that's "missing" between two known frames, with evidence from both sides.

## Common pitfalls

* **Expecting outpainted content far from the edge to be as reliable as inpainted content.** The worked example's own math shows why it can't be — outpainting has only one-sided evidence, which necessarily weakens with distance.
* **Assuming inpainting and outpainting use fundamentally different algorithms.** Both are the same "some pixels locked, some free, minimize a smoothness-plus-prior objective" idea — what differs is only how many sides of the gap have known values.
* **Forgetting a mask's shape matters, not just its size.** A thin gap surrounded almost entirely by known pixels is a much better-constrained inpainting problem than a large gap with a short known boundary.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. Why is inpainting generally more reliable than outpainting?</summary>
Inpainting has known pixels constraining the missing region from multiple directions, while outpainting only has known pixels on one side, leaving the generated content progressively less constrained the further it extends.
</details>

<details><summary>2. In the worked example, what determined how quickly outpainted values decayed toward the prior mean?</summary>
The strength of the prior-pull term, λ — a larger λ caused faster decay toward the prior mean, while a smaller λ let the known anchor's value persist longer.
</details>

<details><summary>3. What's the exact mathematical solution to the inpainting worked example, and why?</summary>
Linear interpolation between the two known anchors — it's the exact minimizer of total squared adjacent differences with both endpoints fixed, a discrete harmonic (smoothness-prior) solution.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Inpainting:** generating a masked region surrounded by known pixels on multiple sides.
* **Outpainting:** extending an image past its original border, with known pixels only on one side of the generated region.
* **Prior mean:** the generic value a one-sided generation process drifts toward as it moves away from known evidence.

## Related

[[ControlNet-Style Structural Conditioning]] · [[Image-to-Image Translation and Style Transfer]] · [[Video Editing and Interpolation]]

## Image-to-Image Translation and Style Transfer

Structural conditioning keeps a generated output faithful to an exact structure; this note covers a different kind of faithfulness — matching an image's *statistics* rather than its exact values, which is what lets a model "paint in the style of" something without copying it pixel for pixel.

**You need:** [[Inpainting and Outpainting]].

## The question it answers

"How do you transform an image's style while keeping its content recognizable?" **Neural style transfer** optimizes a generated image's features to simultaneously match a content image's features *position by position* (preserving what's where) and a style image's **Gram matrix** — the correlations between feature channels, computed across *all* positions at once, which captures texture and color relationships without caring where in the image they occur.

## Intuition

Two photographs of completely different scenes can still share a "feel" — the same palette, the same texture of brushstrokes — without having a single matching shape between them. That shared feel is a statistical property of the whole image (which colors and textures tend to co-occur), not a position-by-position one. Content loss asks "is the right thing in the right place?" Style loss asks a completely different question: "do these same textures and color-relationships show up somewhere, regardless of where?"

## Definition and notation

```text
Gram matrix of feature map F (positions × channels):
  G = FᵗF        (channels × channels; entry (a,b) = Σ over positions of Fₚ,ₐ·Fₚ,ᵦ)

style transfer loss:
  L = α · Σ (generated_position − content_position)²        (content: position-wise)
    + β · ‖Gram(generated) − Gram(style)‖²                   (style: Gram-matrix match)
```

## A worked example

A tiny 4-position, 2-channel "content" feature map with a left-to-right gradient, and a "style" feature map whose channels are much more strongly correlated with each other:

```text
content Gram matrix:  [1.68  0.32]      style Gram matrix:  [16.08  15.92]
                       [0.32  1.68]                           [15.92  16.08]
```

Optimizing a generated feature map to minimize `α·content_loss + β·style_loss` (α=1, β=0.05) by gradient descent, starting from the content image itself:

```text
loss before optimizing: 45.0720
loss after 500 steps:   15.3642

generated Gram matrix after optimizing:  [12.98  11.85]
                                           [11.85  12.98]
```

The generated Gram matrix moved sharply away from content's weakly-correlated `[1.68, 0.32]` pattern toward style's strongly-correlated one — while the generated features themselves still preserve content's original left-to-right ordering (the first position still has a higher first-channel value than the last position does), just rescaled to larger magnitudes consistent with the style's statistics.

## Bench

```bench
id: style-transfer-gram
title: Matching content structure and style statistics
fallback: Step through a gradient-descent optimization that pulls a generated feature map's statistics toward a style image's, while keeping content's structure.
```

**Try this**

1. Step through the optimization and watch the loss fall.
2. Compare the generated values at step 0 against after many steps — the relative ordering across positions should still resemble content's.
3. Reset and step through again, noticing the loss curve's shape doesn't change — it's a deterministic optimization from a fixed starting point.

**What you should notice:** the generated feature map's channel correlations move toward the style's Gram matrix, while the position-by-position structure that encodes "content" is preserved by the separate content-loss term pulling against it.

## Where it appears in AI

* **This is the original Gatys et al. neural style transfer algorithm**, using a pretrained CNN's feature maps (not toy 2-channel vectors) and optimizing pixels directly, usually over hundreds of gradient steps.
* **Diffusion-based image-to-image tools achieve a similar effect differently**, by partially noising a content image and denoising it back out under a different (style- or prompt-) conditioned score, rather than optimizing a Gram-matrix loss directly.
* **The same Gram-matrix idea underlies texture synthesis more broadly**, since a texture is, almost by definition, a pattern defined by its statistics rather than by exact pixel positions.

## Common pitfalls

* **Confusing style transfer's Gram matching with [[ControlNet-Style Structural Conditioning|structural conditioning]]'s exact locking.** Structural conditioning pins specific values exactly; style transfer only matches aggregate statistics across the whole image, leaving individual positions free to vary.
* **Setting the style weight (β) too high relative to content weight (α).** Push it too far and the content's own structure gets overwhelmed, producing something that matches the style's statistics but no longer resembles the original content image at all.
* **Assuming the Gram matrix captures spatial layout.** It explicitly doesn't — it's a sum over all positions, which is exactly why it captures "style" (occurring everywhere) rather than "content" (happening at specific positions).

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. What does a Gram matrix capture, and what does it deliberately throw away?</summary>
It captures how strongly pairs of feature channels are correlated across an entire image; it deliberately throws away *where* in the image those correlations occur, by summing over every position.
</details>

<details><summary>2. In the worked example, what evidence shows the generated features kept content's structure while adopting style's statistics?</summary>
The generated Gram matrix moved from content's weakly-correlated pattern toward style's strongly-correlated one, while the generated feature map's position-by-position ordering still matched content's original left-to-right gradient direction.
</details>

<details><summary>3. Why can two very different-looking images have the same Gram matrix?</summary>
Because the Gram matrix only captures aggregate channel correlations summed over the whole image — it contains no information about which position any particular feature value occurred at.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Gram matrix:** the matrix of correlations between feature channels, summed across every spatial position.
* **Content loss:** a position-by-position comparison between generated and content features, preserving layout.
* **Style loss:** a comparison between generated and style Gram matrices, preserving texture and color statistics without regard to position.

## Related

[[Inpainting and Outpainting]] · [[Instruction-Based Image Editing]] · [[Latent Space Interpolation and Manipulation]]

## Instruction-Based Image Editing

Masks and locked structural coordinates both require drawing an exact region by hand. This note covers editing an image by just describing the change in words instead — and the mechanism that makes "edit the cat, leave the background alone" work without anyone drawing a mask.

**You need:** [[Cross-Attention Conditioning for Generation]].

## The question it answers

"How can an edit instruction know *where* in an image to apply itself, with no mask at all?" The instruction's embedding attends over the image's patches via [[Cross-Attention Conditioning for Generation|the same cross-attention mechanism used for text-to-image conditioning]], and the resulting attention weight for each patch becomes how strongly that patch is nudged toward the edit. Patches the instruction has nothing to do with get low attention and barely change; patches it's clearly about get high attention and change a lot — a *soft*, learned localization, rather than a hard, hand-drawn boundary.

## Intuition

Tell someone "make the cat red" while they're looking at a photo, and they intuitively know to leave the sky and background alone — not because you drew a box around the cat, but because the instruction itself only makes sense applied to the cat. Cross-attention gives a model the same kind of implicit targeting: the instruction "attends" most strongly to whichever parts of the image it's actually about, and the edit is applied in proportion to that attention, with no explicit mask required.

## Definition and notation

```text
instruction embedding → query
image patches         → keys and values

attention weight(patch) = how strongly the instruction's query matches that patch's key
edit strength(patch)    = attention weight(patch)
edited patch = original patch + edit_strength · (target feature − original patch)
```

## A worked example

Four image patches — background, cat-face, cat-body, sky — with the instruction "make the cat red" as the query:

```text
attention to background: 0.190
attention to cat-face:    0.317   ← highest
attention to cat-body:    0.303
attention to sky:         0.190
```

Shifting each patch toward a "red" target feature in proportion to its attention weight:

```text
background edited with strength 0.190 (barely shifted)
cat-face   edited with strength 0.317 (shifted the most)
cat-body   edited with strength 0.303 (shifted almost as much)
sky        edited with strength 0.190 (barely shifted, same as background)
```

Nobody told the model which pixels belong to "the cat" — the two cat-related patches simply had embeddings more similar to the instruction's, earning them higher attention weight and a stronger edit, exactly mirroring how [[Cross-Attention Conditioning for Generation|text-to-image conditioning]] already worked, just applied to an edit instruction instead of a generation prompt.

## Bench

```bench
id: instruction-edit
title: An instruction edits what it attends to
fallback: Choose an edit instruction and see which image patch it attends to most strongly, and how much each patch is edited as a result.
```

**Try this**

1. Try "make the cat red" and confirm the cat patches get the strongest edit.
2. Try "make the sky red" and compare which patches shift most this time.
3. Notice the background patch's edit strength barely changes between the two instructions.

**What you should notice:** which patches get edited strongly is entirely determined by how similar each patch's embedding is to the instruction's — there's no separate step that decides "this is the region the instruction applies to."

## Where it appears in AI

* **Instruction-based image editing models (prompted with "make X do Y" rather than a text-to-image description) rely on exactly this soft localization**, letting one short instruction edit the right region of a photo with no mask drawn by the user.
* **It's a weaker, "soft" version of [[ControlNet-Style Structural Conditioning|structural conditioning]]'s hard locking**: nothing is ever fully exempt from the edit (even the lowest-attention patch still shifts a little), it just shifts far less.
* **Attention maps from this exact mechanism can be visualized directly**, showing which regions of an image an edit instruction actually targeted — a genuine window into why an edit landed where it did.

## Common pitfalls

* **Expecting a hard, mask-like boundary.** Every patch gets edited at least a little, proportional to its attention weight — there's no sharp cutoff between "edited" and "untouched" regions unless the attention weights happen to be extreme.
* **Assuming the instruction's wording alone determines the edit location.** It's the *similarity* between the instruction's embedding and each patch's embedding that determines attention — an ambiguous instruction, or patches with similar embeddings to unrelated content, can misdirect the edit.
* **Confusing this with [[Image-to-Image Translation and Style Transfer|style transfer]].** Style transfer changes statistics across the *whole* image; instruction-based editing specifically concentrates its effect on the patches the instruction's embedding is most similar to.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. What determines how strongly a given image patch is edited by an instruction?</summary>
The cross-attention weight between the instruction's query embedding and that patch's key embedding — a higher similarity means a higher attention weight, and so a stronger edit.
</details>

<details><summary>2. In the worked example, why did the cat-face and cat-body patches receive the strongest edit for "make the cat red"?</summary>
Their feature embeddings were built to be similar to the instruction's embedding, giving them higher attention weights (0.317 and 0.303) than the unrelated background and sky patches (0.190 each).
</details>

<details><summary>3. Is there a sharp boundary between "edited" and "unedited" regions in this mechanism?</summary>
No — every patch is shifted by some amount proportional to its attention weight; low-attention patches shift only a little rather than not at all.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Instruction-based editing:** editing an image by describing the desired change in natural language, with the edit's location determined implicitly by attention rather than a drawn mask.
* **Soft localization:** concentrating an effect on the most relevant regions by degree (via attention weight), rather than with a hard included/excluded boundary.
* **Edit strength:** how much a given patch is shifted toward the target of an edit, proportional to its attention weight.

## Related

[[Cross-Attention Conditioning for Generation]] · [[ControlNet-Style Structural Conditioning]] · [[Image-to-Image Translation and Style Transfer]]

## Audio and Speech Generation

The same generation machinery — learned distributions, conditioning, iterative refinement — applies just as well to sound. This district covers turning model output into audio: speech, a specific voice, and music.

Topics on this stretch of the road:

* [[Vocoders and Neural Audio Synthesis]]: turning an intermediate audio representation into an actual waveform.
* [[Text-to-Speech Pipelines]]: assembling text analysis, an acoustic model and a vocoder into spoken audio.
* [[Voice Cloning and Speaker Adaptation]]: adapting a speech model to a specific speaker's voice from a small sample.
* [[Music Generation]]: generating musical audio or symbolic scores conditioned on style, genre or a melody.

## Vocoders and Neural Audio Synthesis

Every generative model covered so far on this planet outputs some intermediate representation — a latent, a spectrogram-like set of frequencies and amplitudes — but none of that is sound yet. A speaker can't play a spectrogram. This note covers the last step: turning that representation into an actual waveform.

**You need:** [[Text-to-Image Pipelines]].

## The question it answers

"How does a model's intermediate audio representation become an actual sound wave?" A **vocoder** converts a compact acoustic representation (classically, a spectrogram of frequencies and amplitudes over time) into a raw waveform — a long sequence of sample values that, played back at the right rate, produces sound. The simplest version of this is **additive synthesis**: literally summing sine waves at the right frequencies and amplitudes. The hard part isn't the synthesis itself — it's making successive chunks of generated audio fit together without an audible click.

## Intuition

Imagine describing a song to someone only by sheet music — which notes, how loud, how long — and having them actually hum it. That's roughly what a vocoder does: it's handed "here are the frequencies and loudness over time," and has to produce actual sound pressure wiggling at those frequencies. The tricky part shows up if the humming is generated in separate short chunks: unless each chunk picks up exactly where the previous one's pitch wave left off, there's an audible "pop" at every seam — even though each chunk, played alone, sounds perfectly fine.

## Definition and notation

```text
a pure tone, sampled at rate SR, over n samples, starting at phase φ:
  sample[k] = amplitude · sin(φ + 2π · frequency · k / SR)
  (the phase at the end of this frame = φ + 2π · frequency · n / SR)

stitching two frames together smoothly means starting frame 2's phase
exactly where frame 1's phase left off -- not restarting at φ = 0
```

## A worked example

Two 40-sample frames of the same 440Hz tone, stitched together two different ways. Frame 1 ends mid-cycle, at a sample value of 0.7902:

```text
naive restart (frame 2 starts fresh at phase 0):
  frame 2's first sample: 0.0000   →   boundary jump of 0.7902  (a sharp click)

phase-continued (frame 2 starts where frame 1 left off):
  frame 2's first sample: 0.9511   →   boundary jump of 0.1609  (much smaller)
```

Both frames are, individually, a perfectly clean 440Hz tone. The difference is entirely about where in the wave's cycle the second frame *starts* — restarting at phase 0 every frame creates a large, audible discontinuity at every single boundary, while carrying the phase forward keeps the join far smoother.

## Bench

```bench
id: vocoder-phase
title: Stitching audio frames without a click
fallback: Toggle phase continuation on and off and watch the jump at the boundary between two synthesized frames.
```

**Try this**

1. Leave phase continuation off and note the size of the boundary jump.
2. Turn it on and compare.
3. Notice the dashed line marking exactly where the two frames meet.

**What you should notice:** the waveform within each frame doesn't change at all — only what happens exactly at the seam between them does.

## Where it appears in AI

* **Modern neural vocoders (WaveNet, WaveGlow, HiFi-GAN and similar) generate waveforms directly, trained end-to-end**, rather than using hand-built additive synthesis — but they still have to solve the same underlying continuity problem across any chunking of the output.
* **Classical vocoders (phase vocoders, Griffin-Lim reconstruction) explicitly track and reconstruct phase information** for exactly this reason — a magnitude spectrogram alone doesn't specify phase, and phase is what determines whether frames line up smoothly.
* **[[Text-to-Speech Pipelines|a TTS pipeline]] hands its acoustic output to a vocoder as the very last stage**, after duration, pitch and amplitude have already been decided.

## Common pitfalls

* **Assuming any audible artifact must come from an error in the synthesis math.** The worked example shows a technically "correct" tone at both frames still producing a loud click purely from a phase mismatch at the boundary.
* **Forgetting phase is invisible in a magnitude-only spectrogram.** A spectrogram typically records how loud each frequency is at each point in time, but not its phase — recovering or choosing a sensible phase is a separate problem a vocoder has to solve.
* **Treating vocoding as a trivial last step.** It's often the single largest factor in how natural or robotic a generated voice actually sounds, independent of how good the earlier pitch and duration predictions were.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. What causes the audible click in the "naive restart" case of the worked example?</summary>
Frame 2 starts its sine wave at phase 0 regardless of where frame 1's wave actually ended, creating a sudden jump in the sample value right at the boundary.
</details>

<details><summary>2. What does phase continuation actually change between the two stitching methods?</summary>
Only the starting phase of the second frame — everything else about the tone (frequency, amplitude) is identical in both cases.
</details>

<details><summary>3. Why doesn't a magnitude-only spectrogram fully specify a waveform?</summary>
Because it records how loud each frequency is at each time step, but not the phase of each frequency component — and phase determines exactly how sample values line up from one moment to the next.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Vocoder:** a component that converts an acoustic representation (like a spectrogram) into a raw audio waveform.
* **Additive synthesis:** producing a waveform by summing individual sine tones at specified frequencies and amplitudes.
* **Phase continuity:** ensuring a waveform's phase carries forward correctly across chunk boundaries, avoiding audible clicks.

## Related

[[Text-to-Speech Pipelines]] · [[Music Generation]] · [[IO-Aware Attention Computation]]

## Text-to-Speech Pipelines

Turning text into speech means answering several questions at once: how long should each sound last, how should pitch rise and fall, how loud should each part be — and only then, what should the waveform itself look like. This note covers the pipeline that answers them in order.

**You need:** [[Vocoders and Neural Audio Synthesis]].

## The question it answers

"How does written text become spoken audio?" A text-to-speech pipeline breaks a word into **phonemes** (its individual sound units), predicts a **duration**, **pitch** and **amplitude** for each one (together, the *prosody*), assembles those into a sequence of acoustic frames, and finally hands that sequence to a [[Vocoders and Neural Audio Synthesis|vocoder]] to produce the actual waveform. Every stage before the vocoder is deciding *what* should be said and *how* — the vocoder is the only stage that actually produces sound.

## Intuition

Reading a word aloud for the first time, you don't consciously plan "which sound unit, how long, what pitch, how loud" and then separately "now move my vocal cords accordingly" — but a TTS pipeline is forced to make all those decisions explicit and in sequence, because nothing about raw text specifies any of it. "Hello" contains no information at all about how long to hold the "oh" sound or how the pitch should rise on "eh" — a model has to predict all of that from scratch (or, in modern systems, learn to predict it from data).

## Definition and notation

```text
text → phonemes                          (how is it pronounced, as discrete sound units?)
phonemes → duration, pitch, amplitude    (prosody: how long, how high, how loud, per phoneme)
prosody → acoustic frames                (a sequence of per-frame acoustic targets)
acoustic frames → waveform               (the vocoder: the only stage that produces sound)
```

## A worked example

The word "hello" broken into four phonemes, each with its own predicted duration, pitch and amplitude:

```text
phoneme:    h      eh      l      oh
duration: 0.05   0.12    0.06   0.15   (seconds)
pitch:      0    180     170    160    (Hz; 0 = unvoiced)
amplitude: 0.3   0.8     0.6    0.9
```

```text
total duration:  0.05 + 0.12 + 0.06 + 0.15 = 0.380 seconds
```

The "h" phoneme is unvoiced (pitch 0 — it's mostly noise, not a tone) and quiet; "oh" is the longest, loudest, and lowest-pitched of the voiced sounds. None of these four numbers per phoneme came from the text itself — "hello" doesn't say how long the "oh" should last — they're the predictions a TTS pipeline has to make before any audio can be synthesized at all.

## Bench

```bench
id: tts-pipeline
title: Phonemes → duration, pitch and amplitude
fallback: Pick a word and see its phoneme sequence's predicted duration, pitch and amplitude, laid out over time.
```

**Try this**

1. Look at "hello" and note how the four phonemes' durations sum to the total.
2. Switch to "hi" and compare its pitch contour (notice "ai" is both longer and higher-pitched than any phoneme in "hello").
3. Notice the unvoiced "h" phoneme has no pitch bar at all.

**What you should notice:** every phoneme carries its own independent duration, pitch and amplitude — nothing about the word as a whole directly determines any one phoneme's prosody.

## Where it appears in AI

* **Modern TTS systems (Tacotron, FastSpeech, VITS and similar) predict duration, pitch and amplitude jointly from text**, usually without hand-built phoneme lookup tables, though the underlying stages are the same ones shown here.
* **[[Voice Cloning and Speaker Adaptation|voice cloning]] works by adapting exactly this prosody**, rather than by changing the vocoder or the text analysis — a cloned voice typically uses the same pipeline with shifted pitch and timing statistics.
* **Prosody prediction is where most of a synthetic voice's "naturalness" (or lack of it) comes from** — a vocoder reproducing an unnatural prosody faithfully still sounds unnatural.

## Common pitfalls

* **Assuming the vocoder is responsible for how natural speech sounds.** Most of what makes speech sound robotic or flat comes from the duration/pitch/amplitude predictions upstream of the vocoder, not from the waveform synthesis itself.
* **Forgetting unvoiced sounds have no pitch.** Sounds like "h", "s", or "f" are largely noise rather than a tone at a specific frequency — a pitch of exactly 0 (or undefined) is the correct, expected value for them, not a bug.
* **Treating phoneme duration as fixed per phoneme.** The same phoneme's duration varies by context (a stressed syllable, the end of a sentence) — real TTS duration models predict this per occurrence, not from a fixed lookup table.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. What are the four main stages of a text-to-speech pipeline, in order?</summary>
Text to phonemes, phonemes to prosody (duration, pitch, amplitude), prosody to acoustic frames, and acoustic frames to waveform (via a vocoder).
</details>

<details><summary>2. In the worked example, why does the "h" phoneme have a pitch of 0?</summary>
Because "h" is an unvoiced sound — mostly noise rather than a tone at a specific frequency — so it has no meaningful pitch value.
</details>

<details><summary>3. Which stage of the pipeline is the only one that actually produces sound?</summary>
The vocoder — every earlier stage only decides what the eventual sound should contain (phonemes, duration, pitch, amplitude), without producing any actual waveform.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Phoneme:** a discrete unit of sound that makes up spoken language.
* **Prosody:** the duration, pitch and amplitude pattern of speech — how long, how high, and how loud each sound is.
* **Acoustic frame:** one time-slice of the intermediate representation a vocoder converts into sound.

## Related

[[Vocoders and Neural Audio Synthesis]] · [[Voice Cloning and Speaker Adaptation]] · [[Music Generation]]

## Voice Cloning and Speaker Adaptation

A text-to-speech pipeline's prosody predictions describe *some* voice — but making it sound like a *specific* person, from only a few seconds of their recorded speech, is a separate problem. This note covers the simplest version of solving it: matching statistics instead of retraining anything.

**You need:** [[Text-to-Speech Pipelines]].

## The question it answers

"How can a handful of reference recordings change a synthetic voice to sound like that speaker?" The simplest form of **speaker adaptation** measures a statistic of the reference speaker's voice — most directly, their average pitch — from a small number of samples, and rescales a generic voice's own pitch contour to match that target statistic. It's not a full voice clone (the generic voice's phoneme-level style, accent and other characteristics stay unchanged), but it captures one of the most perceptually obvious properties of "whose voice this sounds like."

## Intuition

If you know someone's voice tends to sit noticeably higher or lower than your own, you can roughly impersonate the *pitch* of it just by scaling your own voice up or down by that ratio — without changing anything else about how you speak. That's the entire idea here: measure the target's average pitch from a few samples, compute how much higher or lower that is than the generic voice's average, and apply that same proportional shift across the whole pitch contour.

## Definition and notation

```text
generic mean pitch:     average over the generic voice's pitch contour
reference mean pitch:   average over a few samples of the target speaker's pitch

pitch-shift ratio = reference mean pitch / generic mean pitch

cloned contour[i] = generic contour[i] × pitch-shift ratio
```

## A worked example

A generic voice's pitch contour across five frames, averaging 125 Hz, adapted to a reference speaker whose three sampled frames average 178.67 Hz:

```text
generic contour:    120, 125, 130, 128, 122   (mean 125.00 Hz)
reference samples:  175, 182, 179             (mean 178.67 Hz)

pitch-shift ratio:  178.67 / 125.00 = 1.4293
```

Applying that ratio to every value in the generic contour:

```text
cloned contour:  171.52, 178.67, 185.81, 182.95, 174.38   (mean 178.67 Hz)
```

The cloned contour's mean lands exactly on the reference speaker's measured mean — by construction, since that's exactly what the ratio was chosen to do — while the generic contour's internal shape (which frame is higher or lower than its neighbors) is fully preserved, just uniformly rescaled.

## Bench

```bench
id: voice-clone-pitch
title: Adapting a voice from a few reference samples
fallback: Adjust a reference speaker's measured mean pitch and watch a generic pitch contour get rescaled to match it.
```

**Try this**

1. Raise the reference speaker's mean pitch and watch the cloned contour's bars grow taller.
2. Lower it below the generic mean and watch the cloned contour shrink instead.
3. Compare the *shape* of the two contours — notice it's identical, only the overall scale differs.

**What you should notice:** every cloned value is the same multiple of its generic counterpart — the adaptation changes the voice's overall register, not the pattern of ups and downs within it.

## Where it appears in AI

* **Real speaker adaptation systems go well beyond pitch alone**, adapting timbre, formant structure and speaking style — but pitch-ratio matching remains one of the simplest, most immediately audible components.
* **Few-shot voice cloning (from seconds, not hours, of reference audio) is an active, hard research problem** precisely because a handful of samples give only a noisy estimate of a speaker's true statistics — more reference audio generally means a more reliable clone.
* **It raises the same provenance concerns as any generative technique trained on a specific identifiable person's data** — see [[Content Safety and Red-Teaming|content safety practices]] built around synthetic voice misuse.

## Common pitfalls

* **Assuming a pitch shift alone constitutes a convincing voice clone.** Pitch is one perceptually important statistic, but a real-sounding clone also needs to match timbre, pacing, and other voice qualities this simple method doesn't touch.
* **Using too few reference samples.** A mean estimated from very few samples (as in this worked example) can be noisy — more reference audio gives a more reliable target statistic to adapt toward.
* **Forgetting the shift is applied uniformly.** This method rescales the whole contour by one ratio; it can't capture a reference speaker whose pitch *pattern* (not just average level) differs structurally from the generic voice's.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. What single statistic does this worked example use to adapt a generic voice?</summary>
Mean pitch — the average of the reference speaker's sampled pitch values, compared against the generic voice's own mean pitch.
</details>

<details><summary>2. In the worked example, why does the cloned contour's mean come out to exactly 178.67 Hz?</summary>
Because the pitch-shift ratio was defined specifically as the reference speaker's mean divided by the generic mean, and applying that ratio to every value in the generic contour forces the cloned contour's mean to equal the reference mean exactly.
</details>

<details><summary>3. What aspect of the generic voice does this method leave completely unchanged?</summary>
The relative shape of the pitch contour — which frames are higher or lower than their neighbors — since every value is scaled by the same ratio.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Speaker adaptation:** adjusting a generic synthetic voice to resemble a specific target speaker.
* **Pitch-shift ratio:** the factor by which a generic voice's pitch is rescaled to match a target speaker's measured mean pitch.
* **Few-shot cloning:** adapting a voice from only a small number of reference samples, rather than extensive training data.

## Related

[[Text-to-Speech Pipelines]] · [[Memorization and Training Data Leakage]] · [[Content Safety and Red-Teaming]]

## Music Generation

Speech has to be intelligible; music, rather famously, has to sound *right* in a way that's much harder to pin down — but at least one piece of that is concrete and checkable: whether the notes played actually belong to the key the piece is in.

**You need:** [[Constrained and Structured Generation]].

## The question it answers

"How do you generate a melody that stays in a given musical key?" The same [[Constrained and Structured Generation|grammar masking]] used to force valid arithmetic can force valid *scale membership*: at every step, mask out every note that doesn't belong to the chosen scale before sampling the next one, exactly the way an invalid arithmetic token was masked out earlier on this planet. The underlying note-to-note preferences (a toy model favoring small, stepwise melodic motion) stay exactly the same — only which notes are *available* to express that preference over changes.

## Intuition

A jazz musician improvising over a chord progression isn't choosing from all twelve notes with equal freedom — they're choosing from whichever subset fits the current harmony, and the *feel* of the solo comes from how they move within that restricted set. Masking a generative model's output to a musical scale is the same restriction: it doesn't change what the model finds melodically interesting (stepwise motion, in this toy setup), it changes which notes count as valid choices in the first place.

## Definition and notation

```text
12 chromatic notes, indices 0-11 (C, C#, D, D#, E, F, F#, G, G#, A, A#, B)
C major scale = {0, 2, 4, 5, 7, 9, 11}        (7 of the 12 notes)

toy melodic preference: logit(next | prev) = −0.5 · |next − prev|
  (favors notes close in pitch to the previous one)

scale-constrained generation: mask out every note not in the scale,
  exactly as in grammar-masked decoding, then sample as usual
```

## A worked example

Generating a 10-note melody from the same starting note and the same stepwise-motion preference, with and without a C-major scale mask:

```text
unconstrained:  C D E D# E C# D D# D F# F
  notes outside C major:  D#, C#, D#  (3 off-scale notes)

scale-masked:   C D E E F D D E E G F
  notes outside C major:  (none)
```

Both sequences follow the same underlying preference for small melodic steps — that's why they look similar overall — but the unconstrained version drifts onto chromatic notes (D#, C#) that don't belong to C major whenever they happen to be the closest-pitch option, while the masked version is guaranteed to never do that, regardless of what the underlying preference would otherwise pick.

## Bench

```bench
id: scale-constrained-music
title: Keeping a melody in key
fallback: Toggle a scale mask on and off and see how many notes in a generated melody fall outside the chosen musical scale.
```

**Try this**

1. With the mask off, count how many generated notes fall outside C major.
2. Turn the mask on and confirm that count drops to zero.
3. Notice the overall melodic "shape" — mostly small steps — doesn't change between the two.

**What you should notice:** the mask doesn't change the model's underlying melodic taste, only which notes it's allowed to express that taste through — the exact same relationship between a model's preferences and a grammar mask seen earlier with arithmetic generation.

## Where it appears in AI

* **Real symbolic music generation models (predicting notes or chords, not raw audio) commonly use exactly this kind of scale or chord-tone masking** as a hard constraint layered on top of a learned model's preferences.
* **Audio-domain music generation (producing a waveform directly, rather than symbolic notes) can't apply this mask as cleanly** — a raw audio sample doesn't have a discrete "note" to mask, which is part of why symbolic and audio-domain music generation remain fairly separate approaches.
* **[[Vocoders and Neural Audio Synthesis|turning a generated symbolic melody into actual sound]] still needs a synthesis step afterward** — generating the right notes and generating a pleasant-sounding performance of them are different problems.

## Common pitfalls

* **Assuming a scale mask guarantees "good" music.** It only guarantees the notes belong to the chosen scale — rhythm, harmony, phrasing and structure are entirely separate concerns a note-level mask says nothing about.
* **Forgetting a mask changes what's available, not what's preferred.** The underlying stepwise-motion preference in this worked example is unaffected by the mask — it simply can no longer act on now-forbidden notes.
* **Treating "off-scale" as always wrong in real music.** Deliberate chromaticism (brief excursions outside the home scale) is a normal and expressive part of real composition — a hard mask is a simplification useful for a toy demonstration, not a rule real music always follows.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. What's being masked in scale-constrained melody generation, and what stays unmasked?</summary>
The available next notes are masked down to only those belonging to the chosen scale; the underlying preference for which of the remaining notes to pick (here, favoring small melodic steps) is unchanged.
</details>

<details><summary>2. In the worked example, which notes appeared in the unconstrained melody that the scale mask would have forbidden?</summary>
D#, C#, and D# again — three notes that fall outside the C major scale.
</details>

<details><summary>3. Why is this the same underlying technique as grammar-masked arithmetic generation?</summary>
Both work by setting the logits of disallowed options to −∞ before sampling, guaranteeing the output can never include anything outside the allowed set — only what counts as "allowed" differs between the two domains.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Scale:** a fixed subset of notes (here, 7 of 12) that a piece of music is considered to be "in."
* **Scale masking:** forcing generated notes to belong to a chosen scale by masking out every note that doesn't.
* **Symbolic music generation:** generating discrete musical events (notes, chords) rather than a raw audio waveform directly.

## Related

[[Constrained and Structured Generation]] · [[Vocoders and Neural Audio Synthesis]] · [[Code Generation and Program Synthesis]]

## Video, 3D and Code Generation

Three modalities that each push generation past where images and audio stop: video adds time, 3D adds an extra spatial dimension and viewpoint consistency, and code adds a requirement neither has — the output must actually run.

Topics on this stretch of the road:

* [[Video Generation and Temporal Consistency]]: generating a sequence of frames that stays coherent from one frame to the next.
* [[Video Editing and Interpolation]]: modifying existing footage or generating the frames between two given ones.
* [[3D Asset and Scene Generation]]: generating a three-dimensional object or scene instead of a flat image.
* [[Code Generation and Program Synthesis]]: generating source code, and what makes that different from generating prose.

## Video Generation and Temporal Consistency

Generate a sequence of images one frame at a time, each independently, and you get something that technically shows motion but looks nothing like video — it flickers and jumps, because nothing ties one frame's content to the next. This note covers the specific problem of keeping frames coherent with each other, not just individually plausible.

**You need:** [[Text-to-Image Pipelines]].

## The question it answers

"Why doesn't generating a sequence of plausible images automatically produce a plausible video?" Each frame of a diffusion-generated sequence has its own randomness — its own noise, its own sampling — so two frames generated independently can each look fine on their own while still disagreeing wildly about where things are from one moment to the next. **Temporal consistency** means damping how much a frame is allowed to move away from the previous one, so successive frames stay correlated instead of each being an independent roll of the dice.

## Intuition

Flip through a stack of individually well-drawn photographs of the same scene, each drawn by a different artist with no sight of the others' work, and the "animation" will jump and flicker even though every single photograph looks fine. A flipbook only looks like smooth motion when each page is drawn *with the previous page in view* — exactly the difference between independently sampling every video frame and generating each frame as a damped continuation of the last.

## Definition and notation

```text
without consistency:  frameₜ = frameₜ₋₁ + step_size · score(frameₜ₋₁) + noiseₜ
                       (independent noise every frame → large frame-to-frame jumps)

with consistency (damping factor λ):
  frameₜ = frameₜ₋₁ + (1 − λ) · [step_size · score(frameₜ₋₁) + noiseₜ]
  (λ close to 1: barely move from the previous frame at all;
   λ = 0: identical to the undamped case)
```

## A worked example

Eight toy frames generated from the same starting point and the same random noise sequence, compared with and without a damping term:

```text
no consistency (λ=0):    total frame-to-frame motion = 7.599
with consistency (λ=0.7): total frame-to-frame motion = 2.183
```

Damping with λ=0.7 cut the total motion across all 8 frames by more than 70%, using the exact same underlying noise and the exact same pull toward the data distribution — the only change was how much of each frame's proposed movement was allowed to actually take effect.

## Bench

```bench
id: video-temporal-consistency
title: Jittery frames vs. a temporally consistent sequence
fallback: Adjust a temporal-consistency damping factor and watch the total frame-to-frame motion in a toy generated sequence.
```

**Try this**

1. Set λ to 0 and look at how jagged the resulting path is.
2. Raise λ toward 0.9 and watch the path smooth out into much smaller steps.
3. Compare the total-motion readout across a few different λ values.

**What you should notice:** every frame still ends up somewhere near the data distribution regardless of λ — consistency doesn't change *where* the content tends to go, only how abruptly it gets there from one frame to the next.

## Where it appears in AI

* **Real video diffusion models add temporal attention or 3D convolutions across frames** rather than a simple damping term, letting the model learn consistency directly instead of imposing it as a fixed rule — but the goal is identical to this worked example's.
* **Too much consistency produces a different, equally obvious failure**: a video that barely moves at all, since very high λ suppresses essentially all frame-to-frame change.
* **[[Video Editing and Interpolation|frame interpolation]] solves a related but distinct problem**: filling in frames *between* two already-fixed frames, rather than generating a new frame forward from one.

## Common pitfalls

* **Assuming independently-plausible frames are sufficient for a plausible video.** The worked example is built specifically to show this isn't true — each frame can be individually fine while the sequence as a whole flickers.
* **Treating temporal consistency as purely a post-processing smoothing step.** In the worked example, it's applied *during* generation, shaping every frame as it's produced, not blurring already-finished frames afterward.
* **Pushing the damping factor too high.** Past a point, the sequence stops showing meaningful motion at all — consistency and motion are a genuine trade-off, not a free improvement.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. Why can a sequence of individually plausible frames still fail to look like video?</summary>
Because each frame's own randomness is independent of the others, so even though every single frame looks fine on its own, the content can jump around unpredictably from one frame to the next.
</details>

<details><summary>2. In the worked example, what changed between the two runs, and what stayed the same?</summary>
The damping factor λ changed, reducing how much of each frame's proposed movement was allowed to take effect; the underlying noise sequence and the pull toward the data distribution stayed identical in both runs.
</details>

<details><summary>3. What happens if the temporal-consistency damping factor is set too high?</summary>
The generated sequence barely moves at all from frame to frame, since almost none of each frame's proposed change is allowed to take effect — trading away motion entirely for consistency.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Temporal consistency:** keeping successive frames of a generated sequence correlated with each other, rather than independently sampled.
* **Damping factor:** how much of a frame's proposed change from the previous frame is suppressed to maintain consistency.
* **Frame-to-frame motion:** the total distance moved between consecutive frames across a sequence.

## Related

[[Text-to-Image Pipelines]] · [[Video Editing and Interpolation]] · [[Unified Multimodal Generation]]

## Video Editing and Interpolation

[[Inpainting and Outpainting|inpainting]] fills in missing pixels surrounded by known ones. Frame interpolation is the exact same idea, just rotated: the "gap" to fill is in time rather than space, and what's known on either side is a whole frame instead of a few pixels.

**You need:** [[Inpainting and Outpainting]], [[Video Generation and Temporal Consistency]].

## The question it answers

"How do you generate the frames in between two frames you already have?" **Frame interpolation** treats the in-between frames exactly the way [[Inpainting and Outpainting|inpainting]] treats missing pixels between two known anchors: minimize total squared change between adjacent frames, with the known start and end frames fixed. Because both ends are known, the result is just as well-constrained as spatial inpainting was — unlike [[Video Generation and Temporal Consistency|generating new frames forward]], which only ever has evidence from one direction.

## Intuition

If you have a photo of a ball at the top of a bounce and another photo of it at the bottom, sketching plausible in-between positions is a well-posed problem — you know exactly where the motion starts and ends, you're just filling in a smooth path between them. That's a fundamentally easier task than predicting where the ball is going to end up with no second photo at all, which is what forward video generation has to do.

## Definition and notation

```text
given frame A (position a) and frame B (position b), n frames apart:
  interpolated frame i = a + (i/n)·(b−a)      for i = 0, ..., n

(this is exactly harmonic inpainting from the Image Generation and Editing
district, with "pixel value" replaced by "frame position")
```

## A worked example

Interpolating 3 frames between a known starting frame at position 10 and a known ending frame at position 50:

```text
known frame A:  10
interpolated:   20, 30, 40
known frame B:  50
```

This is the identical computation already verified in [[Inpainting and Outpainting]] — the only thing that changed is calling the sequence "frames over time" instead of "pixels across space." Both known frames are respected exactly, and the interpolated frames fall on a perfectly even path between them.

## Bench

```bench
id: frame-interpolation
title: Interpolating the frames in between
fallback: Choose how many frames to interpolate between two known frames and watch the generated positions fall evenly between them.
```

**Try this**

1. Set the number of interpolated frames low, then high, and watch the sequence stay evenly spaced either way.
2. Compare the two solid (known) endpoints against the hollow (interpolated) frames in between.
3. Notice the interpolated values never depend on anything except the two known endpoints and how many frames separate them.

**What you should notice:** this is the exact same harmonic-interpolation result from [[Inpainting and Outpainting]], applied along a different axis — nothing about the underlying math changed.

## Where it appears in AI

* **Video frame-rate upconversion (making a 30fps video look like 60fps) is built on exactly this idea**, generating new frames between existing ones rather than extending the video forward in time.
* **Real frame interpolation models usually interpolate in a learned feature space informed by motion (optical flow), not a flat linear path** — the toy linear version here shows the well-constrained *shape* of the problem, not the sophistication of a production method.
* **Slow-motion effects from standard-frame-rate footage are a direct application**: interpolating many frames between each pair of real frames to synthesize the missing in-between motion.

## Common pitfalls

* **Confusing frame interpolation with [[Video Generation and Temporal Consistency|forward video generation]].** Interpolation has evidence from both sides of the gap; forward generation only ever has evidence from one side (the past), which is a meaningfully harder-constrained problem.
* **Assuming a straight-line interpolation always looks right.** Real motion is rarely linear in pixel space — a ball's bounce accelerates and decelerates, which is exactly why production systems use learned motion models rather than this toy's flat linear path.
* **Forgetting both endpoints must be real, known frames.** The well-constrained property only holds because both sides of the gap are fixed; interpolating past either known frame is outpainting, not inpainting, and inherits that weaker guarantee.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. Why is frame interpolation better-constrained than forward video generation?</summary>
Because frame interpolation has a known frame on both sides of the gap being filled, while forward generation only has evidence from the preceding frames, with nothing constraining where the sequence "should" end up.
</details>

<details><summary>2. In the worked example, what determines the interpolated frame values?</summary>
Only the two known endpoint positions and how many frames separate them — the same harmonic (linear) interpolation formula used for spatial inpainting.
</details>

<details><summary>3. What's a real limitation of using flat linear interpolation for video frames?</summary>
Real motion is rarely linear — accelerating or decelerating motion (like a bouncing ball) isn't well approximated by evenly-spaced positions, which is why production frame interpolation uses learned, motion-aware methods instead.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Frame interpolation:** generating frames between two known frames, analogous to inpainting across time instead of space.
* **Well-constrained:** having evidence on both sides of a gap, as opposed to only one side.
* **Frame-rate upconversion:** increasing a video's frame rate by interpolating new frames between existing ones.

## Related

[[Inpainting and Outpainting]] · [[Video Generation and Temporal Consistency]] · [[3D Asset and Scene Generation]]

## 3D Asset and Scene Generation

Every generation method so far on this planet produces a flat grid of values — pixels, a spectrogram, a sequence of frames. A genuinely three-dimensional object needs a different kind of representation entirely: something that can answer "is this point inside the shape, or outside it?" for *any* point in space, not just at fixed grid positions.

**You need:** [[ControlNet-Style Structural Conditioning]].

## The question it answers

"How do you represent and generate a three-dimensional shape, rather than a flat image?" A **signed distance function (SDF)** represents a shape implicitly: given any point in space, it returns how far that point is from the shape's surface — negative if the point is inside, positive if outside, zero exactly on the surface. Combining two SDFs with a **smooth minimum** blends their shapes into one rounded union, rather than a sharp, un-blended overlap — one of the simplest building blocks for generating 3D content without ever specifying a fixed grid of voxels or vertices.

## Intuition

A flat image is a fixed table of color values, one per pixel — there's no "value" for a point between pixels unless you interpolate. An SDF is the opposite: it's a *function*, answerable at any point in continuous space, not a fixed table at all. Two SDF shapes placed near each other and combined with a plain minimum would meet at a sharp seam, like two separate lumps of clay just touching. A *smooth* minimum is like actually pressing the clay together — the transition rounds out into one continuous surface instead of staying two distinct shapes with a crease where they meet.

## Definition and notation

```text
signed distance of a point p from a circle of radius r centered at c:
  sd(p) = |p − c| − r          (negative inside, zero on the boundary, positive outside)

plain union of two shapes:        min(d₁, d₂)                  -- sharp seam
smooth union, blend amount k:     smoothMin(d₁, d₂, k)          -- rounded seam
  k = 0 reduces exactly to the plain (sharp) union
```

## A worked example

Two circles (toy 2D stand-ins for spheres), each radius 0.6, centered at `(−0.5, 0)` and `(0.5, 0)` — close enough to overlap. The signed distance exactly at the midpoint between them, `(0, 0)`, under different blend amounts:

```text
k = 0.0 (plain union, sharp seam):     distance at midpoint = −0.1000
k = 0.3 (some blending):               distance at midpoint = −0.1750
k = 0.8 (strong blending):             distance at midpoint = −0.3000
```

As the blend amount increases, the midpoint reads as *further inside* the combined shape than either circle alone would suggest (each circle alone gives exactly −0.1 at that point) — exactly what a smoothly filled-in join between the two shapes should look like, with no sharp crease anywhere in between.

## Bench

```bench
id: sdf-blend-3d
title: Blending two implicit shapes
fallback: Adjust the blend amount between two overlapping implicit shapes and watch the join between them round out.
```

**Try this**

1. Set the blend amount to 0 and look at the sharp seam where the two circles meet.
2. Raise it and watch the seam round into a single smooth shape.
3. Note how the midpoint's signed distance value changes as blending increases.

**What you should notice:** the two circles' individual shapes barely change — almost all the visible difference happens exactly where they overlap, which is precisely where a smooth minimum differs from a plain one.

## Where it appears in AI

* **Many 3D generative models (and classical computer graphics before them) represent shapes as neural or explicit SDFs**, rendered by ray marching (stepping along a ray until the SDF reports a point on the surface) rather than storing an explicit mesh or voxel grid.
* **NeRF-style scene representations use a related but distinct idea** — a learned function of 3D position (and viewing direction) that predicts density and color, rather than signed distance specifically — solving the same core problem of representing 3D content without a fixed grid.
* **[[Video Generation and Temporal Consistency|the same consistency problem from video]] shows up again in 3D**: a generated 3D scene viewed from different angles needs to agree with itself, the spatial analogue of frames needing to agree with each other over time.

## Common pitfalls

* **Confusing "signed distance" with "just distance."** The sign is what makes an SDF useful for defining a shape's interior at all — without it, there's no way to distinguish "inside" from "outside" using the distance value alone.
* **Assuming smooth blending only affects appearance.** It changes the actual signed-distance values (and so, where the true surface boundary lies) in the overlap region — it's a real geometric operation, not a cosmetic rendering effect.
* **Treating k=0 as a special, different algorithm.** It's simply the smooth-minimum formula at its weakest setting, reducing exactly to a plain minimum — not a separate method requiring different code.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. What does a signed distance function return for a point exactly on a shape's surface?</summary>
Zero — positive values mean outside the shape, negative values mean inside it, and zero marks the boundary itself.
</details>

<details><summary>2. In the worked example, why did the midpoint's distance value get more negative as the blend amount increased?</summary>
Because stronger blending fills in the overlap region more fully, making points there read as further inside the combined shape than either individual circle would suggest on its own.
</details>

<details><summary>3. What does the blend amount k=0 case reduce to?</summary>
A plain (sharp) union — the smooth-minimum formula, at its weakest setting, is mathematically identical to just taking the minimum of the two distances.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Signed distance function (SDF):** a function of position that returns distance to a shape's surface, negative inside and positive outside.
* **Smooth minimum:** a blending operation that rounds the join between two combined shapes instead of leaving a sharp seam.
* **Ray marching:** rendering an SDF-defined shape by stepping along a ray until the function reports a point on the surface.

## Related

[[ControlNet-Style Structural Conditioning]] · [[Video Editing and Interpolation]] · [[Any-to-Any Generative Models]]

## Code Generation and Program Synthesis

[[Constrained and Structured Generation|a grammar mask]] guarantees generated arithmetic is syntactically valid — but valid syntax and a program that actually does what you want are two different guarantees entirely. This note covers the second one, and a method that can check it directly: generating candidates and testing whether they actually compute the right thing.

**You need:** [[Constrained and Structured Generation]].

## The question it answers

"How do you generate a program that doesn't just parse, but actually produces a desired result?" **Program synthesis** adds a layer on top of grammar-constrained generation: don't just mask out invalid syntax, also *run* each candidate and check whether it produces the target output. Unlike natural-language generation, code has an unusually sharp advantage here — it's directly executable, so "is this candidate correct?" can often be answered exactly, by running it, rather than only estimated.

## Intuition

Guessing a sentence that correctly describes a situation has no simple check beyond human judgment. Guessing a short arithmetic expression that evaluates to exactly 7, on the other hand, can be checked by literally running the expression and comparing the result — no judgment call required. Program synthesis leans hard into that asymmetry: search (or generate many candidates) and keep only the ones that pass an automatic, exact test.

## Definition and notation

```text
grammar-valid candidate programs: generated (or enumerated) under a syntax
  constraint, as in grammar-masked decoding

program synthesis: additionally keep only candidates c such that
  execute(c) == target
```

## A worked example

Every grammar-valid 5-token postfix (reverse Polish) arithmetic program built from digits `{1, 2, 3}` and operators `{+, -, *}`, in the fixed shape `a b op1 c op2`:

```text
total grammar-valid candidates:  3 × 3 × 3 × 3 × 3 = 243
candidates that evaluate to 7:   10

first few matches:
  1 3 + 3 +  =  7     (1+3=4, 4+3=7)
  2 2 + 3 +  =  7     (2+2=4, 4+3=7)
  2 2 * 3 +  =  7     (2*2=4, 4+3=7)
  2 3 + 2 +  =  7     (2+3=5, 5+2=7)
  2 3 * 1 +  =  7     (2*3=6, 6+1=7)
```

Every one of the 243 grammar-valid candidates is syntactically fine — none would be rejected by a grammar mask. But only 10 of them actually compute 7, and finding those 10 required *executing* each candidate and checking its output, something a grammar mask alone has no way to do.

## Bench

```bench
id: program-synthesis-search
title: Searching for a program that computes a target
fallback: Pick a target value and see how many grammar-valid toy programs, out of all the candidates searched, actually evaluate to it.
```

**Try this**

1. Try a few different target values and compare how many candidates match each one.
2. Notice some targets have many matching programs, while others may have very few.
3. Look at the matching programs' structures — some use `+`, some `*`, in different combinations.

**What you should notice:** every candidate searched is already guaranteed syntactically valid (that's what the grammar enforces); it's execution — not syntax checking — that separates a merely-valid program from a correct one.

## Where it appears in AI

* **Real code-generation models rely on exactly this execution-based check wherever it's available**: running generated code against test cases, compiling it, or checking a unit test, is a far sharper correctness signal than anything available for free-form natural language.
* **This worked example's brute-force search doesn't scale to real programs** — the number of grammar-valid candidates explodes combinatorially with program length, which is exactly why real program synthesis uses a learned model to propose promising candidates rather than enumerating every possibility.
* **[[Self-Consistency and Best-of-N Sampling|best-of-N sampling]] combines naturally with this idea**: generate many candidate programs from a model, execute each one, and keep whichever actually passes.

## Common pitfalls

* **Assuming grammar validity implies correctness.** The worked example's own numbers make this concrete: all 243 candidates are grammar-valid, but only 10 are correct — syntax and correctness are entirely separate properties.
* **Forgetting execution-based checking requires the program to be safely runnable.** Toy arithmetic is trivially safe to execute; real code-generation systems need sandboxing and resource limits before running arbitrary generated code.
* **Treating brute-force search as a real synthesis method.** It works here because the candidate space is tiny (243 programs); real-world code has far too large a space to enumerate, which is why practical synthesis guides the search with a learned model instead.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. What's the key advantage code generation has over natural-language generation, for checking correctness?</summary>
Code is directly executable, so a candidate's correctness can often be checked exactly by running it and comparing the output to a target, rather than only estimated.
</details>

<details><summary>2. In the worked example, why were all 243 candidates "valid" but only 10 "correct"?</summary>
All 243 satisfied the grammar (correct token types in the correct positions); only 10 of them, when actually executed, happened to evaluate to the target value of 7.
</details>

<details><summary>3. Why doesn't brute-force enumeration scale to real program synthesis?</summary>
The number of grammar-valid candidates grows combinatorially with program length, making exhaustive enumeration infeasible for anything beyond very short toy programs — real systems need a model to propose likely candidates instead of checking every possibility.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Program synthesis:** generating a program that satisfies a target behavior, not just valid syntax.
* **Execution-based checking:** verifying a candidate's correctness by actually running it and comparing its output to a target.
* **Postfix (reverse Polish) notation:** writing an expression with operators after their operands, avoiding the need for parentheses.

## Related

[[Constrained and Structured Generation]] · [[Self-Consistency and Best-of-N Sampling]] · [[Building a Generative Product]]

## Multimodal Generation

Every district so far generates one modality at a time. This short district covers models built to generate across modalities from one shared representation, rather than being a separate model per modality glued together.

Topics on this stretch of the road:

* [[Unified Multimodal Generation]]: one model, one shared representation, more than one kind of output.
* [[Any-to-Any Generative Models]]: taking in any supported modality and generating any other, through a single interface.

## Unified Multimodal Generation

[[Multimodal Transformers as an Architecture Pattern|a multimodal transformer]] can take text and image patches as input together. This note covers going one step further: generating *both* text and image content from one model, one shared vocabulary, and one next-token prediction step — with no separate "text head" and "image head" at all.

**You need:** [[Multimodal Transformers as an Architecture Pattern]], [[Byte Pair Encoding]].

## The question it answers

"How can one model generate both text and images using the exact same next-token mechanism?" The trick is making images speak the same discrete language as text. A **codebook** of a fixed number of representative vectors lets any continuous image patch be **quantized** — replaced by the index of whichever codebook entry it's closest to — turning a patch into a discrete token exactly like a word. Once both text tokens and image tokens are just integers in one combined, **unified vocabulary**, a single autoregressive model can predict the next token of either kind, one at a time, with no architectural distinction between them.

## Intuition

Imagine a language that has words for "a", "photo", "of" — and also exactly four extra words, each standing for one specific swatch of visual texture, with no way to express anything in between. Any photograph, chopped into patches, gets described (lossily) using only those four visual words, slotted into sentences right alongside ordinary ones. Once that's true, "predict the next word" and "predict the next patch" are literally the same operation — there's no longer a meaningful line between them.

## Definition and notation

```text
codebook: K fixed vectors c₁, ..., c_K
quantize(patch) = argmin_k ‖patch − cₖ‖²            (nearest codebook entry)

unified vocabulary:  text tokens (ids 0 .. |text vocab|−1)
                      + image codes (ids |text vocab| .. |text vocab|+K−1)
→ one softmax over the combined vocabulary predicts the next token, of either kind
```

## A worked example

A 4-word text vocabulary `{a, photo, of, <img>}` and a 4-entry image codebook, giving a combined vocabulary of size 8. Three different image patches, quantized to their nearest codebook entries:

```text
patch (0.9, 0.1)    →  code 0   (nearest to codebook entry [1, 0])
patch (0.45, 0.52)  →  code 2   (nearest to codebook entry [0.5, 0.5])
patch (-0.8, 0.1)   →  code 3   (nearest to codebook entry [-1, 0])
```

A single unified sequence mixing text and a quantized image patch, using the combined ids directly:

```text
"a photo of <img> code2"   — ids [0, 1, 2, 3, 6]
```

Predicting the next element of this sequence is exactly one softmax over all 8 combined vocabulary entries — the model has no way of "knowing" which of the 8 are text and which are image codes except by what it learned about how they tend to follow each other, because the mechanism itself treats every one of them identically.

## Bench

```bench
id: vq-unified-vocab
title: One vocabulary, text and image tokens together
fallback: Pick an image patch and watch it quantize to a discrete code, placed directly into a shared text-and-image vocabulary sequence.
```

**Try this**

1. Try each of the three patches and check which codebook entry each quantizes to.
2. Notice the unified sequence places a quantized image code directly among the text tokens.
3. Consider: nothing in the sequence's representation marks which tokens came from text versus images.

**What you should notice:** quantization is a lossy compression step — many different continuous patches would all map to the same discrete code — which is the price paid for letting images join the same vocabulary, and the same generation mechanism, as text.

## Where it appears in AI

* **Models like Parti and early versions of DALL·E generate images by predicting a sequence of discrete image-codebook tokens**, using exactly the same autoregressive, next-token machinery as a language model — the codebook (often trained via a VQ-VAE) is what makes that possible.
* **The codebook size is a real design trade-off**: more entries capture visual detail more faithfully, but enlarge the vocabulary (and the prediction problem) correspondingly.
* **[[Any-to-Any Generative Models|any-to-any models]] generalize this idea past two modalities**, giving every supported modality its own quantization scheme into one shared vocabulary (or, alternatively, one shared continuous latent space).

## Common pitfalls

* **Assuming quantization is lossless.** Collapsing a continuous patch to one of a small, fixed number of codebook entries necessarily discards information — the whole point is compression, at the cost of exact fidelity.
* **Thinking the model "knows" which tokens are visual and which are textual.** Nothing in the unified representation marks this distinction explicitly; any such distinction the model exploits is learned from patterns in the data, not built into the mechanism.
