* **Expecting arbitrary resolution from a small codebook.** A codebook with very few entries (as in this toy example) can only represent a small number of distinct visual "words" — real systems use codebooks with thousands of entries for this reason.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. What does quantizing an image patch actually do?</summary>
It replaces a continuous patch vector with the index of whichever fixed codebook entry is closest to it, turning the patch into a discrete token.
</details>

<details><summary>2. In the worked example, why can a single softmax predict either a text token or an image code?</summary>
Because both kinds of token are simply integers in one combined vocabulary — the prediction mechanism has no separate path for either kind, it's one softmax over the whole combined set.
</details>

<details><summary>3. What's lost by representing images as discrete codebook tokens rather than continuous values?</summary>
Fidelity — many different continuous patches can map to the same discrete code, so some visual detail is necessarily discarded in the quantization step.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Codebook:** a fixed set of representative vectors used to quantize continuous inputs into discrete tokens.
* **Quantization:** replacing a continuous value with the nearest entry from a fixed codebook.
* **Unified vocabulary:** a single combined set of token ids spanning more than one modality, letting one model generate across all of them with one mechanism.

## Related

[[Multimodal Transformers as an Architecture Pattern]] · [[Byte Pair Encoding]] · [[Any-to-Any Generative Models]]

## Any-to-Any Generative Models

[[Unified Multimodal Generation|a unified vocabulary]] lets text and image tokens share one generation mechanism. This note covers a more general version of the same idea: encoding *every* supported modality into one shared embedding space, so that generating "any modality out" from "any modality in" is just a matter of which encoder and decoder you plug into the ends.

**You need:** [[Unified Multimodal Generation]].

## The question it answers

"How can one system take in any of several modalities and generate any other, through a single interface?" An **any-to-any model** trains a separate encoder for each supported modality (text, image, audio, ...), all projecting into the *same* shared embedding space — so that "cat" the word, a photo of a cat, and the sound of a cat meowing all land near each other in that space, regardless of which modality they came from. Generation is then: encode whatever input you have into that shared space, then decode the resulting point using whichever modality-specific decoder you want the output in.

## Intuition

Imagine a translator fluent in many languages who doesn't translate directly between any two of them, but instead converts everything into one private internal "meaning," and converts that meaning back out into whichever language is needed. Adding a new output language only means building one new decoder from that shared meaning-space — not a new translation rule for every existing language it might need to connect to. An any-to-any generative model does the same thing with modalities instead of languages: encode into one shared space, decode out to any target.

## Definition and notation

```text
one shared embedding space, dimension d
encoder_text(x), encoder_image(x), encoder_audio(x), ...  →  all map into that same d-dim space

similarity(a, b) = cosine(a, b) = (a · b) / (‖a‖ ‖b‖)

decoding to modality M: find (or generate from) the point in M's own
  representation whose encoding is closest to the shared-space query
```

## A worked example

Four small embeddings in a shared 3-dimensional space, representing the same concept ("cat") and one different concept ("dog") across three different modalities:

```text
image: cat    (0.90, 0.30, 0.10)
text: cat     (0.85, 0.35, 0.05)
audio: meow   (0.88, 0.28, 0.15)
text: dog     (0.10, 0.90, 0.20)
```

Measuring cosine similarity from "image: cat" to each of the others:

```text
cos(image:cat, text:cat)    = 0.9964   ← very close
cos(image:cat, audio:meow)  = 0.9983   ← very close
cos(image:cat, text:dog)    = 0.4295   ← far less similar
```

Despite coming from three completely different modalities, "image: cat," "text: cat," and "audio: meow" all sit nearly on top of each other in the shared space — while "text: dog," a different concept even in the same modality as one of the matches, sits much further away. An any-to-any system exploits exactly this: given "image: cat" as input, decoding to text finds "cat" (not "dog") as the closest match, and decoding to audio finds "meow," purely because of where each one sits in the shared space.

## Bench

```bench
id: any-to-any-shared-space
title: One shared space, any modality in, any modality out
fallback: Pick an input concept and see which other modality's embeddings sit closest to it in a shared embedding space.
```

**Try this**

1. Start from "image: cat" and check which other-modality concept is closest.
2. Switch to "text: dog" and see how little it resembles any of the cat-related embeddings.
3. Notice modality doesn't determine closeness — concept does.

**What you should notice:** closeness in the shared space tracks *meaning*, not modality — two embeddings of the same concept in different modalities sit closer together than two embeddings of different concepts in the same modality.

## Where it appears in AI

* **Models like CLIP build exactly this kind of shared image-text space** (though only for two modalities and for *matching*, not generation) — any-to-any generative systems extend the same idea to more modalities and add decoders that can actually produce content in each one.
* **Adding a new modality to an any-to-any system mainly means training one new encoder and one new decoder** into and out of the existing shared space, rather than redesigning the whole system.
* **[[Unified Multimodal Generation|the discrete codebook approach]] and this shared-embedding approach are two different solutions to a similar problem** — one makes every modality speak through a shared discrete vocabulary, the other through a shared continuous space.

## Common pitfalls

* **Assuming a shared embedding space is automatically well-aligned across all modalities.** It only becomes well-aligned through training on data that links modalities together (a captioned image, for instance) — nothing about having "one space" guarantees meaningful alignment by itself.
* **Confusing cross-modal similarity with cross-modal translation quality.** Being close in the shared space is necessary for finding the right output, but a decoder still has to turn that point into a genuinely good output in the target modality.
* **Forgetting new modalities need a trained encoder and decoder, not just a label.** The shared space doesn't automatically know how to represent a modality it's never seen trained examples of.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. What is the shared embedding space in an any-to-any model actually shared across?</summary>
Every supported modality's encoder maps into the same embedding space, so representations of the same concept from different modalities (e.g., an image of a cat and the word "cat") land near each other regardless of modality.
</details>

<details><summary>2. In the worked example, why was "image: cat" much closer to "audio: meow" than to "text: dog"?</summary>
Because closeness in the shared space tracks concept, not modality or input type — "image: cat" and "audio: meow" represent the same underlying concept, while "text: dog" represents a different one even though it's in the same modality as another embedding.
</details>

<details><summary>3. What does adding support for a new modality require in an any-to-any system?</summary>
Training a new encoder (to map that modality into the shared space) and a new decoder (to generate output in that modality from a point in the shared space) — not redesigning the whole system from scratch.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Any-to-any model:** a system that can take input from any supported modality and generate output in any other, through one shared representation.
* **Shared embedding space:** a common representation that different modalities' encoders all map into, so semantically related content lands close together regardless of modality.
* **Cosine similarity:** a measure of how closely two vectors point in the same direction, used to compare embeddings across modalities.

## Related

[[Unified Multimodal Generation]] · [[Multimodal Transformers as an Architecture Pattern]] · [[Latent Space Interpolation and Manipulation]]

## Evaluating Generative Models

A classifier has a right answer to check against; a generated poem or image usually doesn't. This district covers the metrics and methods built to judge generative output anyway, and what each one actually measures.

Topics on this stretch of the road:

* [[Perplexity as a Generation Metric]]: how surprised a language model is by text, and what that does and doesn't tell you.
* [[n-gram Overlap Metrics (BLEU and ROUGE)]]: scoring generated text by how much it overlaps with a reference.
* [[Distributional Metrics (FID, Inception Score and CLIP Score)]]: comparing generated and real data as whole distributions, not example by example.
* [[Diversity and Mode Collapse in Generation]]: checking whether a generative model produces a genuinely varied range of outputs.
* [[Human Evaluation of Generated Content]]: when automatic metrics aren't enough, and how human judgment is collected reliably.

## Perplexity as a Generation Metric

A classifier's accuracy is easy to check: right or wrong. A language model's quality is harder to pin down with one number — but one very old, very simple metric captures something real: how surprised the model was by what it actually saw.

**You need:** [[Self-Consistency and Best-of-N Sampling]].

## The question it answers

"How confidently does a language model predict the text it's being evaluated on?" **Perplexity** takes the probability a model assigned to each token of a sequence (given everything before it), averages their log-probabilities, and exponentiates the result — producing a single number that can be read as "on average, about how many equally-likely choices did the model seem to be choosing between at each step?" Lower perplexity means the model assigned higher probability to what actually happened — it was less surprised.

## Intuition

If a weather forecaster says "90% chance of rain" the day before it rains, they weren't very surprised; if they said "25% chance of rain" (close to a coin flip among four options) the day before it rains, they were considerably more surprised, even though both forecasts technically "allowed" for rain. Perplexity is exactly that notion of surprise, averaged over every token in a sequence and converted back into an intuitive scale — a perplexity of 4 reads, roughly, as "about as surprised as if choosing uniformly among 4 options every time."

## Definition and notation

```text
perplexity(sequence) = exp( −(1/n) · Σ log P(tokenᵢ | prefix) )

equivalently: perplexity = exp(average cross-entropy, in nats)
  lower perplexity → higher assigned probability → less "surprised"
  perplexity = V for a model that assigns uniform probability 1/V to every token
```

## A worked example

Three toy models' token-by-token probabilities on the same 4-token sequence:

```text
confident & correct:     [0.90, 0.85, 0.80, 0.90]  →  perplexity 1.161
uniform guess (4 tokens): [0.25, 0.25, 0.25, 0.25]  →  perplexity 4.000
unconfident / wrong:     [0.20, 0.15, 0.10, 0.25]  →  perplexity 6.043
```

A model that always assigns exactly 1/4 to a 4-way uniform guess gets perplexity exactly 4 — confirming the "as surprised as choosing among V equally likely options" reading directly. The confident, correct model scores near 1 (almost never surprised); the unconfident, wrong model scores above the uniform baseline — worse than just guessing uniformly would have been.

## Bench

```bench
id: perplexity-metric
title: How surprised was the model?
fallback: Compare the perplexity of three toy models' token probabilities on the same short sequence.
```

**Try this**

1. Compare the confident model's perplexity against the uniform baseline.
2. Notice the unconfident model actually scores *worse* than uniform guessing.
3. Consider what probability sequence would give a perplexity of exactly 1.

**What you should notice:** perplexity near 1 means near-certainty and near-correctness simultaneously — getting it that low requires both confidently assigning probability *and* being right to assign it to.

## Where it appears in AI

* **Perplexity on held-out text is a standard way to compare language models during pretraining**, since lower perplexity on the same evaluation set means the model is systematically less surprised by real text.
* **It only measures how well a model predicts existing text — it says nothing about originality, coherence of generated output, or usefulness**, which is why it's used alongside, not instead of, other evaluation methods.
* **[[n-gram Overlap Metrics (BLEU and ROUGE)|BLEU and ROUGE]] evaluate *generated* text against a reference**; perplexity instead evaluates how well a model predicts *existing* text — a genuinely different question, even though both are often discussed as "language generation metrics."

## Common pitfalls

* **Comparing perplexity across different tokenizers or vocabularies.** Perplexity is sensitive to vocabulary size and how text is split into tokens — two models using different tokenization aren't directly comparable by perplexity alone.
* **Assuming lower perplexity always means better generated text.** A model can achieve very low perplexity by memorizing training data (see [[Memorization and Training Data Leakage]]) without that implying its *novel* generations are good.
* **Forgetting perplexity needs ground-truth text to evaluate against.** It measures how well a model predicts text that actually exists; it can't be computed on a model's own free-form generations with nothing to compare them to.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. What does a perplexity of exactly 4 tell you about a model's predictions?</summary>
On average, the model was about as "surprised" by what it saw as if it had been choosing uniformly at random among 4 equally likely options at each step.
</details>

<details><summary>2. In the worked example, why did the "unconfident / wrong" model score worse than the uniform baseline?</summary>
Its average assigned probability to what actually happened was lower than the uniform guess of 0.25 at every step, meaning it was systematically more surprised than even a flat, uninformed guess would have been.
</details>

<details><summary>3. What does perplexity fail to measure about a language model's generations?</summary>
It only measures how well a model predicts existing (reference) text — it says nothing about the quality, coherence, or usefulness of text the model generates on its own with no reference to compare against.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Perplexity:** the exponentiated average negative log-probability a model assigns to a sequence; lower means less surprised.
* **Cross-entropy:** the average negative log-probability itself, before exponentiating; perplexity is literally e raised to this value.
* **Held-out text:** text not used during training, used to measure how well a model generalizes.

## Related

[[Self-Consistency and Best-of-N Sampling]] · [[n-gram Overlap Metrics (BLEU and ROUGE)]] · [[Human Evaluation of Generated Content]]

## n-gram Overlap Metrics (BLEU and ROUGE)

Perplexity measures how well a model predicts text it's shown; it says nothing about a model's own generated output compared to a correct answer. This note covers the much older, much simpler approach: just count how many words overlap between a generated text and a reference one.

**You need:** [[Perplexity as a Generation Metric]].

## The question it answers

"How closely does a generated piece of text match a reference, by shared words and phrases?" **BLEU** is a *precision*-based score: of all the word sequences (n-grams) the candidate produced, what fraction also appear in the reference? It's commonly used for translation, where producing extra, unsupported content should be penalized. **ROUGE** flips the question into a *recall*-based score: of all the n-grams in the reference, what fraction did the candidate manage to reproduce? It's commonly used for summarization, where missing important reference content should be penalized.

## Intuition

Imagine grading two different kinds of essay answers against a model answer. For a translation, you want to penalize someone who added things that aren't actually in the source — that's precision, BLEU's question: "of what you said, how much was right?" For a summary, you instead want to penalize someone who left out the point entirely, even if everything they *did* write was accurate — that's recall, ROUGE's question: "of what mattered, how much did you capture?"

## Definition and notation

```text
n-gram: a sequence of n consecutive words ("the cat" is a bigram, n=2)

BLEU (precision, with a length-shortfall penalty):
  precisionₙ = (matching n-grams in candidate) / (total n-grams in candidate)
  BLEU = brevity_penalty × geometric_mean(precision₁, precision₂, ...)

ROUGE-n (recall):
  recallₙ = (matching n-grams, clipped to reference counts) / (total n-grams in reference)
```

## A worked example

Reference: `"the cat sat on the mat"`. Three candidates scored against it:

```text
"the cat sat on the mat"  (exact match)
  BLEU = 1.0000      ROUGE-1 recall = 1.0000

"a dog ran in the park"   (unrelated, shares only "the")
  BLEU = 0.0000      ROUGE-1 recall = 0.1667   (1 of 6 reference unigrams matched)
```

The exact match scores perfectly on both metrics, as expected. The unrelated sentence scores exactly 0 on BLEU — it has essentially no matching n-grams of any length, and BLEU's geometric mean over n-gram precisions collapses to zero the moment any one precision does — but ROUGE-1 recall still gives it a small positive score of 0.1667, simply because one shared word ("the") happens to appear in both.

## Bench

```bench
id: bleu-rouge-score
title: Precision (BLEU) vs. recall (ROUGE)
fallback: Compare a candidate sentence's BLEU and ROUGE-1 recall scores against a fixed reference sentence.
```

**Try this**

1. Compare the exact match's scores on both metrics.
2. Compare the paraphrase's BLEU score against its ROUGE score.
3. Notice the unrelated sentence still gets a small nonzero ROUGE score, despite scoring exactly zero on BLEU.

**What you should notice:** BLEU and ROUGE can disagree sharply on the same pair of texts — they're measuring genuinely different things (precision versus recall over shared n-grams), not two versions of the same underlying score.

## Where it appears in AI

* **Machine translation has historically reported BLEU as a standard benchmark metric**, specifically because penalizing unsupported extra content (low precision) matters a lot for faithful translation.
* **Summarization has historically reported ROUGE**, specifically because missing the source's key points (low recall) is the more damaging failure mode there.
* **Both metrics are increasingly supplemented or replaced by [[Human Evaluation of Generated Content|human evaluation]] and learned metrics**, since exact n-gram overlap can't recognize a correct paraphrase that happens to use different words entirely.

## Common pitfalls

* **Using BLEU for summarization or ROUGE for translation without considering which failure mode matters more.** Each metric is built around a specific sensitivity (precision vs. recall) that fits one task's typical error pattern better than the other's.
* **Treating a low score as proof of a bad generation.** A perfectly good paraphrase that avoids repeating the reference's exact wording can score poorly on both metrics, despite being semantically correct — n-gram overlap can't recognize synonyms or restructured sentences.
* **Forgetting BLEU's geometric mean makes it brittle to a single zero precision.** If a candidate happens to share no bigrams at all with the reference, its BLEU score collapses to zero regardless of how good its unigram overlap is.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. What's the key conceptual difference between BLEU and ROUGE?</summary>
BLEU measures precision — how much of what the candidate produced also appears in the reference; ROUGE measures recall — how much of the reference the candidate managed to reproduce.
</details>

<details><summary>2. In the worked example, why did the unrelated sentence score 0 on BLEU but a small positive value on ROUGE?</summary>
BLEU's geometric mean over several n-gram precisions collapses to zero once any one precision (like the bigram precision, with essentially no matches) is zero; ROUGE-1 recall only needed one matching unigram ("the") out of six reference unigrams to register a small nonzero score.
</details>

<details><summary>3. Why might a correct paraphrase score poorly on both BLEU and ROUGE?</summary>
Because both metrics rely on exact n-gram (word-sequence) overlap, which can't recognize that a differently-worded sentence conveys the same meaning as the reference.
</details>

## Key terms

* **BLEU:** a precision-based n-gram overlap metric, commonly used for machine translation.
* **ROUGE:** a recall-based n-gram overlap metric, commonly used for summarization.
* **N-gram:** a sequence of n consecutive tokens, the basic unit both metrics compare.

## Related

[[Perplexity as a Generation Metric]] · [[Distributional Metrics (FID, Inception Score and CLIP Score)]] · [[Human Evaluation of Generated Content]]

## Distributional Metrics (FID, Inception Score and CLIP Score)

BLEU and ROUGE work by comparing a generation directly against *one specific* reference. Images, audio and video usually don't have one "correct" reference to compare against at all — a generated photo of a cat doesn't need to match any particular real photo, just be a *plausible* one. This note covers metrics built for exactly that situation: comparing whole distributions, not individual outputs.

**You need:** [[n-gram Overlap Metrics (BLEU and ROUGE)]].

## The question it answers

"How do you score a generative model when there's no single correct output to compare against?" **Distributional metrics** compare the *statistics* of a set of generated samples against the statistics of real data, rather than matching individual outputs one to one. The **Fréchet distance** (the core of FID, "Fréchet Inception Distance") measures how far apart two distributions' means and (co)variances are. **CLIP score** takes a completely different approach for text-conditioned generation: measuring the cosine similarity between a generated image's embedding and its prompt's embedding directly, via the same kind of shared embedding space from [[Any-to-Any Generative Models]].

## Intuition

You can't check whether a generated photo of a cat "matches" reality by comparing it pixel-for-pixel against any single real cat photo — there's no one right answer. What you *can* check is whether a whole batch of generated cat photos, as a group, has roughly the same statistical "shape" (how varied they are, what the average features look like) as a batch of real cat photos. That's the Fréchet-distance idea: compare two clouds of points by their center and spread, not point by point.

## Definition and notation

```text
Fréchet distance (diagonal-covariance simplification), between real features R and generated features G:
  d = ‖mean(R) − mean(G)‖² + Σᵢ [ var(R)ᵢ + var(G)ᵢ − 2·√(var(R)ᵢ · var(G)ᵢ) ]
  → 0 only when both the means and the variances match exactly, dimension by dimension

CLIP score: cosine(embed(generated image), embed(prompt))
  → high when the image and its prompt land near each other in a shared embedding space
```

## A worked example

Four small 2D "real" feature points clustered near `(1, 2)`, compared against two different generated sets:

```text
real features:         (1, 2), (1.2, 2.1), (0.9, 1.9), (1.1, 2.05)

close match:            (1.05, 1.95), (1.15, 2.08), (0.95, 1.92), (1.0, 2.0)
  distributional distance: 0.0024    ← very close

shifted distribution:   (5, 5), (5.2, 5.1), (4.8, 4.9), (5.1, 5.05)
  distributional distance: 24.8019   ← very far
```

Both generated sets have roughly the same *internal spread* as the real set (each has similar variance among its own four points) — the huge difference between the two scores comes almost entirely from the *mean* term, since the "shifted distribution" set sits in a completely different region of feature space than the real data, despite looking internally just as consistent as the close match.

## Bench

```bench
id: fid-distributional
title: How far apart are two feature distributions?
fallback: Compare two generated feature sets against the same real feature set using a Fréchet-distance-style metric.
```

**Try this**

1. Compare the "close match" generated set's distance against the real set.
2. Switch to the "shifted distribution" set and watch the distance grow sharply.
3. Notice both generated sets have a similar internal spread — the difference is almost entirely about where their mean sits.

**What you should notice:** a distributional metric can't tell you anything about any *individual* generated sample's quality — it's purely a statement about the whole set's statistics compared to the whole real set's statistics.

## Where it appears in AI

* **FID (using real neural network features, not toy 2D points, and full covariance matrices, not just the diagonal) is the standard image-generation benchmark metric**, reported by nearly every major image-generation paper.
* **Inception Score** is a related, older distributional metric that instead measures how confidently and diversely a pretrained classifier labels the generated images — two complementary ways of asking "do these look like real, varied examples of something?"
* **CLIP score directly checks text-image alignment**, answering a different question entirely from FID: not "do generated images look realistic as a group," but "does *this* generated image actually match *this* prompt?"

## Common pitfalls

* **Using a distributional metric to judge a single generated sample.** These metrics are only meaningful computed over a reasonably large set of samples — a "distance" computed from one generated image and one real image doesn't mean what FID normally means.
* **Assuming a low distributional distance guarantees individually high-quality samples.** A generator that reproduces the right overall statistics while still occasionally producing broken individual samples can still score well, since the metric only sees aggregate statistics.
* **Forgetting CLIP score and FID measure different things.** A generated image can match its prompt extremely well (high CLIP score) while still looking statistically different from real images overall (worse FID), or vice versa.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. Why can't BLEU-style, single-reference comparison work for most image generation tasks?</summary>
There's usually no single "correct" reference image a generated image needs to match — many very different images could all be equally valid, so comparing to one specific reference doesn't make sense.
</details>

<details><summary>2. In the worked example, why was the distance so much larger for the "shifted distribution" set despite its internal spread looking similar to the "close match" set?</summary>
The mean term in the distance dominated — the shifted set's average position was far from the real data's average position, even though both generated sets had comparable variance among their own points.
</details>

<details><summary>3. What does CLIP score measure that FID does not?</summary>
How well a specific generated image matches its specific text prompt (via embedding similarity), rather than how statistically similar a whole set of generated images is to a whole set of real images.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Distributional metric:** a score comparing the statistics of a set of generated samples to a set of real samples, rather than comparing individual outputs.
* **Fréchet distance:** a measure of how far apart two distributions' means and (co)variances are.
* **CLIP score:** the cosine similarity between a generated image's embedding and its prompt's embedding in a shared space.

## Related

[[n-gram Overlap Metrics (BLEU and ROUGE)]] · [[Diversity and Mode Collapse in Generation]] · [[Any-to-Any Generative Models]]

## Diversity and Mode Collapse in Generation

A generative model can score well on fidelity — every individual sample looks great — while quietly producing almost the same thing every time. This note covers checking for that specific failure directly, rather than assuming high-quality samples mean a healthy generator.

**You need:** [[Distributional Metrics (FID, Inception Score and CLIP Score)]].

## The question it answers

"Is a generative model actually producing a varied range of outputs, or collapsing onto a few safe ones?" **Mode collapse** is when a generative model stops covering the real diversity of its training distribution and instead produces a narrow range of outputs — sometimes nearly identical ones — regardless of how good any individual sample looks. A simple, direct check is **average pairwise distance**: generate several samples and measure how far apart they typically are from each other; a collapsing generator's samples get closer and closer together over time.

## Intuition

Imagine a student asked to write five different short stories, who instead writes the same basic plot five times with minor cosmetic changes. Each individual story might be perfectly well-written — mode collapse isn't about quality — but something has clearly gone wrong with the *diversity* the assignment actually called for. A generative model that's collapsed behaves the same way: every sample might look plausible on its own, while the set of samples as a whole has stopped exploring the real range of possibilities.

## Definition and notation

```text
average pairwise distance over N samples:
  (1 / C(N,2)) · Σᵢ<ⱼ distance(sampleᵢ, sampleⱼ)

  shrinking average pairwise distance over training ⟹ samples are
  converging toward each other ⟹ a warning sign of mode collapse
```

## A worked example

Eight toy samples drawn at each of several training "epochs," with their spread intentionally shrinking over time to simulate collapse:

```text
epoch 0:  average pairwise distance = 2.348
epoch 2:  average pairwise distance = 1.380
epoch 4:  average pairwise distance = 0.823
epoch 6:  average pairwise distance = 0.201
```

By epoch 6, the samples sit more than ten times closer together on average than they did at epoch 0 — a clear, measurable signature of collapsing diversity, visible directly from the samples themselves with no reference to any particular "correct" output at all.

## Bench

```bench
id: mode-collapse-diversity
title: Sample diversity shrinking over training
fallback: Step through training epochs and watch generated samples cluster more tightly together, along with their average pairwise distance.
```

**Try this**

1. Start at epoch 0 and note how spread out the samples are.
2. Advance through the epochs and watch the samples cluster increasingly tightly.
3. Compare the average-pairwise-distance readout across epochs.

**What you should notice:** nothing about any individual sample looks obviously wrong at any epoch — the collapse is only visible by looking at the *set* of samples together, which is exactly why a diversity-specific check is needed on top of per-sample quality checks.

## Where it appears in AI

* **Mode collapse is a well-known, specific failure mode of GANs**, where the generator can find a narrow range of outputs that reliably fools the discriminator, and has no further incentive (under that training signal alone) to explore beyond it.
* **[[Distributional Metrics (FID, Inception Score and CLIP Score)|FID itself partially captures this]]** — a collapsed generator's variance term diverges sharply from real data's variance — but a direct diversity check like average pairwise distance is simpler to interpret on its own.
* **Diffusion models are generally considered less prone to mode collapse than GANs**, though they aren't immune to related diversity issues, especially under strong [[Classifier-Free Guidance|guidance]] that pushes samples hard toward a narrow target.

## Common pitfalls

* **Judging diversity from a handful of generated samples.** Average pairwise distance (or any diversity measure) needs a reasonably large sample to be meaningful — a small handful of samples can look diverse or collapsed by chance.
* **Confusing low diversity with high quality.** A model that always produces the exact same, very good output has a diversity problem, not a quality success — the two properties are independent, and a generative model is typically expected to have both.
* **Assuming any diversity measure applies unchanged across modalities.** "Distance between two images" and "distance between two sentences" are very different measurements — the general idea here transfers across modalities, but the specific metric has to be adapted to each one.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. What specifically is mode collapse, as distinct from low-quality generation?</summary>
A generative model producing a narrow range of outputs instead of the true diversity of its training distribution — individual samples can still look high-quality; the problem is the lack of variety across samples.
</details>

<details><summary>2. In the worked example, what evidence pointed to mode collapse?</summary>
Average pairwise distance among generated samples shrank sharply across training epochs, from 2.348 down to 0.201 — samples were converging toward each other rather than staying spread out.
</details>

<details><summary>3. Why can't mode collapse be detected by looking at individual samples one at a time?</summary>
Because a collapsed generator's individual samples can each look perfectly plausible on their own — the problem only becomes visible by comparing multiple samples against each other to see how similar they've become.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Mode collapse:** a generative model producing a narrow range of outputs instead of covering its training distribution's real diversity.
* **Average pairwise distance:** the average distance between every pair of samples in a generated set, used as a direct diversity measure.
* **Diversity:** how varied a generative model's outputs are, as distinct from how individually plausible any one output is.

## Related

[[Distributional Metrics (FID, Inception Score and CLIP Score)]] · [[Generative Adversarial Networks]] · [[Classifier-Free Guidance]]

## Human Evaluation of Generated Content

Every metric so far on this planet is automatic — computed from numbers, with no judgment involved. For plenty of generated content, that's exactly the problem: whether a joke is funny, a summary reads naturally, or an image "feels right" doesn't reduce cleanly to an automatic formula. This note covers collecting human judgment directly, and combining many small, noisy opinions into a reliable ranking.

**You need:** [[Distributional Metrics (FID, Inception Score and CLIP Score)]].

## The question it answers

"How do you turn a pile of individual human opinions into one reliable quality ranking?" Asking people to compare two outputs directly ("which is better, A or B?") is usually easier and more reliable than asking them to rate one output on an absolute scale. An **Elo rating system** (the same one used for chess rankings) takes a stream of such pairwise comparisons and updates a running score for each item: beating a highly-rated competitor earns more than beating a weak one, and the ratings converge toward a consistent ranking as more comparisons accumulate.

## Intuition

Asking "is this a 7 out of 10?" invites very different internal scales from different people — one person's 7 is another's 5. Asking "is A better than B?" sidesteps that entirely: it's a much easier, more consistent judgment to make, even for people with wildly different absolute standards. Elo takes a whole stream of these easy, relative judgments and reconstructs a global ranking from them, the same way chess ratings emerge from nothing but a long history of "who beat whom."

## Definition and notation

```text
expected win probability:  P(winner beats loser) = 1 / (1 + 10^((loser_rating − winner_rating)/400))

rating update after one comparison:
  winner_rating += k · (1 − expected)
  loser_rating  -= k · (1 − expected)
  (k controls how much one comparison can move a rating)
```

## A worked example

Three toy models A, B and C with true underlying quality 0.9, 0.6 and 0.3 respectively (used only to simulate which one "wins" a given comparison, with the better one winning more often but not always). Starting every model at rating 1000 and simulating 300 random pairwise comparisons:

```text
final ratings:  A: 1077.4   B: 1031.8   C: 890.9
ranking:        A > B > C
```

With no information given to the rating system except a stream of "which one won" outcomes, Elo recovered exactly the correct ranking (A better than B better than C) that matches the true underlying quality values used to simulate the comparisons — purely from relative, pairwise judgments, with no absolute score ever given to anything.

## Bench

```bench
id: human-eval-elo
title: Pairwise judgments converge to a ranking
fallback: Step through simulated pairwise comparisons and watch Elo ratings converge toward the correct quality ranking.
```

**Try this**

1. Step through a few rounds and watch the ratings start to separate.
2. Keep stepping and see whether the ranking stabilizes at A > B > C.
3. Reset and run again — the specific numbers will differ slightly (it's randomized), but the ranking should settle the same way.

**What you should notice:** with enough comparisons, the specific path each rating takes varies, but the final ranking reliably recovers the true underlying quality order, purely from relative outcomes.

## Where it appears in AI

* **LLM-arena-style leaderboards (where users vote on which of two anonymous model outputs is better) use exactly this Elo-based approach** to turn millions of pairwise human votes into a single ranked leaderboard.
* **Pairwise comparison is also the typical format for training preference-based models** (such as reward models for reinforcement learning from human feedback), for the same reason it's easier and more consistent to collect than absolute ratings.
* **It composes naturally with [[Self-Consistency and Best-of-N Sampling|automated judging]]**: an AI model asked "which of these two is better" can feed the exact same Elo machinery, a common (if imperfect) substitute when human judgment is too slow or expensive to collect at scale.

## Common pitfalls

* **Assuming a single comparison is reliable.** Any one pairwise judgment can go the "wrong" way just from noise (as the worked example's own probabilistic win model shows) — the ranking's reliability comes from aggregating many comparisons, not from any individual one.
* **Confusing Elo rating with an absolute quality score.** Ratings are only meaningful *relative to each other* within the same pool of compared items — an Elo rating of 1077 means nothing on its own, only in comparison to the other rated items.
* **Forgetting rating updates depend on the expected outcome.** Beating a much weaker opponent barely moves a rating; beating an opponent of similar or higher rating moves it more — flat, equal-sized updates regardless of opponent strength wouldn't converge the same way.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. Why is pairwise comparison generally more reliable to collect than absolute ratings?</summary>
People tend to apply inconsistent personal scales when rating something in isolation (one person's 7 may be another's 5), but direct comparisons ("is A better than B?") are a simpler, more consistent judgment to make.
</details>

<details><summary>2. In the worked example, what information was the Elo system given, and what did it recover?</summary>
It was given only a stream of win/loss outcomes from pairwise comparisons, with no absolute quality scores provided at all, and it recovered a ranking that matched the true underlying quality order used to generate those comparisons.
</details>

<details><summary>3. Why does beating a stronger opponent increase a rating more than beating a weaker one?</summary>
The rating update is scaled by how unexpected the outcome was — beating an opponent you were "expected" to lose to moves your rating more than beating one you were already expected to beat.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Human evaluation:** collecting direct human judgments of generated content, used where automatic metrics fall short.
* **Pairwise comparison:** judging which of two outputs is better, rather than rating either one on an absolute scale.
* **Elo rating:** a system that converts a stream of pairwise win/loss outcomes into a consistent relative ranking.

## Related

[[Distributional Metrics (FID, Inception Score and CLIP Score)]] · [[Self-Consistency and Best-of-N Sampling]] · [[Content Safety and Red-Teaming]]

## Risks and Responsible Generation

Generative models fail in ways discriminative models mostly don't: confidently wrong output, reproduced training data, content nobody consented to be trained on, and output that's hard to tell from something real. This district covers those failure modes and the mitigations built around them.

Topics on this stretch of the road:

* [[Hallucination and Factuality]]: generated output that's fluent and confident but not true.
* [[Bias and Representational Harm in Generation]]: how training data imbalances surface as unfair or stereotyped generated content.
* [[Copyright and Training Data Provenance]]: what it means for a model to have learned from copyrighted or unconsented data.
* [[Memorization and Training Data Leakage]]: when a generative model reproduces specific training examples instead of generalizing.
* [[Watermarking and Synthetic Media Provenance]]: marking or detecting generated content so it can be told apart from the real thing.
* [[Content Safety and Red-Teaming]]: testing a generative model deliberately for harmful output before it ships.

## Hallucination and Factuality

Nothing in how a language model generates text requires what it says to be true — it only requires the next token to be a plausible continuation. This note covers the gap that opens up between "sounds right" and "is right," and the specific danger of a model that sounds right while being wrong.

**You need:** [[Human Evaluation of Generated Content]].

## The question it answers

"Why does a model sometimes state false things with the same fluent confidence as true ones?" **Hallucination** is generated content that's fluent and often stated confidently, but doesn't correspond to fact. It's not the same failure as low confidence or obvious gibberish — the dangerous case is specifically when a false claim is delivered with the same tone, structure and apparent certainty as a true one, because nothing about *how* it's phrased distinguishes the two.

## Intuition

A student who's memorized the shape and rhythm of a confident answer, without actually knowing the material, can produce something that sounds exactly like genuine expertise — right up until the content is checked against reality. A language model trained to predict plausible continuations of text has learned the shape of confident, fluent claims extremely well; it has no separate, built-in mechanism that specifically tracks whether each claim is actually true.

## Definition and notation

```text
a claim is a hallucination when:
  it is stated with no hedging (confidently, fluently)
  AND it does not match a known, checkable fact

→ fluency and confidence of phrasing say nothing, by themselves,
  about whether a claim is checkable-true or checkable-false
```

## A worked example

Four claims, each generated with a stated confidence, checked against a small fact base:

```text
"Paris is the capital of France"                       conf 0.97   TRUE   → correct
"The Great Wall of China is visible from the Moon"      conf 0.89   FALSE  → HALLUCINATION
"Water boils at 100°C at sea level"                      conf 0.95   TRUE   → correct
"Napoleon was extremely short for his era"               conf 0.80   FALSE  → HALLUCINATION
```

Two of the four claims are a well-known myth and a long-debunked piece of trivia (Napoleon's height was, in fact, roughly average for his era) — both stated with high confidence, phrased no differently from the two true claims right alongside them. Nothing about *how* any of the four claims were stated distinguishes the true ones from the false ones; only checking each one against an outside source does.

## Bench

```bench
id: hallucination-confidence
title: Confident, and wrong
fallback: Step through generated claims and see which ones, despite sounding equally confident, turn out to be false.
```

**Try this**

1. Step through each claim and track how many turn out to be hallucinations.
2. Notice the stated confidence values don't obviously separate the true claims from the false ones.
3. Consider how you'd have told them apart without a fact base to check against.

**What you should notice:** fluency and confidence of phrasing carry essentially no information about truth on their own — the only way to catch a hallucination is to check the content against something outside the generation itself.

## Where it appears in AI

* **Retrieval-augmented generation (grounding a model in retrieved documents) is one of the main practical mitigations**, specifically because it gives the model something to check claims against, rather than relying purely on parametric memory.
* **Hallucination rates are a standard evaluation axis for LLMs**, usually measured by checking generated claims against a trusted source, exactly as this worked example does by hand.
* **It's distinct from low-confidence uncertainty**: a well-calibrated model that says "I'm not sure" about something it doesn't know is behaving correctly; hallucination specifically means confident, fluent, and wrong.

## Common pitfalls

* **Assuming fluent, confident-sounding text is more likely to be true.** The worked example shows fluency and confidence are present in both the true and false claims — they're not a reliable signal either way.
* **Treating hallucination as a rare edge case.** It's a direct, structural consequence of how generation works (predicting plausible continuations, not verified facts), not an occasional bug limited to unusual inputs.
* **Assuming hallucination only happens on obscure facts.** Models can hallucinate about well-known topics too, particularly ones involving commonly repeated myths (like the Great Wall claim here) that appear confidently stated throughout their training data.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. What makes a generated claim a hallucination, specifically?</summary>
It's stated fluently and with confidence, but it doesn't match a known, checkable fact — the key failure is confident, plausible-sounding falsehood, not obvious uncertainty or gibberish.
</details>

<details><summary>2. In the worked example, what did the two false claims have in common with the two true claims?</summary>
Both pairs were phrased with similar fluency and comparably high stated confidence — nothing about their phrasing distinguished the true claims from the false ones.
</details>

<details><summary>3. Why doesn't a model's confident tone tell you anything reliable about whether a claim is true?</summary>
A model is trained to produce plausible, fluent continuations of text, not to separately track or verify the truth of what it states — confident phrasing reflects learned patterns of how confident claims typically sound, not a checked fact.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Hallucination:** fluent, often confidently stated generated content that doesn't match fact.
* **Grounding:** connecting a model's output to retrieved or verified external sources, to reduce hallucination.
* **Calibration:** how well a model's stated confidence matches its actual correctness — hallucination is a specific, severe failure of calibration.

## Related

[[Human Evaluation of Generated Content]] · [[Bias and Representational Harm in Generation]] · [[Memorization and Training Data Leakage]]

## Bias and Representational Harm in Generation

A model's embeddings encode whatever statistical patterns were in its training data — including patterns nobody deliberately put there. This note covers a direct way to measure one specific kind: whether words associated with a social group sit systematically closer to some concepts than others, in a way that reflects stereotype rather than meaning.

**You need:** [[Any-to-Any Generative Models]].

## The question it answers

"How do you measure whether a model's representations encode a stereotyped association?" A **word embedding association test (WEAT-style)** measures the gap between how strongly one group's embeddings associate with a target concept versus how strongly another group's embeddings associate with that same concept. A consistent, sizeable gap — male-coded terms sitting systematically closer to "career," female-coded terms systematically closer to "family," say — reveals a learned statistical association that mirrors a social stereotype, independent of whether that association reflects anything true about any individual.

## Intuition

If you measured the average distance from "doctor" to a set of male names versus a set of female names in some embedding space, and found a consistent gap, that gap wouldn't mean anything about actual doctors — it would mean the training data the embeddings came from contained that pattern often enough for the model to encode it as a statistical regularity. The test doesn't diagnose any individual word's meaning; it measures a *systematic* gap across a whole set of related words, which is much harder to dismiss as coincidence.

## Definition and notation

```text
mean association of an attribute set A with target concept T:
  meanAssoc(A, T) = (1/|A|) · Σ cosine(a, T)   for a in A

WEAT-style differential:
  meanAssoc(A₁, T) − meanAssoc(A₂, T)
  → a large, consistent gap across target concepts indicates a learned association
```

## A worked example

Toy embeddings for two attribute groups (male-coded, female-coded) and two target concepts (career, family):

```text
male-coded   vs. career:  0.6999        female-coded vs. career:  −0.6255
male-coded   vs. family: −0.6255        female-coded vs. family:   0.6999

differential (male-career minus female-career):  1.3254
```

Male-coded embeddings associate strongly and positively with "career" while female-coded embeddings associate strongly and *negatively* with it — and the pattern flips exactly for "family." The two groups aren't just slightly different; they're near-mirror images of each other across both target concepts, exactly the kind of systematic, large gap the test is built to surface.

## Bench

```bench
id: bias-association-test
title: Which group associates more with which concept?
fallback: Switch between target concepts and compare how strongly two attribute-coded groups associate with each one.
```

**Try this**

1. Look at the association gap for "career."
2. Switch to "family" and watch the gap reverse direction.
3. Consider what a gap of exactly 0 at both concepts would mean.

**What you should notice:** the gap isn't just present for one concept — it shows up consistently, in opposite directions, for both concepts tested, which is what makes it a *systematic* association rather than noise from one arbitrary pair of words.

## Where it appears in AI

* **The real WEAT methodology (Caliskan et al., 2017) used this exact approach on word embeddings trained on ordinary web text**, and found measurable associations mirroring known social stereotypes, confirming such biases get encoded without anyone deliberately introducing them.
* **This generalizes to generative models directly**: a text-to-image model's generated outputs for occupation prompts, or a language model's completions for different demographic framings, can show the same kind of systematic, measurable skew.
* **It's a different question from [[Fairness Metrics|classification fairness]]**: that's about a specific decision's outcomes across groups; this is about whether a model's underlying representations encode a stereotyped association in the first place, which can manifest in generation even without any formal decision being made at all.

## Common pitfalls

* **Treating any single word pair's association as proof of bias.** Individual associations can be noisy; the test's real signal is a *systematic* gap holding across multiple related words and concepts, as in the worked example.
* **Assuming measuring bias is the same as fixing it.** This kind of test diagnoses whether an association exists; removing or correcting it is a separate, genuinely difficult problem — measurement and mitigation are not the same step.
* **Forgetting the test measures statistical association in representations, not intent.** No one has to deliberately encode a stereotype for it to appear — it's a direct consequence of what patterns were present, and how often, in the training data.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. What does a WEAT-style test actually measure?</summary>
The gap between how strongly one group's embeddings associate with a target concept versus how strongly another group's embeddings associate with the same concept, aggregated across multiple related words rather than any single pair.
</details>

<details><summary>2. In the worked example, why is the flip between "career" and "family" significant?</summary>
It shows the association isn't a one-off coincidence for a single concept — the same two groups show a large, opposite-direction gap for a second, related concept, which is much stronger evidence of a systematic encoded pattern.
</details>

<details><summary>3. Does a measured association prove something true about any individual the attribute set represents?</summary>
No — it reveals a statistical pattern present in the training data the embeddings were derived from, not a fact about any individual person or group member.
</details>

## Key terms

* **WEAT (word embedding association test):** a method for measuring systematic association gaps between attribute-coded groups and target concepts in embeddings.
* **Representational harm:** harm arising from how a group is represented (stereotyped, underrepresented, or misrepresented) rather than from a specific denied outcome.
* **Differential association:** the gap between two groups' mean association with the same target concept.

## Related

[[Any-to-Any Generative Models]] · [[Hallucination and Factuality]] · [[Content Safety and Red-Teaming]]

## Copyright and Training Data Provenance

A generative model's training data came from somewhere — and the question of whether that content was licensed, consented to, or even known about by the people who created it is one that measurement, at least, can help with directly, even if the legal and ethical answers are much harder.

**You need:** [[n-gram Overlap Metrics (BLEU and ROUGE)]].

## The question it answers

"How can you check whether generated content reproduces specific training material?" The most direct, mechanical check is **n-gram overlap detection**: compare the generated text's own word sequences against a known corpus, and see how much of it matches verbatim. A high overlap at long n-gram lengths is strong evidence of direct reproduction, not independent generation — exactly the kind of signal that matters for questions of data provenance and potential copyright exposure.

## Intuition

A short phrase matching between two texts is unremarkable — plenty of common short phrases appear everywhere, by coincidence. A long, exact, multi-word sequence matching is a different story: the longer the matching stretch, the less plausible it is that two independent pieces of writing would happen to share it by chance. This is the same logic a plagiarism checker uses, applied here to ask whether a model's generated output traces back to specific pieces of its training data.

## Definition and notation

```text
overlap fraction at n-gram length n:
  (number of the generated text's own n-grams that also appear in the
   reference corpus) / (total n-grams in the generated text)
```

## A worked example

Comparing two candidate texts against a short training-corpus snippet, at several n-gram lengths:

```text
training snippet: "it was the best of times it was the worst of times"

verbatim copy:    "it was the best of times it was the worst of times"
  n=3: 100% overlap    n=5: 100% overlap    n=8: 100% overlap

original text:    "it was a cold and difficult winter that year"
  n=3: 0% overlap      n=5: 0% overlap      n=8: 0% overlap
```

The verbatim copy shows complete overlap at every tested n-gram length — exactly what you'd expect from a direct reproduction. The genuinely original text shows zero overlap at any length, despite starting with the same first two words ("it was"), because no *longer* sequence from it matches the training snippet at all.

## Bench

```bench
id: overlap-provenance
title: Checking for verbatim training-data overlap
fallback: Compare a candidate text against a training-corpus snippet at different n-gram lengths and see how much verbatim overlap is detected.
```

**Try this**

1. Compare the verbatim copy's overlap at a short n-gram length versus a long one.
2. Switch to the original text and watch the overlap drop to zero at every length.
3. Consider what a moderate, partial overlap (neither 0% nor 100%) would suggest.

**What you should notice:** overlap detection at longer n-gram lengths is a much stronger signal than overlap at short lengths — short matches are common by coincidence, long exact matches are not.

## Where it appears in AI

* **Training-data deduplication pipelines use exactly this kind of overlap check**, both to clean training corpora of near-duplicates and to audit whether a model's outputs reproduce specific source material.
* **Legal and policy debates around generative AI training data turn substantially on exactly this question**: whether, and how often, a model's output reproduces identifiable, copyrighted source content rather than producing genuinely novel combinations.
* **[[Memorization and Training Data Leakage|memorization]] is the mechanism behind this kind of overlap**: a model that has memorized a specific training sequence can reproduce it closely enough to register as high overlap, long after training.

## Common pitfalls

* **Treating any overlap as proof of copying.** Short, common phrases will overlap between unrelated texts purely by chance — the signal strengthens specifically as the matching n-gram length grows.
* **Assuming zero measured overlap proves a model learned nothing from its training data.** A model can be heavily influenced by a source's style, structure, or ideas without reproducing any long verbatim sequence from it — overlap detection only catches the specific case of near-exact reproduction.
* **Confusing a detection tool with a legal verdict.** Overlap measurement is evidence that can inform a copyright question; it isn't itself a determination of infringement, which depends on legal standards this note doesn't address.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. Why is a long matching n-gram stronger evidence of direct reproduction than a short one?</summary>
Short phrases can match between unrelated texts purely by coincidence; a long, exact, multi-word match is far less likely to occur by chance, making it stronger evidence of actual copying.
</details>

<details><summary>2. In the worked example, why did the "original text" show 0% overlap at every tested length despite sharing its first two words with the training snippet?</summary>
Overlap is measured at the chosen n-gram length — sharing only the first two words means there's no matching 3-gram (or longer) sequence anywhere in the text, so overlap at n=3 and above is exactly zero.
</details>

<details><summary>3. Does overlap detection alone determine whether something is a copyright violation?</summary>
No — it's a measurement tool that provides evidence relevant to such a question, but the actual determination depends on legal standards and context well beyond what n-gram overlap alone can establish.
</details>

## Key terms

* **N-gram overlap detection:** comparing generated text's word sequences against a reference corpus to measure verbatim reproduction.
* **Data provenance:** tracing what a model's training data consisted of and how it was obtained.
* **Deduplication:** removing near-duplicate content from a training corpus, often using overlap-based detection.

## Related

[[n-gram Overlap Metrics (BLEU and ROUGE)]] · [[Memorization and Training Data Leakage]] · [[Watermarking and Synthetic Media Provenance]]

## Memorization and Training Data Leakage

[[Copyright and Training Data Provenance|overlap detection]] checks whether generated output matches training data verbatim. This note covers detecting the underlying cause from the *model's own behavior* instead of its output: a model that has memorized specific training examples tends to be measurably, suspiciously confident about them.

**You need:** [[Copyright and Training Data Provenance]], [[Perplexity as a Generation Metric]].

## The question it answers

"How can you tell, just from a model's own confidence, whether a specific example was in its training data?" This is a **membership inference** question. A model that has memorized a training example tends to assign it unusually high probability — lower [[Perplexity as a Generation Metric|perplexity]] — compared to a genuinely novel, held-out example it never saw. A sizeable, systematic gap between a model's confidence on "likely training" examples versus held-out ones is a real, measurable signal of memorization, not just better general capability.

## Intuition

Ask someone to recite a passage they memorized word-for-word years ago, versus asking them to read a similar but unfamiliar passage aloud for the first time — the first will come out faster, more fluently, with more confidence about exactly which word comes next. A model behaves similarly: on text it has truly memorized, its next-token predictions are unusually sharp and confident, in a way that goes beyond simply being good at predicting that *kind* of text in general.

## Definition and notation

```text
membership-inference signal:
  perplexity(training example) ≪ perplexity(held-out example of similar kind)

→ a large, consistent gap (not just "the model did okay on both")
  suggests the training example was specifically memorized, rather than
  merely well-predicted because it resembles the training distribution
```

## A worked example

A toy model's assigned probabilities on two four-token sequences of a similar kind — one supposedly seen during training, one genuinely never seen:

```text
seen during training:    probabilities [0.95, 0.97, 0.93, 0.96]  →  perplexity 1.050
never seen (held-out):   probabilities [0.40, 0.35, 0.50, 0.30]  →  perplexity 2.627
```

The training example's perplexity sits barely above 1 — the model is almost never surprised by any token in it. The held-out example's perplexity is well over double that, even though both sequences are of a broadly similar kind. That gap — not either number alone — is the actual memorization signal.

## Bench

```bench
id: membership-perplexity-gap
title: Lower perplexity on training data is a memorization signal
fallback: Compare a model's perplexity on an example it supposedly trained on against one it never saw.
```

**Try this**

1. Look at the "seen during training" example's perplexity.
2. Switch to the "never seen" example and compare.
3. Consider how large a gap would need to be before you'd call it suspicious rather than ordinary variation.

**What you should notice:** the gap between the two perplexities, not either value in isolation, is what carries the signal — a model being generally confident isn't suspicious; being *selectively, unusually* confident on specific examples is.

## Where it appears in AI

* **Membership inference attacks are a standard privacy-research technique**, used to audit whether a model leaks information about what specific data it was trained on — relevant well beyond copyright, including personal or sensitive training data.
* **Larger models, trained for longer on smaller or more-repeated datasets, tend to memorize more**, which is why dataset size, deduplication, and number of training epochs are all discussed as memorization risk factors.
* **Extraction attacks go a step further than measuring a gap**: they actively try to get a model to reproduce specific memorized training content verbatim, using exactly the kind of overlap check from [[Copyright and Training Data Provenance]] to confirm success.

## Common pitfalls

* **Treating any confident prediction as evidence of memorization.** A model can be legitimately confident about common, predictable text (like "the" following "of the") without having memorized any specific training example — the signal is a *gap* relative to a comparable held-out example, not confidence alone.
* **Assuming memorization only matters for exact copyright questions.** It's also a genuine privacy concern when training data includes personal information that a model might later reproduce.
* **Forgetting the comparison needs genuinely comparable examples.** Comparing perplexity on a simple sentence against a complex one conflates "this is an easy example" with "this was memorized" — a fair test needs held-out examples of similar difficulty.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. What specifically signals memorization, rather than just general model competence?</summary>
A large, systematic gap between a model's confidence (low perplexity) on supposedly-seen training examples and its confidence on comparable held-out examples — not high confidence on its own.
</details>

<details><summary>2. In the worked example, how much lower was the training example's perplexity compared to the held-out example's?</summary>
About 1.050 versus 2.627 — the held-out example's perplexity was more than double the training example's.
</details>

<details><summary>3. Why do membership inference tests need to compare against a "comparable" held-out example?</summary>
Because an easy or very typical example will naturally get lower perplexity regardless of memorization — the comparison only reveals memorization if the two examples being compared are of similar inherent difficulty.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Membership inference:** determining whether a specific example was part of a model's training data, based on the model's own behavior.
* **Memorization:** a model reproducing or being unusually confident about specific training examples, rather than generalizing from them.
* **Extraction attack:** deliberately prompting a model to reproduce specific memorized training content.

## Related

[[Copyright and Training Data Provenance]] · [[Perplexity as a Generation Metric]] · [[Watermarking and Synthetic Media Provenance]]

## Watermarking and Synthetic Media Provenance

Detecting memorized training content means comparing a model's behavior against something it saw before. Telling generated content apart from real content is a related but different problem, and one a model's creator can actually engineer a solution for: deliberately biasing generation in a way invisible to a reader but detectable by anyone who knows the rule.

**You need:** [[Memorization and Training Data Leakage]].

## The question it answers

"How can generated text be marked as machine-generated without visibly changing how it reads?" A **green-list watermark** biases which tokens a model is likely to choose, using a rule invisible to a casual reader: the *previous* token deterministically seeds a pseudorandom split of the vocabulary into a "green" list (some fraction, γ) and the rest. Nudging the model to prefer green-list tokens, even slightly, produces text with a green-token fraction well above what random chance would produce — detectable by anyone who knows the seeding rule, without needing to see how the text was generated.

## Intuition

Imagine a secret rule: "whichever word was just said determines a specific, unpredictable-looking half of the dictionary that's temporarily 'preferred.'" Write normally while slightly favoring that preferred half whenever you have a free choice, and the result still reads completely naturally — nothing about any individual sentence looks unusual. But someone who knows the rule can walk through your text afterward, recompute which half was "preferred" at every point, and check: did you use far more preferred-list words than pure chance would predict? If yes, that's the watermark, detected with no need to have watched you write it.

## Definition and notation

```text
green-list rule: previous token's id seeds a pseudorandom split of the
  vocabulary into a green set (fraction γ) and a red set (fraction 1−γ)

generation: bias every green-list token's logit upward by δ before choosing
detection: recompute the green list at every position; measure the
  fraction of generated tokens that landed in their own green list
  → near γ under no watermark; well above γ if the bias was applied
```

## A worked example

200 toy tokens generated two ways — with and without the green-list bias (δ=4, γ=0.5, so about half the vocabulary is "green" at any position) — then checked against the exact same green-list rule used during generation:

```text
unwatermarked generation:  49.2% of tokens land in their own green list
  (matches the ~50% expected by pure chance, with no bias applied)

watermarked generation:    100.0% of tokens land in their own green list
  (far beyond chance — unmistakable evidence of the bias)
```

With no bias, the green-token fraction sits right where random chance predicts (about 50%, since half the vocabulary is green at any step). With the bias applied, every single token in this run happened to land in the green list — a result pure chance would essentially never produce, making the watermark trivially detectable by anyone running the same green-list rule over the text.

## Bench

```bench
id: watermark-detect
title: A hidden bias that's easy to detect, if you know the rule
fallback: Toggle a watermark bias on and off and watch how much the green-token fraction departs from the chance level.
```

**Try this**

1. Turn the watermark off and check the green-token fraction sits near 50%.
2. Turn it on and watch the fraction shoot up.
3. Lower the bias strength (δ) and see how weak the watermark can get before the fraction drops back toward chance.

**What you should notice:** detection doesn't require seeing the generation process at all — it only requires recomputing the same green-list rule over the finished text and checking whether the green fraction is implausibly high to have occurred by chance.

## Where it appears in AI

* **This is a real, deployed technique (closely following Kirchenbauer et al., 2023)**, used by some LLM providers specifically to let anyone with the detection rule check whether a piece of text came from their model.
* **Robustness is the open challenge**: paraphrasing, translation, or heavy editing of watermarked text can wash out the green-list signal, since those operations change which tokens actually appear.
* **It's a fundamentally different approach from [[Copyright and Training Data Provenance|overlap detection]]**: overlap detection looks for evidence a specific training example was reproduced; watermarking is a deliberate signal engineered in at generation time, present whether or not any training data is involved at all.

## Common pitfalls

* **Assuming a watermark is visible or changes the text's readability.** The entire point is that it doesn't — the bias operates purely at the level of which plausible-but-arbitrary token choice gets made, not on content or style.
* **Expecting watermark detection to work without the exact seeding rule.** Detection requires recomputing the same green-list function used during generation; without knowing that rule, the bias is statistically invisible.
* **Treating watermarking as unbreakable.** A sufficiently aggressive rewrite can degrade or destroy the signal, since the watermark lives in specific token choices that a rewrite can simply replace.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. What determines whether a given token counts as "green" at a particular position?</summary>
The token immediately before it — that previous token deterministically seeds a pseudorandom split of the vocabulary into a green set and a red set.
</details>

<details><summary>2. In the worked example, why was 49.2% (unwatermarked) not considered suspicious, while 100.0% (watermarked) clearly was?</summary>
49.2% sits right at the chance level expected when half the vocabulary is green and no bias is applied; 100.0% is so far beyond what chance alone would produce that it's essentially impossible without a deliberate bias toward green tokens.
</details>

<details><summary>3. How does watermark detection differ from overlap-based provenance detection?</summary>
Watermark detection recomputes a known rule over the text and checks for a statistical excess of green tokens, requiring no access to any training data; overlap detection instead compares the text directly against a specific reference corpus to find verbatim matches.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Watermark (green-list):** a deliberate, invisible bias toward a pseudorandomly chosen subset of tokens, detectable by recomputing the same rule.
* **Green list:** the pseudorandomly selected subset of the vocabulary favored at a given generation step.
* **Detection:** checking a piece of text for an implausibly high fraction of green-list tokens under the known seeding rule.

## Related

[[Memorization and Training Data Leakage]] · [[Copyright and Training Data Provenance]] · [[Content Safety and Red-Teaming]]

## Content Safety and Red-Teaming

A watermark is a signal engineered to survive detection. A content-safety classifier faces the opposite adversarial pressure: anyone trying to get harmful content past it is actively looking for ways to make the detector fail, not cooperating with it.

**You need:** [[Watermarking and Synthetic Media Provenance]].

## The question it answers

"How robust is a content-safety filter against someone actively trying to get around it?" **Red-teaming** means deliberately testing a system's defenses the way an adversary would, rather than only checking it against the inputs it was designed for. A simple **keyword-based classifier** is a clear, checkable example of a defense that can look solid against ordinary input while still being easy to slip past using a trivial trick — a single character substitution, in the most basic case — that a real adversary would try as a matter of course.

## Intuition

A bouncer checking IDs only for an exact name match on a list can be fooled by someone spelling their name slightly differently on a fake ID — not because the check is pointless, but because it's checking for one narrow, exact signal rather than the underlying thing it's actually trying to catch. A keyword filter is the same kind of narrow check: it catches the literal word, and anyone motivated to get past it only has to avoid typing that literal word.

## Definition and notation

```text
keyword classifier: flagged(text) = any blocked keyword appears as a
  literal substring of text (case-insensitive)

a red-team probe: a minimal transformation of flagged text designed to
  evade the classifier while preserving its meaning to a human reader
  (character substitution, spacing, synonyms, encoding, translation, ...)
```

## A worked example

Two pairs of requests, each an original and a trivially obfuscated version using a simple character substitution:

```text
original:    "how to build a bomb"        → flagged: true
obfuscated:  "how to build a b0mb"        → flagged: false

original:    "how to hack an account"     → flagged: true
obfuscated:  "how to h4ck an account"     → flagged: false
```

In both cases, swapping a single letter for a visually similar digit is enough to defeat an exact-substring keyword check, while the request's meaning to a human reader is completely unchanged. The classifier isn't "almost" working here — it fails completely on both obfuscated inputs, despite catching both originals perfectly.

## Bench

```bench
id: safety-classifier-evasion
title: A classifier that's easy to slip past
fallback: Compare whether a keyword-based safety classifier flags an original request versus a trivially obfuscated version of it.
```

**Try this**

1. Check that both original requests are flagged.
2. Check that both obfuscated versions are not.
3. Consider how many other simple tricks (spacing, synonyms, different languages) would likely work just as well against this specific classifier.

**What you should notice:** the obfuscation needed almost no sophistication — a single-character substitution was enough — which is exactly why keyword matching alone is considered a weak content-safety mechanism on its own.

## Where it appears in AI

* **Production content-safety systems layer multiple detection methods** (semantic classifiers that understand meaning past exact wording, not just keyword matching) specifically because keyword lists alone are this easy to evade.
* **Red-teaming is now a standard, often required practice before deploying a generative model**, with dedicated teams (internal or external) specifically tasked with finding prompts that produce harmful output the system was supposed to block.
* **The same evasion principle generalizes well past keyword filters**: any safety mechanism relying on a narrow, literal signal — rather than a deeper understanding of meaning or intent — tends to be vulnerable to minor, meaning-preserving changes designed to dodge it.

## Common pitfalls

* **Treating any successful filter as evidence the system is safe.** The worked example's classifier works perfectly on unmodified input — testing only unmodified input would have missed its complete failure on trivially modified input entirely.
* **Assuming red-teaming only has to find exotic attacks.** The worked example's evasion (swapping one character) is about as simple as an attack can be — a thorough red-teaming effort has to check simple tricks first, not just sophisticated ones.
* **Fixing one discovered evasion and declaring the system safe.** Patching the specific evasion found (blocking "b0mb" too) doesn't address the underlying weakness (literal substring matching); a determined adversary tries the next trivial variant.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. Why did a single-character substitution completely defeat the keyword classifier in the worked example?</summary>
