* [[LLM-as-Judge Evaluation]]: using one model to grade another's output, and where that breaks down.
* [[Capability Evaluation vs. Safety Evaluation]]: two different questions — can it, and should it — that need different tests.
* [[Leaderboards and Their Limits]]: what a ranked list of model scores does and doesn't tell you.
* [[Adversarial and Jailbreak Evaluation]]: testing a model against inputs specifically designed to break its guardrails.

## Benchmark Suites (MMLU, HELM, BIG-bench)

Comparing two LLMs fairly requires testing them on the same questions, under the same conditions, at a scale no individual could check by hand. A benchmark suite is exactly that: a large, standardized, repeatable test — but standardized testing has its own well-known blind spot.

**You need:** [[Test-Time Compute Scaling]].

## The question it answers

"How does the field actually measure and compare LLM capability at scale?" **Benchmark suites** (MMLU's broad academic-subject multiple choice, HELM's wide battery of tasks and metrics, BIG-bench's crowd-sourced diverse tasks, among many others) run a model against thousands of fixed questions spanning many categories, then report scores per category and an **overall average** across all of them. The overall average is convenient for ranking models at a glance — and it can also hide a serious weakness in one specific category behind strong performance everywhere else.

## Intuition

A student's overall GPA can look solidly good while hiding a single subject they're genuinely struggling in, if their other grades are strong enough to pull the average up. Anyone looking only at the GPA would never know; anyone looking at the full transcript, subject by subject, would catch it immediately. A benchmark's overall score works exactly the same way — it's a genuinely useful single number, but it's also a number specifically built to average away the detail a per-category breakdown would reveal.

## Definition and notation

```text
overall score = (1/k) · Σ scoreᵢ   across k categories

→ one low-scoring category, averaged with several high-scoring ones,
  can leave the overall score looking comfortably high
```

## A worked example

A toy model's scores across five benchmark categories:

```text
math:        0.85
reading:     0.82
coding:      0.88
safety_qa:   0.40   ← a real weakness
commonsense: 0.80

overall average: 0.750
```

The overall average of 0.750 looks like a solidly competent model — and by four of five categories, it is. But the `safety_qa` category sits at just 0.40, a serious weakness that the overall number alone gives no hint of at all. Anyone comparing models purely by their overall average would never notice this gap unless they specifically looked at the category breakdown.

## Bench

```bench
id: benchmark-category-breakdown
title: One weak score, hidden in the average
fallback: Adjust one category's score and watch how little it moves the overall average, even when that category is seriously weak.
```

**Try this**

1. Set the safety_qa score low and note the overall average.
2. Raise it toward the other categories' level and compare.
3. Consider how different the overall average would need to be before you'd suspect a hidden weak category.

**What you should notice:** the overall average changes only modestly even when one category swings dramatically — averaging across several categories is specifically what dampens the visibility of any single one.

## Where it appears in AI

* **Real benchmark reports (MMLU, HELM, BIG-bench and others) typically do publish per-category breakdowns alongside an overall score**, precisely because the overall number alone is known to obscure category-specific weaknesses.
* **[[Benchmark Contamination and Leakage|a benchmark's score is only meaningful if the model hasn't already seen the test questions]]** — a high score contaminated by leaked test data says nothing real about genuine capability.
* **[[Leaderboards and Their Limits|leaderboards built from these benchmarks]] inherit this same averaging problem**, often compounded by how different leaderboards choose to weight categories against each other.

## Common pitfalls

* **Ranking models purely by overall benchmark score, with no category breakdown.** The worked example shows exactly how a meaningful weakness can hide behind an otherwise-strong average.
* **Assuming a high overall score means uniformly strong performance.** It only means the *average* is high — individual categories can vary far more than the overall number suggests.
* **Treating benchmark categories as equally important for every use case.** A model's weak category might be entirely irrelevant for one application and critical for another — the right way to weigh categories depends on what the model will actually be used for.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. Why can an overall benchmark average hide a serious weakness in one category?</summary>
Because averaging across several categories dampens the visibility of any single one — strong performance in most categories can pull the overall average up even when one specific category is seriously weak.
</details>

<details><summary>2. In the worked example, what was hidden behind the overall average of 0.750?</summary>
A safety_qa score of just 0.40, a real weakness, while the other four categories all scored 0.80 or above.
</details>

<details><summary>3. Why do real benchmark reports typically publish per-category breakdowns alongside an overall score?</summary>
Because the overall score alone is known to obscure category-specific weaknesses — a per-category breakdown is needed to actually see where a model is strong or weak.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Benchmark suite:** a large, standardized set of test questions used to measure and compare model capability.
* **Overall average:** a single score computed by averaging performance across all benchmark categories.
* **Category breakdown:** per-category scores that reveal strengths and weaknesses an overall average can hide.

## Related

[[Test-Time Compute Scaling]] · [[Benchmark Contamination and Leakage]] · [[Leaderboards and Their Limits]]

## Benchmark Contamination and Leakage

A benchmark score only means something if the model is actually being tested, rather than recalling something it already saw. The problem: with pretraining corpora drawn from huge swaths of the internet, there's a real chance a benchmark's own questions — or close paraphrases of them — ended up inside the training data.

**You need:** [[Benchmark Suites (MMLU, HELM, BIG-bench)]], [[Data Deduplication and Quality Filtering]].

## The question it answers

"How can you tell whether a model's high benchmark score reflects genuine capability or memorized test questions?" **Contamination** means a benchmark's test examples (or close variants) appeared in the model's training data. The same [[Data Deduplication and Quality Filtering|n-gram overlap technique]] used to find near-duplicate training documents can be turned around and used to check a specific concern: does a benchmark question show substantial overlap with anything in the training corpus? High overlap is a direct, checkable red flag for contamination.

## Intuition

A standardized test is only meaningful if the person taking it hasn't already seen the answer key. If it later turns out the exact questions (or very close paraphrases) were accidentally included in the study materials beforehand, a high score on that test says a lot less about genuine ability than it first appeared to. Checking a benchmark's questions against a model's training data for suspicious overlap is exactly like checking whether a specific set of exam questions somehow leaked into the study guide ahead of time.

## Definition and notation

```text
contamination check: overlap_fraction(benchmark_question, training_document, n)
  (the exact same n-gram Jaccard overlap mechanism used for deduplication,
   applied here specifically to a benchmark question against training text)

high overlap → the benchmark question (or a close paraphrase)
  was likely present in training data → the score is suspect
```

## A worked example

A benchmark question checked against two different training documents using 5-grams:

```text
benchmark question:  "what is the capital of australia and what is its population"

contaminated document:  "the quiz asks what is the capital of australia and
  what is its population exactly"
  → overlap: 100%   (every 5-gram of the question appears in this document)

clean document:  "canberra became the capital in 1927 after a long design competition"
  → overlap: 0%     (no shared 5-grams at all)
```

The contaminated document shares every single 5-gram with the benchmark question — it clearly contains the question nearly verbatim. The clean document, despite being topically related (it's also about Canberra becoming the capital), shares no 5-grams with the question's exact phrasing at all, and raises no contamination concern.

## Bench

```bench
id: contamination-detection
title: Did the model already see the test?
fallback: Check a benchmark question against two training documents for n-gram overlap, and see which one gets flagged as contaminated.
```

**Try this**

1. Check the question against the contaminated document.
2. Switch to the clean document and compare.
3. Adjust the n-gram length and see how it changes detection sensitivity.

**What you should notice:** topical relatedness alone (the clean document is also about the same subject) doesn't trigger a contamination flag — only substantial overlap in actual phrasing does.

## Where it appears in AI

* **Major benchmark releases now routinely report contamination analyses**, checking how much of the benchmark's content can be found, verbatim or near-verbatim, in commonly used pretraining corpora.
* **Contamination inflates reported capability in a way that's easy to miss without explicitly checking for it** — a contaminated score looks exactly like a genuine high score unless someone specifically goes looking for overlap.
* **It's closely related to [[Memorization and Training Data Leakage|memorization more broadly]]**: contamination is specifically the case where the memorized content happens to be benchmark material, making the resulting evaluation misleading rather than just a general privacy or copyright concern.

## Common pitfalls

* **Treating a high score as proof of contamination without checking overlap directly.** A model can genuinely be good at a benchmark's subject matter without having seen the exact questions — overlap checking distinguishes the two possibilities.
* **Assuming contamination only matters for exact-match questions.** Close paraphrases of benchmark questions, not just verbatim copies, can still meaningfully inflate scores if a model has effectively memorized the pattern.
* **Checking only a tiny sample of benchmark questions for overlap.** A thorough contamination audit needs to check a representative portion of the benchmark, not just a few spot checks, to produce a trustworthy overall assessment.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. What does it mean for a benchmark to be "contaminated"?</summary>
That the benchmark's test examples, or close variants of them, appeared in the model's training data — meaning a high score may reflect memorization rather than genuine capability.
</details>

<details><summary>2. In the worked example, why did the clean document raise no contamination concern despite being on the same topic as the benchmark question?</summary>
Because topical similarity alone doesn't create n-gram overlap — the clean document shared no 5-grams with the question's actual phrasing, even though it discussed the same underlying subject.
</details>

<details><summary>3. Why is contamination checking essentially the same technique as deduplication?</summary>
Both use n-gram overlap to detect when two pieces of text are suspiciously similar — deduplication applies it to find near-duplicate documents within a corpus, while contamination checking applies it to compare specific benchmark questions against the training corpus.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Contamination:** when benchmark test material (or close variants) appears in a model's training data.
* **Leakage:** another term for the same phenomenon — evaluation material unintentionally present in training data.
* **Overlap check:** using n-gram similarity to detect suspicious overlap between a benchmark question and training text.

## Related

[[Benchmark Suites (MMLU, HELM, BIG-bench)]] · [[Data Deduplication and Quality Filtering]] · [[Memorization and Training Data Leakage]]

## LLM-as-Judge Evaluation

Benchmark suites work well for questions with a single checkable right answer. Most interesting LLM output — a summary, a piece of writing, a conversational response — doesn't have one. Using another LLM as the judge scales human-like evaluation far beyond what human raters alone could manage — at the cost of inheriting whatever biases that judge brings with it.

**You need:** [[Benchmark Contamination and Leakage]], [[Constitutional AI and RLAIF]].

## The question it answers

"Can an LLM reliably judge the quality of another LLM's output?" Often, roughly — but not without real, documented biases. One of the best-known is **position bias**: when a judge is shown two responses and asked which is better, its preference can shift measurably just from *which one is shown first*, independent of the responses' actual content.

## Intuition

Asking a human reviewer to compare two near-tied essays, which one they pick can genuinely be swayed by which one they happened to read first — a documented effect in human judgment too, not unique to AI judges. An LLM judge, trained on patterns in human-generated text and human preference data, can inherit exactly this same kind of bias — preferring whichever response occupies a particular position in the prompt, regardless of its actual content.

## Definition and notation

```text
judge_score(response, position) = quality(response) + bias_term(position)

position bias: bias_term("first") > bias_term("second")
  → the SAME response can score differently depending on
    where it's placed in the judge's prompt
```

## A worked example

Two responses, A (quality 0.60) and B (quality 0.65) — B is genuinely slightly better — judged under a toy position bias of +0.15 for whichever is shown first:

```text
A shown first, B second:
  A score: 0.60 + 0.15 = 0.75     B score: 0.65 + 0 = 0.65
  judge prefers: A   ← wrong; B was actually the better response

B shown first, A second:
  A score: 0.60 + 0 = 0.60        B score: 0.65 + 0.15 = 0.80
  judge prefers: B   ← correct
```

The exact same two responses, with the exact same underlying quality, produce opposite judge verdicts purely depending on which one happened to be placed first in the prompt. Nothing about the responses changed between the two trials — only their order did.

## Bench

```bench
id: judge-position-bias
title: The same two answers, a different winner
fallback: Swap which response is shown first and watch the judge's preferred winner flip, even though neither response actually changed.
```

**Try this**

1. Put A first and see which response the judge prefers.
2. Swap the order and compare.
3. Consider what would happen if the quality gap between A and B were much larger than the position bias itself.

**What you should notice:** the judge's verdict flips completely from just swapping presentation order — a clear sign the bias term, not the responses' actual quality, is deciding the outcome in this toy example.

## Where it appears in AI

* **Production LLM-as-judge pipelines commonly randomize or swap response order and average the results**, specifically to cancel out position bias rather than trust a single-order comparison.
* **Other documented LLM-judge biases include length bias (preferring longer responses) and self-preference bias (a model favoring responses similar to its own style)**, both close relatives of the [[Reward Hacking and Sycophancy|reward hacking concerns]] already covered in alignment training.
* **LLM-as-judge is widely used specifically because it's far cheaper and faster than collecting large volumes of human preference judgments** — the biases are a real cost of that scalability, not a reason to discard the approach outright.

## Common pitfalls

* **Trusting a single-order comparison as a fair judgment.** As the worked example shows, that alone can be enough to flip the verdict, with no change to the responses themselves.
* **Assuming LLM-as-judge is strictly worse than human judgment because of these biases.** Humans show related biases of their own (not identical ones, but real presentation effects); the question is how to mitigate rather than eliminate bias entirely.
* **Using LLM-as-judge to evaluate properties the judge itself is unreliable at assessing.** A judge's own blind spots (in factuality-checking, for instance) can limit how trustworthy its evaluations are on exactly those dimensions.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. What is position bias, in the context of LLM-as-judge evaluation?</summary>
A measurable tendency for a judge to prefer whichever response is shown first (or in some other specific position), independent of the responses' actual quality.
</details>

<details><summary>2. In the worked example, why did the judge's preferred response change between the two trials?</summary>
Only the display order changed — B scored higher when shown first, and A scored higher when shown first — the position bias term, not any change in the responses, determined which one "won" each time.
</details>

<details><summary>3. What's a standard mitigation for position bias in LLM-as-judge pipelines?</summary>
Randomizing or swapping which response is shown first and averaging the results across both orderings, to cancel out the position-dependent bias.
</details>

## Key terms

* **LLM-as-judge:** using an LLM to evaluate the quality of generated outputs, often by comparison.
* **Position bias:** a judge's tendency to favor whichever response is shown in a particular position, independent of content.
* **Order randomization:** swapping response order across evaluations to cancel out position bias.

## Related

[[Constitutional AI and RLAIF]] · [[Reward Hacking and Sycophancy]] · [[Capability Evaluation vs. Safety Evaluation]]

## Capability Evaluation vs. Safety Evaluation

"Is this model good?" is really two separate questions wearing one trench coat: can it do the task, and will it behave safely while trying? A single alignment-training decision can push these two scores in opposite directions at once.

**You need:** [[LLM-as-Judge Evaluation]], [[Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF)]].

## The question it answers

"Can a model's capability and its safety be evaluated, and optimized, independently?" Not entirely — they're often linked through the same training decisions. **Capability evaluation** measures whether a model can perform a task well (solve problems, answer correctly, write competently). **Safety evaluation** measures whether it behaves appropriately — refusing genuinely harmful requests, avoiding unsafe outputs. Pushing alignment training harder in one direction (say, to improve safety refusals) can measurably reduce capability on ordinary tasks, and vice versa — the two scores aren't independent dials.

## Intuition

Teaching someone to be more cautious before answering any question at all — double-checking, hedging, sometimes declining to answer when genuinely unsure — makes them safer to rely on in borderline cases, but it can also make them slower and less willing to confidently tackle perfectly ordinary requests they'd have handled fine before. Dialing caution up or down doesn't just change one outcome; it shifts both how often they get things right *and* how often they refuse or hedge on things they didn't need to.

## Definition and notation

```text
capability(alignment_strength): tends to decrease as alignment
  training is pushed harder (more conservative, more refusals)

safety(alignment_strength): tends to increase as alignment
  training is pushed harder

→ the two scores move in roughly opposite directions as the same
  underlying knob (alignment training strength) is adjusted
```

## A worked example

Toy capability and safety scores across a range of alignment training strength:

```text
strength 0.00:  capability 0.850   safety 0.500
strength 0.25:  capability 0.813   safety 0.613
strength 0.50:  capability 0.775   safety 0.725
strength 0.75:  capability 0.738   safety 0.838
strength 1.00:  capability 0.700   safety 0.950
```

Pushing alignment strength from 0 to 1 raises safety by 0.45 (from 0.500 to 0.950) while lowering capability by 0.15 (from 0.850 to 0.700). Neither score moved independently of the other — the same training decision drove both changes simultaneously, in opposite directions.

## Bench

```bench
id: capability-safety-tradeoff
title: Two scores, one knob, opposite directions
fallback: Adjust alignment training strength and watch capability and safety scores move in opposite directions.
```

**Try this**

1. Set alignment strength to 0 and note both scores.
2. Raise it toward 1 and watch both move, in opposite directions.
3. Find a strength where you'd consider the trade-off acceptable, and justify why.

**What you should notice:** there's no single "right" point on this curve in the abstract — where to land depends entirely on how much the deployment context actually weighs capability against safety.

## Where it appears in AI

* **Production deployment decisions routinely involve explicitly choosing a point on exactly this kind of trade-off curve**, informed by what the model is actually being used for and what the real-world cost of each kind of failure is.
* **[[Reward Hacking and Sycophancy|a poorly calibrated safety signal]] can push this trade-off worse than necessary** — a model trained against an overly blunt safety metric might sacrifice more capability than the actual safety gain warrants.
* **Different deployments reasonably land in different places on this curve**: a coding assistant and a general-purpose consumer chatbot facing very different risk profiles might justify very different alignment strengths.

## Common pitfalls

* **Treating capability and safety scores as independently optimizable.** The worked example's own curves move together, in opposite directions, as a function of the same underlying training choice — improving one at this margin generally costs some of the other.
* **Assuming more alignment training is always better.** Past a point, the capability cost can outweigh the safety benefit for a given deployment's actual risk profile.
* **Reporting only one of the two scores.** A model's capability score alone says nothing about its safety behavior, and vice versa — both need reporting for an evaluation to be meaningful.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. Why can't capability and safety generally be maximized independently in this setup?</summary>
Because both are driven by the same underlying training decision (alignment strength) — pushing that knob in one direction tends to move both scores, in opposite directions, rather than letting either be adjusted on its own.
</details>

<details><summary>2. In the worked example, what happened to capability and safety as alignment strength went from 0 to 1?</summary>
Capability dropped from 0.850 to 0.700, while safety rose from 0.500 to 0.950 — a genuine trade-off, not a free improvement in one without cost to the other.
</details>

<details><summary>3. Why might two different deployments reasonably choose different points on this trade-off curve?</summary>
Because the real-world cost of a capability failure versus a safety failure differs by context — a deployment where safety failures are especially costly might reasonably accept lower capability, and vice versa.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Capability evaluation:** measuring whether a model can perform a task well.
* **Safety evaluation:** measuring whether a model behaves appropriately, including refusing harmful requests.
* **Capability-safety trade-off:** the tendency for alignment training strength to move these two scores in opposite directions.

## Related

[[LLM-as-Judge Evaluation]] · [[Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF)]] · [[Adversarial and Jailbreak Evaluation]]

## Leaderboards and Their Limits

A leaderboard promises a simple answer to "which model is best?" — rank them by score, read off the winner. The quiet catch: that ranking depends entirely on a weighting decision that's usually invisible, and a different reasonable weighting can produce a different winner from the exact same underlying scores.

**You need:** [[Capability Evaluation vs. Safety Evaluation]].

## The question it answers

"Can a single leaderboard ranking be trusted as *the* answer to which model is best?" Not without knowing how it was weighted. A leaderboard combines scores across several categories into one ranking number — and which category gets more weight is a real choice, not a neutral default. Two models can trade the #1 spot depending entirely on that weighting, even with their individual category scores held completely fixed.

## Intuition

Ranking job candidates by "overall fit" when one is clearly stronger on technical skill and the other is clearly stronger on communication produces a different winner depending on how much the hiring decision happens to weigh technical skill against communication — neither candidate's individual skills changed, only which one the ranking favors did. A leaderboard combining several evaluation categories into one score is making exactly this kind of weighting decision, usually without making it explicit.

## Definition and notation

```text
weighted leaderboard score(model) = Σᵢ weightᵢ · scoreᵢ(model) / Σᵢ weightᵢ

→ the RANKING between two models can flip entirely depending on
  which weighting is used, even with every individual score fixed
```

## A worked example

Two models with fixed category scores:

```text
Model X:  reasoning 0.90   creativity 0.50   safety 0.70
Model Y:  reasoning 0.60   creativity 0.90   safety 0.70
```

Under a weighting that favors reasoning 3× over the others:

```text
Model X: 0.780      Model Y: 0.680      → Model X leads
```

Under a weighting that favors creativity 3× over the others instead:

```text
Model X: 0.620      Model Y: 0.800      → Model Y leads
```

Neither model's underlying category scores changed at all between the two calculations — only the weighting did, and the leaderboard's declared "winner" flipped completely as a result.

## Bench

```bench
id: leaderboard-reweight
title: The ranking depends on the weighting
fallback: Adjust how heavily a leaderboard weighs one category and watch which of two models comes out on top.
```

**Try this**

1. Set the creativity weight low and note which model leads.
2. Raise the creativity weight and watch the leader flip.
3. Find the weighting where the two models are essentially tied.

**What you should notice:** the flip happens with absolutely no change to either model — it's purely a consequence of the weighting applied to the same fixed underlying scores.

## Where it appears in AI

* **Different public LLM leaderboards genuinely rank the same models differently**, in no small part because they weigh categories (reasoning, safety, creativity, cost, speed) differently, not because they disagree about any individual category score.
* **A leaderboard's weighting choice reflects a judgment about what matters most**, which may or may not match what matters most for a specific downstream use case — the "best" model on a general leaderboard isn't necessarily the best choice for a specific task.
* **[[Choosing a Model for a Task|picking a model for a real application]] should generally look at the relevant category breakdown directly**, rather than relying on a single aggregate leaderboard ranking built around someone else's weighting choices.

## Common pitfalls

* **Treating a leaderboard's #1 ranking as an objective, universal fact.** It's the result of a specific, often unstated weighting decision applied to the underlying category scores — a different reasonable weighting can produce a different #1.
* **Assuming different leaderboards disagreeing means one of them is simply wrong.** Both can be using accurate underlying category scores while still disagreeing on the final ranking, purely due to different weighting choices.
* **Ignoring the category breakdown in favor of the aggregate rank.** The most actionable information — which model is actually better for a specific need — usually lives in the category-level scores, not the single combined ranking number.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. Why can two leaderboards disagree about which model is "best" even when they agree on individual category scores?</summary>
Because the overall ranking depends on how those category scores are weighted and combined — different weighting choices can produce different rankings from identical underlying scores.
</details>

<details><summary>2. In the worked example, what caused the ranking between Model X and Model Y to flip?</summary>
Only the weighting applied to the fixed category scores changed — from favoring reasoning to favoring creativity — with no change at all to either model's actual underlying scores.
</details>

<details><summary>3. What should someone choosing a model for a specific task look at, rather than relying solely on an aggregate leaderboard rank?</summary>
The category-level score breakdown directly, weighted according to what actually matters for their specific use case, rather than trusting a general leaderboard's own (often unstated) weighting choices.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Leaderboard:** a ranking of models by a combined score across evaluation categories.
* **Category weighting:** the relative importance assigned to each evaluation category when combining them into one score.
* **Ranking flip:** a change in which model ranks highest, caused purely by a change in weighting rather than in underlying scores.

[[Capability Evaluation vs. Safety Evaluation]] · [[Benchmark Suites (MMLU, HELM, BIG-bench)]] · [[Choosing a Model for a Task]]

## Adversarial and Jailbreak Evaluation

[[Capability Evaluation vs. Safety Evaluation|safety evaluation]] on ordinary, well-behaved inputs only tells you how a model behaves when nobody's trying to break it. Adversarial evaluation asks the harder, more important question: how does it behave when someone specifically is?

**You need:** [[Capability Evaluation vs. Safety Evaluation]], [[Content Safety and Red-Teaming]].

## The question it answers

"How well do a model's safety guardrails hold up against someone actively trying to defeat them?" **Jailbreak evaluation** measures the **success rate** of specific adversarial strategies — a direct harmful request, a role-play framing that asks the model to "pretend," obfuscated or encoded phrasing, a long prompt priming the model with many examples of compliance — at getting a model to produce output its guardrails are supposed to block. Different strategies succeed at very different rates, and a model's safety can't be fairly judged by its response to direct requests alone.

## Intuition

A lock's resistance to a straightforward attempt at the front door says very little about how it holds up against someone specifically probing for weaknesses — testing the windows, trying a bump key, checking whether a side door was left unlocked. A guardrail's resistance to a plainly-stated harmful request is the lock's front door; jailbreak evaluation is testing every other way in that a motivated attacker would actually try.

## Definition and notation

```text
attack success rate(strategy) = fraction of adversarial attempts
  using that strategy that successfully bypass the model's guardrails

→ different strategies have very different success rates against
  the same model's same guardrails
```

## A worked example

Toy success rates for four attack strategies against the same model's guardrails:

```text
direct request:                    2%    (guardrails hold almost completely)
role-play framing:                35%    ("pretend you're a character who...")
multi-step encoding/obfuscation:   48%    (disguising the request's true content)
many-shot priming:                 55%    (many examples of compliance before the real ask)
```

A direct, plainly-stated harmful request is blocked almost every time — a model evaluated only against this strategy would look extremely safe. But more sophisticated strategies succeed at dramatically higher rates, more than half the time for the most effective one tested here, revealing guardrails that are far less robust than the direct-request number alone would suggest.

## Bench

```bench
id: jailbreak-attack-rates
title: Not every attack is equally effective
fallback: Compare success rates across several adversarial attack strategies against the same model's guardrails.
```

**Try this**

1. Look at the direct-request success rate.
2. Compare it to the most effective strategy tested.
3. Consider what a safety report based only on direct requests would miss.

**What you should notice:** evaluating safety using only the easiest-to-block attack strategy (a direct request) paints an overly optimistic picture — the real test is whether guardrails hold against the strategies most likely to actually succeed.

## Where it appears in AI

* **Red-teaming teams (internal or external) specifically develop and test strategies like these before a model's deployment**, precisely because direct-request testing alone would miss most real vulnerabilities.
* **New jailbreak strategies are continuously discovered as models and guardrails evolve** — adversarial evaluation is an ongoing process, not a one-time certification that stays valid forever.
* **[[Content Safety and Red-Teaming|the same obfuscation principle from earlier on the Generative AI planet]] generalizes here**: a guardrail built around a narrow signal (blocking specific phrasing) is vulnerable to any input that evades that narrow signal while preserving the underlying harmful intent.

## Common pitfalls

* **Reporting safety performance using only direct-request testing.** The worked example shows this can dramatically overstate how robust a model's guardrails actually are.
* **Assuming a guardrail that resists one attack strategy resists all of them.** Different strategies exploit genuinely different weaknesses — resistance to one doesn't imply resistance to the others.
* **Treating adversarial evaluation as a one-time check.** New attack strategies are discovered continuously; a model evaluated as robust against today's known strategies isn't guaranteed to stay that way against tomorrow's.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. Why is testing a model's guardrails only against direct requests insufficient for safety evaluation?</summary>
Because direct requests are typically the easiest for guardrails to block — more sophisticated strategies (role-play framing, obfuscation, priming) can succeed at much higher rates, which direct-request testing alone would never reveal.
</details>

<details><summary>2. In the worked example, which attack strategy was most effective, and by how much did it outperform a direct request?</summary>
Many-shot priming, at 55% success, compared to a direct request's 2% — more than 25 times as effective at bypassing the same guardrails.
</details>

<details><summary>3. Why is adversarial evaluation an ongoing process rather than a one-time check?</summary>
Because new jailbreak strategies are continuously discovered as models and their guardrails evolve — a model found robust against currently known strategies isn't guaranteed to remain robust against future ones.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Jailbreak:** a successful attempt to bypass a model's safety guardrails.
* **Attack success rate:** the fraction of adversarial attempts using a given strategy that successfully bypass guardrails.
* **Adversarial evaluation:** testing a model's safety specifically against strategies designed to defeat its guardrails, not just ordinary inputs.

[[Content Safety and Red-Teaming]] · [[Capability Evaluation vs. Safety Evaluation]] · [[Guardrails and Deployment-Time Safety Filters]]

## The LLM Landscape

Outside the technical mechanics, LLMs exist inside a fast-moving ecosystem of model families, release decisions, licenses and governance frameworks that shape who can actually build on what. This district covers that landscape.

Topics on this stretch of the road:

* [[A History of LLM Families (GPT, BERT, T5, Llama)]]: how today's major model lineages trace back to a handful of architectural decisions.
* [[Open-Weight vs. Closed Models]]: what "open" actually means for a model, and what it doesn't.
* [[Model Cards and Responsible Release]]: the documentation that's supposed to accompany a released model, and why it matters.
* [[Licensing and Model Governance]]: the legal terms that determine what you're actually allowed to do with a model.
* [[Responsible Scaling Policies and Frontier Safety]]: how major labs frame commitments about increasingly capable models.

## A History of LLM Families (GPT, BERT, T5, Llama)

Every architectural choice this road has walked through — encoder-only, decoder-only, encoder-decoder, RoPE, gated feed-forward sublayers — shows up somewhere in a real, named model family. Tracing those choices through a handful of landmark models turns an abstract menu of options into an actual history.

**You need:** [[Architectural Families|Choosing an Architecture Family for a Task]], [[Compute-Optimal Scaling (Chinchilla)]].

## The question it answers

"How do today's major LLM families trace back to the architectural decisions covered earlier on this road?" A small number of landmark models mark the major turns: **BERT** (2018) established encoder-only masked-language-model pretraining; **GPT-2** (2019) showed decoder-only causal language modeling could scale into genuinely fluent, general-purpose generation; **T5** (2019) unified many NLP tasks under one encoder-decoder, text-to-text framing; **GPT-3** (2020) showed that scaling a decoder-only model further unlocked few-shot, in-context capabilities; **Llama 2** (2023) combined a decoder-only architecture with RoPE and other efficiency refinements, at a far smaller parameter count than GPT-3, trained on far more tokens.

## Intuition

Looking at a family tree of cars — the first mass-produced model, the first with a specific safety feature everyone later adopted, the first widely available at a dramatically lower price — tells a clearer story about how the industry got to today's vehicles than reading a list of abstract engineering principles ever could. Tracing a handful of actual LLMs, in order, through the specific architectural and scaling choices that defined each one, does the same for this road's more abstract coverage of tokenization, architecture and scaling.

## Definition and notation

```text
BERT-base (2018):    110M params,   encoder-only
GPT-2 (2019):         1.5B params,  decoder-only
T5-11B (2019):        11B params,   encoder-decoder
GPT-3 (2020):        175B params,   decoder-only
Llama 2 70B (2023):   70B params,   decoder-only
```

## A worked example

Parameter counts across these five landmark models, spanning five years:

```text
2018  BERT-base      1.10 × 10⁸
2019  GPT-2          1.50 × 10⁹
2019  T5-11B         1.10 × 10¹⁰
2020  GPT-3          1.75 × 10¹¹
2023  Llama 2 70B    7.00 × 10¹⁰
```

From BERT-base to GPT-3, parameter count grew by a factor of roughly 1,591× in just two years. Notably, Llama 2 70B (2023) is *smaller* than GPT-3 (2020) despite coming three years later — a direct, concrete instance of [[Compute-Optimal Scaling (Chinchilla)|the Chinchilla-era shift toward training smaller models on relatively more data]], rather than simply scaling parameter count ever upward.

## Bench

```bench
id: llm-family-timeline
title: From millions to hundreds of billions
fallback: Step through major LLM families in order and watch parameter count and architecture family evolve.
```

**Try this**

1. Step through from BERT-base to GPT-3 and watch parameter count climb.
2. Step to Llama 2 70B and notice it's smaller than GPT-3, not larger.
3. Compare each model's architecture family against what you've already covered on this road.

**What you should notice:** parameter count doesn't climb monotonically across this history — Llama 2's smaller size than GPT-3 despite being newer reflects a real, deliberate shift in scaling philosophy, not a step backward.

## Where it appears in AI

* **Each family in this timeline is covered architecturally on [[Architectural Families|Choosing an Architecture Family for a Task]]** on the Transformers planet — this note is specifically about the historical sequence, not re-deriving the architectures themselves.
* **The shift from GPT-3-era scaling to Llama-era scaling is a direct, real-world instance of [[Compute-Optimal Scaling (Chinchilla)|compute-optimal scaling]] changing how the field allocates training budgets.**
* **Later model families (not covered in this small sample) continue evolving along axes this road has covered**: mixture-of-experts routing, longer context windows, multimodal input — each an extension of mechanisms already derived earlier.

## Common pitfalls

* **Assuming parameter count always increases over time.** The worked example's own numbers show this isn't true — Llama 2 70B is smaller than the three-years-older GPT-3.
* **Treating this timeline as exhaustive.** It's a small, illustrative sample of landmark models, not a complete history of every significant LLM family.
* **Confusing a model family's *architecture* with its *training recipe*.** Two models can share an architecture family (decoder-only) while differing enormously in data, scale, and alignment training — the architecture alone doesn't determine the model's capabilities.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. What architectural choice did BERT establish, and how does that differ from GPT-2's?</summary>
BERT used encoder-only masked-language-model pretraining; GPT-2 used decoder-only causal language modeling, predicting the next token rather than filling in masked ones.
</details>

<details><summary>2. In the worked example, why is Llama 2 70B smaller than GPT-3 despite being released three years later?</summary>
It reflects a deliberate shift toward compute-optimal (and often overtrained, cheaper-to-serve) scaling philosophy, training a smaller model on relatively more data rather than simply maximizing parameter count.
</details>

<details><summary>3. What did GPT-3 demonstrate that GPT-2 hadn't, at a smaller scale?</summary>
That scaling a decoder-only model further unlocked genuinely useful few-shot, in-context learning capabilities, without any additional training specific to those tasks.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Model family:** a lineage of models sharing a common architectural approach and naming convention.
* **Landmark model:** a model whose release marked a significant architectural or capability turning point.
* **Scaling philosophy:** the deliberate choices about how much to invest in parameter count versus training data for a given compute budget.

## Related

[[Architectural Families|Choosing an Architecture Family for a Task]] · [[Compute-Optimal Scaling (Chinchilla)]] · [[Open-Weight vs. Closed Models]]

## Open-Weight vs. Closed Models

Two LLMs with similar benchmark scores can offer radically different things to the people using them, depending on whether the weights themselves are published or only an API sits in front of them. That one choice shapes what's actually possible to do with a model, independent of its capability.

**You need:** [[A History of LLM Families (GPT, BERT, T5, Llama)]].

## The question it answers

"What's the practical difference between an open-weight model and a closed, API-only one?" Open-weight release publishes the model's parameters, so anyone can download, inspect, modify and run it themselves. Closed release keeps the weights on the provider's infrastructure; access goes through an API that can be updated, rate-limited or withdrawn at any time.

## Intuition

It's the difference between buying a car and leasing a ride-sharing service. Buying the car means you can modify the engine, drive it with no internet connection, and know it'll drive the same way next year. The ride-sharing service needs no garage or mechanic, and the company keeps the fleet maintained and updated — but you can't open the hood, and the car you ride in next month might not be the one you rode in today.

## Definition and notation

```text
Open-weight:  weights published  → download, inspect, modify, run offline, version is permanent
Closed/API:   weights withheld   → call an endpoint, provider controls updates, version can change
```

Open-weight does not necessarily mean the training data, code or license are also open — see [[Licensing and Model Governance]] for what a license on top of open weights actually permits.

## A worked example

Six concrete capabilities, checked against each access mode:

```text
capability                                          open-weight   closed/API
run fully offline                                        ✓            ✗
inspect/modify the weights                                ✓            ✗
fine-tune locally, any method                             ✓            ✗
guaranteed version never changes under you                ✓            ✗
use without any infrastructure of your own                 ✗            ✓
get provider-managed safety updates automatically          ✗            ✓
```

Open-weight access unlocks 4 of these 6 capabilities; closed access unlocks the other 2. Neither mode is a strict superset of the other — they trade one real set of freedoms for a different real set of conveniences.

## Bench

```bench
id: open-vs-closed-access
title: Different things are actually possible
fallback: Toggle between open-weight and closed access and see which capabilities become possible.
```

**Try this**

1. Switch between open-weight and closed/API-only and watch which capabilities flip from possible to impossible.
2. Notice that the two lists don't overlap — nothing is "possible under both."
3. Think about which of the six capabilities would matter most for a project with no internet access at deployment time.

**What you should notice:** the two access modes aren't "more open = strictly better" — each unlocks a disjoint set of capabilities the other can't offer at all.

## Where it appears in AI

* **A provider's choice between open-weight and closed release shapes who can build on a model** — a startup needing offline deployment or full fine-tuning control can only use open-weight models, regardless of a closed model's capability.
* **[[Licensing and Model Governance]] adds a further layer on top of open-weight release**: publishing weights doesn't by itself guarantee commercial-use rights or redistribution rights.
* **[[Responsible Scaling Policies and Frontier Safety]] treats open-weight release of a highly capable model as a one-way decision** — once weights are public, no later safety fix can be pushed to every downloaded copy.

## Common pitfalls

* **Assuming "open-weight" means "open-source" in the traditional software sense.** Weights, training code, training data and license can each be open or closed independently.
* **Assuming one mode is simply better.** The worked example shows each mode enables capabilities the other cannot offer, not that one is a strict upgrade of the other.
* **Forgetting that closed-model behavior can change without the user's action.** A provider can update, deprecate or restrict an API-only model; an open-weight model you've downloaded cannot change under you.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. Why can't a closed, API-only model guarantee the same version forever?</summary>
The provider controls the weights and can update or withdraw the model behind the API at any time; nothing stops them from changing what the endpoint returns.
</details>

<details><summary>2. Does open-weight release automatically mean a model's training data is also public?</summary>
No — open-weight release is specifically about publishing the model's parameters; the training data, code and license terms are separate decisions, covered under [[Licensing and Model Governance]].
</details>

<details><summary>3. Name one capability each access mode has that the other categorically lacks.</summary>
Open-weight: running fully offline (impossible with an API-only model). Closed/API: using the model with no infrastructure of your own (impossible without downloading and serving an open-weight model yourself).
</details>

## Key terms

* **Open-weight model:** a model whose trained parameters are published for anyone to download and run.
* **Closed model:** a model accessible only through a provider-controlled API, with the weights never released.
* **Version permanence:** the guarantee that a downloaded model's behavior will not change later, which only open-weight release provides.

## Related

[[A History of LLM Families (GPT, BERT, T5, Llama)]] · [[Licensing and Model Governance]] · [[Model Cards and Responsible Release]]

## Model Cards and Responsible Release

A model card is a short document that ships alongside a model, stating what it was trained on, what it's good and bad at, and where it's known to fail. A card with half its sections left blank gives a false sense of transparency — it looks like documentation without functioning as documentation.

**You need:** [[Open-Weight vs. Closed Models]].

## The question it answers

"How do you measure whether a model's documentation actually tells users what they need to know?" A model card is complete when every standard section — intended use, known limitations, training data summary, evaluation results, known biases — is actually filled in, not merely present as an empty heading.

## Intuition

A nutrition label with only "calories" filled in and "allergens," "sugar," and "sodium" left blank technically satisfies "there's a nutrition label" while telling you almost nothing that matters. A model card works the same way: its value comes from what's actually written under each heading, not from the headings existing.

## Definition and notation

```text
completeness(card) = |filled sections| / |total expected sections|
```

Five commonly expected sections: intended use, known limitations, training data summary, evaluation results, known biases.

## A worked example

Two versions of a model card, same five sections:

```text
Card A: intended_use ✓, limitations ✓, training_data ✗, evaluation_results ✗, known_biases ✗
  → 2 of 5 filled → completeness = 0.40 (40%)

Card B: intended_use ✓, limitations ✓, training_data ✓, evaluation_results ✓, known_biases ✓
  → 5 of 5 filled → completeness = 1.00 (100%)
```

Card A states what the model is for and where it struggles, but says nothing about what it was trained on or how it was evaluated — a user can't check its claims or spot likely blind spots. Card B lets a user actually verify the model's fitness for their use case.

## Bench

```bench
id: model-card-completeness
title: A model card is only as good as what's filled in
fallback: Toggle which model-card sections are filled in and watch the completeness score change.
```

**Try this**

1. Start with only "Intended use" and "Known limitations" checked and note the completeness score.
2. Fill in "Training data summary" and "Evaluation results" one at a time and watch the score climb.
3. Uncheck everything and notice the score drops to 0% even though the card headings still exist.

**What you should notice:** completeness tracks what's actually written, not which headings are present — an empty section contributes nothing to the score.

## Where it appears in AI

* **Open-weight releases (see [[Open-Weight vs. Closed Models]]) are often accompanied by a model card**, since there's no other way for downstream users to learn what the provider knows about the model's limitations.
* **[[Responsible Scaling Policies and Frontier Safety]] treats documentation completeness as part of what a responsible release requires**, especially for the known-biases and limitations sections.
* **A leaderboard entry (covered on the Evaluating LLMs stretch of this road) says nothing about a model's documented limitations** — model-card completeness is a separate, complementary signal to benchmark scores.

## Common pitfalls

* **Treating the existence of a model card as equivalent to transparency.** The worked example's Card A has every heading present but tells a user almost nothing actionable.
* **Assuming a high completeness score means the content is accurate.** Completeness measures coverage, not correctness — a filled-in section can still understate real limitations.
* **Expecting every provider to use the same five sections.** Real model cards vary in structure; the principle (write what you actually know, don't leave gaps) matters more than matching a fixed template.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. In the worked example, why does Card A's 40% completeness understate its usefulness problem more than a simple percentage suggests?</summary>
The two sections it's missing — training data summary and evaluation results — are exactly the ones a user would need to verify the model's claims or predict where it's likely to fail, so the gap matters more than "60% missing" alone conveys.
</details>

<details><summary>2. Does filling in every section of a model card guarantee the model has no undisclosed limitations?</summary>
No — completeness measures how much of the expected documentation was written, not whether what's written (or omitted) is fully honest or accurate.
</details>

<details><summary>3. Why might a provider ship a model card with some sections deliberately left blank?</summary>
Possible reasons include not having rigorously evaluated the model along some axis yet, competitive sensitivity about training data, or simple release-deadline pressure — none of which make the blank sections less of a transparency gap for users.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Model card:** a document accompanying a model release stating its intended use, limitations, training data and evaluation results.
* **Completeness score:** the fraction of a model card's expected sections that are actually filled in.
* **Known biases section:** the part of a model card documenting measured or suspected systematic biases in the model's outputs.

## Related

[[Open-Weight vs. Closed Models]] · [[Licensing and Model Governance]] · [[Responsible Scaling Policies and Frontier Safety]]

## Licensing and Model Governance

Publishing a model's weights doesn't by itself say what anyone is actually allowed to do with them. The license attached to a release is a separate, legally binding layer on top of open-weight access, and real licenses differ sharply in what they permit.

**You need:** [[Open-Weight vs. Closed Models]].

## The question it answers

"Given a model's weights are available, what does its license actually let someone do with it?" Three common license styles permit different, specific things: permissive licenses (Apache/MIT-style) allow commercial use, modification and redistribution with no usage cap; open-with-restrictions licenses allow the same three but add a usage-based restriction (such as a user-count cap above which a separate commercial agreement is required); fully closed terms permit commercial use of the service but forbid modifying or redistributing the model itself.

## Intuition

It's the difference between a recipe you're free to cook, tweak, and hand out to anyone, a recipe you can cook and tweak freely but need to call the restaurant first if you plan to open your own restaurant with it above a certain size, and a restaurant meal you can eat and pay for but can't take home the recipe for at all. All three let you eat; only some let you cook, change, or share it yourself.

## Definition and notation

```text
permissive (Apache/MIT-style):        commercial ✓  modify ✓  redistribute ✓  no usage cap ✓
open-with-restrictions (community):    commercial ✓  modify ✓  redistribute ✓  usage cap ✗
fully closed (API terms only):         commercial ✓  modify ✗  redistribute ✗  no usage cap ✓
```

## A worked example

Checking four specific permissions against each license style:

```text
permissive:               4 of 4 freedoms permitted (commercial, modify, redistribute, no cap)
open-with-restrictions:    3 of 4 (commercial, modify, redistribute — but usage-capped)
fully closed:              2 of 4 (commercial use of the API, no usage cap — but no modify, no redistribute)
```

No license style permits exactly zero or exactly all freedoms in the same way as another — a team that needs to redistribute a fine-tuned version of the model can rule out "fully closed" terms immediately, regardless of how capable that model is.

## Bench

```bench
id: license-permission-matrix
title: What a license actually permits
fallback: Switch between license styles and see which freedoms are actually permitted.
```

**Try this**

1. Switch between the three license styles and watch which checkmarks flip.
2. Find the one freedom that "fully closed" terms permit but "open-with-restrictions" doesn't restrict either (no usage cap).
3. Identify which license style a project needing to redistribute a modified model would have to rule out.

**What you should notice:** the three license styles aren't simply more-to-less permissive in a single ordering — "fully closed" and "open-with-restrictions" each permit a different specific freedom the other doesn't.

## Where it appears in AI

* **A model's license is independent of whether its weights are published** ([[Open-Weight vs. Closed Models]]) — open weights under a usage-capped license still restrict large-scale commercial redistribution.
* **A model card ([[Model Cards and Responsible Release]]) documents capabilities and limitations, not legal permissions** — license terms are a separate, usually separately published, document.
* **Deploying a fine-tuned or merged model (covered on the LLMs in Practice stretch of this road) inherits the license terms of every model that went into it** — governance isn't limited to the first release.

## Common pitfalls

* **Assuming "open-weight" and "permissively licensed" mean the same thing.** A model can have openly published weights under a restrictive, usage-capped license, which is the "open-with-restrictions" row in the worked example.
* **Reading "commercial use permitted" as "any commercial use permitted at any scale."** The open-with-restrictions style explicitly caps usage before a separate agreement is required — commercial use and unrestricted commercial use are different permissions.
* **Treating license terms as fixed across versions of the same model family.** A provider can (and often does) change license terms between releases of successive model versions.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. Which of the three license styles in the worked example permits redistribution with no usage cap at all?</summary>
Only the permissive (Apache/MIT-style) license permits both redistribution and no usage cap simultaneously.
</details>

<details><summary>2. A team wants to redistribute a modified version of a model to their own customers. Which license style rules this out entirely?</summary>
Fully closed (API terms only) — it permits commercial use of the service but forbids both modifying and redistributing the model itself.
</details>

<details><summary>3. Does having access to a model's weights guarantee the right to redistribute a fine-tuned version of it?</summary>
No — that depends entirely on the attached license; open-weight access and redistribution rights are governed separately, as the worked example's three license styles show.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Permissive license:** terms allowing commercial use, modification and redistribution with no usage-based restriction.
* **Usage cap:** a license condition requiring a separate commercial agreement once usage (such as user count) crosses a threshold.
* **Model governance:** the combination of license terms, access mode and release policy that determines who may do what with a model.

## Related

[[Open-Weight vs. Closed Models]] · [[Model Cards and Responsible Release]] · [[Responsible Scaling Policies and Frontier Safety]]

## Responsible Scaling Policies and Frontier Safety

As models get more capable, the safety work expected to accompany their release scales up too — a model barely useful for anything dangerous needs far less scrutiny than one capable of meaningfully assisting with serious harm. A responsible scaling policy ties the required safety commitments directly to measured capability, rather than treating every release the same way.

**You need:** [[Model Cards and Responsible Release]], [[Licensing and Model Governance]].

## The question it answers

"How do labs decide how much safety work a given model release needs?" A responsible scaling policy (RSP) sets capability thresholds, each mapping to a safety tier with its own required commitments (more rigorous evaluation, stronger deployment safeguards, tighter access controls); crossing a threshold is what triggers the next tier's requirements, not calendar time or a fixed release schedule.

## Intuition

It's like staged clearance for a new chemical compound: a compound with low toxicity needs minimal paperwork, one with moderate toxicity needs controlled handling procedures, and one that's genuinely hazardous needs restricted access and a dedicated containment plan. Nobody applies the hazardous-compound procedure to every substance, and nobody skips it just because a substance happens to be new — the required tier tracks the measured property, not the calendar.

## Definition and notation

```text
tier 1: capability < 0.30   → baseline safety practices
tier 2: 0.30 ≤ capability < 0.60   → enhanced evaluation
tier 3: 0.60 ≤ capability < 0.85   → strong deployment safeguards
tier 4: capability ≥ 0.85   → the strictest controls (restricted access, dedicated oversight)
```

(The specific thresholds above are illustrative; real policies define their own capability measures and cutoffs.)

## A worked example

Four models with different measured capability scores, checked against the threshold ladder:

```text
capability 0.10  → tier 1 (baseline practices)
capability 0.40  → tier 2 (enhanced evaluation)
capability 0.70  → tier 3 (strong deployment safeguards)
capability 0.90  → tier 4 (strictest controls)
```

A model's required tier is a step function of its measured capability: moving from 0.10 to 0.40 crosses one threshold and jumps straight from tier 1 to tier 2's requirements, with nothing gradual in between.

## Bench

```bench
id: rsp-capability-tier
title: More capable, more required
fallback: Slide a model's measured capability and see which safety tier's commitments it requires.
```

**Try this**

1. Slide capability from 0.10 up past 0.30 and watch the required tier jump from 1 to 2.
2. Keep sliding past 0.60 and 0.85 and watch the tier jump twice more.
3. Notice the tier only changes exactly at a threshold crossing, not gradually.

**What you should notice:** required safety commitments are a step function of measured capability, not a smooth scale — crossing a threshold, however slightly, changes what's required.

## Where it appears in AI

* **Open-weight release ([[Open-Weight vs. Closed Models]]) of a tier-4-level model is a one-way decision under an RSP** — once weights are public, no later safety fix reaches every downloaded copy, which is why the highest tiers often restrict release mode itself.
* **A model card's known-biases and limitations sections ([[Model Cards and Responsible Release]]) are part of what an RSP's evaluation requirements at higher tiers call for.**
* **Benchmark-based capability evaluation (covered on the Evaluating LLMs stretch of this road) is exactly what feeds the capability score an RSP's thresholds are checked against.**

## Common pitfalls

* **Assuming higher-tier requirements apply gradually as capability rises.** The worked example's step function shows requirements jump exactly at each threshold, with no partial tier in between.
* **Treating an RSP's thresholds as universal across labs.** Different organizations define capability differently and set different cutoffs; the worked example's specific numbers are illustrative, not a shared standard.
* **Assuming a lower-capability model needs no safety work at all.** Tier 1 still requires baseline safety practices — the tiers scale required rigor, they don't turn it off entirely at the low end.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. In the worked example, why does a model moving from capability 0.29 to 0.31 face a much bigger change in required commitments than one moving from 0.31 to 0.59?</summary>
0.29 to 0.31 crosses the tier-1/tier-2 threshold, jumping to a new, stricter set of requirements; 0.31 to 0.59 stays within tier 2 the whole way, so the required commitments don't change at all despite the larger capability gap.
</details>

<details><summary>2. Why might an RSP restrict open-weight release specifically at the highest capability tiers?</summary>
Because open-weight release is irreversible — once published, a safety issue discovered later can't be patched in copies already downloaded and run elsewhere, unlike a closed, API-served model the provider can update or restrict.
</details>

<details><summary>3. Does a responsible scaling policy replace the need for a model card?</summary>
No — they serve different purposes: a model card documents what's known about a specific model's behavior and limitations, while an RSP sets the safety process and commitments required before and during a release, scaled to measured capability.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Responsible scaling policy (RSP):** a framework tying required safety commitments to a model's measured capability via defined thresholds.
* **Capability threshold:** the specific measured-capability value at which a model's required safety tier changes.
* **Safety tier:** a bundle of required commitments (evaluation rigor, deployment safeguards, access controls) that applies once a capability threshold is crossed.

## Related

[[Model Cards and Responsible Release]] · [[Licensing and Model Governance]] · [[Open-Weight vs. Closed Models]]

## LLMs in Practice

Topics on this stretch of the road:

* [[Fine-Tuning for a Specific Task]]: adapting a pretrained, aligned model to one narrow job.
* [[Catastrophic Forgetting in Fine-Tuning]]: when teaching a model something new makes it worse at what it already knew.
* [[System Prompts and Prompt Templates]]: the hidden instructions that shape every response before a user's own words arrive.
* [[Structured Output and Tool-Calling APIs]]: getting a model's output into a shape your code can rely on.

* [[Cost and Latency of LLM APIs]]: what actually determines how much a request costs and how long it takes.
* [[Choosing a Model for a Task]]: matching a model's size, cost and capabilities to what a task actually needs.

## Fine-Tuning for a Specific Task

An aligned, general-purpose assistant is often not what a product actually needs — a narrower model trained specifically on one job's data can do that one job better, cheaper, and more predictably. Task-specific fine-tuning is how a general model becomes a specialist.

**You need:** [[Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT)|Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT)]], [[Direct Preference Optimization (DPO)]].

## The question it answers

"After pretraining and alignment, how does a model actually get adapted to one narrow job?" The same supervised fine-tuning mechanism covered earlier on this road — more gradient steps, on a new, narrower dataset — is reused, but now the goal is narrowing the model's behavior to one task rather than broadening it into a general assistant. The practical question is how much of the model to update: a full fine-tune updates every parameter; a low-rank update (already derived on the Generative AI planet as [[Parameter-Efficient Adaptation for Generation|LoRA]]) updates a tiny fraction of that, added on top of the frozen base weights.

## Intuition

Retraining a generalist doctor to become a specialist doesn't mean re-teaching them anatomy from scratch — it means a focused residency on top of everything they already know. Full fine-tuning is closer to re-schooling from scratch (expensive, every parameter moves); a low-rank update is the focused residency: a small number of new, targeted parameters layered on top of a frozen foundation.

## Definition and notation

```text
full fine-tune params  = d²         (every weight in a d×d matrix updated)
LoRA-style params      = 2·d·r      (two low-rank d×r matrices, r ≪ d)
```

This is the exact mechanism already derived in [[Parameter-Efficient Adaptation for Generation|LoRA]]; this topic is about *when* and *why* you'd reach for task-specific fine-tuning at all, not re-deriving the low-rank update itself.

## A worked example

For a hidden size d = 1024 and a low rank r = 8:

```text
full fine-tune: 1024² = 1,048,576 parameters updated
LoRA:           2 × 1024 × 8 = 16,384 parameters updated
ratio: 1,048,576 / 16,384 = 64× fewer trainable parameters with LoRA
```

Updating 64× fewer parameters means far less optimizer state, far less memory, and a far smaller file to store and ship per task — often the deciding factor when a product needs many task-specific variants of the same base model.

## Bench

```bench
id: lora-vs-full-finetune
title: How many parameters actually need to change
fallback: Slide hidden size and rank and compare full fine-tuning's parameter count against LoRA's.
```

**Try this**

1. Start at d=1024, r=8 and note the 64× gap.
2. Raise r toward d and watch the gap shrink — at r=d/2, LoRA's efficiency advantage mostly disappears.
3. Raise d (hidden size) and watch the full fine-tune bar grow quadratically while LoRA's grows only linearly.

**What you should notice:** the full fine-tune's parameter count grows with d², while LoRA's grows only with d·r — the gap between them widens as the base model gets larger, which is exactly when the memory savings matter most.

## Where it appears in AI

* **This reuses the exact low-rank mechanism derived in [[Parameter-Efficient Adaptation for Generation|LoRA]] on the Generative AI planet** — the mechanism doesn't change for LLMs, only the motivation (task specialization rather than style or subject adaptation).
* **A fine-tuned model can be merged with others ([[Model Merging and Weight Averaging]]) or risk forgetting what it knew before fine-tuning ([[Catastrophic Forgetting in Fine-Tuning]])** — both are direct consequences of how fine-tuning updates the model's weights.
* **Choosing whether to fine-tune at all, versus prompting a general model, is part of [[Choosing a Model for a Task]].**

## Common pitfalls

* **Assuming fine-tuning for a task always means a full fine-tune.** In practice, low-rank and other parameter-efficient methods are the default for most task adaptation precisely because of the gap the worked example shows.
* **Expecting fine-tuning to add new knowledge the base model never saw.** Fine-tuning mostly reshapes *how* the model uses what it already learned during pretraining; it's a poor tool for injecting large amounts of new factual knowledge (that's closer to [[Continued Pretraining and Domain Adaptation]] or retrieval).
* **Ignoring catastrophic forgetting.** Narrowing a model to one task can measurably degrade its performance on everything else — covered next.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. Why does the parameter-count gap between full fine-tuning and LoRA widen as the base model's hidden size grows?</summary>
Full fine-tuning's parameter count scales with d² while LoRA's scales with d·r (r fixed and small), so as d grows, the full fine-tune's cost grows quadratically while LoRA's grows only linearly.
</details>

<details><summary>2. Does task-specific fine-tuning typically teach a model large amounts of brand-new factual knowledge?</summary>
Not usually — it mostly reshapes how the model applies knowledge it already has from pretraining; injecting substantial new knowledge is better handled by continued pretraining or retrieval.
</details>

<details><summary>3. What's the main practical benefit of updating 64× fewer parameters, beyond raw training speed?</summary>
Far less optimizer state and memory during training, and a much smaller artifact to store and distribute per task — important when a product needs many task-specific fine-tunes of the same base model.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Task-specific fine-tuning:** further training a pretrained, aligned model on a narrower dataset to specialize it for one job.
* **Full fine-tune:** updating every parameter of the base model during fine-tuning.
* **Low-rank update:** adding a small number of new parameters (two low-rank matrices) on top of a frozen base model, as in LoRA.

## Related

[[Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT)|Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT)]] · [[Catastrophic Forgetting in Fine-Tuning]] · [[Model Merging and Weight Averaging]]

## Catastrophic Forgetting in Fine-Tuning

Fine-tuning a model to be excellent at one narrow task can quietly make it worse at everything it used to do. The same gradient updates that pull the model toward the new task pull it away from whatever made it good at the old one.

**You need:** [[Fine-Tuning for a Specific Task]].

## The question it answers

"Why would teaching a model something new make it worse at something it already knew?" A model's weights are a single, shared resource. Fine-tuning moves those weights toward whatever minimizes loss on the new task's data — and unless that movement happens to also help the old task, it moves the weights away from wherever they were doing well on it. The more fine-tuning steps taken, the further the weights drift and the more of the old capability is lost.

## Intuition

Imagine retraining a generalist nurse into a specialist anesthesiologist by having them practice nothing but anesthesia procedures for months. Their anesthesia skills sharpen fast — but if they never practice general wound care in the meantime, that skill doesn't stay frozen in place; it atrophies. The hours spent get reallocated, and so does the model's capacity.

## Definition and notation

```text
w: the model's weights (toy: a 2D vector)
task A target: [1, 0]      task B target: [0, 1]
lossA(w) = ‖w − [1,0]‖²     lossB(w) = ‖w − [0,1]‖²
fine-tuning step:  w ← w − lr·(w − targetB)
```

## A worked example

Starting at w₀ = [1, 0] (perfectly tuned for task A, lossA = 0), fine-tuning toward task B's target at lr = 0.3:

```text
step 0: w=[1.000, 0.000]  lossA=0.0000  lossB=2.0000
step 1: w=[0.700, 0.300]  lossA=0.1800  lossB=0.9800
step 2: w=[0.490, 0.510]  lossA=0.5202  lossB=0.4802
step 3: w=[0.343, 0.657]  lossA=0.8633  lossB=0.2353
step 4: w=[0.240, 0.760]  lossA=1.1549  lossB=0.1153
step 5: w=[0.168, 0.832]  lossA=1.3842  lossB=0.0565
step 6: w=[0.118, 0.882]  lossA=1.5571  lossB=0.0277
```

By step 6, loss on the new task B has dropped from 2.0 to 0.0277 — but loss on the old task A has climbed from 0 all the way to 1.5571. The model got much better at B by getting much worse at A, exactly as fast.

## Bench

```bench
id: catastrophic-forgetting
title: Learning the new task un-learns the old one
fallback: Step through fine-tuning updates and watch loss on the old task climb as loss on the new task falls.
```

**Try this**

1. Step through all 6 fine-tuning steps and watch both loss curves move in opposite directions.
2. Compare how much lossB drops by step 2 against how much lossA has already risen by then.
3. Reset and imagine stopping fine-tuning early, at step 2 — how would that change the trade-off?

**What you should notice:** the two losses move in lockstep, in opposite directions — there's no point in this trace where the new task improves without the old one getting worse.

## Where it appears in AI

* **This is a direct risk of [[Fine-Tuning for a Specific Task]]** — the more aggressively a model is specialized, the more of its prior general capability it tends to lose.
* **[[Model Merging and Weight Averaging]] is one practical way to recover some of what was lost**, by combining a forgetting specialist's weights back with the original (or another task's) weights.
* **The same phenomenon appears earlier on this road wherever a single model is pushed to serve multiple objectives in sequence** — any time an update moves shared weights toward a new target, it can degrade an old one.

## Common pitfalls

* **Assuming forgetting is binary (either the model forgets everything or nothing).** The worked example shows a smooth trade-off: a small number of fine-tuning steps causes a small amount of forgetting, more steps cause more.
* **Expecting forgetting to be visible from the fine-tuning loss curve alone.** The fine-tuning run's own loss (on the new task) looks great the whole time — the degradation only shows up when you separately measure performance on the old task.
* **Fine-tuning on a narrow task for far longer than needed "just to be safe."** The worked example shows loss on the new task saturating (0.0565 → 0.0277, a small further gain) while the old task keeps getting worse — extra steps past that point are nearly pure forgetting with little new-task benefit.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. In the worked example, does the model's loss on task A ever stop increasing while loss on task B keeps decreasing?</summary>
No — in this trace, every step that decreases lossB increases lossA; they move together because both are driven by the same shared weight update.
</details>

<details><summary>2. Why can't you see catastrophic forgetting just by watching the fine-tuning run's own training loss?</summary>
The training loss only measures performance on the new task's data, which keeps improving — forgetting shows up only when performance on the old task is measured separately, which the fine-tuning run doesn't do by default.
</details>

<details><summary>3. What's one way to reduce how much a fine-tuned model forgets?</summary>
Stop fine-tuning earlier (the worked example shows new-task gains flattening out well before old-task loss stops rising), or merge the fine-tuned weights back with the original model's weights, as in model merging.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Catastrophic forgetting:** the loss of a model's prior capability caused by further training on a new task.
* **Shared weights:** the single set of parameters that every task's gradient update moves, with no separation between what's "for" one task and what's "for" another.
* **Fine-tuning trade-off:** the relationship between how much a model improves on a new task and how much it degrades on tasks it previously performed well.

## Related

[[Fine-Tuning for a Specific Task]] · [[Model Merging and Weight Averaging]] · [[Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT)|Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT)]]

## System Prompts and Prompt Templates

Every request to a deployed LLM usually carries more than the user's own words: a system prompt sets the assistant's persona and rules, and a template arranges the system prompt, conversation history and user turn into the exact format the model was trained to expect.
