None of this is visible to the user, but all of it is sent — and paid for — on every single request.

**You need:** [[Instruction Dataset Construction]].

## The question it answers

"What actually gets sent to the model besides the user's own message?" A system prompt is a block of instructions (persona, rules, output format) prepended to every conversation. A prompt template is the specific arrangement — special tokens, role labels, ordering — that turns a system prompt plus a conversation into the single sequence of tokens the model actually sees, matching the format it was trained (specifically, instruction-tuned, see [[Instruction Dataset Construction]]) on.

## Intuition

A customer-service phone line plays the same recorded greeting and menu before every single call, no matter how short the caller's actual question is. That recording costs the same few seconds whether the call lasts thirty seconds or thirty minutes — and if the company lengthens the recording, every call gets longer and more expensive, even though the caller's own words didn't change at all.

## Definition and notation

```text
per-request tokens = system_tokens + user_tokens + assistant_tokens
system's share      = (system_tokens × n_requests) / (per-request tokens × n_requests)
                     = system_tokens / per-request tokens
```

The system prompt's token count is fixed per request; it's paid for on every request regardless of how short the conversation is.

## A worked example

With a 30-token user turn and a 60-token assistant reply, across 1,000 requests:

```text
short system prompt (20 tokens):
  per request = 20 + 30 + 60 = 110 tokens
  total tokens = 110,000;  system prompt's share = 18.2%

long system prompt (300 tokens):
  per request = 300 + 30 + 60 = 390 tokens
  total tokens = 390,000;  system prompt's share = 76.9%
```

Growing the system prompt 15× (20 → 300 tokens) didn't just add a fixed cost — it took the system prompt from a minor fraction of every request's tokens to the large majority of them, even though the user's and assistant's own turns never changed.

## Bench

```bench
id: system-prompt-overhead
title: A fixed instruction, paid for on every request
fallback: Slide the system prompt's length and the number of requests and watch its share of total tokens change.
```

**Try this**

1. Start at a short system prompt and slide it up toward 300+ tokens; watch its share of total tokens climb past 50%.
2. Hold the system prompt fixed and slide the number of requests up; notice the share doesn't change — only the absolute total does.
3. Imagine two products with identical system prompts but very different average conversation lengths; which one is hit harder by a longer system prompt?

**What you should notice:** the system prompt's *share* of tokens depends only on its length relative to the conversation, not on how many requests are sent — but the *absolute* extra cost from a longer system prompt scales directly with request volume.

## Where it appears in AI

* **A model only follows a prompt template reliably if it was instruction-tuned on data formatted the same way ([[Instruction Dataset Construction]])** — an unexpected template at inference time is a common, silent cause of poor instruction-following.
* **A long, elaborate system prompt directly inflates per-request cost and latency ([[Cost and Latency of LLM APIs]])**, since every token in it is priced and processed like any other input token.
* **[[Structured Output and Tool-Calling APIs]] often relies on instructions placed in the system prompt** (schema definitions, tool descriptions) — another reason system prompts tend to grow over a product's lifetime.

## Common pitfalls

* **Treating the system prompt as "free" because the user never sees it.** It's invisible to the user, but it's still tokenized, transmitted, and billed exactly like visible text.
* **Growing the system prompt indefinitely as a product accumulates more rules and edge cases.** The worked example shows this isn't a one-time cost — it's multiplied by every request, forever, until the prompt is trimmed or restructured.
* **Assuming the template's exact formatting (special tokens, role order) doesn't matter as long as the content is right.** A model instruction-tuned on one template format can behave unpredictably when served a differently formatted prompt at inference time.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. In the worked example, why does the system prompt's share jump from 18.2% to 76.9% when its length only grows 15×?</summary>
The user and assistant turns stay fixed (90 tokens total), so as the system prompt grows, it comes to dominate an ever-larger fraction of a total that's growing almost entirely because of it.
</details>

<details><summary>2. Does increasing the number of requests change the system prompt's *share* of total tokens?</summary>
No — the share only depends on the ratio between system-prompt length and conversation length; increasing request volume scales the absolute totals but not that ratio.
</details>

<details><summary>3. Why might an unexpected prompt template cause a model to follow instructions worse, even if the instructions' content is unchanged?</summary>
Because the model was instruction-tuned on a specific template format; presenting the same content in a different arrangement of roles and special tokens can fall outside what the model reliably learned to follow.
</details>

## Key terms

* **System prompt:** instructions prepended to every conversation, setting the assistant's persona, rules or output format.
* **Prompt template:** the specific arrangement of roles, turns and special tokens that converts a conversation into the token sequence the model expects.
* **Per-request overhead:** the token cost incurred repeatedly on every single request, regardless of how short the user's own message is.

## Related

[[Instruction Dataset Construction]] · [[Cost and Latency of LLM APIs]] · [[Structured Output and Tool-Calling APIs]]

## Structured Output and Tool-Calling APIs

Code that calls an LLM usually needs the response in a specific shape — valid JSON with particular fields, or a specific function call with typed arguments — not free-flowing prose. Hoping the model's free-form text happens to parse correctly is a weaker guarantee than making invalid output structurally impossible.

**You need:** [[Constrained and Structured Generation]].

## The question it answers

"How does an application reliably get a model's output into a shape its code can actually use?" One approach prompts the model to produce JSON (or a tool call) in free-form generation and hopes it's well-formed; parsing then sometimes fails. The more reliable approach, already derived on the Generative AI planet as [[Constrained and Structured Generation|grammar-constrained decoding]], masks out every token that would violate the required schema at each decoding step, so a malformed result is never produced in the first place.

## Intuition

Asking someone to fill out a form freehand on blank paper, in the hope they follow the requested format, will occasionally get you a form you can't process. Handing them a form with labeled boxes — one box per field, the right size for each — makes an invalid submission structurally much harder to produce, because the shape itself constrains what they can write.

## Definition and notation

```text
free-form:        generate text  →  attempt to parse  →  sometimes fails
grammar-masked:    at each step, zero out every token not allowed by the schema  →  always parses
```

## A worked example

Simulating 1,000 free-form generation attempts at a 23% per-attempt malformed-output rate (seed 1):

```text
free-form:        765 of 1,000 attempts parse successfully → 76.5% success rate
grammar-masked:   1,000 of 1,000 (always valid by construction) → 100% success rate
```

A pipeline relying on free-form generation at this failure rate needs to handle roughly 1 in 4 responses failing to parse — retry logic, fallback prompts, or dropped requests. Grammar-masked decoding removes that failure mode entirely, at the cost of needing a schema defined up front.

## Bench

```bench
id: structured-output-success
title: Guaranteed valid, instead of hopefully valid
fallback: Slide the free-form malformed-output rate and compare it against grammar-masked decoding's guaranteed success.
```

**Try this**

1. Set the malformed-output rate low (under 5%) and notice free-form generation still occasionally fails.
2. Raise it toward 50% and watch free-form success collapse while grammar-masked stays at 100%.
3. Consider what it would cost a real pipeline to retry on every one of those free-form failures.

**What you should notice:** grammar-masked decoding's success rate doesn't depend on the slider at all — it's not measuring the same kind of risk, because the failure mode it removes can't occur by construction.

## Where it appears in AI

* **This reuses the exact masking mechanism derived in [[Constrained and Structured Generation|grammar-constrained decoding]] on the Generative AI planet** — a tool-calling API's JSON schema is just another grammar to mask against.
* **A system prompt ([[System Prompts and Prompt Templates]]) often carries the schema or tool definitions a model is meant to follow**, whether or not decoding is actually constrained to match it.
* **An application choosing between free-form and schema-constrained generation is itself part of [[Choosing a Model for a Task]]** — not every provider or model supports constrained decoding equally well.

## Common pitfalls

* **Assuming a well-written prompt alone guarantees well-formed output.** The worked example's free-form case is already being prompted to produce JSON; the gap between 76.5% and 100% is the residual risk even with a good prompt.
* **Treating a parse failure as rare enough to ignore.** At a realistic malformed rate, a high-volume pipeline will see parse failures constantly; the cost of handling them (retries, fallbacks) is real and ongoing.
* **Assuming grammar-masked decoding guarantees the *content* is correct, not just well-formed.** It guarantees the output matches the schema's shape — it says nothing about whether the values inside that shape are accurate.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. In the worked example, what does the 76.5% free-form success rate actually measure?</summary>
The fraction of free-form generation attempts, at a given per-attempt malformed-output rate, that happen to parse successfully as valid structured output.
</details>

<details><summary>2. Why does grammar-masked decoding's success rate stay at 100% regardless of the malformed-output-rate slider?</summary>
Because grammar-masking removes the possibility of producing an invalid token at each decoding step entirely — there's no failure mode left for a "malformed rate" to apply to.
</details>

<details><summary>3. Does guaranteed-valid structure mean the tool-calling arguments a model produces are guaranteed to be correct?</summary>
No — grammar-constrained decoding only guarantees the output's *shape* matches the schema; whether the specific argument values are accurate is a separate question entirely.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Structured output:** a model's response in a specific, machine-parseable shape (JSON, a function call) rather than free-form prose.
* **Tool-calling API:** an interface where a model's output specifies a function name and typed arguments for the application to execute.
* **Grammar-constrained decoding:** masking decoding so that only schema-valid tokens can ever be produced, removing parse failures by construction.

## Related

[[Constrained and Structured Generation]] · [[System Prompts and Prompt Templates]] · [[Choosing a Model for a Task]]

## Model Merging and Weight Averaging

Training a brand-new model that's good at two different tasks usually means training on both tasks' data together. There's a cheaper alternative when two models already exist, each fine-tuned on one task: average their weights directly, with no further training at all.

**You need:** [[Catastrophic Forgetting in Fine-Tuning]].

## The question it answers

"Can two separately fine-tuned models be combined into one without retraining?" Given two models that started from the same base and were each fine-tuned on a different task, averaging their weights parameter-by-parameter often produces a single model that performs reasonably on both tasks — worse than either specialist on its own specialty, but far better than either specialist on the *other* task.

## Intuition

Think of two apprentices who both trained under the same master, then each specialized — one in pastry, one in bread. Averaging their specific techniques doesn't produce someone as good at pastry as the pastry specialist, but it produces someone meaningfully better at both than either specialist alone would be at the other's craft.

## Definition and notation

```text
wA: weights fine-tuned for task A
wB: weights fine-tuned for task B
w_merged = (wA + wB) / 2
```

This only tends to work well when wA and wB started from the same base model and didn't diverge too far from it — merging models with unrelated origins generally doesn't produce anything coherent.

## A worked example

Toy 2D weights, task A's target [1, 0] and task B's target [0, 1], loss = squared distance to the target:

```text
specialist A  (wA = [1, 0]):  lossA = 0.0,  lossB = 2.0
specialist B  (wB = [0, 1]):  lossA = 2.0,  lossB = 0.0
merged        ([0.5, 0.5]):   lossA = 0.5,  lossB = 0.5
```

Each specialist is perfect at its own task and terrible at the other (loss 2.0, the worst possible in this toy setup). The merged model is never perfect, but it's never terrible either — moderate loss (0.5) on both tasks, instead of alternating between 0.0 and 2.0.

## Bench

```bench
id: model-merge-tradeoff
title: One model, moderately good at both
fallback: Compare each task-specialist model's loss against the merged model's, on both tasks.
```

**Try this**

1. Select each specialist model in turn and note how its own task's loss is 0 but the other task's loss is high.
2. Select the merged model and compare both losses to each specialist's corresponding numbers.
3. Consider a situation where you need acceptable performance on both tasks from a single deployed model, with no further training budget — which option would you pick?

**What you should notice:** neither specialist is a good general-purpose choice (each fails badly on the task it wasn't tuned for) — the merged model trades peak performance for balanced performance across both.

## Where it appears in AI

* **Merging is one practical response to [[Catastrophic Forgetting in Fine-Tuning]]** — averaging a narrowly fine-tuned model's weights back toward the original or another task's weights can partially recover what specialization cost it.
* **Merging only works because the models started from the same pretrained-and-aligned base** — it's a direct consequence of how [[Fine-Tuning for a Specific Task]] moves weights from a shared starting point, rather than training from scratch.
* **A product deciding between several fine-tuned variants versus one merged model is a [[Choosing a Model for a Task]] decision**, trading specialist peak performance against operational simplicity.

## Common pitfalls

* **Expecting a merged model to match either specialist's peak performance.** The worked example shows the merged model strictly worse than each specialist on that specialist's own task — merging trades peak capability for balance.
* **Merging models that didn't start from the same base.** The averaging operation assumes the two weight vectors are meaningfully comparable position-by-position, which only holds when they diverged from a shared starting point.
* **Assuming merging always helps.** If the two tasks pull weights in sufficiently conflicting directions, the merged model can end up mediocre at both rather than usefully balanced — the toy example's clean trade-off is an illustration, not a guarantee.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. In the worked example, why is the merged model's loss on task A worse than specialist A's but better than specialist B's?</summary>
The merged weights sit exactly halfway between the two specialists' weights, so its loss on any single task is also roughly "halfway" between how well a specialist in that task and a specialist in the other task would do.
</details>

<details><summary>2. Why does model merging typically require both models to have started from the same base model?</summary>
Averaging assumes the two weight vectors occupy comparable positions in the same parameter space; weights from unrelated training runs don't correspond to each other in any meaningful way, so averaging them produces incoherent results.
</details>

<details><summary>3. When would you prefer a merged model over keeping two separate specialist models?</summary>
When you need one deployed model to handle both tasks reasonably well, with no retraining budget, and can accept lower peak performance on each individual task than a dedicated specialist would give.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Model merging:** combining two or more models' weights, usually by averaging, without further training.
* **Weight averaging:** taking the parameter-by-parameter mean of two models' weights to produce a single combined model.
* **Specialist model:** a model fine-tuned for strong performance on one specific task, typically at the cost of weaker performance elsewhere.

## Related

[[Catastrophic Forgetting in Fine-Tuning]] · [[Fine-Tuning for a Specific Task]] · [[Choosing a Model for a Task]]

## Cost and Latency of LLM APIs

A request to an LLM API has two separate costs that don't move together: how much it costs in money, and how long it takes to come back. Understanding what drives each one separately — not just "bigger request, more expensive" — is what lets a product actually control both.

**You need:** [[KV-Caching for Autoregressive Inference]].

## The question it answers

"What actually determines how much an LLM API request costs, and how long it takes?" Cost is priced per token, input and output, and simply adds up: more tokens in either direction means more money, roughly linearly. Latency is different: a request's input tokens are processed largely in parallel (quick), but output tokens are generated one at a time, each waiting on the last (slow) — so latency is dominated by how many tokens come *out*, almost independent of how many went in.

## Intuition

Reading a long letter takes a fixed, short glance per page — a human (or a model's prefill step) can skim input quickly because it's all there at once. Writing a reply, though, has to happen one word at a time, in order, each one waiting for the last. A very long letter to read barely slows down how fast you can start replying; a very long reply to write takes however long it takes, word by word.

## Definition and notation

```text
cost(request)    = (input_tokens × price_in + output_tokens × price_out) / 1000
latency(request) = fixed_overhead + input_tokens × prefill_per_token + output_tokens × decode_per_token
```

with `prefill_per_token ≪ decode_per_token` — input tokens are processed far faster per token than output tokens are generated.

## A worked example

Illustrative pricing (price_in $0.003/1K tokens, price_out $0.015/1K tokens) and timing (prefill 0.0005s/token, decode 0.02s/token, 0.1s fixed overhead):

```text
short input (50 in, 150 out):   cost = $0.00240   latency = 3.125s
long input  (4000 in, 150 out):  cost = $0.01425   latency = 5.100s
```

Multiplying the input length 80× (50 → 4000 tokens) multiplies cost nearly 6× — but latency only grows from 3.125s to 5.1s, a 1.6× increase. Cost tracks total tokens almost linearly; latency barely notices input length and is dominated by the 150 output tokens both requests share.

## Bench

```bench
id: api-cost-latency
title: Cost scales with tokens, latency with output length
fallback: Slide input and output token counts and watch cost and latency respond very differently.
```

**Try this**

1. Hold output tokens fixed and slide input tokens from 50 to 8000; watch cost climb steadily while latency barely moves.
2. Hold input tokens fixed and slide output tokens up instead; watch latency climb sharply this time.
3. Find a combination where cost and latency move by roughly the same proportion — notice how narrow that range is.

**What you should notice:** cost and latency are driven by different things (total tokens vs. output length specifically) — a request can be expensive but fast, or cheap but slow, depending on the input/output split.

## Where it appears in AI

* **Output-token latency being sequential is a direct consequence of decode-time attention ([[KV-Caching for Autoregressive Inference]])**: each new token's generation depends on every previous one, which is exactly why it can't be parallelized the way prefill can.
* **[[System Prompts and Prompt Templates]] adds to the input-token count on every single request** — mostly a cost lever (since input is cheap per-token but adds up at volume), much less a latency one.
* **Picking a smaller or larger model ([[Choosing a Model for a Task]]) changes both price-per-token and decode speed**, so the same cost/latency trade-off shows up again one level up, at the model-selection stage.

## Common pitfalls

* **Assuming a longer prompt makes a request noticeably slower.** The worked example shows an 80× input increase barely moves latency — the real latency lever is output length.
* **Assuming cost and latency always move together.** They're driven by different factors (total tokens vs. output length specifically), so optimizing one doesn't automatically optimize the other.
* **Ignoring the fixed overhead term.** Even a tiny request pays the fixed_overhead cost; for very short exchanges, that overhead can dominate the total latency.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. In the worked example, why does multiplying input tokens 80× multiply cost by nearly 6× but latency by only 1.6×?</summary>
Cost adds input and output token costs roughly linearly, so an 80× bigger input term still moves the total noticeably; latency's input (prefill) term is tiny per token compared to its output (decode) term, which stayed fixed at 150 tokens in both cases, so the big input increase barely shows up in the total.
</details>

<details><summary>2. If a product wants to reduce latency specifically, which lever matters most: shortening the prompt, or shortening the expected reply?</summary>
Shortening the expected reply (output tokens) — the worked example shows output length is what latency is dominated by, while input length (prompt) barely affects it.
</details>

<details><summary>3. Why are input tokens processed faster per-token than output tokens are generated?</summary>
Input tokens can be processed largely in parallel during prefill, since the whole input is available at once; output tokens must be generated sequentially, each one depending on every token generated before it.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Prefill:** processing a request's input tokens, done largely in parallel and so relatively fast per token.
* **Decode:** generating a request's output tokens one at a time, each depending on all previous ones, so comparatively slow per token.
* **Per-token pricing:** charging separately, and usually at different rates, for input and output tokens.

## Related

[[KV-Caching for Autoregressive Inference]] · [[System Prompts and Prompt Templates]] · [[Choosing a Model for a Task]]

## Choosing a Model for a Task

There's no single "best" LLM — only the best model for a particular task's particular mix of needs. A model that tops every capability benchmark can still be the wrong choice if the task cares more about speed or cost than about squeezing out the last few points of quality.

**You need:** [[Leaderboards and Their Limits]], [[Cost and Latency of LLM APIs]].

## The question it answers

"Given several models of different sizes, how do you pick the right one for a specific task?" The same weighted-scoring mechanism already derived for reweighting a leaderboard ([[Leaderboards and Their Limits]]) applies directly here: score each candidate model on the dimensions the task actually cares about (quality, speed, affordability), weight those dimensions by how much the task values each one, and the model with the highest weighted score is the right choice *for that task* — not necessarily the most capable model in the abstract.

## Intuition

Choosing a vehicle for a job isn't about which vehicle is "best" overall — it's about matching the vehicle to the job. A sports car wins on speed; a cargo van wins on capacity; neither is simply better than the other until you specify what you're hauling and how fast you need to get there. Choosing a model works the same way: specify what the task needs, then rank models against exactly that.

## Definition and notation

```text
score(model, weights) = Σ model[dimension] × weights[dimension]  /  Σ weights[dimension]
```

Exactly the weighted-leaderboard formula from [[Leaderboards and Their Limits]], now applied with task-specific weights instead of a general-purpose leaderboard's weights.

## A worked example

Three model sizes, scored on quality, speed and affordability (0–1, higher is better):

```text
small:  quality 0.60, speed 0.95, affordability 0.95
medium: quality 0.80, speed 0.70, affordability 0.70
large:  quality 0.95, speed 0.30, affordability 0.30
```

Scored under two different task weightings:

```text
latency-sensitive chat (weights: quality 0.2, speed 0.6, affordability 0.2):
  small 0.880  medium 0.720  large 0.430   →  small wins

quality-sensitive offline task (weights: quality 0.9, speed 0.05, affordability 0.05):
  small 0.635  medium 0.790  large 0.885   →  large wins
```

The same three models, the same three scores each — but which one wins flips entirely depending on what the task actually values. Neither "small" nor "large" is the universally right answer.

## Bench

```bench
id: model-choice-weighted
title: The best model depends on what the task actually needs
fallback: Switch between task scenarios and see which model size actually scores best for each.
```

**Try this**

1. Compare the winning model under each scenario and note that it's not the same model both times.
2. Look at how close medium and large are under the quality-sensitive scenario, despite large's much worse speed and affordability scores.
3. Imagine a third scenario that weights all three dimensions equally — which model would you expect to win, and why?

**What you should notice:** "large" isn't a safe default choice even when quality matters most — it only wins when quality is weighted heavily enough to outweigh its much worse speed and affordability scores.

## Where it appears in AI

* **This reuses the exact weighted-scoring mechanism from [[Leaderboards and Their Limits]]**, applied to model selection instead of leaderboard ranking — the same lesson (reweighting flips the winner) shows up at both levels.
* **The "speed" and "affordability" dimensions here are exactly what [[Cost and Latency of LLM APIs]] measures concretely** — this topic is about the decision; that one is about the underlying numbers.
* **A model's capability score itself comes from the kind of benchmark evaluation covered on the Evaluating LLMs stretch of this road** — model choice sits downstream of how models are measured in the first place.

## Common pitfalls

* **Defaulting to the largest, most capable model "to be safe."** The worked example shows this can be a clearly worse choice when the task actually values speed or cost — "most capable" and "best for this task" are different questions.
* **Picking a model based on one dimension's score alone.** A model can look great on a quality benchmark and still be the wrong choice once speed and cost are weighted in at the levels the task actually requires.
* **Assuming the right weighting is obvious or fixed.** Two products that look similar can have very different latency or cost sensitivity, which changes the right choice even with identical candidate models.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. In the worked example, why does the "small" model win the latency-sensitive scenario despite having the lowest quality score of the three?</summary>
Because that scenario weights speed and affordability far more heavily than quality (0.6 and 0.2 versus 0.2), and small scores highest on exactly those two dimensions.
</details>

<details><summary>2. Does picking the model with the single highest quality score always give the best result for a task?</summary>
No — the right choice depends on the task's weighting across all the dimensions that matter to it, not on any one dimension's score alone, as the worked example's two different winners show.
</details>

<details><summary>3. What mechanism does this topic reuse from evaluating LLMs more generally?</summary>
The weighted-scoring formula from leaderboard reweighting — the same arithmetic, applied here to choosing a model for a task instead of to ranking a leaderboard.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Task-specific weighting:** assigning importance to each evaluation dimension (quality, speed, cost) according to what a particular task actually needs.
* **Weighted score:** a single number combining a model's scores across several dimensions, according to a chosen set of weights.
* **Model selection:** choosing which available model to deploy for a task, based on how well it matches that task's specific requirements.

## Related

[[Leaderboards and Their Limits]] · [[Cost and Latency of LLM APIs]] · [[Fine-Tuning for a Specific Task]]

## Guardrails and Deployment-Time Safety Filters

Alignment training shapes what a model tends to do on its own, but a deployed product rarely relies on that alone. A separate filter checks inputs and outputs around the model — catching what training missed, and adding a layer that can be updated without retraining the model itself.

**You need:** [[Adversarial and Jailbreak Evaluation]].

## The question it answers

"What's the difference between a model trained to be safe and a product that's actually safe to deploy?" Alignment training (RLHF, DPO, Constitutional AI, all covered earlier on this road) changes the model's own behavior. A guardrail is a separate, external check — a classifier or rule scoring how risky a request or response looks — that runs *around* the model, blocking anything above a threshold regardless of what the model itself would have done. Looser thresholds catch more unsafe content but also block more safe content by mistake; stricter thresholds reduce false blocks but let more unsafe content through.

## Intuition

A bouncer at a venue's door is a separate check from however well-behaved the venue's own staff are trained to be — even a perfectly behaved staff benefits from someone checking IDs at the entrance. Set the bouncer's standard too loose, and some people who shouldn't get in, do; set it too strict, and legitimate guests get turned away at the door. There's no setting that avoids both kinds of mistakes entirely.

## Definition and notation

```text
false positive rate = (safe content scored above threshold) / (total safe content)
catch rate           = (unsafe content scored above threshold) / (total unsafe content)
```

Both rates move together as the threshold changes — there's no free lunch between over-blocking and under-catching.

## A worked example

Ten safe and ten unsafe example scores (0 = clearly safe, 1 = clearly unsafe), swept across three thresholds:

```text
threshold 0.4:  20% of safe content wrongly blocked,  100% of unsafe content caught
threshold 0.6:   0% of safe content wrongly blocked,   70% of unsafe content caught
threshold 0.8:   0% of safe content wrongly blocked,   40% of unsafe content caught
```

A loose threshold (0.4) catches every unsafe example in this set, but at the cost of blocking a fifth of legitimate requests. A strict threshold (0.8) never over-blocks, but lets 60% of unsafe content through. There's no threshold in this example that gets both numbers to their best value simultaneously.

## Bench

```bench
id: guardrail-threshold
title: Looser catches more, and over-blocks more
fallback: Slide a safety filter's block threshold and watch over-blocking trade off against catching real attacks.
```

**Try this**

1. Slide the threshold down until the false-positive rate first rises above 0%, and note the catch rate at that point.
2. Slide it up until the catch rate drops below 50%, and note the false-positive rate at that point.
3. Try to find a single threshold where both rates are simultaneously at their best possible value — notice it isn't possible here.

**What you should notice:** the two dots sets (safe and unsafe scores) overlap in the middle of the range — any threshold placed inside that overlap necessarily trades one kind of error for the other.

## Where it appears in AI

* **This is the same threshold trade-off [[Adversarial and Jailbreak Evaluation]] measures when testing attack success rates** — a guardrail's catch rate against adversarial attempts is exactly what that evaluation is checking.
* **A guardrail runs independently of the model's own alignment training** — it's a deployment-time addition, not a replacement, for the training-time work covered in Instruction Tuning and Alignment.
* **Updating a guardrail's threshold or rules can happen without retraining the model at all**, unlike [[Responsible Scaling Policies and Frontier Safety]]'s training-time commitments, which is part of why guardrails are a common first line of defense in production.

## Common pitfalls

* **Assuming a stricter guardrail is always safer.** The worked example's strictest threshold (0.8) has zero false positives but lets more than half the unsafe content in this set through — "stricter" reduces one error type at the direct cost of the other.
* **Treating a guardrail as a substitute for alignment training.** A guardrail catches what reaches it at the input/output boundary; it doesn't change what the model would otherwise produce, and sophisticated attacks can be built specifically to evade a known filter.
* **Picking a single global threshold for every use case.** A customer-facing product and an internal research tool often tolerate very different false-positive rates, so the "right" threshold isn't universal even for the same underlying filter.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. In the worked example, why does lowering the threshold from 0.6 to 0.4 increase both the catch rate and the false-positive rate?</summary>
A lower threshold blocks anything scoring at or above it, which includes more of the unsafe examples (raising the catch rate) but also some safe examples that scored just below 0.6 (raising the false-positive rate) — both effects come from the same change.
</details>

<details><summary>2. Does a guardrail replace the need for alignment training, or complement it?</summary>
It complements it — alignment training shapes the model's own tendencies, while a guardrail is a separate check around the model that can catch what training missed and can be updated independently.
</details>

<details><summary>3. Why might two different products reasonably choose different guardrail thresholds for the same underlying filter?</summary>
They can have very different tolerances for over-blocking versus under-catching — a customer-facing product might prioritize not blocking legitimate requests, while a safety-critical context might prioritize catching more unsafe content even at the cost of some false positives.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Guardrail:** a deployment-time filter that checks inputs or outputs against a threshold, separate from the model's own training.
* **False positive rate (in this context):** the fraction of safe content incorrectly blocked by a filter.
* **Catch rate:** the fraction of genuinely unsafe content a filter successfully blocks.

## Related

[[Adversarial and Jailbreak Evaluation]] · [[Responsible Scaling Policies and Frontier Safety]] · [[Reward Hacking and Sycophancy]]

## Capstone: Pretraining to Aligned Assistant, Traced End to End

Every stage this planet's road has covered — pretraining, fine-tuning, preference alignment, deployment — is usually described separately, with its own numbers and its own bench. This capstone follows one model through all four stages in order, reusing the exact same functions each earlier topic already verified, so the whole pipeline's numbers connect end to end.

**You need:** [[Causal Language Modeling as a Pretraining Objective]], [[Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT)|Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT)]], [[Direct Preference Optimization (DPO)]], [[Cost and Latency of LLM APIs]].

## The question it answers

"What does a model actually go through, in order, between raw pretraining and being a deployed, aligned assistant that costs money to run?" Four stages, each one this road already covered in depth: pretraining on raw text with the causal language modeling objective; supervised fine-tuning on assistant-formatted demonstrations; preference alignment (via DPO, no separate reward model needed); and deployment behind an API, where every request now has a real cost and latency.

## Intuition

A single cut of meat moves through butchering, seasoning, cooking and plating before it reaches a table — each stage transforms it further toward "a meal," and each stage has its own techniques worth understanding on their own. But watching the whole sequence happen to one piece, start to finish, makes clear how each stage's result becomes the next stage's starting point.

## Definition and notation

```text
stage 1: pretraining        — clmLoss over raw text, teacher forcing
stage 2: SFT                — same clmLoss objective, over assistant-formatted data
stage 3: DPO alignment      — dpoStep, raising P(preferred) relative to a reference model
stage 4: deployment         — apiCostLatency, pricing and timing a real request
```

## A worked example

Reusing the exact logits and parameters already verified in this planet's own topics:

```text
stage 1 (pretraining):  mean CLM loss = 1.9348
stage 2 (SFT):           mean CLM loss = 0.2670   (same objective, assistant-formatted data)
stage 3 (DPO, 5 steps):  P(preferred response) rises from 0.310 to 0.484
stage 4 (deployment):    an 80-token prompt + 120-token reply → cost $0.00204, latency 2.54s
```

The loss dropping nearly 7× from pretraining to SFT reflects the model learning to produce assistant-style responses specifically, on top of general language modeling. The DPO step then reshapes *preferences* among already-fluent responses, not fluency itself — P(preferred) rising from 0.310 to 0.484 after only 5 steps, with no reward model and no RL loop. The resulting model is then just as subject to per-request cost and latency as any other deployed API.

## Bench

```bench
id: capstone-pretrain-to-assistant
title: One model, through every stage of this road
fallback: Step through pretraining, SFT, DPO alignment and deployment and watch each stage's own verified numbers connect.
```

**Try this**

1. Step through all four stages in order and read each stage's own number.
2. Compare how large the loss drop is from pretraining to SFT against how large the probability shift is from DPO — notice they're not measuring the same kind of quantity.
3. Reset and think about which stage, if skipped, would leave the model least usable as a deployed assistant.

**What you should notice:** each stage's number was independently verified earlier on this planet's own road — this capstone doesn't introduce new mechanics, it chains the same four mechanisms together in the order they actually happen.

## Where it appears in AI

* **Stage 1 reuses [[Causal Language Modeling as a Pretraining Objective]] exactly**, stage 2 reuses [[Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT)|SFT]]'s own worked example, stage 3 reuses [[Direct Preference Optimization (DPO)]]'s own worked example, and stage 4 reuses [[Cost and Latency of LLM APIs]]'s formula — nothing here is new mechanics, only the ordering.
* **Skipping stage 2 or 3 is exactly what distinguishes a base (pretrained-only) model from an instruction-tuned, aligned assistant** — the gap between them is precisely these two stages.
* **Everything downstream of stage 4 — [[Choosing a Model for a Task]], [[Guardrails and Deployment-Time Safety Filters]] — assumes a model has already been through all three earlier stages.**

## Common pitfalls

* **Treating these four stages as interchangeable or reorderable.** Each stage assumes the previous one already happened — SFT assumes a pretrained model, DPO assumes an SFT'd model that can already produce fluent, on-format responses to have preferences *between*.
* **Expecting the loss numbers from stage 1 and 2 to be directly comparable to the probability numbers from stage 3.** They measure genuinely different things (next-token prediction accuracy vs. relative preference between two full responses) — the capstone's point is the pipeline's structure, not a single unified metric.
* **Forgetting that stage 4's cost and latency apply to the final, fully-trained model** — all the training cost in stages 1 through 3 is separate, one-time, and far larger than any single deployment-time request.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. Why does the loss number drop so much more between pretraining and SFT than between any two other adjacent stages?</summary>
Pretraining and SFT use the same loss (next-token prediction via teacher forcing), so their numbers are directly comparable, and the drop from 1.9348 to 0.2670 reflects the model learning to reliably produce exactly the assistant-formatted tokens it's now being trained on — a large, measurable jump on the same scale.
</details>

<details><summary>2. What would be missing from a model that went through stage 1 and stage 2, but skipped stage 3?</summary>
It would be instruction-following and fluent in assistant format, but it wouldn't have been shaped toward human preferences among its own possible responses — it could still produce responses a person would rate as unhelpful, unsafe or low-quality relative to alternatives it could have generated.
</details>

<details><summary>3. Does stage 4's deployment cost reflect the cost of training the model through stages 1 to 3?</summary>
No — stage 4's cost and latency are purely per-request, incurred every time the already-trained model is called; the training cost in stages 1 through 3 is a separate, one-time (or periodically repeated) cost, far larger in absolute terms.
</details>

## Key terms

* **End-to-end pipeline:** the full sequence a model goes through from raw pretraining to a deployed, usable assistant.
* **Stage-specific objective:** the particular loss or update rule that defines what a given training stage is actually optimizing for.
* **Deployment-time cost:** the per-request cost and latency incurred once a model is serving live traffic, separate from however it was trained.

## Related

[[Direct Preference Optimization (DPO)]] · [[Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT)|Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT)]] · [[Cost and Latency of LLM APIs]]

# RAG

## RAG

A language model only knows what was baked into its weights during training — it can't read your company's internal wiki, last week's news, or a PDF you just uploaded. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) fixes that by searching a real collection of documents for relevant passages, and handing those passages to the model as context before it answers. This planet is about engineering that pipeline well: turning documents into searchable chunks, finding the right ones for a query, and getting a model to answer faithfully from what it's given.

**You need:** [[Embeddings and Similarity Search]], [[Long-Context Transformers]], [[Hallucination and Factuality]].

The road through RAG:

* [[Why Retrieval and Grounding]] — why a model's own weights aren't enough, and when retrieval is the right fix.
* [[Document Processing and Chunking]] — turning raw documents into retrievable pieces.
* [[Embeddings for Retrieval]] — the retrieval-specific layer on top of embeddings covered on Math: bi-encoders, cross-encoders, and adapting them to a domain.
* [[Vector Search and Indexing]] — finding the nearest chunks fast, at scale.
* [[Retrieval Strategies]] — sparse, dense, hybrid, and ways to improve what gets retrieved before it's ranked.
* [[Advanced RAG Patterns]] — re-ranking, self-correction, graphs, structured data and multiple modalities.
* [[Generation with Retrieved Context]] — turning retrieved passages into a grounded, attributable answer.
* [[Evaluating RAG Systems]] — measuring retrieval and generation quality separately and together.
* [[RAG in Practice]] — running a RAG system in production, ending in a capstone that traces one question from query to grounded answer.

From here the road leads on to [[Agents]].

## Why Retrieval and Grounding

A model's weights are a fixed snapshot of what it learned during training — they can't be updated with this morning's news or a document it's never seen. This district is about why that limitation matters, and when searching a document collection at answer-time is the right fix for it.

Topics on this stretch of the road:

* [[Parametric vs. Non-Parametric Knowledge]]: two different places a model's "knowledge" can live.
* [[Hallucination and Knowledge Cutoff]]: what happens when a model is asked about something its weights don't cover.
* [[RAG vs. Fine-Tuning vs. Long-Context]]: three different fixes for the same underlying gap, and when each one actually fits.
* [[Anatomy of a RAG Pipeline]]: the stages every retrieval-augmented system has, end to end.

## Parametric vs. Non-Parametric Knowledge

A language model's "knowledge" isn't stored the way a database stores facts. It's baked into millions of weight values during training, which means updating it means retraining — there's no row to edit. Retrieval gives a model a second, very different kind of knowledge: a document store it can search at answer-time, which can be edited the instant a new document arrives.

**You need:** [[Embeddings and Similarity Search]].

## The question it answers

"Where does a model's knowledge actually live, and why does that matter?" **Parametric knowledge** is whatever got compressed into a model's weights during training — implicit, diffuse across millions of parameters, and frozen until the next training run. **Non-parametric knowledge** is an external store (documents, a database) the model consults at answer-time — explicit, inspectable, and editable immediately, with no retraining at all.

## Intuition

Parametric knowledge is like a fact a person memorized years ago from a textbook: it's genuinely theirs, but updating it means re-studying. Non-parametric knowledge is like handing that same person a current reference book before they answer: anyone can add a page to the book the moment new information exists, with no need for the person to "relearn" anything.

## Definition and notation

```text
parametric answer(fact)      = lookup in trained weights         (frozen until retrained)
non-parametric answer(fact)  = lookup in an external document store (editable anytime)
```

## A worked example

A fact that didn't exist when the model was trained, checked before and after a new document is added to the store:

```text
before the document is added:
  parametric model:       "unknown — not in this source"
  retrieval-augmented:    "unknown — not in this source"

after the document is added to the store (no retraining):
  parametric model:       "unknown — not in this source"   (unchanged — its weights never moved)
  retrieval-augmented:    "effective March 2026"            (found the new document instantly)
```

The retrieval-augmented answer changed the moment a document was added. The parametric model's answer didn't move at all — and won't, until it's retrained on data that includes this fact.

## Bench

```bench
id: parametric-vs-retrieved
title: One of these can be updated without retraining
fallback: Add a new document to a store and compare how a parametric and a retrieval-augmented answer respond.
```

**Try this**

1. Note both answers are "unknown" before anything is added.
2. Click to add the new document and see only one answer change.
3. Imagine this fact changing again next month — which approach handles that without any extra training work?

**What you should notice:** adding a document changes what the retrieval-augmented system can answer immediately; it changes nothing about the parametric model, which stays wrong (or honestly "unknown") until someone retrains it.

## Where it appears in AI

* **This is the entire reason retrieval-augmented generation exists**: every topic on this planet is, in one way or another, about building and using the non-parametric half of this picture well.
* **[[Hallucination and Knowledge Cutoff]] is what happens when a model is forced to answer from parametric knowledge alone, past the point where that knowledge is current or complete.**
* **[[RAG vs. Fine-Tuning vs. Long-Context]] compares this topic's two knowledge stores against a third option — stuffing non-parametric information directly into the prompt instead of a searchable store.**

## Common pitfalls

* **Assuming fine-tuning and retrieval solve the same problem.** Fine-tuning changes parametric knowledge (slowly, in bulk, requiring retraining); retrieval adds non-parametric knowledge (instantly, per-document, requiring no retraining) — they're genuinely different mechanisms with different trade-offs.
* **Expecting a parametric model to "know" something just because it's true and recent.** If it wasn't in the training data, it isn't in the weights — there's no partial credit for information existing on the internet somewhere.
* **Forgetting that non-parametric knowledge is only as good as what's actually in the store.** A retrieval-augmented system can't retrieve a fact that was never added to its document collection either.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. In the worked example, why does the parametric model's answer stay "unknown" even after the document is added to the store?</summary>
Adding a document to the store doesn't touch the model's weights at all — the parametric model's answer only changes if the model is retrained on data that includes the new fact.
</details>

<details><summary>2. Is non-parametric knowledge "better" than parametric knowledge in general?</summary>
Not universally — it's better for facts that need to stay current or be added instantly, but parametric knowledge captures patterns, language ability and reasoning that aren't naturally expressed as retrievable documents.
</details>

<details><summary>3. What has to happen for a parametric model's knowledge about a given fact to change?</summary>
Retraining (or fine-tuning) on data that includes that fact — there's no equivalent of "adding a document" for weights that have already been trained.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Parametric knowledge:** information implicitly stored in a model's trained weights, updatable only by retraining.
* **Non-parametric knowledge:** information kept in an external, searchable store, updatable immediately without touching the model.
* **Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG):** combining a model's parametric knowledge with non-parametric knowledge fetched from a document store at answer-time.

## Related

[[Hallucination and Knowledge Cutoff]] · [[RAG vs. Fine-Tuning vs. Long-Context]] · [[Anatomy of a RAG Pipeline]]

## Hallucination and Knowledge Cutoff

Every model has a training cutoff — a date after which nothing happened in its training data. Ask it about something before that date, and it usually answers confidently and correctly. Ask it about something after, and it doesn't say "I don't know" by default — it often produces a fluent, plausible-sounding answer anyway, wrong in a way that's hard to tell apart from being right.

**You need:** [[Parametric vs. Non-Parametric Knowledge]], [[Hallucination and Factuality]].

## The question it answers

"What actually happens when a model is asked about something past its training cutoff?" [[Hallucination and Factuality|Hallucination]] in general covers any confident-but-wrong output; this topic is about one specific, very common cause of it — a knowledge gap the model has no way of knowing it has. The model's confidence in its own unretrieved answer stays high right up to the cutoff, then decays the further past it a question falls, but it never hits zero: a language model is built to produce fluent text, and "I genuinely don't know" isn't the default completion for most questions.

## Intuition

Asking someone who left on a long expedition about recent news gets you confident answers about everything up to the day they left, and increasingly uncertain, outdated, or simply wrong guesses about anything after — but they usually don't just say "I don't know," because people (and models) are built to keep the conversation going, not to flag the exact edge of their own knowledge.

## Definition and notation

```text
confidence(event, cutoff) = 0.95                              if event is before cutoff
                           = max(0.05, 0.95 · e^(−days_past/30))  if event is after cutoff
```

An illustrative decay — the exact shape varies by model and topic, but the direction (confident, then decaying, never literally zero) is the real pattern.

## A worked example

Confidence in an unretrieved answer, at various distances from a training cutoff of January 1, 2024:

```text
365 days before cutoff:  95% confident
 30 days before cutoff:  95% confident
  1 day  before cutoff:  95% confident
  1 day  after  cutoff:  92% confident
 30 days after  cutoff:  35% confident
180 days after  cutoff:   5% confident (floor)
365 days after  cutoff:   5% confident (floor)
```

Confidence doesn't fall off a cliff exactly at the cutoff — it stays high for a short while (recent pre-cutoff training data is sparse too) and then drops sharply over the following weeks, settling at a low floor rather than zero. A model asked about something 180 days past its cutoff isn't refusing to answer; it's guessing with 5% of the confidence it would have for something it actually knows.

## Bench

```bench
id: knowledge-cutoff-confidence
title: Confident up to a point, then guessing
fallback: Slide an event's date relative to a training cutoff and watch confidence decay past it.
```

**Try this**

1. Slide to well before the cutoff and note confidence stays flat and high.
2. Cross the cutoff and watch confidence start falling within the first month.
3. Slide far past the cutoff and notice confidence never reaches exactly zero.

**What you should notice:** there's no sharp "I don't know" boundary at the cutoff — confidence degrades gradually, which is exactly why a hallucinated answer about a post-cutoff event can sound just as fluent as a correct one.

## Where it appears in AI

* **This is a specific, dateable instance of the broader [[Hallucination and Factuality|hallucination]] problem** covered on the Generative AI planet — knowledge cutoff is one concrete, predictable cause among several.
* **Retrieval directly addresses this gap** by giving the model current documents to answer from instead of relying on its own decaying confidence — the motivation behind everything else on this planet.
* **[[RAG vs. Fine-Tuning vs. Long-Context]] treats "freshness" as one of the dimensions that decides whether retrieval is the right fix for a given knowledge gap.**

## Common pitfalls

* **Assuming a model will say "I don't know" when asked about something past its cutoff.** The worked example's confidence floor (5%, not 0%) reflects that models keep answering fluently well past the point where they should be uncertain.
* **Treating the cutoff date as a hard boundary.** Confidence starts sliding within days of the cutoff, not exactly at midnight on the cutoff date — training data near the cutoff is often sparse too.
* **Confusing knowledge cutoff with the model simply not knowing a fact that was always obscure.** Cutoff-related hallucination is specifically about events that didn't exist yet during training, not facts the training data merely omitted.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. In the worked example, why does confidence 1 day after the cutoff (92%) look almost as high as confidence 1 day before it (95%)?</summary>
The decay function only starts applying once an event is past the cutoff, and the exponential decay is still very close to its starting value just one day in — the drop accelerates over the following weeks rather than happening instantly.
</details>

<details><summary>2. Does a model's confidence in an unretrieved answer ever reach exactly zero for events far past its cutoff?</summary>
No — the worked example's confidence floor is 5%, reflecting that models are built to produce fluent completions and rarely default to flat refusal, however far past their knowledge the question falls.
</details>

<details><summary>3. What's the direct fix retrieval offers for this specific problem?</summary>
Giving the model a current document about the event at answer-time, so it can ground its response in real information instead of relying on its own decaying, unretrieved confidence.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Training cutoff:** the date after which no data existed in a model's training set.
* **Hallucination:** a model producing a confident, fluent answer that is factually wrong.
* **Confidence decay:** the gradual drop in reliability of a model's unretrieved answers as a question moves further past its training cutoff.

## Related

[[Hallucination and Factuality]] · [[Parametric vs. Non-Parametric Knowledge]] · [[RAG vs. Fine-Tuning vs. Long-Context]]

## RAG vs. Fine-Tuning vs. Long-Context

A model that doesn't know something, or doesn't behave the way you want, has more than one fix available. Retrieval, fine-tuning, and simply stuffing more into the prompt (long-context) all address a gap between what a model does and what you need — but they're good at different gaps, for different reasons.

**You need:** [[Parametric vs. Non-Parametric Knowledge]], [[Long-Context Transformers]], [[Fine-Tuning for a Specific Task]].

## The question it answers

"Given a gap between what a model knows or does and what's needed, how do you decide which of these three fixes it?" Retrieval (RAG) and long-context both keep the model's weights untouched and supply information at answer-time — RAG searches a large collection for the relevant few documents; long-context relies on stuffing everything that might be relevant directly into the prompt, which only scales as far as the context window and its cost allow. Fine-tuning changes the weights themselves, which is the right tool when the gap is about *behavior* or *style* rather than *facts* — information baked into weights through fine-tuning doesn't update the moment something changes, the way a retrieved document can.

## Intuition

Three different ways to help someone answer questions about an enormous reference library: hand them a search engine over the whole library (RAG); hand them a stack of every book that might be relevant and let them read through it each time (long-context); or send them back to school to actually learn the material (fine-tuning). The search engine scales to a huge library cheaply; handing over physical books gets expensive and slow as the stack grows; sending someone to re-learn material is the right call only when you want them to behave differently, not just to have looked something up once.

## Definition and notation

```text
score(approach, weights) = Σ approach[dimension] × weights[dimension] / Σ weights[dimension]
```

Each approach is scored on freshness (how quickly new information can be reflected), update cost (how cheap it is to incorporate a change), latency cost (how much slower a request gets), transparency (how traceable an answer is to its source), and style (how well it reshapes the model's own behavior).

## A worked example

Three approaches, scored 0–1 on five dimensions, under two different task scenarios:

```text
                freshness  updateCost  latencyCost  transparency  style
RAG                0.95       0.90        0.60          0.90       0.30
fine-tuning        0.20       0.20        0.90          0.30       0.95
long-context       0.95       0.95        0.30          0.70       0.30

freshness-critical knowledge base:  RAG 0.900  long-context 0.860  fine-tuning 0.280  →  RAG wins
writing-style adaptation:            fine-tuning 0.800  RAG 0.4825  long-context 0.405  →  fine-tuning wins
```

For a knowledge base that changes constantly, RAG edges out long-context (similar freshness, but far cheaper to update as the collection grows) and both crush fine-tuning. For adapting a model's writing style, the ranking flips entirely — fine-tuning wins by a wide margin, because style isn't something either RAG or long-context was ever trying to fix.

## Bench

```bench
id: rag-vs-finetune-vs-longcontext
title: Different gaps need different fixes
fallback: Switch between task scenarios and see which approach actually scores best for each.
```

**Try this**

1. Compare the winning approach under each scenario — notice it's a different one each time.
2. Look at how close RAG and long-context are under the freshness scenario, and why RAG still edges ahead.
3. Imagine a scenario that weights latency most heavily — which approach would you expect to suffer most, and why?

**What you should notice:** RAG and long-context solve a similar problem (supplying fresh, non-parametric information) in different ways, while fine-tuning solves a genuinely different problem (changing the model's own behavior) — picking between them is about identifying which kind of gap you actually have.

## Where it appears in AI

* **This reuses the same weighted-scoring mechanism as [[Choosing a Model for a Task]] on the LLMs planet**, applied here to choosing an adaptation strategy instead of a model size.
* **Long-context's latency and cost scale with how much is stuffed into the prompt every single request ([[Cost and Latency of LLM APIs]])** — exactly the trade-off RAG's targeted retrieval is designed to avoid.
* **Fine-tuning's own trade-offs (forgetting, update cost) are covered in depth on the LLMs planet ([[Fine-Tuning for a Specific Task]], [[Catastrophic Forgetting in Fine-Tuning]])** — this topic only covers when fine-tuning is the right tool to reach for in the first place.

## Common pitfalls

* **Treating these three as mutually exclusive.** Production systems routinely combine them — a fine-tuned model that's also retrieval-augmented, with long-context used for a handful of documents too important to risk missing in retrieval.
* **Defaulting to long-context "because context windows are big now."** The worked example shows long-context's update cost is cheap but its *latency* cost is the worst of the three — stuffing more into every single request has a real, recurring price.
* **Reaching for fine-tuning to fix a freshness problem.** The worked example shows fine-tuning scores worst on freshness and update cost by a wide margin — it's the right tool for reshaping behavior, not for keeping facts current.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. In the worked example, why does RAG edge out long-context in the freshness-critical scenario despite both scoring 0.95 on freshness itself?</summary>
The scenario also weights update cost, where RAG scores higher (0.90 vs. 0.95 is close, but long-context's advantage narrows once latency cost — where RAG scores much better, 0.60 vs. 0.30 — is factored in too) — the combination across all weighted dimensions, not freshness alone, decides the winner.
</details>

<details><summary>2. Why does fine-tuning win decisively in the style-adaptation scenario when it scored worst in the freshness scenario?</summary>
The two scenarios weight completely different dimensions — freshness and update cost (where fine-tuning is weakest) barely matter in the style scenario, which instead weights style (where fine-tuning scores 0.95, far above the other two).
</details>

<details><summary>3. Can RAG and fine-tuning be used on the same model at the same time?</summary>
Yes — they address different kinds of gaps (non-parametric facts vs. parametric behavior), so a production system can fine-tune a model for style or task-specific behavior and still retrieve documents for it to answer from.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Long-context:** supplying potentially relevant information directly in the prompt rather than searching for it, limited by the context window and its per-request cost.
* **Adaptation strategy:** the general choice of mechanism (retrieval, fine-tuning, long-context, or some combination) used to close a gap between a model's default behavior and what a task needs.
* **Freshness:** how quickly a change in the real world can be reflected in a system's answers.

## Related

[[Parametric vs. Non-Parametric Knowledge]] · [[Choosing a Model for a Task]] · [[Anatomy of a RAG Pipeline]]

## Anatomy of a RAG Pipeline

Every retrieval-augmented system, however elaborate, is built from the same handful of stages in the same order: a question comes in, it becomes a vector, that vector finds relevant passages, those passages get assembled into context, and the model generates an answer from that context. Everything else on this planet is a deeper look at one of these five stages.

**You need:** [[Embeddings and Similarity Search]].

## The question it answers

"What are the actual steps between a user's question and a grounded answer?" Five stages, in order: **query** (the raw question arrives), **embed** (the query becomes a vector), **retrieve** (that vector is compared against every document's vector, keeping the closest few), **assemble** (the retrieved passages are arranged into a prompt), and **generate** (the model answers, using only what was assembled).

## Intuition

A reference librarian answering a question does roughly the same five things: hears the question, mentally narrows down what kind of thing they're looking for, pulls the handful of books most likely to have the answer, skims and arranges the relevant passages, and only then actually answers — using what they just pulled, not purely from memory.

## Definition and notation

```text
query  → embed  → retrieve (top-k by similarity)  → assemble (context)  → generate (answer)
```

Each arrow is a real engineering decision this planet covers in depth: how to embed ([[Bi-Encoders and Dense Embeddings]]), how to retrieve ([[Dense Retrieval]], [[Sparse Retrieval with TF-IDF and BM25]]), how to assemble ([[Context Assembly and Ordering]]), how to generate faithfully ([[Grounded Generation and Faithfulness]]).

## A worked example

One toy query against four 2D document embeddings, walked through all five stages:

```text
query: "how long do refunds take"
embed: query vector = [0.90, 0.10]

retrieve (cosine similarity against 4 documents):
  "refund timeline"   0.9983
  "returns policy"     0.9980
  "shipping times"     0.8882
  "product warranty"   0.1625
  → top 2 kept: "refund timeline", "returns policy"

assemble: both passages inserted into the prompt, ahead of the question

generate: the model answers using only "refund timeline" and "returns policy" —
  never "product warranty", which scored far lower and was never retrieved
```

The document that actually discusses refunds scores far above the one about an unrelated topic (0.998 vs. 0.163) — exactly the separation retrieval depends on to keep irrelevant content out of the model's context.

## Bench

```bench
id: rag-pipeline-anatomy
title: One question, five stages
fallback: Step through a RAG pipeline's stages on one toy query, from embedding to retrieval to a grounded answer.
```

**Try this**

1. Step through all five stages and read each one's description.
2. At the retrieve stage, compare the similarity scores for all four documents — notice how far "product warranty" trails the other three.
3. Imagine "product warranty" had scored 0.994 instead of 0.163 — would it have changed which documents got assembled?

**What you should notice:** generation only ever sees what survived the retrieve and assemble stages — a document that scores low never reaches the model at all, which is both the whole point of retrieval and exactly where it can go wrong if the wrong documents score highest.

## Where it appears in AI

* **Every later district on this planet is a deeper treatment of one arrow in this diagram**: chunking happens before embedding even starts; embeddings, indexing and retrieval strategies fill in the retrieve stage; assembly and faithful generation fill in the last two.
* **[[RAG vs. Fine-Tuning vs. Long-Context]] compares this entire five-stage pipeline against alternatives that skip some or all of these stages.**
* **The capstone ([[Capstone: A Question Answered, Traced from Query to Grounded Answer]]) walks this same five-stage shape again, at the end of the planet, with every stage built out using the planet's own verified techniques.**

## Common pitfalls

* **Assuming "RAG" means one specific technique.** It names this whole five-stage shape; nearly every other topic on this planet is a different, swappable way to implement one of its stages.
* **Treating retrieval as a single step that either works or doesn't.** The worked example's numeric scores show retrieval is a *ranking*, not a binary decision — "top-k" always involves a cutoff choice with real consequences.
* **Forgetting that assembly is a real stage with real decisions.** Which retrieved passages go first, how they're separated, and how many fit are all choices — not an automatic consequence of retrieval.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. In the worked example, why does "product warranty" never reach the generation stage?</summary>
Its cosine similarity to the query (0.1625) is far below the other three documents', so it falls outside the top 2 kept at the retrieve stage and is never assembled into the prompt the model generates from.
</details>

<details><summary>2. Which stage of the pipeline is responsible for deciding how many retrieved passages actually fit in the model's context?</summary>
The assemble stage — retrieve produces a ranked list, but assemble is where a decision gets made about how many of those ranked passages to actually include.
</details>

<details><summary>3. If retrieval returns the wrong documents, can a strong generation stage still produce a correct answer?</summary>
Not reliably — generation only has access to what was assembled, so a retrieval failure (the right documents never making the top-k) caps how good the final answer can be, regardless of how capable the generating model is.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Query:** the user's raw question before any processing.
* **Top-k:** the number of highest-scoring documents kept after retrieval, out of the full collection.
* **Assembly:** arranging retrieved passages into the prompt the model will actually generate from.

## Related

[[RAG vs. Fine-Tuning vs. Long-Context]] · [[Parametric vs. Non-Parametric Knowledge]] · [[Dense Retrieval]]

## Document Processing and Chunking

Before anything can be retrieved, raw documents — PDFs, web pages, spreadsheets, code — have to become a collection of individually retrievable pieces. How that split happens shapes everything downstream: too coarse and irrelevant text gets dragged along with what's useful; too fine and a passage loses the context it needs to make sense on its own.

Topics on this stretch of the road:

* [[Parsing Documents for Retrieval]]: turning PDFs, HTML and other formats into clean, retrievable text.
* [[Fixed-Size and Recursive Chunking]]: the simplest ways to split a document into pieces.
* [[Semantic and Structure-Aware Chunking]]: splitting by meaning and document structure instead of a fixed character count.
* [[Chunk Overlap and Size Trade-offs]]: how chunk size and overlap change what gets found and what gets missed.
* [[Metadata Extraction and Enrichment]]: attaching the information a chunk can't carry in its own text.
* [[Handling Tables, Code and Structured Content]]: chunking strategies for content that isn't ordinary prose.

## Parsing Documents for Retrieval

A real document isn't just its words. A PDF carries page numbers, headers and footers repeated on every page; a web page carries navigation menus and cookie banners around the actual article. None of that is content a retrieval system should ever match a query against — but it's exactly what a naive "just extract the text" approach drags along for free.

**You need:** [[Anatomy of a RAG Pipeline]].

## The question it answers

"What has to happen before a document is even ready to chunk?" Parsing turns a document's native format (PDF, HTML, a spreadsheet, a scanned image) into clean text, and specifically means stripping boilerplate that repeats across every page or section — page numbers, running headers, confidentiality footers, navigation chrome — none of which answers any real question a user would ask.

## Intuition

Photocopying every page of a report and handing someone the whole stack, headers, footers and page numbers included, buries the one paragraph they actually need in repeated noise. A good parser is the person who goes through first with a highlighter and scissors, keeping only what the report actually says.

## Definition and notation

```text
noise fraction = (raw word count − cleaned word count) / raw word count
```

## A worked example

One raw page from a company policy PDF, before and after stripping repeated boilerplate:

```text
raw page (23 words):
  "Page 7 of 42
   ACME CORP CONFIDENTIAL
   Shipping Policy
   Orders ship within two business days of payment confirmation.
   Footer: acme.com | page 7"

cleaned (11 words):
  "Shipping Policy
   Orders ship within two business days of payment confirmation."

noise fraction: (23 − 11) / 23 = 52.2%
```

Just over half of this raw page's word count was boilerplate repeated on every single page of the document — page numbers, a confidentiality stamp, and a footer. Left in, it would be chunked and embedded right alongside the one sentence that actually answers a question.

## Bench

```bench
id: parsing-noise-vs-signal
title: Half of this page was never content
fallback: Toggle boilerplate stripping and watch how much of a raw page was never real content.
```

**Try this**

1. Look at the raw page and count how much of it repeats the same way on every page of a 42-page document.
2. Toggle stripping on and see exactly which lines get removed.
3. Imagine this boilerplate embedded and chunked across all 42 pages — how much wasted index space does that add up to?

**What you should notice:** the noise isn't a small rounding error — on this page it's over half the word count, and it would repeat identically on every other page of the same document.

## Where it appears in AI

* **Everything downstream assumes parsing already happened**: [[Fixed-Size and Recursive Chunking]] and every later chunking topic operate on text that's assumed to already be boilerplate-free.
* **[[Handling Tables, Code and Structured Content]] is about a parsing decision too** — how to extract structured content without destroying the structure that makes it meaningful.
* **Boilerplate left in a chunk pollutes its embedding** (covered on [[Embeddings and Similarity Search]]), diluting the signal a retrieval system is supposed to match against.

## Common pitfalls

* **Assuming "extracting text" is the whole job.** The worked example shows extraction alone (without cleaning) keeps over half noise — parsing isn't finished until boilerplate is actually removed.
* **Writing one-off cleaning rules per document instead of detecting repeated patterns.** Headers and footers repeat identically or near-identically across pages, which is exactly what makes them detectable and removable systematically.
* **Over-stripping and removing real content that merely looks like boilerplate.** A line like "Section 7: Shipping Policy" can look like a header but is actually the start of real content — cleaning rules need to be specific enough to avoid false positives.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. In the worked example, why does the noise fraction come out above 50%?</summary>
The raw page has only one real sentence of content (12 words) against 11 words of repeated boilerplate (a page counter, a confidentiality stamp, and a footer), so the boilerplate makes up slightly more than half the total word count.
</details>

<details><summary>2. Why does boilerplate matter more on a long, multi-page document than on a single short one?</summary>
The same boilerplate repeats on every page, so its total footprint across the whole document scales with the page count — a document with more pages wastes proportionally more of its chunked, embedded content on identical repeated text.
</details>

<details><summary>3. What's the risk of being too aggressive about stripping "boilerplate"?</summary>
A cleaning rule written too broadly can remove real content that happens to resemble boilerplate (like a section heading), losing information the chunking and retrieval stages downstream never get a chance to see.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Boilerplate:** text that repeats across a document's pages or sections without carrying page-specific content (headers, footers, page numbers).
* **Parsing:** converting a document's native format into clean text suitable for chunking.
* **Noise fraction:** the share of a raw extraction that turns out to be boilerplate rather than real content.

## Related

[[Anatomy of a RAG Pipeline]] · [[Fixed-Size and Recursive Chunking]] · [[Handling Tables, Code and Structured Content]]

## Fixed-Size and Recursive Chunking

The simplest way to split a document is to cut it every N characters and move on. It's trivial to implement and perfectly predictable — and it will, routinely, slice straight through the middle of a word, a sentence, or a fact, with no regard for where the text's own structure would have suggested cutting.

**You need:** [[Parsing Documents for Retrieval]].

## The question it answers

"What's the simplest way to split a document into chunks, and what does that simplicity cost?" **Fixed-size chunking** cuts at a fixed character (or token) count, wherever that count happens to fall. **Recursive chunking** splits on the text's own structure first — paragraphs, then sentences — packing whole units into a chunk until the next one would push it over the size limit, so a cut only ever falls between units, never through the middle of one.

## Intuition

Cutting a loaf of bread into exactly 2-inch slices with a ruler is fast and consistent, but will occasionally slice right through a raisin. Cutting it at the natural gaps between slices the baker already scored is slightly less uniform in size, but it never cuts through anything that was meant to stay whole.

## Definition and notation

```text
fixed-size(text, size)     = text sliced every `size` characters, ignoring word/sentence boundaries
recursive(text, maxSize)   = sentences packed into a chunk until the next one would exceed maxSize,
                             never splitting a sentence itself
```

## A worked example

A 40-character chunk size, applied to a short returns-policy paragraph:

```text
fixed-size (40 chars): 6 chunks, 4 of 5 chunk boundaries cut mid-word
```
