```text
  "Returns are accepted within 30 days. Ite"
  "ms must be unworn and in original packag"
  "ing. Refunds are issued to the original "
  "payment method within 5 business days. S"
  "tore credit is available as an alternati"
  "ve."

recursive (sentence-aware, ≤40 chars): 4 chunks, 0 broken boundaries
  "Returns are accepted within 30 days."
  "Items must be unworn and in original packaging."
  "Refunds are issued to the original payment method within 5 business days."
  "Store credit is available as an alternative."
```

Fixed-size chunking breaks words apart at 4 of its 5 chunk boundaries — "Ite" / "ms", "packag" / "ing", and so on. Recursive chunking produces fewer, slightly longer chunks (one even exceeds the 40-character target, since it keeps a whole sentence rather than cutting it), but never once cuts through a word.

## Bench

```bench
id: fixed-vs-recursive-chunking
title: Splitting by character count vs. by sentence
fallback: Compare fixed-size chunking against recursive, sentence-respecting chunking on the same text.
```

**Try this**

1. Switch to fixed-size and read each chunk — notice how many start or end mid-word.
2. Switch to recursive and notice every chunk starts and ends at a real sentence boundary.
3. Compare the chunk counts — recursive chunking used fewer, because it let one chunk run slightly over 40 characters rather than cut a sentence.

**What you should notice:** recursive chunking trades strict size control for structural integrity — it occasionally produces a chunk longer than the target size, but it never produces one that starts or ends mid-word.

## Where it appears in AI

* **A chunk that cuts a fact in half is exactly the failure mode [[Chunk Overlap and Size Trade-offs]] covers in more detail** — fixed-size chunking's mid-word cuts are a visible symptom of the same underlying problem.
* **[[Semantic and Structure-Aware Chunking]] goes a step further than recursive chunking** — splitting by meaning or document structure instead of just sentence boundaries.
* **A broken chunk still gets embedded and indexed ([[Bi-Encoders and Dense Embeddings]])** — whatever damage happens at chunking time propagates into every later stage of the pipeline.

## Common pitfalls

* **Assuming fixed-size chunking is "good enough" because it's simple.** The worked example shows it breaks 80% of its own boundaries mid-word on ordinary prose — the simplicity comes at a real, measurable cost.
* **Assuming recursive chunking guarantees every chunk fits the target size exactly.** It prioritizes not splitting a sentence over hitting the size limit precisely — a sentence longer than the target still becomes its own, oversized chunk.
* **Applying character-based chunk sizes to text in a language where character count doesn't track token count well.** The same size parameter can mean a very different amount of actual model-visible content depending on the text.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. In the worked example, why does fixed-size chunking break so many of its boundaries mid-word?</summary>
It cuts at a fixed character count with no awareness of where words end — a word that happens to straddle the 40-character mark gets split regardless.
</details>

<details><summary>2. Why does recursive chunking sometimes produce a chunk longer than the target maxSize?</summary>
It refuses to split a sentence in the middle, so when the next sentence would push a chunk over the limit, it still keeps that sentence whole rather than cutting it — prioritizing structural integrity over strict size.
</details>

<details><summary>3. Does recursive chunking eliminate every problem fixed-size chunking has?</summary>
No — it only guarantees chunks don't split sentences; it says nothing about whether a chunk boundary falls at a meaningful change of topic, which is what semantic chunking addresses instead.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Fixed-size chunking:** splitting text at a constant character or token count, regardless of word or sentence boundaries.
* **Recursive chunking:** splitting on structural units (paragraphs, sentences) and packing them up to a size limit without ever cutting one in half.
* **Chunk boundary:** the point where one chunk ends and the next begins.

## Related

[[Parsing Documents for Retrieval]] · [[Chunk Overlap and Size Trade-offs]] · [[Semantic and Structure-Aware Chunking]]

## Semantic and Structure-Aware Chunking

Recursive chunking keeps sentences whole, but a sentence boundary isn't the same thing as a topic boundary — five sentences in a row about the same subject will still get split wherever the size limit happens to land, right through the middle of a coherent idea. Semantic chunking looks at *meaning* instead of character count: it places a boundary exactly where the topic actually shifts.

**You need:** [[Fixed-Size and Recursive Chunking]], [[Embeddings and Similarity Search]].

## The question it answers

"How do you split a document at the points where its meaning actually changes, instead of an arbitrary size limit?" Each sentence gets embedded, and the cosine similarity between consecutive sentences is checked — a high similarity means they're still on the same topic, and a sharp drop marks a real topic shift. A chunk boundary is placed exactly where that drop happens, however long or short the resulting chunks turn out to be. **Structure-aware chunking** uses the same idea at a coarser level, splitting at document structure the author already provided — markdown headings, paragraph breaks — instead of computing similarity at all.

## Intuition

Reading a document and noticing "everything up to here was about returns, and everything after is about shipping" is a judgment about meaning, not a character count. Semantic chunking automates exactly that judgment: it measures how similar each sentence is to the one before it, and calls a sharp drop in similarity the sign of a real topic change.

## Definition and notation

```text
sims[i] = cosine_similarity(sentence_i, sentence_{i+1})
boundary after sentence i   if  sims[i] < threshold
```

## A worked example

Five sentences — two about returns, three about shipping — with their consecutive-sentence similarities:

```text
sentence 0: "Returns are accepted within 30 days."        \ similar (0.998)
sentence 1: "Items must be in original packaging."        /
                                                             ← similarity drops to 0.281
sentence 2: "Shipping takes 3-5 business days."            \
sentence 3: "Orders over $50 ship free."                    | similar (0.998, 0.996)
sentence 4: "Tracking is emailed once shipped."             /

similarities between consecutive sentences: 0.998, 0.281, 0.998, 0.996
→ boundary placed after sentence 1 (the only drop below a 0.5 threshold)
```

Every similarity except one sits above 0.99 — these sentence pairs are clearly on the same topic. The one pair that drops to 0.281 is exactly the pair spanning the actual topic change, from returns to shipping, and that's precisely where the chunk boundary lands.

## Bench

```bench
id: semantic-chunk-boundary
title: A boundary where the topic actually shifts
fallback: Slide a similarity threshold and watch where semantic chunking places its boundary.
```

**Try this**

1. Start with the threshold around 0.5 and note the boundary falls after sentence 1.
2. Lower the threshold toward 0.1 and watch the boundary disappear — 0.281 no longer counts as a "drop."
3. Raise the threshold above 0.99 and watch every gap start to look like a boundary.

**What you should notice:** the threshold has to sit meaningfully below the "same topic" similarity (≈0.99 here) and above the "topic shift" similarity (0.281) for the boundary to land in the one place that actually reflects a real change in subject.

## Where it appears in AI

* **The similarity computation itself is exactly [[Embeddings and Similarity Search|cosine similarity]]**, already covered on the Math planet — this topic is about using it to decide *where* to cut, not re-deriving the metric.
* **Structure-aware chunking is the cheaper, no-embedding alternative**: splitting at a document's own markdown headings or paragraph breaks instead of computing sentence-by-sentence similarity.
* **A badly placed threshold produces the same symptom as naive fixed-size chunking** ([[Fixed-Size and Recursive Chunking]]) — a chunk that straddles two unrelated topics, diluting whatever gets embedded from it.

## Common pitfalls

* **Picking a threshold without checking what "same topic" and "different topic" actually look like in your own data.** The worked example's 0.99-vs-0.28 gap is unusually clean; real text often has a narrower gap, making the threshold choice far more sensitive.
* **Assuming semantic chunking always beats recursive chunking.** It costs an embedding call per sentence just to decide where to cut — for short, already-well-structured documents, that cost may not be worth the improvement.
* **Treating a similarity drop as proof of a *meaningful* topic change, rather than just *a* change.** A drop can also come from a stylistic shift, a quoted aside, or noisy sentence embeddings, not only a genuine subject change.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. In the worked example, why does the similarity between sentence 1 and sentence 2 drop so much more than any other consecutive pair?</summary>
Sentences 0 and 1 are both about returns, and sentences 2 through 4 are all about shipping — sentence 1 and sentence 2 are the only consecutive pair that actually straddles the topic change, so their embeddings are far less similar than any same-topic pair.
</details>

<details><summary>2. What happens to the detected boundary if the similarity threshold is set to 0.1, below the real topic-shift value of 0.281?</summary>
No pair would fall below 0.1, so no boundary would be detected at all — the chunker would treat the whole passage as one chunk, missing the real topic change.
</details>

<details><summary>3. How does structure-aware chunking avoid the cost of computing sentence embeddings just to find a boundary?</summary>
It uses structure the document's author already provided — headings, paragraph breaks — as a proxy for topic boundaries, skipping the similarity computation entirely.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Semantic chunking:** placing chunk boundaries where consecutive sentences' embedding similarity drops, rather than at a fixed size.
* **Structure-aware chunking:** splitting at a document's own structural markers (headings, paragraphs) instead of computing similarity.
* **Similarity threshold:** the cutoff below which two consecutive sentences are considered different enough to warrant a chunk boundary.

## Related

[[Fixed-Size and Recursive Chunking]] · [[Embeddings and Similarity Search]] · [[Chunk Overlap and Size Trade-offs]]

## Chunk Overlap and Size Trade-offs

A fact that happens to straddle a chunk boundary disappears — split in half across two chunks, it may be incomplete in both and never score high enough against a query to be retrieved. Overlap, repeating a few characters at the end of one chunk at the start of the next, can rescue a split fact, but every character of overlap is a character stored and embedded twice.

**You need:** [[Fixed-Size and Recursive Chunking]].

## The question it answers

"How much should consecutive chunks overlap, and what does more overlap actually cost?" With zero overlap, a fact that falls across a chunk boundary is split and may never appear whole in any single chunk. Increasing overlap raises the odds that such a fact lands intact in at least one chunk — but every overlapping character is stored, embedded, and indexed in both chunks, so total redundancy grows directly with overlap.

## Definition and notation

```text
chunk starts: 0, (size − overlap), 2·(size − overlap), ...
redundancy = (total characters across all chunks − document length) / document length
```

## A worked example

A 40-character chunk size, with the phrase "original payment method" (23 characters) sitting right across a chunk boundary at zero overlap:

```text
overlap  0:   6 chunks, 0.0% redundancy,  "original payment method" intact: no
overlap 10:   7 chunks, 29.6% redundancy, "original payment method" intact: no
overlap 20:  11 chunks, 90.1% redundancy, "original payment method" intact: yes
```

At overlap 0 and even at overlap 10, the phrase never lands whole inside a single chunk — it keeps falling across whatever boundary happens to be nearby. Only at overlap 20 (half the chunk size) does it finally land intact in some chunk — at the cost of storing and embedding nearly double the document's actual length.

## Bench

```bench
id: chunk-overlap-tradeoff
title: Rescuing a split fact costs redundant tokens
fallback: Slide chunk overlap and watch a boundary-straddling fact get rescued, at a redundancy cost.
```

**Try this**

1. Start at overlap 0 and confirm the fact is split across chunks.
2. Move to overlap 10 and notice the fact is *still* split — more overlap doesn't guarantee rescue at every step.
3. Move to overlap 20 and watch both the fact become intact and the redundancy spike to 90%.

**What you should notice:** going from "fact split" to "fact intact" isn't a smooth, continuous improvement as overlap rises — it happens at whatever overlap value finally shifts a chunk boundary past the fact's own span, and that threshold can require a surprisingly large overlap relative to the chunk size.

## Where it appears in AI

* **This is the quantitative version of the problem [[Fixed-Size and Recursive Chunking]] shows qualitatively** — a split fact is exactly what a broken chunk boundary produces.
* **Every redundant character here is also a redundant embedding and a redundant index entry** ([[Vector Databases and Index Management]]) — overlap's storage cost isn't just document size, it's indexing cost too.
* **[[Multi-Hop and Iterative Retrieval]] is sometimes a better fix for the same underlying problem**: instead of widening overlap to try to capture a whole fact in one chunk, retrieve multiple related chunks and let generation assemble the fact from them.

## Common pitfalls

* **Assuming more overlap always helps, proportionally.** The worked example shows the fact stays split at both 0% and a meaningfully increased 10-character overlap — the benefit only shows up once overlap crosses a specific threshold tied to where the fact actually falls.
* **Treating overlap as free.** 90% redundancy at overlap 20 means the index is storing and searching through almost twice the actual content — a real cost in storage and retrieval latency, not just a parameter to tune upward by default.
* **Picking a chunk size and overlap once and never revisiting them.** Different document types (dense technical specs vs. conversational FAQs) have very different "typical fact length," which changes what overlap is actually needed.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. In the worked example, why does overlap 10 fail to rescue the fact even though it's larger than overlap 0?</summary>
Increasing overlap shifts where chunk boundaries fall, but it doesn't guarantee a boundary shifts past the exact span of any particular fact — at overlap 10, the boundary still happens to land inside the fact's span.
</details>

<details><summary>2. What's the real cost of raising overlap from 0 to 20 characters in the worked example?</summary>
Redundancy jumps from 0% to 90.1% — nearly double the document's actual content is now duplicated across chunk boundaries, all of which gets stored, embedded and indexed.
</details>

<details><summary>3. Is there a chunk size and overlap combination that guarantees no fact is ever split?</summary>
Not in general — any fixed chunk size can still split a fact longer than the chunk itself, and overlap only helps once it's large enough relative to the specific fact's length and position, which varies fact to fact.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Overlap:** the number of characters (or tokens) repeated between the end of one chunk and the start of the next.
* **Redundancy:** the fraction of total stored characters that are duplicates caused by overlap.
* **Boundary-straddling fact:** a piece of information that falls across where a chunk boundary happens to land, risking being split and lost.

## Related

[[Fixed-Size and Recursive Chunking]] · [[Semantic and Structure-Aware Chunking]] · [[Multi-Hop and Iterative Retrieval]]

## Metadata Extraction and Enrichment

A chunk's text alone often can't say whether it's still true. Three versions of the same shipping policy, written almost identically, differ only in when each one was published — information the chunk's own words don't carry at all. Metadata (a date, a source, a section) attaches exactly that extra context, so a retrieval system can filter on it without re-reading the text.

**You need:** [[Semantic and Structure-Aware Chunking]].

## The question it answers

"What has to be attached to a chunk beyond its own text?" Metadata is structured information about a chunk that isn't part of its searchable content but is essential for deciding whether to use it: the document it came from, the date it was last updated, its section or author, access permissions. Without it, near-duplicate chunks that differ only in currency are indistinguishable to similarity search alone — a retrieval system can rank them all equally relevant and return a stale one right alongside the current one.

## Intuition

Three near-identical memos about an office policy, stapled together with no dates on any of them, are useless for figuring out which one is actually still in effect — the memos read almost the same. Stamp each one with its date, and suddenly "which one is current" becomes a one-line filter instead of a judgment call.

## Definition and notation

```text
freshnessFilter(chunks, cutoffDate) = chunks with date ≥ cutoffDate, most recent first
```

## A worked example

Three near-duplicate chunks about the same shipping policy, differing only in date:

```text
[2022-01-01] "Shipping takes 3-5 days."
[2023-06-01] "Shipping takes 3-5 days."
[2025-09-01] "Shipping takes 2-3 days."

unfiltered top-3 (similarity search alone can't distinguish them): all 3 returned
freshness-filtered (date ≥ 2024-01-01): only [2025-09-01] "Shipping takes 2-3 days."
```

All three chunks are about equally similar to a query like "how long does shipping take" — their text is nearly identical. Without a date filter, a retrieval system has no reason to prefer the current policy over the two outdated ones it happens to also find. With the date attached as metadata, the two stale chunks are excluded before similarity ever comes into play.

## Bench

```bench
id: metadata-freshness-filter
title: Three near-duplicates, only one still true
fallback: Toggle a freshness filter and watch stale duplicate chunks disappear from the results.
```

**Try this**

1. Look at the unfiltered results and notice all three near-identical chunks are returned.
2. Turn on the freshness filter and watch it keep only the most recent one.
3. Imagine a user's answer coming from the 2022 chunk instead of the 2025 one — what would be wrong with it?

**What you should notice:** the three chunks' text alone gives a similarity-based retriever no reason to prefer one over another — the date metadata is what makes "prefer the current one" possible at all.

## Where it appears in AI

* **[[Metadata Filtering and Hybrid Indexes]] covers how a vector database actually executes a metadata filter alongside a similarity search**, combining both into one query.
* **This is a second, independent fix for the staleness problem [[Hallucination and Knowledge Cutoff]] describes at the model level** — here the staleness lives in the document collection itself, not in the model's training data.
* **[[Common RAG Failure Modes]] lists "retrieved the wrong (stale) version of a fact" as one of the recurring ways a RAG system fails** — exactly what this topic's metadata filter prevents.

## Common pitfalls

* **Assuming similarity search alone will prefer the most relevant version.** The worked example shows near-duplicate chunks can score almost identically regardless of which one is actually current — similarity measures topical closeness, not correctness or recency.
* **Extracting metadata inconsistently across a document collection.** A freshness filter is only as reliable as every chunk actually having an accurate date attached — a few chunks missing it undermines the whole mechanism.
* **Filtering so aggressively that relevant older content disappears entirely.** Not every older chunk is wrong — a cutoff needs to reflect when the information in question actually changed, not an arbitrary recency preference.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. In the worked example, why can't cosine similarity alone distinguish the three chunks?</summary>
Their text is nearly identical (two have the exact same wording), so their embeddings are extremely close together — the signal that would distinguish "current" from "outdated" isn't present in the text at all, only in each chunk's date metadata.
</details>

<details><summary>2. What's required for a freshness filter to work reliably across a whole document collection?</summary>
Accurate, consistently extracted date metadata on every chunk — a filter can only exclude what it can correctly identify as stale, so any chunk missing or carrying wrong date metadata silently escapes the filter.
</details>

<details><summary>3. Is a freshness cutoff always the right kind of metadata filter?</summary>
No — recency is just one example; the same mechanism applies to filtering by source, access permission, or section, whatever dimension actually distinguishes which chunks should be eligible for a given query.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Metadata:** structured information about a chunk (date, source, section, permissions) kept separate from its searchable text.
* **Near-duplicate chunks:** chunks with very similar or identical text that differ in some attribute, such as when they were last updated.
* **Freshness filter:** a metadata-based filter that excludes chunks older than a given cutoff date.

## Related

[[Semantic and Structure-Aware Chunking]] · [[Metadata Filtering and Hybrid Indexes]] · [[Hallucination and Knowledge Cutoff]]

## Handling Tables, Code and Structured Content

Flattening a pricing table into one run-on paragraph destroys the one thing that made it useful — knowing which number went with which row. The same chunking advice that works for prose (split by sentence, by topic) actively damages content whose meaning *is* its structure.

**You need:** [[Metadata Extraction and Enrichment]].

## The question it answers

"How should chunking change for content that isn't ordinary prose?" A table's rows, a function's source code, a form's fields all carry meaning in their *structure*, not just their words. Flattening a table into a single paragraph averages its rows together into something that barely resembles any one of them — a query about one specific row ends up matching a vague blur of the whole table instead of the row it's actually asking about.

## Intuition

Reading a spreadsheet aloud as one continuous sentence — "Basic plan nine dollars per month Pro plan forty nine dollars per month Enterprise plan contact sales" — makes it much harder to pick out "how much is the Pro plan" than just pointing at the Pro plan's own row. The information didn't change; the structure that made it easy to use did.

## Definition and notation

```text
flattened:       whole table → one chunk, one embedding, structure lost
row-preserved:    each row (or logical unit) → its own chunk, structure kept
```

## A worked example

A query about one specific row of a pricing table ("what is the price of the Pro plan"), compared against two chunking choices for the same table:

```text
query vector:            [0.90, 0.10, 0.00]
flattened table vector:  [0.30, 0.30, 0.30]   (the whole table averaged into one blob)
row-preserved vector:    [0.88, 0.08, 0.02]   (just "Pro plan: $49/mo" kept as its own chunk)

similarity to flattened table:   0.6376
similarity to row-preserved row: 0.9995
```

Keeping the Pro plan's row as its own chunk scores more than 36 percentage points higher on cosine similarity than the same information buried inside the whole table flattened into prose. The flattened version's embedding sits roughly equidistant from every row's topic, since it's an average of all of them — it's not strongly "about" any one row, including the one the query actually needs.

## Bench

```bench
id: structured-content-similarity
title: A table loses its structure when it's flattened
fallback: Compare a query against a table flattened into prose versus the same table's rows kept separate.
```

**Try this**

1. Check the flattened table's similarity score against the query.
2. Switch to the row-preserved chunk and compare.
3. Imagine a table with 20 rows instead of 3 — would flattening get better or worse as rows are added?

**What you should notice:** a flattened table's embedding dilutes as more unrelated rows get folded into it — the more rows a table has, the worse a flattened chunk's embedding represents any single one of them.

## Where it appears in AI

* **This is a specific instance of the same cost [[Fixed-Size and Recursive Chunking]] and [[Semantic and Structure-Aware Chunking]] cover more generally**: a chunk boundary (or lack of one) that ignores the content's own structure degrades what gets retrieved.
* **[[Retrieval over Structured Data]] goes a step further**, querying a table or database directly instead of retrieving pre-chunked rows at all.
* **Code has the same problem as tables**: a function split mid-body, or flattened together with unrelated functions, loses the structural boundary (a function definition) that should have driven chunking in the first place.

## Common pitfalls

* **Applying prose-chunking rules (sentence boundaries, paragraph breaks) to a table or a code file.** Neither has sentences in the relevant sense — a table's unit is a row; code's unit is a function, class, or block.
* **Flattening structured content "to keep it simple," then being surprised retrieval performs badly on it.** The worked example's gap (0.64 vs. 1.00) shows this isn't a minor quality loss — it can be the difference between retrieving the right row and retrieving nothing useful at all.
* **Preserving structure but losing the surrounding context a row needs to make sense.** A row like "$49/mo" without "Pro plan" and "per month" attached is structurally preserved but semantically incomplete — structure-aware chunking still needs to keep enough context in each chunk to stand alone.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. In the worked example, why does the flattened table's embedding score so much lower against a row-specific query?</summary>
The flattened table's embedding is effectively an average over every row's content, so it isn't strongly aligned with any single row's topic — including the Pro plan row the query actually needs.
</details>

<details><summary>2. Would flattening a 2-row table cause the same problem as flattening a 20-row table?</summary>
To a lesser degree — averaging over fewer, more similar rows dilutes less than averaging over many varied ones, but the underlying problem (losing which content belongs to which row) is the same regardless of table size.
</details>

<details><summary>3. What's the right chunking unit for source code, by the same logic that applies to table rows?</summary>
A function, class or logical block — the structural unit that code's own syntax already defines, analogous to a table's row.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Structured content:** content whose meaning depends on an explicit structure (tables, code, forms) rather than flowing prose.
* **Flattening:** converting structured content into unstructured prose, discarding the structure in the process.
* **Row-preserved chunking:** keeping each structural unit (a table row, a function) as its own chunk.

## Related

[[Metadata Extraction and Enrichment]] · [[Retrieval over Structured Data]] · [[Fixed-Size and Recursive Chunking]]

## Embeddings for Retrieval

Turning a chunk of text into a vector is already covered on the Math planet; this district is about the retrieval-specific engineering on top of that: which kind of model produces the vector, how to make it accurate for a narrow domain, and how to shrink it without losing what makes search work.

Topics on this stretch of the road:

* [[Bi-Encoders and Dense Embeddings]]: encoding queries and documents separately so they can be compared by a single vector each.
* [[Cross-Encoders and Re-Rankers]]: scoring a query and a document together, for accuracy a bi-encoder can't match.
* [[Domain-Adapting Embedding Models]]: fine-tuning a general-purpose embedding model for a specific collection.
* [[Multi-Vector and Late-Interaction Retrieval]]: representing a document as many vectors instead of one.
* [[Embedding Quantization for Retrieval]]: shrinking embeddings to fit a large index in memory.

## Bi-Encoders and Dense Embeddings

Embedding a query and comparing it to embedded documents is a cosine-similarity problem, already covered on the Math planet. A **bi-encoder** is the specific choice of encoding the query and each document *independently*, so every document's vector can be computed once, stored, and reused across every future query — the whole reason retrieval over millions of documents can be fast at all.

**You need:** [[Embeddings and Similarity Search]], [[Anatomy of a RAG Pipeline]].

## The question it answers

"Why does retrieval scale to huge collections when comparing a query to every document directly wouldn't?" A bi-encoder passes the query through an encoder and each document through the *same* encoder, separately — "bi" for the two independent passes. Because documents never need to be re-encoded once a query arrives, their vectors can be computed ahead of time, indexed, and compared against any future query with nothing more expensive than a dot product.

## Intuition

Looking up a word in a dictionary works because every entry was alphabetized once, in advance — finding "retrieval" doesn't require re-sorting the whole dictionary for every lookup. A bi-encoder's precomputed document vectors are the same idea: the expensive part (encoding) happens once per document, forever, and every query only pays the cheap part (one encode, then fast comparisons).

## Definition and notation

```text
doc_vec  = encode(document)        -- computed once, stored
query_vec = encode(query)          -- computed per query
score(query, doc) = cosine_similarity(query_vec, doc_vec)
```

## A worked example

One query against three precomputed document vectors, ranked by cosine similarity:

```text
query: "how long do refunds take" → [0.90, 0.10]

"refund timeline"   [0.95, 0.05]  →  similarity 0.9983
"returns policy"     [0.85, 0.15]  →  similarity 0.9980
"shipping times"     [0.30, 0.20]  →  similarity 0.8882
```

The compute cost tells the real story: with a 1,000-document collection, a bi-encoder spends roughly 1 query encode plus 1,000 cheap dot products (about 1,001 cost units). A cross-encoder, which must jointly process the query with *each* document from scratch, spends roughly 1,000 full forward passes — each far more expensive than a dot product, totaling around 100,000 cost units in this illustration. The gap only widens as the collection grows.

## Bench

```bench
id: bi-encoder-ranking
title: Precompute the documents once, compare cheaply forever
fallback: Rank documents by bi-encoder cosine similarity and compare the per-query compute cost against a cross-encoder's.
```

**Try this**

1. Look at the ranking — it's the same cosine-similarity computation from the Math planet, applied to retrieval.
2. Slide the collection size up and watch the cost gap between bi-encoder and cross-encoder widen.
3. Imagine a collection of a million documents — would re-encoding every one of them for every query still be feasible?

**What you should notice:** the bi-encoder's cost grows roughly linearly with collection size, driven by cheap dot products; a cross-encoder's cost grows the same way but driven by expensive joint forward passes — the same shape of growth, at a vastly different constant factor.

## Where it appears in AI

* **[[Vector Databases and Index Management]] exists specifically to store and search the precomputed document vectors a bi-encoder produces.**
* **[[Cross-Encoders and Re-Rankers]] covers the more accurate, more expensive alternative** that a bi-encoder's speed makes practical to apply only to a short, already-narrowed shortlist.
* **Multi-vector retrieval ([[Multi-Vector and Late-Interaction Retrieval]]) is a middle ground**: still precomputed like a bi-encoder, but keeping several vectors per document instead of pooling into one.

## Common pitfalls

* **Assuming a bi-encoder's precomputed vectors mean zero cost per query.** Encoding the query itself still has a real cost — the savings come from not having to re-encode every *document* for every query.
* **Expecting bi-encoder similarity to always match true relevance exactly.** Encoding the query and document independently is what makes precomputation possible, but it can miss fine-grained interactions a joint encoding would catch — the trade-off [[Cross-Encoders and Re-Rankers]] covers next.
* **Forgetting that document vectors need re-computing if the embedding model changes.** A bi-encoder's speed advantage assumes the stored vectors and any new query vector come from the same model — swapping models means re-indexing the whole collection.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. Why can a bi-encoder's document vectors be computed once and reused for every future query?</summary>
Because the query and document are encoded independently — a document's vector doesn't depend on what query will eventually be compared against it, so it never needs to be recomputed.
</details>

<details><summary>2. In the worked example, why does the cross-encoder's cost grow so much faster than the bi-encoder's as the collection size increases?</summary>
Both costs scale linearly with collection size, but the cross-encoder's per-document cost (a full joint forward pass) is far larger than the bi-encoder's (a single dot product against an already-computed vector), so the same linear growth reaches a much larger total.
</details>

<details><summary>3. What has to happen to a collection's stored vectors if the embedding model used to produce them is replaced?</summary>
Every document has to be re-encoded and re-indexed with the new model — a bi-encoder's stored vectors are only comparable to queries encoded by that same model.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Bi-encoder:** an encoder applied independently to the query and to each document, enabling document vectors to be precomputed.
* **Dense embedding:** a vector representation (as opposed to a sparse, word-count-based one) produced by an encoder like a bi-encoder.
* **Precomputation:** computing and storing document vectors once, ahead of any specific query.

## Related

[[Cross-Encoders and Re-Rankers]] · [[Vector Databases and Index Management]] · [[Dense Retrieval]]

## Cross-Encoders and Re-Rankers

A bi-encoder's speed comes from encoding the query and a document separately — which means it can never let fine details of one influence how the other gets represented. A cross-encoder gives that up: it feeds the query and a document into the model *together*, letting every word of each attend to every word of the other, at the cost of having to do that fresh for every single pair.

**You need:** [[Bi-Encoders and Dense Embeddings]].

## The question it answers

"When does a bi-encoder's ranking get something wrong that a more careful look would catch?" A document that happens to repeat a query's own words can score a high bi-encoder similarity without actually answering the question — its pooled vector looks close to the query's, even though the content is off-topic. A **cross-encoder** jointly processes the query and that document and outputs a single relevance score, catching exactly this kind of mismatch that two independently pooled vectors can miss. Because a cross-encoder has to run once per candidate pair, it's typically used as a **re-ranker**: applied only to the short list a cheap bi-encoder already narrowed down, not the whole collection.

## Intuition

Judging how well two people would get along by comparing each one's résumé independently misses the chemistry that only shows up once they're actually talking to each other. A cross-encoder is the conversation: it looks at the query and the document together, not two separate summaries of each.

## Definition and notation

```text
bi-encoder score(query, doc)    = cosine_similarity(encode(query), encode(doc))     -- independent
cross-encoder score(query, doc) = model(query ⊕ doc) → single relevance score       -- joint
```

## A worked example

Two candidates for the query "how long do refunds take":

```text
A: repeats "refund" twice but is actually off-topic
B: on-topic, but phrased without reusing the query's exact words

bi-encoder ranking (independent cosine similarity):   A 1.000  >  B 0.989
cross-encoder ranking (joint relevance score):         B 0.950  >  A 0.300
```

The bi-encoder ranks A above B — A's surface-level word overlap with the query pulls its pooled vector closer, even though it's off-topic. The cross-encoder, scoring the pair jointly, correctly flips the ranking: B is far more relevant (0.950) and A is recognized as mostly irrelevant (0.300) despite sharing vocabulary with the query.

## Bench

```bench
id: cross-encoder-rerank
title: Scoring the pair together catches what pooling misses
fallback: Compare a bi-encoder's independent-vector ranking against a cross-encoder's joint-scored ranking for the same two candidates.
```

**Try this**

1. Look at the bi-encoder ranking and note which candidate wins.
2. Switch to the cross-encoder ranking and watch the winner flip.
3. Read both candidates' descriptions again — which one would you actually want cited in an answer?

**What you should notice:** the bi-encoder's error isn't a small numerical wobble — it ranks the wrong candidate first by a comfortable margin (1.000 vs. 0.989), while the cross-encoder's joint view corrects it decisively (0.950 vs. 0.300).

## Where it appears in AI

* **This is exactly why [[Re-Ranking Retrieved Results]] exists as a separate stage**: run a cheap bi-encoder over the whole collection to get a shortlist, then run an expensive cross-encoder only over that shortlist.
* **The compute-cost argument from [[Bi-Encoders and Dense Embeddings]] is what makes re-ranking, rather than cross-encoding everything, the practical choice.**
* **[[Multi-Vector and Late-Interaction Retrieval]] sits between these two extremes**: still precomputable like a bi-encoder, but closer to a cross-encoder's sensitivity to specific token-level matches.

## Common pitfalls

* **Running a cross-encoder over an entire large collection "to be safe."** The whole reason bi-encoders exist is that this doesn't scale — a cross-encoder's cost per query grows with collection size the same way a cross-encoder's score itself does, just much more expensively.
* **Assuming a cross-encoder is always right and a bi-encoder is always wrong.** The worked example is a case specifically designed to expose the bi-encoder's blind spot; on many queries the two methods agree closely.
* **Skipping the bi-encoder stage and going straight to cross-encoding "for accuracy."** Without a bi-encoder's cheap first pass to narrow the field, there's no shortlist small enough for a cross-encoder's cost to be affordable.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. Why does candidate A score so highly under the bi-encoder but so poorly under the cross-encoder?</summary>
A's pooled embedding ends up close to the query's because it repeats the query's own words, even though its actual content is off-topic — the cross-encoder, processing the pair jointly, can detect that the surface overlap doesn't correspond to real relevance.
</details>

<details><summary>2. Why is a cross-encoder typically applied only to a shortlist rather than an entire collection?</summary>
Its cost scales with the number of query-document pairs it has to jointly process, and that cost per pair is far higher than a bi-encoder's — applying it to a whole large collection would be far too expensive for most systems.
</details>

<details><summary>3. What's lost by encoding the query and document independently, as a bi-encoder does?</summary>
Any fine-grained interaction between specific parts of the query and specific parts of the document — a bi-encoder's two separate, pooled vectors can't capture the kind of mismatch the worked example's candidate A represents.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Cross-encoder:** a model that jointly processes a query and a document together to produce a single relevance score.
* **Re-ranker:** a (typically cross-encoder) model applied to a short list of already-retrieved candidates to reorder them more accurately.
* **Joint encoding:** processing two inputs together, allowing interactions between them, as opposed to encoding each independently.

## Related

[[Bi-Encoders and Dense Embeddings]] · [[Re-Ranking Retrieved Results]] · [[Multi-Vector and Late-Interaction Retrieval]]

## Domain-Adapting Embedding Models

A general-purpose embedding model learned its sense of "similar" from broad, general text — which means it can genuinely confuse two meanings of the same term if one of them is specific to a domain it rarely saw. "MI" means something very different in a hospital's charts than it does on a map, and a model never shown much medical text has no strong reason to know which sense a query intends.

**You need:** [[Bi-Encoders and Dense Embeddings]], [[Continued Pretraining and Domain Adaptation]].

## The question it answers

"What happens when an embedding model's general-purpose training doesn't match the vocabulary of the collection it's searching?" A term with a rare, specialized meaning (like a medical abbreviation) sits ambiguously in a general-purpose model's embedding space — it may even end up closer to the *wrong*, more common sense. Fine-tuning the embedding model on in-domain text (pairs of medical queries and medical passages, for instance) pulls the ambiguous term's embedding toward the sense that actually matters for that domain's documents.

## Intuition

Someone who's only ever heard "MI" used to mean the state of Michigan will naturally read a new mention of "MI" that way too, unless they spend time specifically immersed in contexts (a hospital, a cardiology textbook) where it means something else entirely. Domain adaptation is that immersion, applied to an embedding model.

## Definition and notation

```text
general-purpose:  similarity("MI", medical sense) and similarity("MI", geographic sense) are close,
                  with no strong training signal for which sense a medical query intends
domain-adapted:   fine-tuned on in-domain (query, relevant passage) pairs, pulling "MI" toward
                  the domain's own dominant sense
```

## A worked example

A query containing the ambiguous term "MI", checked against embeddings for its two senses under both models:

```text
general-purpose model:
  similarity to medical sense:      0.9806
  similarity to geographic sense:   0.9950   ← actually scores HIGHER for the wrong sense

domain-adapted model (fine-tuned on medical text):
  similarity to medical sense:      0.9997
  similarity to geographic sense:   0.2195
```

The general-purpose model doesn't just fail to clearly prefer the medical sense — it scores the *wrong* sense slightly higher. After domain adaptation, the gap flips decisively: the medical sense scores almost perfectly (0.9997) while the geographic sense drops far below it (0.2195).

## Bench

```bench
id: domain-adapted-embedding
title: The same two letters, two very different meanings
fallback: Compare a general-purpose embedding's sense confusion against a domain-adapted one's clean separation.
```

**Try this**

1. Look at the general-purpose model's two similarity scores — notice how close they are, and which one is actually higher.
2. Switch to the domain-adapted model and watch the gap open up decisively in the correct direction.
3. Think of another term that means something completely different inside a specific domain (legal, financial, medical) than it does in everyday language.

**What you should notice:** domain adaptation doesn't just sharpen an existing correct preference — in this worked example, it actually *reverses* a general-purpose model's wrong preference.

## Where it appears in AI

* **This reuses the exact fine-tuning mechanism already covered as [[Continued Pretraining and Domain Adaptation]] on the LLMs planet**, applied here specifically to embedding models rather than generation models.
* **A domain-adapted embedding model is still a bi-encoder ([[Bi-Encoders and Dense Embeddings]])** — adaptation changes what the model has learned to consider similar, not the architecture itself.
* **Getting this wrong directly causes the kind of retrieval failure [[Common RAG Failure Modes]] catalogs**: confidently retrieving a document about the wrong sense of an ambiguous term.

## Common pitfalls

* **Assuming a general-purpose embedding model is "good enough" for any domain.** The worked example shows it can actively prefer the wrong sense of an ambiguous term, not just fail to prefer the right one.
* **Fine-tuning on too little in-domain data to shift the embedding space meaningfully.** Domain adaptation needs enough representative (query, relevant passage) pairs to actually move the ambiguous term's embedding, not just a handful of examples.
* **Over-adapting to one narrow sub-domain and losing general capability.** A model fine-tuned exclusively on cardiology text may develop new blind spots for other medical sub-specialties it saw less of.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. In the worked example, why is the general-purpose model's result more concerning than simply "uncertain"?</summary>
It doesn't just fail to distinguish the two senses — it actually scores the wrong (geographic) sense higher than the right (medical) one, meaning a retrieval system built on it would be actively more likely to retrieve the wrong document.
</details>

<details><summary>2. What kind of training data is needed to domain-adapt an embedding model for this term?</summary>
In-domain (query, relevant passage) pairs — in this case, medical queries paired with the medical passages they should retrieve — so the model learns that in this domain's context, "MI" belongs with the medical sense.
</details>

<details><summary>3. Does domain adaptation change the embedding model's architecture?</summary>
No — it's still a bi-encoder producing dense vectors the same way; adaptation changes what the model has learned to consider similar, via further training on in-domain data.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Domain adaptation:** fine-tuning a general-purpose model on data from a specific domain so it better reflects that domain's vocabulary and conventions.
* **Sense ambiguity:** a term having multiple distinct meanings, with the correct one depending on context or domain.
* **In-domain training pairs:** (query, relevant passage) examples drawn from the specific domain a model is being adapted to.

## Related

[[Bi-Encoders and Dense Embeddings]] · [[Continued Pretraining and Domain Adaptation]] · [[Common RAG Failure Modes]]

## Multi-Vector and Late-Interaction Retrieval

Pooling every token of a document into one vector means a single, strong, exact match can get diluted by everything else in the document — the more unrelated text surrounds it, the weaker its signal looks in the average. Late-interaction retrieval skips the pooling: it keeps one vector per token, and lets the single best match win, no matter how much else is around it.

**You need:** [[Bi-Encoders and Dense Embeddings]], [[Cross-Encoders and Re-Rankers]].

## The question it answers

"Is there a way to get some of a cross-encoder's precision without giving up a bi-encoder's precomputability?" **Multi-vector retrieval** (the ColBERT-style approach) keeps a separate embedding for every token in a document instead of pooling them into one — and because each token vector is still produced independently of the query, they can still be precomputed and stored, just like a bi-encoder's. At query time, **late interaction** scores a document by taking, for each query token, its single best-matching document token (MaxSim), then summing those best-matches across all query tokens.

## Intuition

Judging whether a single paragraph buried inside a long report answers your question by averaging a "relevance score" across the entire report dilutes that one paragraph's strength proportionally to how long the report is. Instead, scanning specifically for the best-matching sentence for each part of your question — and ignoring how much irrelevant text surrounds it — finds the signal regardless of the surrounding noise.

## Definition and notation

```text
MaxSim(query_tokens, doc_tokens) = Σ_q  max_d  cosine_similarity(q, d)
pooled(query_tokens, doc_tokens) = cosine_similarity(mean(query_tokens), mean(doc_tokens))
```

## A worked example

A 2-token query ("refund", "timeline") against a document containing one strongly matching token, with a varying number of unrelated tokens padded in around it:

```text
0 unrelated tokens:  MaxSim 1.580  pooled 0.914
7 unrelated tokens:  MaxSim 1.983  pooled 0.714
```

As unrelated tokens pile up around the one genuinely matching token, the pooled single-vector score drops by about 22% (0.914 → 0.714) — the average gets diluted by everything irrelevant. The MaxSim score doesn't degrade the same way, because it only ever looks at each query token's single *best* match, which the added unrelated tokens can't weaken.

## Bench

```bench
id: multi-vector-maxsim
title: A strong match survives being buried; a pooled average doesn't
fallback: Compare late-interaction MaxSim scoring against single-vector pooled scoring as unrelated document tokens pile up.
```

**Try this**

1. Start at 0 unrelated tokens and note both scores.
2. Slide toward 7 unrelated tokens and watch the pooled score fall while MaxSim holds up.
3. Imagine a 500-word document with just one sentence that answers the question — which scoring method would find it more reliably?

**What you should notice:** pooling is a bottleneck — however strong one token's match is, it has to survive being averaged with every other token in the document; MaxSim never averages anything away.

## Where it appears in AI

* **This sits between [[Bi-Encoders and Dense Embeddings]] (one precomputed vector, cheap but coarser) and [[Cross-Encoders and Re-Rankers]] (no precomputation, finer but expensive)** — multi-vector keeps the precomputability of the first while recovering some of the token-level sensitivity of the second.
* **Storing many vectors per document instead of one is exactly why [[Embedding Quantization for Retrieval]] matters more here** — multi-vector indexes are naturally larger, making compression more valuable.
* **[[Vector Databases and Index Management]] needs specific support for late-interaction scoring**, since it isn't a simple nearest-neighbor lookup against a single vector per document.

## Common pitfalls

* **Assuming multi-vector retrieval is strictly better and should always be used.** It stores and searches many more vectors per document than a bi-encoder, at real memory and compute cost — the worked example's accuracy gain isn't free.
* **Treating MaxSim as equivalent to a cross-encoder.** It's still composed of independently precomputed token vectors with no joint processing — it recovers some token-level precision, not full cross-encoder-level interaction.
* **Forgetting that MaxSim's robustness to distractor tokens isn't unlimited.** It holds up well against unrelated padding, but a document genuinely lacking any strong match for a query token will still score poorly, as it should.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. Why does the pooled single-vector score drop as unrelated tokens are added, while MaxSim doesn't drop the same way?</summary>
Pooling averages every token's vector together, so more unrelated tokens dilute the one strong match's contribution to the average; MaxSim only ever takes each query token's single best match, which stays just as strong regardless of how many weaker tokens are also present.
</details>

<details><summary>2. Can multi-vector document representations still be precomputed ahead of a query, like a bi-encoder's?</summary>
Yes — each document's token vectors are produced independently of any future query, so they can be computed once and stored, the same precomputation advantage a bi-encoder has.
</details>

<details><summary>3. What's the main cost of multi-vector retrieval compared to a single pooled vector per document?</summary>
Storing and searching many vectors per document instead of one, which increases both memory use and the complexity of the index needed to search them efficiently.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Multi-vector retrieval:** representing a document as multiple token-level embeddings instead of one pooled vector.
* **Late interaction:** comparing query and document representations at the token level at query time, after both were encoded independently.
* **MaxSim:** scoring by summing, for each query token, its single highest similarity to any document token.

## Related

[[Bi-Encoders and Dense Embeddings]] · [[Cross-Encoders and Re-Rankers]] · [[Embedding Quantization for Retrieval]]

## Embedding Quantization for Retrieval

A million documents, each with a 768-dimensional embedding stored as 32-bit floats, is already several gigabytes before any text itself is stored. Quantization shrinks every number in every vector down to a much smaller representation — trading a small amount of precision for a large, direct cut in memory.

**You need:** [[Bi-Encoders and Dense Embeddings]].

## The question it answers

"How much can an embedding be shrunk before it stops being useful for retrieval?" Quantization rounds each float32 value in a vector down to a much coarser representation — commonly int8, one byte instead of four — scaled so the rounding error stays small relative to the vector's own range. The question is whether that rounding changes which documents a query would retrieve, not just how much space the vectors take up.

## Intuition

Rounding a set of prices to the nearest dollar instead of keeping every cent barely changes which item is cheapest when prices differ by many dollars — it only risks confusion between items priced within a few cents of each other. Quantizing an embedding is the same trade: coarser numbers, with very little risk of changing the *ranking* unless two candidates were already nearly tied.

## Definition and notation

```text
scale = max(|vector|) / 127
quantized[i]   = round(vector[i] / scale)        -- an integer from −127 to 127
dequantized[i] = quantized[i] × scale            -- back to a float, at reduced precision
```

Four bytes per dimension (float32) become one byte per dimension (int8): a 4× reduction in memory for the vectors themselves.

## A worked example

One embedding, quantized to int8 and converted back to check the precision lost:

```text
original:      [0.9500, 0.0500]
quantized:     [127, 7]            (integers, one byte each)
dequantized:   [0.9500, 0.0524]
similarity between original and dequantized: 0.999997
```

Quantizing and reconstructing this vector changes its cosine similarity to itself by only about 0.0003% — nearly indistinguishable. Checking the same three-document ranking from earlier topics confirms it: the ranking order (refund timeline, returns policy, shipping times) comes out identical whether the document vectors are stored at full float32 precision or quantized to int8.

## Bench

```bench
id: embedding-quantization
title: Four bytes per number, or one
fallback: Quantize an embedding to int8 and compare its similarity and ranking against the original float32 version.
```

**Try this**

1. Compare the float32 and int8 rankings — they come out in the same order.
2. Check the memory figure for each precision level.
3. Imagine a collection of 10 million documents — what does a 4× memory reduction actually mean at that scale?

**What you should notice:** the ranking the query cares about survives quantization intact in this example, while the memory footprint drops to a quarter — a trade that's nearly free when the vectors being compared aren't extremely close to each other to begin with.

## Where it appears in AI

* **Multi-vector retrieval ([[Multi-Vector and Late-Interaction Retrieval]]) stores many more vectors per document**, which is exactly where quantization's memory savings matter most.
* **[[Vector Databases and Index Management]] often applies quantization as one of its built-in storage options**, alongside the index structure itself.
* **[[Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search with IVF and Product Quantization]] takes this idea further**, using quantization not just to save memory but as part of the search algorithm itself.

## Common pitfalls

* **Assuming quantization is always this safe.** The worked example's three documents aren't nearly tied — quantization is far more likely to change a ranking when two candidates' true similarities are extremely close to begin with.
* **Quantizing without checking the actual retrieval quality impact on real queries.** A similarity-preservation check on one vector, as in the worked example, is reassuring but not a guarantee across an entire collection and query distribution.
* **Confusing quantization with dimensionality reduction.** Quantization keeps every dimension but represents each one more coarsely; it doesn't reduce how many numbers make up the vector.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. In the worked example, why does quantizing to int8 barely change the vector's similarity to its own original version?</summary>
The quantization scale is chosen relative to the vector's own maximum absolute value, so the rounding error introduced at each dimension is small relative to the vector's overall magnitude — the reconstructed vector stays very close to the original.
</details>

<details><summary>2. When would quantization be more likely to change a retrieval ranking?</summary>
When two or more candidates' true similarities to the query are extremely close — quantization's small rounding errors are more likely to flip the order of near-ties than they are to change a ranking where the gaps are already large.
</details>

<details><summary>3. Does quantization reduce how many dimensions a vector has?</summary>
No — it keeps the same number of dimensions but stores each one with less precision (fewer bits), which is different from dimensionality reduction, which drops dimensions entirely.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Quantization:** representing each value in a vector with fewer bits, trading precision for reduced memory.
* **int8:** an 8-bit (1-byte) integer representation, commonly used as a quantization target for embeddings originally stored as 32-bit floats.
* **Scale factor:** the value used to convert between a quantized integer and its original floating-point range.

## Related

[[Bi-Encoders and Dense Embeddings]] · [[Multi-Vector and Late-Interaction Retrieval]] · [[Vector Databases and Index Management]]

## Vector Search and Indexing

Once a collection has a few million chunks, each with its own embedding, finding the handful nearest to a query vector stops being a problem you can solve by checking every single one. This district is about the data structures and systems that make that search fast at scale.

Topics on this stretch of the road:

* [[Exact Nearest Neighbor Search]]: finding the true closest vectors, and why it stops being affordable.
* [[Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search with HNSW]]: searching a graph of vectors instead of the whole collection.
* [[Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search with IVF and Product Quantization]]: narrowing the search first, then compressing what's left.
* [[Vector Databases and Index Management]]: what a vector database actually manages beyond the index structure itself.
* [[Metadata Filtering and Hybrid Indexes]]: combining a vector search with exact filters on other fields.

## Exact Nearest Neighbor Search

Finding the true closest vectors to a query is conceptually the simplest possible search: compute the similarity between the query and every single vector in the collection, then keep the highest-scoring ones. It's also the first thing that stops being affordable as a collection grows into the millions.

**You need:** [[Bi-Encoders and Dense Embeddings]].

## The question it answers

"What does it cost to guarantee you've found the actual closest vectors, with no approximation?" Exact nearest neighbor search compares the query against every vector in the collection — a linear scan. It's correct by construction (there's no way to miss the true top-k, since every candidate was checked), but its cost scales directly with collection size: twice as many vectors means twice as many comparisons, for every single query.

## Intuition

Finding the best-matching paint sample by holding your target up against every single can in the store, one at a time, guarantees you'll find the exact best match — but it's a process whose time cost scales directly with how many cans the store has, and a warehouse with a million cans makes that guarantee very expensive to keep.

## Definition and notation

```text
cost(exact search) = N comparisons, where N is the collection size
```

## A worked example

The number of comparisons needed for one exact query, at three collection sizes:

```text
N =         1,000   →         1,000 comparisons
N =     1,000,000   →     1,000,000 comparisons
N =   100,000,000   →   100,000,000 comparisons
```

The cost is exactly linear: a 100,000× larger collection means exactly 100,000× more comparisons for every single query — there's no shortcut built into exact search that changes this relationship.

## Bench

```bench
id: exact-nn-cost
title: Checking every single vector, every single query
fallback: Slide collection size and watch exact nearest-neighbor search's comparison count grow with it.
```

**Try this**

1. Slide from 1,000 up to 10,000,000 and watch the comparison count grow in exact proportion.
2. Imagine this cost paid for every single query your system receives, not just once.
3. Consider a system serving 1,000 queries per second against a 10-million-vector collection — what does that multiply out to?

**What you should notice:** there's nothing to tune here — the cost is a direct, unavoidable consequence of checking every vector, which is exactly why approximate methods exist for any collection large enough to matter.

## Where it appears in AI

* **[[Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search with HNSW]] and [[Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search with IVF and Product Quantization]] both exist specifically to avoid this linear cost**, at the price of no longer guaranteeing the exact true nearest neighbors.
* **A bi-encoder's precomputed document vectors ([[Bi-Encoders and Dense Embeddings]]) are what makes even exact search computationally simple at all** — the expensive part (encoding) already happened; what's left is comparison, not encoding.
* **Small collections (a few thousand documents) often don't need approximation at all** — exact search's guarantee is worth keeping whenever its linear cost is still cheap enough in absolute terms.

## Common pitfalls

* **Assuming exact search is always "too slow" and reaching for approximation prematurely.** For collections small enough that linear scanning is still fast in absolute terms, the simplicity and guaranteed correctness of exact search can be the better choice.
* **Forgetting that the comparison cost is paid per query, not once.** A collection that's expensive to search exactly stays expensive for every subsequent query, not just the first one.
* **Conflating "exact" with "fast."** Exact search is exact by definition — correctness, not speed, is what it guarantees; speed is exactly what it gives up as the collection grows.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. Why does exact nearest neighbor search's cost scale exactly linearly with collection size?</summary>
Because it compares the query against every single vector in the collection with no shortcuts — doubling the collection means doubling the number of comparisons needed to check them all.
</details>

<details><summary>2. Does exact search ever return the wrong top-k result?</summary>
No — because every vector in the collection is checked, it's guaranteed to find the true nearest neighbors; its trade-off is cost, not correctness.
</details>

<details><summary>3. At what point does exact search's linear cost become a practical problem?</summary>
Once the collection size and query volume grow large enough that the total number of comparisons (collection size × queries per second) exceeds what the available hardware can keep up with — exactly when approximate methods become worth the trade-off.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Exact nearest neighbor search:** finding the true closest vectors to a query by comparing against every vector in the collection.
* **Linear scan:** checking every item in a collection one by one, with cost proportional to collection size.
* **Approximation trade-off:** accepting a small risk of missing the true closest results in exchange for a large reduction in search cost.

## Related

[[Bi-Encoders and Dense Embeddings]] · [[Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search with HNSW]] · [[Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search with IVF and Product Quantization]]

## Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search with HNSW

Instead of checking every vector in a collection, HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World) searches a graph where each vector is linked to a handful of its nearest neighbors, plus a few longer-range shortcuts. Starting somewhere and repeatedly hopping to whichever linked neighbor is closer to the query reaches a good answer after checking only a small fraction of the graph.

**You need:** [[Exact Nearest Neighbor Search]].

## The question it answers

"How can a search avoid checking every vector while still usually finding the right one?" A graph where every node links to its nearest neighbors lets a **greedy search** start anywhere, repeatedly move to whichever unvisited linked neighbor is closest to the query, and stop once no neighbor is any closer. Most of the graph never gets touched — only the handful of nodes actually visited along the path. A few long-range links (the "small world" part) are what let the search jump between distant regions of the graph quickly, instead of only crawling locally.

## Intuition

Finding a specific house in an unfamiliar city by asking a local for directions, then asking someone closer each time you get nearer, reaches the destination without ever having to check every house in the city — a handful of well-chosen conversations get you there, as long as each conversation points you reliably closer.

## Definition and notation

```text
greedy_search(query, start):
  current = start
  loop:
    look at current's unvisited linked neighbors
    move to whichever one is closest to the query
    stop once no neighbor is closer than where you already are
```

## A worked example

A graph of 15 points, searched for the one closest to a query at [0.95, 0.90]:

```text
brute-force (exact): checks all 15 points → finds the true nearest, "N", at distance 0

greedy graph search, starting from a distant node "A":
  path: A → H → N
  comparisons made: 8 (vs. 15 for brute force)
  found: "N", distance 0 — the exact same answer, for roughly half the comparisons
```

The greedy search follows two hops along pre-built links — one short link within its starting neighborhood, then a long-range shortcut straight toward the query's region — and lands on the true nearest neighbor after only 8 comparisons instead of checking all 15 points.

## Bench

```bench
id: hnsw-greedy-search
title: A shortcut path instead of checking everyone
fallback: Step a greedy graph search toward a query and compare its comparison count against brute force.
```

**Try this**

1. Step through the search path and watch the distance to the query shrink at each hop.
2. Compare the final comparison count against the number of points in the graph.
3. Imagine this same graph with a million points instead of 15 — would the greedy search's path length grow the same way brute force's cost does?

**What you should notice:** the search doesn't need to get lucky to reach the right answer here — the long-range shortcut link is exactly what lets it cross most of the way to the query's region in a single hop, instead of crawling node by node.

## Where it appears in AI

* **This directly trades [[Exact Nearest Neighbor Search]]'s guarantee for speed** — greedy graph search is not guaranteed to always find the true nearest neighbor; without a well-placed long-range link, it can get stuck in the wrong neighborhood entirely.
* **[[Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search with IVF and Product Quantization]] solves the same problem with a different data structure** (partitioning into clusters instead of a navigable graph) — both trade exactness for speed, differently.
* **[[Vector Databases and Index Management]] typically offers HNSW as one of several index types to choose from**, alongside IVF and others, depending on the collection's size and update patterns.

## Common pitfalls

* **Assuming greedy graph search always finds the true nearest neighbor.** It's an *approximate* method — a graph without enough long-range links can leave the search stranded in the wrong region, finding a decent-but-not-optimal answer, or occasionally a poor one.
* **Building a graph with only short-range links, expecting it to work like this worked example's shortcut-equipped one.** The long-range links are what make the "small world" property work; a purely local graph degenerates toward the kind of local-optimum trap exact search doesn't have to worry about.
* **Treating "fewer comparisons" as automatically "faster in wall-clock time."** Graph traversal has its own overhead (following pointers, maintaining a visited set) that a simple, cache-friendly linear scan doesn't — the comparison-count savings has to be large enough to outweigh that overhead.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. In the worked example, what specifically let the greedy search reach the correct answer in only 8 comparisons?</summary>
A long-range shortcut link connecting node "A" (in a distant region of the graph) directly toward node "H" and then "N" (near the query), letting the search cross most of the distance in two hops instead of crawling through every intermediate node.
</details>

<details><summary>2. Is greedy graph search guaranteed to find the true nearest neighbor on every query?</summary>
No — it's an approximate method; without the right long-range links positioned well relative to a given query, it can get stuck in the wrong local neighborhood and settle on a worse answer.
</details>

<details><summary>3. What's the "small world" idea that makes HNSW's long-range links useful?</summary>
A small number of well-placed long-range connections let a search jump between distant regions of the graph quickly, dramatically shortening the path between any two points compared to a graph with only local, nearest-neighbor links.
</details>

## Key terms

* **HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World):** an approximate nearest-neighbor method based on greedy search over a graph of linked vectors.
* **Greedy search:** repeatedly moving to whichever linked neighbor is closest to the query, stopping once no neighbor improves on the current position.
* **Long-range link:** a graph edge connecting distant regions, letting a search cross large distances in a single hop.

## Related

[[Exact Nearest Neighbor Search]] · [[Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search with IVF and Product Quantization]] · [[Vector Databases and Index Management]]

## Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search with IVF and Product Quantization

Rather than navigating a graph one hop at a time, IVF (inverted file index) takes a different shortcut: group every vector into a cluster ahead of time, and at query time, only search inside the one or few clusters closest to the query — skipping every vector that was never a realistic candidate in the first place.

**You need:** [[Exact Nearest Neighbor Search]], [[Embedding Quantization for Retrieval]].

## The question it answers

"How can clustering avoid searching the whole collection, and what does compressing each cluster add on top of that?" **IVF** partitions a collection into clusters (via k-means or similar), each with a centroid. A query only needs to be compared against the vectors inside whichever cluster's centroid is closest to it — every other cluster is skipped entirely. **Product quantization** (PQ) compresses the vectors *within* each cluster, the same idea as [[Embedding Quantization for Retrieval|embedding quantization]] applied specifically to shrink what IVF has to scan through once it's narrowed down to a cluster.

## Intuition

Looking for a book in a library organized into sections (fiction, history, science) means only browsing one section, not the whole building — IVF's clustering is exactly that sectioning, applied to vectors instead of books. Product quantization is then shrinking each book down to a thinner summary, so browsing that one section goes even faster.

## Definition and notation

```text
cluster(vector)       = nearest centroid, by distance
search(query)         = find query's nearest centroid, then search only vectors in that cluster
```

## A worked example

Eight vectors assigned to three clusters by nearest centroid, then a query searched against only its own cluster:

```text
cluster A (centroid [0.123, 0.133]): a1, a2, a3
cluster B (centroid [0.823, 0.823]): b1, b2, b3
cluster C (centroid [0.125, 0.81]):  c1, c2

query [0.82, 0.84] → nearest centroid: cluster B
→ search only b1, b2, b3 (3 of 8 vectors) instead of all 8
```

The query only ever needs to be compared against the 3 vectors in cluster B — the 5 vectors in clusters A and C are skipped entirely, because their centroids are far enough from the query that nothing inside them could plausibly be the nearest neighbor.

## Bench

```bench
id: ivf-cluster-search
title: Narrow the search to one neighborhood first
fallback: Assign vectors to clusters and search only the query's nearest cluster instead of the whole collection.
```

**Try this**

1. Note which cluster the query falls into and how many vectors get searched.
2. Slide the query toward a different region and watch both the assigned cluster and the searched count change.
3. Imagine a query that falls almost exactly between two clusters — what risk does searching only one cluster introduce?

**What you should notice:** the number of vectors actually compared depends only on the size of the query's own cluster, not on the total collection size — the other clusters' sizes don't matter at all once they're ruled out.

## Where it appears in AI

* **This reuses the same compression idea as [[Embedding Quantization for Retrieval]]**, applied to shrink the vectors inside each cluster rather than the whole collection uniformly.
* **IVF offers a different speed/approximation trade-off than [[Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search with HNSW]]'s graph traversal** — both skip most of the collection, by different mechanisms (clustering vs. graph navigation).
* **[[Vector Databases and Index Management]] typically supports IVF as a configurable index type**, often tunable by how many clusters to search (not just the single nearest one), trading more search time for better recall.

## Common pitfalls

* **Searching only the single nearest cluster when a query falls near a cluster boundary.** A query sitting almost equidistant between two centroids risks having its true nearest neighbor in the *other* cluster — many real IVF systems search several nearby clusters, not just one, to reduce this risk.
* **Assuming cluster sizes are always balanced.** A poorly chosen number of clusters, or naturally uneven data, can leave one cluster far larger than the others, undermining the speedup for queries that land there.
* **Forgetting that cluster assignments need updating as new vectors are added.** A new document's embedding has to be assigned to a cluster at insert time — an index that never rebalances its clusters can drift out of sync with the data's actual distribution.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. In the worked example, why are clusters A and C skipped entirely for this particular query?</summary>
Their centroids are far from the query's position, so nothing inside them is a realistic candidate for the nearest neighbor — only cluster B's centroid is close enough to be worth searching.
</details>

<details><summary>2. What risk does searching only the single nearest cluster introduce?</summary>
A query that falls near the boundary between two clusters might have its true nearest neighbor sitting just inside the *other* cluster, which would be missed entirely if only one cluster is searched.
</details>

<details><summary>3. What does product quantization add on top of IVF's clustering?</summary>
It compresses the vectors within each cluster (the same idea as embedding quantization), so that once IVF has narrowed the search to one cluster, scanning through that cluster's vectors is also faster and uses less memory.
</details>

## Key terms

* **IVF (inverted file index):** an index that clusters vectors ahead of time and searches only the clusters nearest a query.
* **Centroid:** the representative center point of a cluster, used to decide which cluster a query or vector belongs to.
* **Product quantization:** compressing vectors within a cluster to speed up and shrink the memory of searching inside it.

## Related

[[Exact Nearest Neighbor Search]] · [[Embedding Quantization for Retrieval]] · [[Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search with HNSW]]

## Vector Databases and Index Management

An ANN algorithm like HNSW or IVF answers one question well: given a query, which vectors are closest? A real RAG system needs a lot more than that — vectors that can be added and removed as documents change, an index that survives a restart, filtering by metadata, and all of it available to more than one machine at once. That's the gap between a bare search algorithm and a vector database.

**You need:** [[Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search with HNSW]], [[Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search with IVF and Product Quantization]].

## The question it answers

"What does a production system need beyond just an ANN search algorithm?" A bare ANN library is typically built once over a fixed set of vectors and optimized purely for query speed. A vector database wraps that same underlying search algorithm with everything needed to run it as a living system: inserting, updating and deleting vectors after the index already exists; persisting the index so it survives a restart; filtering by metadata alongside similarity; and replicating across machines for availability and scale.

## Intuition
