A sorted phone book is a great index for looking up a name — until someone moves, a number changes, or the book needs printing again next year. A phone *company*, as opposed to a single printed book, handles all of that: updates, storage, and keeping multiple copies in sync. A vector database is the company; a bare ANN library is the one printed book.

## Definition and notation

```text
bare ANN library:    optimized to answer "nearest to this query?" over a fixed set of vectors
vector database:      ANN search + inserts/updates/deletes + persistence + metadata filtering + replication
```

## A worked example

Five capabilities, checked against each kind of system:

```text
capability                                          bare ANN library   vector database
compute nearest neighbors for a query                     ✓                  ✓
insert/update/delete vectors after the index is built      ✗                  ✓
persist the index to disk and reload it                    ✗                  ✓
filter by metadata alongside similarity                     ✗                  ✓
replicate across multiple machines                          ✗                  ✓
```

A bare ANN library handles exactly 1 of these 5 capabilities — the core search itself. Everything a real, continuously updated RAG system also needs is the vector database's job, not the search algorithm's.

## Bench

```bench
id: vector-db-capabilities
title: An index structure is only part of the job
fallback: Compare what a bare ANN library handles against what a full vector database adds on top.
```

**Try this**

1. Switch to "bare ANN library" and note how few capabilities are checked.
2. Switch to "vector database" and see every capability covered.
3. Imagine a document collection that changes daily — which of these capabilities would that requirement make non-negotiable?

**What you should notice:** the ANN algorithm (HNSW, IVF, whichever one) is just one row out of five — most of what a production system actually needs from "the vector store" isn't about search speed at all.

## Where it appears in AI

* **A vector database typically lets you choose which ANN algorithm to use underneath** ([[Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search with HNSW]] or [[Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search with IVF and Product Quantization]]) — the database is the wrapper, not a replacement for either.
* **[[Metadata Filtering and Hybrid Indexes]] is specifically about how the "filter by metadata" row actually gets executed alongside similarity search.**
* **[[Caching and Incremental Indexing]] covers the operational side of the "insert/update/delete" row** — how an index actually stays current as a document collection changes continuously, not just in a one-time rebuild.

## Common pitfalls

* **Assuming any ANN library can be dropped directly into production.** The worked example shows it covers only the search itself — a real system also needs updates, persistence, filtering and availability, none of which come free with a search algorithm alone.
* **Rebuilding the entire index from scratch every time a document changes.** Production vector databases are built specifically to support incremental updates, rather than full rebuilds, for exactly this reason.
* **Choosing a vector database by its ANN algorithm alone.** Two vector databases offering the same underlying algorithm can differ enormously in update support, filtering flexibility, and operational maturity — the algorithm is only one of the five rows.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. In the worked example, what's the one capability a bare ANN library and a vector database both handle?</summary>
Computing nearest neighbors for a query — the core search operation itself.
</details>

<details><summary>2. Why can't a bare ANN library typically handle inserting a new vector after the index is already built?</summary>
Many ANN index structures (especially graph- or cluster-based ones) are optimized for query speed assuming a fixed set of vectors; adding to them efficiently without degrading search quality or requiring a full rebuild is a separate engineering problem a vector database is built to solve.
</details>

<details><summary>3. Why does metadata filtering belong to the vector database layer rather than the ANN algorithm itself?</summary>
The ANN algorithm's job is purely to find vectors close to a query; deciding which of those candidates also satisfy a separate condition (a date range, a permission check) is an additional layer of logic the database adds on top.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Vector database:** a system that wraps an ANN search algorithm with insert/update/delete support, persistence, metadata filtering and replication.
* **Index persistence:** storing a built index to disk so it survives a restart without being rebuilt from scratch.
* **Replication:** maintaining copies of an index across multiple machines for availability and scale.

## Related

[[Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search with HNSW]] · [[Metadata Filtering and Hybrid Indexes]] · [[Caching and Incremental Indexing]]

## Metadata Filtering and Hybrid Indexes

Asking for "the 20 most relevant chunks, but only from documents I have permission to see" sounds like one request — but a vector index has to decide *when* to apply that permission check. Do it after finding the top 20 by similarity, and most of them might belong to documents the user can't see at all, leaving almost nothing behind. Do it first, and the search never wastes effort on candidates that were never eligible.

**You need:** [[Vector Databases and Index Management]], [[Metadata Extraction and Enrichment]].

## The question it answers

"Should a metadata filter be applied before or after the similarity search?" **Post-filtering** runs the ANN search first, gets its top-k by similarity, and only then checks each result against the metadata filter — if the filter and similarity are unrelated to each other, most of the top-k can fail the filter, leaving far fewer usable results than requested. **Pre-filtering** applies the metadata filter first, narrowing the collection down to only eligible candidates, and only then searches for the nearest ones among *those* — guaranteeing the requested number of results, as long as enough eligible candidates exist at all.

## Intuition

Asking a restaurant for "the best vegetarian dish on the menu" by first picking the ten best-reviewed dishes overall and only then checking which ones happen to be vegetarian might leave you with one option, if none of the top ten happen to be vegetarian. Asking by first filtering to just the vegetarian dishes, then ranking only those by review score, reliably gets you a real top choice.

## Definition and notation

```text
post-filter:  top-k by similarity  →  then apply metadata filter  →  survivors ≈ k × match_rate
pre-filter:   apply metadata filter first  →  then rank by similarity within survivors  →  up to k results
```

## A worked example

Requesting the top 20 results from a 1,000-chunk collection where only 5% match a metadata filter (say, a permission check):

```text
post-filter: ANN returns its top 20 by similarity (ignoring the filter),
             then filters → only 1 of the 20 survives

pre-filter:  filter first → 50 eligible chunks (5% of 1,000),
             then rank by similarity within those → up to 20 returned
```

Post-filtering a 5%-match-rate filter against the top 20 leaves, on average, only about 1 usable result — nineteen out of twenty requested results get discarded. Pre-filtering guarantees up to the full 20, limited only by how many eligible chunks actually exist in the collection.

## Bench

```bench
id: prefilter-vs-postfilter
title: Filtering after search can come back nearly empty
fallback: Compare how many results actually survive when a metadata filter is applied before vs. after an ANN search.
```

**Try this**

1. Slide the match rate down toward 1% and watch post-filtering's survivor count collapse.
2. Slide it up toward 50% and watch the gap between the two approaches shrink.
3. Think about a permission filter that only 2% of a collection satisfies for a given user — what would post-filtering return for a request of "give me 20 results"?

**What you should notice:** pre-filtering's advantage is largest exactly when the filter is most restrictive — which is often exactly when getting it right matters most (strict permission checks, narrow date ranges).

## Where it appears in AI

* **This directly extends the freshness-filtering problem from [[Metadata Extraction and Enrichment]]** — the same metadata that lets you *identify* a stale chunk also needs to be applied at the right point in the search to actually exclude it reliably.
* **A hybrid index is what makes efficient pre-filtering possible**: combining a metadata index (fast to check "is this eligible?") with the vector index (fast to check "is this similar?") so pre-filtering doesn't itself become a slow linear scan.
* **[[Common RAG Failure Modes]] lists "returned far fewer results than requested" as a recognizable symptom** — frequently traceable to post-filtering against a restrictive metadata condition.

## Common pitfalls

* **Defaulting to post-filtering because it's simpler to implement on top of an existing ANN index.** The worked example shows this can silently return far fewer usable results than requested, with no error raised — just a quietly short result list.
* **Assuming pre-filtering is always better.** A very restrictive filter still needs enough eligible candidates in the collection in the first place — pre-filtering can't conjure up results that don't exist, it only avoids wasting effort on ineligible ones.
* **Building a metadata index as an afterthought, bolted onto an existing vector index.** Efficient pre-filtering depends on the metadata filter itself being fast to check — a slow metadata lookup undermines the whole point of filtering before the (potentially even more expensive) similarity search.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. In the worked example, why does post-filtering a request for 20 results at a 5% match rate leave only about 1 survivor?</summary>
The ANN search's top 20 were chosen purely by similarity, with no regard for the filter, so only roughly 5% of them — about 1 — happen to also satisfy it; the rest are discarded after the fact.
</details>

<details><summary>2. Does pre-filtering guarantee the requested number of results no matter how restrictive the filter is?</summary>
No — it guarantees up to the requested number, limited by how many eligible candidates actually exist in the collection; an extremely restrictive filter can still leave fewer than requested if there simply aren't enough matching chunks.
</details>

<details><summary>3. What does a hybrid index add that makes pre-filtering practical?</summary>
A fast way to check metadata eligibility combined with the vector index, so narrowing to eligible candidates before the similarity search doesn't itself require a slow scan of the whole collection.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Post-filtering:** applying a metadata filter after an ANN search has already produced its top-k results by similarity.
* **Pre-filtering:** applying a metadata filter before similarity search, ranking only among already-eligible candidates.
* **Hybrid index:** an index combining metadata filtering with vector similarity search, supporting efficient pre-filtering.

## Related

[[Vector Databases and Index Management]] · [[Metadata Extraction and Enrichment]] · [[Common RAG Failure Modes]]

## Retrieval Strategies

Having a fast index doesn't yet say what to search it with. This district covers the different ways of turning a user's question into something retrievable, and how to combine them when any single strategy misses too much.

Topics on this stretch of the road:

* [[Sparse Retrieval with TF-IDF and BM25]]: ranking by matching words, still a strong baseline.
* [[Dense Retrieval]]: ranking by embedding similarity instead of word overlap.
* [[Hybrid Retrieval Fusion]]: combining sparse and dense rankings into one.
* [[Query Expansion and Rewriting]]: improving a query before it's ever searched.
* [[Hypothetical Document Embeddings (HyDE)]]: searching with a guessed answer instead of the question itself.
* [[Multi-Hop and Iterative Retrieval]]: when one search isn't enough to answer the question.

## Sparse Retrieval with TF-IDF and BM25

Counting how many query words a document shares is the simplest possible retrieval method — and it treats every word as equally informative, which "the" and "cat" obviously aren't. TF-IDF and BM25 are two ways of weighting term matches so that rare, distinctive words count for more than common ones, and each has its own particular way of doing that weighting.

**You need:** [[Anatomy of a RAG Pipeline]].

## The question it answers

"How do you rank documents by matching words, without treating every word equally?" **TF-IDF** scores a term by how often it appears in a document (term frequency) multiplied by how rare it is across the whole collection (inverse document frequency) — a term appearing in every document contributes nothing, since it can't distinguish one document from another. **BM25** computes a similar idea but with two refinements: its term-frequency contribution saturates rather than growing without bound, and its idf formula is smoothed so it never degenerates to exactly zero the way TF-IDF's can.

## Intuition

Scoring how well a résumé matches a job posting by counting shared words treats "and" the same as the one specific skill that actually matters. Down-weighting common words and up-weighting rare, specific ones is the whole idea — TF-IDF and BM25 are just two different formulas for doing that weighting.

## Definition and notation

```text
tf-idf(term, doc)  = count(term, doc) × log(N / (1 + doc_count(term)))
bm25(term, doc)    = idf(term) × count(term, doc) × (k1 + 1) / (count(term, doc) + k1 × length_norm)
```

## A worked example

Three tiny documents, scored against the query "cat mat":

```text
d1: "the cat sat on the mat"    (contains both "cat" and "mat")
d2: "the dog sat on the log"    (contains neither)
d3: "a mat for yoga practice"   (contains "mat" only)

raw word overlap:  d1: 2   d2: 0   d3: 1

TF-IDF:  d1: 0.4055   d2: 0.0000   d3: 0.0000
BM25:    d1: 1.4134   d2: 0.0000   d3: 0.4963
```

"Mat" appears in exactly 2 of these 3 documents, which happens to make TF-IDF's idf formula evaluate to exactly zero for it (log(3/3) = 0) — so TF-IDF gives d3 *no* credit at all for containing "mat," indistinguishable from d2's zero overlap. BM25's smoothed idf formula never hits exactly zero this way, correctly giving d3 partial credit (0.4963) for the one term it does share.

## Bench

```bench
id: sparse-tfidf-bm25
title: Weighting matters: raw overlap isn't the only option
fallback: Compare raw word-overlap, TF-IDF and BM25 scores for the same query across a tiny corpus.
```

**Try this**

1. Switch between raw overlap, TF-IDF and BM25 and watch d3's score change.
2. Notice TF-IDF scores d2 (no overlap) and d3 (one shared word) identically — both zero.
3. Confirm BM25 is the only method that distinguishes d2 from d3.

**What you should notice:** TF-IDF's idf formula can land on exactly zero for a term that appears in close to half the collection, silently erasing any credit for documents containing that term — a real, specific edge case BM25's smoothing is designed to avoid.

## Where it appears in AI

* **[[Dense Retrieval]] solves a different problem these methods can't**: a query and a relevant document that share no vocabulary at all score zero under both TF-IDF and BM25, regardless of how well-weighted the terms are.
* **[[Hybrid Retrieval Fusion]] combines a sparse method like BM25 with dense retrieval**, so exact-term-matching strength and semantic-matching strength both contribute to the final ranking.
* **[[Query Expansion and Rewriting]] is one way to work around sparse retrieval's exact-vocabulary requirement** without switching to dense retrieval at all.

## Common pitfalls

* **Assuming TF-IDF and BM25 are interchangeable.** The worked example shows a real, specific case where they disagree — not just by degree, but by TF-IDF giving literally zero credit where BM25 gives meaningful partial credit.
* **Expecting sparse retrieval to handle synonyms or paraphrasing.** Both methods match exact tokens — a document about "automobiles" scores zero against a query about "cars" unless the exact word appears.
* **Treating a high TF-IDF or BM25 score as a guarantee of relevance.** Both measure term-matching strength, not whether the document actually answers the question — a document can share rare terms with a query while being about something else entirely.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. In the worked example, why does TF-IDF give d3 a score of exactly zero despite d3 containing "mat"?</summary>
"Mat" appears in 2 of the 3 documents, which makes TF-IDF's idf formula, log(N/(1+document count)), evaluate to log(3/3) = log(1) = 0 — multiplying by this zero idf wipes out any contribution from "mat" regardless of how often it appears.
</details>

<details><summary>2. Why doesn't BM25 have the same problem?</summary>
BM25's idf formula adds smoothing terms (+0.5) that keep it from ever evaluating to exactly zero, so a term appearing in roughly half the collection still contributes some weight rather than none.
</details>

<details><summary>3. Would either TF-IDF or BM25 score a document highly if it discussed the same topic as the query using entirely different words?</summary>
No — both methods only match exact vocabulary overlap; a topically relevant document using no words in common with the query would score zero under either method, which is exactly the gap dense retrieval is designed to fill.
</details>

## Key terms

* **TF-IDF:** a term-weighting scheme combining term frequency and inverse document frequency.
* **BM25:** a smoothed, saturating refinement of TF-IDF widely used as a strong sparse-retrieval baseline.
* **Sparse retrieval:** ranking documents by weighted exact-term overlap with a query, as opposed to embedding-based similarity.

## Related

[[Dense Retrieval]] · [[Hybrid Retrieval Fusion]] · [[Query Expansion and Rewriting]]

## Dense Retrieval

"Automobile repair" and "car maintenance" share not a single word, yet mean almost the same thing. Sparse retrieval, which can only match vocabulary that actually appears in both the query and the document, scores that pair as having nothing in common. Dense retrieval — ranking by embedding similarity rather than word overlap — catches exactly this case.

**You need:** [[Sparse Retrieval with TF-IDF and BM25]], [[Bi-Encoders and Dense Embeddings]].

## The question it answers

"What can embedding-based retrieval catch that exact word matching can't?" Dense retrieval is the retrieval strategy of ranking documents by [[Bi-Encoders and Dense Embeddings|cosine similarity between dense embeddings]], rather than by shared vocabulary. Two pieces of text that use completely different words for the same underlying concept end up with embeddings that are close together, even though a sparse method like TF-IDF or BM25 would see zero overlap and score them as entirely unrelated.

## Intuition

Someone fluent in two languages recognizes "voiture" and "car" as the same thing instantly, even though the words share no letters. Dense retrieval has learned something like that fluency during training — it's measuring closeness in *meaning*, which doesn't require matching surface vocabulary at all.

## Definition and notation

```text
sparse retrieval:  score = weighted exact-term overlap        (zero if no shared words, regardless of meaning)
dense retrieval:   score = cosine_similarity(embed(query), embed(doc))     (measures meaning, not vocabulary)
```

## A worked example

A query and a document with zero shared vocabulary:

```text
query: "automobile repair"
document: "car maintenance and servicing guide"

sparse (word overlap) score: 0 — not a single shared word
dense (cosine similarity) score: 0.9997 — nearly identical embeddings
```

A sparse method scores this pair as having nothing to do with each other. Dense retrieval scores them as almost the same thing, because the embeddings for "automobile repair" and "car maintenance" land in nearly the same place in the embedding space — the two phrases describe the same real-world concept, regardless of which specific words were used to express it.

## Bench

```bench
id: dense-vs-sparse-vocab
title: No shared words, same meaning
fallback: Compare sparse word-overlap scoring against dense cosine similarity for a query with no shared vocabulary with the relevant document.
```

**Try this**

1. Check the sparse score and confirm it finds zero overlap.
2. Switch to dense and see the similarity score near 1.0.
3. Think of another pair of phrases that mean almost the same thing using completely different words.

**What you should notice:** sparse retrieval isn't a worse version of dense retrieval — on this exact example it fails completely (score of zero), not just scores lower; the two methods are catching genuinely different kinds of relevance.

## Where it appears in AI

* **Dense retrieval is exactly what [[Bi-Encoders and Dense Embeddings]] already covers mechanically** — this topic is about using it as a retrieval *strategy*, in contrast with sparse retrieval, not re-deriving the embedding mechanism.
* **[[Hybrid Retrieval Fusion]] exists because dense retrieval isn't a strict upgrade over sparse either** — a query containing a specific product code or exact phrase can be better served by sparse retrieval's exact matching, which dense retrieval's semantic smoothing can sometimes blur.
* **[[Common RAG Failure Modes]] includes "missed an exact-match query" as a known dense-retrieval weakness**, the mirror image of this topic's zero-overlap sparse-retrieval failure.

## Common pitfalls

* **Assuming dense retrieval is simply "better" than sparse retrieval.** The worked example shows a case where sparse retrieval fails outright — but dense retrieval has its own failure modes, particularly with exact identifiers, codes, or rare proper nouns a model may not represent precisely.
* **Expecting dense retrieval's semantic matching to always align with what a user actually wants.** "Close in embedding space" measures general topical or conceptual similarity, which doesn't always coincide with precise relevance to a specific question.
* **Forgetting that dense retrieval's quality depends entirely on the embedding model.** A model poorly suited to a domain (see [[Domain-Adapting Embedding Models]]) can fail to place conceptually similar texts close together at all.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. Why does sparse retrieval score the worked example's query and document as completely unrelated?</summary>
It only counts shared vocabulary, and the query ("automobile repair") and document ("car maintenance and servicing guide") share no words at all, even though they describe the same concept.
</details>

<details><summary>2. What does a cosine similarity of 0.9997 between the query and document embeddings indicate?</summary>
The two pieces of text, despite using entirely different words, were encoded into nearly the same location in the embedding space — the embedding model has captured that they describe the same underlying concept.
</details>

<details><summary>3. Does dense retrieval have failure modes sparse retrieval doesn't?</summary>
Yes — dense retrieval can struggle with exact identifiers, codes, or rare terms the embedding model doesn't represent precisely, which is exactly where sparse retrieval's literal matching tends to do better.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Dense retrieval:** ranking documents by embedding (cosine) similarity to a query, rather than exact vocabulary overlap.
* **Semantic matching:** finding content related in meaning, even without shared surface vocabulary.
* **Vocabulary mismatch:** the gap between how a query and a relevant document happen to express the same idea in different words.

## Related

[[Sparse Retrieval with TF-IDF and BM25]] · [[Hybrid Retrieval Fusion]] · [[Bi-Encoders and Dense Embeddings]]

## Hybrid Retrieval Fusion

Sparse retrieval and dense retrieval fail in different, complementary ways — one misses semantic matches with no shared vocabulary, the other can blur exact matches it should have caught outright. Hybrid fusion runs both and combines their two separate rankings into one, so a candidate only needs to be a top pick for *one* method to make it into the final result.

**You need:** [[Sparse Retrieval with TF-IDF and BM25]], [[Dense Retrieval]].

## The question it answers

"How do you combine a sparse ranking and a dense ranking into one, without one approach's errors sinking an otherwise-good candidate?" **Reciprocal rank fusion (RRF)** doesn't look at either method's raw scores at all — it only uses each candidate's *rank* (1st, 2nd, 3rd...) within each ranking, and sums 1/(k + rank) across all the rankings a candidate appears in. A candidate ranked first by sparse retrieval and second by dense retrieval gets credit from both; it doesn't need to win both rankings to end up near the top of the fused result.

## Intuition

Combining two different critics' top-ten lists for the same set of restaurants by giving credit for how highly each critic ranked each restaurant — rather than averaging their star ratings, which might use entirely different scales — produces a fair combined ranking where a restaurant beloved by either critic alone still ranks well.

## Definition and notation

```text
RRF_score(doc) = Σ_rankings  1 / (k + rank_of(doc, ranking))
```

`k` (commonly 60) softens the effect of exact rank differences near the top.

## A worked example

Three candidates, ranked differently by sparse and dense retrieval:

```text
sparse ranking (exact-term match wins):  A, B, C
dense ranking (semantic match wins):      B, A, C

fused (RRF) scores:
  A: 0.03252
  B: 0.03252
  C: 0.03175
```

A and B end up tied — each was ranked first by one method and second by the other, so each receives the exact same combined credit. Both clearly outrank C, which never ranked better than last in either method. Fusion doesn't require agreement between the two methods; it rewards *either* method's confidence.

## Bench

```bench
id: hybrid-rrf-fusion
title: Either method's top pick survives fusion
fallback: Fuse a sparse ranking and a dense ranking with reciprocal rank fusion and see which candidates survive.
```

**Try this**

1. Look at the default scenario and note A and B tie while C trails behind.
2. Switch to the scenario where C ranks first on both methods instead, and watch C's fused score jump to the top.
3. Imagine a candidate that ranks 2nd on both methods, versus one that ranks 1st on one and last on the other — which would you expect to score higher under RRF?

**What you should notice:** RRF only cares about rank position, not the raw similarity or BM25 scores — a method's confidence (how big the score gap was) doesn't carry over into the fusion, only where each candidate landed in the order.

## Where it appears in AI

* **This is the direct answer to the complementary failure modes shown in [[Sparse Retrieval with TF-IDF and BM25]] and [[Dense Retrieval]]'s own worked examples** — a candidate either method would have missed on its own can still surface if the other method ranks it well.
* **[[Re-Ranking Retrieved Results]] often runs on top of a fused shortlist like this one**, applying a more expensive cross-encoder only to the candidates fusion already judged worth a closer look.
* **Many production RAG systems run hybrid retrieval as their default first stage** ([[Production RAG Pipeline Architecture]]), precisely because neither sparse nor dense retrieval alone reliably covers both kinds of relevance.

## Common pitfalls

* **Assuming fusion requires both methods to agree for a candidate to rank well.** The worked example shows the opposite — A and B each only won one of the two rankings, and both still beat C decisively.
* **Mixing raw similarity scores and BM25 scores directly instead of using rank.** The two methods' raw scores live on completely different, incomparable scales; RRF sidesteps this entirely by only using rank position, never the raw score values.
* **Treating fusion as a fix for a fundamentally broken retrieval method.** Fusion combines two reasonably good rankings into a better one — if one method is consistently bad on a given query, fusion limits but doesn't eliminate the damage.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. In the worked example, why do candidates A and B receive exactly the same fused score?</summary>
A ranks 1st in the sparse ranking and 2nd in the dense ranking; B ranks 2nd in the sparse ranking and 1st in the dense ranking — the sum of 1/(k+rank) across both rankings comes out identical for each.
</details>

<details><summary>2. Does reciprocal rank fusion use each method's raw similarity or BM25 score?</summary>
No — it only uses each candidate's rank position within each ranking, which avoids the problem of trying to directly compare scores on incompatible scales.
</details>

<details><summary>3. If a candidate ranks 2nd on both sparse and dense rankings, would it score higher or lower than one ranked 1st on one and last on the other?</summary>
It depends on the exact numbers, but RRF is specifically designed so that a strong showing on even one ranking can meaningfully boost a candidate — consistent moderate performance and one-sided strong performance can land close together, which is exactly the trade-off the worked example's tie illustrates.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Hybrid retrieval:** combining sparse and dense retrieval into a single ranking.
* **Reciprocal rank fusion (RRF):** a fusion method that combines rankings using each candidate's rank position, not its raw score.
* **Fusion constant (k):** a smoothing parameter in RRF that softens the effect of small rank differences near the top.

## Related

[[Sparse Retrieval with TF-IDF and BM25]] · [[Dense Retrieval]] · [[Re-Ranking Retrieved Results]]

## Query Expansion and Rewriting

Sparse retrieval only ever matches the exact words a query happens to use. Query expansion sidesteps that limitation at the query side, before any retrieval happens at all — add related words the document might actually use, and a query that originally shared nothing with a document can suddenly share several.

**You need:** [[Sparse Retrieval with TF-IDF and BM25]].

## The question it answers

"Can a query be improved before retrieval even runs?" **Query expansion** adds related terms — synonyms, alternate phrasings, related concepts — to a query before it's matched against documents. For sparse retrieval specifically, this directly compensates for the exact-vocabulary matching problem: a query that originally had zero overlap with a relevant document can gain several matching terms once expanded with the right synonyms.

## Intuition

Searching a library catalog for "automobile" and getting nothing, then thinking to also try "car" and "vehicle," is something a person does instinctively when a first search comes up empty. Query expansion automates exactly that instinct, adding likely alternate words before the search even runs once.

## Definition and notation

```text
expand(query) = query's own terms ∪ known synonyms of each term
```

## A worked example

The query "automobile repair" against a document about "car maintenance and servicing":

```text
original query terms:  automobile, repair
expanded query terms:  automobile, repair, car, vehicle, maintenance, fix, servicing

original overlap with document: 0 terms
expanded overlap with document: 3 terms  (car, maintenance, servicing)
```

With no expansion, a sparse retrieval method sees zero shared vocabulary and scores this document as entirely unrelated. After expansion, three of the document's words now match the expanded query — a sparse method would now rank this document as a real candidate, where before it couldn't have been found at all.

## Bench

```bench
id: query-expansion
title: Matching words the query never used
fallback: Toggle query expansion and watch a zero-overlap query gain matching terms against a document.
```

**Try this**

1. Look at the unexpanded query and note zero terms match the document.
2. Turn on expansion and watch three new matches appear.
3. Consider what happens if the synonym list is wrong or too broad — what risk does that introduce?

**What you should notice:** expansion doesn't change the document or the retrieval algorithm at all — it only changes what the query itself contains before matching ever starts.

## Where it appears in AI

* **This directly targets the exact-vocabulary limitation shown in [[Sparse Retrieval with TF-IDF and BM25]]'s worked example** — expansion is one fix for that limitation; switching to [[Dense Retrieval]] entirely is another.
* **[[Hypothetical Document Embeddings (HyDE)]] takes a related but different approach**: instead of adding synonyms, it generates an entire hypothetical answer and searches with that.
* **A poorly chosen synonym can introduce false matches**, which [[Common RAG Failure Modes]] covers as "retrieved an irrelevant document because of over-broad query expansion."

## Common pitfalls

* **Assuming expansion is free.** Every added term is also a term that can accidentally match an irrelevant document — expansion trades some precision for recall, not purely a win.
* **Using a fixed, hand-built synonym list that doesn't generalize.** A synonym dictionary built for one domain may add the wrong associations in another (medical "MI" expanding toward geography-related terms, for instance).
* **Expanding so aggressively that the query drifts away from its original intent.** Each added synonym should still be something a document actually answering the question might plausibly contain.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. In the worked example, why does the original query have zero overlap with the document?</summary>
The query uses "automobile" and "repair," while the document uses "car," "maintenance," and "servicing" — none of the exact words match, even though both describe the same topic.
</details>

<details><summary>2. What's the main risk of adding too many synonyms to a query?</summary>
Each added term can also match documents that aren't actually relevant, trading away some precision in exchange for the added recall — expansion isn't a pure improvement.
</details>

<details><summary>3. Is query expansion useful for dense retrieval the same way it is for sparse retrieval?</summary>
Less so — dense retrieval already captures semantic similarity through embeddings, so it doesn't suffer from the exact-vocabulary-matching problem expansion is specifically designed to fix for sparse methods.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Query expansion:** adding related terms to a query before retrieval, to compensate for exact-vocabulary matching limitations.
* **Synonym:** a word with a similar meaning used to expand a query's matching vocabulary.
* **Precision/recall trade-off:** the cost of expansion — more matching terms can mean more irrelevant matches too.

## Related

[[Sparse Retrieval with TF-IDF and BM25]] · [[Hypothetical Document Embeddings (HyDE)]] · [[Dense Retrieval]]

## Hypothetical Document Embeddings (HyDE)

A short question and the long passage that answers it don't always sit very close together in embedding space — a question is phrased like a question, while the answer is phrased like an answer, and those are different styles of text. HyDE's trick is to skip embedding the question at all: generate a plausible answer first, then embed *that*, since a generated answer's phrasing is naturally much closer to the real answer's phrasing than the bare question ever was.

**You need:** [[Dense Retrieval]].

## The question it answers

"Can retrieval do better than embedding the query exactly as it was asked?" **HyDE (Hypothetical Document Embeddings)** uses a language model to generate a hypothetical answer to the query — not necessarily a correct one, just a plausible one, written in the style of a real passage — and embeds that generated text instead of the bare question. Because the hypothetical answer is phrased more like the documents being searched than the original question was, its embedding tends to land closer to the real, relevant document.

## Intuition

Looking for a specific paragraph in a textbook by first sketching, from memory, roughly what that paragraph probably says, then searching for text that resembles your sketch, works better than searching with the bare question alone — your sketch is already written in the style of an answer, which is exactly the style the real paragraph is written in too.

## Definition and notation

```text
bare query embedding:          embed(question)
HyDE embedding:                embed(generate_hypothetical_answer(question))
```

## A worked example

Comparing both embeddings against the same real, relevant document:

```text
bare question similarity to real document:        0.7962
hypothetical-answer similarity to real document:  0.9997
```

The generated hypothetical answer — plausible, but not necessarily factually correct — lands far closer to the real document's embedding than the bare question did. The hypothetical answer doesn't need to be *true* to help retrieval; it only needs to be phrased like the kind of passage that would actually answer the question, which makes its embedding naturally closer to real passages that do.

## Bench

```bench
id: hyde-retrieval
title: Embedding a guessed answer instead of the question
fallback: Compare a bare query's similarity to a real document against a generated hypothetical answer's similarity.
```

**Try this**

1. Check the bare question's similarity to the real document.
2. Switch to the hypothetical-answer embedding and see the gap close almost entirely.
3. Consider why a *wrong* hypothetical answer could still help retrieval, as long as it's phrased the right way.

**What you should notice:** the improvement doesn't come from the hypothetical answer being correct — it comes from its phrasing matching the style of real documents far better than a bare question's phrasing does.

## Where it appears in AI

* **This reuses [[Dense Retrieval]]'s exact similarity mechanism** — HyDE changes what gets embedded, not how embeddings are compared.
* **It's a generation-time technique, requiring a call to the generating model *before* retrieval even happens** — an extra cost [[Cost and Latency of RAG Systems]] has to account for.
* **[[Query Expansion and Rewriting]] is a cheaper, non-generative alternative aimed at a similar underlying problem** (query phrasing not matching document phrasing), without needing a model call per query.

## Common pitfalls

* **Assuming the hypothetical answer needs to be factually correct.** It doesn't — HyDE works because of phrasing similarity to real documents, not because the generated guess happens to be true.
* **Ignoring the added cost of generating a hypothetical answer before every single retrieval.** Unlike query expansion's cheap synonym lookup, HyDE requires a full generation call per query, adding real latency and cost.
* **Using HyDE on a domain the generating model knows little about.** A hypothetical answer generated with no real domain knowledge may be phrased badly too, losing the advantage this technique depends on.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. In the worked example, why does the hypothetical answer's embedding land closer to the real document than the bare question's does?</summary>
A generated hypothetical answer is phrased like an answer — similar in style to the real passages being searched — while a bare question is phrased like a question, a different style that happens to sit further away in embedding space from answer-style text.
</details>

<details><summary>2. Does the hypothetical answer need to be factually accurate for HyDE to work?</summary>
No — its usefulness comes from matching the phrasing style of real answers, not from being correct; even a plausible-but-wrong guess can improve retrieval this way.
</details>

<details><summary>3. What extra cost does HyDE add compared to embedding the query directly?</summary>
A full generation call to produce the hypothetical answer, before retrieval can even begin — a real latency and compute cost on top of the embedding and search steps every query already requires.
</details>

## Key terms

* **HyDE (Hypothetical Document Embeddings):** embedding a generated hypothetical answer instead of the bare query, to better match the phrasing of real documents.
* **Hypothetical answer:** a plausible, not-necessarily-correct generated response used only to improve retrieval, not shown to the user.
* **Phrasing mismatch:** the stylistic gap between how a question is phrased and how its answer is phrased, which hurts a bare query's embedding similarity to the real answer.

## Related

[[Dense Retrieval]] · [[Query Expansion and Rewriting]] · [[Cost and Latency of RAG Systems]]

## Multi-Hop and Iterative Retrieval

"What else did the director of Movie X direct?" can't be answered by one search. The first search has to find who directed Movie X; only then does the question "what else did *that person* direct" even exist to search for. One retrieval pass physically cannot answer a question whose second half depends on the first half's answer.

**You need:** [[Anatomy of a RAG Pipeline]].

## The question it answers

"What happens when a single retrieval pass isn't enough to answer a question?" Some questions require chaining facts across documents that don't mention each other directly — no single passage says both "Movie X's director also directed Film A and Film B." **Multi-hop retrieval** runs retrieval more than once: a first search finds an intermediate fact (who directed Movie X), and a second search, using that intermediate answer as its new query, finds the fact that actually answers the original question.

## Intuition

Finding out what else your new neighbor's old roommate does for a living takes two separate lookups: first find out who the old roommate was, then look *that person* up — there's no single directory entry that already connects "your neighbor" to "their old roommate's job." Each lookup only becomes possible once the previous one's answer is in hand.

## Definition and notation

```text
single-hop:  retrieve(question) → answer, if one document directly contains it
multi-hop:   hop1 = retrieve(question)              → intermediate fact
             hop2 = retrieve(question using hop1)    → final answer
```

## A worked example

The question "What else did the director of Movie X direct?":

```text
single-hop retrieval: finds "Movie X was directed by Director Y" —
  answers "who directed Movie X," but not the actual question asked

multi-hop retrieval:
  hop 1 — retrieve: "Movie X" was directed by "Director Y"
  hop 2 — retrieve, using hop 1's answer as the new query: "Director Y" also directed "Film A" and "Film B"
```

A single retrieval pass finds the fact connecting Movie X to its director — useful, but it's not the question that was actually asked. Only the second hop, searching specifically for *Director Y's* other work using the name the first hop just supplied, reaches an answer to the original question.

## Bench

```bench
id: multi-hop-retrieval
title: The second question only exists after the first is answered
fallback: Step through a single-hop retrieval versus a two-hop chain that uses the first hop's answer to retrieve a second fact.
```

**Try this**

1. Step through hop 1 and notice it answers a different, simpler question than the one asked.
2. Step through hop 2 and see it uses hop 1's own answer as its search query.
3. Think of another two-part question that would require the same kind of chaining.

**What you should notice:** the second hop's query didn't exist until the first hop produced an answer — multi-hop retrieval isn't just "search twice," it's specifically using one search's output as the next search's input.

## Where it appears in AI

* **This is the retrieval-side counterpart to [[Tree-of-Thought and Search-Based Reasoning]] on the LLMs planet** — both break a hard problem into intermediate steps, here applied to retrieval queries rather than reasoning steps.
* **[[Chunk Overlap and Size Trade-offs]] mentioned multi-hop retrieval as an alternative fix for a split fact** — sometimes the better answer to "this fact doesn't fit in one chunk" is to retrieve twice rather than widen overlap.
* **[[Common RAG Failure Modes]] includes "question requires combining facts from multiple documents" as a specific failure category** that single-hop retrieval, by design, can never solve.

## Common pitfalls

* **Trying to answer a genuinely multi-hop question with a single retrieval pass.** No amount of better ranking fixes this — the second half of the question doesn't exist as a search target until the first half is answered.
* **Assuming every multi-part-sounding question actually requires multiple hops.** Some questions only sound complex but are directly answered by a single passage — multi-hop retrieval's extra cost (another full retrieval round) should be reserved for questions that genuinely need it.
* **Letting errors in the first hop silently propagate.** If hop 1 retrieves the wrong director, hop 2 will confidently search for the wrong person's other films — multi-hop retrieval has no built-in way to catch a wrong intermediate answer.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. Why can't a single retrieval pass answer "what else did the director of Movie X direct"?</summary>
No single document is likely to state both facts together; the question requires first finding who directed Movie X, then searching specifically for that person's other work — two separate facts that single-hop retrieval has no way to chain together.
</details>

<details><summary>2. What does the second hop's query consist of?</summary>
The first hop's own answer (the director's name), used as the new search query — the second hop's query literally couldn't be formed until the first hop produced a result.
</details>

<details><summary>3. What happens if the first hop retrieves an incorrect intermediate fact?</summary>
The second hop will search using that incorrect fact, likely producing a confidently wrong final answer — multi-hop retrieval has no mechanism of its own to detect or correct an error introduced at an earlier hop.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Multi-hop retrieval:** chaining multiple retrieval passes, where a later search uses an earlier search's result as its query.
* **Intermediate fact:** a piece of information retrieved not because it directly answers the question, but because it's needed to form the next search.
* **Hop:** one retrieval pass within a multi-hop chain.

## Related

[[Anatomy of a RAG Pipeline]] · [[Chunk Overlap and Size Trade-offs]] · [[Tree-of-Thought and Search-Based Reasoning]]

## Advanced RAG Patterns

The basic retrieve-then-generate loop has limits: it trusts whatever came back from a single search, treats every document the same whether it's prose or a spreadsheet, and has no way to notice when retrieval itself failed. This district covers the patterns that address each of those gaps.

Topics on this stretch of the road:

* [[Re-Ranking Retrieved Results]]: a second, more careful pass over what a fast search already found.
* [[Self-RAG and Reflective Retrieval]]: a model that decides for itself whether it needs to retrieve, and whether what it retrieved was good enough.
* [[Corrective RAG]]: catching and recovering from a bad retrieval before it reaches generation.
* [[Graph-Based RAG]]: retrieving from a knowledge graph instead of, or alongside, a flat document collection.
* [[Retrieval over Structured Data]]: answering questions against tables and databases instead of prose.
* [[Multimodal RAG]]: retrieving images, audio or other non-text content alongside, or instead of, text.

## Re-Ranking Retrieved Results

Running a cross-encoder over an entire 10,000-document collection would cost roughly a million units in this planet's own illustrative units — far too much for a live request. Running it only over the 50 documents a cheap bi-encoder already found promising costs a tiny fraction of that, for most of the accuracy benefit.

**You need:** [[Cross-Encoders and Re-Rankers]].

## The question it answers

"How do you get a cross-encoder's accuracy without paying its cost over an entire collection?" Re-ranking is the two-stage pipeline this trade-off implies: a cheap bi-encoder (or sparse method) retrieves a shortlist — the top 50, say — from the full collection, and only *that* shortlist gets passed to a cross-encoder for a more careful, accurate re-score. The expensive stage never sees the documents the cheap stage already ruled out.

## Intuition

A hiring pipeline doesn't have a senior interviewer review every single résumé submitted — a fast initial screen narrows thousands of applicants down to a shortlist, and only that shortlist gets the time-intensive, careful attention a senior interviewer can actually afford to give.

## Definition and notation

```text
cross-encode everything:      N documents × cross-encoder cost per document
funnel (retrieve + re-rank):  N documents × bi-encoder cost  +  shortlist × cross-encoder cost
```

## A worked example

A 10,000-document collection, re-ranking a shortlist of 50:

```text
cross-encoding the entire collection:         10,000 × 100 = 1,000,000 cost units
bi-encoder retrieval + cross-encoder re-rank:  10,000 × 1  +  50 × 100  =  15,000 cost units

speedup: 1,000,000 / 15,000 ≈ 66.7×
```

The funnel costs roughly 1.5% of what cross-encoding the entire collection would — a two-orders-of-magnitude saving, for an accuracy improvement that only matters within the shortlist the cheap first stage already narrowed things down to.

## Bench

```bench
id: rerank-funnel-cost
title: Expensive scoring, saved for a short list
fallback: Compare the cost of cross-encoding an entire collection against a bi-encoder-then-re-rank funnel.
```

**Try this**

1. Slide the shortlist size up and watch the funnel's total cost grow, but stay far below cross-encoding everything.
2. Slide it down toward 10 and watch the speedup increase further.
3. Imagine a shortlist so large it approaches the full collection size — what happens to the speedup?

**What you should notice:** the funnel's cost is dominated by the cheap bi-encoder pass over the *whole* collection, plus a comparatively small cross-encoder cost over just the shortlist — shrinking the shortlist barely changes the total, since the bi-encoder term already dominates.

## Where it appears in AI

* **This is the practical justification for keeping [[Bi-Encoders and Dense Embeddings]] and [[Cross-Encoders and Re-Rankers]] as separate stages**, rather than ever using a cross-encoder as the primary retrieval mechanism.
* **[[Hybrid Retrieval Fusion]] is often the shortlist-producing first stage** that feeds a re-ranker, combining sparse and dense signals before the expensive re-ranking step ever runs.
* **A re-ranked shortlist is exactly what [[Context Assembly and Ordering]] has to decide how to arrange** — re-ranking determines which passages make it into the final context, and roughly in what order of confidence.

## Common pitfalls

* **Assuming a bigger shortlist is always safer.** A larger shortlist does slightly reduce the risk of the cheap first stage missing a truly relevant document, but the worked example shows the funnel's total cost barely changes — the real risk to manage is the first stage's recall, not the re-ranking cost.
* **Skipping the first stage and cross-encoding everything "to be thorough."** The worked example's two-orders-of-magnitude cost gap is exactly why this doesn't scale past small collections.
* **Forgetting that the funnel's final ranking is only as good as the first stage's recall.** If the true best document never makes it into the shortlist, no amount of careful re-ranking can recover it.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. In the worked example, why does the funnel's total cost stay low even as the shortlist size grows?</summary>
The bi-encoder pass over the full 10,000-document collection (10,000 cost units) dominates the total; the cross-encoder's cost over the shortlist only adds 100 units per document kept, which stays small relative to the bi-encoder term for any reasonable shortlist size.
</details>

<details><summary>2. What's the risk of making the shortlist too small?</summary>
If the true most relevant document scores just outside the shortlist cutoff under the cheap first-stage method, it never reaches the cross-encoder at all — no amount of accurate re-ranking can recover a document that was never passed through.
</details>

<details><summary>3. Why is re-ranking not simply "run a cross-encoder on everything, but faster"?</summary>
It's a structurally different approach — a cheap method handles the full collection first, and only the resulting shortlist gets the expensive treatment; the cross-encoder itself isn't optimized to be cheaper, it's just applied to far fewer documents.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Re-ranking:** applying a more accurate (and more expensive) scoring method to a shortlist a cheaper method already produced.
* **Shortlist:** the reduced set of candidates passed from a cheap retrieval stage to an expensive re-ranking stage.
* **Two-stage retrieval:** a pipeline combining a fast, broad first pass with a slow, narrow second pass.

## Related

[[Cross-Encoders and Re-Rankers]] · [[Hybrid Retrieval Fusion]] · [[Context Assembly and Ordering]]

## Self-RAG and Reflective Retrieval

Every query in a basic RAG pipeline gets retrieved for, whether it needs it or not — "what is 2 + 2" triggers the exact same search-then-generate routine as a question about a company's confidential Q3 numbers. Self-RAG adds judgment to that routine: the model itself decides whether retrieval is even necessary, and afterward, whether what came back is actually worth using.

**You need:** [[Anatomy of a RAG Pipeline]].

## The question it answers

"Does every query really need to trigger retrieval, and is every retrieved passage automatically trustworthy?" Self-RAG uses two self-assessment checks instead of always retrieving unconditionally: first, whether the model's own confidence in answering directly is already high enough that retrieval would add little; second, if it does retrieve, whether the retrieved passage actually looks relevant before using it to generate an answer. Both checks can be made by the same model, trained or prompted to produce this kind of self-judgment.

## Intuition

A knowledgeable person answering "what's 2 plus 2" doesn't pause to look anything up — their own confidence is already more than enough. Asked something they're genuinely unsure about, they do look it up — but a good researcher also checks whether what they found actually answers the question before citing it, rather than using the first thing that came back regardless of relevance.

## Definition and notation

```text
retrieve?  = parametric_confidence < threshold
use_passage?  = retrieved_passage.relevance ≥ threshold
```

## A worked example

Two questions, routed by the model's own confidence, followed by a relevance check on what gets retrieved:

```text
"What is 2 + 2?" (confidence 0.98) → answer directly, no retrieval needed
"What were last quarter's returns figures?" (confidence 0.25) → retrieve first

after retrieving for the second question:
  "Q3 returns were up 4%." (relevance 0.91) → used
  "Unrelated HR policy update." (relevance 0.12) → discarded
```

The first question never triggers retrieval at all — the model's own confidence is already well above the threshold. The second question does retrieve, and then applies a second check: one retrieved passage clears the relevance bar and gets used; another, clearly off-topic, gets discarded before it ever reaches generation.

## Bench

```bench
id: self-rag-routing
title: Deciding whether to look something up at all
fallback: Slide a model's own confidence and watch Self-RAG decide whether to retrieve at all, then whether to trust what it found.
```

**Try this**

1. Slide confidence above the retrieval threshold and watch the system skip retrieval entirely.
2. Slide it below, forcing retrieval, then adjust the relevance slider to see the passage get used or discarded.
3. Consider what happens to answer quality if the confidence threshold is set too high, so retrieval almost never triggers.

**What you should notice:** Self-RAG adds two separate decision points to the basic pipeline, not one — skipping unnecessary retrieval and discarding irrelevant retrieved content are each their own judgment call, made independently.

## Where it appears in AI

* **This is a direct refinement of [[Anatomy of a RAG Pipeline]]'s fixed five-stage sequence** — Self-RAG makes the "retrieve" and "assemble" stages conditional rather than automatic.
* **[[Corrective RAG]] takes the relevance-checking idea further**, triggering an actual fallback action (not just discarding) when retrieval quality looks poor.
* **This reuses the same confidence-decay reasoning from [[Hallucination and Knowledge Cutoff]]**: a model's own confidence is exactly the signal Self-RAG checks before deciding whether retrieval is worth the cost.

## Common pitfalls

* **Setting the confidence threshold too low, so retrieval almost always triggers.** This defeats the purpose of skipping retrieval for genuinely easy questions, adding cost and latency with little benefit.
* **Setting it too high, so the model skips retrieval for questions it's only falsely confident about.** A model's own confidence isn't a perfect signal — [[Hallucination and Knowledge Cutoff]] already showed confidence can stay misleadingly high well past where it should be trusted.
* **Trusting the relevance check as infallible.** It's still a model's own judgment, which can itself be wrong — a genuinely relevant passage phrased unusually could be discarded, or an irrelevant one that superficially resembles the query could pass.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. Why does the "What is 2 + 2?" question skip retrieval entirely in the worked example?</summary>
Its parametric confidence (0.98) is above the retrieval threshold, so the system judges that looking anything up wouldn't meaningfully improve an answer it's already essentially certain about.
</details>

<details><summary>2. What happens to the "Unrelated HR policy update" passage after it's retrieved?</summary>
Its relevance score (0.12) falls below the relevance threshold, so it's discarded before reaching the generation stage, rather than being used as context for the answer.
</details>

<details><summary>3. Does Self-RAG eliminate the risk of a model answering confidently but incorrectly?</summary>
No — both of its decision points rely on the model's own self-assessment, which can itself be wrong; it reduces unnecessary retrieval and some irrelevant-context use, but doesn't guarantee correctness.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Self-RAG:** a RAG variant where the model itself decides whether to retrieve and whether to trust what was retrieved.
* **Parametric confidence:** the model's own estimate of how likely its unretrieved answer is to be correct.
* **Relevance check:** a self-assessment of whether a retrieved passage actually bears on the question asked.

## Related

[[Anatomy of a RAG Pipeline]] · [[Corrective RAG]] · [[Hallucination and Knowledge Cutoff]]

## Corrective RAG

Self-RAG discards an individual irrelevant passage; Corrective RAG asks a broader question about the *whole* retrieval — is this collection of results even worth generating from, or should the system take a completely different action instead? A classifier scores the retrieval as a whole and routes to a different fallback depending on how bad it looks.

**You need:** [[Self-RAG and Reflective Retrieval]].

## The question it answers

"What should happen when an entire retrieval looks weak, not just one passage?" Corrective RAG classifies a retrieval's overall quality — by the best relevance score among its results — into three buckets: **correct** (confidently relevant, safe to generate from directly), **ambiguous** (some signal, but not strong enough to trust outright — worth refining the query and trying again), or **incorrect** (nothing relevant found at all — fall back to a broader search, such as a web search, rather than generating from what's clearly the wrong context).

## Intuition

A research assistant handed a weak stack of sources for a report doesn't just write the report anyway using whatever's there — if the sources look thin but plausible, they go back and search more specifically; if the sources are clearly about the wrong topic entirely, they start over with a different search strategy altogether. Writing from bad sources regardless isn't on the list of options.

## Definition and notation

```text
classify(scores) = "correct"    if max(scores) ≥ 0.7
                  = "ambiguous"  if 0.3 ≤ max(scores) < 0.7
                  = "incorrect"  if max(scores) < 0.3
```

## A worked example

Three retrieval scenarios for the same query, classified by their best relevance score:

```text
good retrieval (scores: 0.85, 0.3, 0.1):   best 0.85  →  correct    →  generate from retrieved context
weak retrieval (scores: 0.45, 0.4, 0.2):   best 0.45  →  ambiguous  →  refine query and retrieve again
bad retrieval  (scores: 0.15, 0.1, 0.05):  best 0.15  →  incorrect  →  fall back to a broader search
```

Each scenario triggers a genuinely different action, not just a different confidence label — "ambiguous" tries again with a better query, while "incorrect" abandons the current retrieval strategy entirely rather than trying to patch it.

## Bench

```bench
id: corrective-rag-classifier
title: Checking the retrieval before trusting it
fallback: Classify a retrieval's quality and watch which corrective action it triggers.
```

**Try this**

1. Look at the "good retrieval" scenario and note it proceeds straight to generation.
2. Switch to "weak retrieval" and see it triggers a re-query instead of generating.
3. Switch to "bad retrieval" and see it abandons retrieval-based generation entirely.

**What you should notice:** the classification depends only on the *best* score among the retrieved passages — a retrieval with several mediocre results and one strong one is judged "correct," the same as a retrieval with one spectacular result and nothing else.

## Where it appears in AI

* **This extends [[Self-RAG and Reflective Retrieval]]'s passage-level relevance check to the whole retrieval**, adding genuinely different fallback actions rather than just discarding individual results.
* **The "fall back to a broader search" action is itself just another retrieval strategy** ([[Query Expansion and Rewriting]], or an entirely different data source) — Corrective RAG decides *when* to reach for it, not *how* it works.
* **[[Common RAG Failure Modes]] includes "generated a confident answer from irrelevant retrieved context" as exactly the failure Corrective RAG is designed to intercept before generation ever happens.**

## Common pitfalls

* **Setting the "correct" threshold so low that weak retrievals get treated as trustworthy.** The thresholds in the worked example are a design choice — too permissive a cutoff defeats the purpose of checking at all.
* **Treating "ambiguous" and "incorrect" the same way.** The worked example deliberately gives them different corrective actions — refining a query is a much smaller intervention than abandoning the retrieval strategy altogether, and conflating them wastes the distinction.
* **Relying only on the best score and ignoring how the rest of the results look.** A retrieval with one lucky high-scoring passage and nothing else coherent might still warrant more scrutiny than a single number captures.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. In the worked example, why does the "weak retrieval" scenario trigger a re-query rather than generation or a full fallback?</summary>
Its best score (0.45) falls between the two thresholds — high enough to suggest some real signal exists, but not high enough to trust directly, which is exactly the "ambiguous" bucket's definition and corrective action.
</details>

<details><summary>2. Why does Corrective RAG classify based on the best score among results, rather than the average?</summary>
A single strong, relevant passage can be enough to answer a question even if the rest of the retrieved results are irrelevant noise — averaging would unfairly penalize a good retrieval just for also returning some weak candidates alongside the right one.
</details>

<details><summary>3. What distinguishes Corrective RAG's "incorrect" action from Self-RAG's passage-discarding?</summary>
Self-RAG discards an individual irrelevant passage but still proceeds with whatever else was retrieved; Corrective RAG's "incorrect" verdict abandons the current retrieval approach for the whole query, switching to a different strategy entirely.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Corrective RAG:** classifying a retrieval's overall quality and routing to different corrective actions based on that classification.
* **Retrieval verdict:** the bucket (correct, ambiguous, incorrect) a retrieval is classified into.
* **Fallback action:** an alternative strategy (query refinement, broader search) triggered when a retrieval is judged too weak to generate from directly.

## Related

[[Self-RAG and Reflective Retrieval]] · [[Query Expansion and Rewriting]] · [[Common RAG Failure Modes]]

## Graph-Based RAG

"What did the studio behind Movie X's director also produce?" isn't answered by any single document — it's answered by chaining three separate facts together: who directed Movie X, who they work for, and what that studio produced. A knowledge graph makes those facts, and the connections between them, explicit and traversable, rather than hoping one lucky chunk happens to state the whole chain at once.

**You need:** [[Multi-Hop and Iterative Retrieval]].

## The question it answers

"How can retrieval answer a question whose answer is spread across a chain of relationships, rather than sitting in one document?" A **knowledge graph** stores entities (people, movies, studios) and labeled relationships between them (directed_by, works_at, produced) as explicit edges. **Graph-based RAG** answers a question by *traversing* those edges — following directed_by from "Movie X," then works_at from whatever that led to, then produced from there — building the answer one hop at a time, the same chaining idea as [[Multi-Hop and Iterative Retrieval]], but over an explicit graph structure instead of re-running document search at each step.

## Intuition

Answering "who is my coworker's childhood best friend's current employer" by flipping through a company directory (coworker → their profile) and then a social network (childhood friend → their current job) is exactly graph traversal: each step follows a known, labeled connection to the next entity, rather than hoping a single document states the whole multi-step relationship outright.

## Definition and notation

```text
graph = { entities, edges: [(from, relation, to), ...] }
traverse(start, hops) = follow one matching edge per hop, building a path of entities and relations
```

## A worked example

A 3-edge graph, traversed from "Movie X" to answer a chained question:

```text
edges:
  Movie X  --directed_by-->  Director Y
  Director Y  --works_at-->  Studio Z
  Studio Z  --produced-->  Film A

question: "what did the studio behind Movie X's director also produce?"

flat document retrieval: no single document states this full 3-hop chain
graph traversal (3 hops): Movie X --directed_by--> Director Y --works_at--> Studio Z --produced--> Film A
```

Each edge on its own is a simple, directly stated fact — "Movie X was directed by Director Y" is exactly the kind of sentence a single document would contain. The *question*, though, needs all three facts chained together, which graph traversal does explicitly, one labeled hop at a time.

## Bench

```bench
id: graph-rag-traversal
title: A fact built from three separate edges
fallback: Step through a graph traversal that chains three relations no single document states together.
```

**Try this**

1. Step through all three hops and read each labeled edge as it's followed.
2. Notice each individual edge is a simple fact — the complexity is entirely in chaining three of them.
3. Imagine the same question answered by flat document retrieval alone — what would it find?

**What you should notice:** the graph doesn't need to store the final 3-hop fact anywhere explicitly — it only needs the three individual edges, and traversal reconstructs the chain on demand.

## Where it appears in AI

* **This is the same chaining idea as [[Multi-Hop and Iterative Retrieval]]**, made explicit: instead of re-running a text search at each hop, each hop follows a labeled edge already stored in the graph.
* **Building the graph itself (extracting entities and relations from raw documents) is a document-processing problem**, related to but beyond what [[Metadata Extraction and Enrichment]] covers for simpler per-chunk attributes.
* **[[Retrieval over Structured Data]] is a related but different idea**: querying a table or database directly, rather than traversing a graph of entities and relationships.

## Common pitfalls

* **Assuming a knowledge graph can answer any question flat document retrieval couldn't.** It only helps for questions whose answer genuinely decomposes into a chain of stored relationships — a question with no relevant edges in the graph at all gets no benefit from this approach.
* **Underestimating the cost of building and maintaining the graph itself.** Extracting entities and relationships from raw documents accurately enough to traverse reliably is a substantial undertaking on its own, separate from the traversal mechanism.
* **Following the wrong edge when a node has several relations of the same type.** "Director Y" might work at more than one studio over their career — traversal needs some way to pick the right edge, not just any matching one.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. In the worked example, why can't flat document retrieval answer the full question in one pass?</summary>
The full chain spans three separate facts, each likely stated in a different document — no single document is likely to state "Movie X's director's employer's other production" all at once.
</details>

<details><summary>2. What does each individual edge in the graph represent?</summary>
A single, directly stated fact connecting two entities through a named relationship — simple enough that one document could plausibly state it on its own.
</details>

<details><summary>3. How does graph-based RAG relate to multi-hop retrieval?</summary>
It's the same underlying idea (chaining intermediate facts to reach a final answer), but implemented by following explicit labeled edges in a pre-built graph, rather than re-running a document search at each step.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Knowledge graph:** a structure of entities and labeled relationships (edges) between them.
* **Graph traversal:** following edges from one entity to the next to answer a question spanning multiple relationships.
* **Entity extraction:** identifying entities and relationships from raw documents to build a knowledge graph in the first place.

## Related

[[Multi-Hop and Iterative Retrieval]] · [[Retrieval over Structured Data]] · [[Metadata Extraction and Enrichment]]

## Retrieval over Structured Data

"How many orders were placed in 2024?" has an exact answer sitting in a table of order records — but no chunk of retrieved text, however well-chosen, can ever compute that count. Retrieval returns passages; counting, summing and filtering across many rows is what a structured query actually does.

**You need:** [[Handling Tables, Code and Structured Content]].

## The question it answers

"What happens when a question needs a computed answer over structured data, not a retrieved passage?" Chunk-based retrieval, even with structure preserved ([[Handling Tables, Code and Structured Content]]), still returns *passages* — individual rows or table fragments. A question asking for an aggregate (a count, a sum, an average) across many rows needs a structured query translated from the question, run directly against the table or database, producing an exact computed answer no retrieved chunk could contain on its own.

## Intuition

Asking a librarian "how many books in this library were published after 2020" isn't answered by handing over the single most relevant book — it's answered by actually counting, which requires checking every book's publication year, not retrieving one representative example of one.

## Definition and notation

```text
nl_to_query(question) = {filter, operation}      -- translate the question into a structured query
run(data, query)      = execute filter/aggregate directly against the full table
```

## A worked example

A small orders table, queried for "how many orders were placed in 2024":

```text
orders:
  id 1, year 2023, $50
  id 2, year 2024, $80
  id 3, year 2024, $120
  id 4, year 2024, $60
  id 5, year 2023, $90

structured query: filter year = 2024, count rows
→ result: 3 orders

chunk retrieval over a flattened table: could at best return the whole table's text as one chunk —
  no retrieved passage computes "3" directly; counting still has to happen separately
```

The structured query runs a filter across all five rows and returns an exact count — 3. Retrieval, even if it returned the entire table as a single chunk, would only hand back raw rows; counting how many satisfy the condition is a computation retrieval itself never performs.

## Bench

```bench
id: structured-query-vs-chunks
title: Counting rows is a query, not a passage
fallback: Run an aggregate question as a structured query over a table and compare against what chunk retrieval alone could ever return.
```

**Try this**

1. Slide the year filter and watch the count update exactly.
2. Consider what a chunk-retrieval system would have returned instead for the same question.
3. Think of another question over this table (total revenue in a year, the largest single order) that would need the same kind of structured computation.

**What you should notice:** the count isn't being *found* anywhere in the data — it's being *computed* by checking every row against the filter, which is exactly what a structured query engine does and retrieval alone cannot.

## Where it appears in AI

* **This is the sharper version of the problem [[Handling Tables, Code and Structured Content]] introduced**: even perfectly preserved row-level chunks can't answer an aggregate question across many rows.
* **The "translate the question into a query" step is itself a generation task**, related to [[Structured Output and Tool-Calling APIs]] on the LLMs planet — producing a correctly structured query is a constrained-generation problem.
* **A production RAG system often routes a question to either retrieval or a structured query engine** depending on what kind of question it is — part of the decision [[Production RAG Pipeline Architecture]] has to make.

## Common pitfalls

* **Trying to answer an aggregate question through retrieval alone, however the table is chunked.** No chunking strategy fixes this — the problem isn't how the data is split, it's that computing an aggregate requires checking every row, which retrieving a handful of chunks never does.
* **Assuming every question over structured data needs a structured query.** A question asking about one specific row ("what's in the Pro plan") is answered fine by retrieving that row as a chunk — structured queries matter specifically for aggregates and multi-row computations.
* **Trusting an automatically generated structured query without validating it.** A mistranslated filter (the wrong year, an off-by-one condition) produces a confidently wrong exact number, which can look more trustworthy than a vague retrieved passage precisely because it's a precise-looking number.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. Why can't chunk retrieval answer "how many orders were placed in 2024," even if every row is preserved as its own chunk?</summary>
Retrieval returns a set of passages; it doesn't perform a computation across them — counting how many returned rows satisfy a condition is a separate step that retrieval itself never does.
</details>

<details><summary>2. What has to happen before a natural-language question can be answered as a structured query?</summary>
The question needs to be translated into a structured form — identifying the filter condition (year = 2024) and the operation (count) — before it can be run directly against the table.
</details>

<details><summary>3. Does every question over a table need to become a structured query?</summary>
No — a question asking about one specific row can be answered by retrieving that row as a chunk; structured queries matter specifically for questions requiring computation across many rows.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Structured query:** a precise, executable filter or aggregate operation run directly against structured data.
* **Aggregate:** a computed value (count, sum, average) across multiple rows, as opposed to a single retrieved record.
* **NL-to-query translation:** converting a natural-language question into a structured query's filter and operation.

## Related

[[Handling Tables, Code and Structured Content]] · [[Graph-Based RAG]] · [[Production RAG Pipeline Architecture]]

## Multimodal RAG

A text query can retrieve an image directly — no caption, no text description needed as an intermediary — as long as the text and the image were embedded into the same shared space in the first place. "A photo of a golden retriever" and an actual photo of one land close together in that space, the same way two pieces of text about the same topic would.

**You need:** [[Dense Retrieval]], [[Contrastive Learning]].

## The question it answers

"Can retrieval work across different modalities — text queries finding images, or the reverse?" Multimodal RAG retrieves content in a different modality than the query, by embedding both into the same shared space (built the way [[Contrastive Learning|contrastive learning]] already covered: pulling matching text-image pairs together, pushing unrelated ones apart, during training). Once both modalities share a space, retrieval is the same cosine-similarity operation as always — it just happens to be comparing a text vector to an image vector instead of two text vectors.

## Intuition

A bilingual catalog where every photo and every caption, regardless of which language wrote the caption, gets filed by subject rather than by language lets someone search in one language and find a photo captioned in a different one entirely — because the filing system organizes by *meaning*, not by modality or language. A shared embedding space does the same thing for text and images.

## Definition and notation

```text
shared_space:  embed_text(query) and embed_image(photo) land in the same vector space
score(query, image) = cosine_similarity(embed_text(query), embed_image(image))
```

## A worked example
