A text query ranked against three images, using embeddings in a shared text-image space:

```text
query: "a photo of a golden retriever"

golden_retriever.jpg   similarity 0.9997
invoice_scan.png       similarity 0.7809
siamese_cat.jpg        similarity 0.2815
```

The matching photo scores almost perfectly (0.9997), despite the query never containing a single pixel of image data. A mismatched photo (a cat) scores far lower, and an entirely unrelated image (a scanned invoice) lands in between — closer to the query than the cat photo, interestingly, since it shares no strong signal pulling it toward *either* concept.

## Bench

```bench
id: multimodal-rag-retrieval
title: A text query, ranking images directly
fallback: Rank images by cross-modal similarity to a text query in a shared embedding space.
```

**Try this**

1. Check which image ranks highest for "a photo of a golden retriever."
2. Switch the query to "a photo of a cat" and watch the ranking flip.
3. Consider why the invoice scan's similarity sits between the two animal photos' scores rather than at the very bottom.

**What you should notice:** retrieval itself hasn't changed at all — it's still cosine similarity between two vectors; the only thing multimodal RAG adds is that those two vectors can now come from genuinely different kinds of content.

## Where it appears in AI

* **This reuses [[Dense Retrieval]]'s exact similarity mechanism**, with the only change being which modality each side's embedding comes from.
* **Building the shared space in the first place is exactly [[Contrastive Learning]]**, already covered on the Deep Learning planet — this topic is about using that shared space for retrieval, not re-deriving how it's trained.
* **A multimodal RAG system's generation stage often needs a model capable of reasoning over the retrieved image directly**, not just citing it as text — connecting back to multimodal generation covered on the Generative AI planet.

## Common pitfalls

* **Assuming any embedding model works across modalities by default.** A shared text-image space has to be deliberately trained that way (contrastively, on paired text-image data) — a text-only embedding model has no meaningful way to compare against an image at all.
* **Expecting cross-modal similarity scores to behave exactly like same-modality ones.** The worked example's invoice scan scoring higher than the mismatched cat photo isn't necessarily meaningful — cross-modal similarity scales can behave differently from same-modality comparisons, and absolute score values are less directly interpretable.
* **Retrieving an image without a plan for how generation will actually use it.** Finding the right image is only half the pipeline — the generating model also needs to be able to process that image as input, not just receive a filename.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. Why does "a photo of a golden retriever" retrieve the matching photo without any text caption or description of the image being involved?</summary>
Both the text query and the image were embedded into the same shared space, trained so that matching text-image pairs land close together — the comparison happens directly between the query's text embedding and the image's own embedding.
</details>

<details><summary>2. What training approach builds the shared space multimodal RAG depends on?</summary>
Contrastive learning — pulling matching text-image pairs' embeddings together and pushing unrelated pairs apart during training, the same mechanism already covered for same-modality representation learning.
</details>

<details><summary>3. Does a text-only embedding model support multimodal retrieval?</summary>
No — it has no trained relationship between text embeddings and image embeddings; multimodal retrieval requires an embedding model specifically trained (typically contrastively) on paired data across the modalities involved.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Multimodal RAG:** retrieval where the query and the retrieved content are in different modalities (text and images, for instance).
* **Shared embedding space:** a vector space where content from multiple modalities is embedded so that semantically related items land close together regardless of modality.
* **Cross-modal similarity:** a similarity score computed between embeddings from two different modalities.

## Related

[[Dense Retrieval]] · [[Contrastive Learning]] · [[Multimodal Generation]]

## Generation with Retrieved Context

Retrieval only hands a model raw material; what the model does with that material is a separate problem. This district is about turning a stack of retrieved passages into an answer that's actually grounded in them — ordered sensibly, attributed to its sources, and honest about what the passages don't settle.

Topics on this stretch of the road:

* [[Context Assembly and Ordering]]: deciding what order retrieved passages go in, and why it isn't arbitrary.
* [[Citation and Source Attribution]]: tracing a generated claim back to the passage that supports it.
* [[Handling Noisy or Conflicting Retrieved Context]]: what to do when retrieved passages disagree, or don't actually answer the question.
* [[Context-Window Budgeting for RAG]]: deciding how many passages fit, and which ones to cut when they don't.
* [[Grounded Generation and Faithfulness]]: getting a model to answer from what it was given, instead of what it already "knew."

## Context Assembly and Ordering

Retrieval can rank the single most relevant passage first — and assembly can still bury it in the middle of the prompt, right where a model is statistically least likely to actually use it. Where a passage sits in the assembled context matters every bit as much as whether it was retrieved at all.

**You need:** [[Anatomy of a RAG Pipeline]], [[Context Rot and Lost-in-the-Middle Effects]].

## The question it answers

"Does it matter what order retrieved passages are assembled in?" Yes — this reuses the exact [[Context Rot and Lost-in-the-Middle Effects|lost-in-the-middle]] finding already established on the LLMs planet: a model is most likely to actually use information placed near the start or end of its context, and least likely to use information buried in the middle, regardless of how relevant that information actually is. Assembly is the stage that decides this placement, so it directly controls how much of retrieval's hard-won ranking actually survives into the generated answer.

## Intuition

Handing someone a stack of five documents and asking them to answer a question using the third one from the top, specifically, works less reliably than handing them the same document as either the very first or very last thing they read — not because the document changed, but because where it sits in the stack changes how much attention it tends to get.

## Definition and notation

```text
accuracy(position) = lost-in-the-middle curve: high near the edges, low in the middle
```

(exact formula already derived in [[Context Rot and Lost-in-the-Middle Effects]])

## A worked example

The single most relevant retrieved passage, placed at different positions among 5 assembled passages:

```text
position 1 of 5 (at the start):  95.0% chance it's actually used
position 3 of 5 (in the middle): 55.0% chance it's actually used
position 5 of 5 (at the end):    95.0% chance it's actually used
```

Moving the exact same, most-relevant passage from the start of the assembled context to the middle cuts the odds it actually gets used almost in half — from 95% down to 55% — with nothing about the passage itself changing at all.

## Bench

```bench
id: context-position-accuracy
title: First, last, or buried in the middle
fallback: Slide where the most relevant passage sits in the assembled context and watch the odds it actually gets used.
```

**Try this**

1. Start with the most relevant passage at position 1 and note the high accuracy.
2. Slide it toward the middle and watch accuracy drop.
3. Slide it to the last position and watch accuracy recover.

**What you should notice:** the curve is symmetric — the start and the end are equally good positions, and the dip is centered exactly in the middle of the assembled passages, not biased toward either side.

## Where it appears in AI

* **This is a direct, practical application of [[Context Rot and Lost-in-the-Middle Effects]]'s own worked example**, applied specifically to deciding assembly order rather than measuring the general phenomenon.
* **A re-ranker's job ([[Re-Ranking Retrieved Results]]) isn't finished once it scores passages** — the resulting order still needs to be placed into the context in a way that actually benefits from that ranking.
* **[[Context-Window Budgeting for RAG]] decides how many passages fit at all**; this topic decides where, among the ones that do fit, each one should go.

## Common pitfalls

* **Assembling retrieved passages in an arbitrary order (alphabetical, by document ID) instead of by relevance-aware placement.** The worked example shows a 40-percentage-point accuracy swing purely from positioning — an arbitrary order wastes exactly the ranking signal retrieval worked to produce.
* **Assuming the most relevant passage should always go first.** Depending on the specific lost-in-the-middle curve, the last position can be just as strong — some systems deliberately place the top result last, closest to the question itself.
* **Treating assembly order as a one-time decision that doesn't need revisiting.** The right ordering can depend on the specific model being used, since different models can have somewhat different lost-in-the-middle profiles.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. In the worked example, why does moving the most relevant passage to the middle hurt its odds of being used, when nothing about the passage's content changed?</summary>
The lost-in-the-middle effect is about *position* within the context, not content — a model is statistically less likely to attend to and use information placed in the middle of a long context, regardless of how relevant that information actually is.
</details>

<details><summary>2. Is the start of the context always a better position than the end?</summary>
No — the worked example's curve is symmetric, with both the start and the end scoring equally well (95%); the problem is specifically the middle, not either edge in particular.
</details>

<details><summary>3. What does assembly order control that retrieval ranking alone doesn't?</summary>
Retrieval ranking determines which passages are the most relevant; assembly order determines where those passages physically sit in the prompt, which independently affects how likely the model is to actually use each one.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Context assembly:** arranging retrieved passages into the final prompt sent to the generating model.
* **Lost-in-the-middle effect:** the tendency for information in the middle of a long context to be used less reliably than information at the start or end.
* **Assembly order:** the specific sequence in which retrieved passages are placed within the assembled context.

## Related

[[Context Rot and Lost-in-the-Middle Effects]] · [[Re-Ranking Retrieved Results]] · [[Context-Window Budgeting for RAG]]

## Citation and Source Attribution

An answer that cites its sources lets a reader check it; an answer that doesn't asks for blind trust. Attribution means tracing each specific claim in a generated answer back to the retrieved passage that actually supports it — and noticing when a claim has no such passage at all.

**You need:** [[Dense Retrieval]].

## The question it answers

"How do you know which retrieved passage actually backs up a specific sentence in the generated answer?" For each claim in an answer, attribution finds the retrieved passage whose embedding is most similar to that claim — the passage it's most likely paraphrasing or drawing from — and cites that passage, as long as the similarity clears a minimum threshold. A claim whose best match falls below that threshold isn't cited at all, because nothing retrieved actually supports it closely enough.

## Intuition

Checking a student's essay against the sources they claim to have used means matching each specific sentence back to the source passage that actually contains that information — and flagging any sentence that doesn't match any source closely, because it was either invented or drawn from somewhere not actually cited.

## Definition and notation

```text
best_support(claim) = passage with highest cosine similarity to the claim
cite(claim) = best_support(claim)   if similarity ≥ threshold
            = unsupported            otherwise
```

## A worked example

Three claims in a generated answer, checked against two retrieved passages (one about refunds, one about shipping), at a 0.8 similarity threshold:

```text
"Refunds are issued within 5 business days."  → best match p1 (refunds), similarity 1.000 → cited
"Shipping takes 3-5 days."                     → best match p2 (shipping), similarity 1.000 → cited
"The company was founded in 1998."             → best match p1 (refunds), similarity 0.781 → unsupported
```

The first two claims closely match a retrieved passage and get cited to it directly. The third claim — a fact never actually in either retrieved passage — only reaches a 0.781 similarity to its *closest* match, below the 0.8 threshold, so it's correctly flagged as unsupported rather than falsely attributed to an unrelated passage.

## Bench

```bench
id: citation-attribution
title: Can every claim point back to a source?
fallback: Trace each claim in a generated answer back to its best-supporting passage, flagging anything too weakly supported to cite.
```

**Try this**

1. Look at which claims get cited at the default threshold.
2. Lower the threshold and watch the third claim start getting (falsely) cited too.
3. Raise the threshold and see if either of the first two claims eventually loses its citation.

**What you should notice:** the threshold is doing real work — set it too low, and an unsupported claim gets a false citation that looks just as credible as a real one; set it too high, and genuinely supported claims might lose their citations too.

## Where it appears in AI

* **This reuses the same cosine-similarity mechanism as [[Dense Retrieval]]**, applied after generation rather than before it — attribution is retrieval's comparison operation, run one more time.
* **[[Grounded Generation and Faithfulness]] aggregates exactly this per-claim check into a single score for the whole answer** — attribution is the per-claim mechanism; faithfulness is the summary statistic.
* **A claim that fails attribution is a strong, concrete signal of the kind of problem [[Common RAG Failure Modes]] catalogs as hallucinated content slipping past retrieval's own grounding.**

## Common pitfalls

* **Setting the citation threshold too low.** The worked example shows a genuinely unsupported claim scoring 0.781 — a threshold below that would falsely cite it to an unrelated passage, which looks more credible than no citation at all, and is arguably worse.
* **Assuming a passed citation check guarantees the claim is true.** Attribution checks that a claim is *similar* to a retrieved passage, not that the passage (or the claim drawn from it) is actually accurate.
* **Running attribution only after the full answer is generated, with no way to revise.** A claim that fails attribution has already been written and shown — attribution alone doesn't prevent an unsupported claim from reaching the user, only detects it.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. In the worked example, why does the third claim fail to get cited even though it finds a "best match" among the retrieved passages?</summary>
Every claim has some best match by construction (whichever passage is relatively closest), but that best match's similarity (0.781) falls below the citation threshold (0.8), signaling that even the closest passage isn't actually close enough to count as real support.
</details>

<details><summary>2. What's the risk of setting the citation threshold too low?</summary>
An unsupported or fabricated claim can end up cited to an unrelated passage just because it happens to be the closest match among a weak field — a false citation that looks just as trustworthy as a real one.
</details>

<details><summary>3. Does passing the citation check guarantee a claim is factually correct?</summary>
No — it only confirms the claim is similar to a retrieved passage, which could itself be inaccurate, outdated, or simply misread by the generating model in a way that still happens to resemble its source.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Citation:** linking a specific claim in a generated answer to the retrieved passage that supports it.
* **Source attribution:** the broader practice of tracing generated content back to its retrieved origins.
* **Citation threshold:** the minimum similarity a claim's best-matching passage must reach to be cited rather than flagged unsupported.

## Related

[[Dense Retrieval]] · [[Grounded Generation and Faithfulness]] · [[Common RAG Failure Modes]]

## Handling Noisy or Conflicting Retrieved Context

Retrieval sometimes returns two passages that answer the same question differently — an old policy document and a new one, say, each stating a different number for the same thing. Handing both to the generating model unresolved just moves the conflict downstream, where it's far harder to detect than it was at retrieval time, when the two passages' metadata was right there to check.

**You need:** [[Metadata Extraction and Enrichment]], [[Metadata Filtering and Hybrid Indexes]].

## The question it answers

"What should happen when retrieved passages disagree with each other?" The same metadata that lets a system identify a stale chunk (already covered in [[Metadata Extraction and Enrichment]]) can resolve a conflict between two retrieved passages before generation ever sees both of them: keep the most recent one, as judged by its own metadata, and discard the other — rather than leaving the generating model to somehow notice the contradiction and guess which one to trust.

## Intuition

Handing someone two different printed versions of the same policy, with no publication dates visible, and asking them to figure out which one is current puts them in an impossible position — they have no way to tell without additional information. Checking the dates yourself first and handing over only the current one removes the ambiguity before it ever reaches them.

## Definition and notation

```text
resolve(passages) = passage with the most recent date, among those genuinely answering the same question
```

## A worked example

Two retrieved passages giving different numbers for the same policy:

```text
[2022-01-01] "Shipping takes 3-5 days."
[2025-09-01] "Shipping takes 2-3 days."

unresolved: both passages reach generation — the model has to somehow notice and arbitrate the contradiction
resolved by freshness: only [2025-09-01] "Shipping takes 2-3 days." reaches generation
```

Without resolution, the generating model sees two conflicting numbers with no signal pointing to which one is right — it might blend them, pick one arbitrarily, or even mention both as if the policy itself were ambiguous. Resolving by freshness beforehand removes the conflict entirely: generation only ever sees the one passage judged current.

## Bench

```bench
id: conflicting-context-resolve
title: Two passages, two different answers
fallback: Toggle a freshness-based resolution and watch which of two conflicting passages wins.
```

**Try this**

1. Look at the unresolved view and note both conflicting passages are present.
2. Turn on resolution and see only the more recent one remain.
3. Imagine a case where the *older* passage is actually the correct one (a reverted policy change) — would freshness-based resolution get this wrong?

**What you should notice:** resolving by freshness is a specific, sometimes-wrong heuristic — it works when "more recent" really does mean "more correct," which is common but not universal.

## Where it appears in AI

* **This directly reuses [[Metadata Extraction and Enrichment]]'s freshness-filtering mechanism**, applied here to resolve a conflict between retrieved passages rather than to exclude stale ones from the retrieval set in the first place.
* **[[Corrective RAG]] covers a broader version of "something's wrong with what was retrieved"** — conflicting context is one specific, detectable case among the general retrieval-quality problems it addresses.
* **An unresolved conflict that reaches generation is exactly the kind of input that undermines [[Grounded Generation and Faithfulness]]** — a model can't be faithful to context that contradicts itself.

## Common pitfalls

* **Assuming "more recent" always means "more correct."** A policy that was briefly changed and then reverted could leave an older passage as the actually-correct one — freshness-based resolution would get this backwards.
* **Detecting conflicts only by checking dates, missing conflicts that aren't about recency at all.** Two passages from the same date can still disagree for other reasons (one covering a different region, a different product tier) that freshness-based resolution does nothing to address.
* **Resolving a conflict silently, with no trace that one was ever detected.** Losing the fact that a conflict existed at all makes it harder to audit or debug later why one passage was chosen over another.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. In the worked example, why does resolving by freshness keep the 2025 passage over the 2022 one?</summary>
The resolution rule specifically selects the most recent passage by its date metadata, on the assumption that a more recently published statement is more likely to reflect the current, correct policy.
</details>

<details><summary>2. When would resolving by freshness give the wrong answer?</summary>
When an older passage happens to be the actually-correct one — for instance, if a policy was changed and then reverted, the most recent document about the change might not reflect the policy that's actually back in effect.
</details>

<details><summary>3. What's the cost of leaving a conflict unresolved and passing both passages to generation?</summary>
The generating model has to somehow notice and arbitrate the contradiction on its own, with no guarantee it will — it might blend the two conflicting numbers, pick one arbitrarily, or present the conflict as if the underlying fact were genuinely ambiguous.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Conflicting context:** two or more retrieved passages that answer the same question with different, incompatible information.
* **Freshness-based resolution:** resolving a conflict by keeping the most recently dated passage and discarding the others.
* **Context noise:** retrieved content that is irrelevant, contradictory, or otherwise unhelpful once it reaches generation.

## Related

[[Metadata Extraction and Enrichment]] · [[Corrective RAG]] · [[Grounded Generation and Faithfulness]]

## Context-Window Budgeting for RAG

Retrieved chunks don't get the entire context window to themselves — a running conversation's own history is sitting in there too, and the two are competing for the exact same limited space. The longer a conversation runs, the less room is left for the chunks retrieval just worked to find.

**You need:** [[Multi-Turn Conversation State and Memory]], [[Cost and Latency of LLM APIs]].

## The question it answers

"How many retrieved chunks actually fit once the rest of the context is accounted for?" A fixed context-window budget has to be split between conversation history (which grows as a chat continues, exactly as [[Multi-Turn Conversation State and Memory]] already covers) and newly retrieved chunks. Whatever conversation history claims first, chunk budget has to come out of what's left — there's no separate pool for each.

## Intuition

Packing a suitcase with a fixed size for both a trip's clothes and the souvenirs bought along the way means the more clothes already packed, the fewer souvenirs fit by the time you're deciding what else to bring home — the suitcase doesn't grow just because there's more to put in it.

## Definition and notation

```text
chunks_that_fit = max(0, floor((budget − conversation_tokens) / tokens_per_chunk))
```

## A worked example

A 2,000-token context budget, 150 tokens per retrieved chunk, at three points in a growing conversation:

```text
conversation history   200 tokens  →  12 chunks fit
conversation history   800 tokens  →   8 chunks fit
conversation history 1,500 tokens  →   3 chunks fit
```

As the conversation grows from 200 to 1,500 tokens — nearly the whole budget — the number of retrieved chunks that still fit drops from 12 down to just 3. By the time conversation history alone approaches the full budget, there's barely any room left for retrieval to contribute anything at all.

## Bench

```bench
id: context-budget-tradeoff
title: Conversation history and retrieved chunks compete for the same space
fallback: Slide conversation history length and watch how many retrieved chunks still fit in a fixed context budget.
```

**Try this**

1. Start with a short conversation and note how many chunks fit.
2. Slide conversation length up toward the budget's limit and watch the chunk count collapse.
3. Imagine a long-running support chat — at what point does retrieval stop being able to contribute meaningfully?

**What you should notice:** this isn't a RAG-specific problem invented from scratch — it's the same fixed-budget trade-off [[Multi-Turn Conversation State and Memory]] already covers for conversation history alone, with retrieved chunks now added as a second claimant on the same space.

## Where it appears in AI

* **This directly extends [[Multi-Turn Conversation State and Memory]]'s token-growth problem**, adding retrieved chunks as a second consumer of the same fixed budget conversation history was already competing for.
* **[[Context Window Extension Techniques]] (longer context windows) is one way to relax this trade-off**, though [[Context Rot and Lost-in-the-Middle Effects]] shows a bigger window doesn't automatically mean every chunk inside it gets used equally well.
* **A tighter budget makes [[Re-Ranking Retrieved Results]]'s shortlist size an even more consequential choice** — when only a handful of chunks fit at all, which ones make that handful matters more.

## Common pitfalls

* **Treating the context budget as infinite because "the context window is huge now."** Even a large window has a limit, and conversation history alone can consume a meaningful fraction of it in a long-running chat.
* **Summarizing conversation history to free up room without considering what gets lost.** The same trade-off [[Multi-Turn Conversation State and Memory]] covers (summarization saves tokens but drops detail) applies doubly here, since the freed room goes toward chunks instead of more conversation detail.
* **Keeping chunk count fixed regardless of conversation length, and silently truncating something else when the budget runs out.** Without an explicit allocation rule, running out of room can cut off conversation history, a retrieved chunk, or even part of the question itself in unpredictable ways.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. In the worked example, why does the number of chunks that fit drop so sharply as conversation history grows?</summary>
The chunk budget is whatever's left over after conversation history's share is subtracted from the fixed total — as conversation history claims more of that fixed total, proportionally less remains for chunks, each of which still costs the same 150 tokens.
</details>

<details><summary>2. Does a larger context window eliminate this trade-off entirely?</summary>
It relaxes it by raising the total budget, but doesn't eliminate it — conversation history can still grow to consume a large fraction of any fixed window, and a bigger window introduces its own lost-in-the-middle risk for whatever does fit.
</details>

<details><summary>3. What are the two things competing for the same context-window budget in this topic?</summary>
Conversation history (the accumulated prior turns of the chat) and newly retrieved chunks (the context fetched for the current question) — both need space from the same fixed total.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Context budget:** the fixed total token capacity available for a single request's prompt.
* **Token allocation:** how a fixed budget is divided between competing consumers (conversation history, retrieved chunks).
* **Budget collapse:** the point at which growing conversation history leaves too little room for retrieved content to contribute meaningfully.

## Related

[[Multi-Turn Conversation State and Memory]] · [[Context Window Extension Techniques]] · [[Re-Ranking Retrieved Results]]

## Grounded Generation and Faithfulness

Retrieving the right passages doesn't guarantee the generated answer actually uses them. A model can still fall back on what it already "knows" from pretraining, blending retrieved facts with unretrieved ones in a way that's indistinguishable from the outside — unless each individual claim is checked against what was actually retrieved.

**You need:** [[Citation and Source Attribution]].

## The question it answers

"How do you measure whether an answer is actually grounded in what was retrieved, as a whole?" **Faithfulness** aggregates [[Citation and Source Attribution|the per-claim citation check]] into a single score for the entire answer: the fraction of its claims that have some retrieved passage supporting them above a similarity threshold. An answer where every claim traces back to a retrieved passage is fully grounded; one with claims that don't match anything retrieved has, to that same degree, drawn on something other than what was actually given to it.

## Intuition

Grading an essay for whether it actually uses the assigned readings (as opposed to being well-written in general) means checking, sentence by sentence, whether each claim traces back to something in those readings — a single unsupported claim doesn't necessarily make the whole essay bad, but it does mean the essay isn't fully grounded in the material it was supposed to be based on.

## Definition and notation

```text
faithfulness(answer) = (claims with supporting passage above threshold) / (total claims in answer)
```

## A worked example

A three-claim answer, checked against two retrieved passages at a 0.8 similarity threshold:

```text
"Refunds are issued within 5 business days."  → supported (similarity 1.000)
"Shipping takes 3-5 days."                     → supported (similarity 1.000)
"The company was founded in 1998."             → unsupported (best similarity only 0.781)

faithfulness: 2 of 3 claims supported = 0.667

if the unsupported claim were dropped from the answer: 2 of 2 claims supported = 1.000
```

Two-thirds of this answer is grounded in what was actually retrieved; the third claim appears to have come from somewhere else entirely — the model's own pretrained knowledge, most likely, rather than the passages it was given. Removing that one claim would make the remaining answer fully faithful.

## Bench

```bench
id: faithfulness-score
title: What fraction of the answer is actually grounded?
fallback: Toggle an unsupported claim in/out of an answer and watch the faithfulness score respond.
```

**Try this**

1. Look at the faithfulness score with all three claims included.
2. Remove the unsupported claim and watch the score reach 1.0.
3. Consider what a faithfulness score of exactly 0.0 would mean about an answer.

**What you should notice:** faithfulness measures whether an answer is grounded in its retrieved context — it says nothing about whether the answer is otherwise correct, well-written, or even helpful; a fully faithful answer can still be an unhelpful or incomplete one.

## Where it appears in AI

* **This directly aggregates [[Citation and Source Attribution]]'s per-claim check** into a single number for the whole answer, rather than a list of individual citations.
* **[[Faithfulness and Answer Relevancy Metrics]] covers how this score fits into a broader RAG evaluation suite** — faithfulness measures groundedness specifically, separate from whether the answer actually addresses the question (relevancy).
* **A low faithfulness score is a strong, specific signal pointing to exactly the kind of problem [[Common RAG Failure Modes]] catalogs as "generation ignored or went beyond the retrieved context."**

## Common pitfalls

* **Treating a high faithfulness score as proof the answer is correct.** Faithfulness only measures whether claims trace back to retrieved passages — if those passages are themselves wrong, a fully faithful answer would faithfully repeat that wrongness.
* **Treating a low faithfulness score as proof of a "bad" answer in every sense.** An unsupported claim could be the model correctly adding well-known general knowledge that happens not to be in the retrieved passages — faithfulness flags this as unsupported regardless of whether the claim itself is true.
* **Measuring faithfulness without a sensible similarity threshold.** Too low a threshold credits unsupported claims with false citations (as the worked example's 0.781-scoring claim would be if the threshold were set below that); too high a threshold can mark genuinely supported claims as unfaithful.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. In the worked example, why is the faithfulness score 0.667 rather than some other fraction?</summary>
Two of the answer's three claims have a supporting passage above the 0.8 threshold, and one doesn't — 2 divided by 3 is approximately 0.667.
</details>

<details><summary>2. Does a faithfulness score of 1.0 guarantee the answer is factually correct?</summary>
No — it only means every claim traces back to a retrieved passage above the similarity threshold; if the retrieved passages themselves contain errors, a fully faithful answer would still repeat those errors.
</details>

<details><summary>3. What's the difference between a faithfulness problem and a relevancy problem for a generated answer?</summary>
Faithfulness measures whether the answer's claims are grounded in what was retrieved; relevancy measures whether the answer actually addresses the question asked — an answer can be fully faithful to irrelevant retrieved passages, or relevant to the question while including ungrounded claims.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Faithfulness:** the fraction of a generated answer's claims that are supported by retrieved context.
* **Grounded generation:** generation that draws its claims from retrieved context rather than unretrieved, pretrained knowledge.
* **Unsupported claim:** a generated claim with no sufficiently similar retrieved passage backing it.

## Related

[[Citation and Source Attribution]] · [[Faithfulness and Answer Relevancy Metrics]] · [[Common RAG Failure Modes]]

## Evaluating RAG Systems

A RAG system can fail in two independent places — retrieval can find the wrong passages, or generation can answer badly even from the right ones — and a single end-to-end score can't tell you which. This district covers measuring each half separately, then together.

Topics on this stretch of the road:

* [[Retrieval Metrics: Precision, Recall, MRR and NDCG]]: scoring whether the right passages were found, and how high they ranked.
* [[Faithfulness and Answer Relevancy Metrics]]: scoring whether the generated answer actually uses, and actually answers, what was retrieved.
* [[End-to-End RAG Evaluation Frameworks]]: combining retrieval and generation scores into one evaluation pipeline.
* [[Common RAG Failure Modes]]: the handful of ways a RAG system typically breaks, and which stage each one points to.
* [[Synthetic Test-Set Generation for RAG]]: building an evaluation set without hand-writing every question.
* [[A-B and Online Evaluation of RAG]]: measuring a RAG system against real users instead of a fixed test set.

## Retrieval Metrics: Precision, Recall, MRR and NDCG

Precision and recall, already covered as classification metrics, adapt naturally to retrieval — but a ranked list has structure a classifier's yes/no decision doesn't: *where* a relevant result lands matters, not just whether it's present at all. MRR and NDCG are specifically about that ordering, in two different ways.

**You need:** [[Precision, Recall and F1]].

## The question it answers

"How do you score a ranked list of retrieved documents, not just a yes/no classification?" **Precision@k** and **recall@k** apply [[Precision, Recall and F1|the same precision/recall definitions]] to just the top k results. **MRR (mean reciprocal rank)** looks only at where the *first* relevant result lands — 1/(its position) — rewarding a system that puts something useful right at the top, however the rest of the ranking looks. **NDCG (normalized discounted cumulative gain)** goes further: it uses *graded* relevance (not just relevant/irrelevant) and discounts each result by how far down the ranking it sits, normalized against the best possible ordering of the same results.

## Intuition

Judging a search engine's top 5 results only by how many are relevant (precision@5) misses *where* the good ones landed — a search with the single best result at position 1 feels very different from one with it buried at position 5, even if both have the same precision@5. MRR and NDCG are specifically about rewarding that difference.

## Definition and notation

```text
precision@k = (relevant results in top k) / k
recall@k    = (relevant results in top k) / (total relevant results)
MRR         = 1 / (rank of the first relevant result)
NDCG@k      = DCG@k / ideal_DCG@k,   where DCG@k = Σ gain_i / log2(i + 1)
```

## A worked example

A 5-result ranking, with 2 truly relevant documents (graded relevance 3 and 2) out of a 5-document collection:

```text
rank 1: d3 (relevant, gain 3)
rank 2: d1 (not relevant)
rank 3: d5 (relevant, gain 2)
rank 4: d2 (not relevant)
rank 5: d4 (not relevant)

precision@1: 1.000   recall@1: 0.500
precision@3: 0.667   recall@3: 1.000
precision@5: 0.400   recall@5: 1.000

MRR: 1.000  (the very first result is relevant)
NDCG@3: 0.939
NDCG@5: 0.939  (unchanged past k=3, since nothing relevant appears after rank 3)
```

MRR is a perfect 1.0 because the top result happens to be relevant — it doesn't care that the second relevant result is further down. NDCG@3 at 0.939 reflects that the ranking is *close* to ideal but not quite: the higher-gain document (gain 3) is correctly first, but the gap between that and the true ideal ordering (which would put both relevant documents even more favorably) costs a small amount of discounted gain.

## Bench

```bench
id: retrieval-ranking-metrics
title: Different metrics, same ranked list
fallback: Slide k and switch metrics to see precision, recall, MRR and NDCG score the same ranked list differently.
```

**Try this**

1. Slide k from 1 to 5 and watch precision fall while recall rises.
2. Note that MRR doesn't change at all as k changes — it only depends on the first relevant result's position.
3. Compare NDCG@3 and NDCG@5 — why do they come out identical here?

**What you should notice:** these four metrics aren't redundant — each one is sensitive to a different aspect of the same ranked list (how many of the top k are relevant, how much of all relevant content got surfaced, where the first good result landed, how close to ideal the whole ordering is).

## Where it appears in AI

* **Precision@k and recall@k reuse [[Precision, Recall and F1]]'s exact definitions**, just restricted to the top k results — this topic is about the retrieval-specific adaptation and the two new rank-aware metrics, not re-deriving precision and recall themselves.
* **These metrics are exactly what [[Re-Ranking Retrieved Results]] is trying to improve** — a re-ranker's whole job is to push NDCG and MRR up by getting the ordering closer to ideal, even when the same set of documents was already retrieved.
* **[[End-to-End RAG Evaluation Frameworks]] uses these as the "retrieval half" of a full evaluation suite**, paired with generation-side metrics like faithfulness.

## Common pitfalls

* **Using precision@k alone and ignoring recall.** A system that only ever returns 1 result can score a perfect precision@1 while missing most of the truly relevant documents in the collection — recall catches this, precision alone doesn't.
* **Assuming MRR and NDCG measure the same thing.** MRR only cares about the position of the *first* relevant result; NDCG accounts for every result's graded relevance and position — two rankings can tie on MRR while differing substantially on NDCG.
* **Forgetting that NDCG needs a sensible "ideal" ordering to normalize against.** If the graded relevance values themselves are poorly calibrated, NDCG's normalization won't fix that underlying problem.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. Why does MRR stay the same regardless of which k value you choose, while precision@k and recall@k both change?</summary>
MRR only depends on the position of the single first relevant result in the whole ranking, which doesn't change as you consider more or fewer top results — precision and recall are both computed specifically over the top k, so they shift as k changes.
</details>

<details><summary>2. In the worked example, why is NDCG@3 less than 1.0 even though the highest-gain document is ranked first?</summary>
NDCG compares the actual ranking's discounted gain against the *ideal* ordering's discounted gain; here the second relevant document (gain 2) sits at rank 3 rather than rank 2, so its contribution is discounted slightly more than it would be under the ideal ordering.
</details>

<details><summary>3. When would MRR be a more appropriate metric than NDCG?</summary>
When all that matters is getting at least one good result near the top quickly (as in many search or question-answering use cases) — MRR directly rewards that and ignores the rest of the ranking, which NDCG's full-list weighting doesn't isolate as cleanly.
</details>

## Key terms

* **MRR (mean reciprocal rank):** the reciprocal of the position of the first relevant result in a ranking.
* **NDCG (normalized discounted cumulative gain):** a ranking metric using graded relevance, discounted by position, normalized against the ideal ordering.
* **Graded relevance:** a relevance score with more than two levels (not just relevant/irrelevant), as NDCG uses.

## Related

[[Precision, Recall and F1]] · [[Re-Ranking Retrieved Results]] · [[End-to-End RAG Evaluation Frameworks]]

## Faithfulness and Answer Relevancy Metrics

An answer can be perfectly grounded in its retrieved context and still completely fail to address what was asked — faithful to the wrong thing. Or it can directly, confidently answer the actual question while drawing on nothing that was ever retrieved. Faithfulness and answer relevancy measure these two failure directions separately, because an answer can fail at either one independently of the other.

**You need:** [[Grounded Generation and Faithfulness]].

## The question it answers

"Can an answer fail in two genuinely different ways, and does that require two separate metrics?" [[Grounded Generation and Faithfulness|Faithfulness]] measures whether an answer's claims are grounded in retrieved context. **Answer relevancy** measures something independent: how closely the answer actually addresses the question asked, typically by comparing the question's and the answer's embeddings directly. A grounded-but-off-topic answer and an on-topic-but-ungrounded answer fail in opposite ways, and a single combined score would hide which one happened.

## Intuition

A student asked "what time does the library close" who answers, word for word, something true from the assigned reading about library opening hours is being faithful to their source — and still hasn't answered the actual question. A student who confidently answers "9pm" from memory, with no source at all, has answered relevantly — and has nothing grounding that answer. Both responses fail, in opposite ways.

## Definition and notation

```text
faithfulness(answer)     = fraction of claims grounded in retrieved context
answer_relevancy(answer) = cosine_similarity(embed(question), embed(answer))
```

## A worked example

Two answers to "how long do refunds take," each failing a different one of the two metrics:

```text
"grounded, but off-topic":  answer about shipping (matches a retrieved passage about shipping)
  faithfulness: 1.000  (fully grounded in something retrieved)
  answer relevancy: 0.220  (barely related to the actual question asked)

"on-topic, but ungrounded":  a confident-sounding answer about refund timing, not matching any retrieved passage
  faithfulness: 0.000  (nothing retrieved supports it)
  answer relevancy: 0.998  (closely matches what the question was actually asking)
```

Neither answer scores well on both metrics. The first is entirely faithful to something retrieved, but that something isn't what was asked about. The second directly addresses the question, but has no grounding in anything actually retrieved — exactly the kind of answer that sounds right while potentially being wrong.

## Bench

```bench
id: faithfulness-vs-relevancy
title: Two different ways an answer can go wrong
fallback: Compare two answers that each fail one of faithfulness and answer relevancy, but not the other.
```

**Try this**

1. Look at the "grounded, but off-topic" scenario's two scores.
2. Switch to "on-topic, but ungrounded" and watch which score flips.
3. Consider what an answer scoring well on *both* metrics at once would actually look like.

**What you should notice:** these two scenarios are, in a sense, mirror images of each other — each is strong on exactly the metric the other is weak on, which is precisely why a single blended score would obscure what's actually wrong.

## Where it appears in AI

* **Faithfulness here is exactly the metric [[Grounded Generation and Faithfulness]] already derived** — this topic adds answer relevancy as its necessary complement.
* **[[End-to-End RAG Evaluation Frameworks]] combines both of these with the retrieval-side metrics** ([[Retrieval Metrics: Precision, Recall, MRR and NDCG]]) into a single scorecard that can localize which pipeline stage is actually weak.
* **[[Common RAG Failure Modes]] lists specific symptoms traceable to a low score on one of these two metrics but not the other** — a diagnostic use of exactly this distinction.

## Common pitfalls

* **Averaging faithfulness and answer relevancy into one number before looking at either individually.** The worked example's two scenarios would average to a similar-looking combined score despite failing in completely different ways — the individual breakdown is what actually tells you what's wrong.
* **Assuming a high relevancy score means the answer is trustworthy.** The "on-topic, but ungrounded" scenario scores 0.998 on relevancy while being entirely unsupported — relevancy says nothing about whether the content is grounded.
* **Assuming a high faithfulness score means the answer is useful.** The "grounded, but off-topic" scenario is perfectly faithful to a passage that doesn't answer the question at all.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. Why can an answer score perfectly on faithfulness while scoring poorly on answer relevancy?</summary>
Faithfulness only checks whether an answer's claims trace back to some retrieved passage — it says nothing about whether that passage, or the resulting answer, actually addresses the specific question that was asked.
</details>

<details><summary>2. In the worked example, what specifically makes the "on-topic, but ungrounded" answer risky despite its high relevancy score?</summary>
It directly and confidently addresses the question asked (high relevancy), but nothing in the retrieved context actually supports it (zero faithfulness) — meaning its content may have come entirely from the model's own unretrieved, possibly outdated or incorrect, knowledge.
</details>

<details><summary>3. Why would averaging these two metrics into a single score be misleading?</summary>
Two very different failure modes (grounded-but-irrelevant and relevant-but-ungrounded) could produce similar average scores, hiding which specific problem actually occurred and therefore which stage of the pipeline needs fixing.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Answer relevancy:** how closely a generated answer's embedding matches the question's embedding.
* **Faithfulness:** the fraction of an answer's claims grounded in retrieved context (covered in depth in [[Grounded Generation and Faithfulness]]).
* **Independent failure modes:** two ways an answer can go wrong that don't imply or predict each other.

## Related

[[Grounded Generation and Faithfulness]] · [[End-to-End RAG Evaluation Frameworks]] · [[Common RAG Failure Modes]]

## End-to-End RAG Evaluation Frameworks

Two RAG systems can score identically on an overall end-to-end quality check and still be broken in completely different places — one failing at retrieval, the other at generation. A single pass/fail number can't tell them apart; a full scorecard, broken out by stage, can.

**You need:** [[Retrieval Metrics: Precision, Recall, MRR and NDCG]], [[Faithfulness and Answer Relevancy Metrics]].

## The question it answers

"How do you combine retrieval-side and generation-side metrics into one evaluation that actually localizes problems?" An end-to-end framework runs a scorecard of several metrics at once — retrieval metrics like context precision and context recall, generation metrics like faithfulness and answer relevancy — and looks at the *lowest* score to identify which specific stage of the pipeline is actually weak, rather than relying on one blended number that could hide the problem.

## Intuition

A car that fails inspection on exactly one system — brakes, say — needs the same single clear flag whether every other system passed with flying colors or barely scraped by. A combined "67% roadworthy" score tells you nothing about which system to actually fix; a full checklist, item by item, does.

## Definition and notation

```text
scorecard = { contextPrecision, contextRecall, faithfulness, answerRelevancy, ... }
weakest_stage = the metric with the lowest score, and whichever pipeline stage it belongs to
```

## A worked example

Two systems, each strong on one half of the pipeline and weak on the other:

```text
System A: contextPrecision 0.90, contextRecall 0.85, faithfulness 0.30, answerRelevancy 0.90
  → weakest metric: faithfulness (0.30) → retrieval is fine, generation is the problem

System B: contextPrecision 0.40, contextRecall 0.35, faithfulness 0.90, answerRelevancy 0.85
  → weakest metric: contextRecall (0.35) → generation is fine, retrieval is the problem
```

Both systems could easily land at a similar *average* score across all four metrics — but their weakest individual metric points at completely different places to fix. System A's retrieval is working well; its generation stage is ignoring good context. System B's generation is working well; it's simply not finding enough of the right context to work with in the first place.

## Bench

```bench
id: rag-scorecard
title: The lowest score names the broken stage
fallback: Compare two RAG systems' full metric scorecards and spot which pipeline stage is actually weak in each.
```

**Try this**

1. Look at System A's full scorecard and find its weakest metric.
2. Switch to System B and find its weakest metric.
3. Imagine averaging all four metrics for each system — would that average alone tell you where to look?

**What you should notice:** the weakest individual metric, not the average, is what actually tells you which stage of the pipeline needs attention — the two systems' averages could be deceptively similar despite having opposite problems.

## Where it appears in AI

* **This combines exactly [[Retrieval Metrics: Precision, Recall, MRR and NDCG]] and [[Faithfulness and Answer Relevancy Metrics]]** into one scorecard — the framework's value is in combining them, not in any new metric of its own.
* **Diagnosing System A's problem (good retrieval, bad generation) points directly at [[Grounded Generation and Faithfulness]] as the place to fix it; System B's problem points at the retrieval strategies covered across this planet's earlier districts.**
* **[[Common RAG Failure Modes]] catalogs the specific symptoms each kind of weak metric tends to produce**, giving a faster first guess before running the full scorecard.

## Common pitfalls

* **Reporting a single blended quality score for a RAG system.** The worked example's two systems show exactly how this can mask which stage actually needs work, even when the overall averages look deceptively similar.
* **Running only generation-side metrics because they're easier to compute.** System B's problem is entirely on the retrieval side — a generation-only evaluation would never surface it, and might even look reasonably healthy.
* **Treating the scorecard as a one-time evaluation rather than a recurring check.** A system that scores well today can regress in just one metric after a change (a new embedding model, an index rebuild) — only re-running the full scorecard would catch which specific metric moved.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. In the worked example, why does focusing on the lowest-scoring metric matter more than averaging all four?</summary>
Averaging can produce similar-looking overall scores for systems with completely different underlying problems, while the lowest individual metric directly identifies which stage is actually failing.
</details>

<details><summary>2. What does System A's scorecard suggest about where to focus improvement effort?</summary>
Its context precision and recall are both strong, meaning retrieval is finding good context; its faithfulness is weak, meaning the generation stage isn't actually using that good context well — the fix belongs in generation, not retrieval.
</details>

<details><summary>3. Could a system score well on every metric and still produce a bad answer?</summary>
In principle a system could still produce answers a human judges unsatisfying for reasons none of these specific metrics capture (tone, completeness, formatting) — the scorecard measures the dimensions it's designed to measure, not every possible way an answer can fall short.
</details>

## Key terms

* **End-to-end evaluation framework:** a combined scorecard covering both retrieval-side and generation-side metrics.
* **Context precision/recall:** retrieval-side metrics measuring how much of the retrieved context is relevant, and how much of the relevant content was retrieved.
* **Stage localization:** identifying which specific pipeline stage (retrieval vs. generation) a low score points to.

## Related

[[Retrieval Metrics: Precision, Recall, MRR and NDCG]] · [[Faithfulness and Answer Relevancy Metrics]] · [[Common RAG Failure Modes]]

## Common RAG Failure Modes

Across this planet's road, the same handful of failure symptoms keep recurring — a stale fact, a result count that's mysteriously short, an answer that confidently cites the wrong thing. Recognizing a symptom quickly, and knowing which earlier topic actually fixes it, turns debugging a RAG system from guesswork into a lookup.

**You need:** [[End-to-End RAG Evaluation Frameworks]].

## The question it answers

"When a RAG system misbehaves, what's the shortest path from the symptom to the fix?" Most RAG failures recur across systems because they trace back to one of a small number of root causes, each already covered earlier on this road: a missing metadata filter, a post-filtering mistake, a vocabulary mismatch, a missing relevance check, or a question requiring more than one retrieval hop. Recognizing the symptom and knowing which earlier topic addresses it is faster than re-deriving the fix from scratch each time.

## Intuition

A mechanic who's seen a thousand cars doesn't start from first principles every time an engine makes a specific noise — a particular knock usually means one of a short list of things, checked in order of likelihood. The same recurring symptoms show up across RAG systems because the same handful of pipeline stages are where things most often go wrong.

## Definition and notation

```text
symptom → likely stage → fix (already covered earlier on this road)
```

## A worked example

Six recurring symptoms, each mapped to its likely stage and fix:

```text
"retrieved a stale version of a fact"
  → retrieval (metadata) → add a freshness filter ([[Metadata Extraction and Enrichment]])

"returned far fewer results than requested"
  → retrieval (filtering) → pre-filter instead of post-filter ([[Metadata Filtering and Hybrid Indexes]])

"missed a query using an exact product code"
  → retrieval (strategy) → add sparse retrieval or hybrid fusion ([[Hybrid Retrieval Fusion]])

"generated a confident answer from irrelevant context"
  → generation (grounding) → add a relevance check ([[Self-RAG and Reflective Retrieval]] / [[Corrective RAG]])

"question needs facts from two different documents"
  → retrieval (strategy) → use multi-hop or graph-based retrieval ([[Multi-Hop and Iterative Retrieval]] / [[Graph-Based RAG]])

"answer doesn't actually use the retrieved context"
  → generation (faithfulness) → measure and enforce faithfulness ([[Grounded Generation and Faithfulness]])
```

Each symptom has a specific, previously-covered cause and fix — none of these require inventing a new technique; they require correctly recognizing which earlier topic the symptom is pointing back to.

## Bench

```bench
id: rag-failure-diagnosis
title: Every symptom points at one stage
fallback: Pick a RAG failure symptom and see which stage and fix it actually points to.
```

**Try this**

1. Pick a symptom and check which stage it points to.
2. Notice two of the symptoms both point to "retrieval (strategy)" for different underlying reasons.
3. Think of a RAG system you've used that exhibited one of these symptoms — does the mapped fix match what you'd expect?

**What you should notice:** several distinct symptoms share the same underlying stage — "retrieval (strategy)" covers both an exact-match miss and a missing multi-hop capability, which are different problems with the same general location in the pipeline.

## Where it appears in AI

* **This is a lookup table over nearly every earlier district on this road** — each row's fix is a specific topic already covered, from [[Metadata Extraction and Enrichment]] in District 2 through [[Grounded Generation and Faithfulness]] in District 7.
* **[[End-to-End RAG Evaluation Frameworks]]'s scorecard is what surfaces which symptom a real system is actually exhibiting**, before this topic's lookup table identifies the likely cause.
* **[[Production RAG Pipeline Architecture]] is where these fixes actually get assembled into a running system**, often addressing several of these failure modes simultaneously by design rather than reactively.

## Common pitfalls

* **Treating every low evaluation score as a generation problem.** Several of the worked example's symptoms are retrieval problems that happen to show up as a bad final answer — fixing generation alone wouldn't help any of them.
* **Assuming a single fix addresses every instance of a given symptom.** "Retrieved a stale fact" could also stem from the document collection simply never being updated at all, which no amount of freshness filtering fixes if the current version was never indexed.
* **Debugging by guesswork instead of checking the evaluation scorecard first.** [[End-to-End RAG Evaluation Frameworks]]'s metrics are what tell you *which* symptom you're actually facing before you reach for a specific fix.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. Why do "missed a query using an exact product code" and "question needs facts from two different documents" both get mapped to "retrieval (strategy)" despite being different problems?</summary>
Both are fundamentally about the retrieval strategy being insufficient for a specific kind of query — one needs exact-match capability (sparse or hybrid retrieval) and the other needs multi-step retrieval (multi-hop or graph-based) — different fixes, but both located at the retrieval-strategy stage rather than generation.
</details>

<details><summary>2. What's the fastest way to find out which specific symptom a real RAG system is exhibiting?</summary>
Running the scorecard from [[End-to-End RAG Evaluation Frameworks]] — its breakdown by metric points toward which stage (and likely which symptom from this topic's list) is actually responsible, rather than guessing from the final answer alone.
</details>

<details><summary>3. Does every RAG failure trace back to one of these six specific symptoms?</summary>
No — this is a list of commonly recurring symptoms, not an exhaustive taxonomy; a real system can fail in ways specific to its own data or use case that don't match any of these patterns exactly.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Failure mode:** a recurring, recognizable way a RAG system produces a bad result.
* **Symptom-to-fix mapping:** associating an observed problem with the specific pipeline stage and technique that addresses it.
* **Root cause:** the underlying pipeline stage responsible for a surface-level symptom.

## Related

[[End-to-End RAG Evaluation Frameworks]] · [[Metadata Filtering and Hybrid Indexes]] · [[Production RAG Pipeline Architecture]]

## Synthetic Test-Set Generation for RAG

Hand-writing one evaluation question per chunk doesn't scale — a person can write maybe a few dozen good questions in a day, but a real document collection can hold thousands or millions of chunks. Generating test questions automatically, one per chunk, using a model, scales to the whole collection at once.

**You need:** [[End-to-End RAG Evaluation Frameworks]].

## The question it answers

"How do you build an evaluation set large enough to actually represent a real document collection?" **Synthetic test-set generation** prompts a model to produce a plausible question (and its expected answer) directly from each chunk — automatically creating (question, answer, source chunk) triples at the same rate chunks exist, rather than at the rate a human can write by hand. Coverage scales with the corpus automatically; hand-written coverage is capped by how much human time is available.

## Intuition

Spot-checking a textbook's quality by hand-writing one review question per chapter works fine for a 10-chapter book, but completely fails to scale to a 10,000-page reference library — automating "generate one question per section" is the only way to get evaluation coverage across something that large.

## Definition and notation

```text
hand-written coverage  = min(corpus size, writing rate × hours available)
synthetic coverage     = corpus size   (one generated question per chunk, automatically)
```

## A worked example

Coverage at three corpus sizes, comparing one workday of hand-writing (at 10 questions/hour) against synthetic generation:

```text
corpus    50 chunks:  hand-written covers 50  (100%)   synthetic covers 50  (100%)
corpus   500 chunks:  hand-written covers 80  (16%)    synthetic covers 500 (100%)
corpus 5,000 chunks:  hand-written covers 80  (2%)     synthetic covers 5,000 (100%)
```

At a small corpus size, hand-writing keeps up easily. Past a few hundred chunks, a single workday's hand-written coverage stays flat at 80 questions (the most one person can write in that time) while the corpus keeps growing — coverage collapses to single-digit percentages. Synthetic generation's coverage scales with the corpus by construction, staying at 100% regardless of size.

## Bench

```bench
id: synthetic-testset-coverage
title: One workday of writing questions by hand
fallback: Slide corpus size and compare how much of it a human could hand-write test questions for against automatic synthetic generation.
```

**Try this**

1. Start at a small corpus size and note hand-written coverage is still near 100%.
2. Slide toward 5,000 and watch hand-written coverage collapse toward single digits.
3. Imagine a real production collection with a million chunks — what would hand-written coverage be?

**What you should notice:** hand-written coverage isn't gradually declining — it's capped at a fixed number of questions (however many a workday allows), so its *percentage* coverage drops sharply as the corpus simply grows past that fixed cap.

## Where it appears in AI

* **A synthetic test set is exactly what [[End-to-End RAG Evaluation Frameworks]]'s scorecard needs to run against** — the scorecard's metrics are only as representative as the test set they're computed over.
* **The question-generation step is itself a generation task**, subject to the same risk of producing plausible-but-wrong content covered broadly on the Generative AI planet — a generated question's "expected answer" still needs some form of validation.
* **[[A-B and Online Evaluation of RAG]] is a complementary approach**: instead of a synthetic (or hand-written) fixed test set, it measures quality against real user interactions directly.

## Common pitfalls

* **Trusting generated questions and answers without any validation.** A model generating a question from a chunk can also generate a subtly wrong expected answer — synthetic generation solves the coverage problem, not the correctness problem.
* **Generating only easy, directly-stated questions.** A model prompted naively tends to generate questions that restate a chunk's content almost verbatim, missing the harder multi-hop or inference-based questions a real evaluation should also cover.
* **Assuming 100% chunk coverage means 100% meaningful evaluation.** Covering every chunk with one question each doesn't test multi-chunk reasoning, conflicting-context handling, or any of the failure modes [[Common RAG Failure Modes]] catalogs that only show up with harder, multi-part questions.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. In the worked example, why does hand-written coverage stay at 80 questions regardless of corpus size past a few hundred chunks?</summary>
80 questions is the fixed cap of what one person can write in a single workday at 10 questions per hour — that absolute number doesn't grow just because the corpus does, so its *percentage* of the corpus shrinks as the corpus grows.
</details>

<details><summary>2. Does synthetic test-set generation solve the problem of verifying that generated questions and answers are actually correct?</summary>
No — it solves the coverage problem (having an evaluation question for every chunk), not the correctness problem; generated questions and their expected answers can still be subtly wrong and need their own validation.
</details>

<details><summary>3. What kind of evaluation question does naive synthetic generation tend to miss?</summary>
Harder questions requiring reasoning across multiple chunks or handling conflicting information — a model prompted to generate a question from a single chunk tends to produce questions directly answerable from that one chunk alone.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Synthetic test-set generation:** automatically producing (question, answer, source) evaluation triples from a document collection.
* **Coverage:** the fraction of a corpus that has at least one associated evaluation question.
* **Question-answer triple:** a generated question paired with its expected answer and the source chunk it was derived from.

## Related

[[End-to-End RAG Evaluation Frameworks]] · [[A-B and Online Evaluation of RAG]] · [[Common RAG Failure Modes]]

## A-B and Online Evaluation of RAG

A test set, synthetic or hand-written, measures a RAG system against questions someone anticipated. Real users ask questions nobody anticipated, and their actual satisfaction — a thumbs up, a follow-up question, abandoning the chat — is the measurement that ultimately matters. A/B testing is how you tell whether a change actually helped real users, rather than just scoring better on a fixed benchmark.

**You need:** [[Hypothesis Testing and P-values]], [[End-to-End RAG Evaluation Frameworks]].

## The question it answers

"How do you know a change to a RAG system actually improved things for real users, rather than looking better on paper?" An A/B test routes real traffic to two variants of the system and compares a real outcome metric (thumbs-up rate, follow-up rate) between them. The same [[Hypothesis Testing and P-values|hypothesis-testing]] logic already covered on the Math planet applies directly: an observed difference between two variants' rates isn't automatically trustworthy — it needs enough sample size for the difference to be statistically distinguishable from noise.

## Intuition

Noticing that a coin landed heads 6 times out of 10 flips doesn't prove it's biased — flip it 10,000 times, and a similarly lopsided ratio would be far more convincing. The same logic applies to comparing two RAG variants: a gap that looks real after 100 user interactions each might just be noise, while the identical gap after thousands of interactions each becomes a real signal.

## Definition and notation

```text
z = (p1 − p2) / standard_error(p1, p2, n1, n2)
|z| ≥ 1.96 is the usual cutoff for statistical significance at the 95% confidence level
```

## A worked example

Two RAG variants, A (62% thumbs-up rate) and B (70% thumbs-up rate), tested at two different sample sizes:

```text
n = 100 per variant:   |z| = 1.194  →  not significant at 95% confidence
n = 2,000 per variant: |z| = 5.340  →  significant at 95% confidence
```

The exact same 8-percentage-point gap between A and B isn't trustworthy at a small sample size — it could plausibly be noise. At a larger sample size, the same gap crosses well past the significance threshold, becoming strong evidence that B genuinely performs better, not just that this particular batch of 100 users happened to prefer it.

## Bench

```bench
id: ab-test-significance
title: The same gap, more or less convincing
fallback: Slide sample size and watch the same observed difference between two RAG variants cross the significance threshold.
```

**Try this**

1. Start at a small sample size and note the gap isn't significant.
2. Slide sample size up and watch the z-score cross the 1.96 threshold.
3. Imagine shipping variant B based on the small-sample result alone — what's the risk?

**What you should notice:** the *observed* rates (62% vs. 70%) never change as you slide the sample size — only the *confidence* that this gap reflects something real, rather than noise, changes.

## Where it appears in AI

* **This is a direct application of [[Hypothesis Testing and P-values]]**, already covered in depth on the Math planet — this topic is specifically about applying that logic to RAG variant comparisons, not re-deriving significance testing.
* **An A/B test's outcome metric is often a proxy for exactly what [[Faithfulness and Answer Relevancy Metrics]] measures offline** (a thumbs-up roughly correlating with a relevant, faithful answer) — online evaluation checks whether offline metrics actually predict real user satisfaction.
* **[[Synthetic Test-Set Generation for RAG]] and A/B testing are complementary, not competing**: a synthetic test set catches regressions before deployment; A/B testing catches whether a change that passed offline evaluation actually helps real users.

## Common pitfalls

* **Shipping a change based on a small-sample A/B result that "looks" better.** The worked example's small-sample scenario shows the exact same gap that's meaningful at scale can be statistically indistinguishable from noise with too few observations.
* **Running an A/B test and stopping it as soon as the result looks significant.** Checking significance repeatedly during a test and stopping at the first significant-looking moment inflates the false-positive rate — a pre-committed sample size or duration avoids this.
* **Using an outcome metric that doesn't actually reflect what matters.** A thumbs-up rate is a proxy, not a direct measure of correctness — a system that produces confidently wrong but satisfying-sounding answers could score well on this proxy while actually performing poorly.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. In the worked example, why does the same 8-percentage-point gap between variants A and B become significant only at the larger sample size?</summary>
Statistical significance depends on whether an observed difference is large relative to the *noise* expected from sampling variation, and that noise shrinks as sample size grows — the same absolute gap becomes more and more unlikely to be pure chance as more observations back it up.
</details>

<details><summary>2. What's the risk of shipping a change based on a small, not-yet-significant A/B result?</summary>
The observed improvement might be due to random variation in which users happened to be in each group, rather than the change actually being better — shipping on this basis risks rolling out a change that doesn't actually help, or even hurts, real usage.
</details>

<details><summary>3. Why are A/B testing and offline evaluation (synthetic test sets, the end-to-end scorecard) both still useful, rather than one replacing the other?</summary>
Offline evaluation is fast, repeatable, and catches regressions before anything reaches real users; A/B testing is slower and requires real traffic, but checks whether offline improvements actually translate into better real-world outcomes — each covers a gap the other leaves open.
</details>

## Key terms

* **A/B testing:** comparing two system variants by routing real traffic to each and measuring an outcome metric.
* **Online evaluation:** measuring a system against real user behavior, as opposed to a fixed offline test set.
* **Statistical significance:** whether an observed difference is large enough, relative to sample size, to be distinguishable from random noise.

## Related

[[Hypothesis Testing and P-values]] · [[End-to-End RAG Evaluation Frameworks]] · [[Synthetic Test-Set Generation for RAG]]

## RAG in Practice

Everything on this road so far has covered one piece of a RAG system at a time. This last district is about running the whole thing: the production architecture, what it costs to keep an index current, where it leaks data it shouldn't, and a capstone that follows one question through every stage this planet covered.

Topics on this stretch of the road:

* [[Production RAG Pipeline Architecture]]: how the pieces on this road fit into one running system.
* [[Caching and Incremental Indexing]]: keeping an index current without rebuilding it from scratch.
* [[Cost and Latency of RAG Systems]]: where a RAG request actually spends its time and money, beyond the model call itself.
* [[Security and Data Leakage in RAG]]: what retrieval adds to the list of things that can go wrong with access and privacy.
* [[Capstone: A Question Answered, Traced from Query to Grounded Answer]]: one question, through chunking, embedding, retrieval, re-ranking and grounded generation, end to end.

## Production RAG Pipeline Architecture

Every topic on this road so far has zoomed into one stage of a RAG system. Running the whole thing means those stages have to actually fit together into one pipeline, each one handing its output to the next — and the time each stage takes adds up into a single number a real user actually waits for.

**You need:** [[Anatomy of a RAG Pipeline]], [[Re-Ranking Retrieved Results]].

## The question it answers

"How do all the pieces this planet covered separately fit into one running system?" A production pipeline chains together everything from earlier districts: embed the query, search the vector index, re-rank the shortlist, assemble the context, and generate an answer — each stage built from a specific technique this planet already covered, run in sequence for every single request.

## Intuition

A restaurant kitchen doesn't just have a chef — it has a specific sequence of stations (prep, grill, plating) each handing off to the next, and the total time a diner waits is the sum of however long each station actually takes, not just however good any one station is at its job.

## Definition and notation

```text
total latency = embed_query + vector_search + rerank + assemble + generate
```

## A worked example

A typical request's latency, broken down by stage:

```text
embed query:          15ms   ( 0.6%)
vector search:         20ms   ( 0.8%)
re-rank:                80ms   ( 3.1%)
assemble context:        5ms   ( 0.2%)
generate (LLM call):  2,500ms  (95.4%)
total:                2,620ms
```

Generation dominates the total by a wide margin — everything retrieval contributes (embedding, searching, re-ranking, assembling) adds up to barely 5% of the total request time. The retrieval stages are individually fast; it's the generation call at the end that a user is mostly waiting on.

## Bench

```bench
id: pipeline-latency-breakdown
title: One request, five stages, very unequal shares
fallback: See where a RAG request's total latency actually goes, stage by stage.
```

**Try this**

1. Look at the default breakdown and note how small retrieval's total share is.
2. Slide the re-rank shortlist size up and watch re-ranking's share grow.
3. Imagine re-ranking a shortlist large enough that it actually rivals generation's latency — what shortlist size would that take?

**What you should notice:** even as re-ranking's cost grows with shortlist size, generation stays the dominant cost across a wide range — retrieval has to get dramatically more expensive before it meaningfully changes the total latency a user experiences.

## Where it appears in AI

* **Every stage in this pipeline is a specific technique from an earlier district**: embedding ([[Bi-Encoders and Dense Embeddings]]), searching ([[Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search with HNSW]] or similar), re-ranking ([[Re-Ranking Retrieved Results]]), assembling ([[Context Assembly and Ordering]]), generating ([[Grounded Generation and Faithfulness]]).
* **[[Cost and Latency of RAG Systems]] takes this same breakdown and adds the dollar cost side**, not just timing.
* **[[Caching and Incremental Indexing]] is where this architecture gets optimized further**, specifically targeting the stages whose cost can be avoided on repeated or near-duplicate requests.

## Common pitfalls

* **Optimizing retrieval latency aggressively while generation dominates the total.** The worked example shows retrieval's total share is small enough that even halving it barely moves the overall request time — generation is usually the bigger lever.
* **Assuming every request needs every stage.** [[Self-RAG and Reflective Retrieval]] already showed some queries don't need retrieval at all — a production architecture can route around stages a given request doesn't need.
* **Treating the pipeline as a fixed, one-size-fits-all sequence.** Different query types (a simple lookup vs. a multi-hop question) can benefit from different stage configurations, not the exact same five-stage chain every time.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. In the worked example, why does generation dominate total latency so heavily?</summary>
A single LLM call (2,500ms) is far slower than any of the retrieval-side stages combined (120ms total) — generating text token by token is inherently more time-consuming than the comparison and ranking operations retrieval performs.
</details>
