<details><summary>2. Does optimizing the re-ranking stage meaningfully reduce total latency in this worked example?</summary>
Only modestly — re-ranking is already a small fraction (3.1%) of the total, so even a significant improvement there barely changes the overall request time compared to the dominant generation stage.
</details>

<details><summary>3. Does every RAG request need to go through all five stages?</summary>
Not necessarily — as [[Self-RAG and Reflective Retrieval]] showed, some queries can skip retrieval entirely if the model's own confidence is already high enough.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Production pipeline:** the full chain of stages (embed, search, re-rank, assemble, generate) a real RAG system runs per request.
* **Latency breakdown:** how a request's total time is divided among its constituent stages.
* **Pipeline architecture:** the overall design of how a RAG system's stages connect and hand off to each other.

## Related

[[Anatomy of a RAG Pipeline]] · [[Cost and Latency of RAG Systems]] · [[Caching and Incremental Indexing]]

## Caching and Incremental Indexing

Asking the same question twice shouldn't cost the full pipeline twice — caching the first answer makes the second one nearly free. And adding ten new documents to a hundred-thousand-document index shouldn't mean rebuilding the other 99,990 — incremental indexing updates only what actually changed.

**You need:** [[Production RAG Pipeline Architecture]], [[Vector Databases and Index Management]].

## The question it answers

"How does a production RAG system avoid repeating work it's already done?" **Caching** stores the result of a previous query (or an intermediate step, like an embedding) and serves it again at near-zero cost when the same or a very similar query comes in. **Incremental indexing** adds new documents to an existing index directly, at a cost proportional only to what's being added — rather than rebuilding the entire index from scratch, at a cost proportional to the whole collection, every time anything changes.

## Intuition

A barista who remembers a regular's usual order can make it the moment they walk in, instead of asking every question from scratch each time — that's caching. Expanding a library's catalog by filing ten new books doesn't require re-cataloging the other hundred thousand already on the shelves — that's incremental indexing.

## Definition and notation

```text
cache savings = total_queries × hit_rate × cost_per_query     (approximately free on a cache hit)
incremental index cost  = O(documents added)
full rebuild cost       = O(total documents in the collection)
```

## A worked example

10,000 queries at ~2,620ms each (the full pipeline cost from [[Production RAG Pipeline Architecture]]), at two different cache hit rates:

```text
30% hit rate:  without cache 26,200s total, with cache 18,340s total — 7,860s saved
70% hit rate:  without cache 26,200s total, with cache  7,860s total — 18,340s saved

adding 10 new documents to a 100,000-document index:
  incremental cost: 10 units
  full rebuild cost: 100,000 units
```

A higher cache hit rate saves proportionally more total time, since more of the 10,000 queries skip the full pipeline cost entirely. Adding 10 documents incrementally costs ten-thousandths of what a full rebuild would — rebuilding from scratch every time a handful of documents change is wildly disproportionate to the actual change.

## Bench

```bench
id: cache-incremental-savings
title: A repeated question shouldn't cost the full pipeline twice
fallback: Slide cache hit rate and watch total time saved across a batch of queries; compare incremental indexing against a full rebuild.
```

**Try this**

1. Slide the hit rate up and watch total time saved grow.
2. Compare the incremental and full-rebuild costs for adding 10 documents.
3. Imagine a document collection that changes hourly — what would happen to system cost without incremental indexing?

**What you should notice:** caching's benefit scales with how often queries actually repeat; incremental indexing's benefit scales with how large the existing collection already is relative to what's changing — both exploit the same basic idea of not redoing work that's already settled.

## Where it appears in AI

* **Caching directly reduces the total cost computed in [[Production RAG Pipeline Architecture]]**, by letting a fraction of requests skip the pipeline's full cost entirely.
* **Incremental indexing is a requirement for the "insert/update/delete" capability [[Vector Databases and Index Management]] already identified as something a bare ANN library doesn't handle** — this topic is about why that capability matters operationally.
* **[[Metadata Extraction and Enrichment]]'s freshness filtering depends on new documents actually making it into the index promptly** — a system that can only reindex periodically delays how quickly a freshness filter can reflect new information.

## Common pitfalls

* **Caching without considering when a cached result goes stale.** A cached answer to a question about current information needs some invalidation strategy — caching forever isn't free of the same freshness problems [[Metadata Extraction and Enrichment]] already covers.
* **Rebuilding the full index on every document update "to keep things simple."** The worked example's 10,000x cost gap between incremental and full-rebuild shows this can turn a trivial update into a disproportionately expensive operation.
* **Assuming every ANN index structure supports incremental updates equally well.** Some index types (certain IVF configurations, for instance) handle incremental additions more gracefully than others — this is part of what [[Vector Databases and Index Management]] has to account for when choosing an index type.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. In the worked example, why does a higher cache hit rate save more total time?</summary>
A higher hit rate means a larger fraction of the 10,000 queries skip the full pipeline cost and are instead served near-instantly from the cache, so the total time spent across all queries drops proportionally more.
</details>

<details><summary>2. Why is a full index rebuild disproportionate to adding 10 documents to a 100,000-document collection?</summary>
A full rebuild reprocesses every document in the collection, including the 99,990 that didn't change at all — its cost scales with the whole collection's size, not with how much actually changed.
</details>

<details><summary>3. What risk does caching introduce that incremental indexing doesn't share?</summary>
A cached result can become stale if the underlying information changes after it was cached — incremental indexing, by contrast, is specifically about keeping the index itself current as documents change, not about serving a potentially outdated cached answer.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Caching:** storing and reusing the result of a previous computation (a query's answer, an embedding) instead of recomputing it.
* **Incremental indexing:** adding new documents to an existing index at a cost proportional to what's added, not the whole collection.
* **Cache hit rate:** the fraction of requests that can be served from the cache rather than requiring full computation.

## Related

[[Production RAG Pipeline Architecture]] · [[Vector Databases and Index Management]] · [[Metadata Extraction and Enrichment]]

## Cost and Latency of RAG Systems

A plain LLM call already has its own cost and latency math, already covered on the LLMs planet. RAG adds a handful of extra stages in front of that call — and the question this topic actually answers is how much those extra stages cost on top of a plain generation request, not how generation itself is priced.

**You need:** [[Cost and Latency of LLM APIs]], [[Production RAG Pipeline Architecture]].

## The question it answers

"How much overhead does retrieval actually add to a plain LLM request?" [[Cost and Latency of LLM APIs|Generation's own cost and latency]] is unchanged by RAG — a RAG system still makes the same kind of LLM call at the end. What RAG adds is everything *before* that call: embedding the query, searching the index, and (optionally) re-ranking a shortlist. The real question for a production system is whether that added overhead is large enough to matter next to generation's own cost.

## Intuition

Adding a quick stop at the reference desk before checking out a library book adds some time to the trip — but if checking out the book itself already takes the bulk of the visit, the reference-desk stop is a small addition to an already-dominant cost, not a comparable expense.

## Definition and notation

```text
RAG latency = embed_query + vector_search + rerank + generate   (same generate cost as a plain call)
RAG overhead = RAG latency − plain_LLM_latency
```

## A worked example

A plain LLM call compared against the same call wrapped in a RAG pipeline:

```text
plain LLM call:    2,500ms
RAG pipeline:      2,620ms  (embed 15ms + search 20ms + re-rank 80ms + assemble 5ms + generate 2,500ms)

RAG overhead: 120ms (4.8% more than the plain call)
```

With re-ranking included, RAG adds about 5% to the total latency of an otherwise-identical request. Toggling re-ranking off entirely removes 80 of those 120 added milliseconds — re-ranking is, by a wide margin, the biggest single contributor to RAG's own added latency, even though the whole addition stays modest next to generation's dominant cost.

## Bench

```bench
id: rag-vs-plain-llm-latency
title: Retrieval's overhead, next to the generation it feeds
fallback: Compare a plain LLM call's latency against the full RAG pipeline's, and see where the overhead actually sits.
```

**Try this**

1. Compare the plain call and the RAG pipeline's total latency.
2. Toggle re-ranking off and watch the overhead shrink.
3. Imagine a system where generation itself only took 200ms instead of 2,500ms — would RAG's overhead still look small by comparison?

**What you should notice:** RAG's overhead is a fixed, roughly-constant cost regardless of how expensive generation itself is — a system with faster generation would find RAG's overhead a much larger *relative* share of the total, even though the absolute added milliseconds don't change.

## Where it appears in AI

* **This reuses [[Cost and Latency of LLM APIs]]'s generation cost and latency model directly**, adding only the retrieval-specific stages on top of it.
* **[[Production RAG Pipeline Architecture]]'s own stage-by-stage breakdown is exactly where this overhead comes from** — this topic isolates it specifically as "what RAG adds" relative to a plain call.
* **A cheaper, faster model with lower generation latency ([[Choosing a Model for a Task]]) would make RAG's overhead proportionally more significant**, even though the added milliseconds themselves stay the same.

## Common pitfalls

* **Assuming RAG always adds dramatic latency.** The worked example shows a modest 4.8% overhead on top of a slow generation call — the overhead becomes proportionally more noticeable only when the generation call itself gets much faster.
* **Ignoring re-ranking's outsized share of RAG's own added latency.** The worked example shows re-ranking accounts for two-thirds of RAG's total overhead — it's the first place to look when retrieval-side latency needs trimming.
* **Comparing RAG's total latency only to a plain call, without asking whether the plain call could even answer the question correctly.** RAG's overhead is only meaningful relative to what it buys — an answer a plain call couldn't have given correctly at all.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. In the worked example, why does RAG add only about 5% to the total latency despite running four extra stages?</summary>
Each of those extra stages (embedding, searching, re-ranking, assembling) is individually fast compared to the generation call, which dominates the total — their combined cost (120ms) is small next to generation's 2,500ms.
</details>

<details><summary>2. Which stage contributes the most to RAG's added latency in the worked example?</summary>
Re-ranking, at 80ms out of the total 120ms of added overhead — removing it cuts RAG's overhead by two-thirds.
</details>

<details><summary>3. Would RAG's absolute overhead change if the generating model were replaced with a much faster one?</summary>
Not necessarily — the retrieval-side stages' costs (embedding, searching, re-ranking) are largely independent of which generating model is used, so the absolute overhead could stay similar even as generation's own latency drops, making RAG's overhead a larger relative share of the total.
</details>

## Key terms

* **RAG overhead:** the added latency a RAG pipeline introduces on top of a plain generation call.
* **Retrieval-side latency:** the time spent on embedding, searching, and re-ranking, as opposed to generation itself.
* **Relative overhead:** added latency expressed as a percentage of the baseline (plain call) latency, which shifts as the baseline itself changes.

## Related

[[Cost and Latency of LLM APIs]] · [[Production RAG Pipeline Architecture]] · [[Choosing a Model for a Task]]

## Security and Data Leakage in RAG

Retrieval is a search over documents, and search has always needed access control — a public user's question shouldn't be able to pull an internal finance document into its retrieved context, however relevant that document's content happens to be to the question asked. Relevance and permission are two entirely separate checks, and retrieval has no reason to respect the second one unless it's explicitly told to.

**You need:** [[Metadata Filtering and Hybrid Indexes]], [[Adversarial and Jailbreak Evaluation]].

## The question it answers

"What does retrieval add to the list of ways a system can leak data it shouldn't?" Retrieval searches across a whole document collection by similarity — and similarity alone has no concept of who's allowed to see what. Without an explicit permission check applied as a filter (the same [[Metadata Filtering and Hybrid Indexes|pre-filtering mechanism]] already covered for freshness and other metadata), a sufficiently relevant internal document can end up in a public user's retrieved context, and from there, potentially in the generated answer itself.

## Intuition

A library's card catalog that ranks books purely by subject relevance, with no concept of which books are in the restricted archive, would just as happily point a general patron toward a sealed, access-controlled document as toward a public one — unless the catalog is specifically told to check access rights before returning anything at all.

## Definition and notation

```text
unfiltered retrieval:     ranks by similarity alone, permissions irrelevant to the ranking
permission-filtered:      only chunks matching the requesting user's roles are ever retrievable
```

## A worked example

Three chunks, one restricted to the finance team, retrieved for a public user's query:

```text
[public]       "Public FAQ: shipping takes 3-5 days."
[finance-team] "Internal: Q3 revenue was $4.2M."
[public]       "Public FAQ: refunds in 5 days."

unfiltered top-3: all three chunks returned, including the finance-team-only one
permission-filtered for a public user: only the two [public] chunks returned
```

Without a permission filter, the internal revenue figure sits right alongside the two public FAQ entries in the retrieved results, with nothing distinguishing it except metadata the system never actually checked. With filtering applied before retrieval returns anything, the restricted chunk never reaches this user's results at all.

## Bench

```bench
id: permission-filtered-retrieval
title: Relevant isn't the same as allowed
fallback: Toggle permission filtering and watch an internal, restricted chunk disappear from a public user's results.
```

**Try this**

1. Look at the unfiltered results and note the internal chunk is present.
2. Turn on permission filtering and watch it disappear.
3. Imagine a query specifically crafted to be unusually similar to the internal document's wording — would that make the leak more or less likely without filtering?

**What you should notice:** the restricted chunk's presence in unfiltered results has nothing to do with how relevant it is to the query — it's present simply because nothing checked whether this user was allowed to see it at all.

## Where it appears in AI

* **This reuses the exact pre-filtering mechanism from [[Metadata Filtering and Hybrid Indexes]]**, applied to access control instead of freshness or any other metadata dimension.
* **A retrieved document can also carry a second kind of risk**: a malicious or compromised document instructing the generating model to ignore its instructions — a retrieval-specific variant of the prompt-injection risks [[Adversarial and Jailbreak Evaluation]] already covers for direct user input.
* **[[Guardrails and Deployment-Time Safety Filters]] covers filtering a model's output independently of retrieval** — permission filtering at retrieval time and output guardrails are complementary layers, neither a substitute for the other.

## Common pitfalls

* **Assuming a model won't repeat sensitive content it was never supposed to see, even if it is retrieved.** Once something is in the model's context, nothing stops it from surfacing in the generated answer — the only reliable fix is keeping it out of the context in the first place.
* **Filtering by permission only at the final output stage, after retrieval already happened.** By the time an output filter runs, the sensitive content has already been processed by the model — pre-filtering at retrieval time (as the worked example shows) prevents the exposure earlier and more reliably.
* **Treating retrieved documents as inherently trustworthy instructions.** A document injected into a collection (deliberately or not) that contains text resembling an instruction can attempt to redirect the generating model, the same prompt-injection risk that applies to any untrusted text reaching a model's context.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. In the worked example, why does the finance-team-only chunk appear in unfiltered results at all?</summary>
Unfiltered retrieval ranks purely by similarity to the query, with no check on who's allowed to see each chunk — the internal chunk's content happens to be relevant enough to rank among the top results regardless of permissions.
</details>

<details><summary>2. Why is filtering by permission before retrieval returns results more reliable than filtering the output afterward?</summary>
Filtering beforehand means the restricted content never enters the model's context at all; filtering only the final output still requires catching every possible way that content could leak into the generated answer, which is far less reliable than preventing exposure in the first place.
</details>

<details><summary>3. What's a retrieval-specific version of prompt injection?</summary>
A document in the retrieved collection containing text crafted to look like an instruction to the generating model, which could attempt to redirect its behavior when that document is retrieved and placed into context — a variant of the direct-input prompt-injection risk, but arriving through retrieved content instead.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Data leakage:** unauthorized content reaching a user through a system that wasn't supposed to grant them access to it.
* **Permission filtering:** restricting retrieval to only chunks a given user is authorized to see.
* **Prompt injection via retrieved content:** a retrieved document containing text designed to redirect the generating model's behavior.

## Related

[[Metadata Filtering and Hybrid Indexes]] · [[Adversarial and Jailbreak Evaluation]] · [[Guardrails and Deployment-Time Safety Filters]]

## Capstone: A Question Answered, Traced from Query to Grounded Answer

Every stage this planet covered separately — retrieving by similarity, re-ranking for accuracy, assembling context sensibly, generating with citations — is usually described one at a time, with its own worked example. This capstone follows one real question through all four stages in order, reusing the exact same functions each earlier topic already verified, so the whole pipeline's numbers connect end to end.

**You need:** [[Dense Retrieval]], [[Re-Ranking Retrieved Results]], [[Context Assembly and Ordering]], [[Grounded Generation and Faithfulness]].

## The question it answers

"What does a question actually go through, in order, from arriving as text to becoming a grounded, cited answer?" Four stages, each one this road already covered in depth: embedding the query and retrieving the closest documents by similarity; re-ranking that shortlist with a more careful, joint relevance score; assembling the kept passages into context, aware of where each one lands; and generating an answer whose claims are checked against — and cited to — what was actually retrieved.

## Intuition

A research assistant handling one question does roughly these same four things in order: skims the shelf for the books that look most relevant, reads the few that seem promising more carefully to judge which is actually best, lays out notes from the best ones in a sensible order, and then writes an answer that cites exactly which note supports each claim — rather than writing from memory and hoping it happens to line up with what was actually read.

## Definition and notation

```text
stage 1: embed + retrieve   — cosine similarity against the whole collection, keep the top few
stage 2: re-rank            — a more careful joint score over just the kept shortlist
stage 3: assemble           — place the kept passages into context, aware of position effects
stage 4: generate + cite    — answer, then check each claim against what was retrieved
```

## A worked example

The question "how long do refunds take," traced through all four stages using the exact numbers already verified earlier on this planet:

```text
stage 1 (embed + retrieve): query vs. 4 documents by cosine similarity
  top 2: "refund timeline" (0.998), "returns policy" (0.998)

stage 2 (re-rank): a joint relevance score re-orders the shortlist
  "refund timeline" (0.97) now clearly ahead of "returns policy" (0.80)

stage 3 (assemble): with only 2 passages to place, both sit at context edges —
  neither falls into a lost-in-the-middle position

stage 4 (generate + cite): "Refunds take 5 business days."
  cited to "refund timeline" (similarity 0.9997) — fully grounded
```

Retrieval alone couldn't have told you "refund timeline" was more reliable than "returns policy" — that's what re-ranking's joint score adds. Assembly mattered less here only because there were just two passages to place; with more, their positions would have mattered the way [[Context Assembly and Ordering]] already showed. The final claim's citation confirms the answer didn't drift from what was actually retrieved.

## Bench

```bench
id: rag-capstone
title: One question, every stage of this road
fallback: Step one question through retrieval, re-ranking, assembly and grounded generation, reusing this planet's own verified functions at each stage.
```

**Try this**

1. Step through all four stages and read each one's own number.
2. Compare the retrieval ranking (stage 1) against the re-ranked order (stage 2) — notice the shortlist's membership didn't change, only its order.
3. Reset and imagine skipping stage 4's citation check — would you be able to tell, just from reading the answer, whether it was actually grounded?

**What you should notice:** each stage's number was independently verified earlier on this planet's own road — this capstone doesn't introduce new mechanics, it chains the same four mechanisms together in the order they actually happen.

## Where it appears in AI

* **Stage 1 reuses [[Dense Retrieval]] exactly**, stage 2 reuses [[Re-Ranking Retrieved Results]]'s own worked example, stage 3 reuses [[Context Assembly and Ordering]]'s reasoning, and stage 4 reuses [[Grounded Generation and Faithfulness]]'s citation mechanism — nothing here is new mechanics, only the ordering.
* **[[Common RAG Failure Modes]] names a specific failure for each of these stages** — this capstone is what the pipeline looks like when every stage works as intended, the reference case those failure modes deviate from.
* **[[Production RAG Pipeline Architecture]] is this same four-stage shape, with the operational concerns (latency, cost, caching) layered on top.**

## Common pitfalls

* **Treating these four stages as interchangeable or reorderable.** Each stage assumes the previous one already happened — re-ranking assumes a shortlist retrieval already produced; generation assumes context assembly already placed the passages it's meant to cite.
* **Expecting retrieval's similarity scores to directly predict re-ranking's verdict.** The worked example's stage 1 and stage 2 scores aren't on the same scale and aren't meant to be compared directly — re-ranking's whole purpose is to look more carefully than retrieval's cheap first pass could.
* **Assuming a fully grounded final answer means the pipeline is working perfectly everywhere.** This worked example traces a case where every stage succeeds — a real system also needs the failure-mode handling ([[Corrective RAG]], permission filtering, conflict resolution) covered elsewhere on this road for when a stage doesn't go this cleanly.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. Why does stage 2's re-ranking matter here if stage 1 already retrieved the same two documents?</summary>
Retrieval's cosine similarity scores for the two documents are nearly identical (0.998 vs. 0.998), barely distinguishing them; re-ranking's joint score reveals a much clearer gap (0.97 vs. 0.80), correctly identifying which of the two is actually the stronger source.
</details>

<details><summary>2. Why does context assembly (stage 3) matter less in this specific worked example than it generally would?</summary>
With only two passages to place, both necessarily sit at the edges of the context rather than in a lost-in-the-middle position — assembly order would matter more with a longer list of passages, as [[Context Assembly and Ordering]]'s own worked example shows.
</details>

<details><summary>3. What would it mean if stage 4's citation check had found no supporting passage for the generated claim?</summary>
It would mean the generated answer drew on something other than what was actually retrieved — exactly the ungrounded-claim problem [[Grounded Generation and Faithfulness]] measures, and a signal that the answer shouldn't be trusted as retrieval-backed.
</details>

## Key terms

* **End-to-end trace:** following one request through every stage of a pipeline in order, rather than examining each stage in isolation.
* **Shortlist:** the reduced set of candidates retrieval passes on to re-ranking.
* **Grounded answer:** a generated answer whose claims are verifiably supported by retrieved context.

## Related

[[Dense Retrieval]] · [[Re-Ranking Retrieved Results]] · [[Grounded Generation and Faithfulness]]

# Agents

## Agents

Every planet before this one covered a model answering one request at a time: a prompt goes in, an answer comes out. An agent is different — it's a model given a goal, a loop, and a way to act on the world, which keeps calling itself (and its tools) until the goal is actually done, or it gives up. This planet is about everything that loop needs: planning what to do, using tools reliably, remembering across steps, coordinating with other agents, checking its own work, and being safe to actually run unsupervised.

**You need:** [[Agents and Environments]], [[Structured Output and Tool-Calling APIs]], [[Prompting and In-Context Learning]].

The road through Agents:

* [[Foundations of Agentic Systems]] — what actually turns a single model call into an agent, and what that buys you.
* [[Workflow Patterns Before Autonomy]] — structured, predictable patterns that solve most tasks before you need a fully autonomous loop.
* [[Planning and Task Decomposition]] — breaking a goal into steps, and re-planning when a step doesn't go as expected.
* [[Tool Use and Function Calling]] — picking, calling and trusting the right tool, reliably, at scale.
* [[Memory and State Management]] — what an agent remembers across steps, and what it has to let go of.
* [[Multi-Agent Systems]] — when one agent becomes several, and how they actually coordinate.
* [[Reflection and Self-Improvement]] — an agent checking and correcting its own work, without retraining.
* [[Agent Environments and Action Spaces]] — the browsers, terminals, codebases and simulations an agent actually acts inside.
* [[Evaluating Agents]] — measuring whether an agent actually finished the job, and at what cost.
* [[Agent Safety and Governance]] — how much autonomy is safe to grant, and what has to contain the rest.
* [[Agents in Practice]] — running an agent in production, ending in a capstone that traces one goal from decomposition to a verified result.

## Foundations of Agentic Systems

A single call to a language model, however good, still just returns one response to one prompt. This district is about the specific things added on top of that single call — a loop, tools, memory, a goal that persists across steps — that turn it into something that can actually get a multi-step job done on its own.

Topics on this stretch of the road:

* [[From a Single Call to a Loop]]: the one structural change that separates an agent from a chatbot.
* [[Agents vs. Assistants vs. Workflows]]: three things that get called "AI agents," and what actually tells them apart.
* [[The Augmented LLM]]: tools, memory and retrieval, bolted onto a model, as the shared building block under almost every agent.
* [[Open-Loop vs. Closed-Loop Behavior]]: whether an agent ever checks if its actions actually worked.
* [[Anatomy of an Agent Architecture]]: the pieces every agent architecture has, named consistently, before this road looks at each one separately.

## From a Single Call to a Loop

A single call to a model follows exactly one link in a chain of facts, no matter how the chain continues from there. Asking "what department is Alice's manager's manager in?" in one call gets back Alice's manager — the model answered the first thing it could, not the actual question, because nothing told it to keep going once that first answer wasn't the department.

**You need:** [[Agents and Environments]], [[PDA Loop]].

## The question it answers

"What's the one structural change that turns a single model call into an agent?" A loop: after producing a result, check whether the goal is actually satisfied, and if it isn't, feed that result back in and call the model again. A single call stops after one step regardless of whether the goal was reached; a loop keeps going — following manager after manager, in this example — until it actually lands on the department, or runs out of steps trying.

## Intuition

Asking someone "who manages Alice?" gets an immediate, complete answer — Bob. Asking "what department does Alice's manager's manager work in?" and only getting as far as "Bob" back is a half-finished answer to a question that needed two more hops. A loop is the difference between stopping after the first hop and continuing until the actual question is answered.

## Definition and notation

```text
single call:  result = step(state)
loop:         result = step(state); while (goal_not_met(result)): result = step(result)
```

## A worked example

A tiny organization chart, and the question "what department is Alice's manager's manager in?":

```text
Alice → manager: Bob
Bob   → manager: Carol
Carol → department: Engineering

single call: step(Alice) = "Bob"              (Alice's manager — not the department)
loop:        step(Alice) = "Bob"   (not done, "Bob" has no department)
             step(Bob)   = "Carol" (not done, "Carol" has no department either — wait, it does)
             step(Carol) = "Engineering"  (done — this is a department)
             → 3 steps to reach "Engineering"
```

The single call's answer ("Bob") isn't wrong in isolation — it correctly reports Alice's manager — it's just not an answer to the question that was actually asked. The loop keeps applying the same one-hop lookup, checking after each hop whether it's reached a department yet, until it has.

## Bench

```bench
id: single-call-vs-loop
title: One lookup answers the wrong question
fallback: Step a multi-hop lookup and compare a single call's answer against a looped agent's.
```

**Try this**

1. Compare the single-call answer against the full lookup chain.
2. Step through the loop and watch it stop exactly when it reaches a department.
3. Imagine a four-level-deep organization — would a single call still only get through one hop?

**What you should notice:** the single call and the first step of the loop produce the exact same result — the loop isn't a different kind of lookup, it's the same lookup, repeated and checked.

## Where it appears in AI

* **This is exactly the [[PDA Loop|perceive-decide-act loop]] already covered on the Fundamentals planet**, now specifically framed around *when* that loop needs more than one iteration to reach a goal.
* **[[Goal Decomposition into Subtasks]] is the planning-side version of the same idea** — recognizing in advance that a question needs multiple hops, rather than discovering it only after the first hop falls short.
* **[[Anatomy of an Agent Architecture]] names the specific component (the controller) responsible for deciding whether to loop again** — this topic is about why that component exists at all.

## Common pitfalls

* **Assuming a bigger or better model fixes a problem that's actually about looping.** No amount of model quality changes the fact that a single call only performs one step — the fix is architectural, not a better model.
* **Looping forever when a goal genuinely can't be reached.** A loop needs a step budget or another stopping condition — without one, an agent that can't find a department would keep looking indefinitely.
* **Assuming every task needs a loop.** A question answerable in one real step doesn't benefit from looping — it's specifically multi-hop goals where the difference matters.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. Why isn't the single call's answer ("Bob") simply wrong?</summary>
It correctly answers "who is Alice's manager" — it's a true fact, just not an answer to the actual two-hop question that was asked; the call itself didn't fail, it just never continued past the first hop.
</details>

<details><summary>2. What has to happen after each step of the loop for it to know whether to continue?</summary>
A check against the goal — in the worked example, whether the current result is a department yet — determines whether the loop stops or feeds the result back in for another step.
</details>

<details><summary>3. What would happen if the loop had no step budget and the organization chart had a cycle (A reports to B, B reports to A)?</summary>
The loop would run forever, alternating between A and B and never reaching a department — exactly why a real loop needs a stopping condition beyond just "goal not yet met."
</details>

## Key terms

* **Single call:** one request to a model, producing one result, with no further iteration.
* **Loop:** repeatedly feeding a result back in and calling again until a goal is met or a budget runs out.
* **Multi-hop goal:** a goal that can't be reached in one step because each step's result is needed to determine the next step.

## Related

[[PDA Loop]] · [[Anatomy of an Agent Architecture]] · [[Goal Decomposition into Subtasks]]

## Agents vs. Assistants vs. Workflows

"Agent" gets used loosely enough that a chatbot, a fixed multi-step pipeline, and a genuinely autonomous loop all sometimes get called one. They're not the same thing, and picking the wrong one for a task costs real reliability or real flexibility, depending on which way the mismatch goes.

**You need:** [[From a Single Call to a Loop]].

## The question it answers

"What actually tells an assistant, a workflow and an agent apart?" An **assistant** is a single-turn (or simply-turn-taking) conversational call — fast and cheap, but it can't reliably drive itself through a multi-step task. A **workflow** is a fixed, developer-coded sequence of calls — highly predictable for the specific steps it was built for, but it can't adapt beyond that script. An **agent** decides its own next step at run-time based on what's happened so far — flexible enough for open-ended tasks, at the cost of being far less predictable.

## Intuition

A receptionist who answers one question at a time is the assistant. A printed checklist that always runs the same five steps in the same order is the workflow — reliable, as long as the situation matches what the checklist assumed. A problem-solver who improvises a new plan based on whatever they find is the agent — adaptable, but you can't predict exactly what they'll do next.

## Definition and notation

```text
score(system, weights) = Σ system[dimension] × weights[dimension] / Σ weights[dimension]
```

Each system scored on predictability, flexibility, cost (higher = cheaper) and autonomy (ability to run without a human driving each step).

## A worked example

Three systems, scored 0–1 on four dimensions, under two different task types:

```text
              predictability  flexibility  cost  autonomy
assistant          0.30          0.40      0.95    0.05
workflow           0.95          0.20      0.80    0.50
agent              0.45          0.95      0.30    0.95

well-defined, multi-step task:   workflow 0.815  >  agent 0.520  >  assistant 0.398
open-ended, novel task:           agent 0.835  >  workflow 0.395  ≈  assistant 0.375
```

For a well-defined task, the workflow wins decisively — its high predictability is worth the most when the weights favor getting the same, correct steps done reliably. For an open-ended task, the ranking flips entirely: the agent's flexibility and autonomy make it the clear winner, while the workflow (rigid) and the assistant (can't drive multiple steps at all) both struggle about equally.

## Bench

```bench
id: agent-vs-assistant-vs-workflow
title: Different tasks want different structures
fallback: Switch the task type and see which of an assistant, a workflow or an agent actually scores best.
```

**Try this**

1. Check the well-defined task scenario and note the workflow wins clearly.
2. Switch to the open-ended scenario and watch the ranking flip entirely.
3. Think of a real task you'd assign to each of the three — would your intuition match these numbers?

**What you should notice:** the workflow and the assistant land close together on the open-ended task — neither is actually built for genuine flexibility, so the gap between "rigid but reliable" and "simple but limited" stops mattering once the task stops being well-defined.

## Where it appears in AI

* **This reuses the exact weighted-scoring mechanism already used for choosing a model** ([[Choosing a Model for a Task]]) **and choosing between RAG, fine-tuning and long-context** ([[RAG vs. Fine-Tuning vs. Long-Context]]) — the same lesson (the right structure depends on the task) recurs at this level too.
* **[[Workflow Patterns Before Autonomy]] is specifically about the structured, workflow side of this choice** — the patterns worth reaching for before deciding a task actually needs full agentic autonomy.
* **[[When Planning Hurts More Than It Helps]] covers the symmetric mistake**: reaching for an agent's flexibility on a task simple enough that a workflow (or no loop at all) would have done better.

## Common pitfalls

* **Defaulting to "agent" for every multi-step task.** The worked example shows a workflow beats an agent decisively on a well-defined task — autonomy isn't free, and it costs predictability a well-defined task doesn't need to spend.
* **Assuming a workflow can handle a task it wasn't specifically built for.** A workflow's high predictability only holds for the exact steps it was coded to run — present it with something outside that script and it has no mechanism to adapt.
* **Assuming an assistant can be turned into a workflow or agent just by asking it nicely.** The distinction is architectural (does something outside the single call decide and drive the next step), not a matter of prompting the same single call harder.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. In the worked example, why does the workflow score so much higher than the agent on the well-defined task, despite the agent being more capable overall?</summary>
The well-defined task's weights heavily favor predictability, where the workflow scores far higher (0.95 vs. 0.45) — the agent's extra flexibility and autonomy don't make up for being meaningfully less predictable, when predictability is what the task actually needs.
</details>

<details><summary>2. Why do the workflow and the assistant end up scoring so similarly on the open-ended task?</summary>
Neither is built for genuine adaptability — the workflow is rigid by design, and the assistant can't drive itself through multiple steps at all — so once the task stops being well-defined, their different strengths (reliability vs. simplicity) stop mattering much.
</details>

<details><summary>3. What's the architectural difference between a workflow and an agent, beyond just "a workflow is simpler"?</summary>
A workflow's sequence of steps is fixed by the developer in advance; an agent decides its own next step at run-time based on what's happened so far — the workflow's steps don't change based on intermediate results the way an agent's can.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Assistant:** a single-turn or simply-turn-taking conversational system with no autonomous multi-step drive.
* **Workflow:** a fixed, developer-coded sequence of calls, predictable but inflexible.
* **Agent:** a system that decides its own next step at run-time, flexible but less predictable.

## Related

[[From a Single Call to a Loop]] · [[Workflow Patterns Before Autonomy]] · [[When Planning Hurts More Than It Helps]]

## The Augmented LLM

A bare model call can only ever draw on what was baked into its weights during training. Give it a way to call tools, a way to remember across turns, and a way to search outside documents, and it can suddenly do things none of those weights alone ever could — act on the real world, recall a past conversation, answer from something it's never seen.

**You need:** [[Parametric vs. Non-Parametric Knowledge]], [[Structured Output and Tool-Calling APIs]].

## The question it answers

"What's the minimal set of additions that turns a plain model call into the building block almost every agent is made of?" Three additions, each already derived elsewhere on this road: tools ([[Structured Output and Tool-Calling APIs|the ability to call a function and act]]), memory (state that persists across turns), and retrieval ([[Parametric vs. Non-Parametric Knowledge|a document store searched at answer-time]]). None of these require a different model — they're capabilities wired around the same underlying call.

## Intuition

A brilliant scholar locked in a room with no phone, no notes and no library can only ever answer from what they've already memorized. Give them a phone (tools), a notebook they can write in and read back (memory), and a library card (retrieval), and the same scholar can now do things that were never possible from memorization alone — not because they got smarter, but because they're no longer limited to what's already in their head.

## Definition and notation

```text
augmented LLM = bare LLM + tools + memory + retrieval
```

## A worked example

Four capabilities, checked against a bare LLM and the same model augmented with tools, memory and retrieval:

```text
capability                                          bare LLM   augmented LLM
answer from training data alone                        ✓            ✓
take an action in the real world                         ✗            ✓
recall something from a past conversation                ✗            ✓
answer using a document it's never seen                   ✗            ✓
```

A bare LLM handles exactly 1 of these 4 capabilities — whatever it can answer purely from its own training. Every other capability requires one of the three augmentations: tools to act, memory to recall, retrieval to answer from unseen documents.

## Bench

```bench
id: augmented-llm-capabilities
title: What augmentation actually unlocks
fallback: Compare what a bare LLM can do against the same model augmented with tools, memory and retrieval.
```

**Try this**

1. Switch to "bare LLM" and note only one capability is checked.
2. Switch to "augmented LLM" and see all four checked.
3. Match each newly unlocked capability to the specific augmentation (tools, memory, or retrieval) responsible for it.

**What you should notice:** each of the three new capabilities maps to exactly one augmentation — acting needs tools, recalling needs memory, answering from unseen documents needs retrieval — none of the three substitutes for either of the others.

## Where it appears in AI

* **This is the single building block nearly every pattern on this road is built from** — [[Workflow Patterns Before Autonomy]]'s structured patterns and [[Planning and Task Decomposition]]'s autonomous loops are both arrangements of augmented LLM calls, not a different underlying mechanism.
* **Tools are covered in depth in [[Tool Use and Function Calling]]**, memory in [[Memory and State Management]], retrieval across the entire RAG planet — this topic is only about naming the three as one shared building block.
* **Removing any one augmentation removes exactly the capabilities tied to it** — an agent with tools and memory but no retrieval still can't answer from a document it's never seen, however good its other two augmentations are.

## Common pitfalls

* **Assuming a bigger model closes the gap a bare call has with an augmented one.** The worked example's gap isn't about capability or quality — a bare call, however large the model, still can't take a real-world action without a tool wired to it.
* **Treating the three augmentations as interchangeable.** Memory doesn't help an agent search a document it's never seen, and retrieval doesn't let an agent recall what happened earlier in the same conversation — each covers a specific, non-overlapping gap.
* **Adding all three augmentations to every task regardless of need.** A task that never needs to act on the real world doesn't benefit from tools, and wiring them in anyway only adds complexity and new failure modes.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. Why can't a bare LLM take an action in the real world, no matter how capable it is?</summary>
Taking an action requires something outside the model itself — a tool wired to actually do something — a bare call only produces text, with nothing connecting that text to any real-world effect.
</details>

<details><summary>2. If an agent has tools and retrieval but no memory, what specific capability is it still missing?</summary>
It can't recall something from a past conversation — tools let it act and retrieval lets it search documents, but neither substitutes for state that persists across turns.
</details>

<details><summary>3. Does "augmenting" an LLM require retraining or fine-tuning the model itself?</summary>
No — tools, memory and retrieval are all wired around the existing model call (function definitions, stored state, a search step before generation), not changes to the model's own weights.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Augmented LLM:** a model call combined with tools, memory and retrieval as its three standard additions.
* **Tool:** a function an agent can call to take an action or fetch information beyond its own training.
* **Memory (in this context):** state that persists across turns or runs, as opposed to what's baked into the model's weights.

## Related

[[Structured Output and Tool-Calling APIs]] · [[Tool Use and Function Calling]] · [[Memory and State Management]]

## Open-Loop vs. Closed-Loop Behavior

An agent that fires off four actions in a row and reports "done" might be lying — not out of any intent to deceive, but because it never actually checked whether any of those four actions worked. Whether an agent checks its own results, every single time, is the difference between a silent failure and a caught one.

**You need:** [[From a Single Call to a Loop]].

## The question it answers

"Does an agent ever verify that its own actions actually had the intended effect?" **Open-loop** execution runs a sequence of actions without checking any of their real results — if one silently fails partway through, nothing in the loop notices, and the agent proceeds as if everything worked. **Closed-loop** execution checks the actual outcome after every single action — a silent failure is caught the moment it happens, because the loop looks at the real result before deciding what to do next.

## Intuition

Mailing four letters and assuming all four arrived, with no tracking and no confirmation, is open-loop — if one gets lost in transit, you won't find out unless something else eventually depends on it having arrived. Getting a delivery confirmation for each one before sending the next is closed-loop — a lost letter is caught immediately, right when it happens, not whenever its absence finally causes a problem downstream.

## Definition and notation

```text
open-loop:    run action; move to next action, regardless of what actually happened
closed-loop:  run action; check its real result; only then decide the next step
```

## A worked example

A 4-step action sequence, with a silent failure injected at different steps:

```text
failure at step 2:
  open-loop:    never checks — proceeds through steps 3 and 4, reports success at the end
  closed-loop:  checks after step 2, catches the failure immediately, stops there

failure at step 4 (the last step):
  open-loop:    never checks — still reports success
  closed-loop:  catches it immediately, at step 4
```

However consistently a step's result is injected to fail, open-loop execution never notices by construction — it simply doesn't look. Closed-loop execution catches the failure at exactly the step it happened, regardless of which step that is.

## Bench

```bench
id: open-vs-closed-loop
title: Checking the result, or not
fallback: Slide where a failure happens in a 4-step run and see whether open-loop or closed-loop execution catches it.
```

**Try this**

1. Slide the failure to different steps and watch open-loop's result — it never changes.
2. Watch closed-loop catch the failure at exactly the step you chose, every time.
3. Imagine the failed step was "transfer money" — what's the real-world cost of open-loop missing it?

**What you should notice:** open-loop's blindness isn't a matter of bad luck or an unlucky failure mode — it's structural: nothing in open-loop execution ever looks at the actual result, so there's nothing that could catch a failure regardless of where it happens.

## Where it appears in AI

* **This is the mechanism underneath [[Re-Planning on Failure]]**: re-planning can only happen once a failure has actually been detected, which requires closed-loop checking in the first place.
* **[[Tool Result Verification]] is the specific, tool-level version of this same idea** — checking a tool's actual output before trusting it, rather than assuming the call succeeded.
* **[[Error Attribution Across a Trajectory]] depends on closed-loop checkpoints existing at all** — attributing a later failure to an earlier step requires having actually recorded what each step's real result was.

## Common pitfalls

* **Assuming a tool call "probably worked" without checking its return value.** The worked example shows this is exactly the open-loop failure mode — the assumption holds right up until it doesn't, silently.
* **Checking results inconsistently — sometimes, but not after every action.** A closed loop that skips checking on some steps reduces to open-loop exactly on those steps, reintroducing the same blind spot.
* **Confusing "the action completed" with "the action worked."** A tool call can return without an error while still not having accomplished the intended effect — closed-loop checking needs to verify the actual outcome, not just that the call didn't crash.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. Why does open-loop execution fail to catch the injected failure regardless of which step it happens at?</summary>
Open-loop never checks any step's actual result at all — there's no point in the loop where a failure, wherever it occurs, could be noticed.
</details>

<details><summary>2. What does closed-loop execution need, structurally, that open-loop doesn't?</summary>
A check after every action that compares the action's actual result against what was expected, before deciding what to do next.
</details>

<details><summary>3. Does a tool call returning without an error guarantee the action actually succeeded?</summary>
No — a call can return normally while still not accomplishing its intended effect, which is why closed-loop checking needs to verify the real outcome, not just that the call completed without crashing.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Open-loop execution:** running a sequence of actions without checking their actual results.
* **Closed-loop execution:** checking each action's real outcome before deciding the next step.
* **Silent failure:** an action that fails without raising any error, detectable only by checking its actual effect.

## Related

[[From a Single Call to a Loop]] · [[Re-Planning on Failure]] · [[Tool Result Verification]]

## Anatomy of an Agent Architecture

Every agent architecture this road covers, however different the application, is built from the same five named pieces: something that perceives the current request, something that remembers relevant state, something that plans, something that acts, and something that decides whether to loop again. Naming them consistently here means every later topic can refer to "the planner" or "the controller" without re-explaining what that is.

**You need:** [[The Augmented LLM]], [[Open-Loop vs. Closed-Loop Behavior]].

## The question it answers

"What are the standard named pieces of an agent architecture?" **Perceive** reads the current request and any new observations. **Memory** holds state relevant to the task, checked and updated as the agent works. **Planner** decomposes the goal into steps. **Tool executor** actually carries out a step, calling whatever tool that step requires. **Controller** checks the tool's result against the goal and decides whether to stop, continue to the next planned step, or loop back to the planner entirely.

## Intuition

A restaurant booking made by a competent personal assistant goes through the same five kinds of work every time, whoever's doing it: hearing the request, recalling any relevant preference, figuring out the steps, actually calling the restaurant, and checking whether the booking actually went through before reporting back. Naming these five parts doesn't change what the assistant does — it gives a vocabulary for talking about which part of the process something went wrong in.

## Definition and notation

```text
perceive  →  memory  →  planner  →  tool executor  →  controller  → (loop back to planner, or stop)
```

## A worked example

One request, walked through all five components:

```text
perceive:       reads "book a table for 4 at 7pm"
memory:         retrieves a stored preference, "prefers Italian food"
planner:        decomposes into: search restaurants → check availability → confirm booking
tool executor:  calls the booking tool with the restaurant, time and party size
controller:     checks the tool's result against the goal; loops back to the planner if it
                 didn't work, otherwise stops
```

Each component does one specific, named job. The planner's job is to decide *what* to do; the tool executor's job is to actually *do* it; the controller's job is to check whether it *worked* — three different responsibilities that could each, independently, be the reason a task succeeds or fails.

## Bench

```bench
id: agent-architecture-anatomy
title: The same five components, every time
fallback: Step through the named components of an agent architecture on one toy request.
```

**Try this**

1. Step through all five components and note what each one's job actually is.
2. Notice the controller's decision point: loop back, or stop.
3. Imagine the booking tool fails — which component is responsible for catching that, and what does it do next?

**What you should notice:** "the agent" isn't one undifferentiated thing — it's five components with five distinct responsibilities, and a failure can be isolated to exactly one of them rather than blamed on "the agent" in general.

## Where it appears in AI

* **This is the same shape as [[PDA Loop|the perceive-decide-act loop]] already covered on the Fundamentals planet**, split into finer-grained, named pieces specific to how an agent built on an LLM actually works.
* **Every later district is a deep dive into one of these five components**: [[Planning and Task Decomposition]] is the planner, [[Tool Use and Function Calling]] is the tool executor, [[Memory and State Management]] is memory, and the controller's checking behavior is [[Open-Loop vs. Closed-Loop Behavior]].
* **[[Observability and Tracing for Agent Runs]] depends on being able to log which component produced which part of a run** — naming the components consistently is what makes a trace readable at all.

## Common pitfalls

* **Treating "the agent" as a single opaque thing when debugging a failure.** The worked example shows five distinct places a task can go wrong — a failed booking could be the planner choosing the wrong steps, the tool executor calling the tool incorrectly, or the controller failing to notice the call didn't work.
* **Skipping the controller and letting the tool executor's result flow straight to the final answer.** Without a controller checking the result, there's no mechanism to loop back on failure — this is exactly the open-loop problem from the previous topic, now located in a specific architectural component.
* **Assuming memory and the planner are the same component.** Memory holds state; the planner uses that state (among other things) to decide steps — conflating them makes it harder to reason about which one is responsible when a plan uses the wrong stored preference.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. In the worked example, which component is responsible for deciding that the task needs three steps rather than one?</summary>
The planner — it's specifically responsible for decomposing the goal into an ordered sequence of steps.
</details>

<details><summary>2. If the booking tool call fails, which component notices and decides what to do next?</summary>
The controller — it checks the tool executor's actual result against the goal and decides whether to loop back to the planner or stop.
</details>

<details><summary>3. Why is it useful to give these five components separate names rather than just calling the whole thing "the agent"?</summary>
It lets a specific failure be isolated to one component's responsibility (a bad plan vs. a bad tool call vs. a missed check) instead of being a vague, undifferentiated "the agent didn't work," which makes debugging and improving the system far more tractable.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Perceive:** the component that reads the current request and any new observations.
* **Planner:** the component that decomposes a goal into an ordered sequence of steps.
* **Controller:** the component that checks a step's result against the goal and decides whether to loop again.

## Related

[[PDA Loop]] · [[Planning and Task Decomposition]] · [[Tool Use and Function Calling]]

## Workflow Patterns Before Autonomy

Not every multi-step task needs a fully autonomous agent deciding what to do next. A fixed sequence of LLM calls, wired together by code the developer controls, solves most well-defined tasks more predictably and more cheaply than letting a model improvise the whole plan. This district covers those structured patterns, which stay the right choice right up until a task is genuinely open-ended.

Topics on this stretch of the road:

* [[Prompt Chaining]]: splitting one task into a fixed sequence of smaller LLM calls.
* [[Routing Between Specialized Prompts]]: sending a request to whichever of several specialized prompts actually fits it.
* [[Parallelization: Sectioning and Voting]]: running several LLM calls at once, either on different pieces of a task or on the same piece for a better answer.
* [[Orchestrator-Workers]]: one call that plans the work, several calls that do it, and one call that combines the results.
* [[Evaluator-Optimizer Loops]]: one call that produces an answer, another that critiques it, looping until the critique is satisfied.

## Prompt Chaining

Splitting a task into a fixed sequence of calls — outline, then draft, then polish — lets each step check the previous one's work before building on it. A malformed outline gets caught right there, before it wastes an entire draft written from something that was never going to work.

**You need:** [[Anatomy of an Agent Architecture]].

## The question it answers

"How do you split one task into smaller, checkable steps, without needing full agentic autonomy to do it?" Prompt chaining runs a fixed sequence of LLM calls, each one's output feeding into the next, with a **validation gate** between steps that checks an intermediate result before it's allowed to proceed. The sequence itself (what step comes after what) is decided in advance by the developer — nothing here decides its own next step the way an agent does; the structure is simply broken into smaller, individually checkable pieces.

## Intuition

A copyeditor who reviews a chapter's outline before the author writes a single page of the chapter itself catches a missing section immediately — far cheaper than discovering it's missing only after the whole chapter is drafted around a gap that was never there.

## Definition and notation

```text
chain:  step1 → gate(result1) → step2 → gate(result2) → step3 → ...
gate(result) = passes if result has every field the next step needs
```

## A worked example

Three generated outlines, each checked by a gate requiring an intro, a body, and a conclusion, before any of them would be drafted:

```text
outline 1: intro, body, conclusion  → passes gate → proceeds to draft
outline 2: intro, body              → fails gate → caught before drafting (missing conclusion)
outline 3: intro, body, conclusion  → passes gate → proceeds to draft

2 of 3 proceed; 1 is caught before an entire draft step gets wasted on it
```

Outline 2's problem — a missing conclusion section — is detectable the instant the outline itself is produced. Catching it there, rather than only noticing the final draft has no conclusion, saves an entire wasted drafting step.

## Bench

```bench
id: prompt-chaining-gate
title: Checking the outline before writing the draft
fallback: Step through a chained pipeline and watch its validation gate catch a malformed intermediate result.
```

**Try this**

1. Step through all three outlines and watch the gate's verdict on each.
2. Notice outline 2 is caught *before* any drafting step runs on it.
3. Imagine the gate didn't exist — at what point would the missing conclusion finally get noticed?

**What you should notice:** the gate's check doesn't require understanding the whole task — it only needs to verify the one thing the next step actually depends on, which is cheap to check and catches the problem at the earliest possible point.

## Where it appears in AI

* **This is the structured, developer-controlled version of the gate check [[Open-Loop vs. Closed-Loop Behavior]] already covered**: a chain's gate is exactly a closed-loop check, applied between fixed steps rather than inside an autonomous loop.
* **[[Routing Between Specialized Prompts]] is the other common workflow pattern for splitting work**, choosing which single prompt handles a request rather than running a fixed sequence of several.
* **A chain's steps are themselves the kind of single augmented-LLM calls covered in [[The Augmented LLM]]** — chaining is an arrangement of that building block, not a different mechanism.

## Common pitfalls

* **Skipping the gate "to save a step."** The worked example shows exactly what that costs — a malformed intermediate result flows straight into an expensive next step instead of being caught cheaply where it happened.
* **Writing a gate that checks too little.** A gate that only checks "is there any text at all" would pass outline 2 despite its missing conclusion — the gate needs to check the specific fields the next step actually depends on.
* **Reaching for full agentic autonomy when a fixed chain would do.** If the sequence of steps is known in advance and doesn't need to change based on what happens, a chain is simpler and more predictable than a loop that decides its own next step.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. Why does outline 2 get caught before the draft step, rather than after?</summary>
The gate checks the outline's own fields immediately after it's produced, and a missing conclusion section is detectable right there — there's no need to wait until a draft is written to notice something the outline already lacked.
</details>

<details><summary>2. What's the minimum a gate needs to check to be useful?</summary>
Specifically the fields or properties the *next* step actually depends on — a gate that checks something irrelevant to the next step wouldn't catch the failure that actually matters.
</details>

<details><summary>3. Is prompt chaining an example of agentic autonomy?</summary>
No — the sequence of steps is fixed in advance by the developer; nothing in the chain decides its own next step based on results the way a genuinely autonomous agent would.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Prompt chaining:** a fixed sequence of LLM calls, each one's output feeding into the next.
* **Validation gate:** a check between chained steps that verifies an intermediate result before letting it proceed.
* **Workflow pattern:** a structured, developer-controlled arrangement of calls, as opposed to an autonomous agent's self-directed loop.

## Related

[[Open-Loop vs. Closed-Loop Behavior]] · [[Routing Between Specialized Prompts]] · [[The Augmented LLM]]

## Routing Between Specialized Prompts

One generic handler answering every kind of request is simpler to build than several specialists — and noticeably worse at any one of them. Routing classifies an incoming request first, then sends it to whichever specialized prompt is actually built for that category, instead of asking one prompt to be good at everything at once.

**You need:** [[Prompt Chaining]].

## The question it answers

"Is it better to build one prompt that handles everything, or several specialists plus a router?" Routing classifies each request into a category, then dispatches it to a prompt built and tuned specifically for that category. A billing question goes to a prompt that knows the billing system; a technical question goes to one that knows the product's failure modes. A single generic handler, by contrast, has to do reasonably well at every category at once, which in practice means doing noticeably worse at each one than a specialist would.

## Intuition

A hospital's general triage desk doesn't try to perform every patient's treatment itself — it identifies what kind of problem the patient has and sends them to the specialist actually trained for it. A single doctor trying to be equally expert at cardiology, dermatology and orthopedics all at once would be worse at each than any one specialist.

## Definition and notation

```text
routed accuracy  = Σ (requests of category c) × (specialist_c's accuracy) / total requests
generic accuracy = one flat accuracy, the same for every request regardless of category
```

## A worked example

Three incoming requests (two billing, one technical), compared under routing versus a single generic handler:

```text
billing specialist accuracy:     95%
technical specialist accuracy:   90%
generic handler accuracy:        55% (flat, regardless of category)

routed overall accuracy:   (95% + 95% + 90%) / 3 = 93.3%
generic overall accuracy:                            55.0%
```

Routing each request to the specialist that matches its category lifts overall accuracy from 55% to 93.3% — not because any individual specialist is dramatically better than the generic handler at everything, but because each specialist is genuinely good at exactly the category it actually receives.

## Bench

```bench
id: routing-specialists
title: The right specialist, or one handler for everything
fallback: Compare accuracy when requests are routed to the matching specialist against one generic handler taking everything.
```

**Try this**

1. Check the routed accuracy and note it's close to the weighted average of the two specialists' own accuracy.
2. Switch to the generic handler and see the large drop.
3. Imagine a request that doesn't clearly fit any existing specialist category — what should the router do with it?

**What you should notice:** routing's accuracy gain comes entirely from matching each request to the specialist actually built for its category — the mechanism is simple, but it depends on the classification step itself being accurate.

## Where it appears in AI

* **Routing depends on an accurate classification step**, the same task-classification problem that shows up throughout this road — a misrouted request gets the wrong specialist's accuracy, not the one it should have received.
* **[[Supervisor-Orchestrator Patterns|Supervisor/Orchestrator Patterns]] is the multi-agent version of the same idea**: instead of routing to a specialized *prompt*, a supervisor routes to a specialized *agent*.
* **[[Tool Selection Among Many Candidates]] is a closely related problem one level down**: picking the right tool out of many is routing applied to actions instead of to whole requests.

## Common pitfalls

* **Building one generic handler for a domain with clearly distinct request categories.** The worked example shows this isn't a minor inefficiency — it's a nearly 40-percentage-point accuracy gap, for a mechanism (a classification step plus separate prompts) that isn't especially complex to add.
* **Assuming the router's own classification step is perfect.** Routing's entire benefit depends on correctly identifying each request's category — a router that frequently misclassifies requests pushes accuracy back toward the generic handler's level or worse.
* **Over-splitting into too many narrow specialist categories.** Each additional category needs its own prompt built and maintained, and makes the router's classification job harder — there's a real cost to adding specialists beyond what the request distribution actually calls for.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. In the worked example, why is the routed accuracy (93.3%) closer to the specialists' own accuracy than to the generic handler's?</summary>
Routing sends each request to the specialist that matches its category, so each request gets scored at that specialist's own accuracy (95% or 90%) rather than at the flat 55% the generic handler would have given it.
</details>

<details><summary>2. What's the one additional step routing needs that a single generic handler doesn't?</summary>
A classification step that determines which category an incoming request belongs to, before deciding which specialized prompt to dispatch it to.
</details>

<details><summary>3. What happens to routing's accuracy advantage if the classification step itself is unreliable?</summary>
Misclassified requests get sent to the wrong specialist, whose accuracy for that mismatched category is likely no better (and could be worse) than the generic handler's flat accuracy — routing's benefit shrinks as classification accuracy drops.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Routing:** classifying an incoming request and dispatching it to a specialized prompt built for that category.
* **Specialist prompt:** a prompt built and tuned for one specific category of request.
* **Classification step:** the part of routing that determines which category a request belongs to.

## Related

[[Prompt Chaining]] · [[Supervisor-Orchestrator Patterns|Supervisor/Orchestrator Patterns]] · [[Tool Selection Among Many Candidates]]

## Parallelization: Sectioning and Voting

Running three independent pieces of a task one after another wastes time that didn't need to be spent sequentially at all — none of the three pieces needed the others to finish first. Running the same question several times and taking the most common answer is a different use of the same basic idea: parallel calls, combined afterward.

**You need:** [[Prompt Chaining]].

## The question it answers

"What are the two different reasons to run several LLM calls at once instead of one?" **Sectioning** splits one task into genuinely independent subtasks and runs them in parallel, finishing in however long the *slowest* piece takes rather than the *sum* of all of them. **Voting** runs the identical prompt several times on the same question and takes the most common answer — a form of the self-consistency sampling already covered on the LLMs planet — trading extra compute for a meaningfully more reliable answer.

## Intuition

Three friends cooking three unrelated dishes for the same dinner finish whenever the slowest dish is done, not by adding up all three cooking times — that's sectioning. Asking the same trivia question to five different people and going with whatever most of them say, rather than trusting the first answer alone, is voting — useful specifically because any one person's mistake is unlikely to be the exact same mistake five people happen to share.

## Definition and notation

```text
sectioning:  total time = max(subtask times), not the sum
voting:      majority_vote_accuracy(N, p) = P(more than N/2 of N independent samples, each correct with probability p, agree)
```

## A worked example

Three independent report sections, timed, and a toy voting scenario at 60% per-sample accuracy:

```text
sectioning:
  sequential (one after another): 1200 + 1500 + 900 = 3600ms
  sectioned (run in parallel):    max(1200, 1500, 900) = 1500ms
  speedup: 2.4×

voting (per-sample accuracy 60%):
  N=1: 60.0%     N=3: 64.8%     N=5: 68.3%     N=9: 73.3%
```

Sectioning cuts the total time to whichever single piece takes longest — a 2.4× speedup here, simply by not waiting on pieces that never depended on each other. Voting's accuracy climbs steadily with more samples, though with real diminishing returns: tripling the samples from 3 to 9 buys less than 9 percentage points of accuracy.

## Bench

```bench
id: sectioning-and-voting
title: Splitting work up, or asking several times
fallback: Compare sequential vs. sectioned (parallel) latency, and watch majority-vote accuracy climb with more samples.
```

**Try this**

1. Compare sequential and sectioned latency for the three report sections.
2. Switch to voting and slide N up, watching accuracy climb with diminishing returns.
3. Imagine a per-sample accuracy of 90% instead of 60% — would voting still be worth the extra compute?

**What you should notice:** sectioning's benefit depends on genuine independence between subtasks (nothing to wait on), while voting's benefit depends on wrong answers being inconsistent with each other — if the same mistake keeps recurring, more votes wouldn't out-vote it.

## Where it appears in AI

* **Voting is exactly [[Self-Consistency and Best-of-N Sampling|self-consistency sampling]], already covered on the Generative AI planet** — this topic is about using it as a parallelization pattern alongside sectioning, not re-deriving the sampling mechanism.
* **[[Orchestrator-Workers]] is the natural extension of sectioning** when the subtasks themselves need to be identified dynamically rather than being fixed in advance.
* **Sectioning's speedup assumes genuinely independent subtasks** — a task whose pieces depend on each other's results can't be sectioned this way at all, which is exactly why [[Plan-and-Execute Agents]] exists for tasks that need ordered steps instead.

## Common pitfalls

* **Sectioning a task whose pieces aren't actually independent.** If one section's result is needed by another, running them in parallel either produces a wrong result or requires one to wait on the other anyway, erasing the speedup.
* **Assuming more voting samples always help proportionally.** The worked example shows accuracy gains shrinking as N grows — tripling samples from 3 to 9 buys a much smaller gain than the first jump from 1 to 3.
* **Using voting when wrong answers consistently agree with each other.** Voting's benefit specifically relies on errors being spread across different wrong answers — if every wrong sample converges on the same mistake, the majority vote would confidently pick that mistake too.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. Why does sectioning finish in 1500ms rather than 3600ms in the worked example?</summary>
The three report sections don't depend on each other, so they can run at the same time; the total wait is only as long as the slowest individual section, not the sum of all three.
</details>

<details><summary>2. In the worked example, why does voting's accuracy gain from N=5 to N=9 look smaller than the gain from N=1 to N=3?</summary>
Majority-vote accuracy has diminishing returns as sample count grows — each additional sample contributes less to shifting the majority once the vote is already reasonably likely to be correct.
</details>

<details><summary>3. What assumption does voting's accuracy improvement depend on?</summary>
That wrong answers are inconsistent with each other rather than all converging on the same mistake — if every incorrect sample happened to agree, the majority vote would confidently select that shared wrong answer instead of being corrected by it.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Sectioning:** splitting a task into independent subtasks run in parallel, finishing in the time of the slowest piece.
* **Voting:** running the same prompt multiple times and taking the most common answer.
* **Diminishing returns (in voting):** each additional sample improving accuracy by a progressively smaller amount.

## Related

[[Self-Consistency and Best-of-N Sampling]] · [[Orchestrator-Workers]] · [[Plan-and-Execute Agents]]

## Orchestrator-Workers

A single call asked to analyze a market, project financials, and assess risk, all in one response, often trails off after the first section or two — there was only so much the model would produce before it ran out of room. An orchestrator that first splits the task into exactly those three pieces and assigns each to its own worker call guarantees every piece gets its own fresh output, instead of competing for the same shrinking budget.

**You need:** [[Parallelization: Sectioning and Voting]].

## The question it answers

"What do you do when a task's pieces can't be known in advance, the way sectioning assumes they can?" Sectioning (the previous topic) works when the subtasks are fixed ahead of time — a developer decides "three report sections" before any call runs.
