The **orchestrator-workers** pattern handles the case where the pieces themselves need to be figured out first: an orchestrator call decides what the subtasks *are*, dynamically, then dispatches one worker call per subtask and assembles their results.

## Intuition

A project manager who is handed "write this quarterly report" doesn't try to write the whole thing alone in one sitting — they first decide the report needs a market analysis, financial projections, and a risk assessment, then hand each piece to a specialist who writes just that section. Nobody runs out of room partway through, because nobody is asked to produce all three sections inside one budget.

## Definition and notation

```text
single call:        one generation, fixed length budget, covering as many sections as fit
orchestrator-workers: orchestrator → {subtask₁, subtask₂, subtask₃} → one worker call per subtask → assemble
```

## A worked example

A quarterly report with three required sections, compared under a single big call versus orchestrator-workers:

```text
required sections: market analysis, financial projections, risk assessment

single big call:          covers 2 of 3 sections (market analysis, financial projections)
                           — ran out of room before reaching risk assessment
orchestrator-workers:     covers 3 of 3 sections
                           — each section is its own worker call with its own full budget
```

The single call's shortfall isn't a quirk of one bad generation — it's structural: all three sections compete for the same response budget, so whichever section comes last is the one most likely to be cut short or skipped. Giving each section its own worker call removes that competition entirely.

## Bench

```bench
id: orchestrator-workers
title: Guaranteed coverage, one worker per piece
fallback: Compare a single big call that ran out of room against an orchestrator assigning one worker to each section.
```

**Try this**

1. Look at the single big call's coverage and notice which section never gets reached.
2. Switch to orchestrator-workers and see all three sections covered.
3. Imagine a report with ten required sections instead of three — would the single-call shortfall get better or worse?

**What you should notice:** the orchestrator's job is deciding *what the subtasks are* before any worker runs — unlike sectioning, where the subtasks were already fixed in advance by whoever designed the workflow.

## Where it appears in AI

* **Orchestrator-workers extends [[Parallelization: Sectioning and Voting|sectioning]]** to tasks where the subtasks aren't known ahead of time — the orchestrator's dynamic decomposition step is the one piece sectioning doesn't need.
* **[[Goal Decomposition into Subtasks]] is the general mechanism behind the orchestrator's decomposition step**, applied here specifically to spawning parallel worker calls.
* **[[Supervisor-Orchestrator Patterns|Supervisor/Orchestrator Patterns]] is the multi-agent version of the same structure**: workers become full agents rather than single calls, and the orchestrator's assembly step becomes an ongoing coordination job.

## Common pitfalls

* **Using a single call for a task whose required pieces are numerous or unpredictable.** The worked example's shortfall (missing the third of three sections) only gets worse as more sections are required — eventually no single call's budget covers them all.
* **Skipping the orchestrator's decomposition step and hard-coding subtasks instead.** If the subtasks really are fixed in advance, plain sectioning already covers that case more simply; orchestrator-workers earns its extra complexity only when the decomposition itself needs to happen dynamically.
* **Forgetting the assembly step.** Running three independent worker calls is only half the pattern — something still has to combine market analysis, financial projections, and risk assessment into one coherent report.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. Why does the single big call cover only 2 of 3 sections in the worked example?</summary>
All three sections compete for the same fixed response budget in one generation, so whichever section comes last in the response is the most likely to be cut short or never reached at all.
</details>

<details><summary>2. What does the orchestrator do that a plain sectioning workflow doesn't?</summary>
It decides what the subtasks actually are, dynamically, before dispatching worker calls — sectioning assumes the subtasks were already fixed in advance by the workflow's designer.
</details>

<details><summary>3. Why doesn't giving each section its own worker call reintroduce the single call's shortfall?</summary>
Each worker call gets its own independent response budget, so one section's length no longer competes with another's — nothing is squeezed out by what came before it.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Orchestrator-workers:** a pattern where an orchestrator call dynamically decides a task's subtasks, then dispatches one worker call per subtask and assembles the results.
* **Dynamic decomposition:** figuring out what a task's pieces are at run time, rather than fixing them in advance.
* **Assembly step:** combining the separate worker calls' outputs into one coherent final result.

## Related

[[Parallelization: Sectioning and Voting]] · [[Goal Decomposition into Subtasks]] · [[Supervisor-Orchestrator Patterns|Supervisor/Orchestrator Patterns]]

## Evaluator-Optimizer Loops

A first draft critiqued once gets noticeably better; critiqued a second time, it gets better still, but by less than the first round did. An evaluator-optimizer loop makes that generate-critique-improve cycle explicit: one call generates or revises, a second call evaluates the result and says what's still wrong, and the first call revises again — repeating until the evaluator is satisfied or a round limit is reached.

**You need:** [[Prompt Chaining]].

## The question it answers

"How do you turn a single generation into something that improves itself with feedback?" An evaluator-optimizer loop pairs two roles: an **optimizer** that generates or revises a candidate, and an **evaluator** that judges the candidate and returns specific feedback. The optimizer's next revision responds directly to that feedback, and the two alternate for a fixed number of rounds or until the evaluator passes the result — the same generate-critique-improve cycle as [[Self-Refinement and Iterative Critique|self-refinement]], already covered on the LLMs planet, used here as a workflow pattern rather than a reasoning technique.

## Intuition

A writer who hands a draft to an editor, gets back specific notes ("the ending doesn't land, the second paragraph repeats the first"), and revises accordingly improves faster than one revising blind — and the editor's second round of notes is usually shorter than the first, because most of the big problems already got fixed.

## Definition and notation

```text
loop:    generate → evaluate → feedback → revise → evaluate → feedback → revise → ...
quality after round r = 1 − 0.5^(r+1)        (the self-refinement curve from the LLMs planet)
```

## A worked example

Quality after each evaluator-optimizer round, reusing the exact self-refinement curve already verified on the LLMs planet:

```text
round 0 (first draft):  50.00%
round 1:                75.00%
round 2:                87.50%
round 3:                93.75%
round 4:                96.88%
```

Each round closes half of the remaining gap to a perfect result — round 1 closes half of the 50% that round 0 left open, round 2 closes half of what round 1 left open, and so on. The gains keep shrinking even as they keep coming, which is exactly why a loop like this needs a stopping rule rather than running forever.

## Bench

```bench
id: evaluator-optimizer-loop
title: Generate, critique, improve, repeat
fallback: Step through evaluator-optimizer rounds and watch quality climb with diminishing returns.
```

**Try this**

1. Step through all four rounds and watch the quality bar climb each time.
2. Notice how much smaller the jump from round 3 to round 4 is than the jump from round 0 to round 1.
3. Imagine the evaluator has a fixed quality bar it requires before passing a result — at what round would it likely stop this loop?

**What you should notice:** the loop's gains shrink round over round in exactly the same shape as the self-refinement curve on the LLMs planet — it's the identical mechanism, just run inside a workflow with an explicit evaluator role instead of a single model critiquing its own output.

## Where it appears in AI

* **This is [[Self-Refinement and Iterative Critique|self-refinement]] from the LLMs planet, used as a workflow pattern.** The underlying curve — each round closing half the remaining gap — is the exact same mechanism; what's new here is treating it as a structured loop with its own stopping condition, alongside the other workflow patterns on this road.
* **[[Verifier-Guided Agent Loops]] generalizes this same evaluator role** into a check that runs continuously inside an autonomous agent, rather than a fixed number of workflow rounds.
* **[[Reflection and Self-Improvement|Reflection and self-improvement]], the next district, covers the agent-level version of this same critique-and-revise cycle** happening across an agent's own trajectory rather than inside a fixed workflow.

## Common pitfalls

* **Running the loop for a fixed large number of rounds regardless of returns.** The worked example shows round 4 adds only about 3 percentage points over round 3 — past some point, another round costs more compute than the quality gain is worth.
* **Giving the evaluator no specific feedback to act on.** A pass/fail verdict with no explanation of *what's* wrong gives the optimizer nothing concrete to revise — the loop depends on the evaluator's feedback being specific enough to act on.
* **Confusing this with the agent's own self-correction.** The loop here has a fixed workflow structure with two defined roles; an agent reflecting mid-trajectory (the next district) is doing something related but less structured, with no fixed round count decided in advance.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. In the worked example, why does round 1 add 25 percentage points but round 4 adds only about 3?</summary>
Each round closes half of whatever quality gap was still remaining after the previous round — the gap itself keeps shrinking, so each round's absolute gain shrinks along with it, even though the loop keeps making progress.
</details>

<details><summary>2. What two roles does an evaluator-optimizer loop need?</summary>
An optimizer that generates or revises a candidate, and an evaluator that judges the candidate and returns specific feedback for the optimizer's next revision.
</details>

<details><summary>3. Why would an unlimited number of rounds be a bad default?</summary>
Returns diminish every round, so at some point another round's compute cost exceeds the quality gain it buys — a loop without a stopping rule keeps paying for smaller and smaller improvements indefinitely.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Evaluator-optimizer loop:** a workflow pairing a generating/revising call with an evaluating call that gives feedback, repeated until a stopping condition.
* **Optimizer:** the role that generates or revises a candidate based on feedback.
* **Evaluator:** the role that judges a candidate and returns specific, actionable feedback.

## Related

[[Self-Refinement and Iterative Critique]] · [[Verifier-Guided Agent Loops]] · [[Reflection and Self-Improvement]]

## Planning and Task Decomposition

A genuinely open-ended goal can't be handled by a fixed workflow written in advance — nobody knows the steps until the agent starts looking at the specific situation. This district is about an agent planning its own steps: breaking a goal down, executing that plan, and revising it the moment reality doesn't match what was expected.

Topics on this stretch of the road:

* [[Goal Decomposition into Subtasks]]: turning one large, vague goal into an ordered list of smaller, checkable ones.
* [[Plan-and-Execute Agents]]: writing out the whole plan before executing any of it, instead of deciding one step at a time.
* [[Re-Planning on Failure]]: what an agent does when a step's result doesn't match what the plan assumed.
* [[Hierarchical Task Planning]]: a plan made of subtasks that are themselves planned separately, at a lower level of detail.
* [[When Planning Hurts More Than It Helps]]: the real cost of planning, and the tasks where skipping it entirely does better.

## Goal Decomposition into Subtasks

Told to "launch the product," an agent that lists tasks in whatever order they occur to it can end up trying to launch before the thing it's launching has been tested — the launch step depends on a step that hasn't run yet. Goal decomposition breaks a goal into subtasks and their dependencies explicitly, so the order the agent actually runs them in respects what each one needs to already be true.

**You need:** [[Anatomy of an Agent Architecture]].

## The question it answers

"How does an agent turn one big goal into an ordered sequence of smaller steps it can actually execute?" Goal decomposition identifies a goal's subtasks and the dependencies between them — which subtasks need which others to have finished first — then orders the subtasks so that every dependency is satisfied before the subtask that needs it runs. A **flat** ordering, one that lists subtasks without working out their dependencies, can easily put a subtask before something it secretly depends on.

## Intuition

Told to "throw a dinner party," listing tasks in the order they come to mind — clean the house, buy ingredients, cook the meal, invite guests — puts cooking before buying ingredients and invites after the cooking's already supposed to start. Working out what depends on what first (buy ingredients → cook → invite guests with a time that's actually realistic) gives an order that could actually be followed.

## Definition and notation

```text
subtask graph:  task → [its prerequisite tasks]
dependency violation:  a task appears in the order before one of its own prerequisites has completed
decomposed order = a topological order of the subtask graph (zero violations, by construction)
```

## A worked example

A "launch the product" goal with five subtasks and real dependencies between them, ordered two ways:

```text
dependencies:
  write spec            → (none)
  build backend         → needs: write spec
  build frontend        → needs: write spec
  integration test      → needs: build backend, build frontend
  launch                → needs: integration test

flat order (as first mentioned): launch, write spec, integration test, build backend, build frontend
  → 3 dependency violations

decomposed order (topological):  write spec, build backend, build frontend, integration test, launch
  → 0 dependency violations
```

The flat order isn't a careless mistake — it's what naturally happens when subtasks are listed without first asking what each one needs. Working out the dependency graph and sorting by it is what guarantees zero violations, not luck.

## Bench

```bench
id: goal-decomposition-order
title: Decomposed order, or a flat guess
fallback: Compare a flat task order against one derived from the actual dependencies between subtasks.
```

**Try this**

1. Look at the flat order and find each place a task is marked as needing something that hasn't happened yet.
2. Switch to the decomposed order and confirm every task's prerequisites are already checked off.
3. Imagine adding a sixth subtask that only "launch" depends on — where would decomposition place it?

**What you should notice:** the violations in the flat order aren't about which task is more "important" — they're purely about whether a task's prerequisites happened before it, which is exactly what a dependency graph makes explicit and a flat list doesn't.

## Where it appears in AI

* **[[Orchestrator-Workers]]'s decomposition step is this same mechanism**, applied specifically to splitting a task into pieces that can be assigned to parallel workers — the dependency-tracking half of this topic is what decides whether those pieces can safely run in parallel at all.
* **[[Plan-and-Execute Agents]] uses decomposition's output as its plan**: once subtasks are ordered, a plan-and-execute agent executes them one at a time.
* **A subtask graph with no valid topological order (a cycle) means the goal as stated is unsatisfiable** — two subtasks that each depend on the other can never both run first.

## Common pitfalls

* **Listing subtasks in the order they're mentioned rather than the order their dependencies require.** The worked example shows this isn't a minor risk — three of five tasks violate a real dependency when ordered this way.
* **Assuming decomposition alone guarantees correctness.** Decomposition only guarantees the *order* respects dependencies; it doesn't guarantee the subtasks list itself is complete, or that each subtask is actually achievable.
* **Treating every subtask as independent by default.** The actual dependency structure needs to be worked out, not assumed away — assuming independence is exactly what the flat order implicitly does.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. Why does the flat order in the worked example have exactly 3 violations?</summary>
"Launch" is listed first but needs integration test to finish before it; "integration test" is listed before both "build backend" and "build frontend" have finished — each of those three mismatches between a task's position and its prerequisites' position counts as one violation.
</details>

<details><summary>2. What guarantees the decomposed order has zero violations?</summary>
It's constructed as a topological order of the dependency graph — by definition, a topological order places every task after all of its prerequisites, so no violation can occur.
</details>

<details><summary>3. What does it mean if a goal's subtask graph has no valid topological order?</summary>
There's a cycle of dependencies (some subtask directly or indirectly depends on itself through others), which makes the goal as decomposed unsatisfiable — the subtasks or their stated dependencies need to be reconsidered.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Goal decomposition:** breaking a goal into subtasks and the dependencies between them.
* **Dependency violation:** a subtask appearing in an order before one of its own prerequisites has completed.
* **Topological order:** an ordering of a dependency graph's tasks that places every task after all of its prerequisites.

## Related

[[Anatomy of an Agent Architecture]] · [[Orchestrator-Workers]] · [[Plan-and-Execute Agents]]

## Plan-and-Execute Agents

Deciding every step of a trip itinerary up front, then just following it, takes one planning conversation and one action per stop. Deciding each stop fresh, in the moment, right before taking it, takes roughly twice as many conversations — one to think, one to act — at every single stop. Plan-and-execute agents choose the first shape: decompose the goal into an ordered plan once, then execute each step with no further planning call, unless something goes wrong.

**You need:** [[Goal Decomposition into Subtasks]].

## The question it answers

"Should an agent decide its whole sequence of steps up front, or decide each next step as it goes?" A **plan-and-execute** agent makes one planning call that decomposes the goal into an ordered list of steps, then makes one additional call per step to execute it — no further reasoning about *what* to do next, just doing what the plan already said. An **interleaved** agent (the [[Tool-Augmented Reasoning (ReAct-Style)|ReAct-style]] pattern already covered on the LLMs planet) instead reasons about what to do at every single step, which costs roughly twice as many calls for the same number of steps but can react to new information the plan never anticipated.

## Intuition

A tourist who plans an entire day's itinerary over breakfast, then just follows it stop by stop, needs one planning conversation and one action at each stop. A tourist who stops to think "what should I do next?" before every single stop is doing the same amount of deciding, just spread across every stop instead of concentrated once — at roughly double the total thinking.

## Definition and notation

```text
plan-and-execute calls(n steps) = 1 (planning) + n (one per step)
interleaved calls(n steps)      = 2n (think + act, every step)
```

## A worked example

Total calls for a task broken into a varying number of steps, under both approaches:

```text
n = 3 steps:  plan-and-execute = 4 calls   interleaved = 6 calls
n = 5 steps:  plan-and-execute = 6 calls   interleaved = 10 calls
n = 8 steps:  plan-and-execute = 9 calls   interleaved = 16 calls
```

The gap widens as the number of steps grows — plan-and-execute adds exactly one call per extra step, while interleaving adds two. The saving only holds, though, as long as the original plan stays good; a plan that goes stale partway through needs [[Re-Planning on Failure|re-planning]] to recover, which spends some of that saved budget back.

## Bench

```bench
id: plan-execute-calls
title: One plan then act, or think at every step
fallback: Compare total LLM calls for plan-and-execute against interleaving a think-then-act call at every step.
```

**Try this**

1. Slide the number of steps up and watch both call counts grow.
2. Notice the gap between the two bars widening as steps increase.
3. Imagine a task where step 3's outcome changes what step 4 should be — would plan-and-execute still work as written?

**What you should notice:** the call-count saving is real and grows with plan length, but it comes with a cost the bench doesn't show directly: a plan-and-execute agent can't adapt mid-plan to something it didn't anticipate, which is exactly the gap [[Re-Planning on Failure|re-planning]] exists to close.

## Where it appears in AI

* **Interleaved planning is the [[Tool-Augmented Reasoning (ReAct-Style)|ReAct pattern]] from the LLMs planet**, applied here as the alternative to committing to a full plan up front.
* **[[Re-Planning on Failure]] is what a plan-and-execute agent needs when the world doesn't match the plan it committed to** — without it, a stale plan just keeps executing anyway.
* **[[Hierarchical Task Planning]] extends the same idea** by planning at more than one level of detail, rather than producing one flat list of steps.

## Common pitfalls

* **Assuming plan-and-execute is simply "better" because it costs fewer calls.** The call-count saving only pays off when the plan stays valid — in a fast-changing environment, the saved calls can be dwarfed by the cost of acting on a now-wrong plan.
* **Using plan-and-execute for a task whose later steps genuinely depend on earlier results in ways that can't be anticipated.** If step 4 truly can't be decided until step 3's result is known, the plan has to leave it open, which is closer to interleaving than to a full upfront plan.
* **Forgetting that interleaving's extra cost buys real adaptability.** The comparison isn't "cheap but rigid vs. expensive and pointless" — interleaving's extra think step is what lets it notice and react to things the plan never anticipated.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. Why does plan-and-execute need only 1 + n calls for n steps?</summary>
One call produces the entire ordered plan up front, and then each step is executed with a single call that just carries out what the plan already decided — no further "what should I do" reasoning is needed per step.
</details>

<details><summary>2. Why does interleaving cost roughly twice as many calls as plan-and-execute for the same number of steps?</summary>
Interleaving makes a separate thinking call and a separate acting call at every step, rather than deciding the whole sequence once — so each step costs two calls instead of plan-and-execute's roughly one.
</details>

<details><summary>3. What does plan-and-execute give up in exchange for its lower call count?</summary>
The ability to reconsider what to do next in light of something the original plan didn't anticipate — a plan-and-execute agent just keeps executing the plan it already committed to, unless something explicitly triggers re-planning.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Plan-and-execute:** an agent pattern that decomposes a goal into a full ordered plan once, then executes each step without further planning calls.
* **Interleaved (ReAct-style):** an agent pattern that reasons about what to do at every step, rather than committing to a plan in advance.
* **Call budget:** the number of LLM calls an approach needs for a given number of steps.

## Related

[[Goal Decomposition into Subtasks]] · [[Tool-Augmented Reasoning (ReAct-Style)]] · [[Re-Planning on Failure]]

## Re-Planning on Failure

A plan to book a trip hits a hotel that's sold out on step 3 of 5. An agent that never checks its own results just keeps going — booking a transfer to a hotel address that was never actually confirmed, then "confirming" an itinerary that was never real. An agent that notices the failure and re-plans picks a different hotel and finishes every remaining step successfully.

**You need:** [[Plan-and-Execute Agents]].

## The question it answers

"What happens when a step in an already-committed plan fails, and how does an agent recover?" Re-planning means detecting that a step didn't produce the result the plan assumed, and generating a new plan for the remaining steps instead of blindly continuing the old one. Without it, every later step that depended on the failed one's result either silently fails too or produces output built on a false premise.

## Intuition

A road trip's GPS route hits a closed bridge. A driver who doesn't notice and keeps following the original turn-by-turn directions ends up stuck at the bridge, with every subsequent direction now meaningless. A driver whose GPS notices the closure and recalculates a new route from the current position reaches the destination anyway — the original plan's failure doesn't have to mean the whole trip fails.

## Definition and notation

```text
plan: step₁ → step₂ → ... → stepₙ
failure at stepₖ:
  without re-planning: steps 1..k-1 complete, step k fails, steps k+1..n depend on it and also fail
  with re-planning:    steps 1..k-1 complete, step k's failure is detected, a new plan for steps k..n is made and completes
```

## A worked example

A 5-step trip-booking plan where step 3 (book hotel) fails because the hotel is sold out:

```text
plan: book flight, get visa, book hotel, book transfer, confirm itinerary
failure: step 3 ("book hotel") — the hotel is sold out

without re-planning: 2 of 5 steps complete (flight, visa) — transfer and itinerary both depend on
                      a hotel that was never actually booked, so they fail too
with re-planning:     5 of 5 steps complete — the failure at step 3 is detected, a new hotel is
                      found, and the remaining steps (transfer, itinerary) proceed against it
```

The difference isn't that re-planning avoids the failure itself — the first hotel is still sold out either way. It's that re-planning contains the damage to the one step that actually failed, instead of letting it silently propagate through every step that assumed it had succeeded.

## Bench

```bench
id: replan-on-failure
title: Notice the failure, or plough on
fallback: Step through a 5-step plan where step 3 fails, comparing outcomes with and without re-planning.
```

**Try this**

1. With replanning off, step through all 5 steps and watch steps 4 and 5 get marked as depending on a step that never actually succeeded.
2. Turn replanning on and step through again — notice steps 4 and 5 now complete.
3. Imagine the failure happened at step 1 instead of step 3 — would re-planning still recover all 5 steps?

**What you should notice:** re-planning doesn't require predicting every possible failure in advance — it only requires noticing, after the fact, that a step's actual result didn't match what the plan assumed, which is the same closed-loop check already covered in [[Open-Loop vs. Closed-Loop Behavior]].

## Where it appears in AI

* **Re-planning is [[Open-Loop vs. Closed-Loop Behavior|closed-loop checking]] applied specifically to a multi-step plan**, rather than to a single action — the loop still has to check its own results, just now at the level of "did this step's actual outcome match the plan's assumption."
* **[[Verifier-Guided Agent Loops]], covered later, generalizes the same detect-and-recover mechanism** into a continuous check running throughout an agent's trajectory, not only at a single plan's failure points.
* **A plan-and-execute agent (the previous topic) specifically needs re-planning** to recover the adaptability it gave up by committing to a plan up front.

## Common pitfalls

* **Assuming a failed step's consequences stay contained to that one step.** The worked example shows the opposite — two further steps fail too, purely because they depended on a result that never materialized.
* **Re-planning the entire task from scratch instead of just the remaining steps.** The completed early steps (booking the flight, getting the visa) don't need to be redone — only the steps from the failure point onward need a new plan.
* **Detecting failure too late.** If the failure at step 3 isn't noticed until step 5 is attempted, the agent has already wasted effort executing steps built on a false premise, rather than catching it at step 3 itself.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. Why do steps 4 and 5 fail in the worked example even though nothing is wrong with them individually?</summary>
Both depend on step 3 (the hotel booking) having actually succeeded — booking a transfer to an address that was never confirmed, or confirming an itinerary around a hotel that was never booked, doesn't make sense once step 3 failed.
</details>

<details><summary>2. What does re-planning actually change about the outcome of step 3's failure?</summary>
It doesn't prevent the original failure (the first hotel really is sold out), but it stops that failure from silently propagating — a new plan for the remaining steps (built around a different hotel) lets steps 4 and 5 complete successfully instead of failing too.
</details>

<details><summary>3. What's the minimum an agent needs to re-plan successfully?</summary>
It needs to detect that a step's actual result doesn't match what the plan assumed — the same closed-loop check as open-loop vs. closed-loop behavior, just applied to one step of a larger plan rather than a single action.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Re-planning:** detecting that a plan's step failed and generating a new plan for the remaining steps instead of continuing the original one.
* **Failure propagation:** later steps failing because they depended on an earlier step's result that never actually materialized.
* **Detection point:** the moment a failure is actually noticed, which determines how much wasted effort happens before recovery begins.

## Related

[[Plan-and-Execute Agents]] · [[Open-Loop vs. Closed-Loop Behavior]] · [[Verifier-Guided Agent Loops]]

## Hierarchical Task Planning

"Organize a conference" eventually breaks down into 36 individual primitive actions — booking a specific venue, sending a specific email, printing a specific badge. A flat planner has to consider all 36 at once. A hierarchical planner never considers more than a handful at a time: pick the top-level tasks, then for each one pick its sub-tasks, then for each of those pick its primitive actions — the same 36 actions, reached through a sequence of small decisions instead of one enormous one.

**You need:** [[Goal Decomposition into Subtasks]].

## The question it answers

"How does decomposition stay manageable when a goal has dozens or hundreds of eventual primitive actions?" Hierarchical task planning (the classic **HTN**, hierarchical task network, idea) decomposes a goal into a small number of high-level tasks, then decomposes each of those into its own sub-tasks, continuing down levels until the remaining pieces are primitive actions that can just be executed. At no single level does the planner ever have to reason about more than that level's own handful of choices.

## Intuition

Planning a wedding by listing all several hundred individual tasks at once — order flowers, book the venue, print invitations, choose a song, confirm the caterer's menu — in one giant undifferentiated list is overwhelming. Planning it by first deciding the handful of major areas (venue, catering, guests, ceremony), then working out each area's own handful of tasks, keeps every single decision small, even though the same several hundred tasks eventually get covered.

## Definition and notation

```text
flat planner's branching factor       = total number of primitive actions, all reasoned about at once
hierarchical planner's branching factor = the largest number of choices faced at any single level
```

## A worked example

"Organize a conference," with 3 top-level tasks, each split into 4 sub-tasks, each split into 3 primitive actions:

```text
total primitive actions = 3 × 4 × 3 = 36

flat planner:          reasons about all 36 primitive actions at once → branching factor 36
hierarchical planner:  top level picks among 3, then among 4, then among 3
                        → widest single decision is max(3, 4, 3) = 4
```

The hierarchical planner still has to decide, eventually, over all 36 primitive actions — nothing about the task got smaller. What changed is that no single decision point ever has to weigh more than 4 options at once, instead of one decision point weighing all 36.

## Bench

```bench
id: hierarchical-task-planning
title: One huge choice, or several small ones
fallback: Compare a flat planner's branching factor against a hierarchical planner's widest single choice.
```

**Try this**

1. Note the total primitive actions and the flat planner's branching factor — they're always equal.
2. Slide each of the three levels up and watch the hierarchical planner's branching factor track only the largest single level, not the total.
3. Push all three levels up to their maximum and compare how far apart the two bars get.

**What you should notice:** the hierarchical planner's branching factor is bounded by the *widest single level*, not by the total number of primitive actions — adding more top-level tasks or more primitive actions per sub-task barely moves it, as long as no individual level itself gets wide.

## Where it appears in AI

* **This is the same branching-factor idea behind [[Tree-of-Thought and Search-Based Reasoning|tree-of-thought search]] on the LLMs planet**, applied to planning actions in the world instead of searching over reasoning paths — keeping each level's choice set small is what makes either kind of search tractable at all.
* **[[Goal Decomposition into Subtasks]] is the single-level version of this same mechanism**; hierarchical planning is what happens when decomposition is applied recursively, level after level, rather than just once.
* **A deep hierarchy trades a smaller branching factor at each level for more total levels to plan through** — there's a real cost on the other side of this benefit.

## Common pitfalls

* **Assuming a hierarchical planner "does less work" than a flat one.** The worked example's total of 36 primitive actions doesn't shrink — hierarchical planning only changes how that total is reached, spreading it across several small decisions instead of one big one.
* **Making the hierarchy too deep for the goal's actual complexity.** A hierarchy with many levels for a goal that only has a handful of primitive actions adds planning overhead without reducing any single level's branching factor meaningfully.
* **Choosing level boundaries that don't correspond to anything meaningful.** A hierarchy's levels are useful insofar as they reflect genuine sub-goals (venue, catering, guests) — an arbitrary split that doesn't track real structure just adds bookkeeping without the benefit.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. Why is the flat planner's branching factor always equal to the total number of primitive actions?</summary>
A flat planner reasons about every primitive action in one undifferentiated decision, so its branching factor is exactly the count of all of them — there's no smaller decision to make instead.
</details>

<details><summary>2. In the worked example, why is the hierarchical planner's branching factor 4 rather than something related to 36?</summary>
The hierarchical planner never reasons about more than one level's own choices at a time, and the widest single level here has 4 options (4 sub-tasks per top-level task) — the total of 36 is reached across several separate small decisions, not one combined one.
</details>

<details><summary>3. What's the actual trade-off of going hierarchical rather than flat?</summary>
A smaller branching factor at any single decision point, in exchange for having to plan through more levels overall — the total amount of eventual decision-making doesn't shrink, only how concentrated it is.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Hierarchical task network (HTN):** a planning approach that decomposes a goal into tasks, then those tasks into sub-tasks, continuing down to primitive actions.
* **Branching factor:** the number of choices a planner has to weigh at a single decision point.
* **Primitive action:** a task simple enough to just be executed, with no further decomposition.

## Related

[[Goal Decomposition into Subtasks]] · [[Tree-of-Thought and Search-Based Reasoning]] · [[Plan-and-Execute Agents]]

## When Planning Hurts More Than It Helps

Planning ahead only pays off if the plan is still good by the time it's executed. In a stable environment that barely changes, one upfront plan beats reacting fresh at every single step. In a volatile environment that changes every step, that same upfront plan goes stale almost immediately — by the time step 5 runs, the world it was planned for may no longer exist, and all the planning spent getting there was wasted.

**You need:** [[Plan-and-Execute Agents]].

## The question it answers

"Is planning ahead always worth its cost?" Planning has a real upfront cost — time spent deciding a sequence of steps before acting on any of them. That cost pays for itself only across however many steps the resulting plan stays valid for. In a stable environment, a plan stays valid for a long stretch, so the upfront cost is amortized over many cheap execution steps. In a volatile environment, the plan goes stale fast, forcing frequent re-planning, and a purely reactive policy that never plans at all can end up cheaper overall.

## Intuition

Planning a grocery store trip aisle by aisle before walking in saves time, as long as the store's layout doesn't change mid-trip. If the store's layout were reshuffled every few minutes, re-planning the whole route over and over would cost more time than it saves — at that point, just reacting to whatever's in front of you, aisle by aisle, as you go, would actually be faster.

## Definition and notation

```text
planning total time(horizon, volatility)  = ⌈horizon / volatility⌉ × Tplan + horizon × Texec
reactive total time(horizon)              = horizon × Treactive
    volatility = steps between environment changes (bigger = more stable)
```

## A worked example

A 12-step horizon, with a planning cost of 400ms, a 20ms cost to execute a step that's already planned, and a 150ms cost to reason fresh at every step with no plan at all, compared across three volatilities:

```text
volatility = 12 (stable, never changes):  planning = 640ms   reactive = 1800ms   → planning wins
volatility = 4  (changes every 4 steps):  planning = 1440ms  reactive = 1800ms   → planning wins (barely)
volatility = 3  (changes every 3 steps):  planning = 1840ms  reactive = 1800ms   → reactive wins
volatility = 1  (changes every step):     planning = 5040ms  reactive = 1800ms  → reactive wins (by a lot)
```

The crossover sits between a change every 4 steps and a change every 3 steps. Nothing about reactive execution got cheaper as volatility increased — what changed is how many times planning's 400ms upfront cost had to be paid again, and at high enough volatility, that repeated cost outweighs the entire benefit planning was supposed to provide.

## Bench

```bench
id: planning-vs-reactive
title: Plan ahead, or just react
fallback: Compare total time spent re-planning as the environment changes against a reactive policy that never plans.
```

**Try this**

1. Set the slider to its most stable setting and note how much planning beats reactive.
2. Slide toward more frequent changes and watch for the point where reactive takes over.
3. Imagine Tplan were much cheaper (a smaller upfront planning cost) — would the crossover point move toward more or less volatility?

**What you should notice:** the crossover isn't a fixed property of planning or reacting in general — it depends on the actual numbers (how expensive planning is, how expensive reacting is, how fast the environment changes), so the right choice is an empirical question about the specific environment, not a universal rule.

## Where it appears in AI

* **[[Re-Planning on Failure]] already showed one case where replanning pays for itself** — this topic generalizes that to a spectrum, asking not "should the agent replan when something fails" but "how often is replanning worth it at all, given how often things change."
* **[[Plan-and-Execute Agents]]'s savings assumed a plan stays valid long enough to execute** — this topic makes that assumption explicit and shows what happens when it stops holding.
* **This is the planning-side version of a bias–variance-style trade-off**: more upfront planning reduces per-step decision cost but increases the cost of being wrong when the world changes underneath the plan.

## Common pitfalls

* **Assuming planning is always worth its cost because it "looks more thorough."** The worked example shows a concrete regime (volatility 3 or lower here) where a cheaper, dumber reactive policy actually finishes faster in total.
* **Assuming reactive policies are always worth it because they're simpler.** In the stable regime, reactive execution costs nearly 3× more total time than planning — simplicity isn't free either.
* **Treating the crossover point as universal.** It depends entirely on the actual costs involved (Tplan, Texec, Treactive) for the specific system and environment — a different cost structure moves the crossover to a different volatility.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. In the worked example, why does planning's total time grow so much faster than reactive's as volatility drops?</summary>
Lower volatility means more frequent environment changes, which means more replans within the same 12-step horizon — each replan adds another full 400ms planning cost, while reactive's cost per step (150ms) never changes regardless of volatility.
</details>

<details><summary>2. Why doesn't reactive's total time change across the four volatility settings in the worked example?</summary>
A reactive policy never plans at all — it reasons fresh at every step regardless of how often the environment changes, so its total cost is always horizon × Treactive, independent of volatility.
</details>

<details><summary>3. What determines where the crossover between planning and reactive sits, in general?</summary>
The relative sizes of the planning cost, the plan-execution cost, and the reactive-reasoning cost, together with how often the environment actually changes — change any of those numbers and the crossover point moves.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Volatility:** how often the environment changes, measured here as steps between changes (lower volatility means more frequent change).
* **Amortized planning cost:** a plan's one-time cost spread across however many cheap execution steps it stays valid for.
* **Crossover point:** the volatility at which planning and reactive execution cost the same total time.

## Related

[[Plan-and-Execute Agents]] · [[Re-Planning on Failure]] · [[Hierarchical Task Planning]]

## Tool Use and Function Calling

Calling one tool correctly is a solved problem, already covered on the LLMs planet. An agent calling from a toolbox of fifty tools, across dozens of steps, with some of those calls failing or returning something unexpected, is a different and harder problem — this district is about keeping that reliable at scale.

Topics on this stretch of the road:

* [[Tool Selection Among Many Candidates]]: picking the right tool out of a large toolbox, not just the right arguments for one.
* [[Parallel vs. Sequential Tool Calls]]: when an agent can fire off several tool calls at once, and when one call has to wait for another's result.
* [[Handling Tool Errors and Retries]]: what an agent does when a tool call fails, times out, or returns garbage.
* [[Tool Result Verification]]: checking a tool's output before trusting it, instead of feeding it straight into the next step.
* [[Designing Tools for Agent Reliability]]: what makes a tool's interface easy for an agent to use correctly, versus one it keeps misusing.
* [[Code as a Tool-Calling Interface]]: writing and running a snippet of code as the action itself, instead of calling one fixed tool at a time.

## Tool Selection Among Many Candidates

An agent with 40 tools available for one task has exactly one that's actually correct. Shown all 40 at once with no other signal to go on, picking it by chance alone succeeds 2.5% of the time. Pre-filter to the 3 tools most similar to the task by embedding search — and if the correct one survives that cut — the same blind guess now succeeds a third of the time, simply because there are fewer wrong options left to confuse it with.

**You need:** [[Retrieval Metrics: Precision, Recall, MRR and NDCG]].

## The question it answers

"Does showing an agent more tools make it more capable, or does it make tool selection harder?" Every tool description added to a prompt is one more plausible-looking option the model has to rule out before picking the right one. **Tool retrieval** addresses this the same way retrieval addresses it for documents on the RAG planet: rank the available tools by relevance to the task, keep only the top K, and let the model choose among that smaller set — trading the risk of filtering the right tool out entirely (if K is too small) against the cost of drowning it in distractors (if K is too large).

## Intuition

Handed one knife out of a block of 40 and asked to pick the one meant for bread, you'd have to inspect all 40 to be sure. Handed just the 3 that are clearly bread-adjacent — a bread knife, a serrated utility knife, a cake knife — picking correctly is far easier, precisely because there are fewer plausible wrong answers left standing between you and the right one.

## Definition and notation

```text
recall@K       = 1 if the correct tool is among the top K candidates shown, else 0   (one relevant item)
worst-case accuracy@K = recall@K × 1/K     (a uniform guess among whatever's actually shown)
```

## A worked example

40 available tools; embedding similarity to the task ranks the genuinely correct one 3rd:

```text
K = 1:  correct tool filtered out (rank 3 > K)  → recall = 0   → worst-case accuracy = 0.0%
K = 3:  correct tool survives (rank 3 ≤ K)      → recall = 1   → worst-case accuracy = 33.3%
K = 10: correct tool survives                   → recall = 1   → worst-case accuracy = 10.0%
K = 40: correct tool survives (nothing filtered) → recall = 1  → worst-case accuracy = 2.5%
```

K = 1 is too aggressive — it filters out the very tool the agent needed, guaranteeing failure regardless of how good the final selection step is. K = 40 (showing everything) never risks that, but dilutes the choice so much that a selection with no other signal succeeds barely more than 1 time in 40. K = 3, the smallest K that still keeps the correct tool in view, gets the best of both worlds here.

## Bench

```bench
id: tool-selection-filtering
title: How many candidates to show the model
fallback: Slide the number of pre-filtered candidates and watch recall and worst-case selection accuracy trade off.
```

**Try this**

1. Start at K = 1 and watch the correct tool get filtered out entirely.
2. Slide up to K = 3, the smallest K that keeps it in view, and note the accuracy jump.
3. Keep sliding to K = 40 and watch accuracy keep falling even though recall stays at 100%.

**What you should notice:** recall and worst-case accuracy pull in opposite directions as K grows — recall only ever improves or stays the same, while accuracy keeps shrinking, because every additional candidate shown is one more thing to rule out.

## Where it appears in AI

* **This is tool retrieval, the direct analogue of [[Retrieval Metrics: Precision, Recall, MRR and NDCG|retrieval metrics]] already covered on the RAG planet** — a tool library behaves exactly like a document collection once there are more candidates than fit comfortably in one prompt.
* **[[Routing Between Specialized Prompts]], from the previous district, routes among a handful of whole prompts**; tool selection is the same problem scaled up to dozens or hundreds of fine-grained candidates, which is exactly why a retrieval step becomes necessary here and wasn't for routing.
* **[[Designing Tools for Agent Reliability]], later in this district, addresses a different cause of selection error**: tools that are genuinely similar in description, which pre-filtering alone can't fix.

## Common pitfalls

* **Shrinking K without checking whether the correct tool actually survives.** The worked example's K = 1 shows the failure mode directly — an overly aggressive filter can guarantee failure before selection even begins.
* **Assuming showing every available tool is the "safest" choice.** It maximizes recall, but the worked example shows it comes at real cost: worst-case accuracy here drops to 2.5%, the lowest of any K tested.
* **Treating recall and accuracy as the same metric.** They measure different things — recall asks whether the right tool made it into view at all; accuracy asks whether, given what's in view, the model actually picks it.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. In the worked example, why does K = 1 guarantee the agent can't pick the right tool at all?</summary>
The genuinely correct tool ranks 3rd by similarity, so a cutoff at K = 1 only keeps the top-ranked tool — the correct one never makes it into the candidate set the model actually sees.
</details>

<details><summary>2. Why does worst-case accuracy keep dropping from K = 3 to K = 40 even though recall stays at 100% the whole time?</summary>
Recall only tracks whether the correct tool is present among the candidates; it says nothing about how many other candidates are also present to be confused with it. A uniform guess among 40 candidates succeeds far less often than a uniform guess among 3, even when the right answer is in both sets.
</details>

<details><summary>3. What determines the best choice of K in general?</summary>
It depends on how reliably the correct tool ranks near the top for the task at hand — if relevance ranking is accurate, a small K both preserves recall and keeps the candidate set focused; if ranking is unreliable, a small K risks filtering out the correct tool before selection even starts.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Tool retrieval:** ranking available tools by relevance to a task and keeping only the top K as candidates for selection.
* **Recall@K:** whether the correct item survives being limited to the top K candidates.
* **Worst-case accuracy:** the success rate of a selection that has no signal beyond the candidate set itself.

## Related

[[Retrieval Metrics: Precision, Recall, MRR and NDCG]] · [[Routing Between Specialized Prompts]] · [[Designing Tools for Agent Reliability]]

## Parallel vs. Sequential Tool Calls

Checking flight prices, the weather at the destination, and today's exchange rate are three tool calls that have nothing to do with each other — running them one after another wastes however long the fastest two spent waiting for no reason. Booking a flight, then sending a confirmation for that exact booking, can't be reordered or parallelized at all: the second call needs a result the first one hasn't produced yet.

**You need:** [[Parallelization: Sectioning and Voting]].

## The question it answers

"When can an agent's tool calls run at the same time, and when must they run one after another?" The answer turns entirely on **data dependency**: if no call needs another call's result as an input, they can run in parallel, finishing in however long the *slowest* one takes. If any call's input depends on another call's output, that pair — and everything chained to it — has no choice but to run sequentially, no matter how fast each individual call is.

## Intuition

Three separate errands — mailing a letter, buying groceries, and picking up dry cleaning — can be done in any order or even delegated to three different people at once, because none of them depends on how any other turns out. Baking a cake can't be parallelized the same way: you can't frost it before it's baked, because frosting needs the baked cake as an input.

## Definition and notation

```text
independent calls: sequential total = Σ latencies      parallel total = max(latencies)
dependent chain:    sequential total = Σ latencies      parallel total = not possible
```

## A worked example

Three independent lookups, and a three-step dependent booking chain, each with real per-call latencies:

```text
independent (flight search 800ms, weather check 300ms, exchange rate 150ms):
  sequential total: 800 + 300 + 150 = 1250ms
  parallel total:   max(800, 300, 150) = 800ms

dependent (search flight 800ms → book flight 400ms → send confirmation 200ms):
  sequential total: 800 + 400 + 200 = 1400ms
  parallel total:   not possible — each step needs the previous step's result
```

The independent calls save 450ms just by recognizing they don't need to wait on each other. The dependent chain can't be sped up the same way at all — the only way to shorten it is to make an individual step faster, not to reorder or parallelize the calls themselves.

## Bench

```bench
id: parallel-vs-sequential-tools
title: Run them together, or one after another
fallback: Compare total latency for independent tool calls run in parallel against a dependent chain that can only run sequentially.
```

**Try this**

1. Look at the independent calls and note the gap between sequential and parallel totals.
2. Switch to the dependent chain and see that no parallel option exists at all.
3. Imagine the "check weather" call also needed the flight search's destination city as an input — would it still be independent?

**What you should notice:** the saving from parallelizing has nothing to do with how many calls there are — it comes entirely from whether any of them actually needs another's result, which is a property of the task, not a setting to toggle.

## Where it appears in AI

* **This is exactly [[Parallelization: Sectioning and Voting|sectioning]] from the previous district**, applied specifically to tool calls instead of whole sub-prompts — the mechanism (independent work finishes in the time of its slowest piece) doesn't change.
* **[[Goal Decomposition into Subtasks]]'s dependency graph is what actually determines which tool calls are independent** — a correct decomposition identifies this before any call is made, rather than discovering it by trial and error.
* **A chain of dependent tool calls is a small instance of [[Plan-and-Execute Agents|plan-and-execute]]'s step-by-step execution**, where each step genuinely needs the step before it.

## Common pitfalls

* **Running calls sequentially out of habit even when nothing connects them.** The worked example's independent case wastes 450ms this way — time that bought nothing, since none of the three calls needed to wait for another.
* **Trying to parallelize calls that are actually dependent.** Attempting to send a booking confirmation before the booking call has returned a confirmation number doesn't just fail to save time — it fails outright, because the second call has nothing valid to send yet.
* **Misjudging independence because two calls look unrelated on the surface.** Two calls can still be dependent through a shared input (both needing a destination city determined by a first call) even if neither obviously depends on the other's full output.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. Why does the independent case's parallel total equal 800ms rather than something smaller?</summary>
Even running all three calls at once, the overall wait is bounded by whichever single call takes the longest — here, the 800ms flight search — so nothing can finish before that, no matter how fast the other two are.
</details>

<details><summary>2. Why can't the dependent chain's total time be reduced by reordering or parallelizing its three calls?</summary>
Each call in the chain needs a specific result from the call before it (a booking needs a flight search result, a confirmation needs a booking result) — there's no valid order to run them in except the one the dependencies require, and no way to start two of them at once.
</details>

<details><summary>3. What property of a set of tool calls determines whether they can be parallelized?</summary>
Whether any call's input depends on another call's output — calls with no such dependency between them can run in parallel; any dependency at all forces that part of the sequence to run one after another.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Data dependency:** one tool call needing another call's result as an input.
* **Independent calls:** tool calls with no data dependency between them, which can run in parallel.
* **Dependent chain:** a sequence of tool calls where each one needs the previous one's result, forcing sequential execution.

## Related

[[Parallelization: Sectioning and Voting]] · [[Goal Decomposition into Subtasks]] · [[Plan-and-Execute Agents]]

## Handling Tool Errors and Retries

A flaky network call that succeeds 70% of the time individually succeeds 99.19% of the time within four tries — failures that are transient are exactly the kind retrying is good for. A call that fails because its arguments are malformed succeeds 0% of the time no matter how many times it's retried, because nothing about trying again fixes a request that was wrong to begin with.

**You need:** [[Re-Planning on Failure]].

## The question it answers

"When does retrying a failed tool call actually help, and when is it pointless?" A **transient** error (a timeout, a momentary rate limit, a flaky network) has some real chance of succeeding if tried again under the same conditions — each retry is an independent new chance. A **permanent** error (malformed arguments, calling a tool that doesn't exist, a request the API will reject in exactly the same way every time) will fail identically on every retry, because nothing about the retry itself changes what made it fail.

## Intuition

A coffee shop having a brief run of noisy, dropped orders might fill yours correctly if you ask again — the problem was circumstantial, not about what you ordered. Ordering an item that's not on the menu at all will keep failing no matter how many times you repeat the exact same order — repeating it doesn't make the item exist.

## Definition and notation

```text
success within n tries = 1 − (1 − p)ⁿ      where p = per-try success probability
transient error:  p > 0   → success probability climbs toward 100% with more tries
permanent error:  p = 0   → success probability stays at 0% no matter how many tries
```

## A worked example

A transient error with a 70% per-try success rate, and a permanent error that always fails, both retried up to four times:

```text
transient (p = 0.70):
  1 try:  70.00%
  2 tries: 91.00%
  3 tries: 97.30%
  4 tries: 99.19%

permanent (p = 0):
  any number of tries: 0.00%
```

Four retries of the transient call turn a 30%-chance-of-failure single attempt into a call that fails only about 1 time in 125. The permanent error's probability never moves at all — the formula itself shows why: with p = 0, every term in (1 − p)ⁿ stays at 1, so 1 minus it stays at 0 regardless of n.

## Bench

```bench
id: tool-retry-success
title: Retrying a flaky call, or a broken one
fallback: Step through retries of a transient and a permanent tool error and watch cumulative success probability.
```

**Try this**

1. Step through all four tries on the transient error and watch the probability climb toward 100%.
2. Switch to the permanent error and step through the same four tries.
3. Imagine a per-try success probability of 95% instead of 70% — would fewer retries reach the same cumulative success?

**What you should notice:** retrying only ever helps when the failure has some non-zero chance of not recurring — the bench's permanent-error case isn't a different retry strategy, it's a demonstration that no retry strategy helps when the underlying cause is deterministic.

## Where it appears in AI

* **This is the same detect-and-recover shape as [[Re-Planning on Failure]]**, but at the level of a single tool call rather than a whole plan — the key judgment call in both cases is distinguishing a fixable failure from one that will recur identically.
* **[[Designing Tools for Agent Reliability]], later in this district, is about reducing how often permanent errors happen in the first place** — a well-designed tool interface prevents many "malformed arguments" failures before any retry logic is even needed.
* **Blind retries without this distinction waste calls and money on errors retrying can never fix**, which is exactly why production agent systems need to classify an error before deciding whether to retry it at all.

## Common pitfalls

* **Retrying every failure the same way regardless of its cause.** The worked example makes the cost of this explicit: retrying a permanent error four times spends four calls to arrive at exactly the same 0% success the first call already showed.
* **Giving up after one failure without trying again.** For a genuinely transient error, this throws away most of the benefit — a single try at 70% leaves a 30% failure rate that four tries would cut to under 1%.
* **Assuming every error that "looks" like a server hiccup is actually transient.** A malformed request might happen to also return a generic server error, making a permanent problem look retryable when it isn't — the error needs to be inspected, not just its symptom.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. Why does success probability keep climbing with more tries for the transient error but not for the permanent one?</summary>
A transient error has some real chance (70% here) of not recurring on the next try, so each additional try adds a genuine independent chance of success. A permanent error has a 0% per-try success rate by its nature, so every additional try adds exactly nothing.
</details>

<details><summary>2. What's the practical difference between treating an error as transient versus permanent?</summary>
Treating it as transient means retrying is worth spending more calls on, since each one has a real chance of succeeding; treating it as permanent means retrying is pointless and the actual request needs to be fixed (or a different tool used) instead.
</details>

<details><summary>3. What does the formula 1 − (1 − p)ⁿ reveal about why permanent errors can never be fixed by retrying?</summary>
With p = 0, the term (1 − p) equals 1, and 1 raised to any power n is still 1 — so the whole expression stays at 1 − 1 = 0 regardless of how large n gets.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Transient error:** a failure with some real chance of not recurring if the same call is tried again.
* **Permanent error:** a failure that will recur identically on every retry, because its cause doesn't change between tries.
* **Cumulative success probability:** the chance that at least one of n independent tries succeeds.

## Related

[[Re-Planning on Failure]] · [[Designing Tools for Agent Reliability]] · [[Tool Result Verification]]

## Tool Result Verification

A weather tool call that returns no exception isn't the same as a weather tool call that actually returned a usable result. Five calls, none of which raised an error, still include one that silently came back empty and one that came back missing the temperature field entirely — only three of the five actually have everything the agent needs to act on.

**You need:** [[Prompt Chaining]].

## The question it answers

"Is it enough to check that a tool call didn't error out?" No — a tool call can complete successfully by every signal the calling code checks (no exception, a 200 status, a non-null return value) while still returning a result that's empty, incomplete, or simply wrong for what the agent actually needs next. **Result verification** is a separate check, applied after the call returns successfully, confirming the result itself has the specific fields or properties the next step depends on — the same validation-gate idea already covered for chained workflows, now applied to a tool's output.

## Intuition

A vending machine that takes your money and makes the correct sounds and lights isn't actually a successful purchase if nothing drops into the tray. The machine reported no error — it just didn't deliver what you paid for. Checking that the transaction "went through" and checking that you actually got a snack are two different checks, and only the second one tells you whether you can eat lunch.

## Definition and notation

```text
no exception:              the call returned without raising an error
passes verification(result, requiredFields) = every required field is actually present in the result
```

## A worked example

Five calls to a weather tool, none of which raised an exception, checked against the three fields the agent actually needs:

```text
required fields: temperature, conditions, location

call 1: temperature, conditions, location  → ✓ has every required field
call 2: temperature, conditions, location  → ✓ has every required field
call 3: conditions, location               → ✗ missing temperature
call 4: (empty result)                     → ✗ missing everything
call 5: temperature, conditions, location  → ✓ has every required field

calls with no exception:        5 of 5
calls that pass verification:   3 of 5
```

Every single call "succeeded" by the only signal a bare try/catch would check. Verification is the only thing that catches that two of those five successes were actually unusable.

## Bench

```bench
id: tool-result-verification
title: No exception isn't the same as a usable result
fallback: Compare five tool calls that all completed without an exception against which of them actually pass result verification.
```

**Try this**

1. Look at which calls are missing a required field despite none of them raising an exception.
2. Compare the "no exception" count against the "passes verification" count.
3. Imagine a sixth call that returns a plausible-looking but factually wrong temperature — would field-presence verification catch that?

**What you should notice:** this verification check only catches *structural* problems (a field that's missing), which is why call 4's empty result and call 3's missing field both get caught — but it says nothing about whether a present value is actually correct, which the Quick check below asks you to notice.

## Where it appears in AI

* **This is the same validation gate from [[Prompt Chaining]], applied to a tool's output instead of a chained step's output** — the mechanism (check the fields the next step actually depends on) doesn't change.
* **[[Handling Tool Errors and Retries]] only catches failures the call itself signals** — an exception, a timeout, an error code. Result verification catches the failures that the call reports as a success.
* **[[Designing Tools for Agent Reliability]], later in this district, is about reducing how often a tool can silently return an incomplete result in the first place** — verification is the safety net for whatever still gets through.

## Common pitfalls

* **Trusting "no exception" as proof the result is usable.** The worked example shows two of five calls pass this bar while still being missing data the next step actually needs.
* **Verifying only that fields are present, not that their values make sense.** A result with a temperature field present but holding an absurd value (say, 400 degrees) passes a presence check while still being wrong — presence and correctness are different things to verify.
* **Skipping verification because a tool "usually" works.** The whole value of verification is catching the cases that don't — the worked example's rate (2 of 5 silently incomplete) would be exactly the kind of failure a skipped check lets through unnoticed.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. Why do calls 3 and 4 both "succeed" by a bare exception check, yet fail verification?</summary>
Neither call raised an exception — by that signal alone, both completed successfully. But call 3's result is missing the temperature field and call 4's result is entirely empty, so neither actually has what the required-fields check needs.
</details>

<details><summary>2. What's the difference between checking that a call didn't error and verifying its result?</summary>
Checking for an exception only tells you the call mechanism itself didn't break (no timeout, no crash); verifying the result tells you whether what came back actually has the specific content the next step depends on — a call can pass the first check while failing the second.
</details>

<details><summary>3. Does the field-presence check in the worked example catch a result with a present but factually wrong value?</summary>
No — it only checks whether required fields exist in the result, not whether their values are correct. A temperature field holding an implausible number would pass this specific check while still being wrong.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Result verification:** checking that a tool call's returned result actually has the content the next step needs, beyond just confirming the call didn't raise an error.
* **Silent failure:** a tool call that reports success while returning an incomplete or empty result.
* **Validation gate:** a check applied to an intermediate result before letting it proceed to the next step.

## Related

[[Prompt Chaining]] · [[Handling Tool Errors and Retries]] · [[Designing Tools for Agent Reliability]]

## Designing Tools for Agent Reliability

A tool with a free-text date field lets an agent write "03/14/2025," "March 14, 2025," or "14/03/2025" — three formats, at least two of them genuinely ambiguous about which number is the month. Three of five realistic attempts fail to parse. The same tool with a schema that only accepts ISO-8601 (`2025-03-14`) and rejects anything else before it ever reaches the tool's logic has nowhere for that ambiguity to enter at all — all five attempts parse.

**You need:** [[Tool Result Verification]].

## The question it answers

"How much of an agent's unreliability comes from the agent, and how much comes from how its tools are built?" A tool's interface — its parameter types, how strictly it validates input, what it does when something's wrong — directly shapes how often an agent calling it succeeds. A loosely specified tool (free-text fields, silent failures, no schema) leaves room for an agent to produce something technically valid-looking but wrong; a tightly specified one (strict types, enums instead of free text, validation that rejects malformed input immediately) removes much of that room before the agent's own reasoning is even a factor.

## Intuition

A form that asks "when?" with a blank text box invites a dozen different answers for the same date. A form with separate year, month, and day dropdowns makes an ambiguous answer structurally impossible — not because whoever's filling it out got smarter, but because the form itself no longer accepts anything else.

## Definition and notation

```text
free-text field:    accepts any string; parsing ambiguity is discovered only when the tool tries to use it
strict schema:      accepts only a defined format; anything else is rejected before the tool's logic runs
```

## A worked example

The same "book an event" tool's date parameter, given five realistic values under each design:

```text
free-text field:
  "03/14/2025"      → ✗ fails to parse (month or day? ambiguous)
  "2025-03-14"      → ✓ parses
  "March 14, 2025"  → ✗ fails to parse (not the expected format)
  "14/03/2025"      → ✗ fails to parse (day-first, misread as month-first)
  "2025-03-14"      → ✓ parses
  → 3 of 5 calls fail to parse

strict ISO-8601 schema (anything else rejected before this point):
  "2025-03-14" × 5  → ✓ all 5 parse
  → 0 of 5 calls fail to parse
```

Nothing about the agent changed between the two columns — the same reasoning produced every attempt. What changed is whether the tool's own interface left room for an ambiguous or malformed value to reach it in the first place.

## Bench

```bench
id: tool-schema-reliability
title: A field that accepts anything, or a schema that doesn't
fallback: Compare a free-text date field's parse failures against a strict ISO-8601 schema's.
```

**Try this**

1. Look at the free-text attempts and identify which ones are genuinely ambiguous rather than simply wrong.
2. Switch to the strict schema and see every attempt already forced into the one accepted format.
3. Imagine a strict schema with an unreasonably narrow format real inputs rarely match — what new failure mode would that introduce?

**What you should notice:** a strict schema doesn't make the agent reason better — it narrows what the agent is even allowed to produce, so the ambiguity that caused 3 of 5 free-text failures simply has nowhere left to occur.

## Where it appears in AI

* **This directly reduces the permanent-error rate from [[Handling Tool Errors and Retries]]** — a malformed-argument failure caused by an ambiguous field design is exactly the kind of permanent error no amount of retrying fixes; a stricter schema prevents it from happening at all.
* **[[Tool Result Verification]] is the safety net for whatever reliability problems a tool's design doesn't prevent** — the two are complementary, not alternatives: design reduces how often bad calls happen, verification catches the ones that still get through.
* **[[Code as a Tool-Calling Interface]], next in this district, is itself a tool-interface design choice** at a larger scale — the same reliability questions (how much room is left for ambiguity or error) apply there too.

## Common pitfalls

* **Blaming the agent for failures that are actually the tool's design.** The worked example's free-text failures happen with identical reasoning to the strict-schema successes — the difference is entirely in what the tool accepts.
* **Making a schema so strict it rejects legitimate variation.** A schema that's too narrow for the task's actual range of valid inputs trades one reliability problem (ambiguity) for another (false rejections of correct input).
* **Assuming better prompting alone fixes an unreliable tool.** Asking the agent more clearly to "use ISO-8601 format" can reduce but not eliminate the ambiguity that a schema which simply doesn't accept anything else removes by construction.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. Why does "14/03/2025" fail to parse under the free-text design but not necessarily under a schema?</summary>
As free text, it's genuinely ambiguous whether 14 is meant as the day or an invalid month depending on the reader's assumed format; a strict schema sidesteps the ambiguity entirely by only accepting one defined format (ISO-8601), so a value like this is simply rejected before any ambiguous interpretation is attempted.
</details>

<details><summary>2. What's the key difference between fixing this with a stricter schema versus fixing it by retrying failed calls?</summary>
A stricter schema prevents the ambiguous or malformed value from being accepted in the first place, reducing how often the failure happens at all; retrying (from the previous topic) only helps with failures that have some chance of not recurring, and a parsing failure caused by a genuinely ambiguous format will recur identically on every retry.
</details>

<details><summary>3. What's the trade-off of making a tool's schema stricter?</summary>
A stricter schema reduces ambiguity-driven failures but risks rejecting inputs that are actually valid if the schema is narrower than the real range of acceptable values — reliability gained on one side can cost false rejections on the other if the schema is miscalibrated.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Tool interface design:** the choices (parameter types, validation strictness, error behavior) that shape how a tool can be called.
* **Free-text field:** a parameter that accepts any string, leaving format ambiguity undetected until the tool tries to use the value.
* **Strict schema:** a parameter definition that only accepts a defined format, rejecting anything else before the tool's own logic runs.

## Related

[[Tool Result Verification]] · [[Handling Tool Errors and Retries]] · [[Code as a Tool-Calling Interface]]

## Code as a Tool-Calling Interface

Applying a discount to 200 items one tool call at a time costs 200 separate round trips, each one a full request and response. Writing a short piece of code that loops over all 200 items and calls the same underlying function internally costs one round trip — the model produces the loop once, and a sandbox runs it however many times is needed.

**You need:** [[Designing Tools for Agent Reliability]].

## The question it answers

"Does every action an agent takes need to be its own separate tool call?" Structured function calling gives the model one discrete, schema-checked call per action — reliable and easy to validate, but a loop over many items costs one call per item. Letting the model instead write a short piece of **code** that calls already-defined functions, with real loops and conditionals, lets a single generated call express arbitrarily much control flow, executed all at once in a sandbox rather than round-tripped back to the model at every step.

## Intuition

Asking an assistant to update 200 spreadsheet rows one instruction at a time ("update row 1," wait for confirmation, "update row 2," wait again...) takes 200 back-and-forth exchanges. Handing the assistant a short script that says "for each row, do this update" and letting them run it once accomplishes exactly the same 200 updates in a single instruction.

## Definition and notation

```text
structured tool calls(n items) = n            (one call per item)
code-as-tool calls              = 1            (one call, however many items the code loops over)
```

## A worked example

Applying one operation to a growing number of items, under both interfaces:

```text
n = 10 items:   structured calls = 10    code-as-tool calls = 1
n = 50 items:   structured calls = 50    code-as-tool calls = 1
n = 200 items:  structured calls = 200   code-as-tool calls = 1
```
