The structured interface's call count scales directly with the number of items — ten times the items, ten times the calls. The code interface's call count never moves, because the looping itself happens inside the one call's generated code, not across repeated round trips to the model.

## Bench

```bench
id: code-as-tool-interface
title: One call per item, or one loop
fallback: Compare total tool calls needed to process a growing number of items under structured calling versus code as the interface.
```

**Try this**

1. Slide the item count up and watch the structured-calls bar grow while the code-as-tool bar stays flat.
2. Imagine each structured call also costs a fixed network round-trip delay — how would that change the total time, not just the call count, as items grow?
3. Think of an operation where each item's handling genuinely depends on the result of handling the previous one — would code-as-tool still save calls the same way?

**What you should notice:** the saving comes specifically from moving a loop that's genuinely repetitive into the generated code itself — it isn't a universal replacement for structured calls, just a better fit whenever the actual task is "do this same thing many times."

## Where it appears in AI

* **This is the same call-count logic behind [[Orchestrator-Workers]] and sectioning, in reverse**: those patterns split one task into many separate calls when the pieces genuinely need independent handling; code-as-tool collapses many repetitive pieces back into one call when they don't.
* **[[Code-Execution Agents]], covered in the next district, is the full environment built around this idea** — an execution sandbox, state carried between code snippets, and the broader question of what an agent can do once code itself is its action space. This topic is specifically about the *interface* choice; that one is about the environment it runs in.
* **Structured function calling still has real advantages this topic doesn't erase**: its schema makes every individual action easy to validate and log, which a freeform code blob makes harder to inspect before it runs.

## Common pitfalls

* **Using code-as-tool for operations that genuinely need per-item oversight.** Collapsing 200 individually risky actions (each needing a human or verification check before proceeding) into one uninterrupted loop removes the checkpoints a structured per-item call would have given.
* **Assuming the call-count saving means code-as-tool is strictly better.** It trades call count for a loss of per-action granularity and schema validation — a real cost, not a free win, for tasks where that granularity mattered.
* **Writing code that calls undefined or unsafe operations.** The safety of this pattern depends entirely on the sandbox only exposing the same already-vetted functions a structured interface would have exposed directly — it isn't a license for the model to call anything it can imagine.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. Why does the structured interface's call count scale directly with the number of items while code-as-tool's doesn't?</summary>
Structured calling requires a separate round trip for every action, so repeating an action n times costs n calls. Code-as-tool expresses the repetition as a loop inside one generated snippet, so the loop itself runs inside a single call regardless of how many times it iterates.
</details>

<details><summary>2. What does code-as-tool give up in exchange for its lower call count?</summary>
Per-item granularity and schema validation — a structured call can be checked and logged individually before it runs, while a code snippet's internal loop iterations aren't individually inspected the same way before the whole thing executes.
</details>

<details><summary>3. When would code-as-tool not actually save any calls compared to structured calling?</summary>
When each item's handling genuinely depends on an earlier item's result in a way that needs to be checked or decided by the model between iterations — at that point the task isn't a simple repetitive loop, and collapsing it into one call loses exactly the oversight that made per-item calls useful.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Code as a tool-calling interface:** letting a model express an action (including loops and conditionals) as generated code executed in a sandbox, rather than as one discrete structured call per action.
* **Structured function calling:** a schema-checked tool call representing exactly one discrete action.
* **Call count:** the number of model-to-tool round trips a given approach requires for a task.

## Related

[[Designing Tools for Agent Reliability]] · [[Orchestrator-Workers]] · [[Code-Execution Agents]]

## Memory and State Management

An agent running for hundreds of steps can't keep everything it's ever seen in its context window — and some of what it learns along the way needs to survive past the current run entirely. This district is about what an agent actually keeps, for how long, and how it finds the right piece of it again later.

Topics on this stretch of the road:

* [[Short-Term vs. Long-Term Agent Memory]]: what lives only in the current run's context, and what's meant to persist across runs entirely.
* [[Episodic Memory and Experience Logs]]: recording what an agent actually did and what happened, as a resource for later.
* [[Memory Retrieval as Agent-Time RAG]]: pulling the right remembered fact back out of a large memory store, mid-task.
* [[Memory Compression and Forgetting]]: what has to be summarized or dropped once memory itself grows too large to use directly.
* [[Shared State Across a Multi-Step Task]]: the working state a single long task keeps passing from one step to the next.

## Short-Term vs. Long-Term Agent Memory

Everything an agent reads during one run — the request, the tool results so far, its own earlier reasoning — disappears the moment that run ends, unless something deliberately writes it somewhere that outlives the run. **Short-term memory** is whatever fits in the current context; **long-term memory** is whatever gets written to storage that the next run can read back.

**You need:** [[Anatomy of an Agent Architecture]].

## The question it answers

"What's the difference between what an agent remembers and what it forgets the moment the run ends?" Short-term memory is the agent's working context for the current run: the request, intermediate results, anything perceived or reasoned about so far. It's immediate and complete, but it vanishes when the run finishes. Long-term memory is anything deliberately persisted to external storage — a file, a database, a vector store — that a *later*, separate run can read back. Nothing moves from short-term to long-term automatically; a fact only survives past the current run if something explicitly writes it somewhere durable.

## Intuition

A contractor who finishes a job and walks away with nothing written down starts the next visit from zero, no matter how much they learned on the first one. A contractor who jots preferences in a notebook before leaving picks up exactly where they left off next time — the notebook is what makes the difference between "remembered" and "re-asked every visit."

## Definition and notation

```text
short-term memory:  current run's context — gone when the run ends
long-term memory:   written to external storage — read back by a later, separate run
```

## A worked example

A user states a preference once; what happens across the next few sessions depends entirely on whether that preference was ever written to long-term storage:

```text
short-term only (nothing persists):
  session 1: user states preference → used this session → session ends → gone
  session 2: preference is restated          (asked again)
  session 3: preference is restated          (asked again)
  total times restated across 3 sessions: 3

long-term memory (written once, read back each time):
  session 1: user states preference → written to storage
  session 2: read back from storage          (not re-asked)
  session 3: read back from storage          (not re-asked)
  total times restated across 3 sessions: 1
```

Nothing about the model changed between the two cases — the only difference is whether the preference was ever written somewhere that outlives a single run. That one write is what turns three repeated questions into one.

## Bench

```bench
id: short-term-vs-long-term-memory
title: Restating a fact, or remembering it
fallback: Compare how many times a fact must be restated across sessions with and without persistent memory.
```

**Try this**

1. Slide the number of sessions up with memory off and watch the restated count climb with it.
2. Turn persistent memory on and see the count drop to 1 regardless of session count.
3. Imagine a preference that changes over time (the user moves, their deadline shifts) — what does a long-term memory store need to do differently than just "write once, read forever"?

**What you should notice:** the gap between short-term and long-term memory isn't about model capability at all — it's entirely about whether something wrote the fact down somewhere that survives past the current run.

## Where it appears in AI

* **This is the memory component named in [[Anatomy of an Agent Architecture]]**, looked at specifically through the lens of what does and doesn't survive past one run.
* **[[Episodic Memory and Experience Logs]] is a specific, structured kind of long-term memory**: not just facts, but a record of what the agent actually did and what happened.
* **This is a different problem from [[Multi-Turn Conversation State and Memory|managing a single long conversation's context]], already covered on the LLMs planet** — that's about keeping one ongoing conversation's context bounded; this is about whether anything survives at all once a run ends entirely.

## Common pitfalls

* **Assuming a model "remembers" something just because it was mentioned earlier in a long context.** That's still short-term memory — it disappears the moment the run ends unless it was separately written somewhere durable.
* **Writing everything to long-term memory indiscriminately.** Not every fact from a run is worth persisting — a long-term store that saves every detail of every run becomes exactly the problem [[Memory Compression and Forgetting]] exists to solve.
* **Forgetting that long-term memory needs its own retrieval step.** Writing a fact to storage doesn't help unless a later run actually reads it back at the right moment — which is why [[Memory Retrieval as Agent-Time RAG]] exists as its own topic.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. In the worked example, why does the long-term memory case still ask once, at session 1?</summary>
Session 1 is when the preference is first stated; it has to be captured and written to storage at least once before any later session can read it back — the saving comes from every session *after* that no longer needing to ask again.
</details>

<details><summary>2. What makes a fact "long-term memory" rather than just "something in the context"?</summary>
It was deliberately written to external storage that persists after the current run ends, so a separate, later run can read it back — nothing about being mentioned in context alone makes it long-term.
</details>

<details><summary>3. Does a model automatically decide which facts to persist to long-term memory?</summary>
No — nothing moves from short-term to long-term automatically; a fact only survives past the current run if some part of the system explicitly writes it to durable storage.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Short-term memory:** the current run's working context, gone once the run ends.
* **Long-term memory:** anything deliberately written to external storage that a later, separate run can read back.
* **Persist:** to write a fact somewhere that outlives the current run.

## Related

[[Anatomy of an Agent Architecture]] · [[Episodic Memory and Experience Logs]] · [[Memory Retrieval as Agent-Time RAG]]

## Episodic Memory and Experience Logs

The first time an agent faces a task, it has to actually discover which approach works — try something, see it fail, try something else. Without a record of that, every later instance of the same recurring task pays the discovery cost all over again. Logging what was tried and what happened, an **episodic memory**, is what lets a later instance skip straight to what already worked.

**You need:** [[Short-Term vs. Long-Term Agent Memory]].

## The question it answers

"What specifically should an agent remember about its own past runs, beyond plain facts?" An episodic memory records *episodes*: what task was attempted, what approach was tried, and what the outcome was — not a fact about the world, but a record of the agent's own experience. When the same (or a similar) task recurs, the agent can look up what it logged last time instead of rediscovering the right approach from scratch.

## Intuition

A technician who writes "tried swapping the battery first, didn't fix it — the actual issue was a loose cable" in a repair log saves the next technician (or themselves) from redoing the same failed first attempt on a similar fault. The notebook isn't a fact about the machine in general — it's a record of what was tried on this specific kind of problem and what actually worked.

## Definition and notation

```text
episode = (task, approach tried, outcome)
without episodic log:  every instance rediscovers the working approach from scratch
with episodic log:     only the first instance discovers it; later instances recall it
```

## A worked example

A recurring task where the first attempt at an approach fails and a second attempt succeeds, repeated across 5 instances:

```text
without episodic log:  every instance tries approach A (fails), then B (succeeds) — 2 attempts each
  5 instances × 2 attempts = 10 total attempts

with episodic log:     instance 1 tries A (fails), then B (succeeds), logs "B worked" — 2 attempts
                        instances 2-5 recall the log, go straight to B — 1 attempt each
  2 + (4 × 1) = 6 total attempts
```

The saving isn't from the agent getting smarter at the task itself — the second instance's B still succeeds for exactly the same reason it did the first time. The saving is entirely from not re-running a failed experiment (approach A) that the log already knows doesn't work.

## Bench

```bench
id: episodic-memory-log
title: Rediscovering what works, or recalling it
fallback: Compare total attempts spent on a recurring task with and without an episodic memory log.
```

**Try this**

1. Slide the number of instances up with the log off and watch the total climb by 2 every time.
2. Turn the log on and see every instance after the first drop to 1 attempt.
3. Imagine the task's correct approach changes over time (what worked last month stops working) — what would a pure "recall the log" agent miss that an agent which still occasionally re-checks wouldn't?

**What you should notice:** the log's benefit depends on the task actually recurring in a similar enough form that last time's outcome is still relevant — a one-off task gets no benefit from logging it at all.

## Where it appears in AI

* **This is a specific, structured application of [[Short-Term vs. Long-Term Agent Memory|long-term memory]]**: not arbitrary facts, but a record of the agent's own past attempts and outcomes.
* **[[Self-Critique Loops in Agents]] produces the kind of outcome judgment an episodic log actually stores** — a critique of what happened is exactly the information worth logging for next time.
* **[[Learning from Feedback Without Weight Updates]] is the general principle this topic is one concrete mechanism for**: changing future behavior from past experience without touching the model's weights at all.

## Common pitfalls

* **Logging episodes for tasks that never recur.** A log entry for a genuinely one-off task is pure overhead — it will never be looked up again, which is exactly why this topic specifies a *recurring* task.
* **Logging only successes.** The worked example's saving comes specifically from knowing that approach A *doesn't* work — a log that only records what succeeded would still let every instance waste an attempt rediscovering that A fails.
* **Assuming a logged outcome stays valid forever.** An approach that worked under past conditions can stop working if something in the environment changes — a log entry is evidence from a specific past attempt, not a permanent guarantee.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. In the worked example, why do instances 2 through 5 need only 1 attempt instead of 2?</summary>
The episodic log already recorded that approach B worked and approach A didn't, so each later instance can go straight to B instead of re-trying the already-known-to-fail A first.
</details>

<details><summary>2. What does an episodic memory entry actually store — a fact, or something else?</summary>
Something else: an episode, a record of what task was attempted, what approach was tried, and what the outcome was — the agent's own experience, not a general fact about the world.
</details>

<details><summary>3. Why does episodic memory provide no benefit for a task that never recurs?</summary>
The whole saving comes from a later instance looking up what an earlier instance already discovered — if the task never happens again, there is no later instance to benefit from the log entry.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Episode:** a record of a specific task attempt, the approach tried, and its outcome.
* **Episodic memory:** a long-term memory store specifically of an agent's own past episodes.
* **Rediscovery cost:** the attempts spent finding a working approach from scratch, paid again by every instance that lacks access to a log of what already worked.

## Related

[[Short-Term vs. Long-Term Agent Memory]] · [[Self-Critique Loops in Agents]] · [[Learning from Feedback Without Weight Updates]]

## Memory Retrieval as Agent-Time RAG

An agent with thousands of stored memories can't dump all of them into context on every step — it needs to pull back only the handful actually relevant to what it's doing right now. That's retrieval, running at agent time instead of at answer-a-question time: the exact mechanism already covered on the RAG planet, applied to an agent's own memory store instead of a document collection.

**You need:** [[Short-Term vs. Long-Term Agent Memory]].

## The question it answers

"Once an agent has a large memory store, how does it find the few memories actually relevant right now?" The answer is retrieval: embed the current situation into a vector, embed every stored memory the same way, and rank memories by similarity — identical in mechanism to [[Bi-Encoders and Dense Embeddings|dense retrieval]] on the RAG planet, just retrieving from a store of the agent's own past facts and experiences instead of a document corpus.

## Intuition

A doctor with a thick patient file doesn't re-read the whole file before every question — they pull up the specific entries relevant to today's complaint. Which entries are relevant changes with the question being asked right now, which is exactly why this has to be a *retrieval* step at the moment it's needed, not something decided once in advance.

## Definition and notation

```text
cosine similarity(q, m) = (q · m) / (‖q‖ ‖m‖)
retrieved memories = top-K stored memories by similarity to the current query
```

## A worked example

A query vector against four stored memories, ranked by cosine similarity exactly as on the RAG planet:

```text
query:  "what units does the user want?"           q = (0.8, 0.6)

m1  "the user prefers metric units"                 v = (1, 0)   similarity = 0.800
m2  "the user's deadline is Friday"                 v = (0, 1)   similarity = 0.600
m3  "the user prefers metric and works in km"       v = (1, 1)   similarity = 0.990
m4  "the user prefers imperial units"                v = (-1, 0)  similarity = -0.800

top 2 retrieved: m3 (0.990), m1 (0.800)
```

m2's deadline fact and m4's directly contradicted preference both score low or negative — exactly what should happen, since neither is relevant to a question about units. The ranking does the filtering automatically; nothing had to specially mark m2 and m4 as irrelevant in advance.

## Bench

```bench
id: memory-retrieval-rag
title: Pulling the right memory back out
fallback: Rank an agent's stored memories against the current query by cosine similarity.
```

**Try this**

1. Read the ranked list and check that the two memories about units score highest.
2. Slide K down to 1 and notice which single memory wins.
3. Imagine the query were instead "when is this due?" — which memory should now score highest, and why does the embedding step have to change for that?

**What you should notice:** the same similarity mechanism that ranks documents against a question on the RAG planet ranks an agent's own memories against whatever it's currently doing — nothing about retrieval itself changes when the store is memories instead of documents.

## Where it appears in AI

* **This is exactly [[Bi-Encoders and Dense Embeddings|dense retrieval]] from the RAG planet**, applied to a store of the agent's own memories rather than an external document collection — the embedding and ranking mechanism is identical.
* **[[Memory Compression and Forgetting]] determines what's even left in the store to retrieve from** — a memory that was compressed away or dropped can't be retrieved no matter how relevant it would have been.
* **A [[Anatomy of a RAG Pipeline|RAG pipeline]]'s retrieval step runs once per user question; this runs continuously, at every point in an agent's own task** where it needs to recall something relevant to the step it's on.

## Common pitfalls

* **Treating memory retrieval as a one-time lookup at the start of a task.** Relevance changes as the task progresses — the right memories to retrieve partway through a multi-step task can be completely different from the ones relevant at the start.
* **Retrieving too few memories (missing something relevant) or too many (burying the genuinely relevant ones in noise).** K is a real tuning knob here exactly as it is in RAG retrieval generally — there's no single right value independent of the memory store's size and redundancy.
* **Assuming a high similarity score guarantees usefulness.** A memory can be topically similar but outdated or contradicted by a more recent one (m4 contradicts m1 directly) — similarity ranks relevance to the query's wording, not correctness or recency on its own.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. In the worked example, why does m3 score higher than m1, even though m1 is also about metric units?</summary>
m3's vector (1, 1) has a direction closer to the query's (0.8, 0.6) than m1's (1, 0) does — cosine similarity measures the angle between vectors, and m3 happens to point more directly toward the query's direction.
</details>

<details><summary>2. Why does m4 score negative instead of just low?</summary>
m4's vector (-1, 0) points in roughly the opposite direction from the query — it directly contradicts the metric-units preference the query is about, and cosine similarity can go negative exactly when two vectors point in substantially opposite directions.
</details>

<details><summary>3. What's the key difference between this topic and retrieval on the RAG planet?</summary>
The mechanism (embed, rank by cosine similarity, take the top K) is identical — the only difference is what's being retrieved from: the agent's own memory store of facts and past experience, instead of an external document collection.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Agent-time retrieval:** running a retrieval step continuously during an agent's task, rather than once per external question.
* **Memory store:** the collection of an agent's embedded past facts and experiences that retrieval ranks against.
* **Top-K:** the number of highest-similarity memories actually pulled back for use.

## Related

[[Bi-Encoders and Dense Embeddings]] · [[Memory Compression and Forgetting]] · [[Anatomy of a RAG Pipeline]]

## Memory Compression and Forgetting

A memory store that keeps every fact and every logged episode forever grows without bound — eventually too large to search efficiently, let alone fit anywhere near a context window. Compression keeps the store usable by periodically folding old entries into a smaller summary and, deliberately, forgetting whatever didn't make the cut.

**You need:** [[Episodic Memory and Experience Logs]].

## The question it answers

"What happens once an agent's memory store itself gets too large to use?" Left alone, a raw log of everything an agent has ever done grows linearly with how long it's been running — nothing about an ever-growing store collapses it back down on its own. Memory compression periodically summarizes older entries into a bounded budget, trading detail from the past for a store that stays usable no matter how long the agent keeps running.

## Intuition

A doctor's chart that keeps every visit's full notes forever becomes unwieldy after decades of care — a good chart periodically folds older visits into a brief summary ("stable hypertension since 2019, no other chronic conditions") and keeps only recent visits in full detail. Something is genuinely lost in that folding, but the chart stays usable precisely because it doesn't try to keep everything.

## Definition and notation

```text
raw store size(turns) = turns × tokens_per_turn          — grows without bound
summarized size        = a fixed cap, regardless of turns
compression ratio       = raw store size / cap
```

## A worked example

A transcript growing at 120 tokens per turn, against a fixed 400-token summary budget:

```text
10 turns:   raw = 1,200 tokens   cap = 400   ratio =  3.0×
50 turns:   raw = 6,000 tokens   cap = 400   ratio = 15.0×
200 turns:  raw = 24,000 tokens  cap = 400   ratio = 60.0×
```

The raw store keeps growing in direct proportion to how long the agent has been running; the summarized version doesn't grow at all past the first compression. The ratio between them is exactly how much detail compression is discarding to keep the store at a fixed size — a ratio that itself keeps climbing the longer the agent runs.

## Bench

```bench
id: memory-compression
title: Keeping everything, or keeping a summary
fallback: Compare raw transcript size against a fixed summarization budget as a conversation grows.
```

**Try this**

1. Slide turns up from 10 to 200 and watch the raw bar grow while the summary bar stays fixed.
2. Read off the compression ratio at a few different turn counts.
3. Imagine a specific detail from turn 3 (an exact number the user mentioned) is needed again at turn 180 — what has to be true about the summarization step for that detail to still be recoverable?

**What you should notice:** the summary budget staying fixed is exactly what keeps the store usable — but that fixed budget is also exactly why detail from the past gets lost, which is the actual trade compression is making, not a bug in how it's implemented.

## Where it appears in AI

* **This is the same trade-off as [[Multi-Turn Conversation State and Memory|summarization-based conversation memory]] on the LLMs planet**, applied to an agent's whole long-term memory store rather than just one conversation's context.
* **[[Memory Retrieval as Agent-Time RAG]] can only retrieve what the store still has** — a detail compressed away or dropped during forgetting is gone from retrieval too, no matter how relevant it would have been.
* **[[Memory Compression and Forgetting|Forgetting]] deliberately, bounded by a budget, is different from losing information by accident** — the budget is a design decision about how much of the past to keep, not a failure to keep anything at all.

## Common pitfalls

* **Never compressing at all.** The worked example's 60× ratio at 200 turns shows exactly where an uncompressed store ends up — eventually too large to search efficiently or fit in any reasonable context budget.
* **Compressing too aggressively and losing details that matter later.** A fixed small budget that discards specifics (exact numbers, names, decisions) can make the store confidently wrong rather than just incomplete, if the summary states a vague approximation as if it were the original fact.
* **Assuming compression is lossless.** Folding detail into a summary is a genuine trade, not a free optimization — something always has the possibility of being dropped, which is exactly why what to keep (and for how long) is a real design decision.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. In the worked example, why does the compression ratio keep climbing as turns increase, rather than staying constant?</summary>
The raw store's size grows in direct proportion to the number of turns, while the summary budget is fixed — so the ratio between a growing numerator and a constant denominator keeps increasing.
</details>

<details><summary>2. What's actually being traded away when a store is compressed?</summary>
Detail from older entries — compression keeps the overall store at a fixed, usable size specifically by giving up the ability to recall older information with full fidelity.
</details>

<details><summary>3. Is forgetting, in this sense, a failure of the memory system?</summary>
No — it's a deliberate design choice, trading detail for a bounded, usable store size; the alternative (keeping everything forever) isn't actually free, since the worked example shows it growing without bound.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Memory compression:** periodically folding older memory entries into a bounded summary.
* **Compression ratio:** the raw store size divided by the fixed summarized size.
* **Forgetting (deliberate):** discarding detail on purpose, as the cost of keeping the overall store at a usable, bounded size.

## Related

[[Multi-Turn Conversation State and Memory]] · [[Memory Retrieval as Agent-Time RAG]] · [[Shared State Across a Multi-Step Task]]

## Shared State Across a Multi-Step Task

A five-step task that needs today's date can fetch it five separate times, once per step — or fetch it once and write it somewhere every later step can just read. That shared somewhere, a **blackboard**, is what lets a long task's steps build on each other instead of each starting from nothing.

**You need:** [[Memory Compression and Forgetting]].

## The question it answers

"How do the different steps of one long task share information with each other?" Without shared state, each step only has whatever's in its own immediate context — anything another step already figured out or fetched has to be rediscovered or re-fetched from scratch. With a shared blackboard, any step can write a value once and every later step can read it back, without needing to know which earlier step produced it.

## Intuition

A relay team where each runner has to independently figure out the race conditions from scratch wastes effort every single leg; a team with a shared whiteboard at the exchange zone — wind direction, the competition's pace — lets every runner benefit from what the earlier ones already learned, without needing to ask them directly.

## Definition and notation

```text
no shared state:    each step fetches the needed value independently     → n fetches for n steps
shared blackboard:   first step fetches and writes it once; later steps read it → 1 fetch total
```

## A worked example

A 5-step research task where every step needs to know today's date:

```text
no shared state:
  step 1: fetches today's date itself
  step 2: fetches today's date itself
  step 3: fetches today's date itself
  step 4: fetches today's date itself
  step 5: fetches today's date itself
  total external calls: 5

shared blackboard:
  step 1: fetches today's date, writes it to shared state
  steps 2-5: read today's date from shared state
  total external calls: 1
```

Every one of the five calls in the first case returns exactly the same value — the repetition buys nothing, since the date hasn't changed between steps 1 and 5. The shared blackboard removes exactly that redundancy, at the cost of needing somewhere both to write to and to read consistently from across steps.

## Bench

```bench
id: shared-state-blackboard
title: Fetching it again, or reading it off the blackboard
fallback: Compare external calls needed for a piece of shared context, with and without a shared blackboard.
```

**Try this**

1. Slide the step count up with shared state off and watch external calls climb one-for-one.
2. Turn shared state on and see the total drop to 1 regardless of step count.
3. Imagine two steps run in parallel (as in [[Parallelization: Sectioning and Voting|sectioning]]) and both need to write to the same blackboard entry — what has to be true about how writes are handled to avoid one step's write silently overwriting the other's?

**What you should notice:** the saving here isn't from any step doing less work on its own problem — it's from not repeating a fetch whose answer was already available from an earlier step in the same task.

## Where it appears in AI

* **This is [[Memory Compression and Forgetting|memory]] at the scale of a single task rather than across sessions** — a shared blackboard is a short-lived, task-scoped store, built and torn down within one run rather than persisted long-term.
* **[[Coordination Failures and Deadlock]] covers what goes wrong when shared state is read or written inconsistently** by multiple agents or steps working on it at once.
* **[[Supervisor-Orchestrator Patterns|Supervisor/Orchestrator Patterns]]'s orchestrator often owns exactly this shared state**, handing each worker only the piece of it that worker's step actually needs.

## Common pitfalls

* **Re-fetching a value every step "to be safe."** The worked example shows this costs real external calls for no benefit when the value genuinely hasn't changed — the safety concern is valid only when the value actually *can* change mid-task.
* **Sharing state that does change mid-task without any staleness check.** A blackboard entry written once and trusted forever can go stale if the underlying value changes after it was written — shared state removes redundant fetches, not the need to know when a cached value is no longer valid.
* **Using a shared blackboard as a substitute for episodic or long-term memory.** A blackboard is scoped to one task's run; nothing on it survives the task ending unless it's separately written to the kind of persistent store covered by [[Short-Term vs. Long-Term Agent Memory]].

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. In the worked example, why is five separate fetches wasteful when the shared-blackboard version only needs one?</summary>
Today's date doesn't change across the five steps of the task, so every one of the five independent fetches returns the identical value — the blackboard removes exactly that repeated, redundant work.
</details>

<details><summary>2. What distinguishes shared state here from long-term memory?</summary>
Shared state is scoped to a single task's run and disappears once that run ends, unless separately persisted — long-term memory is specifically about writing something to storage that a later, different run can still read.
</details>

<details><summary>3. When would re-fetching a value on every step actually be the right choice?</summary>
When the value can genuinely change during the task — a cached value trusted for the whole run would then go stale, so the redundant-looking re-fetch is actually necessary freshness checking rather than waste.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Shared state (blackboard):** a store any step of a task can write to and any other step can read from, scoped to that one task's run.
* **Redundant fetch:** re-retrieving a value another step already obtained, when nothing about that value has changed.
* **Staleness:** a cached shared value no longer matching the current true value, because something changed after it was written.

## Related

[[Memory Compression and Forgetting]] · [[Coordination Failures and Deadlock]] · [[Supervisor-Orchestrator Patterns|Supervisor/Orchestrator Patterns]]

## Multi-Agent Systems

One agent can only hold one line of thought at a time. Splitting a task across several agents — each specialized, each potentially working in parallel — can get more done, but only if they're coordinated well enough that the pieces actually fit back together. This district is about the concrete patterns for wiring several agents together, and the specific ways that wiring can fail.

Topics on this stretch of the road:

* [[Supervisor-Orchestrator Patterns|Supervisor/Orchestrator Patterns]]: one agent that routes work to specialists and never lets them talk to each other directly.
* [[Pipeline and Sequential Handoff]]: a fixed chain of agents, each one handing its output to the next.
* [[Swarm and Peer-to-Peer Coordination]]: agents that coordinate directly through shared state, with no central router.
* [[Debate and Adversarial Multi-Agent Setups]]: agents arguing opposite sides of a question to surface a better answer than either alone.
* [[Role Specialization in Agent Teams]]: giving each agent in a team a distinct job, instead of running identical copies of the same prompt.
* [[Coordination Failures and Deadlock]]: the specific ways a multi-agent system gets stuck, talks past itself, or duplicates work.

## Supervisor-Orchestrator Patterns

A supervisor agent never does the specialized work itself — it decides which specialist should handle a piece of a task, hands it off, and collects the result. Every specialist talks only to the supervisor; none of them talk to each other. That hub-and-spoke shape is simple to reason about, but it puts the whole system's coordination through one place.

**You need:** [[Routing Between Specialized Prompts]].

## The question it answers

"What's the simplest way to wire several specialized agents together?" A supervisor/orchestrator pattern puts one agent in charge of routing: it receives the overall task, decides which specialist agent should handle each piece, sends that piece to the specialist, and collects the result back. This is exactly [[Routing Between Specialized Prompts|routing]], one level up — instead of dispatching a request to a specialized *prompt*, the supervisor dispatches a subtask to a specialized *agent* capable of running its own multi-step loop.

## Intuition

A general contractor on a job doesn't personally do the plumbing, the electrical work, and the drywall — they decide which subcontractor handles which piece, hand off the work, and check it comes back done. The plumber and the electrician never coordinate directly with each other; everything routes through the contractor, who's the only one with the full picture of the job.

## Definition and notation

```text
star topology: supervisor ↔ each of n specialists      (n links; specialists never link to each other)
full mesh:     every pair of n agents linked directly    (n(n−1)/2 links)
```

## A worked example

A supervisor coordinating 4 specialist agents, compared to what a fully connected peer-to-peer version of the same 4 agents would need:

```text
supervisor (star) topology:  4 links — one from the supervisor to each specialist
full peer mesh, same 4 agents:  4×3/2 = 6 links — every pair connected directly
```

Every specialist in the star only ever has to know how to talk to the supervisor — not to the other three. That's 2 fewer connections than a full mesh would need at this size, and the gap only widens as more specialists are added, since the star grows linearly while the mesh grows quadratically.

## Bench

```bench
id: supervisor-orchestrator-topology
title: Routing through one hub, or everyone to everyone
fallback: Compare a supervisor's hub-and-spoke communication edges against a fully connected peer mesh of the same agents.
```

**Try this**

1. Slide the specialist count up and watch the star's edge count grow in a straight line.
2. Compare it to the mesh's edge count at the same specialist count.
3. Imagine the supervisor itself fails — what happens to the specialists' ability to coordinate with each other at all?

**What you should notice:** the star's simplicity (fewer connections, one place that knows the whole picture) comes with a cost that the last question points at directly — explored next in [[Coordination Failures and Deadlock]] and contrasted with [[Swarm and Peer-to-Peer Coordination]].

## Where it appears in AI

* **This is [[Routing Between Specialized Prompts|routing]] applied to full agents instead of prompts** — the mechanism (classify, then dispatch to whichever specialist handles that category) is identical; what's new is that each specialist can now run its own multi-step loop rather than returning in one call.
* **[[Pipeline and Sequential Handoff]] is a different wiring of the same kind of specialist agents**: fixed order and direct handoff between stages, instead of a central router deciding where each piece goes.
* **[[Swarm and Peer-to-Peer Coordination]] is the explicit alternative to this topology**: no central hub at all, at the cost of more connections to manage.

## Common pitfalls

* **Letting specialists communicate directly "to save a round-trip."** The moment two specialists talk to each other outside the supervisor, the system stops being a clean star — and loses the property that made it easy to reason about in the first place: everything routing through one place.
* **Treating the supervisor as just a router with no judgment.** Beyond classifying which specialist handles a subtask, a supervisor often also has to decide what to do when a specialist's result isn't good enough — that's a real decision, not a mechanical dispatch.
* **Not noticing the single point of failure.** The star's simplicity is bought at a specific cost: if the supervisor itself goes down, every specialist loses its only link to the rest of the system at once.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. Why does the star topology need only 4 links for 4 specialists, while a full mesh of the same 4 agents needs 6?</summary>
In a star, each specialist needs exactly one link, to the supervisor — that's n links total. A full mesh needs a separate link for every pair of agents, which is n(n−1)/2 — 6 for n=4, since specialists in a mesh also connect directly to each other.
</details>

<details><summary>2. What's the one thing a specialist in a supervisor pattern never does?</summary>
Talk directly to another specialist — every piece of communication, in both directions, goes through the supervisor.
</details>

<details><summary>3. What does a supervisor pattern have in common with plain routing between prompts?</summary>
The same core mechanism: classify the incoming work and dispatch it to whichever specialist is built to handle that category — the only difference is that the specialist here is a full agent rather than a single prompt.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Supervisor (orchestrator):** the single agent that routes subtasks to specialists and collects their results, with no direct specialist-to-specialist communication.
* **Star (hub-and-spoke) topology:** a communication structure where every participant links only to a central hub, never to each other.
* **Single point of failure:** a component whose failure disconnects every participant that depended solely on it.

## Related

[[Routing Between Specialized Prompts]] · [[Pipeline and Sequential Handoff]] · [[Swarm and Peer-to-Peer Coordination]]

## Pipeline and Sequential Handoff

A research agent hands its findings to a drafting agent, which hands its draft to a review agent, which hands its approval to a finalizing agent. Each stage is a fixed, known step in a chain — the order never changes, and each stage only ever talks to the one right after it.

**You need:** [[Supervisor-Orchestrator Patterns|Supervisor/Orchestrator Patterns]].

## The question it answers

"What's the simplest way to wire several specialist agents in a fixed sequence?" A pipeline runs a fixed chain of agents, each one handing its output directly to the next — no central router deciding where things go, because the order is already known in advance. This is [[Prompt Chaining|prompt chaining]], one level up: the "steps" in the chain are now full agents rather than single calls, and the validation gate between them can check an entire stage's output before the next agent ever sees it.

## Definition and notation

```text
pipeline: stage1 → gate(result1) → stage2 → gate(result2) → stage3 → stage4
no gate:  a flaw at stage k flows into every later stage, wasting (total − k) stages
gate:     a flaw at stage k is caught at the handoff — 0 later stages wasted
```

## Intuition

An assembly line where each station passes its work straight to the next one, and nowhere in between, only works smoothly if a flawed part gets caught at the handoff rather than quietly continuing down the line. A line with inspection at every handoff stops wasting the later stations' work on something already broken; a line without it keeps assembling around a flaw until the final inspection finally catches it.

## A worked example

A 4-stage report pipeline, with a flaw introduced at stage 2, compared with and without a validation gate at each handoff:

```text
stages: research → draft → review → finalize
flaw appears at stage 2 (draft)

no gate between stages:
  stage 1 (research): runs normally
  stage 2 (draft):     produces the flaw
  stage 3 (review):    runs anyway, on flawed input     ← wasted
  stage 4 (finalize):  runs anyway, on flawed input     ← wasted
  stages wasted: 4 − 2 = 2

gated handoff:
  stage 1 (research): runs normally
  stage 2 (draft):     produces the flaw
  → caught at the handoff, before stage 3 ever runs
  stages wasted: 0
```

The gate doesn't make stage 2 any less likely to produce a flaw — what it changes is how much gets wasted *after* the flaw happens, by catching it at the very next handoff instead of letting it propagate.

## Bench

```bench
id: pipeline-handoff-gate
title: A flaw caught at handoff, or three stages later
fallback: Compare stages wasted on a flawed handoff with and without a per-stage validation gate.
```

**Try this**

1. Slide the flaw's stage earlier and later and watch how many stages get wasted without a gate.
2. Turn the gate on and see wasted stages drop to 0 regardless of where the flaw appears.
3. Imagine a flaw that the gate's check doesn't actually test for — what happens to the gate's benefit in that case?

**What you should notice:** the earlier a flaw appears in an ungated pipeline, the more later stages get wasted running on it — which is exactly why a gate's value grows with pipeline length, not just with how often flaws happen.

## Where it appears in AI

* **This is [[Prompt Chaining|prompt chaining]] with full agents as the chain's steps**, and its validation gate is the same mechanism, now checking an agent's whole output rather than one call's result.
* **[[Supervisor-Orchestrator Patterns|Supervisor/orchestrator patterns]] wire specialists through a central router instead**; a pipeline is the simpler case where the order is fixed enough that no router is needed at all.
* **[[Orchestrator-Workers]] runs its workers in parallel on independent subtasks**; a pipeline's stages are sequential and dependent on each other specifically because each one needs the previous stage's output.

## Common pitfalls

* **Treating a pipeline as fault-tolerant just because each stage is specialized.** Specialization helps each individual stage do its job well — it does nothing to stop a flawed result from flowing straight into the next stage unless something actually checks it at the handoff.
* **Putting the gate at the very end instead of between every stage.** A single check after the last stage catches a problem no earlier than the worked example's ungated case — the benefit specifically comes from checking at *every* handoff, not just the final one.
* **Assuming sequential means slow.** A pipeline's stages are sequential because each depends on the previous one's output, not because sequential execution is inherently the only option — independent work still belongs in [[Parallelization: Sectioning and Voting|sectioning]] instead.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. In the worked example, why are exactly 2 stages wasted when the flaw appears at stage 2 of 4, without a gate?</summary>
Every stage after the one that produced the flaw (stages 3 and 4) runs on the flawed input anyway, since nothing checks it at the handoff — that's 4 total stages minus the 2 stages up to and including where the flaw appeared, leaving 2 wasted.
</details>

<details><summary>2. What's the key structural difference between a pipeline and a supervisor pattern?</summary>
A pipeline's order is fixed in advance and each stage hands off directly to the next; a supervisor pattern instead routes each piece of work through a central decision-maker that decides which specialist handles it.
</details>

<details><summary>3. Does adding a gate make a pipeline's individual stages less likely to produce a flaw?</summary>
No — the gate doesn't change how often a stage produces a flawed result; it changes how much work gets wasted after a flaw happens, by catching it at the very next handoff instead of letting it propagate further down the pipeline.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Pipeline:** a fixed sequence of specialist agents, each handing its output directly to the next.
* **Handoff:** the point where one stage's output becomes the next stage's input.
* **Validation gate (agent-level):** a check at a handoff that verifies a stage's output before the next stage runs on it.

## Related

[[Prompt Chaining]] · [[Supervisor-Orchestrator Patterns|Supervisor/Orchestrator Patterns]] · [[Orchestrator-Workers]]

## Swarm and Peer-to-Peer Coordination

Remove the supervisor from a star topology and every specialist loses its only connection to the rest of the system at once. A swarm avoids that single point of failure by connecting agents directly to each other, with no central hub — at the cost of needing far more connections to manage as the group grows.

**You need:** [[Supervisor-Orchestrator Patterns|Supervisor/Orchestrator Patterns]].

## The question it answers

"What's the alternative to routing every piece of coordination through one central agent?" A swarm (peer-to-peer) system connects agents directly to each other through shared state, with no central router deciding who talks to whom. Any agent can read or write what another has produced. The trade is connections: a full peer mesh of n agents needs n(n−1)/2 links, compared to a star's n — but no single agent's failure disconnects the rest of the group from each other.

## Intuition

A team that only ever communicates through one project manager loses all internal coordination the instant that manager is unavailable — nobody else knows who's doing what. A team that also talks directly to each other keeps functioning even if one member drops out; the remaining members were never dependent on routing everything through a single point.

## Definition and notation

```text
star:  n links (supervisor to each specialist); hub fails → 0 links remain among specialists
mesh:  n(n−1)/2 links (every pair of agents); one peer fails → remaining (n−1) agents keep all (n−1)(n−2)/2 links among themselves
```

## A worked example

4 agents, comparing what survives when one participant fails under each topology:

```text
star (supervisor pattern):
  before:  4 links (supervisor ↔ each specialist)
  supervisor fails → 0 links remain: every specialist loses its only connection

peer mesh (swarm):
  before:  4×3/2 = 6 links (every pair of the 4 agents)
  one peer fails → the remaining 3 agents keep all 3×2/2 = 3 links among themselves
```

The star's 4 links all pass through one agent, so losing that agent loses all of them at once. The mesh's 6 links are spread across every pair, so losing any single peer only removes that peer's own 3 links — the other 3 agents keep coordinating with each other exactly as before.

## Bench

```bench
id: swarm-mesh-resilience
title: One hub going down, or one peer going down
fallback: Compare a peer mesh's connectivity before and after one agent fails, against a star topology's single point of failure.
```

**Try this**

1. Set the topology to star and watch what happens to the link count after a failure.
2. Switch to mesh and compare how many links the survivors keep among themselves.
3. Slide the agent count up on the mesh — how fast does the link count grow compared to the star's?

**What you should notice:** the mesh's resilience to any one agent failing comes at a real, growing cost — the number of connections to manage climbs quadratically with agent count, while the star's climbs only linearly.

## Where it appears in AI

* **This is the direct alternative to [[Supervisor-Orchestrator Patterns|supervisor/orchestrator patterns]]**: no central hub, trading simplicity and fewer connections for resilience against any single agent's failure.
* **A swarm's shared state is exactly [[Shared State Across a Multi-Step Task|a blackboard]]**, now read and written by multiple independent agents instead of multiple steps of one task.
* **[[Coordination Failures and Deadlock]] covers what specifically goes wrong when several agents read and write that shared state inconsistently** — a risk the mesh's lack of central coordination makes more likely, not less.

## Common pitfalls

* **Choosing a swarm for its resilience without budgeting for its connection cost.** The worked example's 6-vs-4 link count is already more at just 4 agents — that gap only widens, and at a large enough agent count a full mesh's connections become impractical to maintain.
* **Assuming "no central hub" means "no coordination problems."** Removing the supervisor removes the single point of failure, but doesn't remove the need for agents to agree on shared state consistently — if anything, it makes that problem harder, since there's no one place enforcing consistency.
* **Using a full mesh when a partial one would do.** Not every pair of agents actually needs a direct link — a sparser peer topology can keep most of the resilience benefit without paying for every single pairwise connection.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. In the worked example, why does the star lose all 4 links when the supervisor fails, but the mesh only loses 3 when one peer fails?</summary>
Every one of the star's 4 links passes through the single supervisor, so losing it removes all of them at once; the mesh's 6 links are spread across different pairs, so losing one peer only removes that peer's own links, leaving the other agents' links to each other intact.
</details>

<details><summary>2. What's the real cost a swarm pays for its resilience to single-agent failure?</summary>
A much larger number of connections to maintain — a full mesh needs n(n−1)/2 links for n agents, growing quadratically, compared to a star's n links growing linearly.
</details>

<details><summary>3. Does removing the central supervisor eliminate coordination problems?</summary>
No — it removes the single point of failure, but agents still need to agree on shared state consistently, and with no central hub enforcing that consistency, coordination failures like inconsistent reads and writes can become more likely, not less.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Swarm (peer-to-peer):** a multi-agent system where agents coordinate directly through shared state, with no central router.
* **Full mesh:** a topology where every pair of agents has a direct link.
* **Single point of failure:** a component whose failure disconnects every participant that depended solely on it — present in a star, absent in a mesh.

## Related

[[Supervisor-Orchestrator Patterns|Supervisor/Orchestrator Patterns]] · [[Shared State Across a Multi-Step Task]] · [[Coordination Failures and Deadlock]]

## Debate and Adversarial Multi-Agent Setups

A single agent that states a claim has no one checking its arithmetic. A second agent whose explicit job is to challenge that claim — recompute it, look for the mistake — catches exactly the kind of error that would otherwise sail through unexamined.

**You need:** [[Supervisor-Orchestrator Patterns|Supervisor/Orchestrator Patterns]].

## The question it answers

"Can having two agents argue opposite sides of a question catch errors a single agent would miss?" A debate setup gives one agent the job of proposing an answer and a second agent the job of challenging it — recomputing, probing for mistakes, arguing the other side. A judge (sometimes a third agent, sometimes the same mechanism built into the exchange) decides the outcome once the challenge has been raised. The point isn't politeness or compromise — it's that an error the proposer didn't catch in its own reasoning is exactly the kind of thing a dedicated challenger, starting fresh, is positioned to catch.

## Intuition

A courtroom doesn't just ask one side to state their case and accept it — a dedicated opposing side is specifically tasked with finding the holes in it. The opposing side isn't being difficult for its own sake; an unchallenged claim and a claim that survived a real challenge carry very different evidentiary weight, precisely because the second one was actually tested.

## Definition and notation

```text
proposer:   generates a claim
challenger: independently re-derives the answer and checks it against the claim
mismatch → debate overrides to the recomputed answer
```

## A worked example

A proposer's arithmetic claim, checked by a challenger that redoes the computation independently:

```text
proposer:    "17 × 23 = 381."
(single agent, no debate: accepts the claim as final — final answer: 381, wrong)

challenger:  recomputes independently — 17 × 23 = 391.
mismatch found (381 ≠ 391) → debate overrides to the recomputed answer

final answer, with debate: 391 (correct)
```

Nothing about the proposer's claim looked obviously wrong on its own — 381 is a plausible-looking three-digit number. The error only becomes visible because the challenger redid the actual computation independently, rather than reviewing the proposer's reasoning for a mistake it might not even state.

## Bench

```bench
id: debate-adversarial-check
title: An unchecked claim, or one a challenger recomputes
fallback: Step through a proposer's claim and a challenger's recomputation catching a genuine error.
```

**Try this**

1. Step through and see the single-agent case accept the wrong claim.
2. Continue stepping and watch the challenger's independent recomputation catch the mismatch.
3. Imagine the challenger made the identical arithmetic mistake as the proposer, independently — would the mismatch still be caught?

**What you should notice:** the challenger's value here comes specifically from recomputing *independently*, not from reviewing the proposer's stated reasoning — a shared blind spot that both agents happen to share wouldn't be caught by this mechanism at all.

## Where it appears in AI

* **This is one specific structure built from [[Role Specialization in Agent Teams|role-specialized agents]]**: proposer and challenger are deliberately different roles, not two copies of the same agent doing the same thing.
* **[[Self-Critique Loops in Agents]] is the single-agent version of a similar idea**: one agent critiquing its own output, rather than a second, independent agent doing the challenging.
* **[[LLM-as-Judge for Agent Trajectories]] often plays the role of the judge deciding between a debate's competing claims**, once the challenge has actually been raised.

## Common pitfalls

* **Treating any two-agent exchange as a real debate.** If the challenger doesn't independently re-derive anything and just restates agreement, no actual checking happened — the worked example's benefit specifically comes from independent recomputation, not from having two agents talk.
* **Assuming debate catches every kind of error.** A mistake that both the proposer and the challenger happen to make identically and independently — a shared misconception, not an arithmetic slip — would survive a debate exactly as it would survive a single agent, since nothing here checks against ground truth directly.
* **Running debate on tasks with no checkable ground truth.** The worked example depends on the challenger being able to independently verify the proposer's claim (here, by redoing real arithmetic) — a genuinely subjective judgment has no equivalent "recompute and compare" step.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. In the worked example, why does the single-agent case end up with the wrong final answer?</summary>
With no challenger, nothing re-derives or checks the proposer's claim — it's accepted as final exactly as stated, including whatever error it contains.
</details>

<details><summary>2. What specifically does the challenger do that catches the error?</summary>
It independently recomputes the same calculation from scratch, rather than reviewing the proposer's stated reasoning — the mismatch between the two independent results is what reveals the error.
</details>

<details><summary>3. Would debate catch a mistake that both the proposer and the challenger happen to make identically?</summary>
No — if both agents share the same error independently, their results would agree with each other despite both being wrong, since this mechanism only checks for disagreement between the two, not against an external ground truth.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Proposer:** the agent that generates an initial claim or answer.
* **Challenger:** the agent whose role is to independently check or dispute the proposer's claim.
* **Debate:** a multi-agent setup where opposing roles argue a question before a judgment is reached.

## Related

[[Role Specialization in Agent Teams]] · [[Self-Critique Loops in Agents]] · [[LLM-as-Judge for Agent Trajectories]]

## Role Specialization in Agent Teams

Three identical copies of the same generalist agent are each mediocre at every required skill. Three agents, each built and tuned for exactly one of those skills, are each excellent at theirs — and together cover the same ground far better, for the same number of agents.

**You need:** [[Supervisor-Orchestrator Patterns|Supervisor/Orchestrator Patterns]].

## The question it answers

"Does it help to give each agent in a team a distinct job, rather than running identical copies of the same agent?" Role specialization assigns each required skill to an agent built and tuned specifically for it, rather than asking every agent in the team to be equally capable at everything. This is exactly the weighted-average mechanism behind [[Routing Between Specialized Prompts|routing]], now applied at the level of a persistent team's structure rather than per-request classification.

## Intuition

A three-person team where every member is a generalist, equally mediocre at coding, writing, and research, gets roughly the same mediocre result no matter which member handles which task. A three-person team where one member is an excellent coder, one an excellent writer, and one an excellent researcher — each handling only their own specialty — covers all three far better, with exactly the same headcount.

## Definition and notation

```text
generalist team accuracy   = one flat accuracy, the same regardless of which skill is needed
specialized team accuracy  = Σ (skill's specialist accuracy) / number of skills
```

## A worked example

Three required skills, compared under a team of identical generalists versus a team with one specialist per skill:

```text
required skills:  coding, writing, research

3 identical generalists:   60% accuracy on every skill (flat)
1 specialist per skill:     coding 95%, writing 95%, research 95%

generalist team overall accuracy:    60.0%
specialized team overall accuracy:   (95% + 95% + 95%) / 3 = 95.0%
```

Both teams have exactly three agents — the difference is entirely in what each agent is built to be good at. The specialized team's 35-point accuracy gain comes from each agent handling only the one skill it was actually built for, instead of every agent splitting its competence across all three.

## Bench

```bench
id: role-specialization-team
title: Three generalists, or one specialist per skill
fallback: Compare a team of identical generalist agents against one with a specialist per required skill.
```

**Try this**

1. Check the generalist team's flat accuracy across all three skills.
2. Switch to the specialized team and see each skill handled at its own specialist's accuracy.
3. Imagine a fourth required skill appears that none of the three specialists is built for — what happens to the specialized team's advantage?

**What you should notice:** the accuracy gain isn't from adding more agents — both teams have exactly three — it's entirely from matching each skill to an agent actually built for it, the same lesson as routing, now applied to a team's lasting structure.

## Where it appears in AI

* **This reuses the exact weighted-accuracy mechanism from [[Routing Between Specialized Prompts]]**, applied once to define a team's standing roles rather than per-request to a single classification decision.
* **[[Debate and Adversarial Multi-Agent Setups]] is a specific pair of specialized roles** (proposer and challenger) built for exactly this reason: each role does one job well, rather than one agent doing both jobs adequately.
* **[[Coordination Failures and Deadlock]] becomes more likely as specialization increases**, since a team of distinct roles depends on handoffs between them working correctly — a risk a team of interchangeable generalists doesn't face in the same way.

## Common pitfalls

* **Over-specializing until the team can't cover an unanticipated need.** The worked example's three specialists cover exactly three skills — a fourth required skill with no matching specialist gets no better than a generalist's accuracy on it, or worse.
* **Assuming specialization requires more agents.** The worked example uses exactly three agents in both cases — the gain comes from what each agent is built to do, not from team size.
* **Specializing roles without a way to route work to the right one.** Role specialization only pays off if subtasks actually reach the agent built for them — which is exactly what [[Supervisor-Orchestrator Patterns|a supervisor]] or a pipeline's fixed handoff is responsible for.

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. In the worked example, why does the specialized team score 95.0% overall rather than each specialist's individual 95%?</summary>
95.0% is already the exact overall figure — since all three specialists happen to score identically at 95% on their own skill, the weighted average across the three skills comes out to that same 95.0%.
</details>

<details><summary>2. What's the actual source of the specialized team's accuracy advantage?</summary>
Matching each required skill to an agent specifically built and tuned for it, rather than team size — both teams in the worked example have exactly three agents.
</details>

<details><summary>3. What happens to a specialized team's advantage when a new required skill appears with no matching specialist?</summary>
The team has no agent built for that skill, so it falls back to whatever accuracy some other agent can offer on it — likely no better than a generalist's flat accuracy, and possibly worse if none of the specialists has any competence in that area at all.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Role specialization:** assigning each required skill in a team to an agent built and tuned specifically for it.
* **Generalist agent:** an agent built to be adequate across many skills rather than excellent at one.
* **Weighted team accuracy:** the overall accuracy across required skills, each scored at whichever agent actually handles it.

## Related

[[Routing Between Specialized Prompts]] · [[Debate and Adversarial Multi-Agent Setups]] · [[Coordination Failures and Deadlock]]

## Coordination Failures and Deadlock

Two agents, each waiting on a result only the other can produce, aren't making progress — they're stuck in a circular wait. A different failure: two agents, unaware of each other's progress, both redo the same piece of work neither needed to repeat. Different symptoms, same underlying cause: nothing coordinated who does what, or who waits on whom.

**You need:** [[Swarm and Peer-to-Peer Coordination]].

## The question it answers

"What specifically goes wrong when a multi-agent system isn't coordinated well enough?" Two distinct, concrete failure modes: **circular wait** (deadlock), where each of two agents is blocked on a result only the other can produce, so neither can proceed; and **duplicated work**, where agents unaware of each other's progress each independently redo a subtask that only needed doing once. Both come from the same root cause — a lack of shared awareness of who's doing what — but they produce opposite-looking symptoms: one freezes everything, the other wastes effort while still finishing.

## Intuition

Two coworkers each waiting for the other to send their half of a joint report first will wait forever if neither goes first — that's circular wait. Two coworkers who don't check in with each other and both independently write the same section from scratch get the report done, just with wasted, duplicated effort — a different failure, but from the same gap: neither knew what the other was doing.

## Definition and notation

```text
circular wait = (A waits on B) AND (B waits on A)             — true deadlock, 0 progress
duplicated work units = 2 × necessary units  (uncoordinated)
                        = 1 × necessary units  (coordinated)
```

## A worked example

The two failure modes, shown separately:

```text
circular wait:
  Agent A: waiting on B's result
  Agent B: waiting on A's result
  → deadlocked: neither can proceed, no matter how long they wait

duplicated work (3 shared subtasks):
  uncoordinated: both agents independently complete all 3 subtasks  → 6 total work units
  coordinated:   each of the 3 subtasks is done exactly once         → 3 total work units
```

Circular wait is a binary condition — either both agents are mutually blocked, in which case progress is exactly zero, or at least one isn't, in which case things proceed. Duplicated work is a matter of degree — the uncoordinated case still finishes the task, just at twice the necessary cost.

## Bench

```bench
id: coordination-failures-deadlock
title: Stuck waiting, or doing the same work twice
fallback: Show a circular-wait deadlock and duplicated-work coordination failures, and what fixes each.
```

**Try this**

1. In the deadlock mode, toggle each agent's wait condition and watch when the system becomes genuinely stuck.
2. Switch to duplicated work and compare coordinated versus uncoordinated total work units.
3. Imagine a three-agent cycle (A waits on B, B waits on C, C waits on A) — does breaking just one of those three wait conditions resolve it?

**What you should notice:** circular wait requires *both* directions of waiting to be true at once — breaking either one alone (not just both) is enough to let progress resume, which is exactly why a timeout or an arbitration rule on just one side is often all a fix needs.

## Where it appears in AI

* **Both failures are specific risks of [[Swarm and Peer-to-Peer Coordination]]'s shared state**, with no central hub enforcing who does what or who waits on whom — a cost explicitly flagged when that topology was introduced.
* **[[Shared State Across a Multi-Step Task]]'s blackboard is exactly the mechanism duplicated work needs to avoid**: a shared record of which subtasks are already claimed or completed prevents two agents from redoing the same one.
* **[[Supervisor-Orchestrator Patterns|A supervisor]] avoids circular wait by construction**: since every dependency routes through one central agent, two specialists can never end up directly waiting on each other.

## Common pitfalls

* **Adding more agents to a stuck system, hoping it unblocks.** If the actual problem is a circular wait, adding a third agent that doesn't break either waiting direction does nothing — the fix has to target the cycle itself, not the agent count.
* **Coordinating only after the fact, by comparing finished results.** Checking for duplicated work after both agents have already finished catches the waste too late to prevent it — the fix needs to happen before the redundant work starts, via shared state both agents check first.
* **Assuming a peer-to-peer system is inherently more failure-prone than a supervisor pattern.** It's specifically *more exposed* to these two failure modes because nothing centrally enforces coordination — but a supervisor pattern isn't failure-free either, it simply trades these particular risks for the single-point-of-failure risk covered in [[Swarm and Peer-to-Peer Coordination]].

## Quick check

<details><summary>1. Why does breaking just one agent's wait condition resolve a circular wait, rather than needing to fix both?</summary>
Circular wait requires both directions of waiting to hold simultaneously (A waits on B AND B waits on A) — if either one is false, at least one agent can proceed, which breaks the cycle.
</details>

<details><summary>2. In the worked example, why does the coordinated case still need 3 work units rather than 0?</summary>
The 3 subtasks genuinely need to be done once each — coordination removes the redundant, duplicated second pass, not the necessary work itself.
</details>

<details><summary>3. What do circular wait and duplicated work have in common, despite looking like opposite problems?</summary>
Both come from the same root cause: a lack of shared awareness between agents about who is doing what, or who is waiting on whom — one results in zero progress, the other in wasted but still-completed progress.
</details>

## Key terms

* **Circular wait (deadlock):** a cycle of agents each blocked on a result only another in the cycle can produce, so none can proceed.
* **Duplicated work:** independent agents each redoing a subtask that only needed to be completed once.
* **Shared awareness:** knowledge, available to every relevant agent, of what's already been claimed, completed, or is being waited on.

## Related

[[Swarm and Peer-to-Peer Coordination]] · [[Shared State Across a Multi-Step Task]] · [[Supervisor-Orchestrator Patterns|Supervisor/Orchestrator Patterns]]

## Reflection and Self-Improvement

An agent that never looks back at its own work repeats the same mistake at every step that triggers it. Reflection is an agent, or a second pass over the same agent's work, checking whether a step actually succeeded and correcting course — without any weights ever being updated.

Topics on this stretch of the road:

* [[Self-Critique Loops in Agents]]: an agent generating a critique of its own last action, and using that critique to decide what to do next.
* [[Error Attribution Across a Trajectory]]: figuring out which step in a long chain of actions actually caused a failure that only showed up later.
* [[Learning from Feedback Without Weight Updates]]: an agent's behavior changing within a single run, purely from what it's observed so far, with no training step involved.
* [[Verifier-Guided Agent Loops]]: a separate checker that scores each step, steering the agent toward the steps that check out.

## Self-Critique Loops in Agents

An arithmetic mistake made at step two of a four-step calculation doesn't stay contained to step two — every later step builds on the wrong number, and the final answer comes out wrong even though steps three and four were each computed correctly. Self-critique is an agent pausing after its own output, checking that output against what it should have been, and correcting it on the spot before anything downstream ever sees the mistake.

**You need:** [[Evaluator-Optimizer Loops]].

## The question it answers

"Can an agent catch its own mistakes without a separate evaluator role or an external verifier?" A self-critique loop has the agent examine its own last action or output — re-deriving it, checking it against a constraint, or simply asking "does this look right?" — before moving on to the next step. It's the single-role version of the generate-critique-improve cycle: the same agent that produced the output is the one checking it, inline, as part of its own trajectory, rather than handing the check to a second evaluator call.

## Intuition

A careful arithmetic student doesn't just write down each line of a multi-step calculation and move on — they glance back at the line they just wrote, re-derive it in their head, and fix it immediately if it doesn't match, rather than discovering three lines later that the final answer is wrong and having no idea which line broke it.

## Definition and notation

```text
without self-critique:  step[i] = produced(step[i-1])            (used as-is, even if wrong)
with self-critique:     step[i] = produced(step[i-1])
                         if produced(step[i-1]) ≠ recompute(step[i-1]): step[i] = recompute(step[i-1])
```

## A worked example

A 4-step calculation starting from 12: multiply by 4, subtract 10, divide by 2. Step 1 (the multiply) contains an injected error — it should produce 48 but actually produces 52:

```text
without self-critique:  12 → 52 → 42 → 21   (error at step 1 propagates to the final answer)
with self-critique:     12 → 48 → 38 → 19   (step 1's error caught and corrected immediately)

corrections caught: 1
```

Without self-critique, 52 (not 48) feeds into every later step, so the final answer — 21 — is wrong even though the subtract-10 and divide-by-2 steps were each computed correctly from what they were given. With self-critique, the agent recomputes step 1 from its own formula, notices 52 doesn't match the recomputed 48, substitutes the corrected value, and every later step proceeds from the right number.

## Bench

```bench
id: self-critique-loop
title: Catching the error before it spreads
fallback: Step through a 4-step trajectory with self-critique on or off and watch where an injected error gets caught.
```

**Try this**

1. Step through all 4 steps with self-critique off and watch the wrong value propagate.
2. Turn self-critique on, reset, and step through again — watch the correction happen at step 1.
3. Imagine the error were injected at step 3 instead of step 1 — would self-critique still need to catch it at every step, or just that one?

**What you should notice:** self-critique only needs to catch an error once, at the step where it actually happened — it doesn't need to understand the whole trajectory, just whether its own last output matches what it should have produced.

## Where it appears in AI

* **This is the single-agent version of [[Evaluator-Optimizer Loops|the evaluator-optimizer loop]]** covered as a workflow pattern — there, a second call plays the evaluator; here, the same agent plays both roles inline, as part of one continuous trajectory.
* **[[Error Attribution Across a Trajectory]] covers what happens when self-critique isn't run at every step** and a mistake is only noticed much later — attribution is the harder problem of finding which earlier step actually caused it.
* **[[LLM-as-Judge for Agent Trajectories]], covered later, is a more thorough version of the same checking instinct**, applied by an evaluator after the fact rather than by the agent itself mid-trajectory.

## Common pitfalls
